questions.prompt: The abdomen extends superiorly into the thoracic cage up to the:
questions.explanation: The diaphragm forms the superior boundary and domes upward into the thorax.

questions.prompt: The main anterolateral abdominal wall muscles include external oblique, internal oblique and:
questions.explanation: These three flat muscles form the layered abdominal wall.

questions.prompt: Rectus abdominis lies within the:
questions.explanation: The aponeuroses of flat muscles form the rectus sheath.

questions.prompt: The linea alba is formed by:
questions.explanation: It is the midline tendinous raphe between rectus muscles.

questions.prompt: The umbilicus is commonly at the level of:
questions.explanation: The umbilicus is a useful surface landmark near L3-L4.

questions.prompt: The inguinal ligament extends from ASIS to:
questions.explanation: It is the rolled lower border of external oblique aponeurosis.

questions.prompt: The superficial inguinal ring is an opening in:
questions.explanation: The spermatic cord exits through the superficial ring.

questions.prompt: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in:
questions.explanation: It is the entrance to the inguinal canal.

questions.prompt: The roof of inguinal canal is formed mainly by:
options: Arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis
questions.answer: Arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis
questions.explanation: These fibers arch over the canal.

questions.prompt: The posterior wall of inguinal canal is formed mainly by:
questions.explanation: It is reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.

questions.prompt: A swelling appears above and medial to the pubic tubercle and increases on coughing. Which canal is involved?
questions.explanation: Inguinal hernias present above and medial to the pubic tubercle.

questions.prompt: A hernia passes through the deep inguinal ring, traverses the canal and may enter the scrotum. What type is it?
questions.explanation: Indirect hernia follows the path of the processus vaginalis through the deep ring.

questions.prompt: A hernia pushes through Hesselbach triangle without entering the deep ring. Which type is it?
questions.explanation: Direct hernia protrudes through the posterior wall of the canal in Hesselbach triangle.

questions.prompt: During abdominal incision, the surgeon chooses the linea alba. Why does this reduce bleeding?
options: It contains the inferior epigastric artery
It is a relatively avascular tendinous raphe
It is full of muscle belly
questions.answer: It is a relatively avascular tendinous raphe
questions.explanation: The linea alba has fewer vessels and avoids cutting muscle fibers.

questions.prompt: A lower abdominal incision injures iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves. What postoperative problem may follow?
options: Weak abdominal wall and sensory loss in groin
questions.answer: Weak abdominal wall and sensory loss in groin
questions.explanation: These L1 nerves supply lower abdominal wall motor and sensory territories.

questions.prompt: The kidneys are primarily:
questions.explanation: Kidneys lie on posterior abdominal wall behind peritoneum.

questions.prompt: The right kidney lies lower than the left because of the:
questions.explanation: The large right lobe of liver depresses the right kidney.

questions.prompt: The renal hilum transmits vein, artery and pelvis arranged anterior to posterior as:
questions.explanation: Mnemonic VAP from anterior to posterior.

questions.prompt: The left renal vein crosses anterior to the:
questions.explanation: It passes between SMA and aorta to reach IVC.

questions.prompt: The suprarenal glands lie on the:
questions.explanation: They cap the kidneys.

questions.prompt: The right suprarenal vein drains into:
questions.explanation: Right suprarenal vein is short and drains directly to IVC.

questions.prompt: The left suprarenal vein drains into:
questions.explanation: It commonly joins the left renal vein.

questions.prompt: The ureter crosses the pelvic brim near bifurcation of:
questions.explanation: This is one common site of ureteric narrowing.

questions.prompt: Ureteric constrictions occur at pelviureteric junction, pelvic brim and:
questions.explanation: Stones lodge at the three anatomical narrowings.

questions.prompt: Renal pain may radiate from loin to groin because afferents follow:
questions.explanation: Ureteric pain follows sympathetic afferents to lower thoracic/upper lumbar segments.

questions.prompt: A stone at the ureterovesical junction causes pain radiating to scrotum or labium. Why?
options: Shared segmental innervation with genitofemoral/ilioinguinal areas
questions.answer: Shared segmental innervation with genitofemoral/ilioinguinal areas
questions.explanation: Lower ureter pain may refer to groin and external genital region.

questions.prompt: A left renal vein is compressed between SMA and aorta. Which condition does this describe?
questions.explanation: The left renal vein passes through the aortomesenteric angle.

questions.prompt: A posterior abdominal stab near the 12th rib injures the upper pole of kidney. Which pleural relation matters?
options: Diaphragm and costodiaphragmatic recess lie nearby
questions.answer: Diaphragm and costodiaphragmatic recess lie nearby
questions.explanation: Upper kidney is related to diaphragm and pleura, especially near 12th rib.

questions.prompt: During hysterectomy, the ureter is at risk near the uterine artery. What relation is remembered?
questions.explanation: Water under the bridge: ureter under uterine artery.

questions.prompt: A renal hilum mass compresses the most anterior structure first. Which structure is affected?
questions.explanation: At the hilum, renal vein is most anterior.

questions.prompt: The liver lies mainly in right hypochondrium and:
questions.explanation: The liver occupies right upper abdomen and extends into epigastrium.

questions.prompt: The bare area of liver is related to:
questions.explanation: The bare area lacks peritoneal covering and contacts diaphragm.

questions.prompt: The porta hepatis transmits portal vein, hepatic artery and:
questions.explanation: These structures form the portal triad.

questions.prompt: The portal vein is formed behind the neck of pancreas by union of splenic vein and:
questions.explanation: SMV and splenic vein unite to form portal vein.

questions.prompt: The gallbladder lies on the visceral surface of liver between right lobe and:
questions.explanation: The gallbladder fossa separates right and quadrate lobes.

questions.prompt: The cystic duct joins common hepatic duct to form:
questions.explanation: CBD carries bile to the duodenum.

questions.prompt: The cystic artery usually arises from:
questions.explanation: It is classically found in Calot triangle.

questions.prompt: Calot triangle is bounded by cystic duct, common hepatic duct and:
questions.explanation: Modern hepatocystic triangle includes liver inferiorly.

questions.prompt: Bile duct opens into the second part of duodenum at:
questions.explanation: CBD joins main pancreatic duct and opens at major papilla.

questions.prompt: Portal-systemic anastomosis at lower esophagus involves left gastric vein and:
questions.explanation: This site can form esophageal varices.

questions.prompt: A patient with gallstones has pain referred to the right shoulder tip. Which nerve pathway explains this?
questions.explanation: Inflammation near diaphragm can refer pain through C3-C5 phrenic pathways.

questions.prompt: During cholecystectomy, the surgeon identifies Calot triangle mainly to find which artery?
questions.explanation: Cystic artery is controlled during gallbladder removal.

questions.prompt: A stone impacted at the ampulla causes jaundice and pancreatitis. Why are both systems affected?
options: Common bile duct and pancreatic duct join near the ampulla
questions.answer: Common bile duct and pancreatic duct join near the ampulla
questions.explanation: The hepatopancreatic ampulla receives bile and pancreatic ducts.

questions.prompt: Caput medusae around umbilicus occurs in portal hypertension due to reopening of which vein?
questions.explanation: Paraumbilical veins connect portal system to superficial abdominal wall veins.

questions.prompt: A liver abscess ruptures superiorly through bare area. Which cavity is most directly threatened?
questions.explanation: Bare area is against diaphragm, so infection may track subphrenically or toward thorax.

questions.prompt: The pancreas is mainly:
questions.explanation: Except tail, pancreas is retroperitoneal.

questions.prompt: The head of pancreas lies within the curve of:
questions.explanation: The duodenum embraces the pancreatic head.

questions.prompt: The tail of pancreas reaches the:
questions.explanation: The tail passes in the splenorenal ligament to splenic hilum.

questions.prompt: The main pancreatic duct usually joins:
questions.explanation: It joins CBD near the hepatopancreatic ampulla.

questions.prompt: The splenic artery runs along the superior border of:
questions.explanation: It is tortuous and closely related to pancreas.

questions.prompt: The spleen lies mainly in the:
questions.explanation: Spleen is protected by left lower ribs.

questions.prompt: The spleen is related to ribs:
questions.explanation: Its long axis follows the 10th rib.

questions.prompt: The splenorenal ligament contains splenic vessels and:
questions.explanation: The pancreatic tail reaches splenic hilum through this ligament.

questions.prompt: Accessory spleens are commonly found near:
questions.explanation: Splenunculi often occur near hilum or splenic ligaments.

questions.prompt: The spleen develops in:
questions.explanation: Spleen is a mesodermal derivative in dorsal mesogastrium.

questions.prompt: A carcinoma in the head of pancreas causes painless progressive jaundice. Which structure is compressed?
questions.explanation: CBD passes through/behind pancreatic head.

questions.prompt: A posterior gastric ulcer erodes into the pancreas. Why can pain radiate to the back?
questions.explanation: The stomach bed includes pancreas; posterior ulcers can involve it.

questions.prompt: A child with left lower rib fracture develops shock and left upper quadrant tenderness. Which organ is most at risk?
questions.explanation: Spleen is protected by ribs 9-11 and may rupture with rib trauma.

questions.prompt: During splenectomy, injury to the pancreatic tail may cause leakage of which secretion?
questions.explanation: The tail of pancreas lies close to the splenic hilum.

questions.prompt: A splenic rupture irritates the diaphragm and causes left shoulder pain. What is this referred pain called?
questions.explanation: Blood under the diaphragm irritates phrenic nerve, referring pain to shoulder.

questions.prompt: The peritoneum lining the abdominal wall is:
questions.explanation: Parietal peritoneum lines the body wall.

questions.prompt: The peritoneum covering abdominal organs is:
questions.explanation: Visceral peritoneum invests organs.

questions.prompt: The greater sac communicates with lesser sac through the:
questions.explanation: The foramen of Winslow connects the two peritoneal sacs.

questions.prompt: The anterior boundary of epiploic foramen contains the:
questions.explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament contains portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct.

questions.prompt: The greater omentum hangs from the greater curvature of stomach and:
questions.explanation: It descends from stomach/proximal duodenum and attaches to transverse colon.

questions.prompt: The lesser omentum extends from liver to lesser curvature of stomach and:
questions.explanation: It includes hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments.

questions.prompt: Mesentery transmits vessels, nerves and lymphatics to:
questions.explanation: The mesentery suspends small intestine from posterior abdominal wall.

questions.prompt: A retroperitoneal organ is:
questions.explanation: Most of duodenum is secondarily retroperitoneal.

questions.prompt: An intraperitoneal organ is:
questions.explanation: Spleen is invested by peritoneum and suspended by ligaments.

questions.prompt: Paracolic gutters allow spread of fluid between abdomen and:
questions.explanation: These channels guide intraperitoneal fluid spread.

questions.prompt: A posterior gastric ulcer erodes through the stomach wall and causes severe bleeding. Which artery behind the stomach is at risk?
questions.explanation: The splenic artery runs tortuously along the superior border of pancreas behind the stomach.

questions.prompt: During surgery, the hepatoduodenal ligament is compressed to control hepatic bleeding. Which maneuver is this?
questions.explanation: Compression of portal triad in hepatoduodenal ligament reduces inflow to liver.

questions.prompt: A perforated anterior duodenal ulcer spills contents into the greater sac. Why is generalized peritonitis likely?
options: Omentum always seals all leaks instantly
questions.explanation: Intraperitoneal leakage irritates peritoneum and can spread widely.

questions.prompt: A patient with appendicitis first has vague periumbilical pain, then right iliac fossa pain. What changed?
options: Visceral pain became parietal peritoneal irritation
questions.answer: Visceral pain became parietal peritoneal irritation
questions.explanation: Early visceral afferents refer to umbilicus; local parietal peritoneum gives sharp localized pain.

questions.prompt: A pelvic abscess is drained through the posterior fornix of vagina. Which peritoneal pouch is accessed?
questions.explanation: The pouch of Douglas is the lowest peritoneal recess in females when upright.

questions.prompt: The stomach begins at the:
questions.explanation: The esophagus enters the stomach at the cardiac orifice.

questions.prompt: The pylorus continues as the:
questions.explanation: The pyloric canal opens into the first part of duodenum.

questions.prompt: The lesser curvature gives attachment to:
questions.explanation: The hepatogastric ligament attaches along the lesser curvature.

questions.prompt: The greater curvature gives attachment to:
questions.explanation: Greater omentum descends from the greater curvature.

questions.prompt: The arterial supply of stomach along lesser curvature includes left gastric and:
questions.explanation: Right and left gastric arteries anastomose along lesser curvature.

questions.prompt: The gastroduodenal artery lies posterior to:
questions.explanation: Posterior duodenal ulcer may erode it.

questions.prompt: The duodenum is mostly:
questions.explanation: Parts 2-4 are fixed retroperitoneally.

questions.prompt: The major duodenal papilla opens into the:
questions.explanation: Bile and main pancreatic ducts open here.

questions.prompt: The duodenojejunal flexure is supported by:
questions.explanation: The ligament of Treitz supports the flexure.

questions.prompt: The stomach bed includes pancreas, spleen, left kidney and:
questions.explanation: These posterior relations form the stomach bed.

questions.prompt: A posterior duodenal ulcer causes sudden hematemesis and shock. Which vessel was most likely eroded?
questions.explanation: Gastroduodenal artery runs behind the first part of duodenum.

questions.prompt: A gastric ulcer near the lesser curvature may bleed from which arterial arcade?
questions.explanation: The gastric arteries run along lesser curvature.

questions.prompt: Vomiting after annular pancreas is due to compression of which duodenal part?
questions.explanation: Annular pancreas encircles the descending duodenum.

questions.prompt: A tumor at the major duodenal papilla causes obstructive jaundice. Why?
options: Bile duct opens there with pancreatic duct
questions.answer: Bile duct opens there with pancreatic duct
questions.explanation: Obstruction at papilla blocks bile flow into duodenum.

questions.prompt: Pain from a foregut organ such as stomach is commonly referred to which region?
questions.explanation: Foregut visceral pain commonly refers to the epigastric region.

questions.prompt: The corpus striatum includes caudate nucleus and:
questions.explanation: Caudate plus lentiform nucleus form corpus striatum.

questions.prompt: The lentiform nucleus includes putamen and:
questions.explanation: Putamen and globus pallidus form lentiform nucleus.

questions.prompt: The thalamus is the major relay for:
questions.explanation: Most sensory pathways relay in thalamus before cortex.

questions.prompt: The hypothalamus is important for:
questions.explanation: It regulates homeostasis, autonomic output and pituitary function.

questions.prompt: The lateral geniculate body relays:
questions.explanation: Visual fibers from optic tract relay in LGN.

questions.prompt: The medial geniculate body relays:
questions.explanation: Auditory pathway relays in MGN.

questions.prompt: The subthalamic nucleus lesion classically causes:
questions.explanation: Contralateral flinging movements follow subthalamic lesions.

questions.prompt: Dopaminergic input to basal ganglia comes mainly from:
questions.explanation: Nigrostriatal dopamine modulates movement circuits.

questions.prompt: The pineal gland is part of the:
questions.explanation: Pineal lies in epithalamic region.

questions.prompt: The mammillary bodies belong to:
questions.explanation: They are hypothalamic nuclei involved in memory circuits.

questions.prompt: A patient has resting tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia. Loss of neurons in which structure explains this?
questions.explanation: Parkinsonism follows degeneration of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons.

questions.prompt: A lacunar stroke in thalamus causes contralateral sensory loss. Which role of thalamus explains this?
questions.explanation: Thalamic nuclei relay somatosensory information to cortex.

questions.prompt: A lesion of subthalamic nucleus causes violent flinging movements of opposite limbs. What is the movement disorder?
questions.explanation: Subthalamic nucleus lesions reduce indirect pathway control.

questions.prompt: A pituitary tumor compresses hypothalamic region and optic chiasm. Which endocrine-control center is nearby?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus lies above pituitary and controls hypophyseal secretion.

questions.prompt: Memory impairment with mammillary body damage is classically seen in which syndrome?
questions.explanation: Mammillary bodies are part of Papez circuit and affected in thiamine deficiency.

questions.prompt: The internal carotid artery gives rise to anterior cerebral and:
questions.explanation: ICA terminal branches include ACA and MCA.

questions.prompt: The vertebral arteries unite to form the:
questions.explanation: Vertebral arteries join at pontomedullary junction.

questions.prompt: Posterior cerebral artery is usually a terminal branch of:
questions.explanation: The basilar bifurcates into PCAs.

questions.prompt: Anterior communicating artery connects the:
questions.explanation: It completes the anterior part of circle of Willis.

questions.prompt: Posterior communicating artery connects internal carotid to:
questions.explanation: It forms the lateral connection in circle of Willis.

questions.prompt: Middle cerebral artery supplies much of the:
questions.explanation: MCA supplies lateral frontal, parietal and temporal cortex.

questions.prompt: Anterior cerebral artery supplies mainly:
questions.explanation: ACA territory includes medial leg motor/sensory areas.

questions.prompt: Posterior cerebral artery supplies:

questions.prompt: The basic unit of heredity is called what?
questions.explanation: Genes carry hereditary information and influence traits.

questions.prompt: Human somatic cells normally contain how many chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Most human body cells are diploid with 46 chromosomes.

questions.prompt: Autosomal dominant disorders usually appear in which pattern in a family pedigree?
questions.explanation: Autosomal dominant traits often affect successive generations.

questions.prompt: A child has an affected parent and a dominant single-gene disorder. What is the approximate risk to each child if the parent is heterozygous?
questions.explanation: A heterozygous affected parent transmits the mutant allele to half of children on average.

questions.prompt: Autosomal recessive disorders commonly occur when both parents are what?
questions.explanation: Carrier parents can have affected children despite being clinically normal.

questions.prompt: Consanguineous marriage increases risk mainly of which type of genetic disorders?
questions.explanation: Related parents are more likely to share recessive disease alleles.

questions.prompt: X-linked recessive disorders usually affect males more often because males have how many X chromosomes?
questions.explanation: A male with a pathogenic allele on his single X chromosome expresses the disorder.

questions.prompt: A boy has haemophilia and his maternal uncle was also affected. Which inheritance pattern is suggested?
questions.explanation: Haemophilia classically follows X-linked recessive inheritance.

questions.prompt: Multifactorial inheritance results from interaction of multiple genes and what?
questions.explanation: Many common diseases reflect genetic susceptibility plus environmental influences.

questions.prompt: A family has several members with hypertension, obesity and diabetes without a single-gene pattern. Which inheritance concept fits best?
questions.explanation: Common chronic diseases often have polygenic and environmental determinants.

questions.prompt: Community genetics applies genetic knowledge to improve health at which level?
questions.explanation: Community genetics uses prevention, screening and counselling for populations.

questions.prompt: Genetic registers can help provide follow-up, counselling and what?
questions.explanation: Registers help identify families needing services while respecting confidentiality.

questions.prompt: Confidentiality in genetic services is important because genetic information may affect whom?
questions.explanation: Genetic results can have implications for relatives and future children.

questions.prompt: A public health programme screens newborns for treatable metabolic diseases. Which level of prevention is this?
questions.explanation: Newborn screening detects disease early so treatment can prevent disability.

questions.prompt: Teratogens are harmful exposures during pregnancy that may cause what?
questions.explanation: Teratogens can disrupt fetal development and produce birth defects.

questions.prompt: Rubella immunization before pregnancy helps prevent which fetal condition?
questions.explanation: Preventing maternal rubella protects the fetus from congenital rubella syndrome.

questions.prompt: Fetal alcohol exposure can lead to growth restriction, facial features and what?
questions.explanation: Alcohol is a teratogen affecting growth and brain development.

questions.prompt: A pregnant woman takes an unprescribed teratogenic drug in early pregnancy. What is the main concern?
questions.explanation: Early organogenesis is a sensitive period for teratogenic malformations.

questions.prompt: Public education in genetics should reduce stigma and improve understanding of what?
questions.explanation: Education helps families seek counselling and avoid blame or myths.

questions.prompt: Screening relatives of an index case with hereditary disease is called what?
questions.explanation: Cascade screening traces at-risk relatives from a known affected person.

questions.prompt: Down syndrome is most commonly due to trisomy of which chromosome?
questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 is the commonest chromosomal cause of Down syndrome.

questions.prompt: The risk of Down syndrome increases with increasing what?
questions.explanation: Advanced maternal age increases risk of meiotic nondisjunction.

questions.prompt: Turner syndrome usually has which chromosomal pattern?
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome is monosomy X or related sex-chromosome mosaicism.

questions.prompt: A newborn has hypotonia, flat facial profile, single palmar crease and congenital heart disease. Which condition is likely?
questions.explanation: These are classic clinical features of Down syndrome.

questions.prompt: Klinefelter syndrome is classically associated with which karyotype?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is most commonly 47,XXY.

questions.prompt: Sickle cell disease is inherited in which pattern?
questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease occurs when both beta-globin alleles are affected.

questions.prompt: Thalassaemia prevention in public health relies strongly on screening, carrier detection and what?
questions.explanation: Carrier screening and counselling help couples understand reproductive risk.

questions.prompt: A couple are both beta-thalassaemia carriers. What is the chance of an affected child in each pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Two carrier parents have a one in four risk of an affected child per pregnancy.

questions.prompt: Phenylketonuria causes preventable intellectual disability if untreated and is detected by what?
questions.explanation: Newborn screening allows early dietary treatment of phenylketonuria.

questions.prompt: A neonate detected with congenital hypothyroidism on screening is treated early to prevent what?
questions.explanation: Early treatment prevents avoidable intellectual disability and developmental delay.

questions.prompt: Genetic counselling is a communication process that helps families understand genetic risk and what?
questions.explanation: Counselling supports informed decisions about testing, reproduction and care.

questions.prompt: Primary prevention of genetic disease includes avoiding consanguineous marriage where relevant and what?
options: Preventing exposure to mutagens and teratogens
questions.answer: Preventing exposure to mutagens and teratogens
questions.explanation: Primary prevention reduces occurrence by reducing risks before disease appears.

questions.prompt: Secondary prevention of genetic disease mainly involves early detection through screening and what?
questions.explanation: Screening is useful when early treatment or reproductive planning can reduce harm.

questions.prompt: A woman with previous child affected by neural tube defect asks for prevention before pregnancy. Which measure is important?
questions.explanation: Folic acid before conception and early pregnancy reduces neural tube defect risk.

questions.prompt: Prenatal diagnosis is most useful when a pregnancy is at high risk for what?
questions.explanation: Prenatal testing is offered when inherited or chromosomal disease risk is significant.

questions.prompt: Amniocentesis is a prenatal diagnostic procedure that samples what?
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid contains fetal cells and biochemical markers for testing.

questions.prompt: Carrier screening is especially useful for diseases that are common in a population and have what?
questions.explanation: Carrier detection allows risk estimation before affected births occur.

questions.prompt: A couple with family history of haemophilia seeks advice before pregnancy. Which service is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Genetic counselling explains inheritance, testing and reproductive options.

questions.prompt: Newborn screening programmes should target conditions where early diagnosis leads to what?
options: Effective treatment or prevention of disability
questions.answer: Effective treatment or prevention of disability
questions.explanation: Screening is justified when early action improves health outcomes.

questions.prompt: A positive screening test for a genetic disorder should usually be followed by what?

questions.prompt: Community diagnosis means identifying and quantifying health problems and resources of what?
questions.explanation: Community diagnosis studies health needs and available resources in a population.

questions.prompt: Community diagnosis helps plan services according to local needs and what?
questions.explanation: It guides priority setting and resource allocation.

questions.prompt: Important components of community diagnosis include demography, morbidity, mortality and what?
questions.explanation: Community diagnosis covers population, health status, services and environment.

questions.prompt: A PHC team surveys households and finds high anaemia, poor diet and low IFA compliance. What is the next use of this information?
questions.explanation: Community diagnosis should lead to action based on identified needs.

questions.prompt: Comprehensive health care includes promotive, preventive, curative and what services?

questions.prompt: Family folder records help health workers maintain continuing information on what?
questions.explanation: Family records support continuity, follow-up and community assessment.

questions.prompt: Home visiting is useful in community health because it allows assessment of family environment and what?
questions.explanation: Home visits reveal living conditions, risks and care practices.

questions.prompt: During a home visit, an ANM finds a newborn is cold, poorly feeding and lethargic. What should she do?
questions.explanation: Poor feeding and lethargy in a newborn are danger signs needing urgent care.

questions.prompt: Community-based rehabilitation aims to improve quality of life of persons with disability through health, education, livelihood and what?
questions.explanation: CBR promotes inclusion and functioning within the community.

questions.prompt: A child with cerebral palsy receives physiotherapy guidance, assistive support and school linkage near home. Which service is this?
questions.explanation: Community-based rehabilitation supports function and participation close to home.

questions.prompt: A subcentre in rural health services is commonly staffed by ANMs and what other frontline worker?
questions.explanation: Subcentre staff provide basic preventive, promotive and selected curative services.

questions.prompt: A primary health centre functions as a referral unit for subcentres and provides integrated what?
questions.explanation: PHCs support subcentres and provide first-level medical care.

questions.prompt: A community health centre usually serves as a higher referral centre with specialist services for how many PHCs?
questions.explanation: CHCs are referral units above PHCs with specialist care.

questions.prompt: ASHAs mainly act as community-level link workers between households and what?
questions.explanation: ASHAs mobilize communities and link families to health care.

questions.prompt: An ASHA motivates a pregnant woman for ANC, institutional delivery and immunization. What role is she performing?
questions.explanation: ASHAs support awareness, mobilization and access to services.

questions.prompt: Anganwadi workers under ICDS mainly support supplementary nutrition, preschool education and what?
questions.explanation: Anganwadi centres provide nutrition and early childhood services.

questions.prompt: The village health sanitation and nutrition committee promotes local planning and what?
questions.explanation: VHSNCs support decentralized health action at village level.

questions.prompt: A malnourished child is weighed monthly at an anganwadi and counselled for feeding. Which service is shown?
questions.explanation: Anganwadi services include child growth monitoring and nutrition education.

questions.prompt: Multipurpose health workers are important because they deliver several programmes through what approach?
questions.explanation: Multipurpose workers provide multiple primary health services in the field.

questions.prompt: A health worker provides immunization, antenatal follow-up, malaria slides and health education during field visits. Which concept fits?
questions.explanation: Field workers commonly deliver integrated services for several programmes.

questions.prompt: The arithmetic mean is calculated by dividing the sum of observations by what?

questions.prompt: The median is the value that divides an ordered series into how many equal parts?
questions.explanation: Median is the middle value after arranging observations.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: The mode is the observation that occurs with what?
questions.explanation: Mode is the most frequent value.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: In a highly skewed income distribution, which average is usually more appropriate?
questions.explanation: Median is less affected by extreme values than mean.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Range is calculated as the difference between the highest value and what?
questions.explanation: Range is the simplest measure of dispersion.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Standard deviation measures dispersion of observations around which value?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation describes spread around the mean.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Coefficient of variation is useful for comparing variability between series because it is what?
questions.explanation: CV expresses standard deviation as a percentage of the mean.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics

questions.prompt: A child's weight is at the 3rd percentile for age. What does this primarily indicate?
options: Low position compared with reference population

questions.explanation: Percentiles show relative position in a reference distribution.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Qualitative data describe attributes such as sex, blood group and what?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Birth weight measured in kilograms is which type of variable?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: A frequency distribution shows how observations are arranged according to what?
questions.explanation: Frequency tables summarize how often each value or class occurs.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: A bar diagram is most suitable for presenting what type of data?
questions.explanation: Bar charts compare separate categories.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: A histogram is used to display frequency distribution of what?
questions.explanation: Histograms show frequencies across continuous class intervals.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: A health worker compares malaria cases in four villages by village name. Which diagram is suitable?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: A pie chart is used to show parts of a whole as what?
questions.explanation: Pie diagrams display component percentages of a total.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: A scatter diagram is useful for studying relation between two what?
questions.explanation: Scatter plots show paired numerical observations and possible correlation.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: A health information system is used to collect, process, analyse and use data for what?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Good health information should be reliable, timely, complete and what?
questions.explanation: Useful information must be accurate, timely, complete and relevant to decisions.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Vital registration mainly records births, deaths and what?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: A district officer uses monthly malaria case reports to detect a sudden rise. Which function of health information is this?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Census provides information on size, composition and distribution of what?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Notification of disease means reporting specified diseases to whom?
questions.explanation: Notifiable disease reporting enables public health action.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Medical certification of cause of death improves the quality of what statistics?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Health management information systems are especially useful for monitoring service coverage and what?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: If immunization coverage reports are incomplete from several subcentres, what data quality problem is present?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Probability expresses the chance of occurrence of an event and ranges from zero to what?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: The null hypothesis usually states that there is what?
questions.explanation: Statistical tests commonly begin with a hypothesis of no difference.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: A p value less than the chosen significance level suggests rejecting which hypothesis?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics

The treatment is always clinically important

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Type I error means rejecting a null hypothesis when it is actually what?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: Type II error means failing to reject a null hypothesis when it is actually what?
questions.explanation: Type II error is a false negative conclusion.

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: The chi-square test is commonly used to test association between what type of variables?

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics

questions.chapterTitle: Health Information and Basic Medical Statistics
questions.prompt: A study compares mean haemoglobin between two independent treatment groups. Which test is commonly used?

questions.prompt: Implementation means putting a health plan into what?

questions.prompt: Operational planning translates broad objectives into detailed activities, responsibilities and what?

questions.prompt: Process indicators measure activities such as sessions held, visits made and what?
questions.explanation: Process indicators track implementation activities.

questions.prompt: An immunization plan reports number of outreach sessions conducted this month. Which indicator type is this?

questions.prompt: Output indicators measure immediate results such as coverage and what?

questions.prompt: Outcome indicators measure changes in health status, behaviour or what?

questions.prompt: Impact indicators often measure long-term changes such as mortality reduction and what?

questions.prompt: Management is commonly described through functions such as planning, organizing, staffing, directing and what?

Blocks muscarinic signaling in vestibular pathways and the vomiting center

Muscle calcium channels are opened directly

questions.topic: Neuromuscular Junction and Autonomic Ganglia; Nicotine, Muscle Relaxants, and Spasmolytics

questions.topic: Neuromuscular Junction and Autonomic Ganglia; Nicotine, Muscle Relaxants, and Spasmolytics

questions.topic: Neuromuscular Junction and Autonomic Ganglia; Nicotine, Muscle Relaxants, and Spasmolytics
questions.prompt: Baclofen helps painful flexor spasms after spinal cord injury mainly by activating:

questions.topic: Neuromuscular Junction and Autonomic Ganglia; Nicotine, Muscle Relaxants, and Spasmolytics

Acetylcholine synthesis in cholinergic nerve terminals

Less codeine is converted to morphine

Giving more opioid to restore miosis

questions.explanation: Dopamine agonists can overstimulate mesolimbic pathways and cause hallucinations or impulse-control disorders.

questions.explanation: Anti-D prophylaxis prevents maternal sensitization to Rh-positive fetal RBCs.

questions.explanation: Vaccination exposes the immune system to antigen and induces active immunity.

questions.explanation: Histocompatibility antigens and HLA typing are important for graft/transplant compatibility.

questions.explanation: Low albumin lowers colloid osmotic pressure, favoring movement of fluid into tissues.

questions.explanation: Albumin has important transport functions for several poorly soluble substances.

options: Reduced albumin and clotting factor synthesis

questions.explanation: Liver disease can reduce albumin and clotting protein synthesis, causing edema and coagulation defects.

questions.prompt: Which dietary factor most directly supports synthesis of plasma proteins?
questions.explanation: Dietary proteins are listed among factors affecting plasma protein synthesis.

questions.prompt: Platelets are derived from:
questions.explanation: Platelets are cytoplasmic fragments produced from megakaryocytes.

questions.prompt: The normal platelet count is approximately:
questions.explanation: The chapter gives the normal platelet count in the usual range of about 1.5-4 lakh per microlitre.

questions.prompt: A patient with chronic inflammatory disease has a high ESR on testing. What does this finding most commonly indicate?

questions.explanation: Iron deficiency impairs haemoglobinization, producing small pale RBCs.

questions.prompt: Unconjugated bilirubin formation is mainly related to breakdown of:

questions.prompt: Physiological jaundice of newborn is related mainly to immature handling of:
questions.explanation: The chapter discusses neonatal physiological jaundice under bilirubin and jaundice mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Which cells are granulocytes?

questions.prompt: Which cells become macrophages in tissues?

questions.prompt: Which WBC is central to acquired immunity?
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes, including B and T cells, mediate acquired immune responses.

questions.prompt: Leucocytosis means:

questions.prompt: Leucopenia means:

questions.prompt: Medullary vasomotor centre controls:

questions.prompt: Chemoreceptor reflex is stimulated by hypoxia, hypercapnia and:

questions.prompt: Electron microscopy shows the plasma membrane as a trilayer unit membrane. What is its approximate total thickness?
questions.explanation: The source describes the cell membrane as a trilayer unit membrane with total thickness of 7-10 nm.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate biochemical composition of the cell membrane stated in the source?
questions.explanation: The membrane is described as a mixture of lipids 40%, proteins 55% and carbohydrates 5%.

questions.prompt: Which model of membrane structure was proposed by Singer and Nicholson in 1972?
questions.explanation: Singer and Nicholson proposed the fluid mosaic model of membrane structure.

questions.prompt: According to the fluid mosaic model, why can the plasma membrane tolerate considerable changes in cell shape?
options: All membrane proteins are fixed permanently
The glycocalyx replaces the lipid bilayer
Phospholipids are present in fluid form within a bilayer
The membrane is made of rigid cellulose
questions.answer: Phospholipids are present in fluid form within a bilayer
questions.explanation: Fluidity of the phospholipid bilayer makes the membrane flexible and helps preserve structural integrity during shape change.

questions.prompt: A lipid-soluble anesthetic rapidly crosses a cell membrane, while electrolytes cross poorly without channels. Which membrane feature explains this?
options: Hydrophobic lipid bilayer forms a major barrier to water-soluble molecules
questions.answer: Hydrophobic lipid bilayer forms a major barrier to water-soluble molecules
questions.explanation: The lipid bilayer is semipermeable: it restricts water-soluble molecules but allows fat-soluble substances like oxygen, fatty acids and alcohol to pass more easily.

questions.prompt: In the phospholipid bilayer, how are lipid molecules oriented?
options: Hydrophilic heads face extracellular and intracellular fluid, hydrophobic tails face the membrane centre
Hydrophobic tails face water on both sides, hydrophilic heads face the centre
All heads face only the cytoplasm
All tails are exposed to extracellular fluid
questions.answer: Hydrophilic heads face extracellular and intracellular fluid, hydrophobic tails face the membrane centre
questions.explanation: Polar hydrophilic heads face the aqueous extracellular and intracellular phases; nonpolar hydrophobic tails point toward the centre.

questions.prompt: A hormone binds to a cell surface molecule and initiates intracellular physiologic change. Which membrane protein function is being used?
questions.explanation: Some membrane proteins act as receptors for hormones and neurotransmitters, initiating intracellular changes.

questions.prompt: Which membrane proteins form active transport systems such as Na+-K+ ATPase, K+-H+ ATPase and Ca2+ pump?
questions.explanation: The source lists pumps as membrane proteins that form active transport systems, including Na+-K+ ATPase and Ca2+ pump.

questions.prompt: Which statement about peripheral extrinsic proteins is correct?
options: They are found only inside mitochondria
They are on the outer surface and can dissociate readily from the membrane
They always cross the entire lipid bilayer
They are the fatty acid tails of phospholipids
questions.answer: They are on the outer surface and can dissociate readily from the membrane
questions.explanation: Extrinsic or surface proteins are located on the outer surface and are not tightly associated with the membrane.

questions.prompt: A membrane carbohydrate defect reduces close fixation between adjacent epithelial cells. Which structure/function is most directly affected?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates form the glycocalyx, which helps in tight fixation of cells with one another.

questions.prompt: A typical cell seen by light microscopy is described as having three basic components. Which set is correct?
questions.explanation: The source describes the typical cell as consisting of cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines the cell membrane in cell physiology?
options: It is the contractile protein of skeletal muscle
It is a protective sheath that separates cell contents from the external environment
It is the site of ribosomal RNA synthesis
It is a temporary cytoplasmic inclusion
questions.answer: It is a protective sheath that separates cell contents from the external environment
questions.explanation: The plasma membrane envelops the cell body, separates intracellular from extracellular fluid and controls exchange.

questions.prompt: A skeletal muscle fibre requires rapid release and sequestration of calcium during contraction. Which organelle is modified for this function?
questions.explanation: In skeletal and cardiac muscle, smooth ER is modified into sarcoplasmic reticulum for calcium release and sequestration.

questions.prompt: Which organelle is especially numerous in metabolically active cells because it is a major site of aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are major sites of aerobic respiration and are more numerous in metabolically active cells.

questions.prompt: A plasma cell has abundant Russell bodies and a pancreatic acinar cell actively synthesizes proteins. Which structure is expected to be well developed?
questions.explanation: Rough ER bears ribosomes and is well developed in cells active in protein synthesis, including plasma cells and pancreatic acinar cells.

questions.prompt: Which function is most directly associated with the Golgi apparatus?
options: Packaging proteins synthesized in rough ER into vesicles
questions.answer: Packaging proteins synthesized in rough ER into vesicles
questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus packages rough ER proteins into vesicles and also participates in secretion, glycosylation and lysosomal enzyme formation.

questions.prompt: A macrophage is engaged in phagocytosis and digestion of engulfed material. Which organelle is particularly abundant and functionally important?
questions.explanation: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes and are abundant in phagocytic cells such as neutrophils and macrophages.

questions.prompt: Which cytoplasmic organelle contains oxidases and catalases and is prominent in hepatocytes and tubular epithelial cells?
questions.explanation: Peroxisomes contain oxidases and catalases and are described as predominant in hepatocytes and tubular epithelial cells.

questions.prompt: Which cytoskeletal element is composed of alpha- and beta-tubulin and forms a transport system for organelles and proteins?
questions.explanation: Microtubules are hollow structures made of alpha- and beta-tubulin and act as a cellular transport system.

questions.prompt: A patient has fragile skin with blistering due to abnormal mechanical integration of cell organelles. Which cytoskeletal structure is most consistent with this defect?
questions.explanation: The source notes that abnormal intermediate filaments in humans are associated with skin blistering because cells rupture more easily.

questions.prompt: Which are the three main types of intercellular junctions described in this chapter?
options: Tight junction, adherens junction and gap junction
Synapse, neuromuscular junction and motor end plate
questions.answer: Tight junction, adherens junction and gap junction
questions.explanation: The chapter classifies intercellular junctions into tight, adherens and gap junctions.

questions.prompt: A junction obliterates the space between neighbouring cells by fusion of outer layers of the cell membranes. What is it called?
questions.explanation: In tight junctions, the outer layers of neighbouring cell membranes fuse, obliterating the intercellular space.

questions.prompt: What is the main barrier function of tight junctions?
options: They generate ATP through Krebs cycle
They block movement of ions and solutes from one cell to another
questions.answer: They block movement of ions and solutes from one cell to another
questions.explanation: Tight junctions form a barrier to movement of ions and other solutes from one cell to another.

questions.prompt: A leaky epithelial barrier allows excessive paracellular movement of ions and solutes. Which junction is most likely functionally compromised?

questions.prompt: In an adherens junction, what is the usual width of the space separating adjacent cell membranes?
questions.explanation: The source describes adherens junctions as having adjacent membranes separated by a 15-20 nm space.

questions.prompt: Which adherens junction has thickened focal areas on both apposing cell membranes?

questions.prompt: A blistering disorder involves failure of strong focal attachment between epidermal cells. Which junctional structure best matches this attachment mechanism?

questions.prompt: What protein subunits surround each half-channel of a gap junction?
questions.explanation: Each half of the gap junction channel is surrounded by six protein subunits called connexins.

questions.prompt: Gap junctions reduce the intercellular space to approximately what distance?
questions.explanation: At gap junctions, the intercellular space is reduced from the usual 15-20 nm to 2-3 nm.

questions.prompt: Rapid propagation of electrical potential changes from one cardiac muscle cell to another depends mainly on which junction?

questions.prompt: What is meant by membrane potential in a living cell?
options: Absence of electrical charge in resting cells
Only the ATP content of the plasma membrane
Potential difference across the cell membrane with inside usually negative
Equal distribution of all ions across the membrane
questions.answer: Potential difference across the cell membrane with inside usually negative
questions.explanation: The source defines membrane potential as the potential difference across living cell membranes, with the inside negative in relation to outside.

questions.prompt: A resting nerve cell has a membrane potential of about -70 mV. What happens during excitation according to the source example?
options: It becomes -130 mV because calcium exits
It may become about +30 mV inside positive
questions.answer: It may become about +30 mV inside positive
questions.explanation: The chapter gives nerve cell resting potential as about -70 mV and excited/action potential as about +30 mV.

questions.prompt: The term resting membrane potential means the cell is not undergoing which change?
questions.explanation: The source clarifies that rest does not mean metabolic quiescence; it means the cell is not undergoing electrical change.

questions.prompt: The membrane potential measured during the excited state of a cell is called what?
questions.explanation: The membrane potential during the excited state is called the action potential.

questions.prompt: Which is the basic reason for genesis of membrane potential?
options: Complete impermeability to sodium and potassium
Unequal distribution of ions across the cell membrane
Equal movement of all proteins across the membrane
questions.answer: Unequal distribution of ions across the cell membrane
questions.explanation: Membrane potential is basically due to unequal ion distribution across the membrane, produced by combined forces acting on ions.

questions.prompt: Which set contains the factors listed for genesis of membrane potential?
options: Only oncotic pressure and plasma protein concentration
Selective permeability, Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium, Nernst equation, GHK equation and Na+-K+ ATPase
Only ribosomes, lysosomes and Golgi apparatus
questions.answer: Selective permeability, Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium, Nernst equation, GHK equation and Na+-K+ ATPase
questions.explanation: The chapter lists selective permeability, Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium, Nernst equation, constant field Goldmann equation and Na+-K+ ATPase pump.

questions.prompt: Which ions are described as diffusible ions in the selective permeability section?
questions.explanation: Na+, K+, Cl- and HCO3- are listed as diffusible ions in this section.

questions.prompt: In resting membrane permeability, the membrane is freely permeable to which ions according to the source?
questions.explanation: The source states the membrane is freely permeable to K+ and Cl- and moderately permeable to Na+.

questions.prompt: Why are intracellular proteins and organic phosphate important for membrane potential?
options: They are pumped out by Na+-K+ ATPase
They are non-diffusible negatively charged ions
They diffuse freely through sodium channels
questions.answer: They are non-diffusible negatively charged ions
questions.explanation: The membrane is practically impermeable to intracellular proteins and organic phosphate, which are negatively charged non-diffusible ions.

questions.prompt: According to Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium, what must be true for each solution separated by a semipermeable membrane at equilibrium?
options: One solution must carry only positive charge
questions.explanation: Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium requires each solution to remain electrically neutral, with total cation charge equal to total anion charge.

questions.prompt: If non-diffusible anions are present on one side of a semipermeable membrane, what ion distribution is expected by Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium?
options: Perfectly equal Na+ and Cl- on both sides
questions.explanation: With non-diffusible anions on one side, Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium produces asymmetrical distribution of diffusible ions.

questions.prompt: The Nernst equation is used to calculate which value?
options: Equilibrium potential for an individual ion
questions.answer: Equilibrium potential for an individual ion
questions.explanation: The source states that the magnitude of equilibrium potential for an ion can be determined by the Nernst equation.

questions.prompt: For a mammalian spinal motor neuron in the table, what is the equilibrium potential for sodium?
questions.explanation: Table 1.4-1 lists sodium equilibrium potential as +60 mV.

questions.prompt: For a mammalian spinal motor neuron in the table, what is the equilibrium potential for potassium?
questions.explanation: Table 1.4-1 lists potassium equilibrium potential as -90 mV.

questions.prompt: For a mammalian spinal motor neuron in the table, which ion has an equilibrium potential of about +130 mV?
questions.explanation: Table 1.4-1 lists calcium equilibrium potential as +130 mV.

questions.prompt: Why is the Goldmann-Hodgkin-Katz equation needed in addition to the Nernst equation?
options: It calculates osmolarity from glucose alone
It records membrane potential with electrodes
It accounts for Na+, K+ and Cl- distributions and their permeabilities together
questions.answer: It accounts for Na+, K+ and Cl- distributions and their permeabilities together
questions.explanation: Nernst calculates one ion individually; GHK integrates Na+, K+ and Cl- distributions with their membrane permeabilities.

questions.prompt: In nerve and muscle fibres, which ions are most important for development of membrane potentials according to the GHK inference?
questions.explanation: The GHK inferences state that Na+, K+ and Cl- are the most important ions for membrane potentials in nerve and muscle fibres.

questions.prompt: Signal transmission in nerves is primarily due to rapid changes in permeability of which ions?
questions.explanation: The source states nerve signal transmission is primarily due to changes in sodium and potassium permeability during impulse conduction.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of Na+-K+ ATPase in membrane potential genesis according to this chapter?
options: Building and maintaining sodium and potassium concentration gradients
Producing the entire membrane potential by itself
Making the membrane impermeable to chloride
Recording action potentials on an oscilloscope
questions.answer: Building and maintaining sodium and potassium concentration gradients
questions.explanation: Na+-K+ ATPase mainly builds concentration gradients by pumping back Na+ that diffuses in and K+ that diffuses out.

questions.prompt: A physiology practical asks for essential instruments used to record activity of excitable tissue. Which set is correct?
options: ECG limb leads, tuning fork and ophthalmoscope
Microelectrodes, electronic amplifiers and cathode ray oscilloscope
questions.answer: Microelectrodes, electronic amplifiers and cathode ray oscilloscope
questions.explanation: The chapter lists microelectrodes, electronic amplifiers and cathode ray oscilloscope as essential recording instruments.

questions.prompt: Cardiac muscle fibres are best described as:
questions.explanation: The comparison table describes cardiac muscle as striated with branching and functional connections forming a syncytium.

questions.prompt: Cardiac muscle is controlled by which nervous system?
questions.explanation: The table lists cardiac muscle as involuntary and supplied by autonomic nerves.

questions.prompt: The resting membrane potential of cardiac muscle in the comparison table is approximately:
questions.explanation: The comparison table lists cardiac resting membrane potential as about -90 mV.

questions.prompt: What action potential shape is typical of cardiac muscle in the comparison table?
options: Pacemaker wave only in all fibres
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle has a plateau action potential lasting about 100-300 ms.

questions.prompt: Sustained fused contraction would prevent ventricular filling. Which property of cardiac muscle prevents tetanus?
questions.explanation: The table states tetanus is not possible due to the long refractory period.

questions.prompt: Cardiac muscle has many mitochondria mainly reflecting:
options: High oxygen consumption and continuous work
questions.answer: High oxygen consumption and continuous work
questions.explanation: The comparison table notes many mitochondria and high oxygen consumption in cardiac muscle.

questions.prompt: A fall in extracellular calcium reduces myocardial contractile force. This reflects that cardiac excitation-contraction coupling is partly dependent on:
questions.explanation: The comparison table states cardiac contraction is partly dependent on extracellular calcium concentration.

questions.prompt: Which property is listed for cardiac muscle but not skeletal muscle in the comparison table?
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle has autorhythmicity, while skeletal muscle does not.

questions.prompt: Cardiac muscle obeys all-or-none law at the level of:
questions.explanation: The table states cardiac muscle obeys all-or-none law as a whole muscle because it behaves as a functional syncytium.

questions.prompt: A physiology teacher explains why the heart relaxes between beats instead of remaining in sustained contraction. Which principle best explains this?
questions.explanation: The long refractory period prevents tetanus, allowing rhythmic contraction-relaxation cycles essential for pumping.

questions.prompt: What is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system?
questions.explanation: The source defines the neuron or nerve cell as the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.

questions.prompt: Absence of which structure explains why destroyed neurons are not replaced by cell division?
questions.explanation: The neuronal cell body lacks a centrosome, indicating loss of ability for division.

questions.prompt: Which neuronal component is composed of rough endoplasmic reticulum and indicates high protein synthesis?
questions.explanation: Nissl granules are basophilic rough ER and indicate high protein synthesis in neurons.

questions.prompt: After a peripheral nerve is cut during trauma, the neuron shows chromatolysis of Nissl bodies. Which event is most directly responsible for this change?
questions.explanation: The source notes that Nissl bodies disintegrate in fatigue, poisoning and after sectioning of the axon.

questions.prompt: Which part of a neuron conducts impulses away from the cell body?
questions.explanation: Axons perform the specialized function of conducting impulses away from the cell body.

questions.prompt: What are nodes of Ranvier?
options: Periodic gaps between myelinated Schwann cell segments
questions.answer: Periodic gaps between myelinated Schwann cell segments
questions.explanation: Nodes of Ranvier are short periodic gaps at junctions between myelin segments.

questions.prompt: A child with a contaminated wound develops tetanus after toxin travels from the wound toward the spinal cord. Which neuronal transport mechanism explains this spread?
questions.explanation: The source mentions tetanus toxin and viruses such as polio, herpes simplex and rabies can travel by retrograde flow.

questions.prompt: Which connective tissue sheath covers each fasciculus of a peripheral nerve?
questions.explanation: Each nerve fasciculus is covered by perineurium, whose cells act as a barrier.

questions.prompt: What is the resting membrane potential recorded inside a nerve fibre in the source example?
questions.explanation: With one microelectrode inside the axon, a steady potential difference of about -70 mV is recorded.

questions.prompt: A nerve fibre receives a weak stimulus that causes small local depolarization but no propagated impulse. Propagation begins only when the membrane reaches about:
questions.explanation: The source gives firing level as about -55 mV, after which abrupt propagated action potential occurs.

questions.prompt: What is the neuromuscular junction?
options: Synapse between a motor nerve terminal and skeletal muscle fibre
Gap junction between smooth muscle cells
questions.answer: Synapse between a motor nerve terminal and skeletal muscle fibre
questions.explanation: The chapter describes NMJ as the junction where a motor nerve terminal communicates with skeletal muscle.

questions.prompt: Which neurotransmitter mediates transmission at the skeletal neuromuscular junction?
questions.explanation: Neuromuscular transmission at skeletal muscle uses acetylcholine released from nerve terminals.

questions.prompt: Where is acetylcholine stored before release at the NMJ?
questions.explanation: The source describes acetylcholine synthesis and storage in vesicles at the nerve terminal.

questions.prompt: Entry of which ion into the nerve terminal triggers acetylcholine release?
questions.explanation: Calcium entry into the nerve terminal triggers release of acetylcholine vesicles.

questions.prompt: Acetylcholine acts on the postsynaptic membrane to produce which local potential?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine opens channels at the motor end plate and develops the end plate potential.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme removes acetylcholine from the neuromuscular junction?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine is removed mainly by acetylcholinesterase at the junction.

questions.prompt: A patient has fluctuating skeletal muscle weakness due to impaired postsynaptic transmission at the motor end plate. Which site is primarily affected?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is discussed with neuromuscular disorders and classically affects postsynaptic transmission.

questions.prompt: A toxin blocks acetylcholine release from motor nerve terminals. What immediate functional effect is expected in skeletal muscle?
questions.explanation: Without acetylcholine release, the end plate potential cannot adequately activate the muscle fibre.

questions.prompt: The motor end plate belongs to which muscle type in this source contrast?
questions.explanation: The source contrasts skeletal muscle motor end plates with smooth muscle varicosities that do not form direct motor end plates.

questions.prompt: A patient receives a drug that inhibits acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction. Which effect is expected at the end plate?
options: Acetylcholine action at the end plate
questions.answer: Acetylcholine action at the end plate
questions.explanation: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase delays acetylcholine removal and prolongs its junctional action.

questions.prompt: Skeletal muscle fibres are described as which structural type?
questions.explanation: The comparison table describes skeletal fibres as cylindrical and striated.

questions.prompt: Which regulatory protein complex is present in skeletal muscle thin filaments?
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle contraction is regulated by troponin-tropomyosin on thin filaments.

questions.prompt: The T-tubule system of skeletal muscle is part of which function?
questions.explanation: The sarcotubular system, including T-tubules, carries excitation inward for excitation-contraction coupling.

questions.prompt: During skeletal muscle contraction, thin filaments slide over thick filaments due to:
questions.explanation: The source explains contraction by molecular cross-bridge cycling and sliding of thin over thick filaments.

questions.prompt: Which ion binds to troponin to initiate skeletal muscle contraction?
questions.explanation: Calcium binds to troponin, allowing actin-myosin interaction in skeletal muscle.

questions.prompt: What is a motor unit?
options: One actin and one myosin molecule
One Schwann cell and one node
One motor neuron and the muscle fibres it supplies
questions.answer: One motor neuron and the muscle fibres it supplies
questions.explanation: The motor unit is the functional group of a motor neuron and its innervated muscle fibres.

questions.prompt: A man holds a heavy suitcase steady without visible shortening of the biceps. Which type of muscle contraction is occurring?
questions.explanation: In isometric contraction, tension develops without change in muscle length.

questions.prompt: During lifting of a dumbbell, the biceps shortens while moving the load. Which type of contraction is this?
questions.explanation: In isotonic contraction, muscle length changes while moving a load.

questions.prompt: A patient with suspected myopathy is evaluated by recording electrical activity from skeletal muscle. Which investigation is being used?
questions.explanation: The chapter discusses electromyography and electromyogram for skeletal muscle electrical activity.

questions.prompt: Muscular dystrophy, myotonia and myasthenia gravis are listed under:
questions.explanation: These are listed under common disorders of skeletal muscles in the chapter.

questions.prompt: Smooth muscle fibres are typically:
options: Long cylindrical fibres with peripheral nuclei
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle fibres are long spindle-shaped myocytes with a central nucleus.

questions.prompt: Which junction allows adjacent single-unit smooth muscle cells to communicate?
questions.explanation: Adjacent smooth muscle cells communicate through gap junctions, especially in single-unit smooth muscle.

questions.prompt: Compared with skeletal muscle, smooth muscle lacks which regulatory protein?
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle thin filaments lack troponin; calcium acts through calmodulin.

questions.prompt: In smooth muscle, calcium binds to which protein to activate contraction?
questions.explanation: Calcium-calmodulin activates myosin light chain kinase in smooth muscle.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme phosphorylates the myosin regulatory light chain in smooth muscle?
questions.explanation: MLCK uses ATP to phosphorylate the myosin regulatory chain, enabling cross-bridge formation.

questions.prompt: Depolarization in smooth muscle action potentials is mainly due to entry of:
questions.explanation: The source states smooth muscle depolarization occurs due to calcium entry rather than sodium entry.

questions.prompt: A strip of intestinal smooth muscle shows rhythmic slow waves that trigger periodic contractions. These slow waves are produced by:
questions.explanation: Slow wave or pacemaker potentials underlie rhythmic contractions in many visceral smooth muscles.

questions.prompt: The latch phenomenon in smooth muscle helps maintain contraction with:
questions.explanation: The chapter lists latch phenomenon as a characteristic allowing sustained smooth muscle contraction efficiently.

questions.prompt: Autonomic fibres supplying visceral smooth muscle do not end as motor end plates; instead transmitter is released from bead-like swellings. These swellings are:
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle autonomic fibres have beaded varicosities that release neurotransmitter into interstitial fluid.

questions.prompt: A bright light stimulates constriction of the pupil through smooth muscle that behaves as separate motor units. This is an example of smooth muscle responding mainly to:
questions.explanation: The source says multiunit smooth muscles, including iris and piloerector muscles, usually respond to nerve stimuli.

questions.prompt: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons arise mainly from which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: Sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar.

questions.prompt: Parasympathetic outflow is described as what?
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic fibres arise from brainstem nuclei and sacral cord.

questions.prompt: The neurotransmitter at all autonomic ganglia is what?
questions.explanation: Preganglionic autonomic neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors.

questions.prompt: A patient with Horner syndrome has ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis due to interruption of which pathway?
questions.explanation: Horner syndrome follows sympathetic pathway damage.

questions.prompt: Most postganglionic sympathetic neurons release which neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: Most sympathetic postganglionic fibres are adrenergic.

questions.prompt: Sweat glands are an exception because their sympathetic postganglionic fibres release what?
questions.explanation: Eccrine sweat glands receive cholinergic sympathetic fibres.

questions.prompt: Parasympathetic stimulation of heart primarily causes what?
questions.explanation: Vagal activity slows SA node firing.

questions.prompt: A patient with autonomic neuropathy develops postural dizziness. Which reflex is impaired?
questions.explanation: Autonomic failure impairs vasoconstriction on standing.

questions.prompt: Alpha-1 receptor stimulation usually causes which vascular response?
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 activation contracts vascular smooth muscle.

questions.prompt: Organophosphate poisoning causes salivation, lacrimation and bronchospasm by increasing which neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: Acetylcholinesterase inhibition increases acetylcholine at muscarinic synapses.

questions.prompt: The cerebellum is especially important for which function?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates timing, force and accuracy of movements.
