options: Storage material accumulates in mononuclear phagocytes and parenchymal cells
questions.answer: Storage material accumulates in mononuclear phagocytes and parenchymal cells
questions.explanation: Progressive substrate accumulation expands affected cells and organs.

questions.prompt: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Tay-Sachs disease results from HEXA mutations and GM2 ganglioside accumulation.

questions.prompt: Gaucher disease is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disorder involving glucocerebroside accumulation.

questions.prompt: A cherry-red spot may be seen in:
questions.explanation: Ganglioside accumulation in retinal ganglion cells can leave the fovea appearing cherry red.

questions.prompt: Gaucher cells have a characteristic cytoplasm described as:
questions.explanation: Lipid-laden macrophages in Gaucher disease have fibrillary, wrinkled cytoplasm.

questions.prompt: Niemann-Pick disease types A and B involve deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Types A and B Niemann-Pick disease are caused by sphingomyelinase deficiency.

questions.prompt: Niemann-Pick disease type C is primarily a defect in:
questions.explanation: NPC1/NPC2 defects impair cholesterol movement out of lysosomes.

questions.prompt: I-cell disease occurs because lysosomal enzymes:
options: Fail to receive mannose-6-phosphate targeting markers
Are encoded only by the Y chromosome
questions.answer: Fail to receive mannose-6-phosphate targeting markers
questions.explanation: Without mannose-6-phosphate, lysosomal enzymes are secreted rather than delivered to lysosomes.

questions.prompt: Pompe disease is a glycogen storage disease caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Pompe disease is glycogen storage disease type II and affects lysosomal glycogen degradation.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: Familial hypercholesterolemia most commonly involves defective:
questions.explanation: Reduced LDL receptor function decreases hepatic LDL uptake.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: Statins are useful in many patients with familial hypercholesterolemia because they:
options: Repair the LDL receptor gene directly
Increase hepatic LDL receptor expression by lowering intracellular cholesterol synthesis
Block all cholesterol absorption in lysosomes
questions.answer: Increase hepatic LDL receptor expression by lowering intracellular cholesterol synthesis
questions.explanation: By inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, statins increase LDL receptor expression when receptor function remains.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: The major plasma lipid abnormality in familial hypercholesterolemia is:
questions.explanation: LDL accumulates in plasma when receptor-mediated clearance is impaired.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: A clinical finding associated with familial hypercholesterolemia is:
questions.explanation: Cholesterol-rich deposits in tendons and skin can form xanthomas.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: The most serious consequence of familial hypercholesterolemia is:
options: Premature atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease
questions.answer: Premature atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease
questions.explanation: High LDL accelerates atheroma formation and vascular disease.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: LDL receptors are normally clustered in membrane regions called:
questions.explanation: LDL binds receptors in coated pits, which are internalized by endocytosis.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: After LDL receptor-mediated endocytosis, LDL is degraded mainly in:
questions.explanation: The LDL particle dissociates from its receptor and is degraded in lysosomes.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: PCSK9 promotes hypercholesterolemia by:
questions.explanation: PCSK9 binds LDL receptors and targets them for degradation after endocytosis.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: A homozygous LDL receptor defect is more severe than heterozygous disease because:
options: LDL is cleared by red cells only
LDL receptor activity is nearly absent rather than partially reduced
questions.answer: LDL receptor activity is nearly absent rather than partially reduced
questions.explanation: Gene dosage strongly affects LDL clearance and age of cardiovascular disease onset.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: Intracellular cholesterol normally suppresses cholesterol synthesis by inhibiting:
questions.explanation: Free cholesterol downregulates HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis.

questions.prompt: A missense mutation is best defined as:
options: A base substitution that changes one amino acid to another
A mutation that creates a premature stop codon
A deletion of an entire chromosome
A repeat expansion that always silences a gene
questions.answer: A base substitution that changes one amino acid to another
questions.explanation: Missense mutations alter the meaning of a codon and substitute one amino acid in the protein.

questions.prompt: Genetic heterogeneity means:
options: One mutation always produces many unrelated effects
Mutations at different loci can produce a similar clinical phenotype
A gene is expressed only from the paternal allele
questions.answer: Mutations at different loci can produce a similar clinical phenotype
questions.explanation: Clinically similar disorders such as childhood deafness may arise from mutations in many different genes.

questions.prompt: A nonsense mutation produces disease by:
options: Replacing one amino acid with a similar amino acid
Changing an amino acid codon into a stop codon
questions.answer: Changing an amino acid codon into a stop codon
questions.explanation: Nonsense mutations create premature termination codons, often yielding truncated unstable proteins.

questions.prompt: A frameshift mutation usually results from:
options: Insertion or deletion of bases not in multiples of three
questions.answer: Insertion or deletion of bases not in multiples of three
questions.explanation: Because codons are read in triplets, non-triplet insertions or deletions alter the downstream reading frame.

questions.prompt: A mutation in a promoter or enhancer may cause disease mainly by:
options: Changing the number of chromosomes in every cell
questions.explanation: Regulatory sequence mutations can impair transcription factor binding and reduce mRNA production.

questions.prompt: A point mutation in an intron can be pathogenic when it:
questions.explanation: Intronic splice-site mutations can prevent proper processing of the primary RNA transcript.

questions.prompt: A conservative missense mutation is usually less harmful because:
options: The substituted amino acid has similar biochemical properties
It always restores the normal codon
It creates a full chromosomal monosomy
questions.answer: The substituted amino acid has similar biochemical properties
questions.explanation: A chemically similar substitution may preserve enough protein structure and function.

questions.prompt: The sickle cell mutation is a classic example of:
questions.explanation: Sickle hemoglobin results from substitution of valine for glutamic acid in beta-globin, changing protein properties.

questions.prompt: A three-base-pair deletion within a coding exon is less likely to cause a frameshift because:
options: All deletions are corrected by mismatch repair
The reading frame remains aligned after loss of one codon
questions.answer: The reading frame remains aligned after loss of one codon
questions.explanation: In-frame deletions remove amino acid(s) but preserve codon grouping downstream.

questions.prompt: Pleiotropism means:
options: One mutant gene produces multiple phenotypic effects
Several genes produce the same phenotype
questions.answer: One mutant gene produces multiple phenotypic effects
questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is pleiotropic because one beta-globin mutation causes anemia, vaso-occlusion, organ infarcts, and more.

questions.prompt: Autosomal dominant disorders are typically expressed in:
questions.explanation: A single mutant autosomal allele is sufficient to produce many dominant phenotypes.

questions.prompt: A new mutation is especially common in severe autosomal dominant disorders because:
options: Autosomal genes mutate only after birth
Affected individuals often have reduced reproductive fitness
questions.answer: Affected individuals often have reduced reproductive fitness
questions.explanation: When disease limits reproduction, many cases arise from new germline mutations rather than inheritance.

questions.prompt: If an affected heterozygous parent has an autosomal dominant disorder and the other parent is unaffected, each child has what risk?
questions.explanation: Each child has a one-in-two chance of inheriting the mutant allele.

questions.prompt: Autosomal recessive disorders usually require:
options: A mutant allele only on the Y chromosome
One dominant allele in every affected person
Mutant alleles on both homologous chromosomes
questions.answer: Mutant alleles on both homologous chromosomes
questions.explanation: Most autosomal recessive diseases manifest in homozygotes or compound heterozygotes.

questions.prompt: A key reason autosomal recessive disorders are more common in consanguineous families is:
options: Relatives are more likely to carry the same rare mutant allele
questions.answer: Relatives are more likely to carry the same rare mutant allele
questions.explanation: Shared ancestry increases the chance both parents carry the same pathogenic recessive variant.

questions.prompt: Incomplete penetrance means:
options: The phenotype is always identical in all carriers
Some individuals with the disease genotype do not express the phenotype
The gene is located only in mitochondria
questions.answer: Some individuals with the disease genotype do not express the phenotype
questions.explanation: Penetrance describes the proportion of genotype-positive individuals who show the trait.

questions.prompt: Variable expressivity means:
options: Only half of carriers have any phenotype
All daughters of affected fathers are unaffected
The same genotype produces different severity or features among affected individuals
questions.answer: The same genotype produces different severity or features among affected individuals
questions.explanation: Expressivity refers to the range of manifestations in people who express the disease.

questions.prompt: X-linked recessive disorders are usually expressed more severely in males because males are:
questions.explanation: Males have one X chromosome, so a mutant X-linked allele lacks a normal counterpart.

questions.prompt: An affected male with an X-linked recessive disorder and an unaffected noncarrier female will transmit the mutant allele to:
options: Half of sons and half of daughters
questions.explanation: Fathers pass their X chromosome to daughters and Y chromosome to sons.

questions.prompt: A heterozygous female carrier of an X-linked disorder may show symptoms because of:
questions.explanation: Lyonization can leave a substantial fraction of cells expressing the mutant X chromosome.

questions.topic: Nonclassic Inheritance and Molecular Genetic Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Fragile X syndrome is caused by expansion of:
questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome results from CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene.

questions.topic: Nonclassic Inheritance and Molecular Genetic Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Next-generation sequencing is powerful because it can:
options: Always detect every balanced translocation without other tests
Sequence many genomic regions in parallel
questions.answer: Sequence many genomic regions in parallel
questions.explanation: NGS massively parallelizes DNA sequencing, enabling panels, exomes, and tumor profiling.

questions.topic: Nonclassic Inheritance and Molecular Genetic Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Mitochondrial DNA disorders are usually inherited from:
questions.explanation: Oocytes contribute most mitochondria to the embryo, so mtDNA is maternally inherited.

questions.topic: Nonclassic Inheritance and Molecular Genetic Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Genomic imprinting means:
options: All genes are expressed equally from both parents
Gene expression depends on whether the allele is inherited from the mother or father
questions.answer: Gene expression depends on whether the allele is inherited from the mother or father
questions.explanation: Imprinting is parent-of-origin-specific gene expression due to epigenetic marking.

questions.topic: Nonclassic Inheritance and Molecular Genetic Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Anticipation in trinucleotide-repeat disorders refers to:
options: Earlier onset or increased severity in successive generations
Equal expression of maternal and paternal alleles
questions.answer: Earlier onset or increased severity in successive generations
questions.explanation: Repeat expansions can enlarge during transmission, worsening disease in descendants.

questions.topic: Nonclassic Inheritance and Molecular Genetic Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Full Fragile X mutations usually cause disease by:
questions.explanation: Large CGG expansions promote methylation and transcriptional silencing of FMR1.

questions.topic: Nonclassic Inheritance and Molecular Genetic Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Prader-Willi syndrome usually results from loss of genes on:
questions.explanation: Paternal 15q11-q13 deletion or maternal uniparental disomy can cause Prader-Willi syndrome.

questions.topic: Nonclassic Inheritance and Molecular Genetic Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Angelman syndrome usually results from loss of function of genes on:
questions.explanation: Angelman syndrome reflects loss of the maternally active allele in the same imprinted region.

questions.topic: Nonclassic Inheritance and Molecular Genetic Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Heteroplasmy in mitochondrial disease means:
options: A cell contains a mixture of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA
All mitochondria are inherited from the father
Every cell has identical mutant autosomes
Only one X chromosome is active
questions.answer: A cell contains a mixture of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA
questions.explanation: Variable proportions of mutant mtDNA help explain variable severity and threshold effects.

questions.topic: Nonclassic Inheritance and Molecular Genetic Diagnosis
questions.prompt: FISH is especially useful for detecting:
options: Single-base substitutions across the entire genome only
Specific chromosomal deletions or rearrangements using fluorescent probes
questions.answer: Specific chromosomal deletions or rearrangements using fluorescent probes
questions.explanation: FISH uses labeled DNA probes to localize particular genomic regions in cells.

questions.topic: Sex Chromosome Disorders and Disorders of Sex Development
questions.prompt: Klinefelter syndrome most commonly has which karyotype?
questions.explanation: The classic Klinefelter karyotype is 47,XXY.

questions.topic: Sex Chromosome Disorders and Disorders of Sex Development
questions.prompt: True hermaphroditism is defined by the presence of:
options: Only testes with female external genitalia
Only ovaries with male external genitalia
One extra X chromosome in all males
questions.explanation: Ovotesticular disorder of sex development contains both ovarian and testicular gonadal tissue.

questions.topic: Sex Chromosome Disorders and Disorders of Sex Development
questions.prompt: Turner syndrome most commonly involves:
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome is usually 45,X or mosaic variants involving X chromosome loss.

questions.topic: Sex Chromosome Disorders and Disorders of Sex Development
questions.prompt: A common clinical feature of Turner syndrome is:
options: Hyperphagia and obesity from paternal 15q deletion
questions.explanation: Short stature and gonadal dysgenesis are classic Turner features.

questions.topic: Sex Chromosome Disorders and Disorders of Sex Development
questions.prompt: Klinefelter syndrome classically presents with:
questions.explanation: Seminiferous tubule dysgenesis causes small firm testes, infertility, and hypogonadism.

questions.topic: Sex Chromosome Disorders and Disorders of Sex Development
questions.prompt: Barr body number is generally equal to:
options: Number of X chromosomes minus one
Number of Y chromosomes plus one
questions.answer: Number of X chromosomes minus one
questions.explanation: All but one X chromosome are inactivated in somatic cells.

questions.topic: Sex Chromosome Disorders and Disorders of Sex Development
questions.prompt: A classic cardiovascular association of Turner syndrome is:
options: Aortic root dilation from fibrillin defect
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome is associated with congenital cardiovascular defects, including coarctation.

questions.topic: Sex Chromosome Disorders and Disorders of Sex Development
questions.prompt: Why are sex chromosome aneuploidies often better tolerated than autosomal aneuploidies?
options: X inactivation and limited Y chromosome gene content reduce gene dosage imbalance
questions.answer: X inactivation and limited Y chromosome gene content reduce gene dosage imbalance
questions.explanation: Dosage compensation blunts the effect of extra X chromosomes, and the Y has relatively few genes.

questions.topic: Sex Chromosome Disorders and Disorders of Sex Development
questions.prompt: In Klinefelter syndrome, increased gonadotropins occur because:
options: There is excess LDL receptor activity
Primary testicular failure reduces sex steroid and inhibin feedback
questions.answer: Primary testicular failure reduces sex steroid and inhibin feedback
questions.explanation: Gonadal failure leads to hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

questions.topic: Sex Chromosome Disorders and Disorders of Sex Development
questions.prompt: A phenotypic female with streak ovaries, webbed neck, and lymphedema most likely has:
questions.explanation: These findings are classic for Turner syndrome.

questions.topic: Biochemical and Molecular Basis of Single-Gene Disorders
questions.prompt: Most inborn errors of metabolism are caused by defects in:
questions.explanation: Many metabolic diseases are autosomal recessive enzyme deficiencies.

questions.topic: Biochemical and Molecular Basis of Single-Gene Disorders
questions.prompt: Patient-tailored therapy based on drug-metabolizing gene variants is an example of:
questions.explanation: Pharmacogenetic information can guide drug selection or dose for an individual patient.

questions.topic: Biochemical and Molecular Basis of Single-Gene Disorders
questions.prompt: A receptor or transport-system defect classically causes:
options: A balanced karyotype in every cell
Impaired uptake or movement of a molecule
questions.answer: Impaired uptake or movement of a molecule
questions.explanation: Mutations in transporters or receptors block normal cellular handling of specific molecules.

questions.topic: Biochemical and Molecular Basis of Single-Gene Disorders
questions.prompt: Pharmacogenetics studies:
questions.explanation: Genetic variants in drug-metabolizing enzymes, transporters, or receptors can influence toxicity and efficacy.

questions.topic: Biochemical and Molecular Basis of Single-Gene Disorders
questions.prompt: Loss of enzyme activity may cause disease by:
options: Accumulation of substrate or deficiency of product
questions.answer: Accumulation of substrate or deficiency of product
questions.explanation: Enzyme defects often cause toxic substrate buildup or inadequate production of downstream metabolites.

questions.topic: Biochemical and Molecular Basis of Single-Gene Disorders
questions.prompt: Why are many enzyme deficiencies autosomal recessive?
options: Enzymes are encoded only on mitochondrial DNA
Half-normal enzyme activity is often sufficient
Heterozygotes always lack all enzyme activity
questions.answer: Half-normal enzyme activity is often sufficient
questions.explanation: Carriers often remain healthy because one normal allele provides enough enzyme function.

questions.topic: Biochemical and Molecular Basis of Single-Gene Disorders
questions.prompt: A dominant-negative mutation causes disease because the mutant protein:
options: Interferes with function of the normal protein
questions.answer: Interferes with function of the normal protein
questions.explanation: Structural proteins made of multimers are vulnerable to dominant-negative mutant subunits.

questions.topic: Biochemical and Molecular Basis of Single-Gene Disorders
questions.prompt: Haploinsufficiency refers to disease caused when:
options: One normal allele does not produce enough functional protein
The gene product is never needed
questions.answer: One normal allele does not produce enough functional protein
questions.explanation: Some genes require two working copies to provide adequate protein dosage.

questions.topic: Biochemical and Molecular Basis of Single-Gene Disorders
questions.prompt: G6PD deficiency is often clinically silent until oxidant drug exposure because:
options: The enzyme defect becomes important under oxidative stress
questions.answer: The enzyme defect becomes important under oxidative stress
questions.explanation: G6PD helps maintain red cell glutathione; oxidant stress can trigger hemolysis in deficient cells.

questions.topic: Biochemical and Molecular Basis of Single-Gene Disorders
questions.prompt: A mutation affecting a collagen chain can produce dominant disease because:
options: Mutant chains can disrupt assembly of normal collagen triple helices
Collagen is encoded only by mitochondrial DNA
questions.answer: Mutant chains can disrupt assembly of normal collagen triple helices
questions.explanation: Abnormal structural subunits can poison the function of multimeric protein complexes.

questions.topic: Structural Protein Disorders: Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
questions.prompt: Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations affecting:
questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome usually results from FBN1 mutations encoding fibrillin-1.

questions.topic: Structural Protein Disorders: Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
questions.prompt: The dermatosparaxis type of EDS is autosomal recessive because it involves:
options: A dominant structural collagen chain defect
questions.explanation: Enzyme deficiencies often require both alleles to be defective before disease appears.

questions.topic: Structural Protein Disorders: Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
questions.prompt: The major organ systems affected in Marfan syndrome are:
questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome prominently affects connective tissues rich in microfibrils.

questions.topic: Structural Protein Disorders: Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
questions.prompt: Ehlers-Danlos syndromes are primarily disorders of:
questions.explanation: EDS variants involve defective collagen or collagen-processing proteins.

questions.topic: Structural Protein Disorders: Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
questions.prompt: A dangerous cardiovascular complication of Marfan syndrome is:
questions.explanation: Weakness of the aortic media predisposes to dilation, regurgitation, and dissection.

questions.topic: Structural Protein Disorders: Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
questions.prompt: Lens dislocation in Marfan syndrome reflects weakness of:
questions.explanation: Fibrillin-rich zonular fibers help suspend the lens.

questions.topic: Structural Protein Disorders: Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
questions.prompt: Excess TGF-beta signaling contributes to Marfan syndrome because fibrillin normally:
options: Helps sequester latent TGF-beta in extracellular matrix
questions.answer: Helps sequester latent TGF-beta in extracellular matrix
questions.explanation: Fibrillin defects increase TGF-beta bioavailability, contributing to tissue abnormalities.

questions.topic: Structural Protein Disorders: Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
questions.prompt: Classic EDS commonly presents with:
questions.explanation: Defective collagen weakens skin, ligaments, and other connective tissues.

questions.topic: Structural Protein Disorders: Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
questions.prompt: The vascular type of EDS is especially associated with defects in:
questions.explanation: Type III collagen is abundant in vessels and hollow organs, explaining rupture risk.

questions.topic: Structural Protein Disorders: Marfan Syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
questions.prompt: Autosomal dominant inheritance in some EDS variants is explained by:
options: Dominant-negative effects of abnormal collagen chains
questions.answer: Dominant-negative effects of abnormal collagen chains
questions.explanation: A mutant collagen chain can disrupt the collagen molecule even when a normal allele is present.

questions.prompt: Adaptive immunity is mediated mainly by:
questions.explanation: T and B cells provide antigen-specific immunity and memory.

questions.prompt: A virus produces proteins in the cytosol of an infected epithelial cell. Peptides are generated in proteasomes, transported into the ER, and displayed to lymphocytes that kill the infected cell. Which MHC pathway is being used?
options: Class II MHC presentation to CD4+ cells
Class I MHC presentation to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells
questions.answer: Class I MHC presentation to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells
questions.explanation: Cytosolic antigens are presented on MHC I to CD8 CTLs.

questions.prompt: The enzyme complex required for antigen receptor gene recombination is encoded by:
questions.explanation: RAG proteins mediate V(D)J recombination in developing lymphocytes.

questions.prompt: Class I MHC molecules present peptides mainly to:
questions.explanation: CD8 T cells recognize cytosolic peptides displayed by MHC class I.

questions.prompt: Class II MHC molecules present peptides mainly to:
questions.explanation: CD4 T cells recognize extracellularly derived peptides on MHC class II.

questions.prompt: Which cells are the most efficient antigen-presenting cells for activating naive T lymphocytes?
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells capture antigens in tissues and present them in T-cell zones of lymphoid organs.

questions.prompt: The principal costimulatory signal for naive T-cell activation is:
options: B7 on APCs binding CD28 on T cells
questions.answer: B7 on APCs binding CD28 on T cells
questions.explanation: Signal 2 is provided by B7/CD28, ensuring T cells respond to danger-associated antigens.

questions.prompt: Follicular dendritic cells mainly help B-cell responses by:
options: Displaying antibody- or complement-coated antigen in germinal centers
questions.answer: Displaying antibody- or complement-coated antigen in germinal centers
questions.explanation: FDCs retain immune complexes for selection of high-affinity B cells.

questions.prompt: A lymph node biopsy shows many lymphocytes with different immunoglobulin gene rearrangements after infection. Another node shows one dominant rearrangement pattern in nearly all B cells. What is the key diagnostic use of antigen receptor gene rearrangement testing here?
options: Distinguishing polyclonal reactive proliferation from monoclonal lymphoma
questions.answer: Distinguishing polyclonal reactive proliferation from monoclonal lymphoma
questions.explanation: Each lymphocyte clone has a unique rearrangement; monoclonality suggests neoplasia.

questions.prompt: A vaccine protein is injected with an adjuvant. The antigen is recognized by T cells, but robust T-cell activation occurs only because the adjuvant stimulates dendritic cells to express B7 and cytokines. What principle explains this?
options: Naive T cells require antigen plus costimulation
questions.answer: Naive T cells require antigen plus costimulation
questions.explanation: Signal 1 alone may induce tolerance; costimulation links adaptive responses to innate danger signals.

questions.prompt: Amyloid is composed of misfolded proteins arranged as:
questions.explanation: Amyloid fibrils share beta-pleated sheet structure.

questions.prompt: An elderly patient develops restrictive cardiomyopathy from transthyretin deposition, without a plasma cell neoplasm or chronic inflammatory disorder. The fibrils still share beta-pleated sheet structure and Congo red positivity. Which category best fits?
questions.explanation: Transthyretin can form senile systemic or hereditary amyloid deposits, especially in heart.

questions.prompt: Congo red-stained amyloid shows what under polarized light?
questions.explanation: Congo red produces apple-green birefringence with amyloid.

questions.prompt: AL amyloid is derived from:

questions.prompt: AA amyloid is derived from:

questions.prompt: A common cause of systemic reactive AA amyloidosis is:
questions.explanation: Persistent inflammation elevates SAA, predisposing to AA amyloid.

questions.prompt: The kidney in amyloidosis commonly presents with:

questions.prompt: Dialysis-associated amyloidosis is related to accumulation of:

questions.prompt: A patient with multiple myeloma develops nephrotic-range proteinuria and restrictive cardiomyopathy. Tissue biopsy shows Congo red-positive deposits with apple-green birefringence composed of monoclonal light-chain fragments. Which amyloid type is present?
questions.explanation: Plasma cell dyscrasias produce monoclonal light chains that form AL amyloid.

questions.prompt: A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops enlarged waxy kidneys and heavy proteinuria. The amyloid fibrils are derived from an acute-phase reactant made by the liver during chronic inflammation. Which precursor protein is involved?
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation causes AA amyloidosis from SAA.

questions.prompt: HIV primarily infects cells expressing:
questions.explanation: HIV uses CD4 and CCR5 or CXCR4 to enter cells.

questions.prompt: A person homozygous for a loss-of-function CCR5 mutation is highly resistant to infection by common transmitted HIV strains. Which step in the viral life cycle is impaired?
questions.explanation: CCR5 is a required entry coreceptor for many HIV strains.

questions.prompt: The defining immune defect in AIDS is loss of:
questions.explanation: Progressive CD4 T-cell depletion causes opportunistic infections and tumors.

questions.prompt: HIV is a:
questions.explanation: HIV is an RNA retrovirus that uses reverse transcriptase.

questions.prompt: CCR5-tropic HIV strains usually infect:
questions.explanation: CCR5 is used by many transmitted macrophage-tropic strains.

questions.prompt: Reverse transcriptase allows HIV to:
questions.explanation: Reverse transcriptase converts RNA genome into DNA for integration.

questions.prompt: AIDS is diagnosed clinically by opportunistic infections or tumors, often when CD4 count falls below:
questions.explanation: CD4 counts below 200/µL are associated with AIDS-defining opportunistic disease.

questions.prompt: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in HIV reflects defective:
questions.explanation: T-cell depletion predisposes to opportunistic fungal pneumonia.

questions.prompt: Soon after HIV exposure, a patient has fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, high viremia, and a transient drop in CD4 cells. Symptoms improve, but virus persists in lymphoid tissues with ongoing replication. Which phase is this?
options: Acute retroviral syndrome followed by clinical latency
questions.answer: Acute retroviral syndrome followed by clinical latency
questions.explanation: Primary HIV infection causes high viremia; latency is clinically silent but virologically active.

questions.prompt: An untreated HIV patient develops progressive weight loss, chronic diarrhea, oral candidiasis, and Kaposi sarcoma. CD4 count is 80/µL. Which mechanism best explains the broad susceptibility to infections and tumors?
options: Severe depletion and dysfunction of CD4+ helper T cells
questions.answer: Severe depletion and dysfunction of CD4+ helper T cells
questions.explanation: CD4 T cells coordinate macrophage, B-cell, and CTL responses; their loss cripples immunity.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: Type I hypersensitivity is mediated primarily by:

questions.topic: Type I and Type II Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: A patient has hemoptysis, renal failure, linear IgG staining along glomerular basement membranes, and antibodies against a noncollagenous domain of type IV collagen. Which type II pattern best fits this disease?
options: Antibody-mediated tissue injury against fixed basement membrane antigen
questions.answer: Antibody-mediated tissue injury against fixed basement membrane antigen
questions.explanation: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by antibodies binding fixed BM antigens, activating complement and leukocytes.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: The main vasoactive amine released from mast cell granules is:
questions.explanation: Histamine causes vasodilation, vascular leakage, and bronchoconstriction.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: Type II hypersensitivity is caused by antibodies directed against:
questions.explanation: Type II reactions involve IgG or IgM binding fixed antigens on cells or matrix.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: Anaphylaxis is an example of:
questions.explanation: Widespread IgE-mediated mast cell activation causes systemic vascular leakage and bronchospasm.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is an example of:
questions.explanation: IgG or complement on RBCs leads to phagocytosis or lysis.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: Goodpasture syndrome involves antibodies against:
questions.explanation: Anti-basement membrane antibodies injure glomeruli and alveoli.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: Myasthenia gravis is type II hypersensitivity because antibodies:
questions.explanation: Antibodies alter receptor function without necessarily destroying cells.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: Minutes after a bee sting, a sensitized patient develops bronchospasm, hypotension, urticaria, and laryngeal edema. Serum tryptase is elevated, and symptoms improve with epinephrine. Which mechanism produced the acute event?
options: IgE cross-linking on mast cells with mediator release
questions.answer: IgE cross-linking on mast cells with mediator release
questions.explanation: Systemic immediate hypersensitivity reflects mast cell degranulation after IgE cross-linking.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: A woman develops weakness that worsens with repeated use of muscles. Autoantibodies bind the acetylcholine receptor and reduce neuromuscular transmission, but the receptor is not a soluble antigen. Which hypersensitivity mechanism is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is a functional type II antibody-mediated disease.

questions.topic: Type III and Type IV Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: Type III hypersensitivity is mediated by:
questions.explanation: Soluble antigen-antibody complexes deposit and trigger complement and inflammation.

questions.topic: Type III and Type IV Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: A renal biopsy shows granular immune deposits in glomeruli after infection, with complement consumption and neutrophilic inflammation. The target antigen is not fixed in the basement membrane before antibody binding. Which pattern distinguishes this from Goodpasture syndrome?
options: Linear antibody binding to fixed antigen
Immune complex deposition with granular staining
questions.answer: Immune complex deposition with granular staining
questions.explanation: Type III lesions show granular immune complex deposits; anti-GBM disease shows linear staining.

questions.topic: Type III and Type IV Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: Type IV hypersensitivity is mediated by:
questions.explanation: Delayed-type and cytotoxic T-cell reactions are type IV hypersensitivity.

questions.topic: Type III and Type IV Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: The tuberculin skin test is a classic example of:
questions.explanation: Prior sensitization leads to Th1-mediated macrophage inflammation after 24 to 72 hours.

questions.topic: Type III and Type IV Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: Serum sickness is caused by:
options: T-cell killing of tumor cells only
questions.explanation: Circulating immune complexes deposit in vessels, joints, and kidneys.

questions.topic: Type III and Type IV Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: An Arthus reaction is:
questions.explanation: Preexisting IgG reacts with injected antigen and forms local immune complexes.

questions.topic: Type III and Type IV Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: Complement activation in type III hypersensitivity recruits:
questions.explanation: C5a attracts neutrophils, which release enzymes and cause tissue injury.

questions.topic: Type III and Type IV Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: Contact dermatitis from poison ivy is mediated mainly by:
questions.explanation: Small chemicals act as haptens and elicit type IV T-cell inflammation.

questions.topic: Type III and Type IV Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: A child receives heterologous antiserum and 8 days later develops fever, urticaria, arthralgias, proteinuria, and low complement. Biopsy shows granular immune deposits in small vessels. Which mechanism explains the disease?
options: Systemic type III hypersensitivity from circulating immune complexes
questions.answer: Systemic type III hypersensitivity from circulating immune complexes
questions.explanation: Serum sickness occurs when soluble immune complexes form and deposit after antibody appears.

questions.topic: Type III and Type IV Hypersensitivity
questions.prompt: A purified protein derivative skin test is read at 48 hours and shows induration, not just erythema. The lesion contains T cells and activated macrophages rather than immune-complex neutrophilic vasculitis. Which cytokine is central?
questions.explanation: Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma, activating macrophages in delayed-type hypersensitivity.

questions.prompt: Primary immunodeficiencies are most often caused by:
options: Inherited defects in immune development or function
questions.answer: Inherited defects in immune development or function
questions.explanation: Primary immunodeficiencies are genetic disorders of immune components.

questions.prompt: A child has recurrent staphylococcal abscesses and granulomas. Neutrophils ingest bacteria but cannot generate an oxidative burst on testing. Which immune defect is responsible?
options: NADPH oxidase defect in chronic granulomatous disease
questions.answer: NADPH oxidase defect in chronic granulomatous disease
questions.explanation: CGD impairs respiratory burst-dependent microbial killing.

questions.prompt: Severe combined immunodeficiency involves defective:
questions.explanation: SCID severely impairs cellular and humoral immunity.

questions.prompt: X-linked agammaglobulinemia is caused by mutation in:
questions.explanation: BTK is required for B-cell maturation.

questions.prompt: DiGeorge syndrome causes T-cell deficiency because of:
questions.explanation: 22q11.2 deletion impairs thymic development and T-cell maturation.

questions.prompt: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome classically includes:
options: Aortic aneurysm, lens dislocation, and tall stature
Dry eyes, dry mouth, and lymphoma only
questions.explanation: WAS affects cytoskeletal responses in hematopoietic cells.

questions.prompt: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is associated with:
options: Defective lysosomal trafficking and giant granules
questions.answer: Defective lysosomal trafficking and giant granules
questions.explanation: LYST mutation causes abnormal granule fusion and impaired microbial killing.

questions.prompt: C3 deficiency predisposes especially to:
questions.explanation: C3 is central to opsonization and complement activation.

questions.prompt: An infant develops recurrent bacterial infections after maternal IgG wanes. Tonsils and lymph nodes are very small, mature B cells are absent, and serum immunoglobulins of all classes are markedly reduced. T-cell numbers are preserved. Which defect is most likely?
options: X-linked agammaglobulinemia due to BTK mutation
questions.answer: X-linked agammaglobulinemia due to BTK mutation
questions.explanation: BTK deficiency blocks pre-B-cell maturation, causing absent mature B cells and antibodies.

questions.prompt: A newborn has chronic diarrhea, thrush, Pneumocystis pneumonia, and failure to thrive. Both cellular immunity and antibody responses are poor, and lymphocyte numbers are very low. Which category best describes the disease?
questions.explanation: SCID causes profound T-cell deficiency with secondary impairment of B-cell immunity.

questions.prompt: The first line of defense that is ready before antigen exposure is called:
questions.explanation: Innate immunity is constitutively present and responds rapidly to microbes and damaged cells.

questions.prompt: Bacterial peptides containing N-formylmethionine are detected by leukocyte G-protein-coupled receptors. Neutrophils then migrate up the concentration gradient toward the infected tissue. Which innate immune function is being illustrated?
questions.explanation: N-formylated bacterial peptides act as chemoattractants for innate leukocytes.

questions.prompt: Which cells are the principal rapid phagocytes recruited from blood during innate immune responses?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages are central innate phagocytes.

questions.prompt: Epithelia contribute to innate immunity mainly by:
options: Providing barriers and producing antimicrobial molecules
Presenting antigen only on MHC class II
questions.answer: Providing barriers and producing antimicrobial molecules
questions.explanation: Skin and mucosal epithelia block entry and secrete defensins and other antimicrobial products.

questions.prompt: Toll-like receptors are important because they:
options: Bind peptide-MHC complexes on T cells
Recognize conserved microbial products and activate inflammatory genes
questions.answer: Recognize conserved microbial products and activate inflammatory genes
questions.explanation: TLRs are pattern-recognition receptors for microbial PAMPs and damage signals.

questions.prompt: The inflammasome promotes inflammation chiefly by increasing production of:
questions.explanation: Inflammasomes activate caspase-1, which processes pro-IL-1 beta into active IL-1.

questions.prompt: Natural killer cells kill abnormal cells when:
options: Activating signals exceed inhibitory MHC class I signals
questions.answer: Activating signals exceed inhibitory MHC class I signals
questions.explanation: NK cells integrate activating stress ligands and inhibitory recognition of self MHC I.

questions.prompt: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity by NK cells depends on:
questions.explanation: NK-cell CD16 recognizes IgG-coated targets and triggers killing.

questions.prompt: A virus-infected cell downregulates MHC class I and expresses stress-induced ligands on its surface. A nearby lymphocyte lacks a TCR but contains cytotoxic granules and secretes IFN-gamma. Which cell is best suited to eliminate this target?
questions.explanation: Loss of MHC I removes NK inhibition, while stress ligands activate NK-cell cytotoxicity.

questions.prompt: A patient has recurrent fever attacks from excessive inflammasome activity but no autoantibodies or antigen-specific T-cell response. Symptoms improve dramatically with IL-1 blockade. This pattern is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Autoinflammatory syndromes arise from dysregulated innate immunity, often IL-1 driven.

questions.prompt: IL-2 produced by activated T cells primarily functions as:
questions.explanation: IL-2 drives clonal expansion of antigen-stimulated T cells.

questions.prompt: A child has recurrent mucocutaneous fungal infections due to impaired IL-17 signaling. Neutrophil numbers are normal, but epithelial chemokine responses are weak. Which helper T-cell subset function is most impaired?
options: Th17-mediated recruitment of neutrophils and barrier defense
questions.answer: Th17-mediated recruitment of neutrophils and barrier defense
questions.explanation: Th17 cells are crucial for neutrophil-rich responses at mucosal barriers, especially against fungi.

questions.prompt: Th1 cells characteristically secrete:
questions.explanation: Th1 cells activate macrophages through IFN-gamma.

questions.prompt: Th2 cells are especially important in defense against:
questions.explanation: Th2 cytokines promote IgE, eosinophils, mast cells, and anti-helminth responses.

questions.prompt: Th17 cells promote inflammation mainly by:
questions.explanation: Th17 cytokines induce chemokines and recruit inflammatory leukocytes.

questions.prompt: CD40 ligand on helper T cells is important because it:
options: Binds MHC I on infected cells
Serves as an antibody Fc receptor
Activates macrophages and helps B-cell class switching
questions.answer: Activates macrophages and helps B-cell class switching
questions.explanation: CD40L-CD40 interactions are central to T-cell help for macrophages and B cells.

questions.prompt: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes kill infected cells mainly using:
questions.explanation: CTL granules induce apoptosis in antigen-bearing target cells.

questions.prompt: Affinity maturation of antibodies occurs in:
questions.explanation: Somatic hypermutation and selection in germinal centers increase antibody affinity.

questions.prompt: A patient with a CD40L mutation has recurrent pyogenic and opportunistic infections with very high IgM but little IgG, IgA, or IgE. Germinal centers are poorly developed. Which failed process best explains this syndrome?
questions.explanation: CD40L deficiency causes hyper-IgM syndrome by blocking class switching and germinal center reactions.

questions.prompt: A macrophage contains viable intracellular mycobacteria. A nearby CD4+ T cell recognizes microbial peptide on MHC II, expresses CD40L, and secretes IFN-gamma. What is the main intended result?
options: Classical macrophage activation with enhanced microbicidal killing
questions.answer: Classical macrophage activation with enhanced microbicidal killing
questions.explanation: Th1 CD40L and IFN-gamma activate macrophages to kill ingested microbes.

questions.prompt: Systemic lupus erythematosus is classically associated with antibodies against:
questions.explanation: ANA and anti-dsDNA/anti-Sm antibodies are characteristic of SLE.

questions.prompt: A patient develops tight skin of the fingers, Raynaud phenomenon, dysphagia from esophageal fibrosis, and pulmonary hypertension. The disease involves endothelial injury and fibroblast activation rather than immune complex deposition alone. Which disease fits best?
questions.explanation: Systemic sclerosis is marked by vasculopathy and progressive fibrosis of skin and organs.

questions.prompt: The most specific antibody for SLE among common tests is:
questions.explanation: Anti-Sm is highly specific, though not very sensitive, for SLE.

questions.prompt: Sjögren syndrome primarily affects:
questions.explanation: Autoimmune destruction of exocrine glands causes dry eyes and dry mouth.

questions.prompt: Anti-dsDNA antibodies in SLE correlate especially with:
questions.explanation: Anti-dsDNA immune complexes are associated with renal involvement.

questions.prompt: Libman-Sacks endocarditis in SLE is characterized by:
options: Sterile vegetations on either side of valve leaflets
questions.answer: Sterile vegetations on either side of valve leaflets
questions.explanation: SLE can cause sterile verrucous endocarditis.

questions.prompt: Sjögren syndrome increases risk of:
questions.explanation: Chronic B-cell stimulation in Sjögren syndrome predisposes to MALT-type lymphoma.

questions.prompt: Systemic sclerosis is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Scleroderma combines vascular injury, immune activation, and collagen deposition.

questions.prompt: A woman has photosensitive malar rash, arthritis, low complement, and proteinuria. Renal biopsy shows granular deposits of IgG and complement in glomeruli. Which mechanism best explains the nephritis?
options: Type III immune complex disease due to anti-nuclear antibodies
questions.answer: Type III immune complex disease due to anti-nuclear antibodies
questions.explanation: SLE nephritis is largely immune complex-mediated, producing granular deposits.

questions.prompt: A patient has dry eyes, dry mouth, parotid enlargement, anti-SSA antibodies, and a monoclonal B-cell proliferation in salivary tissue. Which long-term complication is most directly linked to the chronic autoimmune process?
questions.explanation: Sjögren syndrome may evolve into extranodal marginal zone lymphoma from chronic B-cell activation.

questions.prompt: The major barrier to organ transplantation is mismatch in:
questions.explanation: HLA polymorphism is the main determinant of graft recognition.

questions.prompt: After bone marrow transplantation, a recipient develops rash, jaundice, diarrhea, and mucosal ulceration. The graft contains mature donor T cells, and the recipient is immunosuppressed. Which immunologic event is central?
options: Recipient IgE against donor mast cells
Preformed recipient antibodies to kidney endothelium
Donor T cells reacting against recipient antigens
questions.answer: Donor T cells reacting against recipient antigens
questions.explanation: GVHD occurs when donor T cells recognize host alloantigens.

questions.prompt: Hyperacute rejection is usually mediated by:
questions.explanation: Preexisting antibodies cause immediate endothelial injury and thrombosis.

questions.prompt: Graft-versus-host disease occurs when:
options: Donor T cells attack recipient tissues
Recipient antibodies attack donor RBCs only
questions.answer: Donor T cells attack recipient tissues
questions.explanation: Immunocompetent donor T cells react against host antigens.

questions.prompt: Acute cellular rejection is mediated mainly by:
questions.explanation: Recipient T cells attack graft parenchyma and vessels.

questions.prompt: Acute antibody-mediated rejection primarily targets:
questions.explanation: Antibodies to donor antigens injure graft vessels through complement and inflammation.

questions.prompt: Chronic rejection is characterized by:
options: Progressive vascular narrowing and interstitial fibrosis
questions.answer: Progressive vascular narrowing and interstitial fibrosis
questions.explanation: Chronic rejection causes graft ischemia and fibrosis over months to years.

questions.prompt: Direct allorecognition means recipient T cells recognize:
options: Intact donor MHC molecules on donor APCs
Only donor peptides on recipient MHC
questions.answer: Intact donor MHC molecules on donor APCs
questions.explanation: Direct recognition is a strong T-cell response to foreign MHC itself.

questions.prompt: Minutes after kidney transplantation, the graft becomes cyanotic and fails to perfuse. Histology shows neutrophils, fibrin thrombi, and endothelial injury. The recipient had circulating antibodies against donor blood group/HLA antigens. What is the rejection pattern?
questions.explanation: Preformed antibodies cause immediate complement-mediated vascular thrombosis.

questions.prompt: Months after transplant, a patient develops gradual renal graft dysfunction. Biopsy shows intimal smooth muscle proliferation, luminal narrowing, tubular atrophy, and interstitial fibrosis. There is no sudden thrombosed graft. Which process is most likely?
questions.explanation: Chronic rejection is dominated by vascular occlusion and fibrosis.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms

questions.explanation: Metastasis is unequivocal evidence of malignancy in solid tumors.

questions.prompt: Differentiation refers to:

questions.answer: Resemblance of tumor cells to normal cells of origin

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: Anaplasia means:
questions.explanation: Anaplasia is a hallmark of many malignant tumors.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: Carcinoma in situ means malignant epithelial cells:

questions.prompt: Dysplasia is most often recognized by:

Disordered epithelial growth with pleomorphism and architectural loss

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: Benign tumors usually grow by:

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: Which feature favors malignancy over benignity?
options: Tumor giant cells with abnormal mitoses
questions.answer: Tumor giant cells with abnormal mitoses
questions.explanation: Marked pleomorphism and atypical mitoses suggest anaplasia and malignancy.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: A cervical biopsy shows full-thickness epithelial atypia, loss of maturation, hyperchromatic nuclei, and mitoses above the basal layer. The basement membrane is intact, and no stromal invasion is identified. Which diagnosis best matches these findings?
questions.explanation: Full-thickness dysplasia without basement membrane invasion is carcinoma in situ.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: A smoker’s bronchial biopsy shows replacement of ciliated columnar epithelium by squamous epithelium. A later biopsy shows pleomorphic basal-like cells and abnormal mitoses, but no invasion. Which sequence best describes the progression?
options: Metaplasia to dysplasia to carcinoma in situ
questions.answer: Metaplasia to dysplasia to carcinoma in situ
questions.explanation: Chronic injury can cause metaplasia, then dysplasia, then preinvasive carcinoma.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Tumor grade is based mainly on:
options: Degree of differentiation and mitotic activity
questions.answer: Degree of differentiation and mitotic activity
questions.explanation: Grade estimates biologic aggressiveness from histology.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: A man with pancreatic carcinoma loses marked weight despite adequate caloric intake and no mechanical obstruction. He has muscle wasting, anorexia, and elevated inflammatory mediators. Which mechanism best explains this systemic effect?
options: Cancer cachexia mediated by cytokines and metabolic changes

questions.explanation: Cachexia is a cytokine-driven wasting syndrome not fully reversed by nutrition.

questions.prompt: Tumor stage is based mainly on:

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: For most solid tumors, prognosis correlates better with:
questions.explanation: Anatomic extent is usually more prognostically important than grade.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Cachexia in cancer is driven partly by:
questions.explanation: Cancer cachexia involves systemic inflammation and metabolic wasting.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Paraneoplastic syndromes are symptoms caused by:
options: Only direct compression by tumor mass
Hormone-like or immune effects not explained by local tumor spread
questions.answer: Hormone-like or immune effects not explained by local tumor spread
questions.explanation: Paraneoplastic syndromes are remote effects of cancer.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: A classic paraneoplastic endocrine syndrome in small cell lung carcinoma is:

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: A definitive cancer diagnosis most often requires:
questions.explanation: Tissue diagnosis remains central to tumor classification.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: A colon cancer invades through muscularis propria and has metastases in regional lymph nodes but no distant metastasis. Another colon cancer is poorly differentiated but confined to mucosa. Which parameter usually has greater prognostic weight?
options: Presence of a capsule in all cancers

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: A patient with lung cancer develops hypercalcemia, but imaging shows no bone metastases. Laboratory testing reveals tumor production of a parathyroid hormone-related peptide. Which clinical category best explains this finding?

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: Defective DNA repair predisposes to cancer by causing:

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: Mismatch repair defects are associated with:
questions.explanation: Mismatch repair loss causes length changes in microsatellite repeats.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: BRCA1 and BRCA2 participate in repair of:
options: Double-strand DNA breaks by homologous recombination
questions.answer: Double-strand DNA breaks by homologous recombination
questions.explanation: BRCA proteins help high-fidelity double-strand break repair.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: Lynch syndrome is caused by germline defects in:
questions.explanation: Inherited mismatch repair defects predispose to colon and endometrial cancers.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from defective:
questions.explanation: XP impairs repair of UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: Microsatellite instability is most useful as a marker of:
questions.explanation: MSI reflects insertion/deletion errors at short repeats due to MMR loss.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: Cancers with high mutation burdens may be more responsive to immune checkpoint blockade because they:
questions.explanation: More mutations can create tumor-specific peptides recognized by T cells.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: A young patient develops colon cancer, and tumor testing shows loss of MLH1/MSH2 function with length variation in multiple microsatellite markers. The tumor has numerous frameshift mutations in growth-regulatory genes. Which inherited syndrome is most likely?
questions.explanation: Lynch syndrome is caused by germline mismatch repair defects and MSI.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: A child develops multiple skin cancers on sun-exposed areas, severe photosensitivity, and inability to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. The underlying defect lies in excising bulky helix-distorting lesions. Which repair pathway is abnormal?
questions.explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum involves nucleotide excision repair defects.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: Cancer is fundamentally caused by:
options: Genetic and epigenetic alterations in a cell clone
questions.answer: Genetic and epigenetic alterations in a cell clone
questions.explanation: Neoplasms arise from heritable changes that confer growth and survival advantages.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: A small carcinoma remains clinically dormant until a clone emerges that secretes VEGF, degrades basement membrane, and survives in blood. The new clone expands because it has a selective advantage within the tumor. What process best explains this evolution?
questions.explanation: Tumors evolve by selection of subclones with advantageous mutations.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: Driver mutations are mutations that:
