questions.prompt: Bioavailability refers to the fraction of administered drug that
questions.explanation: Bioavailability determines the amount of active drug reaching systemic circulation.

questions.prompt: First-pass metabolism most strongly reduces bioavailability after
questions.explanation: Orally absorbed drugs pass through gut wall and liver before systemic circulation.

questions.prompt: An elderly patient develops digoxin toxicity after dehydration and acute kidney injury. The main pharmacokinetic reason is
options: Reduced renal clearance increases drug accumulation
questions.answer: Reduced renal clearance increases drug accumulation
questions.explanation: Digoxin is substantially renally cleared, so AKI raises serum levels and toxicity risk.

questions.prompt: Volume of distribution is increased when a drug
options: Leaves plasma extensively and distributes into tissues
questions.answer: Leaves plasma extensively and distributes into tissues
questions.explanation: Large apparent volume of distribution reflects extensive tissue binding or partitioning.

questions.prompt: The loading dose of a drug is mainly determined by
options: Target concentration and volume of distribution
questions.answer: Target concentration and volume of distribution
questions.explanation: Loading dose quickly fills the apparent distribution space to achieve a target level.

questions.prompt: Maintenance dose is most directly related to
options: Drug clearance and target steady-state concentration
questions.answer: Drug clearance and target steady-state concentration
questions.explanation: Maintenance dosing replaces drug removed per unit time.

questions.prompt: A patient receiving vancomycin has rising trough levels after creatinine doubles. The best response is to
options: Extend the dosing interval or reduce dose based on renal function and levels
Give larger doses because infection is severe
questions.answer: Extend the dosing interval or reduce dose based on renal function and levels
questions.explanation: Renally cleared drugs need dose adjustment and monitoring when kidney function worsens.

questions.prompt: Steady state is usually reached after about
questions.explanation: Repeated dosing approaches steady state over several elimination half-lives.

questions.prompt: A drug with zero-order elimination has
options: A constant amount eliminated per unit time
A constant fraction eliminated per unit time
Elimination independent of dose at all concentrations
questions.answer: A constant amount eliminated per unit time
questions.explanation: Zero-order kinetics occur when elimination pathways are saturated.

questions.prompt: A patient on phenytoin has disproportionate toxicity after a small dose increase. The explanation is
options: Saturable metabolism causing nonlinear rise in concentration
questions.answer: Saturable metabolism causing nonlinear rise in concentration
questions.explanation: Phenytoin can show capacity-limited metabolism, so small dose changes may sharply raise levels.

questions.prompt: Potency refers to the
options: Dose or concentration needed to produce a given effect
Maximum effect a drug can produce
questions.answer: Dose or concentration needed to produce a given effect
questions.explanation: Potency compares how much drug is required for an effect.

questions.prompt: Efficacy refers to the
options: Maximum effect achievable by a drug
questions.answer: Maximum effect achievable by a drug
questions.explanation: Efficacy reflects maximal response, independent of dose needed to reach it.

questions.prompt: A patient taking nitrates for angina develops severe hypotension after sildenafil. The mechanism is
questions.explanation: PDE-5 inhibitors amplify nitrate-mediated vasodilation and can cause dangerous hypotension.

questions.prompt: A competitive antagonist shifts an agonist dose-response curve
options: To the right with preserved maximum response if enough agonist is present
questions.answer: To the right with preserved maximum response if enough agonist is present
questions.explanation: Surmountable competitive antagonism reduces apparent potency but not maximal effect.

questions.prompt: A partial agonist has lower intrinsic activity than a full agonist and can
options: Antagonize a full agonist in the same receptor system
questions.answer: Antagonize a full agonist in the same receptor system
questions.explanation: Partial agonists occupy receptors but produce submaximal activation.

questions.prompt: Idiosyncratic drug reactions are usually
options: Unpredictable reactions not explained by usual pharmacologic action
questions.answer: Unpredictable reactions not explained by usual pharmacologic action
questions.explanation: Idiosyncratic reactions are uncommon and patient-specific.

questions.prompt: A patient on warfarin starts trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and presents with high INR and bleeding. The interaction is best described as
options: Reduced warfarin metabolism and increased anticoagulant effect
questions.answer: Reduced warfarin metabolism and increased anticoagulant effect
questions.explanation: Several antibiotics inhibit warfarin metabolism or alter vitamin K balance, raising INR.

questions.prompt: Therapeutic index compares
questions.explanation: A narrow therapeutic index means small concentration changes can cause toxicity.

questions.prompt: A type A adverse drug reaction is generally
questions.explanation: Type A reactions are augmented pharmacologic effects and often dose dependent.

questions.prompt: A patient develops urticaria, wheeze and hypotension minutes after penicillin injection. The reaction is
questions.explanation: Rapid multisystem allergic reaction after exposure is anaphylaxis and needs immediate treatment.

questions.prompt: Rational prescribing begins with
options: Defining the therapeutic objective and choosing the safest effective option
questions.answer: Defining the therapeutic objective and choosing the safest effective option
questions.explanation: Good prescribing links diagnosis, treatment goal, patient factors and evidence.

questions.prompt: Medication reconciliation is important because it
options: Detects omissions, duplications, interactions and incorrect doses across care transitions
questions.answer: Detects omissions, duplications, interactions and incorrect doses across care transitions
questions.explanation: Transitions of care are high-risk times for medication errors.

questions.prompt: An older patient is admitted with confusion after starting a sedating antihistamine. The best interpretation is
options: Anticholinergic adverse effect is more likely in older adults
questions.answer: Anticholinergic adverse effect is more likely in older adults
questions.explanation: Older adults are vulnerable to anticholinergic delirium, urinary retention and falls.

questions.prompt: Prescribing in pregnancy should consider
options: Gestational age, fetal risk, maternal benefit and safer alternatives
That all drugs are harmless after implantation
That no treatment is ever allowed
questions.answer: Gestational age, fetal risk, maternal benefit and safer alternatives
questions.explanation: Risk-benefit assessment changes with trimester and disease severity.

questions.prompt: Teratogenic risk is greatest for many structural malformations during
questions.explanation: Major organ formation occurs early in pregnancy.

questions.prompt: A pregnant patient has severe hypertension. The safest prescribing principle is to
options: Treat maternal disease with agents known to be safer in pregnancy
Stop all antihypertensives regardless of BP
questions.answer: Treat maternal disease with agents known to be safer in pregnancy
questions.explanation: Untreated severe maternal hypertension is dangerous, but drug choice must avoid known fetal harm.

questions.prompt: In liver disease, drug toxicity may increase because of impaired
options: Metabolism, protein synthesis and biliary excretion
questions.answer: Metabolism, protein synthesis and biliary excretion
questions.explanation: Hepatic dysfunction alters clearance and free drug concentration.

questions.prompt: Polypharmacy is clinically important because it increases
options: Drug interactions, adverse effects and prescribing cascades
questions.answer: Drug interactions, adverse effects and prescribing cascades
questions.explanation: More medicines create more opportunities for harm and interactions.

questions.prompt: A patient has persistent cough after starting enalapril for hypertension. The appropriate change is
options: Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker if RAAS blockade is still desired
Ignore because drug cough is impossible
questions.answer: Switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker if RAAS blockade is still desired
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitor cough often resolves after stopping the ACE inhibitor; ARBs avoid bradykinin accumulation.

questions.prompt: When stopping long-term glucocorticoids, tapering is needed mainly to prevent
questions.explanation: Chronic steroids suppress endogenous cortisol production, so abrupt withdrawal can be dangerous.

questions.prompt: K x-ray fluorescence instruments measure lead levels in bone, which reflect
options: Only exposure in the last hour
questions.explanation: Chapter 449 states that KXRF measures bone lead, reflecting cumulative exposure over many years, unlike blood lead which mostly reflects recent exposure.

questions.prompt: Blood lead levels mostly reflect
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 contrasts blood lead as mainly recent exposure with bone lead as cumulative exposure.

questions.prompt: Serious cadmium poisoning in Japan caused itai-itai disease, named for painful
questions.explanation: Chapter 449 describes itai-itai disease as cadmium-induced bone toxicity leading to painful fractures.

questions.prompt: A patient from a mining-contaminated region has severe bone pain, fractures and renal calciuric effects after food and water exposure. Which metal is most likely?
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 links cadmium contamination of food and water with bone toxicity, fractures and renal calciuric effects.

questions.prompt: A chronically exposed patient develops increased risk of coronary heart disease, stroke and lung function impairment. Which heavy metal exposure fits Medicine 1?
questions.explanation: The heavy metal chapter lists arsenic exposure associations including coronary heart disease, stroke and lung function impairment.

questions.prompt: Thallium is absorbed by ingestion, inhalation and through the
questions.explanation: Chapter 449 states that thallium is absorbed through the skin as well as by ingestion and inhalation.

questions.prompt: Severe thallium poisoning follows a single ingested dose greater than 1 g or greater than
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 gives severe poisoning thresholds of >1 g or >8 mg/kg.

questions.prompt: A patient with suspected acute thallium ingestion presents within 4-6 hours. Induced emesis or gastric lavage may be indicated, and which oral agent prevents absorption?
questions.explanation: Chapter 449 states Prussian blue prevents thallium absorption and is given orally.

questions.prompt: Unlike many other metal poisonings, thallium poisoning may be less severe when activated charcoal interrupts
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 notes activated charcoal may reduce thallium severity by interrupting enterohepatic circulation.

questions.prompt: A poisoned patient has nausea, abdominal pain, hematemesis followed by confusion, psychosis and coma after radiopaque metal ingestion. Which poisoning fits best?
questions.explanation: Chapter 449 describes thallium poisoning with early GI symptoms followed by neuropsychiatric findings and notes thallium is radiopaque.

questions.prompt: Medicine 1 table 450-1 classifies poisoning physiologic states as stimulated, depressed, discordant and
questions.explanation: The poisoning differential table organizes poisonings by physiologic state including normal.

questions.prompt: AGMA-inducing poisonings in table 450-1 include ethylene glycol, methanol, iron and
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 lists alcohol ketoacidosis, ethylene glycol, iron, methanol, other alcohols, salicylate and toluene as AGMA inducers.

questions.prompt: Fundamental poisoning management begins with supportive care including airway protection, oxygenation and
questions.explanation: Table 450-3 includes airway protection, oxygenation/ventilation, treatment of arrhythmias and hemodynamic support.

questions.prompt: During the pretoxic phase before symptoms begin, the highest treatment priority is
questions.explanation: Chapter 450 states that before onset of poisoning, decontamination is the highest priority and treatment is based on history.

questions.prompt: A patient arrives soon after a potentially lethal ingestion but is not yet symptomatic. Which intervention goal has highest priority in this pretoxic phase?
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 emphasizes decontamination to prevent absorption during the pretoxic phase.

questions.prompt: Activated charcoal is the preferred gastrointestinal decontamination method in most situations because it has comparable or greater efficacy and fewer
questions.explanation: Chapter 450 states charcoal is preferred over ipecac or gastric lavage because of efficacy and fewer contraindications and complications.

questions.prompt: The generally recommended activated charcoal dose is
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 gives 1 g/kg as the generally recommended activated charcoal dose.

questions.prompt: Activated charcoal is not recommended after corrosive ingestion because it obscures
questions.explanation: Chapter 450 notes charcoal is not recommended for corrosives because it obscures endoscopy.

questions.prompt: A cyclic antidepressant overdose causes ventricular tachydysrhythmias with QRS prolongation. Specific treatment is hypertonic sodium
questions.explanation: Table 450-4 recommends hypertonic sodium bicarbonate or saline for ventricular tachydysrhythmias with QRS prolongation in cyclic antidepressant poisoning.

questions.prompt: A patient on SSRI and tramadol develops agitation, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, diarrhea, fever and tachycardia. Severe cases may benefit from
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 describes serotonin syndrome and notes cyproheptadine may help severe cases after stopping offending agents.

questions.prompt: The most important prehospital care for venomous snakebite is rapid transport to a facility with supportive care and
questions.explanation: Chapter 451 states rapid transport to a facility equipped for ABC support and antivenom is the most important prehospital care.

questions.prompt: After snakebite, jewelry or tight clothing near the bite should be removed to avoid constriction from anticipated
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 advises removing jewelry and tight clothing because swelling is anticipated.

questions.prompt: Incising and applying suction to a snakebite should be avoided because these measures worsen local tissue damage and increase
questions.explanation: Chapter 451 states incision/suction exacerbate tissue damage, increase infection risk and are not effective.

questions.prompt: A hiker is bitten by a pit viper. Friends want to cut and suction the wound. The best advice is
options: Avoid incision and suction and arrange rapid transport
questions.answer: Avoid incision and suction and arrange rapid transport
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 discourages incision/suction and prioritizes rapid transport for snakebite care.

questions.prompt: In U.S. and Canadian venomous snakebite management, prophylactic antibiotics are unnecessary unless prehospital care included incision or
questions.explanation: Table 451-1 states prophylactic antibiotics are unnecessary unless incision or mouth suction was used.

questions.prompt: A snakebite victim has severe pain but evolving coagulopathy is a concern. Medicine 1 advises avoiding salicylates/NSAIDs and using acetaminophen and/or
questions.explanation: The management table recommends acetaminophen and/or opioids while avoiding salicylates and NSAIDs.

questions.prompt: Scombroid poisoning symptoms usually develop within
questions.explanation: Chapter 451 states symptoms of scombroid poisoning develop within 15-90 minutes after ingestion.

questions.prompt: A patient develops flushing, tingling of lips, nausea and abdominal discomfort 30 minutes after eating unrefrigerated tuna. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 describes scombroid poisoning after dark/red-fleshed fish with symptoms beginning 15-90 minutes after ingestion.

questions.prompt: Tick paralysis usually begins with symmetric lower-extremity weakness about how long after tick attachment?
questions.explanation: Chapter 452 states weakness begins symmetrically in the lower extremities 6 days after tick attachment.

questions.prompt: A child has ascending symmetric weakness, absent reflexes, normal sensation and normal lumbar puncture; a tick is found in the scalp. The key treatment is
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 states diagnosis depends on finding the tick and removal generally leads to rapid improvement.

questions.prompt: The central obligation of the physician-patient relationship is to
options: Place the patient's welfare and informed choices at the center of care
Follow family preferences over patient preferences
questions.answer: Place the patient's welfare and informed choices at the center of care
questions.explanation: Professional care combines beneficence, respect for autonomy and honest communication.

questions.prompt: A complete clinical encounter should integrate disease diagnosis with assessment of
options: The patient's illness experience, values and functional context
questions.answer: The patient's illness experience, values and functional context
questions.explanation: Good medicine treats the patient who has the disease, not only the disease label.

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old with heart failure says she cannot take diuretics because she fears being unable to travel for work. The best next step is to
options: Explore her goals and barriers before revising the treatment plan
Document noncompliance and end the visit
Ask the family to decide for her
questions.answer: Explore her goals and barriers before revising the treatment plan
questions.explanation: Adherence improves when the plan fits the patient's life and concerns.

questions.prompt: Shared decision-making is most important when
options: More than one medically reasonable option exists with different trade-offs
The patient is unconscious without a surrogate
A laboratory value is being transcribed
questions.answer: More than one medically reasonable option exists with different trade-offs
questions.explanation: Preference-sensitive decisions require clear explanation of risks, benefits and alternatives.

questions.prompt: The most useful opening question in history taking is usually one that
options: Allows the patient to describe the problem in their own words
Immediately narrows to a yes-or-no symptom
questions.answer: Allows the patient to describe the problem in their own words
questions.explanation: An open beginning reveals symptoms, sequence and concerns that closed questions can miss.

questions.prompt: A patient with newly diagnosed cancer asks, 'Am I going to die soon?' The best response is to
options: Acknowledge the fear and ask what they understand before giving clear information
Say there is nothing to worry about
Change the subject to chemotherapy protocols
Give survival statistics without checking readiness
questions.answer: Acknowledge the fear and ask what they understand before giving clear information
questions.explanation: Serious conversations need empathy, assessment of understanding and honest information.

questions.prompt: The main reason to summarize the patient's story back to them is to
options: Confirm accuracy and show that their concerns were heard
questions.answer: Confirm accuracy and show that their concerns were heard
questions.explanation: Reflection catches errors and strengthens therapeutic alliance.

questions.prompt: In chronic disease care, the physician's role includes helping the patient to
options: Develop self-management skills and realistic goals
questions.answer: Develop self-management skills and realistic goals
questions.explanation: Long-term outcomes depend heavily on informed patient participation.

questions.prompt: A patient repeatedly misses diabetes visits because clinic timing conflicts with daily wages. The most patient-centered response is to
options: Identify practical access barriers and arrange a feasible follow-up plan
Dismiss the patient from care immediately
questions.answer: Identify practical access barriers and arrange a feasible follow-up plan
questions.explanation: Social and logistical barriers must be addressed as part of clinical care.

questions.prompt: A hospitalized patient refuses a recommended procedure after understanding the risks. The physician should
options: Respect the informed refusal and discuss alternative management
Proceed because the doctor knows best
Hide the refusal from the chart
questions.answer: Respect the informed refusal and discuss alternative management
questions.explanation: Capacitous patients may refuse treatment even when refusal increases risk.

questions.prompt: A diagnostic hypothesis should be revised most strongly when
options: New findings are inconsistent with the working diagnosis
questions.answer: New findings are inconsistent with the working diagnosis
questions.explanation: Sound reasoning updates probability as new evidence arrives.

questions.prompt: Premature closure in diagnosis means
options: Accepting a diagnosis before adequate consideration of alternatives
questions.answer: Accepting a diagnosis before adequate consideration of alternatives
questions.explanation: Premature closure is a common cognitive error leading to missed diagnoses.

questions.prompt: A 55-year-old with chest discomfort is diagnosed as gastritis without ECG despite diaphoresis and risk factors. The reasoning error is most likely
questions.explanation: Stopping at a benign explanation before excluding dangerous alternatives is premature closure.

questions.prompt: The pretest probability of disease is mainly estimated from
options: Clinical context, history, examination and disease prevalence
questions.answer: Clinical context, history, examination and disease prevalence
questions.explanation: Test interpretation depends on probability before the test is ordered.

questions.prompt: A highly sensitive test is most useful for
options: Ruling out disease when the result is negative
questions.answer: Ruling out disease when the result is negative
questions.explanation: Sensitive tests have few false negatives, so a negative result reduces probability.

questions.prompt: A highly specific test is most useful for
options: Ruling in disease when the result is positive
questions.answer: Ruling in disease when the result is positive
questions.explanation: Specific tests have few false positives, so a positive result is persuasive.

questions.prompt: A low-risk patient requests a whole-body scan. The best explanation against indiscriminate testing is that it
options: May produce false positives and downstream harm without likely benefit
questions.answer: May produce false positives and downstream harm without likely benefit
questions.explanation: Testing low-probability populations can cause overdiagnosis, anxiety and invasive follow-up.

questions.prompt: A D-dimer is negative in a patient with low clinical probability of pulmonary embolism. The appropriate interpretation is
options: CT pulmonary angiography is mandatory for all patients
questions.explanation: A sensitive D-dimer helps exclude PE in low-probability patients.

questions.prompt: Bayesian reasoning in clinical diagnosis means that
options: Test results are interpreted by how much they change prior probability
Every disease is considered equally likely
One positive test always proves disease
questions.answer: Test results are interpreted by how much they change prior probability
questions.explanation: Likelihood ratios modify the probability estimated before testing.

questions.prompt: A patient has recurrent syncope. The physician documents arrhythmia, seizure, orthostatic hypotension and structural heart disease before testing. This is an example of
questions.explanation: A differential organizes plausible causes and guides targeted evaluation.

questions.prompt: Valid informed consent requires disclosure, voluntariness and
options: A relative's signature in every case
questions.explanation: Consent is valid only when a capable patient understands and freely chooses.

questions.prompt: Decision-making capacity is task-specific and includes the ability to
options: Understand, appreciate, reason about options and communicate a choice
questions.answer: Understand, appreciate, reason about options and communicate a choice
questions.explanation: Capacity concerns the decision at hand, not a global label.

questions.prompt: A confused patient with sepsis refuses antibiotics but cannot explain the consequences. The physician should first
options: Assess and treat reversible causes of impaired capacity while seeking surrogate input
Accept the refusal as fully informed
questions.answer: Assess and treat reversible causes of impaired capacity while seeking surrogate input
questions.explanation: Delirium can impair capacity and urgent care may require surrogate or emergency standards.

questions.prompt: Confidentiality may be breached without consent when
options: There is a serious, legally recognized risk to others or mandatory reporting requirement
questions.answer: There is a serious, legally recognized risk to others or mandatory reporting requirement
questions.explanation: Confidentiality is strong but not absolute when law or serious preventable harm applies.

questions.prompt: The ethical principle of autonomy primarily protects the patient's right to
options: Make informed decisions about their own body and care
questions.answer: Make informed decisions about their own body and care
questions.explanation: Autonomy requires respect for informed choices within professional and legal limits.

questions.prompt: A patient with tuberculosis refuses isolation and plans to travel in a crowded bus. The physician's duty includes
options: Taking public health steps to prevent serious transmission
Keeping the plan secret under all circumstances
Calling relatives before notifying health authorities
questions.answer: Taking public health steps to prevent serious transmission
questions.explanation: Contagious diseases can create duties to protect others through lawful public health action.

questions.prompt: Medical paternalism is least justified when
options: A capable patient has made an informed preference-sensitive decision
Immediate emergency care is needed and no surrogate is available
questions.answer: A capable patient has made an informed preference-sensitive decision
questions.explanation: Capable informed patients should not be overruled merely because the clinician disagrees.

questions.prompt: Truth telling in medicine is best understood as
options: Clear, compassionate disclosure adjusted to the patient's readiness and preferences
questions.answer: Clear, compassionate disclosure adjusted to the patient's readiness and preferences
questions.explanation: Honesty and compassion are both required in difficult conversations.

questions.prompt: A family asks the doctor not to tell a competent patient about metastatic cancer. The best response is to
options: Ask the patient how much information they want and whom they want involved
Tell the family to leave permanently
questions.answer: Ask the patient how much information they want and whom they want involved
questions.explanation: The patient controls information preferences if they have capacity.

questions.prompt: A medical student wants to post a de-identified rare case with enough details for recognition. The correct action is to
options: Avoid posting unless proper consent and institutional rules are satisfied
Post if the name is removed
Post only in a private social media group
Change the patient's age by one year
questions.answer: Avoid posting unless proper consent and institutional rules are satisfied
questions.explanation: Confidentiality can be breached even without names if details identify the patient.

questions.explanation: Most safety improvement comes from better systems, not individual blame alone.

questions.prompt: A near miss is important because it
options: Reveals a hazard before patient harm occurs

options: Reported and analyzed as a near miss
Handled only by scolding the prescriber
questions.answer: Reported and analyzed as a near miss
questions.explanation: Learning from intercepted errors improves future safety.

questions.prompt: Root cause analysis is used after serious adverse events to
options: Identify contributory system factors and prevention strategies
questions.answer: Identify contributory system factors and prevention strategies
questions.explanation: RCA looks beyond the final act to conditions that allowed harm.

questions.prompt: The safest handoff communication is one that
options: Uses structured, concise transfer of diagnosis, status, risks and pending tasks
questions.answer: Uses structured, concise transfer of diagnosis, status, risks and pending tasks
questions.explanation: Structured handoffs reduce omissions during transitions of care.

questions.topic: Quality, Safety and Systems of Care
questions.topicTitle: Quality, Safety and Systems of Care
questions.prompt: A postoperative patient deteriorates overnight after abnormal vitals were not escalated during shift change. The best quality intervention is
options: Create a reliable escalation and handoff process for abnormal vital signs
Tell staff to be more careful only
questions.answer: Create a reliable escalation and handoff process for abnormal vital signs
questions.explanation: A dependable trigger and communication process addresses the system failure.

questions.topic: Quality, Safety and Systems of Care
questions.topicTitle: Quality, Safety and Systems of Care
questions.prompt: Clinical practice guidelines are best used as
options: Evidence-based aids adapted to the individual patient's context
questions.answer: Evidence-based aids adapted to the individual patient's context
questions.explanation: Guidelines support but do not replace individualized clinical reasoning.

questions.topic: Quality, Safety and Systems of Care
questions.topicTitle: Quality, Safety and Systems of Care
questions.prompt: Checklists improve safety mainly by
options: Reducing omission of critical steps in complex workflows
Increasing paperwork for its own sake
questions.answer: Reducing omission of critical steps in complex workflows
questions.explanation: Checklists protect against predictable memory and coordination failures.

questions.topic: Quality, Safety and Systems of Care
questions.topicTitle: Quality, Safety and Systems of Care
questions.prompt: A central line team uses full barrier precautions and a checklist, then infection rates fall. This improvement targets
questions.explanation: Insertion bundles reduce catheter-related bloodstream infections.

questions.prompt: Open disclosure after a harmful medical error should include
options: Honest explanation, apology where appropriate and steps to reduce future harm
questions.answer: Honest explanation, apology where appropriate and steps to reduce future harm
questions.explanation: Transparency maintains trust and supports learning after harm.

questions.prompt: Professionalism in medicine includes competence, integrity, accountability and
questions.explanation: Medicine is a social profession with duties beyond technical skill.

questions.prompt: Lifelong learning is essential because medical practice
options: Changes as evidence, technology and population needs evolve
questions.answer: Changes as evidence, technology and population needs evolve
questions.explanation: Continuing competence requires updating knowledge and skills.

questions.prompt: A physician realizes a new drug they commonly prescribe has important updated safety restrictions. The professional response is to
options: Review the evidence and adjust practice promptly
Ignore it until the next textbook edition
Delete patient messages about adverse effects
questions.answer: Review the evidence and adjust practice promptly
questions.explanation: Professional competence requires responding to credible new safety information.

questions.prompt: Conflict of interest is problematic because it can
options: Bias judgment or undermine trust even when no harm is intended
questions.answer: Bias judgment or undermine trust even when no harm is intended
questions.explanation: Financial and nonfinancial interests can influence decisions or perception.

questions.prompt: The best response to a pharmaceutical gift that may influence prescribing is to
options: Follow institutional policy and preserve independent clinical judgment
Accept it because all gifts are harmless
questions.answer: Follow institutional policy and preserve independent clinical judgment
questions.explanation: Managing conflicts protects trust and decision quality.

questions.prompt: A patient cannot afford the first-line medicine. Professional care requires the physician to
options: Discuss affordable effective alternatives and access options
Assume the patient will be nonadherent
questions.answer: Discuss affordable effective alternatives and access options
questions.explanation: Cost is a real determinant of treatment success and should be addressed.

questions.prompt: Cultural humility in clinical practice means
options: Eliciting the patient's beliefs and avoiding assumptions while providing evidence-based care
questions.answer: Eliciting the patient's beliefs and avoiding assumptions while providing evidence-based care
questions.explanation: Respectful care asks rather than assumes and still explains medical reasoning.

questions.prompt: A patient with limited English nods to a surgical consent discussion but cannot explain the operation. The best next step is
options: Use a trained medical interpreter and reassess understanding
Ask a child relative to translate complex risks
questions.answer: Use a trained medical interpreter and reassess understanding
questions.explanation: Language access is necessary for valid informed consent.

questions.prompt: Team-based care is important because complex illness often requires
options: Coordinated contributions from multiple health professionals
One physician making all decisions alone
questions.answer: Coordinated contributions from multiple health professionals
questions.explanation: Good outcomes depend on communication across disciplines and settings.

questions.prompt: A junior doctor is asked to perform a procedure they have never done unsupervised. The professional response is to
options: Seek supervision and disclose their level of experience
Ask the patient not to worry
Document it as completed by a senior
questions.answer: Seek supervision and disclose their level of experience
questions.explanation: Recognizing limits and seeking help protects the patient and supports learning.

questions.prompt: In Medicine 1 chapter 278, most respiratory diseases presenting with cough or dyspnea are grouped into obstructive, restrictive and which third major category?
options: Diseases limited to the upper airway
questions.explanation: Chapter 278 classifies common respiratory presentations into obstructive lung disease, restrictive disorders and pulmonary vascular abnormalities.

questions.prompt: Which group is listed as obstructive lung disease in the opening approach to respiratory disorders?
options: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, kyphoscoliosis and pleural effusion
Pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension and venoocclusive disease
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 names asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis and bronchiolitis as airway-predominant obstructive disorders.

questions.prompt: A patient with chronic cough and dyspnea is being evaluated. Which history is essential because it raises risk for COPD, bronchogenic lung cancer and some parenchymal lung diseases?
options: Current and previous cigarette smoking with pack-years
questions.answer: Current and previous cigarette smoking with pack-years
questions.explanation: Chapter 278 emphasizes asking all respiratory patients about cigarette smoking and quantifying pack-years.

questions.prompt: Which home exposure in chapter 278 is specifically relevant to hypersensitivity pneumonitis-type respiratory disease?
questions.explanation: The book lists home exposures such as pet bird excrement among inhalational exposures to explore.

questions.prompt: Initial chest imaging in many respiratory disorders generally begins with ultrasound or
options: A plain chest radiograph, preferably posteroanterior and lateral films
questions.answer: A plain chest radiograph, preferably posteroanterior and lateral films
questions.explanation: Chapter 278 recommends chest ultrasound or plain chest radiography as early imaging in most respiratory evaluations.

questions.prompt: A bedside ultrasound rapidly detects pneumothorax, pleural effusion and consolidation in an acutely dyspneic patient. This use is supported in which diagnostic chapter?
options: Approach to the Patient with Disease of the Respiratory System
questions.answer: Approach to the Patient with Disease of the Respiratory System
questions.explanation: Medicine 1 chapter 278 notes ultrasound can rapidly diagnose pneumothorax, pleural effusion and consolidation.

questions.prompt: During forced spirometry, which value is the amount of air exhaled in the first second?
questions.explanation: Chapter 280 defines FEV1 as the volume exhaled in the first second of the forced vital capacity maneuver.

questions.explanation: Medicine 1 describes FEV1/FVC as typically reduced in airflow obstruction, though severe air trapping may sometimes mask this.

questions.prompt: Retinal photocoagulation treats retinal tears by creating:

questions.prompt: Excimer laser reshapes the cornea using:

questions.prompt: LASIK corrects refractive error by applying excimer laser to the:

questions.prompt: Diode laser cyclophotocoagulation lowers IOP by damaging:

questions.prompt: Leukaemia may involve the fundus with:

questions.explanation: Night blindness and Bitot spots are classic xerophthalmia findings.

questions.prompt: Ishihara plates are used to test:

questions.prompt: Direct ophthalmoscopy gives a magnified view of the:

questions.prompt: Tonometry measures:
questions.explanation: Tonometry estimates IOP for glaucoma diagnosis and monitoring.

questions.prompt: Goldmann applanation tonometry is based on flattening a fixed area of:
questions.explanation: Applanation tonometry estimates pressure from the force needed to flatten the cornea.

questions.prompt: A patient has severe ocular pain, halos and cloudy cornea. Which practical measurement is urgent?
questions.explanation: Acute angle closure is confirmed by raised IOP and needs urgent treatment.

questions.prompt: Schiotz tonometer is an indentation tonometer affected by:

questions.prompt: A patient has watering with regurgitation from opposite punctum during syringing. This suggests:

questions.prompt: A patient has burning eyes and normal Schirmer wetting but tear film breaks up rapidly after blinking. The test evaluates:

questions.prompt: Keratometry measures:

questions.prompt: A cataract patient needs IOL power calculation. Which measurements are essential?
questions.explanation: Biometry combines corneal power and axial length to calculate IOL power.

questions.prompt: A-scan ultrasonography measures:

questions.prompt: B-scan ultrasonography is especially useful when:

questions.answer: Fundus view is obscured by opaque media

questions.prompt: Retinoscopy is an objective method for estimating:
questions.explanation: Retinoscopy observes reflex movement to determine refractive status.

questions.prompt: A child with suspected latent hypermetropia is examined after cycloplegic drops. This is done to:

questions.prompt: During subjective refraction, a patient with residual meridional blur is tested with a Jackson cross-cylinder. It is used for refining:
questions.explanation: JCC refines cylinder power and axis during subjective refraction.

questions.prompt: Trial frame and trial lenses are used during:
questions.explanation: Trial lenses help determine the correction giving best visual acuity.

questions.prompt: Cover-uncover test detects:
questions.explanation: Movement of the uncovered eye indicates manifest deviation.

questions.prompt: Alternate cover test reveals:

questions.prompt: A 46-year-old woman has painless cervical lymphadenopathy. A lymph-node biopsy shows closely packed follicles composed predominantly of small lymphocytes. Cytogenetic analysis demonstrates t(14;18), resulting in overexpression of BCL2. The affected lymphocytes survive substantially longer than normal germinal-center B cells. Which of the following events is most directly inhibited by the overexpressed protein in these cells?
options: Release of cytochrome c through the outer mitochondrial membrane
Cleavage of an inhibitor of caspase-activated DNase
Externalization of phosphatidylserine on the plasma membrane
Formation of a death-inducing signaling complex
questions.answer: Release of cytochrome c through the outer mitochondrial membrane
questions.explanation: BCL2 is an anti-apoptotic protein that preserves outer mitochondrial membrane integrity and prevents cytochrome c from entering the cytosol. The other options describe downstream execution events or components of the extrinsic death-receptor pathway.

questions.answer: Target hemoglobin of 7–8 g/dL (restrictive transfusion strategy)
questions.explanation: In acute variceal hemorrhage, a restrictive transfusion strategy targeting a hemoglobin of 7–8 g/dL is standard. Overzealous transfusion raises central venous pressure and portal venous pressure, dislodging fresh hemostatic clots at the variceal rupture site and significantly increasing re-bleeding rates and mortality.
tags: Metabolic Response, Shock and Fluid Balance
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 30-year-old male weighing 70 kg sustains full-thickness flame burns covering his entire anterior trunk, entire right upper limb, and anterior aspect of both lower limbs. According to Wallace's Rule of Nines, what is the total percentage of body surface area burned?
questions.explanation: According to Wallace's Rule of Nines: Anterior trunk = 18%; Entire right upper limb = 9%; Anterior aspect of both lower limbs = 9% each (18% total). Total Body Surface Area (TBSA) burned = 18 + 9 + 18 = 45%.
tags: Metabolic Response, Shock and Fluid Balance
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: For the 70-kg patient with 45% TBSA thermal burn, calculate the total fluid requirement in the first 24 hours using the Parkland formula, and determine the volume to be infused over the first 8 hours post-injury.
options: Total 6,300 mL; infuse 3,150 mL in the first 8 hours
Total 12,600 mL; infuse 6,300 mL in the first 8 hours
Total 15,400 mL; infuse 7,700 mL in the first 8 hours
Total 8,400 mL; infuse 4,200 mL in the first 8 hours
questions.answer: Total 12,600 mL; infuse 6,300 mL in the first 8 hours
questions.explanation: The Parkland formula dictates: 4 mL × Body weight in kg × % TBSA burn. Here: 4 mL × 70 kg × 45 = 12,600 mL of Ringer's lactate in the first 24 hours. Half of this total volume (6,300 mL) must be infused within the first 8 hours calculated from the exact time of burn injury, and the remaining half (6,300 mL) is infused over the subsequent 16 hours.
tags: Metabolic Response, Shock and Fluid Balance
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 40-year-old male sustains full-thickness circumferential burns to the right forearm. Four hours later, he complains of severe deep aching pain, paresthesias in the fingers, and progressive loss of radial pulse. Compartment pressures measure 38 mmHg. What is the urgent operative intervention?
options: Emergency bedside escharotomy along the mid-lateral and mid-medial lines
Application of tight compressive crepe bandaging
questions.answer: Emergency bedside escharotomy along the mid-lateral and mid-medial lines
questions.explanation: Circumferential full-thickness burns form an inelastic, rigid eschar. As post-burn tissue edema develops beneath the eschar, interstitial compartment pressures rise rapidly, impairing arteriolar flow and inducing compartment syndrome. Emergency escharotomy involves incising the full depth of the non-elastic burned dermis into subcutaneous fat along mid-axial neutral lines without breaching the deep muscular fascia.
tags: Metabolic Response, Shock and Fluid Balance
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which topical antimicrobial agent used in extensive thermal burns is known to penetrate thick eschar effectively, making it useful in infected burn wounds and auricular burns, but carries the specific adverse effect of severe burning pain and metabolic acidosis from carbonic anhydrase inhibition?
questions.explanation: Mafenide acetate diffuses rapidly through avascular eschar, making it effective for deep bacterial colonization, suppurative chondritis of the ear, and electrical burns. Its major limitation is inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in renal tubules, leading to alkaline diuresis, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, compensatory hyperventilation, and marked local application pain.
tags: Metabolic Response, Shock and Fluid Balance
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: An unhealed burn scar on the anterior aspect of the lower leg of 24 years duration develops a proliferative, non-healing ulcer with raised, everted, indurated borders and foul-smelling discharge. Punch biopsy reveals well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. What is the eponym for this malignancy?
questions.explanation: Marjolin's ulcer is a malignant transformation—classically aggressive squamous cell carcinoma (rarely basal cell carcinoma or melanoma)—arising in chronic, non-healing burn scars, chronic venous ulcers, or sinus tracts of chronic osteomyelitis. Characterized by dense, avascular fibrous scar tissue, it exhibits late regional lymph node metastasis, but once metastasis occurs, the prognosis is poor.
tags: Metabolic Response, Shock and Fluid Balance
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In Jackson's burn wound model of local thermal injury, which concentric zone represents tissue with reversible microvascular stasis that is salvageable with prompt and adequate fluid resuscitation?
questions.explanation: Jackson's burn wound model describes three concentric zones: 1. Zone of coagulation: innermost area of irreversible cellular death and protein denaturation; 2. Zone of stasis: middle zone of compromised perfusion, microvascular thrombosis, and stasis, which can either recover with optimal fluid resuscitation and wound care or progress to irreversible necrosis; 3. Zone of hyperemia: outermost zone of minimal injury and vasodilation that spontaneously recovers.

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old female presents with an unsightly, raised, erythematous, pruritic scar over her sternum 6 months after sternotomy. The lesion projects well beyond the original boundaries of the surgical incision and invades adjacent normal dermal margins. Histological examination shows thick, disorganized, hyalinized collagen bands. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Keloids characteristically extend beyond the confines of the original wound margin and invade surrounding normal tissue without spontaneous regression, occurring preferentially over presternal skin, deltoid, and ear lobes. Hypertrophic scars remain confined within the boundaries of the original incision, contain predominantly type III collagen parallel to the epidermis, and frequently regress over 1–2 years.

questions.prompt: A burn patient with extensive 50% TBSA burns on day 10 develops sudden epigastric pain, coffee-ground vomiting, and melena with dropping hemoglobin. Endoscopy reveals acute multiple superficial punctate ulcerations and mucosal erosions in the stomach and duodenum. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Curling's ulcer refers to acute stress ulceration of the gastric and duodenal mucosa arising as a severe complication of extensive thermal burn injury, mediated by splanchnic hypoperfusion, mucosal ischemia, and decreased mucosal barrier defenses. Cushing's ulcer, by contrast, is associated with elevated intracranial pressure or severe head trauma and is driven by vagal hyperstimulation causing gastric acid hypersecretion.

questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which phase of normal surgical wound healing is characterized by peak fibroblast proliferation, capillary endothelial sprouting, and conversion of type III collagen to robust type I collagen?
questions.explanation: The proliferative phase (days 4 to 21) encompasses angiogenesis, fibroplasia, granulation tissue formation, and epithelialization. Fibroblasts synthesize large quantities of ground substance and extracellular matrix (primarily type III collagen initially), laying the structural lattice for subsequent wound contraction and remodeling.

questions.prompt: An electrician suffers an entry electrical burn on his right hand and an exit wound on his right heel from a 11,000-volt power line. Despite minimal skin surface burns, his urine is dark reddish-brown. Urine dipstick is positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red blood cells. What is the urgent priority to prevent acute kidney injury?
options: Aggressive fluid resuscitation targeting urine output of 1.5–2 mL/kg/hr, urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate, and intravenous mannitol
Fluid restriction to 500 mL/day to avoid pulmonary edema
Immediate bilateral lower-extremity fasciotomy without intravenous fluids
questions.answer: Aggressive fluid resuscitation targeting urine output of 1.5–2 mL/kg/hr, urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate, and intravenous mannitol
questions.explanation: High-voltage electrical injury generates massive internal resistance heating and deep muscular necrosis, releasing myoglobin into the circulation. In acidic urine, myoglobin precipitates as ferrihemate casts, causing acute tubular necrosis. Management requires higher fluid rates targeting urine output of 1.5–2.0 mL/kg/hr (75–100 mL/hr in adults), intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize urine (pH > 6.5) to keep myoglobin soluble, and osmotic diuresis with mannitol.

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old agricultural laborer sustains a deep laceration on his thigh contaminated with soil. Forty-eight hours later, he presents with excruciating disproportionate pain, tachycardia out of proportion to fever, a thin watery brownish discharge with a sweetish foul odor, and palpable soft tissue crepitus. Gram stain demonstrates large Gram-positive bacilli devoid of polymorphonuclear leukocytes. What is the definitive diagnosis and primary surgical management?
options: Staphylococcal pyomyositis; aspiration and oral cephalexin
Clostridial gas gangrene (myonecrosis); emergency radical surgical debridement of all non-viable muscle, high-dose intravenous crystalline penicillin, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy
Erysipelas; oral erythromycin and warm compression
Streptococcal toxic shock; intravenous immunoglobulin without surgery
questions.answer: Clostridial gas gangrene (myonecrosis); emergency radical surgical debridement of all non-viable muscle, high-dose intravenous crystalline penicillin, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy
questions.explanation: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis, most commonly Clostridium perfringens) is a surgical emergency characterized by rapid spread, alpha-toxin (lecithinase) tissue destruction, gas production, and absence of inflammatory cells on smear. Emergency management hinges on radical debridement of dead muscle (which fails to contract, bleed, or exhibit normal turgor), high-dose crystalline penicillin G and clindamycin, and hyperbaric oxygen.

questions.prompt: According to the CDC surgical wound classification system, into which category is an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic cholelithiasis classified when there is controlled entry into the bile duct with no gross bile spillage?
questions.explanation: Clean-contaminated wounds (Class II) are operative wounds in which a hollow viscus (respiratory, alimentary, genital, or urinary tract) is entered under controlled conditions without unusual contamination or gross spillage. Elective cholecystectomy, gastric surgery, and appendectomy without perforation fall into this category.

questions.prompt: A 58-year-old diabetic male presents with scrotal swelling, severe perineal pain, high-grade fever, and marked toxemia. Examination reveals rapidly spreading blackened skin necrosis, extensive crepitus extending from the scrotum into the perineum and lower abdominal wall, with foul-smelling dishwater pus. What is the diagnosis and urgent course of action?
options: Fournier's gangrene; immediate wide surgical debridement of all necrotic fascia, broad-spectrum triple antibiotics, and resuscitation
Simple scrotal carbuncle; outpatient oral antibiotics and warm sits baths
Testicular torsion; immediate emergency unilateral orchidectomy
Strangulated inguinal hernia; immediate reduction by taxis
questions.answer: Fournier's gangrene; immediate wide surgical debridement of all necrotic fascia, broad-spectrum triple antibiotics, and resuscitation
questions.explanation: Fournier's gangrene is a necrotizing fasciitis of the perineal, genital, and perianal regions, typically polymicrobial (aerobic and anaerobic synergy) in immunocompromised or diabetic patients. It causes endarteritis obliterans of the subcutaneous vessels. Immediate intervention requires aggressive resuscitation, broad-spectrum coverage, and emergency radical surgical debridement back to healthy bleeding fascia.

questions.prompt: An unimmunized 35-year-old construction worker presents 8 days after stepping on a rusty nail with lockjaw (trismus), risus sardonicus, painful reflex muscular spasms triggered by acoustic and tactile stimuli, and opisthotonos. Sensorium is completely clear. What is the mechanism of action of the causative toxin?
options: Tetanospasmin retrogradely travels up motor axons to block the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (glycine and GABA) in the spinal cord and brainstem
Tetanolysin causes direct lysis of acetylcholine receptors at the motor endplate
Botulinum toxin prevents the presynaptic exocytosis of acetylcholine
Alpha toxin causes lecithinase-mediated cellular membrane disruption
questions.answer: Tetanospasmin retrogradely travels up motor axons to block the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (glycine and GABA) in the spinal cord and brainstem
questions.explanation: Clostridium tetani elaborates tetanospasmin, an exotoxin that enters motor neuron terminals and travels via retrograde intra-axonal transport to inhibitory interneurons (Renshaw cells) in the spinal cord and brainstem. There, it cleaves synaptobrevin, preventing the presynaptic release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), leading to unregulated, continuous excitatory motor discharge and reflex tetanic spasms.

questions.prompt: What is the optimal timing for the administration of single-dose intravenous prophylactic antibiotics prior to elective clean-contaminated abdominal surgery to achieve peak bactericidal tissue concentrations at the time of skin incision?
options: Within 30 to 60 minutes prior to surgical incision
24 hours prior to surgery in the ward
Immediately after the skin has been closed at the end of surgery
At induction followed by mandatory continuation for 5 postoperative days
questions.answer: Within 30 to 60 minutes prior to surgical incision
questions.explanation: Surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis is intended to establish peak bactericidal drug concentration in the dermis and target tissues before incisional contamination occurs. Administering the agent within 30 to 60 minutes prior to skin incision (or 120 minutes for vancomycin/fluoroquinolones due to prolonged infusion times) optimizes tissue protection. Postoperative continuation beyond 24 hours provides no benefit and fosters antimicrobial resistance.
tags: Metabolic Response, Shock and Fluid Balance
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 42-year-old female presents with a solitary, firm, painless thyroid nodule in the right lobe measuring 2.5 cm. Ultrasound reveals microcalcifications, marked hypoechogenicity, irregular borders, and taller-than-wide dimensions. FNAC shows ground-glass nuclei with pseudoinclusions and longitudinal nuclear grooves. What is the diagnosis and the most common mode of metastasis?
options: Follicular thyroid carcinoma; hematogenous metastasis to bones and lungs
Papillary thyroid carcinoma; lymphatic metastasis to regional cervical lymph nodes
Medullary thyroid carcinoma; direct local invasion only
Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma; systemic dissemination within weeks
questions.answer: Papillary thyroid carcinoma; lymphatic metastasis to regional cervical lymph nodes
questions.explanation: The cytological features (Orphan Annie eye ground-glass nuclei, nuclear pseudoinclusions, and longitudinal grooves) together with microcalcifications (psammoma bodies) are diagnostic of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). PTC is the most common thyroid malignancy (80–85%) and predominantly metastasizes via lymphatic pathways to ipsilateral and central compartment (Level VI) cervical lymph nodes.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Why can fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) NOT reliably differentiate between a follicular thyroid adenoma and a follicular thyroid carcinoma?
options: FNAC cannot assess cellular atypia or nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio
Distinction requires architectural demonstration of capsular invasion and/or vascular invasion, which requires histological evaluation of the intact capsule
Follicular thyroid carcinoma does not take up standard Papanicolaou stain
Thyroid follicles contain high colloid concentrations that dissolve cytological specimens
questions.answer: Distinction requires architectural demonstration of capsular invasion and/or vascular invasion, which requires histological evaluation of the intact capsule
questions.explanation: Both follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma present with identical cytological appearances of uniform microfollicles and crowded follicular epithelial cells. The definitive diagnosis of follicular carcinoma hinges exclusively on histopathological demonstration of transcapsular invasion (full-thickness penetration of the fibrous capsule) or angioinvasion (tumor cells invading veins in or beyond the capsule), which can only be determined on formal histological sectioning of the resected specimen.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 35-year-old male is diagnosed with medullary thyroid carcinoma. Serum calcitonin is markedly elevated. A family history of sudden death and hypertension is reported. Which mandatory preoperative investigation must be performed prior to thyroidectomy to prevent a lethal intraoperative hypertensive crisis?
options: Serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) and 24-hour urinary metanephrines/catecholamines to exclude pheochromocytoma
Serum gastrin and calcium levels to exclude Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
CT angiography of the circle of Willis
questions.answer: Serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) and 24-hour urinary metanephrines/catecholamines to exclude pheochromocytoma
questions.explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) originates from parafollicular C cells and can occur as part of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) 2A or 2B, both caused by germline RET proto-oncogene mutations. Because pheochromocytoma may coexist, all MTC patients must be screened with 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines/plasma metanephrines. If a pheochromocytoma is present, it must always be resected first before neck surgery to avoid fatal hypertensive crisis during anesthesia and neck exploration.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During total thyroidectomy, ligating the superior thyroid vessels close to the upper pole of the gland protects which specific nerve, and what clinical impairment occurs if this nerve is inadvertently injured?
options: Recurrent laryngeal nerve; causes permanent complete aphonia
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; causes loss of high-pitch phonation and early vocal fatigue due to cricothyroid muscle paralysis
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; causes paralysis of the thyroarytenoid muscle
Cervical sympathetic trunk; causes bilateral Horner's syndrome
questions.answer: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; causes loss of high-pitch phonation and early vocal fatigue due to cricothyroid muscle paralysis
questions.explanation: The superior thyroid artery runs in close proximity to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN). To safeguard this nerve, the superior vascular pedicle must be ligated individually right on the capsule at the apex of the superior thyroid pole. Injury to the EBSLN paralyzes the cricothyroid muscle (the chief tensor of the vocal fold), causing loss of high-frequency voice range, voice fatigue, and weakness of projection.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Four hours after an uncomplicated total thyroidectomy, a patient develops sudden severe respiratory distress, stridor, and a rapidly expanding tense swelling deep to the neck incision. What is the immediate life-saving bedside action?
options: Emergency transfer to the radiology suite for ultrasound neck
Immediate bedside removal of all skin sutures and clips, opening the deep cervical fascia to evacuate the hematoma, followed by urgent transfer to the OR
Immediate intravenous injection of 100 mg hydrocortisone and racemic epinephrine nebulization
Placement of a wide-bore nasogastric tube to decompress the pharynx
questions.answer: Immediate bedside removal of all skin sutures and clips, opening the deep cervical fascia to evacuate the hematoma, followed by urgent transfer to the OR
questions.explanation: A postoperative tension hematoma deep to the investing layer of cervical fascia compresses venous drainage, causing rapid supraglottic laryngeal edema and acute airway obstruction. This is a surgical emergency. The surgeon or on-duty clinician must immediately open the wound at the bedside, cut all sutures, spread the strap muscles, and evacuate the clot to relieve venous compression, followed by transfer to the operating theater for definitive hemostasis.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 48-year-old female undergoes total thyroidectomy for high-risk papillary carcinoma. Six weeks postoperatively, she is scheduled for radioactive iodine (RAI, I-131) ablation. Which tumor marker is measured serially to detect persistent, recurrent, or metastatic disease during long-term follow-up?
questions.explanation: Following total thyroidectomy and radioiodine ablation, normal thyroid tissue is eliminated. In this setting, thyroglobulin (Tg) is an exquisitely sensitive tumor marker. Any detectable or rising serum Tg reflects persistent, recurrent, or metastatic thyroid carcinoma. Anti-Tg antibodies must always be measured simultaneously because their presence can falsely lower measured Tg levels.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which anatomical triangle or landmark provides the standard surgical trajectory to identify the recurrent laryngeal nerve during capsular dissection of the inferior thyroid pole?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is located in the tracheoesophageal groove, passing deep to or through the ligament of Berry and close to the branches of the inferior thyroid artery. Simon's triangle (bounded by the carotid sheath laterally, trachea/esophagus medially, and inferior thyroid artery superiorly) and Beahrs' landmark are classic surgical anatomical spaces used to identify and preserve the nerve.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 70-year-old female presents with a 4-week history of a rapidly enlarging, stony-hard, fixed neck mass associated with dysphagia, dyspnea, and hoarseness. Core needle biopsy shows sheets of pleomorphic giant cells, marked spindle cell proliferation, and numerous abnormal mitotic figures. What is the diagnosis and general prognosis?
options: Hashimoto's thyroiditis; complete resolution with thyroxine
Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma; extremely aggressive with median survival under 6 months
Riedel's thyroiditis; excellent response to tamoxifen alone
Benign colloid multinodular goiter; managed with subtotal thyroidectomy
questions.answer: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma; extremely aggressive with median survival under 6 months
questions.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is an undifferentiated tumor that accounts for 1–2% of thyroid malignancies, typically presenting in elderly females as a rapidly growing, fixed, invasive thyroid mass causing tracheal and esophageal compression. It is one of the most lethal human solid tumors, with median survival typically under 6 months; treatment is mostly palliative (airway protection, radiation, chemotherapy).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In the preoperative preparation of a patient with primary hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease) scheduled for subtotal or total thyroidectomy, what is the rationale for administering Lugol's iodine (or saturated solution of potassium iodide) for 10–14 days immediately preceding surgery?
options: To stimulate iodine uptake and increase postoperative hormone synthesis
To induce the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, reducing thyroid vascularity, friability, and glandular blood flow to minimize operative hemorrhage
To destroy residual parathyroid glands and prevent hypercalcemia
To prevent allergic reactions to volatile general anesthetics
questions.answer: To induce the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, reducing thyroid vascularity, friability, and glandular blood flow to minimize operative hemorrhage
questions.explanation: Pharmacologic doses of inorganic iodine (Lugol's iodine: 5% iodine + 10% potassium iodide) inhibit thyroid hormone release through the acute Wolff-Chaikoff effect. Crucially for the surgeon, it markedly reduces glandular vascularity and friability, converting a hypervascular gland into a firmer, less hemorrhagic organ during surgical dissection.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 52-year-old male presents with recurrent renal calculi, generalized bone aches, and constipation. Serum calcium is 11.8 mg/dL, serum phosphate is 2.1 mg/dL, and intact PTH is elevated at 145 pg/mL. A 99mTc-Sestamibi SPECT scan demonstrates persistent focal tracer retention inferior to the left thyroid lobe. What is the diagnosis and surgical management?
options: Secondary hyperparathyroidism; subtotal parathyroidectomy of all 4 glands
Primary hyperparathyroidism due to a solitary parathyroid adenoma; focused targeted minimally invasive parathyroidectomy with intraoperative PTH monitoring
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism; total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1; bilateral total adrenalectomy
questions.answer: Primary hyperparathyroidism due to a solitary parathyroid adenoma; focused targeted minimally invasive parathyroidectomy with intraoperative PTH monitoring
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and elevated intact PTH indicate primary hyperparathyroidism, which is caused by a single benign parathyroid adenoma in 85–90% of cases. Accurate localization with 99mTc-Sestamibi and ultrasound permits targeted, minimally invasive parathyroidectomy. Complete excision is confirmed intraoperatively by demonstrating a > 50% fall in PTH level 10 minutes post-excision compared to baseline (Miami criterion).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old female presents with a painless, slow-growing, mobile swelling in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland of 4 years duration. Facial nerve examination is intact. FNAC confirms a pleomorphic adenoma. Why is simple enucleation of this tumor strictly contraindicated in favor of superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation?
options: Pleomorphic adenoma lacks any histological capsule
The tumor possesses microscopic pseudopodial extensions penetrating through its false capsule; enucleation results in high recurrence rates and facial nerve injury
Pleomorphic adenoma is an obligate high-grade malignancy requiring radical neck dissection
Enucleation invariably causes malignant transformation to mucoepidermoid carcinoma
questions.answer: The tumor possesses microscopic pseudopodial extensions penetrating through its false capsule; enucleation results in high recurrence rates and facial nerve injury
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumor) has a delicate, pseudocapsule with microscopic projections (pseudopodia) extending into surrounding salivary parenchyma. Simple enucleation breaches this capsule, seeding tumor cells and leading to recurrence rates of 20–45% in a scarred field where facial nerve branches are at high risk. The standard minimum oncologic procedure is superficial parotidectomy with anatomical facial nerve dissection.
tags: Salivary Gland Tumors and Neck Swellings
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old male presents with a hard parotid mass, rapid growth over 2 months, and right-sided lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy (inability to close the eye, drooping of angle of mouth). FNAC reveals malignant cells. What is the most common malignant neoplasm of the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common primary malignant tumor of the salivary glands, representing roughly 30% of parotid malignancies. High-grade variants invade the facial nerve, cause pain, and metastasize to regional lymph nodes, whereas low-grade tumors follow a more indolent course.
tags: Salivary Gland Tumors and Neck Swellings
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 22-year-old male presents with a painless, smooth, cystic swelling located along the anterior border of the upper third of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, deep to the deep cervical fascia. The cyst contains turbid fluid rich in cholesterol crystals on aspiration. What is the diagnosis?
options: Branchial cleft cyst (second branchial cleft anomaly)
questions.answer: Branchial cleft cyst (second branchial cleft anomaly)
questions.explanation: A branchial cyst arises from the persistence of the cervical sinus of the second branchial cleft. It typically presents in young adults (20–30 years) as a painless, non-transilluminant cyst at the junction of the upper third and lower two-thirds of the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Needle aspiration typically yields characteristic opalescent, straw-colored fluid containing cholesterol crystals.
tags: Salivary Gland Tumors and Neck Swellings
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 7-year-old child presents with a midline anterior neck mass located just below the hyoid bone. On clinical examination, the mass moves upward with swallowing AND characteristically moves upward upon protrusion of the tongue. What is the definitive operative procedure for this condition?
questions.explanation: A thyroglossal duct cyst develops along the embryological migratory pathway of the thyroid gland from the foramen cecum to the base of the neck. Attachment to the foramen cecum at the tongue base causes it to rise on tongue protrusion. To prevent high recurrence rates, Sistrunk's operation is the definitive procedure: en-bloc resection of the cyst, the entire epithelial tract, the middle third of the body of the hyoid bone, and a core of muscle up to the foramen cecum.
tags: Salivary Gland Tumors and Neck Swellings
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 48-year-old female presents with a painless mass at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery. On examination, the mass can be moved easily from side to side (laterally) but cannot be moved vertically along the carotid axis. What is this classic clinical sign, and what is the underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fontaine's sign (mobility in the horizontal plane, fixed in the vertical axis) is pathognomonic for carotid body tumor (paraganglioma / chemodectoma). Arising from neural crest paraganglia at the carotid bifurcation, the tumor splays the internal and external carotid arteries (the Lyre sign on angiography) and is constrained along the longitudinal axis of the carotid sheath.
tags: Salivary Gland Tumors and Neck Swellings
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 52-year-old postmenopausal female presents with an ill-defined, hard, painless 3-cm lump in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast with overlying skin tethering (peau d'orange). Triple assessment is initiated. What three components constitute the standard 'Triple Assessment' in evaluating suspected breast malignancy?
options: Clinical breast examination, digital bilateral mammography (with ultrasound), and core needle biopsy (or FNAC)
Breast self-examination, chest radiograph, and serum CA 15-3 level
MRI breast, PET-CT scan, and open excisional biopsy
Thermography, ductoscopy, and fine needle aspiration
questions.answer: Clinical breast examination, digital bilateral mammography (with ultrasound), and core needle biopsy (or FNAC)
questions.explanation: Triple assessment is the gold standard diagnostic triad for evaluating all discrete breast lumps, achieving an overall diagnostic accuracy > 99%. It consists of: 1. Clinical examination; 2. Imaging (bilateral digital mammography in women > 35–40 years, ultrasound for younger/dense breasts); 3. Pathological evaluation (core needle biopsy is preferred over FNAC because it provides tissue architecture, invasive vs in-situ status, and ER/PR/HER2 receptor status).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the precise pathophysiological cause of the 'peau d'orange' (orange-peel) appearance of the skin overlying an advanced breast carcinoma?
options: Infiltration and shortening of the suspensory ligaments of Astley Cooper
Tumor emboli causing obstruction of subdermal lymphatic vessels, leading to localized cutaneous edema with tethering at hair follicles and sweat duct orifices
Direct malignant ulceration through the epidermis
Hypervascular neoplastic angiogenesis causing cutaneous venous congestion
questions.answer: Tumor emboli causing obstruction of subdermal lymphatic vessels, leading to localized cutaneous edema with tethering at hair follicles and sweat duct orifices
questions.explanation: Peau d'orange occurs when malignant tumor emboli invade and plug the subdermal cutaneous lymphatic plexus. This induces lymphedema of the overlying dermis. Because hair follicles and sweat gland ducts are deeply anchored to the subcutaneous fascia, they remain tethered while the surrounding skin balloons with fluid, creating the characteristic dimpled orange-peel texture (classified as T4b disease). Dimpling, by contrast, is caused by shortening of the ligaments of Cooper.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In a patient with early invasive breast cancer (cT1cN0M0) undergoing breast conservation surgery, sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is performed using dual-tracer technique (radiocolloid 99mTc-sulfur colloid and isosulfan blue). What is the definition of a sentinel lymph node?
options: The largest lymph node palpable in Level I axilla
The first lymph node(s) in the regional lymphatic basin that directly receives lymphatic drainage from the primary tumor
Any lymph node located medial to the pectoralis minor muscle
The apical lymph node at Halsted's ligament
questions.answer: The first lymph node(s) in the regional lymphatic basin that directly receives lymphatic drainage from the primary tumor
questions.explanation: The sentinel lymph node (SLN) is the initial lymph node (or group of nodes) that receives primary lymphatic drainage directly from the tumor bed. If the sentinel node is histopathologically negative for micrometastatic and macrometastatic disease on serial sectioning/immunohistochemistry, the remaining axillary nodes are highly likely to be uninvolved (> 95–98%), sparing the patient the morbidity of axillary lymph node dissection (lymphedema, nerve injury).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During modified radical mastectomy (Auchincloss or Patey modification), axillary clearance is performed. The surgeon inadvertently injures a nerve coursing along the lateral thoracic wall in the mid-axillary line on the surface of serratus anterior. What clinical deformity will the patient develop postoperatively?
options: Loss of sensation over the medial arm (intercostobrachial nerve injury)
Winged scapula due to paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle (long thoracic nerve of Bell injury)
Weakness of adduction and internal rotation of the arm due to latissimus dorsi paralysis (thoracodorsal nerve injury)
questions.answer: Winged scapula due to paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle (long thoracic nerve of Bell injury)
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve of Bell (arising from C5, C6, C7 roots) descends along the medial wall of the axilla directly on the fascia of the serratus anterior muscle. Inadvertent transection or traction injury paralyzes the serratus anterior, resulting in 'winging of the scapula'—the vertebral border and inferior angle of the scapula project backwards when the patient pushes forward against a wall with outstretched arms.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 48-year-old female presents with persistent, unilateral, eczema-like red scaling, excoriation, and superficial ulceration of the left nipple-areolar complex that has failed to heal with topical corticosteroids. Full-thickness nipple wedge biopsy demonstrates large, intraepithelial, pale cells with vacuolated cytoplasm (Paget's cells). What underlying pathology is almost universally present?
options: Underlying intraductal carcinoma (DCIS) or invasive ductal carcinoma in the deeper breast parenchyma
questions.answer: Underlying intraductal carcinoma (DCIS) or invasive ductal carcinoma in the deeper breast parenchyma
questions.explanation: Paget's disease of the nipple is an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma presenting as an eczematous, pruritic, eroding lesion of the nipple-areolar complex. In over 95–98% of cases, it is associated with an underlying ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or invasive ductal carcinoma located elsewhere in the breast, representing malignant cells migrating along lactiferous ducts into the epidermis.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old female with invasive ductal carcinoma has a receptor profile showing Estrogen Receptor (ER) negative, Progesterone Receptor (PR) negative, and HER2/neu negative ('Triple Negative Breast Cancer'). Which statement regarding this molecular subtype is correct?
