options: It responds exceptionally well to targeted oral tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors
It represents Luminal A subtype and has an exceptionally favorable long-term prognosis
It is associated with BRCA1 mutations, carries a higher rate of visceral and brain metastasis, and relies primarily on systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy rather than targeted endocrine therapy
Trastuzumab (Herceptin) is the primary first-line targeted antibody
questions.answer: It is associated with BRCA1 mutations, carries a higher rate of visceral and brain metastasis, and relies primarily on systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy rather than targeted endocrine therapy
questions.explanation: Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) accounts for approximately 15% of breast cancers. Lacking ER, PR, and HER2 amplification, it is refractory to both endocrine therapy (tamoxifen, letrozole) and anti-HER2 antibodies (trastuzumab). It is frequently associated with germline BRCA1 mutations, behaves aggressively with early visceral and CNS relapse, and requires cytotoxic polychemotherapy (e.g., anthracyclines and taxanes, often combined with platinum agents or immunotherapy).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 21-year-old unmarried female presents with a 2-cm, well-circumscribed, painless, firm, lobulated swelling in the right breast. On examination, the mass is extraordinarily mobile, slipping freely beneath the examining fingers without fixing to the skin or pectoral fascia. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast neoplasm in young females (15–30 years), arising from the terminal duct lobular unit as an aberration of normal development and involution (ANDI). Because of its lack of fixation, firm rubbery consistency, and extreme mobility within the surrounding mobile breast parenchyma, it is clinically termed the 'breast mouse'.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 44-year-old female presents with spontaneous, unilateral, single-duct serosanguinous (blood-stained) discharge from the left nipple without any palpable breast lump. Mammography and ultrasound are unremarkable. What is the most common cause of unilateral bloody nipple discharge?
options: Solitary intraductal papilloma in a major lactiferous duct
questions.answer: Solitary intraductal papilloma in a major lactiferous duct
questions.explanation: A solitary benign intraductal papilloma arising within the primary lactiferous ducts just beneath the areola is the single most common cause (approx. 50–70%) of spontaneous, single-pore bloody or serosanguinous nipple discharge. Definitive management is microdochectomy (selective excision of the involved single duct and papilloma) or subareolar duct excision (Hadfield's operation) in older women.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which clinical trial benchmark definitively established that Breast Conservation Surgery (lumpectomy/wide local excision + axillary evaluation) combined with whole-breast radiotherapy yields equivalent overall survival to Modified Radical Mastectomy (MRM) in early breast cancer?
options: NSABP B-06 trial / Milan I trial (Veronesi et al.)
questions.answer: NSABP B-06 trial / Milan I trial (Veronesi et al.)
questions.explanation: The landmark NSABP B-06 (National Surgical Adjuvant Breast and Bowel Project) trial and the Milan I trial directed by Umberto Veronesi definitively demonstrated that breast-conserving therapy (lumpectomy followed by adjuvant whole-breast radiotherapy) provides equivalent long-term disease-free and overall survival compared to modified radical mastectomy in women with Stage I and Stage II breast carcinoma.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 55-year-old female presents with a massive 12-cm rapidly growing, lobulated, bosselated, painless breast lump. Overlying skin is thinned with prominent dilated superficial veins, but is not fixed. Axillary lymph nodes are non-palpable. Core needle biopsy confirms a low-grade Phyllodes tumor. What is the definitive surgical treatment of choice?
options: Wide local excision with a mandatory clear surgical margin of at least 1 cm (or simple mastectomy if breast-to-tumor ratio is unfavorable), without routine axillary lymphadenectomy
Modified radical mastectomy with complete Level I–III axillary clearance
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by lumpectomy without margins
Incisional biopsy and primary whole-breast radiation therapy
questions.answer: Wide local excision with a mandatory clear surgical margin of at least 1 cm (or simple mastectomy if breast-to-tumor ratio is unfavorable), without routine axillary lymphadenectomy
questions.explanation: Phyllodes tumors (fibroepithelial tumors) have an aggressive stromal component with potential for local recurrence and hematogenous (not lymphatic) metastasis in malignant variants. Treatment requires complete surgical excision with an adequate negative margin of at least 1 cm (or total mastectomy if the tumor occupies the majority of the breast). Because lymphatic spread is rare (< 1%), routine axillary dissection is not indicated unless lymph nodes are pathologically proven to contain tumor.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In a patient presenting with primary lower limb varicose veins, which clinical examination test specifically assesses competence of the saphenofemoral junction (SFJ)?
questions.explanation: The Brodie-Trendelenburg test evaluates saphenofemoral junction competence. The patient lies supine and the leg is elevated to empty the varicose veins. A tourniquet is placed just below the saphenofemoral junction (approx. 2.5–3.5 cm below the pubic tubercle). The patient stands. If the veins remain collapsed and then fill rapidly from above downwards upon release of the tourniquet within 30 seconds, saphenofemoral junction incompetence is confirmed (Trendelenburg positive/test 1).
tags: Varicose Veins, DVT and Arterial Disease
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Why is Perthes' test mandatory prior to planning surgical ligation or stripping of the great saphenous vein in a patient with varicose veins?
options: To detect arterial insufficiency in the dorsalis pedis artery
To verify the patency and competence of the deep venous system; if the deep veins are thrombosed, superficial veins serve as the sole venous outflow and stripping is strictly contraindicated
To localize perforating veins in the adductor canal
To assess venous valve cusps under direct visual illumination
questions.answer: To verify the patency and competence of the deep venous system; if the deep veins are thrombosed, superficial veins serve as the sole venous outflow and stripping is strictly contraindicated
questions.explanation: Perthes' test assesses deep venous patency. A tourniquet is applied at the upper thigh to occlude superficial veins, and the patient walks vigorously. If the calf muscle pump empties the superficial varicosities through competent, patent deep veins, the veins collapse. If deep veins are obstructed (e.g., chronic DVT), the varicosities become tensely engorged and the patient experiences severe bursting calf pain, proving that superficial varicosities are collateral pathways that must never be ablated or stripped.
tags: Varicose Veins, DVT and Arterial Disease
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During classical flush ligation of the saphenofemoral junction (Trendelenburg operation), what anatomical rule must be strictly observed to prevent recurrence of varicose veins from collateral tributaries?
options: Ligate the great saphenous vein 5 cm distal to the femoral vein without dividing any tributaries

Divide and ligate all 5–6 named tributaries (superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, superficial external pudendal, deep external pudendal, and lateral/medial accessory saphenous) flush with the anterior wall of the femoral vein
Ligate the superficial femoral artery alongside the vein
Strip the saphenous nerve alongside the vein into the foot
questions.answer: Divide and ligate all 5–6 named tributaries (superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, superficial external pudendal, deep external pudendal, and lateral/medial accessory saphenous) flush with the anterior wall of the femoral vein
questions.explanation: A true flush ligation demands dissecting the saphenofemoral junction until the glistening white adventitia of the femoral vein is cleanly visualized, followed by individual identification, division, and ligation of all terminal tributaries. Leaving any tributary intact permits retrograde venous reflux into superficial venous networks, which is the primary cause of postoperative recurrent varicosities.
tags: Varicose Veins, DVT and Arterial Disease
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In modern endovenous ablation of the great saphenous vein (using Endovenous Laser Ablation - EVLA or Radiofrequency Ablation - RFA), what is the function of infiltrating generous perivenous 'tumescent anesthesia' under ultrasound guidance prior to energy delivery?
options: To lyse existing endoluminal red blood cells
To provide local anesthesia, act as a protective heat sink safeguarding surrounding skin and the saphenous nerve from thermal damage, and compress the vein onto the catheter for optimal wall contact
To chemically dissolve the venous endothelium through sclerotherapy
To dilate the vein to facilitate smooth catheter withdrawal
questions.answer: To provide local anesthesia, act as a protective heat sink safeguarding surrounding skin and the saphenous nerve from thermal damage, and compress the vein onto the catheter for optimal wall contact
questions.explanation: Tumescent local anesthesia (dilute lidocaine, epinephrine, and sodium bicarbonate in cold saline) injected circumferentially into the perivenous saphenous sheath serves three vital functions: 1. Complete pain control; 2. Thermal insulation, protecting the overlying skin and adjacent saphenous nerve from heat injury; 3. Mechanical compression of the vein lumen around the ablation fiber, ensuring efficient transmural thermal injury and fibrotic occlusion.
tags: Varicose Veins, DVT and Arterial Disease
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 58-year-old male with chronic venous insufficiency presents with a large, shallow, painless ulcer with sloping edges, pale granulation tissue, and brownish-black hemosiderin pigmentation over the medial malleolus (gaiter zone). What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism generating this venous ulcer?
options: Severe endarteritis obliterans leading to acute ischemic infarction
Ambulatory venous hypertension transmitting high hydrostatic pressures to capillary beds, causing extravasation of RBCs (hemosiderin deposition), fibrin cuff formation, and tissue hypoxia
Malignant transformation of eccrine sweat glands
questions.answer: Ambulatory venous hypertension transmitting high hydrostatic pressures to capillary beds, causing extravasation of RBCs (hemosiderin deposition), fibrin cuff formation, and tissue hypoxia
questions.explanation: Valvular incompetence in the deep, superficial, or perforating veins impairs the calf muscle pump, creating sustained ambulatory venous hypertension. This raises microvascular capillary bed pressure, leading to endothelial gap formation, extravasation of red blood cells (which breakdown into hemosiderin, causing stasis pigmentation) and fibrinogen. Polymerized pericapillary fibrin cuffs, along with trapped leukocytic activation, obstruct oxygen diffusion, triggering local tissue ischemia, lipodermatosclerosis, and ulceration.
tags: Varicose Veins, DVT and Arterial Disease
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 60-year-old female presents on postoperative day 6 following total hip arthroplasty with sudden unilateral left calf swelling, tenderness, pitting edema, and marked pain on passive dorsiflexion of the ankle. What is the eponym for this sign, and what is the primary diagnostic imaging modality?
options: Homans' sign; Compression duplex Doppler ultrasonography
questions.answer: Homans' sign; Compression duplex Doppler ultrasonography
questions.explanation: Homans' sign refers to calf pain elicited upon passive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee extended, suggestive of deep vein thrombosis (DVT). While Homans' sign lacks sensitivity and specificity, the definitive first-line diagnostic investigation is compression duplex Doppler ultrasound of the lower extremity veins (revealing non-compressibility of the lumen and absent flow signals).
tags: Varicose Veins, DVT and Arterial Disease
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 68-year-old chronic smoker presents with severe cramping pain in his right calf that comes on after walking 150 meters and is promptly relieved after 3 minutes of rest. The Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) on the affected side is measured at 0.65. What stage of peripheral arterial disease does this represent, and where is the anatomical arterial obstruction most commonly located?
options: Intermittent claudication (Fontaine Stage II); superficial femoral artery occlusion in Hunter's (adductor) canal
Critical limb ischemia (Fontaine Stage III); digital microarterial spasm
Acute limb ischemia; popliteal artery embolism
questions.answer: Intermittent claudication (Fontaine Stage II); superficial femoral artery occlusion in Hunter's (adductor) canal
questions.explanation: Fontaine Stage II represents intermittent claudication: reproducible muscular pain brought on by exercise and relieved by rest. An ABI between 0.5 and 0.8 confirms moderate arterial stenosis. The single most common anatomical site of atherosclerotic stenosis in the lower limb causing calf claudication is the superficial femoral artery where it traverses the adductor (Hunter's) canal through the adductor magnus hiatus.
tags: Varicose Veins, DVT and Arterial Disease
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 54-year-old male presents with bilateral buttock claudication, marked muscle atrophy of the gluteal and thigh musculature, absent femoral pulses bilaterally, and erectile dysfunction (impotence). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Leriche syndrome is chronic aortoiliac occlusive disease caused by atherosclerotic occlusion of the distal abdominal aorta at its bifurcation. It classically presents with the clinical triad of: 1. Claudication of the buttocks, thighs, and calves; 2. Absent or markedly diminished femoral and distal pulses; 3. Erectile dysfunction (vasculogenic impotence due to internal iliac hypoperfusion).
tags: Varicose Veins, DVT and Arterial Disease
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 30-year-old male heavy bidi smoker presents with severe rest pain and blackish dry gangrene of the tips of the right 2nd and 3rd toes. Radial and pedal pulses are diminished, but femoral and popliteal pulses are fully palpable. Histopathology shows segmental, acute and chronic transmural inflammation with occlusive inflammatory thrombi and preservation of the internal elastic lamina. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Thromboangiitis obliterans (TAO or Buerger's disease) is a non-atherosclerotic, segmental, inflammatory vasculitis that predominantly affects small- and medium-sized arteries and veins of the extremities in young male smokers (< 40–45 years). It typically presents with digital ischemia, rest pain, superficial thrombophlebitis migrans, and Raynaud's phenomenon. Pathognomonically, the internal elastic lamina remains intact without medial calcification.
tags: Varicose Veins, DVT and Arterial Disease
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 72-year-old patient with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden onset of excruciating pain in the right lower extremity of 3 hours duration. Physical examination reveals the '6 Ps': Pain, Pallor, Poikilothermia (coldness), Pulselessness, Paresthesias, and Paralysis. What is the definitive emergency surgical intervention to salvage the limb?
options: Urgent Fogarty balloon catheter embolectomy under local anesthesia
Long-term oral aspirin therapy and leg elevation
Intravenous antibiotic infusion and bed rest
questions.answer: Urgent Fogarty balloon catheter embolectomy under local anesthesia
questions.explanation: Acute limb ischemia due to cardiogenic arterial embolism (frequently lodging at the femoral bifurcation) is a surgical emergency with a golden window of 6 hours before irreversible muscle necrosis sets in. Emergency surgical intervention is catheter-directed balloon embolectomy using a Fogarty catheter, typically performed through a transverse femoral arteriotomy under local anesthesia, alongside systemic heparinization.
tags: Varicose Veins, DVT and Arterial Disease
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 42-year-old female presents with progressive dysphagia to both liquids and solids of 2 years duration, regurgitation of undigested food, and 8 kg weight loss. Barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus with smooth, symmetric tapering at the gastroesophageal junction ('bird's beak' appearance). High-resolution esophageal manometry confirms failure of lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation and absent peristalsis. What is the gold-standard surgical treatment of choice?
options: Laparoscopic Heller's cardiomyotomy with partial anterior fundoplication (Dor) or posterior (Toupet)
questions.answer: Laparoscopic Heller's cardiomyotomy with partial anterior fundoplication (Dor) or posterior (Toupet)
questions.explanation: Achalasia cardia is an esophageal motility disorder caused by degeneration of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, leading to incomplete LES relaxation and aperistalsis. The gold standard surgical management is laparoscopic Heller's cardiomyotomy (dividing the circular and longitudinal muscle fibers of the lower esophagus 5–6 cm above and 2–3 cm onto the gastric cardia) combined with a partial fundoplication (Dor anterior 180° or Toupet posterior 270°) to prevent severe gastroesophageal reflux.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 60-year-old male with a 20-year history of heavy alcohol intake and chronic smoking presents with rapidly progressive dysphagia, initially for solids and later for liquids, accompanied by significant weight loss. Endoscopy demonstrates an ulcerated, friable, obstructing mass in the middle third of the thoracic esophagus. Histopathology confirms squamous cell carcinoma. What is the standard radical two-stage transthoracic esophagectomy procedure named?
options: Ivor Lewis esophagectomy (laparotomy and right thoracotomy with intrathoracic esophagogastric anastomosis)
questions.answer: Ivor Lewis esophagectomy (laparotomy and right thoracotomy with intrathoracic esophagogastric anastomosis)
questions.explanation: The Ivor Lewis esophagectomy is a classic two-stage operation for tumors of the middle and lower third of the esophagus: 1. Abdominal stage (laparotomy or laparoscopy) for gastric mobilization, celiac lymphadenectomy, and tubularization of the stomach; 2. Right thoracotomy (or thoracoscopy) for esophageal resection, mediastinal lymph node dissection, and intrathoracic esophagogastric anastomosis above the azygos vein.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 38-year-old male with a history of recurrent duodenal ulcers presents to the emergency room with sudden, severe, agonising epigastric pain that rapidly spread to the entire abdomen 3 hours ago. On examination, the patient lies still, abdomen shows wooden, board-like rigidity, and liver dullness is obliterated on percussion. An erect chest X-ray confirms free gas under the right dome of the diaphragm. What is the immediate definitive surgical management?
options: Emergency diagnostic laparoscopy and therapeutic total gastrectomy
Emergency exploratory laparotomy with primary repair of the perforation reinforced with a live pedicled omental patch (Graham's omentopexy/patch)
High-dose intravenous proton pump inhibitor infusion alone without surgery
Endoscopic clip application and immediate discharge
questions.answer: Emergency exploratory laparotomy with primary repair of the perforation reinforced with a live pedicled omental patch (Graham's omentopexy/patch)
questions.explanation: Perforated peptic (duodenal) ulcer presents with acute chemical and subsequent bacterial peritonitis, board-like abdominal rigidity, loss of liver dullness, and pneumoperitoneum. After initial resuscitation with nasogastric decompression, crystalloids, and broad-spectrum antibiotics, the gold-standard surgical procedure is Cellan-Jones or Graham's omentopexy (suturing a pedicled tongue of vascularized greater omentum over the perforation) alongside thorough peritoneal lavage.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 56-year-old male with a long-standing history of recurrent peptic ulcer disease presents with severe projectile vomiting of foul-smelling, undigested food ingested 24–48 hours earlier, devoid of bile. Physical examination reveals a visible gastric peristaltic wave moving from left to right and a positive succession splash elicited 4 hours after meals. What is the diagnosis and the classic metabolic abnormality expected on blood gas analysis?
options: Acute pancreatitis; hypercalcemia and metabolic acidosis
Gastric outlet obstruction (pyloric stenosis); hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
questions.answer: Gastric outlet obstruction (pyloric stenosis); hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
questions.explanation: Gastric outlet obstruction from cicatricial contraction of chronic duodenal ulcer scarring causes intractable non-bilious projectile vomiting containing food eaten days before, visible gastric peristalsis, and a positive succussion splash. Chronic vomiting of gastric juice rich in hydrochloric acid and potassium leads to volume depletion, hypochloremia, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and compensatory renal excretion of hydrogen ions (paradoxical aciduria).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In a patient presenting with advanced gastric adenocarcinoma, on physical examination you identify a hard, non-tender, fixed metastatic lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa between the heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. What is the eponym for this sign, and what anatomical lymphatic channel explains this specific predilection?
options: Sister Mary Joseph's nodule; falciform ligament lymphatic plexus
Troisier's sign (Virchow's node); retrograde malignant dissemination via the thoracic duct into the left jugulo-subclavian venous confluence
Irish's node; anterior axillary pectoral pathway
Blumer's shelf; transcoelomic pouch of Douglas seeding
questions.answer: Troisier's sign (Virchow's node); retrograde malignant dissemination via the thoracic duct into the left jugulo-subclavian venous confluence
questions.explanation: Virchow's node (Troisier's sign) refers to metastatic enlargement of the left supraclavicular lymph node, indicative of advanced intra-abdominal visceral malignancy (most classically gastric adenocarcinoma). It occurs because the thoracic duct, which drains almost the entire abdomen and lower body, ascends into the left neck and empties into the left internal jugular and subclavian vein junction, communicating directly with left supraclavicular nodal channels.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the defining criterion and standard surgical clearance for a 'D2 lymphadenectomy' in the radical curative resection of gastric adenocarcinoma?
options: Resection of perigastric lymph nodes only along the lesser and greater curvatures (stations 1–6)

Resection of all perigastric lymph nodes (stations 1–6) PLUS second-tier lymph nodes along the left gastric artery, common hepatic artery, celiac axis, splenic hilum, and splenic artery (stations 7–12a)
Para-aortic lymph node dissection from diaphragm to aortic bifurcation (stations 16a/b)
Complete mesenteric lymphadenectomy down to the ileocolic vessels
questions.answer: Resection of all perigastric lymph nodes (stations 1–6) PLUS second-tier lymph nodes along the left gastric artery, common hepatic artery, celiac axis, splenic hilum, and splenic artery (stations 7–12a)
questions.explanation: According to the Japanese Gastric Cancer Association (JGCA) classifications, D1 lymphadenectomy removes tier-1 perigastric stations (1 to 6). A standard D2 lymphadenectomy requires en-bloc resection of stations 1 through 6 plus tier-2 stations along the branches of the celiac trunk: left gastric artery (7), common hepatic artery (8a), celiac axis (9), splenic artery (11p/11d), and hepatoduodenal ligament (12a). D2 clearance is the global standard for curative-intent gastrectomy.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 50-year-old male undergoes a distal gastrectomy with Billroth II gastrojejunostomy for gastric carcinoma. Two weeks after resuming meals, he complains of palpitations, diaphoresis, epigastric fullness, flushing, and explosive watery diarrhea occurring 20–30 minutes after every meal. What is this syndrome, and what physiological mechanism causes it?
options: Late dumping syndrome; reactive hypoglycemia due to exaggerated insulin surge
Early dumping syndrome; rapid transit of hyperosmolar carbohydrate-rich chyme into the proximal jejunum, drawing massive fluid shifts from the intravascular space into the bowel lumen
Afferent loop syndrome; chronic obstruction of the biliopancreatic limb
Alkaline reflux gastritis; bile acid mucosal injury
questions.answer: Early dumping syndrome; rapid transit of hyperosmolar carbohydrate-rich chyme into the proximal jejunum, drawing massive fluid shifts from the intravascular space into the bowel lumen
questions.explanation: Early dumping syndrome occurs 15–30 minutes postprandially following gastrectomy with loss of pyloric sphincter function. Rapid emptying of hypertonic chyme into the jejunum creates an osmotic gradient that shifts large volumes of extracellular fluid into the intestinal lumen, causing acute hypovolemia (palpitations, dizziness, diaphoresis, hypotension) alongside vasoactive neurohormone release (serotonin, neurotensin, bradykinin). Late dumping occurs 2–3 hours postprandially due to reactive hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old male presents with recurrent massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Endoscopy reveals a submucosal, well-circumscribed gastric fundic mass with a central 'bull's eye' or 'target' mucosal ulceration. Immunohistochemistry of core biopsy is strongly positive for CD117 (c-KIT receptor tyrosine kinase) and DOG-1. What is the diagnosis, and what targeted pharmacological agent is used for high-risk or metastatic disease?
questions.explanation: GISTs are mesenchymal neoplasms arising from the interstitial cells of Cajal (pacemaker cells of the gut) driven by activating mutations in the KIT (CD117) or PDGFRA receptor tyrosine kinase genes. They characteristically appear as submucosal lesions with central umbilication. Surgical wedge resection with negative margins without routine lymphadenectomy is primary management. Imatinib mesylate (a selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor) is standard neoadjuvant and adjuvant therapy for intermediate- and high-risk GISTs.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: On upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, a 48-year-old patient with severe chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease shows salmon-pink, velvety, tongue-like mucosal projections extending 4 cm proximal to the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsies confirm specialized intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells (Barrett's esophagus). What is the primary clinical significance of this finding?
options: It represents an irreversible benign infection with no oncological risk
It is a premalignant condition that confers a 30- to 40-fold increased risk of developing esophageal adenocarcinoma, necessitating regular surveillance endoscopy
It carries a mandatory indication for immediate total esophagectomy
It invariably leads to squamous cell carcinoma of the proximal esophagus
questions.answer: It is a premalignant condition that confers a 30- to 40-fold increased risk of developing esophageal adenocarcinoma, necessitating regular surveillance endoscopy
questions.explanation: Barrett's esophagus is an acquired metaplastic conversion of normal stratified squamous esophageal epithelium into specialized columnar epithelium containing intestinal goblet cells in response to chronic acid and bile reflux. It is the single most critical premalignant precursor for adenocarcinoma of the distal esophagus and gastroesophageal junction, requiring structured endoscopic surveillance with targeted four-quadrant biopsies.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 42-year-old male with recurrent, refractory, multiple peptic ulcers located in atypical sites (second and third part of duodenum and jejunum) accompanied by chronic watery diarrhea has a fasting serum gastrin level of 1,200 pg/mL (normal < 100 pg/mL). Gastric acid secretion shows basal acid output (BAO) > 15 mEq/hr. What is the diagnosis, and which anatomical triangle defines the location of the majority of these tumors?
questions.explanation: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES) is caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma) driving hyperchlorhydria, refractory atypical peptic ulceration, and diarrhea. Over 85–90% of gastrinomas reside within the **Gastrinoma Triangle of Passaro**, anatomically demarcated by: 1. Superiorly: Junction of cystic duct and common bile duct; 2. Inferiorly: Junction of the second and third parts of the duodenum; 3. Medially: Junction of the neck and body of the pancreas.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 44-year-old obese female presents with severe, colicky right upper quadrant pain radiating to the inferior angle of the right scapula following a fatty meal, accompanied by nausea. On examination, deep palpation in the right subcostal margin elicits sharp catch in breath upon inspiration. What is this sign, and what is the definitive gold-standard elective management?
options: Boas' sign; extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy
Rovsing's sign; medical dissolution with ursodeoxycholic acid
questions.explanation: Murphy's sign (arrest of inspiration on deep palpation of the right subcostal region due to acute inflammation of the gallbladder descending against the examiner's fingers) is a hallmark of acute cholecystitis. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the definitive gold-standard treatment, ideally performed within 72 hours of symptom onset (early laparoscopic cholecystectomy). Boas' sign refers to hyperesthesia over the right 9th to 11th ribs posteriorly.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What are the anatomical boundaries of the hepatobiliary triangle (Calot's triangle) that must be skeletonized to achieve the 'Critical View of Safety' during laparoscopic cholecystectomy?
options: Inferior surface of liver superiorly, cystic duct inferiorly, and common hepatic duct medially
Falciform ligament, portal vein, and inferior vena cava
Right branch of portal vein, common bile duct, and gastroduodenal artery
Cystic artery superiorly, hepatic duct laterally, and duodenum medially
questions.answer: Inferior surface of liver superiorly, cystic duct inferiorly, and common hepatic duct medially
questions.explanation: The hepatobiliary triangle of Calot is bounded superiorly by the visceral under-surface of liver segment V, inferiorly/laterally by the cystic duct, and medially by the common hepatic duct. The cystic artery and Calot's lymph node (node of Lund) reside within this triangle. Achieving the Critical View of Safety (Strasberg) requires clearing all fibrofatty tissue in this triangle so only two structures (cystic duct and cystic artery) are seen entering the lower third of the gallbladder, with the liver bed clearly visible.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 65-year-old male presents with deep, progressive jaundice, clay-colored stools, high-colored urine, and generalized pruritus. On abdominal examination, a smooth, non-tender, pear-shaped cystic swelling is palpable in the right hypochondrium that moves with respiration. According to Courvoisier's law, what is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Impacted stone in the common bile duct (choledocholithiasis)
Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas or periampullary carcinoma
questions.answer: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas or periampullary carcinoma
questions.explanation: Courvoisier's law states that in the presence of obstructive jaundice, if the gallbladder is palpably enlarged and non-tender, the cause is unlikely to be a gallstone because chronic inflammation from prior cholelithiasis renders the gallbladder fibrotic and non-distensible. Instead, it signifies malignant obstruction of the lower biliary tract, most commonly carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, ampullary carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, or duodenal carcinoma.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 58-year-old female presents with fever with chills, right upper quadrant pain, and fluctuating jaundice (Charcot's triad), accompanied by confusion and hypotension (Reynold's pentad). Total bilirubin is 8.5 mg/dL, and ultrasound shows common bile duct dilatation (14 mm) with an acoustic shadow in the distal duct. What is the emergency treatment of choice?
options: Emergency open cholecystectomy and choledochotomy within 2 hours
Aggressive resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and urgent biliary decompression via Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with biliary sphincterotomy and stenting
questions.answer: Aggressive resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and urgent biliary decompression via Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with biliary sphincterotomy and stenting
questions.explanation: Reynold's pentad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain, confusion, septic shock) indicates acute suppurative ascending cholangitis, a life-threatening emergency caused by infected biliary obstruction under high pressure. Immediate management requires aggressive fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and urgent emergent biliary drainage—optimally via therapeutic ERCP with biliary sphincterotomy and stent placement (or percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage if ERCP fails).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 46-year-old chronic alcoholic male presents with severe, unrelenting epigastric pain boring through to the back, relieved somewhat by leaning forward, associated with repeated vomiting. Serum lipase is 1,850 U/L (reference < 60 U/L). On day 3, bruising is noted around the umbilicus and across both flanks. What are the eponyms for these signs, and what do they signify?
options: Kehr's sign and Murphy's sign; splenic rupture
Cullen's sign (periumbilical) and Grey Turner's sign (flanks); retroperitoneal necrotizing hemorrhagic pancreatitis
Trousseau's sign and Chvostek's sign; acute hypomagnesemia
Boas' sign and Blumberg's sign; acute gangrenous appendicitis
questions.answer: Cullen's sign (periumbilical) and Grey Turner's sign (flanks); retroperitoneal necrotizing hemorrhagic pancreatitis
questions.explanation: Cullen's sign (periumbilical ecchymosis) and Grey Turner's sign (flank ecchymosis) represent tracking of retroperitoneal blood and pancreatic enzymes along the falciform ligament to the umbilicus and through the retroperitoneal fascial planes to the flanks. They are physical hallmarks of severe acute necrotizing hemorrhagic pancreatitis and indicate high clinical severity.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Four weeks following an episode of acute necrotizing pancreatitis, a patient presents with persistent early satiety, fullness, and a smooth, non-tender, cystic mass in the epigastrium. Contrast-enhanced CT reveals a 7-cm well-circumscribed fluid collection within the lesser sac, completely devoid of an epithelial lining. What is the diagnosis and appropriate definitive intervention if symptomatic?
options: Pancreatic pseudocyst; internal drainage (cystogastrostomy or cystojejunostomy) once the mature fibrous wall has formed (> 6 weeks)
Hydatid cyst of liver; albendazole therapy alone
True epithelial retention cyst; observation only
questions.answer: Pancreatic pseudocyst; internal drainage (cystogastrostomy or cystojejunostomy) once the mature fibrous wall has formed (> 6 weeks)
questions.explanation: A pancreatic pseudocyst is a localized collection of amylase-rich pancreatic fluid enclosed by a non-epithelial wall composed of granulation tissue and dense collagenous fibrosis, typically located in the lesser sac following pancreatitis or trauma. Maturation of the cyst wall requires at least 4–6 weeks. Symptomatic, persistent, or enlarging (> 6 cm) pseudocysts are managed by internal drainage: endoscopic or surgical cystogastrostomy (connecting the pseudocyst into the posterior gastric wall) or Roux-en-Y cystojejunostomy.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 35-year-old sheep farmer presents with dull right hypochondrial pain. Ultrasound reveals a 9-cm well-defined cystic lesion in the right lobe of the liver with multiple internal daughter cysts and a double-layered wall ('water-lily sign' on detachment of the endocyst). If PAIR (Puncture, Aspiration, Injection, Re-aspiration) is performed, what scolicidal agent must NEVER be used due to the risk of chemical sclerosing cholangitis if a biliary communication exists?
questions.explanation: In hydatid disease of the liver (Echinococcus granulosus), scolicidal agents like 20% hypertonic saline or 95% ethanol are instilled into the cyst to kill protoscolices. Formalin and silver nitrate are strictly contraindicated as scolicidal agents because accidental entry into communicating intrahepatic bile ducts induces catastrophic, irreversible corrosive chemical sclerosing cholangitis.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In liver surgery, what is the 'Pringle maneuver', and what vascular structures are temporarily occluded within the free margin of the lesser omentum (epiploic foramen of Winslow)?
options: Clamping of the hepatic veins as they enter the inferior vena cava
Non-crushing vascular cross-clamping of the hepatoduodenal ligament, occluding the proper hepatic artery and the portal vein to control intraoperative hepatic parenchymal hemorrhage
Selective ligation of the middle colic vessels
Occlusion of the inferior vena cava alone
questions.answer: Non-crushing vascular cross-clamping of the hepatoduodenal ligament, occluding the proper hepatic artery and the portal vein to control intraoperative hepatic parenchymal hemorrhage
questions.explanation: The Pringle maneuver (described by J. Hogarth Pringle in 1908) involves compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament across the foramen of Winslow with an atraumatic vascular clamp (or tourniquet). This occludes both incoming afferent blood supplies to the liver—the hepatic artery and the portal vein—to arrest torrential liver hemorrhage during trauma or parenchymal liver transection. Continuous ischemic clamp time is typically limited to 15–20 minutes to prevent warm ischemia-reperfusion injury.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 58-year-old male with resectable adenocarcinoma of the head of the pancreas is scheduled for pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple's procedure). Which sequence of anatomical reconstructions correctly restores gastrointestinal, biliary, and pancreatic continuity?
options: Pancreaticojejunostomy, followed by Hepaticojejunostomy, followed by Gastrojejunostomy (or Duodenojejunostomy)
Gastrojejunostomy first, followed by Pancreaticogastrostomy, followed by Hepaticoduodenostomy
Hepaticojejunostomy first, followed by primary Pancreaticoduodenostomy, followed by Esophagojejunostomy
Pancreaticocutaneous fistula creation followed by cholecystoenterostomy
questions.answer: Pancreaticojejunostomy, followed by Hepaticojejunostomy, followed by Gastrojejunostomy (or Duodenojejunostomy)
questions.explanation: The classic Whipple reconstruction brings a single loop of jejunum through the retrocolic window and performs the anastomoses in precise proximal-to-distal sequence: 1. Pancreaticojejunostomy (end-to-end or end-to-side, to protect the vulnerable pancreatic anastomosis from digestive enzymes); 2. Hepaticojejunostomy (biliary drainage, approx. 10–15 cm downstream); 3. Gastrojejunostomy or duodenojejunostomy (approx. 40–50 cm downstream, to prevent biliary reflux into the stomach).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 75-year-old female presents with signs of mechanical small bowel obstruction (colicky abdominal pain, distension, vomiting). An abdominal radiograph reveals the classic 'Rigler's triad'. What is Rigler's triad, and what is the underlying diagnosis?
options: Rigler's triad: Pneumoperitoneum, ascites, and pleural effusion; perforated peptic ulcer
Rigler's triad: Mechanical small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia (gas in the biliary tree), and an ectopic radio-opaque gallstone in the intestinal lumen; Gallstone ileus
Rigler's triad: Renal enlargement, ureteral calculus, and hydronephrosis; renal colic
Rigler's triad: Splenomegaly, portal hypertension, and ascites; cirrhosis
questions.answer: Rigler's triad: Mechanical small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia (gas in the biliary tree), and an ectopic radio-opaque gallstone in the intestinal lumen; Gallstone ileus
questions.explanation: Gallstone ileus occurs when a large gallstone erodes through the gallbladder wall into the adjacent duodenum via a cholecystoduodenal fistula. The stone traverses the small bowel until it impacts at the narrowest point—classically the ileocecal valve. Rigler's triad on plain radiograph or CT comprises: 1. Pneumobilia (air in the biliary tree); 2. Dilated small bowel loops indicating mechanical obstruction; 3. An aberrantly located calcified gallstone in the right iliac fossa/pelvis.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: An 18-year-old male presents with dull, poorly localized periumbilical abdominal pain of 12 hours duration that has now shifted and localized to the right iliac fossa as sharp, continuous pain. What neuroanatomical pathway explains the initial periumbilical referral of pain in acute appendicitis?
options: Somatic sensory afferents from the parietal peritoneum via the L1 iliohypogastric nerve
Visceral sympathetic afferent fibers travelling via the lesser splanchnic nerves to the T10 spinal cord segment responding to appendiceal luminal distension
Parasympathetic vagal afferents terminating in the nucleus tractus solitarius
questions.answer: Visceral sympathetic afferent fibers travelling via the lesser splanchnic nerves to the T10 spinal cord segment responding to appendiceal luminal distension
questions.explanation: Early acute appendicitis causes visceral pain due to luminal obstruction and distension. Visceral afferents from the midgut appendiceal serosa travel with sympathetic fibers in the lesser splanchnic nerves to the T10 spinal cord segment, projecting pain to the T10 dermatome (periumbilical area). Once transmural inflammation breaches the visceral peritoneum and irritates the adjacent somatic parietal peritoneum, pain shifts and localizes sharply to the right iliac fossa (somatic pain).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Where is McBurney's point anatomically located, representing the point of maximum tenderness in classic acute appendicitis?
options: Midpoint of a line joining the umbilicus and the right anterior superior iliac spine
At the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line joining the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus
At the junction of the lateral two-thirds and medial one-third of a line joining the right anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle
Two inches above the pubic symphysis in the midline
questions.answer: At the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line joining the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus
questions.explanation: McBurney's point lies at the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of the spinoumblical line (drawn between the right anterior superior iliac spine and the umbilicus). It corresponds to the anatomical base of the vermiform appendix where it arises from the posteromedial wall of the cecum.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: On clinical examination of a 24-year-old male suspected of acute appendicitis, pressure applied in the left iliac fossa elicits sharp pain referred to the right iliac fossa. What is the eponym for this clinical sign?
questions.explanation: Rovsing's sign is the elicitation of pain in the right lower quadrant when continuous palpation pressure is applied to the left lower quadrant. Pressure forces colonic gas retrogradely through the descending colon, transverse colon, and cecum, distending the inflamed cecum and appendix against the sensitive parietal peritoneum of the right iliac fossa.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In evaluating an atypical presentation of retrocecal appendicitis, which clinical sign is elicited by placing the patient in the left lateral decubitus position and passively hyperextending the right hip joint?
questions.explanation: The Psoas sign (iliopsoas test) is elicited when passive extension of the right hip stretches the psoas major muscle, or when active flexion of the right hip against resistance contracts it. Friction against an inflamed retrocecal or retrocolic appendix overlying the psoas fascia elicits deep retroperitoneal pain. The obturator sign (internal rotation of flexed hip) indicates pelvic appendicitis.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 22-year-old male has an Alvarado score calculated for suspected acute appendicitis. Which two clinical parameters in the 10-point Alvarado (MANTRELS) scoring system are awarded 2 points each, with all other parameters carrying 1 point?
options: Localized tenderness in the right lower quadrant and Leukocytosis (WBC count > 10,000/μL)
Rebound tenderness and Shift of neutrophils to the left
questions.answer: Localized tenderness in the right lower quadrant and Leukocytosis (WBC count > 10,000/μL)
questions.explanation: The Alvarado (MANTRELS) score totals 10 points: Symptoms: Migration of pain (1), Anorexia (1), Nausea/vomiting (1); Signs: Tenderness in RLQ (2 points), Rebound tenderness (1), Elevation of temperature (1); Laboratory: Leukocytosis > 10,000/μL (2 points), Shift to left of neutrophils > 75% (1). A score ≥ 7 strongly predicts acute appendicitis warranting surgical intervention.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 30-year-old male presents on day 5 of acute right iliac fossa pain with high fever. On examination, a well-defined, tender, firm, non-mobile 6-cm mass is palpated in the right iliac fossa without generalized peritonitis. Ultrasound confirms an appendicular mass (phlegmon). What is the standard classical management strategy?
options: Ochsner-Sherren conservative regimen (bed rest, IV fluids, analgesia, broad-spectrum antibiotics, serial abdominal charting) followed by interval appendectomy after 6–8 weeks
questions.answer: Ochsner-Sherren conservative regimen (bed rest, IV fluids, analgesia, broad-spectrum antibiotics, serial abdominal charting) followed by interval appendectomy after 6–8 weeks
questions.explanation: An appendicular mass comprises the inflamed appendix walled off by the greater omentum, cecum, and loops of terminal ileum. Emergency surgery in this friable, inflamed mass carries high risk of fecal fistula, iatrogenic bowel perforation, and conversion to right hemicolectomy. The Ochsner-Sherren regimen conserves the patient while resolution occurs. Failure of conservative treatment (rising pulse, spreading mass, increasing peritonitis) prompts drainage of an abscess or surgery. Interval appendectomy is typically performed 6–8 weeks later.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During open appendectomy, the surgeon uses a muscle-splitting gridiron incision. Which anatomical muscle layers and aponeuroses are divided along their respective fibers in sequence?
options: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, External oblique aponeurosis split along its fibers, Internal oblique and Transversus abdominis muscles split transversely/horizontally, Fascia transversalis, and Parietal peritoneum
Skin, Rectus sheath opened vertically, Rectus abdominis transected completely
Division of the inguinal ligament and pectineal fascia
questions.answer: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, External oblique aponeurosis split along its fibers, Internal oblique and Transversus abdominis muscles split transversely/horizontally, Fascia transversalis, and Parietal peritoneum
questions.explanation: The gridiron incision (McBurney's incision) splits abdominal wall layers in the direction of their fibers without cutting muscular tissue: external oblique aponeurosis is split downwards and medially; internal oblique and transversus abdominis are split horizontally across their muscle bellies; fascia transversalis and extraperitoneal fat are incised; and the parietal peritoneum is picked up and opened carefully between hemostats to avoid underlying cecal injury.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the single most common anatomical position of the vermiform appendix observed in clinical surgical practice?
questions.explanation: According to anatomical surveys (e.g., Wakeley's classification), the retrocecal and retrocolic position is the most common anatomical location of the vermiform appendix, occurring in approximately 65% of individuals. The second most frequent is the pelvic position (approx. 31%), followed by subcecal (approx. 2%), preileal (approx. 1%), and postileal (approx. 0.5%).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: An appendectomy is performed for acute appendicitis. Histopathology unexpectedly reveals a 1.2-cm well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor (carcinoid tumor) located at the tip of the appendix with negative surgical margins and no mesoappendiceal or vascular invasion. What further treatment is indicated?
options: Right hemicolectomy with formal mesenteric lymphadenectomy within 2 weeks
Simple appendectomy already performed is curative; no further surgery required
questions.answer: Simple appendectomy already performed is curative; no further surgery required
questions.explanation: The appendix is the most common site for gastrointestinal neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors. For appendiceal carcinoids < 1 cm located at the tip with negative margins, simple appendectomy is fully curative. Right hemicolectomy is indicated only if: tumor size is > 2 cm, the tumor is located at the base of the appendix involving the cecal margin, there is invasion of the mesoappendix > 3 mm, high mitotic index/Ki-67 > 2%, or goblet cell carcinoid histology.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A patient with generalized purulent peritonitis secondary to perforated appendicitis presents with persistent spiking fever, swinging chills, right hypochondrial tenderness, and jaundice on postoperative day 10. CT scan of the abdomen shows multiple small septic abscesses throughout the liver and thrombosis of the superior mesenteric vein. What is this severe complication named?
questions.explanation: Pylephlebitis is suppurative infective thrombophlebitis of the portal venous system arising from an uncontrolled intra-abdominal or pelvic septic focus (most commonly appendicitis or diverticulitis). Septic emboli travel from the appendicular veins via the superior mesenteric vein into the intrahepatic portal branches, leading to portal vein thrombosis, high fever, jaundice, and multiple liver abscesses.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 55-year-old female with a history of open hysterectomy presents with central colicky abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, progressive abdominal distension, and absolute constipation (failure to pass flatus and feces). Supine abdominal radiograph shows multiple dilated centrally located small bowel loops with transverse mucosal folds traversing the entire diameter of the lumen. What are these characteristic mucosal folds called?
questions.explanation: On plain abdominal radiograph, dilated small bowel loops (jejunal/ileal) are centrally positioned and exhibit valvulae conniventes (plicae circulares) which extend completely across the lumen from wall to wall at close intervals (the 'step-ladder pattern'). In contrast, large bowel loops are peripheral, have haustrations that do not completely cross the transverse diameter, and contain indentations spaced further apart.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the single most common cause of mechanical small bowel obstruction in adult patients in developed and developing countries who have previously undergone abdominal surgery?
questions.explanation: Postoperative peritoneal adhesions and bands account for approximately 60–75% of all mechanical small bowel obstructions in adults with prior abdominopelvic surgery. In unoperated virgin abdomens, strangulated or incarcerated external hernias remain the leading cause of intestinal obstruction.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 70-year-old male with chronic constipation presents with massive painless abdominal distension, vomiting, and absolute constipation. Plain abdominal radiograph demonstrates a hugely distended, ahaustral, U-shaped loop of bowel projecting from the pelvis toward the right upper quadrant ('coffee-bean sign' or bent inner tube sign). What is the diagnosis and initial emergency therapeutic intervention?
options: Sigmoid volvulus; rigid sigmoidoscopy with gentle placement of a flatus tube (derotation and decompression) if no signs of gangrene or peritonitis exist
questions.answer: Sigmoid volvulus; rigid sigmoidoscopy with gentle placement of a flatus tube (derotation and decompression) if no signs of gangrene or peritonitis exist
questions.explanation: Sigmoid volvulus (torsion of a redundant sigmoid colon on its narrow mesenteric base) produces massive colonic distension and the classic 'coffee bean sign' on X-ray. In the absence of transmural strangulation, gangrene, or peritonitis, the initial treatment of choice is non-operative detorsion via rigid or flexible sigmoidoscopy and placement of a soft rectal/flatus tube past the twisted segment, achieving immediate decompression. Elective resection is scheduled subsequently due to high recurrence rates (> 50%).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In acute mechanical closed-loop intestinal obstruction (e.g., in the presence of a competent ileocecal valve with an obstructing sigmoid cancer), which site in the gastrointestinal tract is at greatest risk of ischemic perforation according to Laplace's law?
questions.explanation: According to Laplace's law (Wall tension = Pressure × Radius), wall tension is directly proportional to the radius of the cylinder. Because the cecum has the largest diameter (greatest radius) of any segment of the colon, it experiences the highest intramural wall tension during distal closed-loop obstruction. When the cecal diameter exceeds 10–12 cm, intramural capillary perfusion ceases, predisposing to gangrenous ischemic perforation (diastatic perforation of the cecum).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 68-year-old female with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden, excruciating, generalized abdominal pain of 4 hours duration. On abdominal examination, the abdomen is soft and non-tender, with normal bowel sounds, representing 'pain out of proportion to physical findings'. Arterial blood gas shows severe metabolic acidosis with hyperlactatemia. What is the diagnosis and gold-standard imaging investigation?
options: Perforated duodenal ulcer; erect plain abdominal radiography
Acute mesenteric ischemia (superior mesenteric artery embolism); Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) of the mesenteric vessels
questions.answer: Acute mesenteric ischemia (superior mesenteric artery embolism); Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) of the mesenteric vessels
questions.explanation: Acute mesenteric ischemia (most commonly caused by an acute embolus from atrial fibrillation lodging in the superior mesenteric artery distal to the middle colic origin) classically presents with severe, unremitting abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to physical exam findings early in its course. CT angiography of the mesenteric vasculature is the diagnostic gold standard, demonstrating the arterial filling defect, bowel wall thickening or pneumatosis intestinalis.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 9-month-old infant presents with bouts of screaming, episodic inconsolable crying with drawing up of legs, vomiting, and passage of red stool mixed with mucus ('red currant jelly stool'). A sausage-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant, with emptiness in the right iliac fossa (Signe de Dance). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Intussusception is the invagination of a proximal bowel segment (intussuscipiens) into an immediately distal segment (intussusceptum), most commonly ileocolic in infants aged 3–12 months secondary to hypertrophied Peyer's patches following viral gastroenteritis. The triad of episodic colicky abdominal pain, a sausage-shaped abdominal mass with an empty right iliac fossa (Dance's sign), and passage of 'red currant jelly' stools (blood and mucus from venous engorgement) is pathognomonic. Ultrasound shows the 'target' or 'donut' sign.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male presents with recurrent painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding. A 99mTc-pertechnetate scintigraphy (Meckel's scan) is positive. What embryological structure fails to obliterate in Meckel's diverticulum, and what ectopic mucosa is most commonly responsible for ulceration and bleeding?
options: Persistent vitellointestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct; ectopic gastric mucosa
Persistent thyroglossal tract; thyroid follicular tissue
Remnant of cloacal membrane; squamous epithelium
questions.answer: Persistent vitellointestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct; ectopic gastric mucosa
questions.explanation: Meckel's diverticulum is a true congenital diverticulum arising on the antimesenteric border of the ileum (approx. 2 feet proximal to the ileocecal valve) due to failure of complete obliteration of the vitellointestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct. It frequently contains ectopic gastric mucosa (approx. 50%), which secretes acid and causes peptic ulceration and painless hemorrhage in the adjacent ileal mucosa. 99mTc-pertechnetate concentrates in ectopic gastric parietal cells.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In differentiating viable from non-viable intestine during exploratory laparotomy for strangulated mechanical obstruction, what are the standard intraoperative clinical criteria that confirm bowel viability?
options: Color changes from dark purple/black to pink, visible active peristalsis elicited by tapping or warm saline packs, and palpable or Doppler-detectable arterial pulsations in adjacent mesenteric arcades
Complete lack of bleeding when the serosa is nicked
Loss of normal glistening sheen and flaccid, thin wall
questions.answer: Color changes from dark purple/black to pink, visible active peristalsis elicited by tapping or warm saline packs, and palpable or Doppler-detectable arterial pulsations in adjacent mesenteric arcades
questions.explanation: Assessing bowel viability after releasing strangulation involves wrapping the loop in warm saline-soaked pads for 10–15 minutes and delivering 100% oxygen. Definite criteria of viability are: 1. Color: return of normal pink sheen from dark purple; 2. Peristalsis: presence of active contraction waves spontaneously or upon gentle flicking; 3. Arterial pulsations: palpable or acoustic Doppler pulsation in the marginal mesenteric arcades; 4. Bleeding: bright red active bleeding from cut serosa or margins.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 78-year-old bedridden nursing-home resident with severe Parkinson's disease presents with marked abdominal distension and obstipation. Abdominal X-ray demonstrates massive dilatation of the cecum and colon down to the rectum without an identifiable mechanical obstructing lesion on water-soluble contrast enema or CT. What is this syndrome?
questions.explanation: Ogilvie's syndrome (acute colonic pseudo-obstruction) is massive functional dilatation of the colon without an underlying mechanical obstruction, typically occurring in elderly, debilitated, hospitalized patients with neurological disorders, metabolic derangements, or trauma. It is mediated by autonomic imbalance (excess sympathetic suppression or deficient parasympathetic tone). Intravenous neostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) or colonoscopic decompression is used if cecal diameter exceeds 10–12 cm.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which vascular territory is the most common 'watershed' ischemic zone in the colon, making it exquisitely vulnerable to hypoperfusion and non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia (NOMI)?
options: Griffiths' point at the splenic flexure (junction of SMA and IMA territories) and Sudeck's point at the rectosigmoid junction
questions.answer: Griffiths' point at the splenic flexure (junction of SMA and IMA territories) and Sudeck's point at the rectosigmoid junction
questions.explanation: Watershed areas of the colon lie at the anatomical junctions between major arterial circulations where collateral marginal flow (Drummond's artery) is vulnerable: 1. Griffiths' point at the splenic flexure (watershed between the superior mesenteric artery via the middle colic and the inferior mesenteric artery via the left colic); 2. Sudeck's critical point at the rectosigmoid junction (watershed between the lowest sigmoid branch of the IMA and the superior rectal artery).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: How does the classic clinical presentation of an adenocarcinoma of the right colon (cecum and ascending colon) differ typically from an adenocarcinoma of the left colon (rectosigmoid junction)?
options: Right colon presents with early intestinal obstruction; left colon presents with painless hematemesis

Right colon (large lumen, liquid contents, exophytic polypoid growth) presents with occult blood loss, iron deficiency anemia, weakness, and a palpable mass; Left colon (narrow lumen, solid stool, annular napkin-ring growth) presents with altered bowel habits, pencil stools, and mechanical obstruction
Right colon presents strictly with bright red rectal bleeding; left colon never causes bleeding
There is no clinical or pathological difference between right and left colon malignancies
questions.answer: Right colon (large lumen, liquid contents, exophytic polypoid growth) presents with occult blood loss, iron deficiency anemia, weakness, and a palpable mass; Left colon (narrow lumen, solid stool, annular napkin-ring growth) presents with altered bowel habits, pencil stools, and mechanical obstruction
questions.explanation: Right-sided colon carcinomas typically present as fungating, ulcerating masses into a wide cecal lumen carrying liquid chyme; they bleed insidiously, presenting with profound iron deficiency anemia, lethargy, and a palpable right iliac fossa mass without early obstruction. Left-sided colon tumors are annular, infiltrating 'napkin-ring' lesions in a narrower caliber lumen containing firm stool, presenting early with change in bowel habits (alternating diarrhea and constipation), progressive obstipation, and bowel obstruction.
tags: Colorectal Carcinoma, Anal Canal and Hemorrhoids
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In performing a curative oncological resection for a primary adenocarcinoma of the cecum (Right Hemicolectomy), which vessels must be ligated flush at their origins alongside high central lymphadenectomy?
options: Left colic artery and inferior mesenteric vein
Ileocolic artery, right colic artery, and the right branch of the middle colic artery
Splenic artery and left gastroepiploic artery
Superior rectal artery and sigmoidal branches
questions.answer: Ileocolic artery, right colic artery, and the right branch of the middle colic artery
questions.explanation: A formal oncologic right hemicolectomy requires high ligation of the ileocolic artery, right colic artery, and the right branch of the middle colic artery near their take-off from the superior mesenteric artery. The resection encompasses the terminal 10–15 cm of ileum, the cecum, ascending colon, hepatic flexure, and proximal third of the transverse colon with its draining lymph nodes, followed by ileotransverse anastomosis.
tags: Colorectal Carcinoma, Anal Canal and Hemorrhoids
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In modern rectal cancer surgery, what is the surgical principle of Total Mesorectal Excision (TME) pioneered by R.J. Heald, and what distal clear surgical margin is considered oncologically safe for mid-to-low rectal adenocarcinoma?
options: Sharp, complete, en-bloc excision of the rectum and intact mesorectum within the visceral pelvic fascial envelope (the 'holy plane'), achieving at least a 1–2 cm distal mural margin and negative circumferential resection margin (CRM)
Blunt finger dissection of the rectum leaving mesorectal fat behind with a 10-cm distal margin
Removal of the bladder and prostate in all cases
questions.answer: Sharp, complete, en-bloc excision of the rectum and intact mesorectum within the visceral pelvic fascial envelope (the 'holy plane'), achieving at least a 1–2 cm distal mural margin and negative circumferential resection margin (CRM)
questions.explanation: Total Mesorectal Excision (TME) requires precise sharp dissection under direct vision along the embryological plane between the visceral mesorectal fascia and the parietal presacral fascia ('the holy plane'). Removing the intact mesorectal envelope intact prevents tumor breach and clears all perirectal lymph nodes, reducing local recurrence rates from 30% to < 5%. For mid and low rectal tumors, a distal mural clearance of 1–2 cm (and a negative circumferential resection margin > 1 mm) is oncologically acceptable.
tags: Colorectal Carcinoma, Anal Canal and Hemorrhoids
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 60-year-old male is diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the lower third of the rectum located only 1.5 cm from the anal verge, invading the external anal sphincter mechanism. What definitive radical surgical procedure is mandatory?
options: Low anterior resection (LAR) with coloanal anastomosis
Abdominoperineal Resection (APR / Miles' operation) with permanent end colostomy
questions.answer: Abdominoperineal Resection (APR / Miles' operation) with permanent end colostomy
questions.explanation: When a rectal cancer directly infiltrates the external anal sphincter or levator ani musculature, or when an adequate 1–2 cm distal margin cannot be achieved without compromising sphincteric continence, sphincter preservation is impossible. Abdominoperineal resection (APR / Miles' procedure) is required, entailing en-bloc removal of the rectum, mesorectum, anal canal, and sphincter apparatus with creation of a permanent left iliac end colostomy.

questions.prompt: At what anatomical positions around the anal circumference are primary internal hemorrhoids (piles) consistently located, corresponding to the terminal branches of the superior rectal artery?
options: 3, 7, and 11 o'clock positions (Left lateral, Right posterior, and Right anterior)
Equally distributed at all 12 radial positions
questions.answer: 3, 7, and 11 o'clock positions (Left lateral, Right posterior, and Right anterior)
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery divides into a right branch and a left branch. The left branch continues as a single vessel to supply the left lateral quadrant (3 o'clock position). The right branch subdivides into an anterior branch supplying the right anterior quadrant (11 o'clock) and a posterior branch supplying the right posterior quadrant (7 o'clock). Primary internal hemorrhoids therefore consistently occupy the 3, 7, and 11 o'clock positions in the lithotomy position.

questions.prompt: According to Banov's classification, how are 3rd-degree internal hemorrhoids defined clinically?
options: Bleed only; do not prolapse out of the anal canal
Prolapse on defecation but reduce spontaneously
Prolapse on defecation or straining and require manual digital reduction back into the anal canal
questions.answer: Prolapse on defecation or straining and require manual digital reduction back into the anal canal
questions.explanation: Internal hemorrhoids are graded as: Grade I: Prominent vascular cushions that bleed but do not prolapse; Grade II: Prolapse through the anal canal during defecation but reduce spontaneously; Grade III: Prolapse with defecation/straining and require manual replacement; Grade IV: Permanently prolapsed, irreducible, with chronic mucosal exteriorization.

questions.prompt: A 32-year-old female presents with excruciating, sharp, knife-like pain during defecation lasting for several hours afterward, accompanied by small streaks of bright red blood on toilet paper. Digital rectal examination cannot be completed due to severe anal spasm. Inspection of the posterior midline reveals a longitudinal tear with a swollen skin tag ('sentinel pile') at its lower margin and a hypertrophied anal papilla at the upper end. What is the diagnosis and gold-standard surgical treatment for chronic refractory cases?
options: Chronic anal fissure; Lateral Internal Sphincterotomy (LIS)
questions.answer: Chronic anal fissure; Lateral Internal Sphincterotomy (LIS)
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation (severe defecatory pain, bleeding, sentinel skin tag, hypertrophied papilla, and posterior midline fissure) is diagnostic of chronic fissure-in-ano. Ischemia of the posterior midline anal anoderm secondary to severe spasm and high resting tone of the internal anal sphincter prevents healing. Partial division of the lower third of the internal sphincter (Lateral Internal Sphincterotomy, Notaras technique) reduces resting anal canal pressure, restores mucosal blood flow, and achieves > 95% cure rates.

questions.prompt: According to Goodsall's Rule for anal fistulas, where does the internal opening enter the anal canal if an external fistula opening is located in the posterior perianal quadrant (posterior to a transverse line bisecting the anus)?
options: It tracks directly radially inward to the nearest crypt
It follows a curved path to open in the posterior midline at the 6 o'clock crypt
It tracks anteriorly to open at the 12 o'clock position
Goodsall's rule applies only to congenital urethral fistulas
questions.answer: It follows a curved path to open in the posterior midline at the 6 o'clock crypt
questions.explanation: Goodsall's rule states that for an external fistula opening located posterior to a transverse line drawn across the center of the anus, the fistula tract follows a curving path to enter the anal canal at the posterior midline crypt (6 o'clock position). For an external opening anterior to this line, the tract usually runs straight and radially inward to open into the crypt at that radial meridian (exception: an anterior opening > 3 cm from the verge may track to the posterior midline).

questions.prompt: What is the primary etiology and pathogenesis of an anorectal fistula (fistula-in-ano) in the cryptoglandular hypothesis formulated by Parks?
options: Primary tuberculous infection of the anoderm
Infection and suppuration of an anal gland in the intersphincteric plane discharging at the dentate line (crypt of Morgagni), which forms an abscess and then tracks to the perianal skin
Direct malignant extension from squamous cell carcinoma
Trauma from chronic constipation with direct rupture
questions.answer: Infection and suppuration of an anal gland in the intersphincteric plane discharging at the dentate line (crypt of Morgagni), which forms an abscess and then tracks to the perianal skin
questions.explanation: The cryptoglandular theory of Eisenhammer and Parks states that > 90% of anorectal abscesses and fistulae originate from infection of the anal glands. The glands arise from the crypts of Morgagni at the dentate line and penetrate into the intersphincteric plane. Obstruction of the gland duct by debris or stool causes stasis, suppuration, and intersphincteric abscess formation. As the abscess tracks downward, it produces a perianal or ischiorectal abscess, which on spontaneous rupture or inadequate drainage leaves a chronic epithelialized fistula-in-ano.

questions.prompt: A 56-year-old female presents with an exophytic, ulcerated, bleeding lesion at the anal margin. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal. What is the standard primary definitive curative treatment of choice?
options: Nigro protocol (concurrent chemoradiotherapy using external beam radiation, 5-Fluorouracil, and Mitomycin-C)
Wide local excision with permanent loop colostomy
questions.answer: Nigro protocol (concurrent chemoradiotherapy using external beam radiation, 5-Fluorouracil, and Mitomycin-C)
questions.explanation: Unlike rectal adenocarcinoma (which is surgical), primary squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal is treated with primary chemoradiotherapy (the Nigro protocol: definitive external beam radiation therapy combined with 5-fluorouracil and mitomycin-C). This achieves complete cure rates exceeding 80–90% while preserving anal sphincter function. Abdominoperineal resection (APR) is reserved for persistent or recurrent disease after chemoradiotherapy (salvage APR).
