questions.prompt: Anatomically, what are the three precise boundaries of Hesselbach's triangle, and what type of inguinal hernia traverses through this space?
options: Inferior epigastric artery laterally, lateral border of the rectus abdominis medially, and inguinal ligament inferiorly; Direct inguinal hernia
Inferior epigastric artery medially, anterior superior iliac spine laterally, and pectineal ligament inferiorly; Indirect inguinal hernia
Femoral vein laterally, lacunar ligament medially, and inguinal ligament superiorly; Femoral hernia
Internal oblique muscle superiorly, transversus abdominis inferiorly, and iliopubic tract laterally; Pantaloon hernia
questions.answer: Inferior epigastric artery laterally, lateral border of the rectus abdominis medially, and inguinal ligament inferiorly; Direct inguinal hernia
questions.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded: Laterally by the inferior epigastric vessels; Medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle (linea semilunaris); Inferiorly by the inguinal ligament (Poupart's ligament). The floor of this triangle is formed by the fascia transversalis reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon. Direct inguinal hernias protrude directly forward through the floor of Hesselbach's triangle (medial to the inferior epigastric artery).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During the clinical internal ring occlusion test in a 28-year-old male with an inguinal swelling, where is the deep (internal) inguinal ring accurately surface marked?
options: 1.25 cm (half an inch) above the midinguinal point (midpoint between anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis)
Midpoint of the inguinal ligament (midpoint between ASIS and pubic tubercle)
Two inches lateral to the umbilicus
questions.answer: 1.25 cm (half an inch) above the midinguinal point (midpoint between anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis)
questions.explanation: The deep (internal) inguinal ring is a U-shaped defect in the fascia transversalis situated 1.25 cm (half an inch) above the **midinguinal point** (the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis, where the femoral artery pulse is felt). Occluding this point with the thumb prevents an indirect hernia from descending upon coughing, whereas a direct hernia will still bulge medial to the finger.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In the open tension-free mesh repair of an inguinal hernia described by Irving Lichtenstein, what anatomical structures are used to anchor the prosthetic polypropylene mesh inferiorly and medially?
options: Inferiorly to the shelving edge of the inguinal ligament (down to the pubic tubercle with a 1.5–2 cm medial overlap) and superiorly to the conjoint tendon/internal oblique aponeurosis
Anchored directly to the femoral nerve and femoral vein
Sutured exclusively to the subcutaneous Dartos fascia
Fixed to the psoas minor tendon and iliopectineal line
questions.answer: Inferiorly to the shelving edge of the inguinal ligament (down to the pubic tubercle with a 1.5–2 cm medial overlap) and superiorly to the conjoint tendon/internal oblique aponeurosis
questions.explanation: Lichtenstein's tension-free hernioplasty places a flat polypropylene mesh (approx. 7.5 × 15 cm) over the posterior wall of the inguinal canal. The inferior border is sutured with continuous nonabsorbable suture (prolene) to the shelving margin of the inguinal ligament, starting 1.5–2 cm medial to the pubic tubercle over the rectus sheath. The superior edge is anchored to the internal oblique aponeurosis/conjoint tendon with interrupted sutures, and the lateral tails are split around the spermatic cord and tacked to the inguinal ligament.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Why is a femoral hernia associated with a substantially higher risk of incarceration, obstruction, and strangulation (up to 30–40%) compared to an indirect inguinal hernia?
options: Because the femoral canal contains the inferior epigastric artery
Because the femoral ring is small, narrow, rigid, and surrounded by unyielding ligamentous structures (lacunar ligament medially, inguinal ligament anteriorly, and pectineal ligament posteriorly)
Because femoral hernias contain only Meckel's diverticulum
Because femoral hernias lack a peritoneal sac
questions.answer: Because the femoral ring is small, narrow, rigid, and surrounded by unyielding ligamentous structures (lacunar ligament medially, inguinal ligament anteriorly, and pectineal ligament posteriorly)
questions.explanation: The femoral ring has rigid, unyielding fibrous boundaries: anteriorly the inguinal ligament, medially the sharp crescentic margin of Gimbernat's (lacunar) ligament, posteriorly Astley Cooper's (pectineal) ligament, and laterally the femoral vein. Because these boundaries are completely inelastic, any viscus herniating through this narrow aperture is subject to acute constriction, early venous congestion, and rapid progression to strangulation.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In laparoscopic preperitoneal inguinal hernia repair (TEP or TAPP), what two anatomical danger triangles must the surgeon recognize on the posterior surface of the groin to avoid major vascular catastrophe and neuropathic chronic pain?
options: Triangle of Doom (containing external iliac vessels) and Triangle of Pain (containing lateral femoral cutaneous and femoral branch of genitofemoral nerves)
Triangle of Petit and Grynfelt's triangle
questions.answer: Triangle of Doom (containing external iliac vessels) and Triangle of Pain (containing lateral femoral cutaneous and femoral branch of genitofemoral nerves)
questions.explanation: In posterior laparoscopic inguinal anatomy: 1. **Triangle of Doom**: bounded medially by the vas deferens and laterally by the spermatic vessels, with apex at the deep ring; it contains the external iliac artery and vein—tacks placed here risk fatal vascular injury. 2. **Triangle of Pain**: bounded by the spermatic vessels medially and the iliopubic tract laterally/superiorly; it contains the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh and the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve—staples or tacks here cause severe chronic inguinodynia.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 65-year-old male with an incarcerated groin hernia is taken for emergency exploration. Only a portion of the antimesenteric circumference of a loop of small bowel is trapped and strangulated in the hernia sac, with no signs of luminal bowel obstruction. What is this special type of hernia called?
questions.explanation: Richter's hernia is a hernia in which only a portion of the antimesenteric wall of the intestine is trapped in the hernia defect. Because the entire luminal continuity is not occluded, symptoms of mechanical bowel obstruction (vomiting, distension, obstipation) are typically absent, yet the pinched wall undergoes ischemia, necrosis, and perforation, often presenting insidiously.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is a 'Littre's hernia' defined as?
options: A hernia sac containing Meckel's diverticulum as its content
A hernia containing the vermiform appendix (Amyand's hernia)
A hernia containing the ovary and fallopian tube
A double loop of bowel in the sac with intermediate loop strangulated inside the abdomen (W-hernia)
questions.answer: A hernia sac containing Meckel's diverticulum as its content
questions.explanation: Littre's hernia is specifically defined as any hernia sac (inguinal, femoral, or umbilical) containing a Meckel's diverticulum. A hernia containing an inflamed appendix in an inguinal sac is Amyand's hernia (or De Garengeot's hernia if in a femoral sac). A 'W' hernia with a retrograde loop strangulated intra-abdominally is Maydl's hernia.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In a 'sliding hernia' (hernie par glissement), which retroperitoneal organ most commonly forms part of the posterior wall of the indirect hernia sac on the left side, and what on the right side?
options: Sigmoid colon on the left; Cecum and ascending colon on the right
Urinary bladder on both sides exclusively
Spleen on the left; Gallbladder on the right
Left kidney on the left; Appendix on the right
questions.answer: Sigmoid colon on the left; Cecum and ascending colon on the right
questions.explanation: A sliding hernia is one in which a partially retroperitoneal visceral organ forms a portion of the wall of the hernia sac rather than being freely contained within it. On the left side, the sigmoid colon (and mesosigmoid) is most commonly involved; on the right side, the cecum and ascending colon are typical. The urinary bladder can slide in direct hernias on either side. Care must be taken not to open the posterior wall of the sac to prevent iatrogenic enterotomy.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Where is the anatomical retroperitoneal space for sublay (Rives-Stoppa) mesh placement in the repair of large incisional ventral hernias?
options: Subcutaneous space directly beneath the dermis (onlay)
In the retrorectus plane (between the posterior surface of the rectus abdominis muscle and the posterior rectus sheath)
Intraperitoneal cavity attached directly to the small bowel serosa
Within the internal oblique muscle belly
questions.answer: In the retrorectus plane (between the posterior surface of the rectus abdominis muscle and the posterior rectus sheath)
questions.explanation: The Rives-Stoppa (retrorectus sublay) repair places a large prosthetic mesh in the avascular retromuscular space behind the rectus abdominis muscles and anterior to the posterior rectus sheath (extending down to the space of Retzius). Intra-abdominal pressure naturally holds the mesh against the anterior abdominal wall without requiring heavy fixation, separating the prosthesis from intra-abdominal viscera with low recurrence and infection rates.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: An infant presents with a small 1-cm umbilical hernia at 6 months of age. The mother states the swelling bulges outward when the infant cries but easily reduces with gentle pressure. What is the standard management?
options: Immediate emergency herniotomy with mesh placement
Reassurance and conservative observation; over 80–90% of congenital indirect umbilical hernias spontaneously close by 2 to 3 years of age
Application of an umbilical adhesive coin binder
questions.answer: Reassurance and conservative observation; over 80–90% of congenital indirect umbilical hernias spontaneously close by 2 to 3 years of age
questions.explanation: Congenital umbilical hernia in infants results from delayed contraction of the umbilical ring. The vast majority (> 80–90%) close spontaneously as the rectus abdominis muscles approximate in the midline by 2–3 years of age. Strangulation is extremely rare. Conservative observation is standard; surgical repair (simple Mayo or direct suture herniotomy) is indicated only if the hernia persists beyond 3–4 years of age, is unusually large (> 1.5–2 cm), or becomes symptomatic.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 32-year-old male presents with sudden onset of excruciating spasmodic right flank pain radiating along the course of the groin to the ipsilateral testis and inner thigh, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and microscopic hematuria. Which investigation is currently the gold-standard imaging modality of choice for confirming acute urolithiasis?
options: Non-Contrast Computed Tomography of Kidneys, Ureters, and Bladder (NCCT KUB)
questions.answer: Non-Contrast Computed Tomography of Kidneys, Ureters, and Bladder (NCCT KUB)
questions.explanation: Non-Contrast Computed Tomography of Kidneys, Ureters, and Bladder (NCCT KUB) is the diagnostic imaging gold standard for acute renal and ureteric colic (> 98% sensitivity and specificity). It visualizes virtually all urinary stones regardless of composition (including radiolucent uric acid stones, with the sole exception of rare indinavir stones), accurately measures stone size, Hounsfield density, and skin-to-stone distance, and identifies obstruction (hydronephrosis, perinephric stranding) and non-urological differentials.
tags: Urinary Calculi, BPH and Bladder Tumors
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old female with recurrent Proteus mirabilis urinary tract infections has an abdominal radiograph showing a large radio-opaque branched calculus completely filling the renal pelvis and major and minor calyces of the left kidney (Staghorn calculus). What is the chemical composition of this calculus?
options: Struvite (Triple phosphate: Magnesium ammonium phosphate with carbonate apatite)
questions.answer: Struvite (Triple phosphate: Magnesium ammonium phosphate with carbonate apatite)
questions.explanation: Staghorn calculi are infection stones composed of struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) and carbonate apatite. They form in alkaline urine (pH > 7.2) produced by urea-splitting organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Ureaplasma) that secrete urease. Urease hydrolyzes urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, raising urinary pH and supersaturating struvite.
tags: Urinary Calculi, BPH and Bladder Tumors
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the single most common chemical type of renal calculus encountered in global clinical surgical practice (approx. 70–80%), and what is its appearance on plain abdominal radiography?
options: Calcium oxalate calculus (monohydrate/dihydrate); densely radio-opaque with sharp, spiky, mulberry-like surface
Cystine calculus; faintly radiolucent ground-glass appearance
questions.answer: Calcium oxalate calculus (monohydrate/dihydrate); densely radio-opaque with sharp, spiky, mulberry-like surface
questions.explanation: Calcium stones (predominantly calcium oxalate, either monohydrate/Whewellite or dihydrate/Weddellite, often mixed with calcium phosphate) account for 75–80% of all urinary tract calculi. Because calcium has a high atomic number, they are sharply radio-opaque on plain radiography. Calcium oxalate monohydrate stones are dark, extremely hard, and jagged ('mulberry stones'), causing hematuria as they traverse the ureter.
tags: Urinary Calculi, BPH and Bladder Tumors
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 68-year-old male presents with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS): weak stream, hesitancy, terminal dribbling, intermittency, frequency, and nocturia 4 times per night. In McNeal's zonal anatomy of the prostate, in which zone does benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) characteristically originate, and where does carcinoma of the prostate most commonly develop?
options: BPH originates in the Transition Zone; Carcinoma originates in the Peripheral Zone
BPH originates in the Peripheral Zone; Carcinoma originates in the Central Zone
BPH originates in the Anterior Fibromuscular Stroma; Carcinoma originates in the Transition Zone
Both arise exclusively in the periurethral verumontanum
questions.answer: BPH originates in the Transition Zone; Carcinoma originates in the Peripheral Zone
questions.explanation: According to McNeal's zonal anatomy: BPH originates in the **Transition Zone** (surrounding the proximal prostatic urethra), explaining why even modest adenomatous enlargement causes early circumferential compression of the urethra and lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). Carcinoma of the prostate originates predominantly (70–75%) in the **Peripheral Zone** (posterolateral aspect of the gland), which explains why it is palpable on digital rectal examination (DRE) but may not produce early obstructive urinary symptoms.
tags: Urinary Calculi, BPH and Bladder Tumors
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During classical monopolar transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), non-conductive 1.5% glycine solution is used for continuous irrigation. If substantial fluid is absorbed into open venous sinuses, what life-threatening clinical syndrome (TURP syndrome) ensues, and what is its core biochemical hallmark?
options: Hypercalcemic crisis and severe metabolic alkalosis
Intravascular volume overload, dilutional hyponatremia (< 120 mEq/L), hypo-osmolality, glycine neurotoxicity (visual disturbances/blindness), and cerebral edema
questions.answer: Intravascular volume overload, dilutional hyponatremia (< 120 mEq/L), hypo-osmolality, glycine neurotoxicity (visual disturbances/blindness), and cerebral edema
questions.explanation: TURP syndrome occurs when large volumes of hypotonic non-electrolyte irrigation fluid (1.5% glycine) are absorbed through unsealed open capsular veins during prolonged resections (> 60 minutes) under high irrigant pressure. The syndrome is characterized by hypervolemia, acute dilutional hyponatremia, confusion, visual disturbances (glycine acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the retina), bradycardia, seizures, and cerebral edema. It is prevented by limiting resection time, using bipolar resection with normal saline, and maintaining low irrigation bags.
tags: Urinary Calculi, BPH and Bladder Tumors
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old male chronic smoker presents with recurrent, painless, total hematuria with the passage of worm-like clots. Urine cytology is positive for malignant cells. Cystoscopy shows a papillary exophytic growth in the lateral bladder wall. What is the most common histological type of bladder cancer in India and the Western world?
questions.explanation: Urothelial carcinoma (formerly transitional cell carcinoma) accounts for over 90–95% of all bladder cancers. Painless, intermittent, gross total hematuria is the cardinal presenting sign in > 80% of patients. Squamous cell carcinoma accounts for < 5% generally, though it is the predominant histological subtype in areas endemic for Schistosoma haematobium infection due to chronic irritation.
tags: Urinary Calculi, BPH and Bladder Tumors
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In a patient undergoing transurethral resection of a bladder tumor (TURBT), histopathology reveals high-grade urothelial carcinoma invading deeply into the muscularis propria (detrusor muscle layer, stage T2). What is the standard curative treatment for muscle-invasive bladder cancer?
options: Repeated TURBT with intravesical BCG immunotherapy alone
Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy followed by Radical Cystectomy with bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy and urinary diversion (e.g., ileal conduit or orthotopic neobladder)
Oral targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors only
External beam radiation without lymph node evaluation
questions.answer: Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy followed by Radical Cystectomy with bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy and urinary diversion (e.g., ileal conduit or orthotopic neobladder)
questions.explanation: Bladder cancers are stratified into non-muscle-invasive (NMIBC: Ta, T1, CIS) and muscle-invasive (MIBC: T2, T3, T4). NMIBC is treated by TURBT followed by intravesical chemotherapy/BCG. Once tumor penetrates the muscularis propria (Stage T2, muscle-invasive), local TURBT is inadequate; the standard of care is neoadjuvant cisplatin-based polychemotherapy followed by radical cystectomy (including prostate/seminal vesicles in men, uterus/anterior vagina in women) with bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy and urinary diversion.
tags: Urinary Calculi, BPH and Bladder Tumors
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the classical triad of clinical presentation in Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC / Grawitz's tumor), and what percentage of patients present with all three features simultaneously?
options: Flank pain, palpable abdominal mass, and gross hematuria; seen in only 10–15% of patients (Too late triad)
Fever, jaundice, and weight loss; seen in 80% of patients
Oliguria, hypertension, and edema; seen in 90% of patients
Dysuria, frequency, and strangury; seen in 50% of patients
questions.answer: Flank pain, palpable abdominal mass, and gross hematuria; seen in only 10–15% of patients (Too late triad)
questions.explanation: The classic Guyon's triad of renal cell carcinoma consists of: 1. Gross hematuria; 2. Flank pain; 3. Palpable abdominal/flank mass. Today, more than 60% of RCCs are discovered incidentally on cross-sectional imaging for unrelated indications (incidentalomas). The complete triad occurs in only 10–15% of cases and almost always indicates locally advanced or metastatic disease (hence termed the 'too-late triad').
tags: Urinary Calculi, BPH and Bladder Tumors
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 55-year-old male presents with a new-onset, non-tender, non-reducible left-sided varicocele that does NOT decompress when he assumes the supine position. What underlying intra-abdominal pathology must be urgently ruled out?
options: Left-sided renal cell carcinoma with tumor thrombus invading the left renal vein and obstructing the left testicular vein
Deep vein thrombosis of the femoral vein
questions.answer: Left-sided renal cell carcinoma with tumor thrombus invading the left renal vein and obstructing the left testicular vein
questions.explanation: The left testicular (gonadal) vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle, whereas the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. A left-sided varicocele that is sudden in onset, non-collapsible in the recumbent position, or occurs in an older man is a clinical red flag for a retroperitoneal mass or left renal cell carcinoma with tumor thrombus obstructing the left renal vein, impeding venous outflow from the left testicular vein.
tags: Urinary Calculi, BPH and Bladder Tumors
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In managing a 28-year-old male presenting with a hard, painless, non-transilluminant testicular mass, scrotal ultrasound confirms an intratesticular lesion. Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and beta-hCG are elevated. Why is transscrotal needle biopsy strictly contraindicated?
options: Needle biopsy carries a high risk of developing acute bacterial orchitis

Transscrotal biopsy breaches the anatomical scrotal barriers, altering lymphatic drainage from retroperitoneal nodes to inguinal nodes and causing local tumor seeding; diagnosis and management require radical high inguinal orchiectomy
The testicular parenchyma does not yield diagnostic cytological material
Needle biopsy invariably triggers testicular torsion
questions.answer: Transscrotal biopsy breaches the anatomical scrotal barriers, altering lymphatic drainage from retroperitoneal nodes to inguinal nodes and causing local tumor seeding; diagnosis and management require radical high inguinal orchiectomy
questions.explanation: The testes develop in the retroperitoneum and maintain their primary lymphatic drainage to the para-aortic/paracaval retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Scrotal skin, however, drains to superficial inguinal lymph nodes. Any incisional or needle violation of the scrotum breaches the tunica dartos and scrotal lymphatic watershed, contaminating the scrotal skin and rerouting tumor metastasis to inguinal lymph node basins. All suspected testicular tumors must be accessed via an inguinal incision with early vascular control at the deep ring (radical high inguinal orchiectomy).
tags: Urinary Calculi, BPH and Bladder Tumors
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male is brought to the emergency room following blunt abdominal trauma from a steering-wheel impact. He is hemodynamically stable. Contrast-enhanced CT reveals a subcapsular splenic hematoma involving 35% of the surface area and a 2.5-cm parenchymal laceration not involving trabecular vessels. According to the AAST splenic injury scale, what grade of injury is this?
questions.explanation: According to the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) Splenic Injury Scale: Grade I: Subcapsular hematoma < 10% surface area, laceration < 1 cm depth; Grade II: Subcapsular hematoma 10–50% surface area, parenchymal laceration 1–3 cm depth not involving trabecular vessels; Grade III: Subcapsular hematoma > 50% surface area, parenchymal laceration > 3 cm depth or involving trabecular vessels; Grade IV: Laceration involving segmental or hilar vessels producing > 25% devascularization; Grade V: Completely shattered spleen or hilar vascular avulsion.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Following splenectomy, patients are at lifelong risk of Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection (OPSI). Which triad of encapsulated bacteria is primarily responsible for OPSI, requiring mandatory pre-splenectomy or early postoperative immunization?
options: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b
Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Proteus mirabilis
Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Clostridium difficile
Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Salmonella typhi, and Shigella sonnei
questions.answer: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b
questions.explanation: The spleen is essential for phagocytosis of unopsonized encapsulated bacteria via splenic macrophages and for IgM memory B-cell generation. In asplenic individuals, encapsulated organisms can rapidly cause fatal bacteremia and septic shock (OPSI, with mortality up to 50–70%). The three primary pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae (approx. 50–70%), Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b. Patients require vaccination against all three pathogens (optimally 2 weeks prior to elective surgery or 14 days post-emergency splenectomy).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During elective splenectomy, which vascular structures located in the gastrosplenic ligament must be carefully ligated and divided without compromising the greater curvature of the stomach?
options: Short gastric arteries (vasa brevia) and left gastroepiploic vessels
Splenic artery trunk at the celiac axis
questions.answer: Short gastric arteries (vasa brevia) and left gastroepiploic vessels
questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic ligament connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the splenic hilum. It contains the short gastric arteries (4 to 6 branches arising from the splenic artery) and the left gastroepiploic vessels. When dividing the short gastric vessels, the surgeon must place ties well away from the gastric wall to prevent ischemic necrosis of the gastric fundus and catastrophic gastric fistula.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: On peripheral blood smear examination 4 weeks following splenectomy, which characteristic erythrocyte inclusion bodies are routinely observed due to the absence of the splenic 'pitting' function?
options: Auer rods in circulating myeloid precursor cells
Russell bodies in immunoglobulin-producing plasma cells
Döhle bodies in the cytoplasm of neutrophils
questions.explanation: The normal spleen removes intraerythrocytic inclusions through its specialized filtration/pitting function in the cords of Billroth without destroying the red blood cell. Following splenectomy, characteristic cellular inclusions persist in circulation: Howell-Jolly bodies (basophilic nuclear DNA fragments), Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin), Pappenheimer bodies (iron granules), along with target cells and acanthocytes.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 22-year-old female presents with severe recurrent epistaxis, petechiae, and a platelet count of 18,000/μL. Bone marrow shows megakaryocytic hyperplasia, and anti-platelet IgG antibodies are present, confirming Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP). First-line high-dose corticosteroid and IVIG therapies fail. If splenectomy is performed for refractory ITP, why must a meticulous search for an accessory spleen (splenunculus) be carried out?
options: Because an overlooked accessory spleen will rapidly hypertrophy and cause disease recurrence in up to 15% of patients
Because accessory spleens invariably undergo malignant transformation
Because accessory spleens cause acute portal hypertension
Because accessory spleens secrete excessive erythropoietin
questions.answer: Because an overlooked accessory spleen will rapidly hypertrophy and cause disease recurrence in up to 15% of patients
questions.explanation: In hematological conditions where splenectomy is performed for antibody-mediated cytopenia (e.g., ITP, hereditary spherocytosis), accessory spleens (splenunculi, present in 15–20% of the population, most commonly in the splenic hilum, gastrosplenic ligament, or greater omentum) must be scrupulously identified and excised. If left behind, an accessory spleen can undergo compensatory hypertrophy under reticuloendothelial drive, causing late relapse of thrombocytopenia.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old female is scheduled for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Prior to surgery, the surgeon discusses the indication, surgical procedure, common and serious potential complications (including bile duct injury and conversion to open procedure), alternatives, and the consequences of not undergoing surgery. The patient understands, asks relevant questions, and signs the consent form voluntarily. Which type of consent has been legally and ethically obtained?
questions.explanation: Informed consent requires providing adequate information regarding diagnosis, proposed procedure, alternatives, potential risks and benefits, and consequences of refusing treatment, ensuring the patient possesses capacity and gives voluntary agreement without coercion.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In an operative theatre, a surgeon finishes an appendectomy and removes soiled laparotomy sponges, gauzes, and human tissue specimens. According to current Biomedical Waste Management guidelines, into which color-coded container must the contaminated anatomical human tissue and cotton gauze dressings be discarded?
options: Blue cardboard container with leak-proof liner
questions.explanation: Human anatomical tissues, soiled cotton dressings, plasters, swabs, and linen contaminated with blood or body fluids are categorized under Yellow category bags for incineration or plasma pyrolysis.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During a monthly surgical department meeting, the team undertakes a systematic critical analysis of surgical site infection (SSI) rates over the preceding six months against recognized national benchmarks, identifies a lack of timely prophylactic antibiotic administration, implements an automated checklist, and re-evaluates infection rates after three months. What quality improvement process does this sequence exemplify?
options: Morbidity and mortality root cause analysis
questions.explanation: A clinical audit cycle involves choosing a topic, setting standards, measuring current performance against established standards, identifying deficiencies, implementing change, and re-auditing to complete the audit loop.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Where should contaminated disposable surgical scalpels, disposable trocars, suture needles, and surgical blade fragments be discarded immediately following skin closure?
questions.explanation: Contaminated sharps including needles, scalpels, surgical blades, and contaminated sharp metal items must be segregated into white translucent, puncture-proof, tamper-proof containers to undergo dry heat sterilization or autoclaving followed by shredding.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 22-year-old unconscious male is brought to the casualty following polytrauma with active hemoperitoneum and profound hypotension (BP 60/40 mmHg). No relatives or legal surrogates are present. Emergency laparotomy is required to save his life. Which legal and ethical principle empowers the surgical team to proceed without waiting for next of kin?
questions.explanation: Under the doctrine of emergency and necessity, when a patient lacks decision-making capacity and immediate surgical intervention is essential to preserve life or prevent grave permanent damage, treatment can be provided without formal consent.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) Surgical Safety Checklist, which critical pause takes place immediately before the skin incision?
questions.explanation: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist comprises three phases: 'Sign In' (before induction of anaesthesia), 'Time Out' (after induction and immediately prior to skin incision), and 'Sign Out' (before any member of the surgical team leaves the operating room).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which of the following is considered an absolute contraindication for selecting an elective surgical procedure as day-care (ambulatory) surgery?
options: Controlled hypertension on a single drug
Lack of a responsible adult companion at home for 24 hours postoperatively
questions.answer: Lack of a responsible adult companion at home for 24 hours postoperatively
questions.explanation: Social criteria are paramount in day-care surgery: the patient must have a responsible adult escort to accompany them home, care for them for at least 24 hours, and have convenient telephone access and rapid transport to emergency facilities.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 58-year-old male with chronic ischemic heart disease is on lifelong aspirin (75 mg/day). He is scheduled for elective open mesh repair of an uncomplicated inguinal hernia. What is the standard guideline regarding perioperative continuation of his low-dose aspirin therapy?
options: Stop aspirin 14 days before surgery and bridge with heparin
Continue low-dose aspirin perioperatively because cardiovascular risk outweighs bleeding risk
Stop aspirin 7 days before surgery and do not bridge
Switch aspirin to clopidogrel 3 days prior to surgery
questions.answer: Continue low-dose aspirin perioperatively because cardiovascular risk outweighs bleeding risk
questions.explanation: In non-cardiac low-to-moderate bleeding risk surgeries like hernia repair, low-dose aspirin (monotherapy) used for secondary cardiovascular prevention is continued perioperatively to prevent adverse thromboembolic and cardiac events.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: According to Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols, what is the recommended preoperative fasting guideline for elective procedures in patients without delayed gastric emptying?
options: Fasting midnight for all solids and liquids (nil by mouth)
Clear fluids permitted up to 2 hours, and light solids up to 6 hours before induction
Clear fluids permitted up to 30 minutes, solids up to 4 hours
Fasting 12 hours for liquids, 24 hours for solids
questions.answer: Clear fluids permitted up to 2 hours, and light solids up to 6 hours before induction
questions.explanation: ERAS protocols recommend avoiding prolonged dehydration and catabolism by permitting clear carbohydrate-rich fluids up to 2 hours before anaesthesia induction and light meals/solids up to 6 hours before surgery.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 64-year-old male with chronic COPD is scheduled for elective major abdominal surgery. Which of the following preoperative interventions has the greatest documented impact on reducing postoperative pulmonary complications (atelectasis and pneumonia)?
options: Cessation of smoking for at least 4 to 8 weeks prior to surgery and preoperative incentive spirometry
Routine prophylactic amoxicillin-clavulanate starting 3 days before surgery
Preoperative systemic corticosteroid pulse therapy for 5 days
Cessation of smoking 24 hours prior to surgery
questions.answer: Cessation of smoking for at least 4 to 8 weeks prior to surgery and preoperative incentive spirometry
questions.explanation: Smoking cessation for at least 4 to 8 weeks before elective major surgery significantly reduces postoperative respiratory complications by allowing ciliary clearance and airway mucus recovery. Smoking cessation < 24-48 hours only reduces carboxyhemoglobin.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What are the standard operational parameters (temperature, pressure, and exposure time) for autoclaving wrapped surgical steel instruments?
questions.explanation: Moist heat sterilization in a standard gravity displacement autoclave requires saturated steam at 121°C (250°F) at a pressure of 15 pounds per square inch (psi) holding for at least 15 to 20 minutes to eliminate all vegetative organisms and bacterial spores.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the primary chemical agent used for high-level disinfection and cold sterilization of heat-sensitive optical endoscopic and laparoscopic instruments (e.g. laparoscopes, choledochoscopes)?
questions.explanation: Activated 2% buffered alkaline glutaraldehyde (with an exposure time of 20-30 minutes for high-level disinfection, or up to 10 hours for complete sporicidal sterilization) is the benchmark chemical disinfectant for heat-sensitive optical and flexible/rigid endoscopes.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 52-year-old female is undergoing an elective right hemicolectomy for colon adenocarcinoma. When should the single intravenous dose of prophylactic antibiotic (e.g., cefazolin plus metronidazole) be administered to achieve maximum tissue antimicrobial levels during surgical incision?
options: The evening prior to surgery at bedtime
At the time of admission in the preoperative ward 4 hours before surgery
Within 60 minutes prior to surgical skin incision (during induction of anaesthesia)
Immediately upon skin closure at the end of the operation
questions.answer: Within 60 minutes prior to surgical skin incision (during induction of anaesthesia)
questions.explanation: Prophylactic antibiotics must achieve peak bactericidal tissue concentrations at the exact moment of skin incision. Administering the IV dose within 60 minutes prior to incision (usually at induction of anaesthesia) is standard practice.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) wound classification, an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy for chronic calculus cholecystitis with minor controlled bile spillage from the gallbladder during extraction falls under which wound class?
questions.explanation: Class II (Clean-contaminated) wounds involve elective, controlled entry into the respiratory, alimentary, genital, or urinary tract without unusual contamination or gross spillage.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the biological indicator organism used to validate the efficacy of ethylene oxide (EtO) sterilization and dry heat sterilization?
questions.explanation: Bacillus atrophaeus (formerly Bacillus subtilis var. niger) spores are used for testing dry heat and ethylene oxide gas sterilization, whereas Geobacillus stearothermophilus is the biological indicator for steam autoclaves.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.topic: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.topicTitle: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.prompt: Following major surgical trauma, the neuroendocrine-metabolic response is classically divided into the 'ebb' and 'flow' phases (Cuthbertson classification). Which of the following features characterizes the initial 'ebb' phase?
options: Hyperthermia, tachycardia, and peak protein catabolism
Marked negative nitrogen balance with maximal gluconeogenesis
Hypovolemia, decreased metabolic rate, depressed core temperature, and reduced oxygen consumption
Sustained hyperglycemia mediated by profound insulin resistance
questions.answer: Hypovolemia, decreased metabolic rate, depressed core temperature, and reduced oxygen consumption
questions.explanation: The initial 'ebb phase' (typically lasting 24-48 hours after injury) is characterized by reduced cardiac output, depressed oxygen consumption, hypothermia, and hypoperfusion as the body prioritizes conserving blood volume and hemodynamic stability.
tags: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.topic: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.topicTitle: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.prompt: A 62-year-old severely malnourished patient with long-standing esophageal cancer and a 20% weight loss over 3 months is started on aggressive high-carbohydrate total parenteral nutrition (TPN). On day 3, the patient develops severe muscle weakness, cardiac dysrhythmias, and respiratory failure. What electrolyte abnormality is the hallmark cause of this condition (refeeding syndrome)?
questions.explanation: Refeeding syndrome occurs when carbohydrate reintroduction stimulates high insulin secretion, driving phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells to form ATP and phosphorylated glycolytic intermediates. Severe hypophosphatemia results in diaphragmatic weakness, arrhythmias, and death.
tags: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.topic: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.topicTitle: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.prompt: Why is enteral nutrition (EN) preferred over total parenteral nutrition (TPN) whenever the gastrointestinal tract is functional in surgical patients?
options: Enteral nutrition provides faster positive nitrogen balance than parenteral nutrition
Enteral nutrition preserves intestinal mucosal architecture, prevents bacterial translocation, and carries lower infection risks
Enteral nutrition requires zero monitoring of blood glucose levels
Enteral nutrition completely eliminates hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
questions.answer: Enteral nutrition preserves intestinal mucosal architecture, prevents bacterial translocation, and carries lower infection risks
questions.explanation: Enteral feeding provides luminal nutrients to enterocytes, maintains gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT), prevents mucosal atrophy, decreases bacterial translocation across the mucosal barrier, and avoids central venous catheter infections.
tags: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.topic: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.topicTitle: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.prompt: What is the standard daily maintenance caloric and protein requirement for a stable adult postoperative surgical patient?
questions.explanation: Standard maintenance in a surgical patient requires 25 to 30 kcal/kg/day of total non-protein energy and 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day of protein (yielding a non-protein calorie-to-nitrogen ratio of approximately 100:1 to 150:1).
tags: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.topic: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.topicTitle: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.prompt: Which specific conditionally essential amino acid is the primary metabolic fuel for enterocytes, colonocytes, and rapidly dividing lymphocytes in surgical stress states?
questions.explanation: Glutamine is the principal energy substrate for enterocytes and immune cells. During acute surgical trauma, sepsis, or critical catabolism, endogenous stores rapidly deplete, making glutamine conditionally essential.
tags: Nutritional Support & Metabolic Response to Injury
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) Analgesic Ladder, what is the appropriate stepped escalation for treating moderate acute postoperative pain (Step 2) not controlled by paracetamol alone?
options: Switch directly to intravenous fentanyl infusion
Add a weak opioid (e.g. tramadol or codeine) combined with non-opioid analgesics
questions.answer: Add a weak opioid (e.g. tramadol or codeine) combined with non-opioid analgesics
questions.explanation: The WHO analgesic ladder recommends: Step 1 = Non-opioids (paracetamol, NSAIDs); Step 2 (Moderate pain) = Weak opioid (tramadol, codeine) +/- non-opioids; Step 3 (Severe pain) = Strong opioid (morphine, fentanyl, hydromorphone).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) utilizing intravenous morphine, what is the fundamental purpose of programming a 'lockout interval'?
options: To prevent the pump from battery exhaustion
To ensure peak drug effect is attained before the patient can administer a subsequent dose, preventing opioid overdose
To restrict total analgesic duration to under 12 hours
To administer an automatic continuous basal infusion
questions.answer: To ensure peak drug effect is attained before the patient can administer a subsequent dose, preventing opioid overdose
questions.explanation: The lockout interval (typically 5 to 10 minutes for IV morphine) prevents the patient from redosing before the previous dose has achieved its peak clinical central nervous system effect, thereby avoiding cumulative drug toxicity and respiratory depression.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the primary rationale for utilizing multimodal (balanced) analgesia in postoperative surgical protocols (ERAS)?
options: To eliminate the need for postoperative vital sign monitoring
To combine drugs acting through distinct mechanisms, maximizing analgesia while minimizing opioid requirements and adverse effects
To substitute oral medications exclusively with epidural catheters
To accelerate suture tensile strength absorption
questions.answer: To combine drugs acting through distinct mechanisms, maximizing analgesia while minimizing opioid requirements and adverse effects
questions.explanation: Multimodal analgesia combines agents with differing mechanisms (e.g., paracetamol, NSAIDs, gabapentinoids, local anesthetic nerve blocks, and weak opioids), achieving synergistic analgesia while reducing opioid consumption, postoperative nausea/vomiting, and ileus.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 56-year-old postoperative patient receiving continuous thoracic epidural analgesia with bupivacaine and fentanyl complains of numbness ascending to the nipple line, accompanied by a sudden drop in blood pressure to 80/50 mmHg and heart rate of 52 bpm. What is the diagnosis and immediate management?
options: High sympathetic thoracic blockade; administer IV fluids, ephedrine/atropine, and titrate down the infusion
questions.answer: High sympathetic thoracic blockade; administer IV fluids, ephedrine/atropine, and titrate down the infusion
questions.explanation: Sensory block up to T4 (nipple level) results in significant thoracic sympathetic chain blockade, loss of vasomotor tone (vasodilation), and blockade of cardioaccelerator fibers (T1-T4), manifesting as hypotension and bradycardia. Treatment involves IV fluids, alpha/beta-agonists, and dose reduction.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which regional fascial plane block is widely utilized to provide somatic analgesia for the anterior abdominal wall in midline exploratory laparotomies?
options: Transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block or rectus sheath block
questions.answer: Transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block or rectus sheath block
questions.explanation: TAP blocks and bilateral rectus sheath blocks deposit local anesthetic in the neurovascular plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis, targeting anterior rami of intercostal nerves T7-L1 to provide somatic analgesia for the abdominal wall.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the standard definition of a 'Massive Blood Transfusion' in an adult surgical patient?
options: Transfusion of > 2 units of packed red blood cells within 24 hours
Transfusion of >= 10 units of packed red blood cells in 24 hours (or replacement of >= 1 circulating blood volume within 24 hours)
Transfusion of any amount of platelets within 6 hours
Infusion of 4 units of fresh frozen plasma in 8 hours
questions.answer: Transfusion of >= 10 units of packed red blood cells in 24 hours (or replacement of >= 1 circulating blood volume within 24 hours)
questions.explanation: Massive blood transfusion is traditionally defined as the replacement of >= 10 units of packed red blood cells in 24 hours, or the transfusion of >= 4 units within 1 hour, or replacing 50% of total blood volume in 3 hours.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Within 2 hours of initiating a blood transfusion, a 48-year-old female develops acute dyspnea, hypoxemia (SpO2 84%), tachycardia, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray. Her central venous pressure (CVP) and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) are normal (< 12 mmHg), and no signs of circulatory volume overload or elevated JVP are evident. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: TRALI is characterized by non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema with acute hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 < 300) and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates within 6 hours of transfusion without circulatory overload. It is mediated by anti-HLA or anti-HNA donor antibodies activating recipient neutrophils.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During rapid massive blood transfusion of cold, stored bank blood, which of the following biochemical and physiological complications is most likely to develop?
questions.explanation: Stored blood accumulates potassium from erythrocyte lysis (hyperkalemia) and contains citrate preservative which chelates ionized calcium causing hypocalcemia. Rapid cold blood infusion causes hypothermia.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the single most critical immediate step if an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR) is suspected intraoperatively?
options: Slow the infusion rate to 10 drops per minute
Immediately stop the transfusion and maintain IV access with normal saline
Administer 100 mg hydrocortisone and continue transfusion
Infuse two units of fresh frozen plasma immediately
questions.answer: Immediately stop the transfusion and maintain IV access with normal saline
questions.explanation: The moment an acute hemolytic reaction is suspected, the transfusion must be stopped immediately. IV access is preserved using 0.9% normal saline while notifying the blood bank and initiating supportive care to prevent renal shutdown and DIC.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the primary operational ratio of Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBC) : Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) : Platelets in contemporary damage-control resuscitation for traumatic hemorrhagic shock?
questions.explanation: Modern balanced damage-control resuscitation protocols (such as PROPPR trial guidelines) employ a 1:1:1 ratio of PRBCs, FFPs, and platelets to reconstitute whole blood and prevent trauma-induced coagulopathy.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 40-year-old male with persistent vomiting from pyloric stenosis presents with dehydration. Arterial blood gas (ABG) shows pH 7.52, PaCO2 48 mmHg, and HCO3- 36 mEq/L. Serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L and chloride is 82 mEq/L. Urine examination reveals acidic pH (paradoxical aciduria). What is the underlying acid-base and electrolyte disturbance?
options: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
questions.answer: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
questions.explanation: Loss of gastric HCl leads to hypochloremia and metabolic alkalosis. As volume depletion activates aldosterone, the distal renal tubules exchange sodium for potassium and hydrogen ions. In severe hypokalemia, H+ is preferentially excreted in urine, producing paradoxical aciduria.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the standard intravenous crystalloid of choice for resuscitating hypovolemic surgical shock, and why is large-volume 0.9% normal saline resuscitation avoided?
options: 5% Dextrose, because it provides prompt cellular calories
Balanced crystalloid (e.g. Ringer's Lactate / Hartmann's solution); large volume 0.9% saline causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and renal vasoconstriction
0.45% Saline with 20 mEq KCl; saline causes hypochloremia
Colloid gelatins; balanced crystalloids cause hypothermia
questions.answer: Balanced crystalloid (e.g. Ringer's Lactate / Hartmann's solution); large volume 0.9% saline causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and renal vasoconstriction
questions.explanation: 0.9% Normal Saline contains 154 mEq/L of chloride, which exceeds normal plasma chloride (96-106 mEq/L). Infusing large volumes produces hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, reduced renal blood flow, and renal impairment.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 55-year-old postoperative patient with severe acute pancreatitis develops oliguria and serum potassium rises to 6.8 mEq/L. ECG reveals tall peaked T waves and widening of the QRS complex. What is the immediate first-line pharmacological agent administered to protect the myocardium against lethal ventricular arrhythmias?
options: Intravenous 10% Calcium gluconate (10 mL over 5-10 minutes)
questions.answer: Intravenous 10% Calcium gluconate (10 mL over 5-10 minutes)
questions.explanation: Intravenous calcium gluconate immediately antagonizes the membrane excitability effects of hyperkalemia and stabilizes cardiac myocytes without altering serum potassium concentration. Insulin-dextrose and beta-2 agonists are then used to shift potassium intracellularly.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the daily maintenance fluid requirement for a healthy 60-kg adult using the standard 4-2-1 hourly rule (or ~30 mL/kg/day)?
questions.explanation: Using 30-35 mL/kg/day or the 4-2-1 rule (40 mL/hr for first 10 kg + 20 mL/hr for second 10 kg + 1 mL/kg/hr for remaining 40 kg = 100 mL/hr), the 24-hour maintenance volume is 2400 mL/day, containing approximately 1-2 mmol/kg/day sodium and 1 mmol/kg/day potassium.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In correcting chronic severe symptomatic hyponatremia (serum Na+ < 118 mEq/L), why must the rate of sodium correction not exceed 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours?
options: To prevent acute pulmonary capillary leak syndrome
To avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis)
To prevent cerebral edema and uncal herniation
questions.answer: To avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis)
questions.explanation: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia causes rapid fluid shifts out of brain cells, resulting in osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis) with dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, and coma.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old carpenter presents with acute throbbing pain and swelling of the right index finger 4 days after a puncture wound. Examination reveals uniform symmetrical sausage-like swelling, slight flexion of the digit at rest, marked tenderness along the entire flexor tendon sheath, and excruciating pain upon passive extension of the finger. What clinical sign-complex is present?
options: Felon's signs of closed pulp infection
Kanavel's four cardinal signs of acute flexor tenosynovitis
Paronychia signs of eponychial fold collection
questions.answer: Kanavel's four cardinal signs of acute flexor tenosynovitis
questions.explanation: Kanavel's four cardinal signs of acute suppurative flexor tenosynovitis are: (1) symmetrical sausage-like swelling of the digit, (2) flexed posture at rest, (3) tenderness along the anatomic course of the flexor sheath, and (4) severe pain elicited by passive extension of the finger.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 42-year-old manual laborer presents with painful throbbing swelling of the terminal pulp of the right thumb. On examination, the pulp is tense, erythematous, exquisitely tender, and indurated. Why is urgent surgical decompression essential in a felon (whitlow)?
options: To prevent ascending digital nerve neuroma formation
Because vertical fibrous septa create a closed compartment, risking ischemic necrosis and osteomyelitis of the distal phalanx
To prevent spontaneous rupture into the midpalmar space
To obtain immediate skin biopsy for malignant transformation
questions.answer: Because vertical fibrous septa create a closed compartment, risking ischemic necrosis and osteomyelitis of the distal phalanx
questions.explanation: The pulp of the distal phalanx contains strong vertical fibrous septa anchoring skin to the periosteum. Increased compartment pressure from pus rapidly compromises microvascular perfusion to the distal phalanx, resulting in ischemic necrosis and terminal phalangeal osteomyelitis.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 35-year-old agricultural worker from South India presents with chronic, painless, progressive swelling of the right foot with multiple discharging sinuses. The discharge contains visible granular particles ('sulfur granules' / black grains). X-rays reveal soft tissue swelling with periosteal reaction and 'dot-in-circle' signs on MRI. What is the classic condition?
questions.explanation: Madura foot (mycetoma) is a chronic granulomatous infection of the subcutaneous tissue, characterized by the clinical triad of: painless subcutaneous mass, multiple sinuses discharging characteristic pigmented grains (eumycotic or actinomycotic), and progressive destruction of bone and fascial planes.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 40-year-old farmer presents with a firm, indurated swelling at the angle of the jaw following dental extraction, which breaks down into multiple discharging sinuses. Gram stain of the purulent discharge reveals filamentous, branching Gram-positive anaerobic bacilli with sulfur granules. What is the definitive first-line antibiotic regimen?
options: High-dose intravenous crystalline penicillin G for 2 to 6 weeks followed by oral amoxicillin for 6 to 12 months
questions.answer: High-dose intravenous crystalline penicillin G for 2 to 6 weeks followed by oral amoxicillin for 6 to 12 months
questions.explanation: Cervicofacial actinomycosis caused by Actinomyces israelii requires prolonged antibiotic therapy due to extensive avascular fibrous induration. The treatment of choice is high-dose IV penicillin G (18-24 million units/day) for 2 to 6 weeks, followed by oral penicillin or amoxicillin for 6 to 12 months.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: An infection originating in the flexor synovial sheath of the little finger (fifth digit) frequently spreads directly into which space and can communicate with the radial bursa to form a 'horseshoe abscess'?
options: Lumbrical canal of the second digit
questions.explanation: The digital synovial sheath of the little finger is continuous proximally with the ulnar bursa in over 80% of individuals. Because the ulnar bursa often communicates with the radial bursa (sheath of flexor pollicis longus), suppurative tenosynovitis readily tracks across, forming a classic horseshoe abscess.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 52-year-old male presents with a chronic, shallow ulcer above the medial malleolus of the right lower leg. The ulcer floor shows healthy red granulation tissue, the edges are sloping, and surrounding skin demonstrates lipodermatosclerosis and brownish hyperpigmentation. Dorsal pedal pulses are easily palpable. What is the primary etiology?
questions.explanation: Venous ulcers typically occur in the 'gaiter area' (medially above the malleolus), featuring sloping edges, shallow granulated base, and surrounding stasis changes like hemosiderin hyperpigmentation, stasis eczema, and lipodermatosclerosis.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 60-year-old long-standing diabetic male presents with a deep, painless, punched-out ulcer over the plantar aspect of the first metatarsophalangeal head. The ulcer is surrounded by thick hyperkeratotic callus, and monofilament testing demonstrates absence of protective sensation. Peripheral pulses are palpable. What type of ulcer is this?
questions.explanation: Neuropathic ulcers occur on weight-bearing pressure points of the plantar foot (metatarsal heads, heel) in diabetic patients with sensory peripheral neuropathy. They are painless, circular, 'punched out' with surrounding callous hyperkeratosis, while arterial perfusion is preserved.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 75-year-old bedridden patient in the intensive care unit is found to have a full-thickness skin loss over the sacrum with visible subcutaneous fat and slough, but no exposure of bone, tendon, or muscle. According to the National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel (NPIAP) staging system, what stage pressure injury is present?
questions.explanation: Stage 3 pressure injury involves full-thickness tissue loss with visible adipose tissue in the ulcer, potentially with granulation and slough; however, bone, tendon, and muscle are NOT exposed. (Stage 4 involves direct exposure or palpability of bone, tendon, or muscle).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: An ulcer characterized by deeply undermined, purplish, ragged edges, watery thin discharge with necrotic slough, typically located on the calf of young females, is known as Bazin's disease (erythema induratum). What is the underlying pathophysiological association?
questions.explanation: Bazin's disease (erythema induratum) is a nodular vasculitis of the lower legs, predominantly affecting young women, that represents a chronic tuberculid hypersensitivity reaction to M. tuberculosis.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 58-year-old male with a 15-year history of an unhealed burn scar ulcer over the posterior leg notices sudden everted, raised rolled edges, rapid ulcer expansion, foul odor, and blood-stained discharge. An edge biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. What is this malignant transformation termed?
questions.explanation: Marjolin's ulcer is a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma arising in chronic unhealed scars, burn contractures, chronic osteomyelitis sinus tracts, or long-standing venous ulcers. It features everted margins and carries high metastatic potential once it breaches the avascular scar capsule.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the clinical classification of primary lymphedema based on the patient's age of presentation?
options: Type A (< 5 yrs), Type B (5–20 yrs), Type C (> 20 yrs)
Congenital (present at birth or < 1 yr; Milroy's disease), Praecox (onset between 1 and 35 yrs; Meige's disease), and Tarda (onset after 35 yrs)
Class I (mild), Class II (moderate), Class III (severe)
questions.answer: Congenital (present at birth or < 1 yr; Milroy's disease), Praecox (onset between 1 and 35 yrs; Meige's disease), and Tarda (onset after 35 yrs)
questions.explanation: Primary (idiopathic) lymphedema is categorized by age of onset: Lymphedema congenita (onset at birth or < 1 year; autosomal dominant form is Milroy's disease); Lymphedema praecox (onset around puberty up to 35 years; Meige's disease); and Lymphedema tarda (onset after 35 years).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: On physical examination of a swollen lower extremity, the inability to pinch a fold of skin over the base of the second toe due to subcutaneous fibrosis is a pathognomonic diagnostic indicator of chronic lymphedema. What is this clinical sign?
questions.explanation: Stemmer's sign is positive when the skin over the dorsum of the base of the second toe cannot be pinched or lifted into a fold because of cutaneous thickening and subcutaneous fibrosis, strongly indicating lymphedema over lipedema or simple venous edema.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 26-year-old male presents with painless enlargement of cervical lymph nodes. He gives a history of cyclical high fever lasting 1 to 2 weeks alternating with afebrile periods of similar duration (Pel-Ebstein fever). Excisional lymph node biopsy confirms Hodgkin lymphoma with Reed-Sternberg cells. Which histological subtype of classic Hodgkin lymphoma is most common in young adults and typically displays collagen bands dividing the node into nodules?
questions.explanation: Nodular sclerosis classic Hodgkin lymphoma (NSCHL) is the most common subtype (60-70% of cases), typically presenting in adolescents and young adults with cervical/mediastinal nodes. Histology shows broad bands of birefringent collagen encircling nodules containing lacunar Reed-Sternberg cell variants.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 64-year-old female who underwent radical mastectomy with axillary dissection 12 years ago has severe chronic postmastectomy lymphedema of the right arm. She now develops multiple tender, rapidly growing purple-red subcutaneous vascular plaques and nodules across the lymphedematous limb. Biopsy reveals lymphangiosarcoma. What is this clinical entity?
questions.explanation: Stewart-Treves syndrome is the development of a highly aggressive angiosarcoma/lymphangiosarcoma in a background of chronic, long-standing lymphedema, classically seen in the ipsilateral upper extremity years following radical mastectomy and axillary node clearance.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the primary cornerstone non-operative management for Stage II moderate-to-severe lymphedema?
options: Complete Decongestive Therapy (CDT) incorporating manual lymphatic drainage, multilayer short-stretch bandaging, skin care, and exercises
Prophylactic wide excision of all subcutaneous fat (Charles procedure)
questions.answer: Complete Decongestive Therapy (CDT) incorporating manual lymphatic drainage, multilayer short-stretch bandaging, skin care, and exercises
questions.explanation: Complete Decongestive Therapy (CDT) is the gold standard conservative treatment for lymphedema, consisting of Phase 1 (reduction phase: skin hygiene, manual lymphatic drainage, multi-layer short-stretch compression wraps, remedial exercises) followed by Phase 2 (maintenance phase: compression garments). Diuretics are contraindicated.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 65-year-old fair-skinned male presents with a painless, slow-growing pearly nodule with rolled, beaded translucent borders and prominent surface telangiectasias located on the side of the nose above the line joining the angle of the mouth and tragus of the ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) characteristically arises on sun-exposed head and neck areas above a line joining the angle of the mouth to the ear lobule. Classical features include pearly translucent nodular border, telangiectasia, and central ulceration (rodent ulcer). Metastasis is exceedingly rare.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: According to the ABCDE criteria used for clinical screening and early identification of malignant melanoma, what does 'D' represent?
options: Diameter greater than 6 mm (size of a pencil eraser)
questions.answer: Diameter greater than 6 mm (size of a pencil eraser)
questions.explanation: The ABCDE mnemonic for melanoma screening stands for: A = Asymmetry, B = Border irregularity, C = Color variegation (shades of brown, black, blue, white, red), D = Diameter > 6 mm, and E = Evolution / Elevation.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: On histopathological examination of an excisional biopsy of a cutaneous malignant melanoma, what is the single most important microstaging parameter that dictates surgical re-excision margins and overall prognosis?
options: Breslow tumor thickness (depth measured in millimeters from granular layer)
questions.answer: Breslow tumor thickness (depth measured in millimeters from granular layer)
questions.explanation: Breslow thickness (measured in millimeters with an ocular micrometer from the top of the epidermal granular layer to the deepest invading melanoma cell) is the gold standard prognostic factor and directly determines recommended wide local excision surgical margins and indications for sentinel node biopsy.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the recommended radial wide local excision margin for a confirmed invasive cutaneous melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 1.5 mm (intermediate thickness: 1.01 to 2.0 mm)?
options: 1 to 2 cm margin down to the deep muscular fascia
5 cm margin requiring routine primary amputation
questions.answer: 1 to 2 cm margin down to the deep muscular fascia
questions.explanation: Standard oncological guidelines for wide local excision of melanoma: In situ = 0.5 cm; <= 1.0 mm thickness = 1.0 cm margin; 1.01 to 2.0 mm thickness = 1 to 2 cm margin; > 2.0 mm thickness = 2.0 cm margin. Excision should extend down to, but need not sacrifice, healthy deep fascia.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which clinical subtype of malignant melanoma is the most common form observed in dark-skinned individuals and Asian populations, characteristically arising on the palms, soles, and subungual nail beds?
questions.explanation: Acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) accounts for the majority of melanomas in Asian, African, and dark-skinned individuals. It develops on glabrous skin of soles, palms, and beneath nail plates (subungual melanoma, presenting with Hutchinson's sign).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 48-year-old male presents with a painless, gradually enlarging 7-cm mass deep in the anterior thigh beneath the fascia lata. MRI shows an intramuscular, heterogeneous mass without bone involvement. What is the mandatory biopsy technique to establish histopathological subtype and grade before planning definitive limb-salvage resection?
options: Core needle biopsy (CNB) placed longitudinally along the anticipated future definitive surgical incision line
Transverse excisional biopsy through the skin
Incisional biopsy with extensive lateral undermining
questions.answer: Core needle biopsy (CNB) placed longitudinally along the anticipated future definitive surgical incision line
questions.explanation: Core needle biopsy oriented strictly along the longitudinal axis of the limb (in line with the proposed definitive resection incision) is the standard method. Transverse incisions or broad undermining contaminate adjacent tissue planes and jeopardize limb-salvage surgery.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Why is simple 'enucleation' of a soft tissue sarcoma (STS) along its apparent fibrous capsule associated with an unacceptably high local recurrence rate (> 80%)?
options: The capsule is an artifact of formalin fixation
The apparent capsule is a pseudo-capsule composed of compressed neoplastic cells and microvascular tumor projections
Sarcomas only spread via intra-articular ligaments
questions.answer: The apparent capsule is a pseudo-capsule composed of compressed neoplastic cells and microvascular tumor projections
questions.explanation: Soft tissue sarcomas lack a true anatomical capsule; their 'capsule' is a pseudocapsule formed by compressed surrounding normal tissue, inflammatory cells, and invasive tumor fingers. Shelling out the tumor leaves microscopic disease behind.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the single most common anatomical site of distant hematogenous metastasis in extremity soft tissue sarcomas?
questions.explanation: Extremity soft tissue sarcomas metastasize almost exclusively via the hematogenous route to the lungs (accounting for > 80% of metastases). Routine baseline staging requires a non-contrast or contrast CT of the thorax.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: While soft tissue sarcomas typically spread hematogenously, a few rare histological variants show a marked predilection for regional lymph node metastasis. Which of the following STS subtypes has the highest propensity for nodal spread?
options: Synovial sarcoma, Rhabdomyosarcoma, Epithelioid sarcoma, and Clear cell sarcoma
questions.answer: Synovial sarcoma, Rhabdomyosarcoma, Epithelioid sarcoma, and Clear cell sarcoma
questions.explanation: Unlike most sarcomas, five distinct variants frequently metastasize to regional lymph nodes: Rhabdomyosarcoma, Epithelioid sarcoma, Synovial sarcoma, Clear cell sarcoma, and Angiosarcoma (mnemonic: S-R-E-C-A).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the defining clinical sign on physical examination of a subcutaneous lipoma that distinguishes it from a cystic lesion or deep fibroma?
options: Positive 'slip sign' and lobulated surface with pseudofluctuation
Fixity to underlying deep skeletal muscle
questions.answer: Positive 'slip sign' and lobulated surface with pseudofluctuation
questions.explanation: A lipoma classically demonstrates the 'slip sign'—as the examining fingers gently compress the edge of the swelling, the tumor slips away from under the fingers into the surrounding subcutaneous fat. It is lobulated and soft.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 50-year-old chronic tobacco and betel nut chewer presents with progressive inability to open his mouth (severe trismus), burning sensation in the mouth on eating spicy foods, and pale, blanched, leathery oral mucosa with palpable vertical fibrous bands. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Oral submucous fibrosis (OSMF) is a chronic, progressive premalignant condition strongly associated with areca nut/betel quid chewing. It is characterized by fibroelastic changes in the lamina propria, dense vertical fibrous bands, progressive trismus, mucosal blanching, and an elevated risk of transformation to squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.prompt: A 58-year-old male presents with an unhealed, indurated ulcer with everted edges on the lateral border of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. An edge punch biopsy confirms well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (T2N1M0). Why does carcinoma of the tongue carry a notably poorer prognosis than carcinoma of the lip?
options: The tongue has zero arterial supply
Rich lymphatic network with cross-drainage across the midline, constant muscular mobility, and high propensity for early occult nodal metastasis
Tongue tumors are resistant to radiation therapy
Lip carcinomas always metastasize to the lungs first
questions.answer: Rich lymphatic network with cross-drainage across the midline, constant muscular mobility, and high propensity for early occult nodal metastasis
questions.explanation: The oral tongue has an extensive, interconnected lymphatic plexus with rich bilateral drainage to levels I, II, and III. Constant mobility during speech and mastication promotes early lymphatic embolization and nodal metastasis.

questions.prompt: What is the standard surgical timing for primary repair of cleft lip using the Millard rotation-advancement flap, according to the classic 'Rule of 10s'?
options: 10 days of age, 10 ounces body weight, and 10 WBC count
10 weeks of age, 10 pounds (4.5 kg) weight, and hemoglobin of 10 g/dL
10 months of age, 10 kg weight, and 10 teeth erupted
questions.answer: 10 weeks of age, 10 pounds (4.5 kg) weight, and hemoglobin of 10 g/dL
questions.explanation: Wilhelmsen and Musgrave's 'Rule of 10s' for cleft lip repair specifies: age >= 10 weeks, body weight >= 10 pounds (~4.5 kg), hemoglobin >= 10 g/dL, and white blood cell count < 10,000/mm3 to ensure safety under general anaesthesia.

questions.prompt: In the oncological evaluation of maxillary sinus (antrum) malignancies, what does 'Ohlgren's line' represent?
options: A radiographic line connecting the frontal sinus to the sella turcica
An imaginary plane extending from the medial canthus of the eye to the angle of the mandible, dividing the antrum into anteroinferior (favorable) and posterosuperior (unfavorable) infrastructure
A line drawn between the mastoid tip and mental protuberance
The incision line for a Weber-Fergusson maxillectomy
questions.answer: An imaginary plane extending from the medial canthus of the eye to the angle of the mandible, dividing the antrum into anteroinferior (favorable) and posterosuperior (unfavorable) infrastructure
questions.explanation: Ohlgren's line is an imaginary line from the medial canthus to the angle of the mandible. Tumors anteroinferior to this plane (infrastructure) have better resectability and prognosis, while posterosuperior tumors (suprastructure) invade the orbit, pterygopalatine fossa, and skull base, carrying a poor prognosis.

questions.prompt: What is a 'ranula' and what is its standard surgical treatment when simple marsupialization fails or recurs?
options: Infection of Stensen's duct treated by parotidectomy
Mucus extravasation pseudocyst arising from the sublingual salivary gland on the floor of the mouth; definitive treatment is complete excision of the sublingual gland with the ranula
Adenocarcinoma of the palate treated by maxillectomy
Epidermoid cyst of the tongue requiring partial glossectomy
questions.answer: Mucus extravasation pseudocyst arising from the sublingual salivary gland on the floor of the mouth; definitive treatment is complete excision of the sublingual gland with the ranula
questions.explanation: A ranula is a bluish, translucent cystic swelling on the floor of the mouth arising from extravasation of saliva from the damaged ducts of Rivinus of the sublingual gland. Definitive management of recurrent or plunging ranulas is excision of the ipsilateral sublingual gland.
