questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which malignant salivary gland neoplasm is characteristically renowned for perineural invasion (creeping along nerve sheaths), pain, late distant metastases, and a high rate of recurrence even after a 10-to-20 year disease-free interval?
questions.explanation: Adenoid cystic carcinoma characteristically exhibits marked perineural spread along cranial nerves, pain, swiss-cheese (cribriform) histological pattern, and relentless late distant pulmonary metastases despite apparent early radical local control.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Six months following superficial parotidectomy, a 44-year-old male complains of localized erythema, warmth, and profuse sweating over the preauricular skin whenever he smells or eats appetizing food (gustatory sweating). What is the underlying pathophysiology of Frey's syndrome?
options: Recurrence of pleomorphic adenoma infiltrating skin
Aberrant regeneration of severed postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers (auriculotemporal nerve) into sympathetic sweat glands and dermal blood vessels
Cutaneous fistula from persistent Stensen's duct stump
questions.answer: Aberrant regeneration of severed postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers (auriculotemporal nerve) into sympathetic sweat glands and dermal blood vessels
questions.explanation: Frey's syndrome (auriculotemporal syndrome) is caused by misdirected regeneration of severed parasympathetic secretomotor axons of the auriculotemporal nerve into vacant sympathetic pathways supplying overlying skin sweat glands and vasodilators, leading to gustatory sweating and flushing.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During superficial parotidectomy, what is the most reliable and consistent anatomical landmark used to identify the main trunk of the facial nerve as it exits the stylomastoid foramen?
options: Tympanomastoid suture, tragal pointer, and posterior belly of the digastric muscle
questions.answer: Tympanomastoid suture, tragal pointer, and posterior belly of the digastric muscle
questions.explanation: Key landmarks to find the facial nerve trunk are: (1) Tragal pointer (nerve lies 1 cm deep and inferior), (2) Tympanomastoid fissure (nerve exits 6-8 mm deep), (3) Upper border of the posterior belly of the digastric muscle, and (4) Styloid process.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 52-year-old female presents with recurrent nephrolithiasis, generalized bone aches, abdominal constipation, and fatigue ('bones, stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans'). Serum calcium is 11.8 mg/dL, phosphate is 2.1 mg/dL, and intact PTH is elevated at 145 pg/mL (normal 15-65). What is the single most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism?
options: Ectopic PTHrP production by bronchogenic carcinoma
questions.explanation: A solitary parathyroid adenoma accounts for approximately 80 to 85% of all cases of primary hyperparathyroidism, followed by multiglandular parathyroid hyperplasia (10-15%) and parathyroid carcinoma (< 1%).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which preoperative functional nuclear imaging scan has the highest sensitivity for localizing a hyperfunctioning parathyroid adenoma prior to targeted minimally invasive parathyroidectomy?
questions.explanation: Tc-99m sestamibi SPECT/CT scintigraphy (especially dual-phase washout technique or subtraction imaging) is the premier imaging modality for preoperative localization of solitary parathyroid adenomas, showing delayed retention in mitochondrial-rich oxyphil cells.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 36-year-old female presents with episodic pounding headaches, profuse diaphoresis, palpitations, and severe paroxysmal hypertension (220/120 mmHg). 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are markedly elevated. Abdominal CT identifies a 4.5-cm right adrenal medullary mass. Why is preoperative administration of alpha-adrenergic blockade (phenoxybenzamine) mandatory BEFORE initiating beta-blocker therapy?
options: Beta-blockers can precipitate acute adrenal cortical necrosis
Unopposed alpha-receptor stimulation would cause catastrophic hypertensive crisis, acute heart failure, and cerebral hemorrhage
Alpha-blockers are required to lower blood glucose levels
questions.answer: Unopposed alpha-receptor stimulation would cause catastrophic hypertensive crisis, acute heart failure, and cerebral hemorrhage
questions.explanation: In pheochromocytoma, blocking beta-2 mediated vasodilation with a beta-blocker prior to adequate alpha-1 receptor blockade leaves circulating catecholamines to act unopposed on alpha-receptors, resulting in severe vasoconstriction and life-threatening hypertensive crisis.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 48-year-old male undergoes non-contrast abdominal CT for renal colic, which unexpectedly reveals an incidental 2.5-cm right adrenal mass ('adrenal incidentaloma'). The lesion has a lipid-rich low unenhanced attenuation (< 10 Hounsfield Units) and homogeneous borders. Functional biochemical screening confirms it is non-functioning. What is the standard management strategy?
options: Conservative surveillance with repeat non-contrast CT at 6 to 12 months
Image-guided fine needle percutaneous core biopsy
questions.answer: Conservative surveillance with repeat non-contrast CT at 6 to 12 months
questions.explanation: An adrenal incidentaloma < 4 cm with benign imaging features (< 10 HU, rapid contrast washout > 60%) and absence of biochemical hypersecretion is benign (adrenocortical adenoma) and managed conservatively with follow-up imaging. Lesions >= 4 cm or with suspicious features warrant surgical excision.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which anatomical relationship reliably separates the superior parathyroid glands from the inferior parathyroid glands with respect to the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN)?
options: Superior glands lie posterior to the plane of the RLN, whereas inferior parathyroid glands lie anterior to the plane of the RLN
Superior glands lie anterior to the carotid sheath; inferior glands lie inside the thyroid capsule
Both superior and inferior glands lie strictly medially to the trachea
Superior glands lie ventral to the RLN, and inferior glands lie dorsal
questions.answer: Superior glands lie posterior to the plane of the RLN, whereas inferior parathyroid glands lie anterior to the plane of the RLN
questions.explanation: Anatomically, the superior parathyroid glands (derived from the 4th pharyngeal pouch) are located dorsal/posterior to the coronal plane of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, while the inferior parathyroid glands (derived from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch) migrate anterior/ventral to the nerve.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old female secretary presents with numbness, paresthesias, and pain in the medial aspect of her right forearm and hand (ulnar nerve distribution), aggravated by carrying heavy bags. Physical examination shows radial pulse obliteration on hyperabduction and external rotation of the arm with the neck extended and head turned to the affected side (positive Adson's test). What is the underlying diagnosis?
options: Thoracic outlet syndrome (cervical rib / scalenus anticus syndrome)
questions.answer: Thoracic outlet syndrome (cervical rib / scalenus anticus syndrome)
questions.explanation: Thoracic outlet syndrome results from compression of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1) and/or subclavian vessels in the scalene triangle or costoclavicular space (due to a cervical rib or tight scalene muscle band). Adson's test and Roos test are classic physical examination signs.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 54-year-old male with a 15-year history of chronic GERD undergoes surveillance upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Biopsy of salmon-pink velvety mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastroesophageal junction shows intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells (Barrett's esophagus) and confirmed high-grade dysplasia (HGD). What is the current standard treatment of choice?
options: Endoscopic eradication therapy (Endoscopic Mucosal Resection of visible nodules plus Radiofrequency Ablation)
Immediate total gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y reconstruction
questions.answer: Endoscopic eradication therapy (Endoscopic Mucosal Resection of visible nodules plus Radiofrequency Ablation)
questions.explanation: For Barrett's esophagus with confirmed high-grade dysplasia without submucosal invasion, endoscopic eradication therapy (endoscopic mucosal resection of nodular lesions combined with radiofrequency ablation of flat metaplastic mucosa) is the standard of care, offering cure rates comparable to esophagectomy with much lower morbidity.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old male develops sudden, excruciating retrosternal and epigastric pain following an episode of violent retching after alcohol binge drinking. On examination, he is tachypneic, hypotensive, and has subcutaneous emphysema palpable over the suprasternal notch and neck (Mackler's triad). Chest X-ray reveals left pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Boerhaave's syndrome is a full-thickness rupture of the esophagus (classically on the left posterolateral wall of the lower third) caused by sudden elevation of intraluminal pressure against a closed cricopharyngeus. Mackler's triad consists of vomiting, lower chest pain, and subcutaneous emphysema.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: An elderly male presents with halitosis, regurgitation of undigested food eaten hours earlier, gurgling in the neck upon swallowing (Boyce's sign), and a soft fluctuant swelling on the left side of the neck. Barium swallow demonstrates an outpouching through Killian's dehiscence. What is this pouch?
questions.explanation: Zenker's diverticulum is a pulsion pseudodiverticulum herniating through Killian's dehiscence (the potential anatomical weak area between the oblique thyropharyngeus and transverse cricopharyngeus muscles). Key features include dysphagia, halitosis, regurgitation, and Boyce's gurgling sign.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 38-year-old male presents with high-grade spiking fevers, right upper quadrant pain, and tender hepatomegaly. Ultrasound shows a solitary 8-cm liquefied abscess in the right lobe of the liver. Diagnostic aspiration yields thick, reddish-brown, odorless 'anchovy-sauce' fluid. What is the definitive initial medical management?
options: Immediate open surgical deroofing and laparotomy
Oral or intravenous Metronidazole (750 mg thrice daily for 10 days) plus a luminal amebicide
Broad-spectrum IV Meropenem and Vancomycin for 6 weeks
questions.answer: Oral or intravenous Metronidazole (750 mg thrice daily for 10 days) plus a luminal amebicide
questions.explanation: Amoebic liver abscess (caused by Entamoeba histolytica) characteristically contains sterile chocolate-colored 'anchovy sauce' pus. Over 90% respond successfully to medical therapy with Metronidazole (or Tinidazole) followed by a luminal amebicide (e.g. Paromomycin or Diloxanide furoate).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: According to the internationally accepted Milan Criteria, which solitary hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patient with cirrhosis is an eligible candidate for deceased or living-donor liver transplantation?
options: Single tumor <= 5 cm in diameter, or up to 3 lesions none exceeding 3 cm, with no macrovascular invasion and no extrahepatic spread
Any single tumor up to 10 cm without portal vein thrombosis
Multiple bilateral nodules up to 5 lesions none > 5 cm
Tumor invading the main portal vein trunk but confined to one lobe
questions.answer: Single tumor <= 5 cm in diameter, or up to 3 lesions none exceeding 3 cm, with no macrovascular invasion and no extrahepatic spread
questions.explanation: The Milan criteria for liver transplantation in cirrhotic patients with HCC require: (1) single lesion <= 5 cm, OR up to 3 lesions all <= 3 cm; (2) no macrovascular invasion; and (3) no extrahepatic nodal or distant metastasis, yielding post-transplant 5-year survival rates > 70%.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In the Couinaud classification of hepatic functional segmental anatomy, which anatomical structure subdivides the liver into functional right and left hemiliver (along Cantlie's line)?
options: Middle hepatic vein (running from gallbladder fossa to the IVC)
questions.answer: Middle hepatic vein (running from gallbladder fossa to the IVC)
questions.explanation: The principal functional plane (Cantlie's line) runs from the middle of the gallbladder fossa anteriorly to the middle of the inferior vena cava posteriorly. The middle hepatic vein lies in this main scissura, dividing the liver into the true right functional lobe (segments V, VI, VII, VIII) and left functional lobe (segments II, III, IV).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 46-year-old male with chronic calcific pancreatitis presents with intractable, disabling epigastric pain radiating to the back and exocrine insufficiency. Contrast CT and MRCP demonstrate marked dilatation of the main pancreatic duct (10 mm, 'chain of lakes' appearance) with intraductal calculi throughout the body and tail, but no focal inflammatory mass in the head of the pancreas. What is the surgical drainage procedure of choice?
questions.explanation: For chronic pancreatitis with a significantly dilated main pancreatic duct (>= 6-7 mm) and no inflammatory head mass, longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy (Partington-Rochelle / modified Puestow procedure) provides optimal surgical ductal decompression and pain relief.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: According to the Revised Atlanta Classification for acute pancreatitis, how is a persistent, encapsulated fluid collection with a well-defined inflammatory wall and negligible necrosis, developing > 4 weeks after the onset of interstitial edematous pancreatitis, defined?
questions.explanation: In interstitial edematous pancreatitis, fluid collections occurring < 4 weeks are acute peripancreatic fluid collections (APFC). When persisting > 4 weeks and maturing into an encapsulated collection with a well-defined wall containing no solid necrotic tissue, it is defined as a Pancreatic Pseudocyst.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: On postoperative day 10 following laparotomy for a perforated duodenal ulcer, a patient develops swinging high fevers, right shoulder-tip pain (Kehr's sign), hiccoughs, and right basal pulmonary atelectasis with pleural effusion. Abdominal ultrasound reveals a fluid collection between the superior surface of the right hepatic lobe and the diaphragm. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A right subphrenic abscess lies between the right hepatic lobe and the inferior diaphragmatic surface. Diaphragmatic irritation irritates the phrenic nerve (C3-C5), producing referred pain to the right shoulder tip, hiccoughs, and reactive sympathetic pleural effusion.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 16-year-old boy presents with a painless, mobile abdominal mass. On physical examination, the mass is freely mobile in a direction perpendicular to the line of attachment of the mesentery (from left upper to right lower quadrant) but restricted along the mesenteric axis (Tillaux's sign). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tillaux's sign is pathognomonic of a mesenteric cyst: the mass moves freely in a plane perpendicular to the attachment of the root of the mesentery, but exhibits limited or no mobility along the axis of mesenteric attachment.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old male with massive burn trauma and vigorous crystalloid resuscitation develops a tense, drum-like abdomen, progressive oliguria (< 15 mL/hr), elevated peak inspiratory airway pressures (42 cm H2O), and worsening hypercapnia. Intravesical urinary bladder catheter manometry records a sustained pressure of 26 mmHg. What condition is present, and what is the definitive surgical intervention?
options: Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS); perform urgent decompressive laparotomy with temporary abdominal closure
Paralytic ileus; place a nasogastric tube
questions.answer: Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS); perform urgent decompressive laparotomy with temporary abdominal closure
questions.explanation: Abdominal compartment syndrome is defined as sustained intra-abdominal pressure > 20 mmHg associated with new-onset organ dysfunction (e.g. oliguria, elevated ventilatory pressures, refractory hypotension). Urgent surgical decompressive laparotomy with open abdomen (laparostomy) is life-saving.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which anatomical space forms the dependent, lowest recess of the peritoneal cavity in an upright or semi-recumbent patient, making it the most frequent location for pelvic abscess collections following generalized peritonitis?
options: Rectovesical pouch (in males) or Rectouterine pouch of Douglas (in females)
questions.answer: Rectovesical pouch (in males) or Rectouterine pouch of Douglas (in females)
questions.explanation: The rectovesical pouch in males and pouch of Douglas (rectouterine pouch) in females represents the most gravity-dependent recess of the peritoneal cavity. Gravitational tracking of purulent exudate after peritonitis results in pelvic abscesses, presenting with tenesmus, diarrhea, and boggy pelvic fullness on digital rectal examination.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In differentiating intestinal tuberculosis from Crohn's disease during surgical exploration and pathology, which of the following gross features is characteristic of intestinal tuberculosis?
options: Longitudinal ulcers along the mesenteric border with 'fat wrapping' (creeping fat)
Transverse ulcers oriented perpendicular to the long axis of the bowel, caseating granulomas, and circumferential stricturing
Continuous mucosal involvement extending from rectum proximally
Cobblestone mucosa with non-caseating sarcoid-like granulomas
questions.answer: Transverse ulcers oriented perpendicular to the long axis of the bowel, caseating granulomas, and circumferential stricturing
questions.explanation: Tubercular ulcers follow circular lymphatic channels around the bowel circumference, producing transverse ulcers perpendicular to the long axis that heal with ring-like circumferential strictures, accompanied by caseating granulomas in mesenteric lymph nodes. In contrast, Crohn's ulcers are longitudinal and non-caseating.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During the third week of illness with Salmonella typhi (enteric fever), a 22-year-old male develops sudden acute lower abdominal pain, guarding, and free gas under the diaphragm. Where is the classic surgical site of enteric perforation located?
options: Terminal ileum (within 60 cm of the ileocecal valve on the antimesenteric border)
questions.answer: Terminal ileum (within 60 cm of the ileocecal valve on the antimesenteric border)
questions.explanation: Enteric (typhoid) ulcers result from necrosis of Peyer's patches in the terminal ileum, classically occurring within the distal 60 cm of the antimesenteric border of the terminal ileum during the 2nd to 3rd week of typhoid fever.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 52-year-old female presents with episodic cutaneous flushing of the face and upper chest, watery secretory diarrhea, and dyspnea with right-sided heart murmur (tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis). Urinary 24-hour excretion of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) is markedly elevated. Why does carcinoid syndrome typically manifest only AFTER hepatic metastasis has occurred in primary midgut neuroendocrine tumors?
options: The primary tumor produces zero serotonin
Serotonin and vasoactive mediators released from gut NETs into the portal venous circulation are completely metabolized by hepatic monoamine oxidases
The heart secretes serotonin antagonists until liver failure ensues
Midgut NETs only synthesize 5-HIAA inside hepatic sinusoids
questions.answer: Serotonin and vasoactive mediators released from gut NETs into the portal venous circulation are completely metabolized by hepatic monoamine oxidases
questions.explanation: In primary gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumors, vasoactive secretions (serotonin, bradykinin) are drained by the portal vein and cleared by first-pass hepatic metabolism. When liver metastases develop, secretions directly enter the hepatic veins and systemic circulation, triggering carcinoid syndrome.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which anatomical criteria define 'Short Bowel Syndrome' in adult patients following extensive small bowel resection?
options: Resection of > 50 cm of small intestine
Remaining functional small bowel length of less than 200 cm (especially < 100 cm without an intact colon)
Loss of the appendix and terminal 10 cm of ileum
questions.answer: Remaining functional small bowel length of less than 200 cm (especially < 100 cm without an intact colon)
questions.explanation: Short bowel syndrome results from extensive bowel resection leaving < 200 cm of functional small intestine (normal small bowel is 400-600 cm). Patients with < 100 cm and an end-enterostomy typically require long-term home total parenteral nutrition.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which of the following factors is well-known to prevent spontaneous closure of an enterocutaneous fistula (mnemonic: FRIENDS)?
options: Foreign body, Radiation, Infection/Inflammation, Epithelialization of tract, Neoplasm, Distal obstruction, Short tract (< 2 cm)
questions.answer: Foreign body, Radiation, Infection/Inflammation, Epithelialization of tract, Neoplasm, Distal obstruction, Short tract (< 2 cm)
questions.explanation: The 'FRIENDS' mnemonic lists the established adverse factors that prevent spontaneous healing of an enterocutaneous fistula: Foreign body, Radiation enteritis, Infection/abscess, Epithelialization of the tract, Neoplasm, Distal obstruction, and Short tract length (< 2 cm).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: According to the modified Hinchey classification of acute colonic diverticulitis, what characterizes Stage III?
options: Pericolic phlegmon or confined pericolic abscess
Generalized purulent peritonitis without fecal contamination (ruptured purulent abscess)
Generalized feculent peritonitis with frank colonic wall perforation
questions.answer: Generalized purulent peritonitis without fecal contamination (ruptured purulent abscess)
questions.explanation: The Hinchey classification grades diverticulitis: Stage I = Pericolic abscess; Stage II = Pelvic/distant retroperitoneal abscess; Stage III = Generalized purulent peritonitis; Stage IV = Generalized feculent peritonitis from non-communicating colonic rupture.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 2-week-old newborn presents with continuous clear, watery discharge from the umbilicus that tests strongly positive for urea and creatinine. Catheterization and fistulogram demonstrate direct communication with the dome of the urinary bladder. What congenital anomaly is present?
questions.explanation: A patent urachus occurs due to complete failure of obliteration of the embryonic allantois connecting the bladder dome to the umbilicus, causing continuous or intermittent urinary discharge from the umbilicus.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: On postoperative day 7 following an emergency midline exploratory laparotomy for peritonitis, a patient's wound dressing is soaked with profuse, serosanguinous ('salmon-pink') peritoneal fluid. On gentle examination, loop of small bowel is felt directly under the skin sutures. What is this surgical emergency, and what is the primary management?
options: Superficial surgical site infection; remove two skin sutures and irrigate
Abdominal wound dehiscence (burst abdomen); apply sterile saline-soaked packs and perform urgent operative re-closure in the operating theatre
Incisional hernia; provide an abdominal binder and follow up in clinic in 6 months
Hematoma of the rectus sheath; order conservative ultrasound
questions.answer: Abdominal wound dehiscence (burst abdomen); apply sterile saline-soaked packs and perform urgent operative re-closure in the operating theatre
questions.explanation: Profuse serosanguinous ('salmon-pink') wound discharge is the classic harbinger of fascial dehiscence (burst abdomen). Immediate management consists of covering exposed viscera with sterile moist saline-soaked laparotomy pads and preparing for urgent operative re-closure with non-absorbable mass closure or retention sutures.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 30-year-old multiparous female presents with a firm, painless, slow-growing mass in the anterior abdominal wall within the right rectus abdominis muscle. Biopsy reveals benign monoclonal fibroblastic and myofibroblastic proliferation with abundant collagen, expressing nuclear beta-catenin, without cytologic atypia or mitoses. What is this lesion?
questions.explanation: Desmoid tumors (aggressive fibromatosis) are locally infiltrative, non-metastasizing fibroblastic neoplasms that frequently arise from the musculoaponeurotic structures of the abdominal wall, particularly in young postpartum females or patients with Gardner syndrome (APC gene mutations).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 68-year-old female on therapeutic warfarin presents with acute, severe, well-localized unilateral lower abdominal pain following a bout of severe coughing. Examination shows a tender, non-pulsatile abdominal mass that does not cross the midline and remains palpable and painful when she tenses her abdominal muscles by raising her head and shoulders (positive Fothergill's sign). What is the diagnosis?
options: Rectus sheath hematoma (rupture of inferior epigastric vessels)
questions.answer: Rectus sheath hematoma (rupture of inferior epigastric vessels)
questions.explanation: A positive Fothergill's sign (the mass remains palpable and fixed when abdominal rectus muscles are contracted) distinguishes an abdominal wall mass (such as a rectus sheath hematoma resulting from rupture of the inferior epigastric vessels) from an intra-abdominal lesion.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the defining clinical characteristic of 'Divarication of Recti' (diastasis recti), and why is mesh repair generally NOT indicated?
options: It is an incarcerated true hernia with high risk of strangulation
It is a separation of the rectus abdominis muscles due to stretching of the linea alba without a true fascial hernia defect, carrying zero risk of bowel strangulation
It represents congenital agenesis of the transversalis fascia
It is an umbilical endometrioma requiring wide resection
questions.answer: It is a separation of the rectus abdominis muscles due to stretching of the linea alba without a true fascial hernia defect, carrying zero risk of bowel strangulation
questions.explanation: Divarication of recti is a widening of the linea alba with lateral separation of the rectus muscles, common in multiparous women and elderly males. Because the aponeurosis remains intact with no narrow hernia neck or defect, bowel strangulation does not occur, and routine surgery is not indicated.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In an unstable blunt abdominal trauma patient arriving in the resuscitation bay, what are the four standard acoustic windows examined in Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST)?
options: Hepatorenal space (Morison's pouch), Splenorenal recess, Suprapubic (pelvic) pouch, and Pericardial (subxiphoid) window
Scrotum, Inguinal canal, Umbilicus, and Xiphoid
questions.answer: Hepatorenal space (Morison's pouch), Splenorenal recess, Suprapubic (pelvic) pouch, and Pericardial (subxiphoid) window
questions.explanation: FAST exam evaluates four dependent anatomic areas for pathological free fluid (blood): (1) Perihepatic / Morison's pouch, (2) Perisplenic / splenorenal recess, (3) Pelvic / retrovesical or pouch of Douglas, and (4) Subxiphoid / pericardial view.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What are the three core physiological components of the 'Lethal Triad of Trauma' that mandate execution of Damage Control Surgery (DCS) rather than prolonged definitive reconstruction?
options: Hypothermia (core temp < 35°C), Coagulopathy, and Metabolic Acidosis (pH < 7.2)
questions.answer: Hypothermia (core temp < 35°C), Coagulopathy, and Metabolic Acidosis (pH < 7.2)
questions.explanation: The lethal triad in severe exsanguinating trauma comprises hypothermia, metabolic acidosis, and coagulopathy. When these emerge, definitive multi-hour anatomical reconstruction is aborted in favor of rapid damage control surgery: rapid hemostasis, contamination control, temporary abdominal closure, and resuscitation in the ICU.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old restrained driver involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision sustains a blunt handlebar/steering wheel blow to the epigastrium. Forty-eight hours later, he develops bilious vomiting and epigastric discomfort. Abdominal CT demonstrates a retroperitoneal gas collection outlining the right kidney and psoas shadow. What organ injury is classically suspected?
options: Rupture of the second/third part of the duodenum
questions.answer: Rupture of the second/third part of the duodenum
questions.explanation: Blunt steering wheel or bicycle handlebar injuries crush the fixed retroperitoneal duodenum (2nd and 3rd parts) against the rigid lumbar vertebral column. Because the posterior duodenal wall is retroperitoneal, perforation produces retroperitoneal air and fluid tracking along the right kidney and psoas margin.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In mass casualty triage protocols (START system), what color tag is designated for a critically injured trauma victim with compromised airway, respiratory rate > 30/min, or absent radial pulse, who requires immediate life-saving surgical intervention?
questions.explanation: In START disaster triage: Red = Immediate priority (critical life-threatening injuries with high likelihood of survival if treated immediately); Yellow = Delayed priority; Green = Minor walking wounded; Black = Deceased or expectant (injuries incompatible with life).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Which anatomical zone of a retroperitoneal hematoma discovered during exploratory laparotomy for blunt trauma MUST ALWAYS be explored surgically due to high risk of injury to the abdominal aorta, IVC, or visceral vessels?
options: Zone 1 (centromedial retroperitoneum, extending from diaphragmatic hiatus to sacral promontory)
Retrohepatic caval zone without active bleeding
questions.answer: Zone 1 (centromedial retroperitoneum, extending from diaphragmatic hiatus to sacral promontory)
questions.explanation: Retroperitoneal hematomas are classified into Zone 1 (centromedial), Zone 2 (flank/perirenal), and Zone 3 (pelvic). In blunt trauma, Zone 1 hematomas ALWAYS require mandatory surgical exploration to address major vascular injuries (aorta, IVC, celiac/SMA trunks), whereas unexpanding blunt Zone 2 and 3 hematomas are usually managed non-operatively.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old female presents with a firm, irregular mass in the right iliac fossa associated with altered bowel habits, evening pyrexia, weight loss, and anemia. Barium enema shows an pulled-up cecum, obtuse ileocecal angle, and conical cecum with a gaping ileocecal valve (Fleischner's sign). What is the primary diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hyperplastic ileocecal tuberculosis characteristically causes cicatrization and contracture of the cecum, pulling it up into the lumbar region, with narrowing of the terminal ileum (string sign of Stierlin) and gaping of the ileocecal valve (Fleischner's sign).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old male presents with a hard, irregular nodular mass at the umbilicus ('Sister Mary Joseph's nodule'). What does this clinical finding indicate?
options: Cutaneous metastasis from an advanced intra-abdominal malignancy (most commonly gastric, colonic, or pancreatic adenocarcinoma)
Primary adenocarcinoma of the umbilical skin
questions.answer: Cutaneous metastasis from an advanced intra-abdominal malignancy (most commonly gastric, colonic, or pancreatic adenocarcinoma)
questions.explanation: Sister Mary Joseph's nodule is an umbilical cutaneous metastasis from an advanced intra-abdominal adenocarcinoma (classically stomach, ovary, or colon) spreading via lymphatic channels or remnants of the falciform ligament/obliterated umbilical vein.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: On physical examination, how does an examiner clinically distinguish a renal lump in the right lumbar region from an enlarged right hepatic lobe or gallbladder?
options: A renal mass is bimanually palpable and ballotable, has a band of colonic resonance anteriorly on percussion, and fingers can be insinuated between the mass and costal margin
A renal mass moves markedly with respiration and has dullness to percussion anteriorly
A hepatic mass is ballotable from the loin
The gallbladder is always resonant to percussion
questions.answer: A renal mass is bimanually palpable and ballotable, has a band of colonic resonance anteriorly on percussion, and fingers can be insinuated between the mass and costal margin
questions.explanation: A renal mass is retroperitoneal: it is bimanually palpable, ballotable, overlaid by resonant ascending colon, and the examiner's fingers can be insinuated between the upper border of the kidney and the costal margin. In contrast, liver masses are not ballotable and lack an upper palpable border.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 50-year-old male presents with a large, smooth, painless mass occupying the left hypochondrium and lumbar region that moves downwards and medially with inspiration. The examiner can palpate a distinct notch on the anterior border, and fingers CANNOT be insinuated between the mass and the left costal margin. Percussion over the mass is uniformly dull. What organ is enlarged?
questions.explanation: Characteristics of an enlarged spleen: moves along the axis of the 10th rib toward the right iliac fossa with respiration; has a palpable splenic notch on its anterior border; examiner cannot get above it; uniformly dull to percussion without overlying colonic resonance; and not ballotable.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 60-year-old female presents with progressive abdominal distension, ascites, and a pelvic mass. Digital rectal examination reveals a shelf-like, hard nodular ridge projecting into the anterior rectal wall in the rectouterine pouch ('Blumer's shelf'). What does this finding indicate?
options: Metastatic transcoelomic peritoneal drop metastasis into the pouch of Douglas from an upper GI or ovarian malignancy
questions.answer: Metastatic transcoelomic peritoneal drop metastasis into the pouch of Douglas from an upper GI or ovarian malignancy
questions.explanation: Blumer's shelf is a firm, shelf-like nodular ridge palpable on digital rectal or vaginal examination in the pouch of Douglas. It represents transcoelomic gravitational drop metastasis of an intra-abdominal adenocarcinoma (e.g. stomach, pancreas, colon, or ovary).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old male chronic smoker presents with intermittent, painless, total gross hematuria with the passage of worm-like blood clots. Physical examination is unremarkable. What is the mandatory, gold-standard initial diagnostic investigation combination to evaluate for urothelial malignancy of the upper and lower urinary tracts?
options: Urine routine microscopy and plain abdominal X-ray KUB
CT Urography (multi-phase computed tomography) combined with flexible cystoscopy
questions.answer: CT Urography (multi-phase computed tomography) combined with flexible cystoscopy
questions.explanation: Painless gross hematuria in an older patient or smoker is considered urothelial malignancy until proven otherwise. Standard evaluation requires complete visualization of both the upper tract (via multiphasic CT Urography) and the lower tract (via white-light flexible cystoscopy).

questions.prompt: In an infant male presenting with recurrent febrile urinary tract infections, what is the investigation of choice to diagnose and grade Vesicoureteric Reflux (VUR) and rule out Posterior Urethral Valves (PUV)?
questions.explanation: Micturating cystourethrography (MCU/VCUG) is the gold standard imaging modality for demonstrating vesicoureteric reflux (graded I to V), bladder diverticula, and anatomical urethral obstruction like posterior urethral valves during active voiding.

questions.prompt: Which radiotracer dynamic renal scan is the gold standard for measuring differential renal function (split renal function) and distinguishing non-obstructive pelvicalyceal dilatation from true mechanical pelviureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction using diuretic furosemide challenge?
questions.explanation: Tc-99m MAG3 (mercaptoacetyltriglycine) dynamic renography with furosemide (diuretic renogram) provides split renal tubular clearance function and distinguishes mechanical PUJ obstruction (washout half-time T1/2 > 20 min after Lasix) from hypotonic non-obstructed dilatation.

questions.prompt: What does 'initial hematuria' (blood appearing only at the beginning of micturition, with clear urine thereafter) localize the bleeding source to?
options: Urinary bladder trigone or posterior urethra
questions.explanation: In three-glass urinalysis: Initial hematuria indicates an anterior urethral lesion (urethritis, trauma, stricture). Terminal hematuria arises from the bladder neck, trigone, or prostate. Total hematuria (throughout urination) indicates upper tract bleeding (kidneys, ureters) or diffuse bladder wall bleeding.

questions.prompt: Which static cortical renal imaging agent is superior for detecting permanent renal cortical scarring and pyelonephritic damage in pediatric patients with vesicoureteric reflux?
questions.explanation: Tc-99m DMSA binds fixedly to the proximal renal tubular cells of the renal cortex, producing high-resolution anatomical cortical images to assess functional tubular mass and identify focal cortical scarring resulting from reflux nephropathy or chronic pyelonephritis.

questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male involved in a high-speed road traffic accident sustains a severe pelvic fracture with diastasis of the pubic symphysis. On examination, blood is seen trickling at the external urethral meatus, he is unable to void, and digital rectal examination reveals a 'high-riding' boggy prostate. What injury is suspected, and what is the absolute contraindication?
options: Anterior urethral bulbous rupture; contraindication is suprapubic catheterization
Posterior urethral rupture (membranous urethra disruption); blind Foley catheterization is absolutely contraindicated and urgent retrograde urethrography (RUG) must be performed
Bladder dome rupture; intravenous fluids are contraindicated
questions.answer: Posterior urethral rupture (membranous urethra disruption); blind Foley catheterization is absolutely contraindicated and urgent retrograde urethrography (RUG) must be performed
questions.explanation: The classic triad of posterior (membranous) urethral disruption following pelvic fracture includes: blood at the external urethral meatus, inability to micturate with palpable distended bladder, and a displaced high-riding prostate. Blind catheterization can convert a partial tear into a complete transection; an emergency retrograde urethrogram (RUG) is mandatory.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 30-year-old male with a full bladder sustains a blunt kick to the lower abdomen during a brawl. He presents with severe lower abdominal pain, guarding, and inability to void. Retrograde cystography demonstrates extravasation of contrast outlining bowel loops and pooling in the paracolic gutters. What is the diagnosis and standard treatment?
options: Extraperitoneal bladder rupture; manage conservatively with Foley catheter drainage alone
Intraperitoneal bladder rupture (perforation of the peritoneal-covered dome); mandatory emergency exploratory laparotomy and primary two-layer bladder wall closure
Spigelian hernia; manage with elective laparoscopic mesh repair
questions.answer: Intraperitoneal bladder rupture (perforation of the peritoneal-covered dome); mandatory emergency exploratory laparotomy and primary two-layer bladder wall closure
questions.explanation: Blunt trauma to a distended bladder bursts the dome (the only peritoneal-covered portion), causing intraperitoneal urine extravasation and peritonitis. Intraperitoneal ruptures ALWAYS mandate emergency laparotomy and formal two-layer surgical repair, whereas extraperitoneal ruptures are typically managed conservatively with catheter drainage.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old male sustains a fall-astride (straddle) injury onto a bicycle crossbar. He presents with scrotal and perineal swelling, perineal pain, and blood at the meatus. Urine and blood extravasate into the scrotum, penis, and lower anterior abdominal wall deep to Scarpa's fascia, but DO NOT track into the thighs. Why is fluid prevented from extending into the thighs?
options: Because Colle's fascia is firmly attached to the ischiopubic rami and fascial lata just below the inguinal ligament along the line of Holdsworth
Because the rectus sheath blocks fluid entry
Due to the dartos muscle contraction
Due to the femoral canal septum crurale
questions.answer: Because Colle's fascia is firmly attached to the ischiopubic rami and fascial lata just below the inguinal ligament along the line of Holdsworth
questions.explanation: In anterior urethral (bulbar) rupture with breach of Buck's fascia, urine extravasates into the superficial perineal pouch deep to Colles' fascia. Colles' fascia is attached to the fascia lata of the thigh just below the inguinal ligament (Holdsworth's line), preventing urine from tracking down into the lower limbs.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: According to McNeal's anatomical zonal architecture of the human prostate, in which zone do > 70% of prostate adenocarcinomas arise, and in which zone does benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) predominantly develop?
options: Cancer in Central Zone; BPH in Peripheral Zone
Cancer in Peripheral Zone; BPH in Transition Zone
Cancer in Anterior Fibromuscular Stroma; BPH in Central Zone
Both Cancer and BPH originate exclusively in the Periurethral Zone
questions.answer: Cancer in Peripheral Zone; BPH in Transition Zone
questions.explanation: Prostate adenocarcinoma arises primarily in the Peripheral Zone (~70-80% of cancers), making it palpable on digital rectal examination. Conversely, Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) develops in the Transition Zone surrounding the proximal urethra, leading to early urinary obstructive symptoms.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the pharmacological mechanism of 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (such as finasteride and dutasteride) in the medical management of symptomatic Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia?
options: Blockade of post-synaptic alpha-1A adrenergic receptors on prostatic smooth muscle
Inhibition of the enzyme converting testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), reducing prostate volume by 20–25% over 6 months
Direct competitive antagonism of estrogen receptors in the bladder neck
questions.answer: Inhibition of the enzyme converting testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), reducing prostate volume by 20–25% over 6 months
questions.explanation: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors block the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the active androgen driving prostate epithelial proliferation. This reduces prostate volume by approximately 20-25%, decreases hematuria, and reduces the risk of acute urinary retention and need for surgery.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 70-year-old male with newly diagnosed metastatic adenocarcinoma of the prostate presents with severe low back pain from osteoblastic lumbar vertebral metastases. What venous anatomical plexus explains the preferential, early hematogenous spread of prostate cancer cells to the lumbar vertebrae without traversing the lungs or caval circulation?
questions.explanation: Batson's vertebral venous plexus is a valveless, low-pressure network of veins linking the prostatic venous plexus to the internal vertebral venous plexus. Transient increases in intra-abdominal pressure cause retrograde flow directly to the lumbar spine, pelvis, and skull, bypassing the caval and pulmonary systems.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 16-year-old boy presents with sudden, excruciating left hemiscrotal pain, nausea, and vomiting of 3 hours' duration. On physical examination, the left testis is swollen, exquisitely tender, retracted superiorly into the upper scrotum, and oriented horizontally ('bell-clapper deformity'). Elevation of the scrotum fails to relieve the pain (negative Prehn's sign). What is the mandatory management timeline?
options: Immediate oral ciprofloxacin and follow up in clinic after 48 hours
Emergency scrotal exploration within 6 hours with bilateral orchidopexy
Elective outpatient ultrasound scheduled next week
questions.answer: Emergency scrotal exploration within 6 hours with bilateral orchidopexy
questions.explanation: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency with a critical golden window of 6 hours to prevent irreversible ischemic necrosis of the testicular germinal epithelium. Immediate surgical exploration via scrotal incision with untwisting and bilateral orchidopexy (due to bilateral bell-clapper anatomical predisposition) is mandatory.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 26-year-old male presents with a painless, dull dragging ache in the left scrotum, aggravated by prolonged standing. Examination in the upright position reveals a soft, compressible scrotal mass resembling a 'bag of worms' above and behind the testis that disappears when lying supine. Why does varicocele occur predominantly on the left side (in > 85% of cases)?
options: The left testis is smaller than the right
The left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a perpendicular right angle, is 8–10 cm longer than the right, and may be compressed between the SMA and aorta (nutcracker effect)
The left pampiniform plexus lacks valves, while the right has hundreds of valves
The left internal iliac artery causes local hypoplasia
questions.answer: The left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a perpendicular right angle, is 8–10 cm longer than the right, and may be compressed between the SMA and aorta (nutcracker effect)
questions.explanation: Left-sided varicocele predominates because: (1) left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a 90-degree right angle (high hydrostatic pressure), (2) it is 8-10 cm longer than the right vein which empties obliquely into the IVC, (3) compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery ('nutcracker phenomenon'), and (4) absence or incompetence of valves.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 56-year-old diabetic male presents with severe perineal and scrotal pain, high fevers, toxicity, and rapidly spreading blackish necrotic patches with crepitus over the scrotal skin. What is this life-threatening polymicrobial necrotizing fasciitis termed, and what is the definitive immediate management?
options: Fournier's gangrene; immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and aggressive emergency surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue
Peyronie's disease; oral vitamin E therapy
questions.answer: Fournier's gangrene; immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and aggressive emergency surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue
questions.explanation: Fournier's gangrene is a fulminant polymicrobial (synergistic aerobic and anaerobic) necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and external genitalia. Immediate resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering aerobes/anaerobes, and emergent radical surgical debridement of necrotic fascial planes are life-saving.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During evaluation of a primary hydrocele of the tunica vaginalis, which physical examination test confirms that the swelling contains translucent serous fluid rather than solid tumor tissue or blood?
questions.explanation: Primary vaginal hydroceles contain clear, amber-colored serous fluid that brightly transilluminates in a darkened room using a torch and roll of cardboard, confirming its cystic serous nature. Solid testicular tumors and hematocele do not transilluminate.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male arrives at the emergency department with severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, and hypotension (BP 70/40 mmHg) following a penetrating stab wound to the right hemithorax. Examination reveals hyper-resonance to percussion and absent breath sounds over the right lung field, distended neck veins, and tracheal deviation to the contralateral left side. What is the immediate life-saving intervention?
options: Immediate formal exploratory emergency thoracotomy in theatre
Immediate needle thoracostomy decompression in the 2nd intercostal space (mid-clavicular line) or 5th intercostal space (anterior axillary line), followed by insertion of an intercostal chest tube
Urgent non-contrast CT of the chest
Endotracheal intubation with high positive end-expiratory pressure
questions.answer: Immediate needle thoracostomy decompression in the 2nd intercostal space (mid-clavicular line) or 5th intercostal space (anterior axillary line), followed by insertion of an intercostal chest tube
questions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate needle decompression without waiting for chest radiography, converting the one-way valve tension pneumothorax into an open pneumothorax. A definitive intercostal chest tube (ICD) with an underwater seal is placed immediately thereafter.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What defines a 'Flail Chest' following blunt thoracic trauma, and what is its pathognomonic clinical feature on inspection during spontaneous breathing?
options: Fracture of any two ribs causing subcutaneous emphysema
Fracture of >= 3 consecutive ribs in >= 2 places each, producing paradoxical chest wall movement (inward drawing on inspiration, outward bulging on expiration)
Unilateral diaphragmatic avulsion with bowel herniation
Fracture of the sternum with bilateral pneumothoraces
questions.answer: Fracture of >= 3 consecutive ribs in >= 2 places each, producing paradoxical chest wall movement (inward drawing on inspiration, outward bulging on expiration)
questions.explanation: Flail chest occurs when >= 3 contiguous ribs are fractured at >= 2 points each, detaching a segment of chest wall from the thoracic cage. This segment exhibits paradoxical motion (moving inward during inspiration and outward during expiration), accompanied by severe underlying pulmonary contusion.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Following a motor vehicle crash with severe steering wheel impact, a patient presents with hypotension, distended neck veins, and distant, muffled heart sounds. Pulsus paradoxus is present. What classic triad is described, and what is the underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Beck's triad of acute cardiac tamponade comprises: (1) systemic arterial hypotension, (2) distended jugular veins, and (3) distant muffled heart sounds. Subxiphoid FAST ultrasound confirms pericardial effusion, and emergency pericardiocentesis or pericardial window is life-saving.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What are the standard mediastinal compartment boundaries and the classic lesions representing the '4 Ts' of an anterior mediastinal mass?
options: Thymoma, Teratoma (germ cell tumors), Thyroid (substernal goitre), and Terrible lymphoma
questions.answer: Thymoma, Teratoma (germ cell tumors), Thyroid (substernal goitre), and Terrible lymphoma
questions.explanation: The anterior mediastinum (anterior to the pericardium and great vessels) is the site for the classic '4 Ts': Thymoma/thymic carcinoma, Teratoma/germ cell tumor, Thyroid retrosternal goiter, and 'Terrible' lymphoma (Hodgkin/Non-Hodgkin).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the threshold criteria of chest tube blood drainage that indicates massive hemothorax and mandates immediate emergency exploratory thoracotomy?
options: Initial chest tube drainage of >= 1500 mL immediately upon insertion, or continuous ongoing bleeding of >= 200 mL/hr for 2 to 4 consecutive hours
Initial drainage of 200 mL over 12 hours
Any blood drainage exceeding 50 mL in 24 hours
Presence of air bubbles in the water-seal chamber alone
questions.answer: Initial chest tube drainage of >= 1500 mL immediately upon insertion, or continuous ongoing bleeding of >= 200 mL/hr for 2 to 4 consecutive hours
questions.explanation: According to ATLS thoracic trauma guidelines, indications for emergency operative thoracotomy in massive hemothorax include: immediate chest tube output >= 1500 mL of blood upon initial ICD tube placement, or persistent hemorrhage >= 200 mL/hr for 2 to 4 consecutive hours with hemodynamic instability.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male sustains a blow to the temporal region during a cricket match. He experiences brief loss of consciousness, regains complete lucidity for 2 hours ('lucid interval'), and then rapidly deteriorates with severe headache, vomiting, ipsilateral dilated sluggish pupil, and contralateral hemiparesis. Non-contrast CT of the brain demonstrates a biconvex (lentiform) hyperdense extra-axial collection that does not cross cranial suture lines. What is the vessel injured and the diagnosis?
options: Bridging subdural cortical veins; Acute subdural hematoma
Middle meningeal artery (pterion fracture); Extradural (epidural) hematoma
Internal carotid artery cavernous aneurysm rupture
questions.answer: Middle meningeal artery (pterion fracture); Extradural (epidural) hematoma
questions.explanation: Extradural hematoma (EDH) typically results from fracture at the pterion injuring the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery. The classical clinical course includes trauma, temporary recovery ('lucid interval'), followed by rapid neurological decompensation. Non-contrast CT shows a lens-shaped / biconvex hyperdensity restricted by cranial sutures.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: An 80-year-old male with cerebral cortical atrophy and mild dementia presents with a 3-week history of fluctuating confusion, lethargy, and mild right hemiparesis following a minor trivial fall. Non-contrast CT brain shows a crescentic, concave hypodense collection along the left cerebral convexity crossing suture lines. What is the source of bleeding in chronic subdural hematoma?
options: Tearing of bridging cortical cerebral veins traversing the subdural space to the superior sagittal sinus
questions.answer: Tearing of bridging cortical cerebral veins traversing the subdural space to the superior sagittal sinus
questions.explanation: In elderly patients with cerebral atrophy, the brain shrinks away from the dura, stretching bridging veins that drain cerebral cortex into the superior sagittal sinus. Minor trauma shears these stretched veins, leading to slow subdural venous bleeding and a crescent-shaped hematoma that freely crosses cranial suture lines.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A head-injured patient opens his eyes only to painful stimuli (E2), produces incomprehensible sounds (V2), and demonstrates decerebrate (abnormal extensor) posturing in response to pain (M2). What is this patient's total Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score, and what severity category does it represent?
questions.explanation: GCS score: Eye opening to pain = 2; Verbal incomprehensible sounds = 2; Motor abnormal extension (decerebrate) = 2. Total GCS = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. Head injury severity: GCS 13-15 = Mild; GCS 9-12 = Moderate; GCS <= 8 = Severe head injury (mandating airway protection with endotracheal intubation).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is Cushing's Triad, and what life-threatening pathophysiological state does it herald in a neurosurgical patient?
options: Tachycardia, Hypotension, and Tachypnea; hypovolemic shock
Hypertension with widened pulse pressure, Bradycardia, and Irregular/depressed respirations; acute impending brainstem herniation from dangerously raised intracranial pressure
Fever, Jaundice, and RUQ pain; ascending cholangitis
Flushing, Diarrhea, and Wheezing; carcinoid crisis
questions.answer: Hypertension with widened pulse pressure, Bradycardia, and Irregular/depressed respirations; acute impending brainstem herniation from dangerously raised intracranial pressure
questions.explanation: Cushing's triad consists of: (1) marked systolic hypertension with widened pulse pressure, (2) bradycardia, and (3) irregular respiration (Cheyne-Stokes or ataxic breathing). It represents a late pre-terminal reflex to brainstem ischemia caused by critically elevated ICP and imminent transtentorial or tonsillar herniation.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Following a base-of-skull fracture involving the cribriform plate of the ethmoid, a patient presents with watery nasal discharge. Which biochemical test on the nasal fluid reliably confirms the presence of Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea?
options: Detection of Beta-2 transferrin (or Beta-trace protein)
questions.answer: Detection of Beta-2 transferrin (or Beta-trace protein)
questions.explanation: Beta-2 transferrin (a desialylated isoform of transferrin) is found almost exclusively in CSF, perilymph, and ocular aqueous humor, making its electrophoretic detection the most specific and sensitive non-invasive diagnostic test to confirm CSF fistula/rhinorrhea.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During preoperative airway assessment, on opening the mouth wide with tongue protruded, the examiner visualizes the soft palate and the base of the uvula only; the tonsillar pillars and tip of the uvula are completely obscured by the base of the tongue. According to the modified Mallampati airway classification, what class is this?
questions.explanation: Modified Mallampati classification: Class I = Soft palate, fauces, uvula, and anterior/posterior tonsillar pillars visible; Class II = Soft palate, fauces, and uvula visible; Class III = Soft palate and base of uvula visible; Class IV = Only hard palate visible (soft palate not visible at all). Class III and IV predict difficult intubation.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: During general anaesthesia with halothane and succinylcholine, a 20-year-old male develops sudden unexplained tachycardia, severe masseter muscle rigidity (trismus), hypercarbia (ETCO2 rising rapidly to 85 mmHg refractory to hyperventilation), metabolic acidosis, and core temperature rising by 1°C every 5 minutes. What is the specific life-saving antidote for Malignant Hyperthermia?
options: Intravenous Dantrolene sodium (2.5 mg/kg initial bolus)
questions.answer: Intravenous Dantrolene sodium (2.5 mg/kg initial bolus)
questions.explanation: Malignant Hyperthermia is an autosomal dominant pharmacogenetic crisis triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine, caused by uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via defective ryanodine receptors (RYR1). Intravenous Dantrolene sodium blocks ryanodine receptors, halting calcium release.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: A patient undergoing wide local excision under local infiltration with 0.5% bupivacaine suddenly complains of circumoral numbness, metallic taste in the mouth, auditory tinnitus, followed within minutes by tonic-clonic convulsions and cardiovascular collapse with broad-complex ventricular arrhythmias. What is the definitive targeted rescue therapy for Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST)?
questions.explanation: Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST), particularly from lipophilic agents like bupivacaine, is managed with immediate airway protection, seizure suppression, and administration of Intravenous 20% Lipid Emulsion (1.5 mL/kg initial bolus followed by infusion), which acts as a 'lipid sink' and restores myocardial fatty acid oxidation.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: In an adult patient, at what vertebral interspace is a lumbar puncture or spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthesia safely performed, and why?
options: L1-L2 space; because spinal cord ends at T10
L3-L4 or L4-L5 space (along Tuffier's line connecting the iliac crests); because the spinal cord (conus medullaris) terminates at the lower border of L1 in adults
T12-L1 space; because the cauda equina begins at S1
questions.answer: L3-L4 or L4-L5 space (along Tuffier's line connecting the iliac crests); because the spinal cord (conus medullaris) terminates at the lower border of L1 in adults
questions.explanation: In adults, the conus medullaris terminates at the lower border of L1 (or upper L2). Spinal needle insertion is therefore performed safely at L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspaces (identified by Tuffier's line crossing the highest points of the iliac crests at the L4 spine) to avoid puncturing the spinal cord.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the specific cyclodextrin encapsulating agent used for rapid and complete chemical reversal of profound neuromuscular blockade induced by rocuronium or vecuronium?
questions.explanation: Sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin that selectively binds and encapsulates steroidal non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (rocuronium > vecuronium) in a 1:1 ratio, lowering free plasma concentration and reversing even deep or immediate neuromuscular blockade without anticholinesterase side effects.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Within minutes to hours of un-clamping the donor renal vascular anastomosis during renal transplantation, the graft turns mottled, cyanotic, soft, flaccid, and fails to produce any urine. Biopsy demonstrates diffuse microvascular thrombosis, neutrophilic infiltration, and fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles. What type of allograft rejection is this?
questions.explanation: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to hours after revascularization. It is caused by preformed donor-specific anti-HLA or ABO cytotoxic antibodies in the recipient binding to vascular endothelial antigens, activating the complement cascade and causing diffuse microvascular thrombosis and cortical necrosis.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What are the three essential components required to establish the clinical diagnosis of 'Brainstem Death' for deceased organ donation?
options: Flat EEG, loss of cardiac pacemaker activity, and coma
Deep unresponsive coma of known irreversible etiology, absence of all brainstem reflexes, and a positive apnea test (PaCO2 rising >= 60 mmHg without spontaneous respiration)
GCS score of 3 for 12 hours alone
questions.answer: Deep unresponsive coma of known irreversible etiology, absence of all brainstem reflexes, and a positive apnea test (PaCO2 rising >= 60 mmHg without spontaneous respiration)
questions.explanation: Brainstem death diagnosis requires: (1) irreversible coma of known cause with exclusion of reversible confounders (hypothermia, depressant drugs, severe metabolic derangements); (2) absence of all brainstem cranial nerve reflexes (pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, oculovestibular, gag, cough); and (3) documented apnea despite hypercarbia (PaCO2 >= 60 mmHg or >= 20 mmHg above baseline).
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the intracellular molecular target and mechanism of action of the calcineurin inhibitor Tacrolimus (FK506) in maintenance immunosuppression?
options: Binds to FKBP-12, inhibiting calcineurin phosphatase and blocking dephosphorylation of NFAT, thereby preventing transcription of interleukin-2 (IL-2) in T-helper cells
Direct competitive antagonism of IL-2 receptors (CD25)
Depletion of circulating B cells via CD20 opsonization
questions.answer: Binds to FKBP-12, inhibiting calcineurin phosphatase and blocking dephosphorylation of NFAT, thereby preventing transcription of interleukin-2 (IL-2) in T-helper cells
questions.explanation: Tacrolimus binds intracellularly to FK506-binding protein-12 (FKBP-12). This complex inhibits calcineurin, a calcium-dependent phosphatase, blocking dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T cells) and shutting down IL-2 gene transcription.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: Where is the donor kidney anatomically placed during routine adult heterotopic renal transplantation?
options: In the native retroperitoneal renal fossa following bilateral native nephrectomy
In the iliac fossa extraperitoneally, anastomosing the renal vessels to the external iliac vessels and ureter to the bladder (Lich-Gregoir technique)
Intraperitoneally attached to the splenic vessels
In the lesser sac anterior to the pancreas
questions.answer: In the iliac fossa extraperitoneally, anastomosing the renal vessels to the external iliac vessels and ureter to the bladder (Lich-Gregoir technique)
questions.explanation: Renal allografts are transplanted heterotopically into the right or left iliac fossa (extraperitoneal placement). The donor renal vein is anastomosed to the external iliac vein, renal artery to the external or internal iliac artery, and donor ureter is implanted into the bladder with an anti-reflux tunnel.
questions.subject: General Surgery

questions.prompt: What is the maximum permissible cold ischemia time (CIT) for safely preserving a donor organ in University of Wisconsin (UW) solution before irreversible preservation injury occurs in: (1) Heart, and (2) Kidney?
questions.explanation: Tolerable cold ischemia times vary substantially by organ: heart and lung allografts are most sensitive to hypothermia and ischemia, tolerating only 4 to 6 hours; liver tolerates up to 12 hours; whereas kidneys can be safely preserved for 24 to 36 hours (or even longer with hypothermic machine perfusion).

questions.prompt: What are the classic '4 Rs of Radiobiology' that govern the therapeutic rationale and biological benefit of fractionated radiation therapy over single large doses?
options: Repair of sublethal cellular DNA damage in normal cells, Repopulation of healthy tissues, Reassortment (redistribution) into sensitive cell-cycle phases, and Reoxygenation of hypoxic tumor cells
questions.answer: Repair of sublethal cellular DNA damage in normal cells, Repopulation of healthy tissues, Reassortment (redistribution) into sensitive cell-cycle phases, and Reoxygenation of hypoxic tumor cells
questions.explanation: Fractionation exploits the '4 Rs': (1) Repair of sublethal injury in normal tissue between fractions, (2) Reoxygenation of hypoxic radioresistant tumor core, (3) Redistribution/reassortment of surviving tumor cells into radiosensitive G2/M phases, and (4) Repopulation of critical normal stem cells.

questions.prompt: What is the primary oncological objective of 'Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy' administered prior to definitive surgical resection?
options: To substitute for all future radiation therapy
To downstage the primary tumor, improve resectability, treat occult micrometastases early, and assess in vivo tumor biological response
To avoid performing intraoperative histopathological frozen section
questions.answer: To downstage the primary tumor, improve resectability, treat occult micrometastases early, and assess in vivo tumor biological response
questions.explanation: Neoadjuvant (preoperative) systemic chemotherapy aims to downstage large or borderline resectable primary tumors, convert inoperable tumors to operable ones, facilitate organ-preserving surgery (e.g. breast conservation), eradicate early micrometastatic disease, and assess tumor responsiveness.

questions.prompt: Which phase of the eukaryotic cell cycle is classically the MOST sensitive to ionizing radiation-induced cell kill?
questions.explanation: Cells are most radiosensitive in the G2 and M (mitosis) phases of the cell cycle because chromosome condensation and mitotic apparatus assembly facilitate double-strand DNA breaks. Conversely, late S phase is the most radioresistant due to peak DNA repair enzyme activity.

questions.prompt: During peripheral intravenous infusion of Doxorubicin (Adriamycin), the patient complains of severe burning and stinging at the cannula site with erythema and swelling. What is the immediate required protocol for handling vesicant extravasation?
options: Flush the cannula with 50 mL normal saline and speed up the infusion

Immediately stop the infusion, aspirate as much extravasated drug as possible through the cannula, remove cannula, elevate extremity, apply cold compresses, and administer the specific antidote Dexrazoxane
Apply hot packs immediately and massage the arm
questions.answer: Immediately stop the infusion, aspirate as much extravasated drug as possible through the cannula, remove cannula, elevate extremity, apply cold compresses, and administer the specific antidote Dexrazoxane
questions.explanation: Anthracyclines (doxorubicin) are potent DNA-binding vesicants. Extravasation causes progressive severe tissue necrosis and ulceration. Management includes immediately stopping infusion, gently aspirating residual drug, extremity elevation, dry cold compresses, and intravenous Dexrazoxane (iron-chelating topoisomerase-II inhibitor antidote).

questions.prompt: What form of radiation delivery involves placing radioactive sealed sources (such as Iridium-192 or Cesium-137 wires/seeds) directly into or immediately adjacent to the tumor bed (e.g. in tongue carcinoma or cervical cancer)?
questions.explanation: Brachytherapy (sealed source radiotherapy) delivers radiation from radioactive sources positioned directly inside (interstitial, e.g. tongue carcinoma) or immediately contiguous to (intracavitary, e.g. cervix) the target lesion. Following the inverse square law, it delivers high tumor doses with rapid dose fall-off sparing adjacent normal tissues.

questions.prompt: During an abdominal hysterectomy, the surgeon prepares to clamp and ligate the uterine artery at the level of the internal os. What is the precise anatomical relationship of the ureter to the uterine artery at this critical surgical landmark?
questions.question: During an abdominal hysterectomy, the surgeon prepares to clamp and ligate the uterine artery at the level of the internal os. What is the precise anatomical relationship of the ureter to the uterine artery at this critical surgical landmark?
options: The ureter passes 1.5 to 2 cm superior and anterior to the uterine artery
The ureter passes approximately 1.5 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix, running inferior and posterior to the uterine artery ('water under the bridge')
The ureter runs medial to the uterine artery along the anterior vaginal wall
The ureter is enclosed inside the round ligament of the uterus
questions.answer: The ureter passes approximately 1.5 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix, running inferior and posterior to the uterine artery ('water under the bridge')
questions.explanation: At the level of the internal os, approximately 1.5 to 2 cm lateral to the supravaginal cervix, the uterine artery crosses transversely above and in front of the ureter within the base of the broad ligament (cardinal ligament), described as 'water (ureter) under the bridge (uterine artery)'.

questions.prompt: Which ligamentous condensation of pelvic endopelvic fascia provides the principal and strongest primary support preventing apical uterine descent and vault prolapse?
questions.question: Which ligamentous condensation of pelvic endopelvic fascia provides the principal and strongest primary support preventing apical uterine descent and vault prolapse?
options: Cardinal (Mackenrodt's / transverse cervical) and uterosacral ligament complex
questions.answer: Cardinal (Mackenrodt's / transverse cervical) and uterosacral ligament complex
questions.explanation: The cardinal ligaments (Mackenrodt's / transverse cervical ligaments) and uterosacral ligaments form the primary apical support suspension apparatus (Level I support of DeLancey), anchoring the cervix and upper vagina to the lateral pelvic walls and sacrum.

questions.prompt: During a retroperitoneal pelvic lymph node dissection for gynecologic cancer, the surgeon identifies the pelvic diaphragm. Which muscle group constitutes the greatest muscular mass of the pelvic floor and forms the levator ani?
questions.question: During a retroperitoneal pelvic lymph node dissection for gynecologic cancer, the surgeon identifies the pelvic diaphragm. Which muscle group constitutes the greatest muscular mass of the pelvic floor and forms the levator ani?
questions.explanation: The levator ani muscle forms the bulk of the pelvic diaphragm and consists of three components: puborectalis (forming the U-shaped sling around the anorectum), pubococcygeus, and iliococcygeus.

questions.topicTitle: Histology of the Female Genital Tract
questions.prompt: In the uterine cervix, what epithelial transition defines the physiological 'Transformation Zone' where squamous metaplasia occurs and where over 90% of cervical intraepithelial neoplasias develop?
questions.question: In the uterine cervix, what epithelial transition defines the physiological 'Transformation Zone' where squamous metaplasia occurs and where over 90% of cervical intraepithelial neoplasias develop?
options: Transition from transitional epithelium to pseudostratified columnar epithelium
The dynamic area between the original squamocolumnar junction and the new physiological squamocolumnar junction
The junction between non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and peritoneal mesothelium
The border between the endometrial functionalis and basalis
questions.answer: The dynamic area between the original squamocolumnar junction and the new physiological squamocolumnar junction
questions.explanation: The transformation zone is the area of the cervix between the original squamocolumnar junction and the new, physiological squamocolumnar junction where continuous physiological squamous metaplasia takes place, rendering it uniquely vulnerable to oncogenic HPV integration.

questions.prompt: On histopathological evaluation of an endometrial biopsy performed on cycle day 17 (3 days post-ovulation) in an ovulatory cycle, what is the earliest pathognomonic morphological hallmark of progesterone action?
questions.question: On histopathological evaluation of an endometrial biopsy performed on cycle day 17 (3 days post-ovulation) in an ovulatory cycle, what is the earliest pathognomonic morphological hallmark of progesterone action?
options: Extensive stromal decidualization and spiral arteriolar prominence
Subnuclear glycogen-rich vacuoles in the glandular epithelial cells
Marked stromal edema with dense neutrophilic infiltration
Tortuous saw-toothed glands with intraluminal secretory exhaustion
questions.answer: Subnuclear glycogen-rich vacuoles in the glandular epithelial cells
questions.explanation: Subnuclear vacuolation (appearance of glycogen-rich vacuoles pushing epithelial nuclei toward the luminal border) is the earliest histological evidence of post-ovulatory progesterone stimulation, appearing typically around post-ovulatory day 2 to 3 (cycle day 16–17).

questions.question: Which epithelial lining characterizes the mucosa of the human fallopian tube (oviduct)?
options: Simple columnar ciliated cells interspersed with non-ciliated secretory (peg) cells
questions.answer: Simple columnar ciliated cells interspersed with non-ciliated secretory (peg) cells
questions.explanation: The fallopian tube mucosa is lined by simple columnar epithelium comprising ciliated cells (which beat toward the uterus to facilitate gamete and blastocyst transport) and non-ciliated secretory cells (peg cells, providing nutritional and fluid support).

questions.prompt: A 32-year-old parous female presents for a routine gynecological checkup. During pelvic examination, which instrument is specifically designed for self-retaining visualization of the vaginal walls and cervix without requiring an assistant?
questions.question: A 32-year-old parous female presents for a routine gynecological checkup. During pelvic examination, which instrument is specifically designed for self-retaining visualization of the vaginal walls and cervix without requiring an assistant?
questions.explanation: Cusco's bivalve speculum is self-retaining, holding open the anterior and posterior vaginal walls simultaneously, making it the premier instrument for outpatient cervical visualization, Pap smear collection, and IUD insertion without an assistant.
