questions.prompt: What differential tissue agonist/antagonist profile characterizes the Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) Tamoxifen?
questions.question: What differential tissue agonist/antagonist profile characterizes the Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) Tamoxifen?
options: Pure antagonist in all human tissues
Estrogen receptor antagonist in breast tissue, but partial agonist in the endometrium and bone
Agonist in breast, antagonist in bone
questions.answer: Estrogen receptor antagonist in breast tissue, but partial agonist in the endometrium and bone
questions.explanation: Tamoxifen is a SERM that competitively antagonizes estrogen receptors in mammary tissue (used in ER+ breast cancer), while displaying partial agonistic properties in bone (preserving bone density) and the endometrium (increasing risk of endometrial polyps, hyperplasia, and carcinoma).

questions.prompt: Why is 'add-back therapy' (low-dose estrogen plus progestin or tibolone) co-prescribed when treating severe endometriosis or uterine fibroids with GnRH agonists (e.g. leuprolide) for longer than 6 months?
questions.question: Why is 'add-back therapy' (low-dose estrogen plus progestin or tibolone) co-prescribed when treating severe endometriosis or uterine fibroids with GnRH agonists (e.g. leuprolide) for longer than 6 months?
options: To restore follicular development and trigger rapid ovulation
To reduce hot flushes and hypoestrogenic bone loss
To prevent drug-related hepatotoxicity during prolonged treatment
To induce immediate amenorrhea through enhanced pituitary suppression
questions.answer: To reduce hot flushes and hypoestrogenic bone loss
questions.explanation: Prolonged administration of GnRH agonists produces profound medical castration with severe bone demineralization (~5% trabecular bone loss in 6 months) and severe vasomotor flushes. Low-dose add-back therapy prevents bone loss and flushes without compromising endometriosis/fibroid control.

Binds progesterone receptors to inhibit or delay follicular rupture and luteinizing hormone surge even when LH has already begun rising
questions.answer: Binds progesterone receptors to inhibit or delay follicular rupture and luteinizing hormone surge even when LH has already begun rising
questions.explanation: Ulipristal acetate (30 mg oral) is a second-generation SPRM that delays or prevents ovulation. Unlike levonorgestrel which is ineffective once LH has begun to rise, ulipristal remains effective at inhibiting follicular rupture even immediately prior to ovulation.

questions.prompt: According to the two-cell, two-gonadotropin hypothesis of ovarian steroidogenesis, which hormone acts on the theca interna cells and which enzyme does it activate?
questions.question: According to the two-cell, two-gonadotropin hypothesis of ovarian steroidogenesis, which hormone acts on the theca interna cells and which enzyme does it activate?
options: LH acts on theca cells to synthesize androgens from cholesterol; FSH acts on granulosa cells to stimulate aromatase (CYP19A1)
FSH acts on theca cells to stimulate 17-hydroxylase; LH acts on granulosa cells to convert progesterone into estradiol
LH acts on granulosa cells to produce testosterone; FSH acts on theca cells to produce estrone
FSH acts on theca cells to stimulate StAR protein; LH acts on granulosa cells to stimulate 21-hydroxylase
questions.answer: LH acts on theca cells to synthesize androgens from cholesterol; FSH acts on granulosa cells to stimulate aromatase (CYP19A1)
questions.explanation: In ovarian folliculogenesis, the two-cell, two-gonadotropin system explains estrogen synthesis: (1) Theca interna cells express LH receptors; LH stimulates cholesterol uptake and converts cholesterol into androgens (androstenedione and testosterone) via 17α-hydroxylase (CYP17A1). (2) Granulosa cells express FSH receptors; FSH activates the aromatase enzyme (CYP19A1), which converts androgens diffusing from theca cells into estrogens (estrone and 17β-estradiol). Granulosa cells cannot synthesize androgens de novo due to lacking 17α-hydroxylase.

questions.prompt: What critical serum estradiol threshold and duration are required to trigger the positive feedback mid-cycle LH surge in a normal ovulatory cycle?
questions.question: What critical serum estradiol threshold and duration are required to trigger the positive feedback mid-cycle LH surge in a normal ovulatory cycle?
options: Serum estradiol >= 200 pg/mL sustained for at least 36-48 hours
Serum estradiol >= 50 pg/mL sustained for 12 hours
Serum estradiol >= 500 pg/mL sustained for 6 hours
Serum estradiol >= 100 pg/mL sustained for 7 days
questions.answer: Serum estradiol >= 200 pg/mL sustained for at least 36-48 hours
questions.explanation: Throughout the early and mid-follicular phases, estradiol exerts negative feedback on gonadotropin release. However, as the dominant follicle matures, it produces high concentrations of estradiol. When serum estradiol reaches or exceeds a threshold of 200 pg/mL and is maintained for at least 36 to 48 hours, it flips from negative to positive feedback at the anterior pituitary and hypothalamus, triggering the mid-cycle surge of LH (and FSH).

12 hours after the onset; 2 hours after the peak
72 hours after the onset; 48 hours after the peak
24 hours after the onset; 24 hours after the peak
questions.answer: 34-36 hours after the onset of the LH surge; 10-12 hours after the peak of the LH surge
questions.explanation: Ovulation occurs consistently approximately 34 to 36 hours after the initial onset (first rise) of the LH surge, and approximately 10 to 12 hours after the LH surge reaches its peak concentration. This precise temporal relationship is the basis for scheduling intrauterine insemination (IUI) or oocyte retrieval following recombinant hCG administration in ART cycles.

questions.prompt: What is the normal lifespan of the human corpus luteum in a non-conception menstrual cycle?
questions.question: What is the normal lifespan of the human corpus luteum in a non-conception menstrual cycle?
questions.explanation: In an ovulatory menstrual cycle without conception, the functional lifespan of the corpus luteum is remarkably constant at 14 days (+/- 2 days). In the absence of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) from a blastocyst, the corpus luteum undergoes programmed luteolysis with regression into the fibrous corpus albicans, causing a precipitous drop in progesterone and estradiol that precipitates menstrual shedding.

questions.question: Which dimeric glycoprotein hormone is selectively secreted by developing antral follicles in the follicular phase to inhibit pituitary FSH secretion?
questions.explanation: Inhibin B is produced primarily by the granulosa cells of small growing antral follicles during the follicular phase, reaching its peak in the mid-follicular phase and selectively suppressing pituitary FSH secretion. In contrast, Inhibin A is produced by the dominant pre-ovulatory follicle and the corpus luteum, peaking during the luteal phase.

questions.prompt: What is the primary vascular mechanism that initiates endometrial shedding during menstruation?
questions.question: What is the primary vascular mechanism that initiates endometrial shedding during menstruation?
options: Intense vasoconstriction and spasm of spiral arterioles followed by ischemia, necrosis, and extravasation
Dilatation of radial arteries with hyperemic capillary bursting
questions.answer: Intense vasoconstriction and spasm of spiral arterioles followed by ischemia, necrosis, and extravasation
questions.explanation: Following luteolysis and withdrawal of progesterone, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and endothelin are released in the endometrium. This triggers profound, rhythmic vasoconstriction and spasms of the spiral arterioles supplying the stratum functionale, causing ischemic necrosis of the functional layer, vascular wall breakdown, and shedding of menstrual blood and necrotic decidual fragments.

questions.prompt: What is the physiological role of pulsatile GnRH secretion versus continuous non-pulsatile GnRH exposure?
questions.question: What is the physiological role of pulsatile GnRH secretion versus continuous non-pulsatile GnRH exposure?
options: Pulsatile secretion (every 60-90 minutes) stimulates gonadotropin release; continuous administration downregulates GnRH receptors causing profound hypogonadism
Continuous administration stimulates FSH; pulsatile secretion inhibits LH
Pulsatile secretion induces ovulation; continuous administration accelerates follicular recruitment
Continuous secretion stimulates corpus luteum progesterone production
questions.answer: Pulsatile secretion (every 60-90 minutes) stimulates gonadotropin release; continuous administration downregulates GnRH receptors causing profound hypogonadism
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic GnRH must be released in a pulsatile rhythm (every 60 to 90 minutes in the follicular phase and every 180 to 240 minutes in the luteal phase) to maintain pituitary sensitivity and stimulate normal LH/FSH secretion. Continuous non-pulsatile exposure to GnRH or long-acting GnRH agonists (e.g., leuprolide, goserelin) leads to initial flare followed by desensitization and downregulation of pituitary GnRH receptors, producing reversible medical hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (medical oophorectomy).

questions.prompt: What is the normal chronological sequence of pubertal milestones in a female?
questions.question: What is the normal chronological sequence of pubertal milestones in a female?
options: Thelarche -> Adrenarche/Pubarche -> Peak height velocity (Growth spurt) -> Menarche
questions.answer: Thelarche -> Adrenarche/Pubarche -> Peak height velocity (Growth spurt) -> Menarche
questions.explanation: Normal female puberty follows an orderly sequence: (1) Thelarche (breast bud development, usually age 8-10 years, first sign of estrogen action); (2) Adrenarche/Pubarche (development of pubic and axillary hair under adrenal and ovarian androgens, ~age 10-11); (3) Peak height velocity (maximum growth spurt, ~age 11-12); (4) Menarche (onset of menses, occurring ~2 to 2.5 years after thelarche, average age 12.5 years).

questions.prompt: What is the clinical definition of precocious puberty in girls, and what is the drug of choice for central (GnRH-dependent) precocious puberty?
questions.question: What is the clinical definition of precocious puberty in girls, and what is the drug of choice for central (GnRH-dependent) precocious puberty?
options: Development of secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years of age (or menarche before 9.5-10 years); Depot GnRH agonists (e.g., leuprolide acetate)
Development of secondary sexual characteristics before 10 years of age; High-dose combined oral contraceptives
Menarche before 12 years of age; Danazol
Breast budding before 6 years of age; Letrozole
questions.answer: Development of secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years of age (or menarche before 9.5-10 years); Depot GnRH agonists (e.g., leuprolide acetate)
questions.explanation: Precocious puberty in girls is traditionally defined as the onset of secondary sexual characteristics (breast budding or pubic hair) before 8 years of age or menarche before 9.5-10 years of age. In central (true/GnRH-dependent) precocious puberty, early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis occurs. The treatment of choice is continuous long-acting depot GnRH agonists (e.g., leuprolide depot 3.75-11.25 mg), which downregulate pituitary GnRH receptors, halt sexual development, and prevent premature epiphyseal fusion to preserve adult height.

questions.prompt: According to the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) criteria, what are the diagnostic diagnostic criteria for Premature Ovarian Insufficiency (POI)?
questions.question: According to the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) criteria, what are the diagnostic diagnostic criteria for Premature Ovarian Insufficiency (POI)?
options: Oligo/amenorrhoea for at least 4 months before age 40 years, with elevated FSH > 25 IU/L on two occasions at least 4 weeks apart
Amenorrhoea for 12 months before age 45 years with FSH > 10 IU/L
Single FSH level > 40 IU/L before age 35 years regardless of menstrual cycle history
Absence of menses for 6 months after age 40 with low AMH < 1.0 ng/mL
questions.answer: Oligo/amenorrhoea for at least 4 months before age 40 years, with elevated FSH > 25 IU/L on two occasions at least 4 weeks apart
questions.explanation: ESHRE guidelines define premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) by: (1) Oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea for at least 4 months, (2) in a woman younger than 40 years of age, and (3) elevated serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) > 25 IU/L measured on two separate occasions at least 4 weeks apart. Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) is typically undetectable or extremely low.

questions.prompt: What is the predominant circulating estrogen in postmenopausal women, and what is its primary site of biosynthesis?
questions.question: What is the predominant circulating estrogen in postmenopausal women, and what is its primary site of biosynthesis?
options: Estrone (E1); Synthesized in peripheral adipose tissue by aromatization of adrenal androstenedione
Estradiol (E2); Synthesized in the ovarian stroma
Estriol (E3); Synthesized in the liver by sulfation
Estetrol (E4); Synthesized in the adrenal cortex
questions.answer: Estrone (E1); Synthesized in peripheral adipose tissue by aromatization of adrenal androstenedione
questions.explanation: In reproductive-aged women, 17β-estradiol (E2) is the predominant circulating estrogen, secreted by ovarian granulosa cells. Following menopause, ovarian follicular estrogen secretion ceases, and estrone (E1) becomes the predominant circulating estrogen. Estrone is synthesized peripherally, primarily in subcutaneous adipose tissue stroma and liver, through the enzymatic aromatization of adrenal-derived androstenedione.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme deficiency is responsible for more than 90-95% of cases of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) presenting with 46,XX virilization and salt wasting?
questions.question: Which enzyme deficiency is responsible for more than 90-95% of cases of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) presenting with 46,XX virilization and salt wasting?
questions.explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (due to CYP21A2 gene mutations) accounts for > 90-95% of CAH. Impaired conversion of 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) to 11-deoxycortisol causes cortisol deficiency, which stimulates ACTH hypersecretion, driving steroid precursors into the adrenal androgen pathway. This leads to marked accumulation of 17-OHP and androgens, causing clitoromegaly and ambiguous genitalia in 46,XX females. In the classic salt-wasting form, concomitant aldosterone deficiency causes neonatal hyponatremic hyperkalemic shock.

questions.prompt: What clinical and hormonal features distinguish Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS) from Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome?
questions.question: What clinical and hormonal features distinguish Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS) from Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome?
options: CAIS: 46,XY karyotype, absent pubic/axillary hair, male serum testosterone levels; MRKH: 46,XX karyotype, normal pubic/axillary hair, female serum testosterone levels
CAIS: 46,XX karyotype with hirsutism; MRKH: 46,XY karyotype without gonads
CAIS patients have functioning ovaries; MRKH patients have cryptorchid testes
CAIS presents with cyclic pelvic pain; MRKH presents with secondary amenorrhoea
questions.answer: CAIS: 46,XY karyotype, absent pubic/axillary hair, male serum testosterone levels; MRKH: 46,XX karyotype, normal pubic/axillary hair, female serum testosterone levels
questions.explanation: Both CAIS and MRKH present with primary amenorrhoea, excellent breast development, and an absent/blind-ending vagina with absent uterus. However, they are distinguished by: (1) Karyotype: CAIS is 46,XY; MRKH is 46,XX. (2) Body hair: In CAIS, androgen receptor insensitivity prevents pubic and axillary hair development (sparse or absent hair); in MRKH, androgen receptors and hair are normal. (3) Gonads: CAIS has cryptorchid or labial testes producing normal/elevated male testosterone; MRKH has normal functioning pelvic ovaries producing female testosterone levels.

questions.prompt: In a 46,XY patient with Swyer syndrome (pure gonadal dysgenesis), what is the status of the internal genital organs and what is the lifetime risk of gonadal malignancy (gonadoblastoma/dysgerminoma)?
questions.question: In a 46,XY patient with Swyer syndrome (pure gonadal dysgenesis), what is the status of the internal genital organs and what is the lifetime risk of gonadal malignancy (gonadoblastoma/dysgerminoma)?
options: Normal uterus, cervix, and fallopian tubes are present; Gonadal malignancy risk is 25-30%
Absent uterus and fallopian tubes; Malignancy risk is < 1%
Normal male internal Wolffian structures; Malignancy risk is 75%
Ambiguous internal genitalia; Malignancy risk is 0%
questions.answer: Normal uterus, cervix, and fallopian tubes are present; Gonadal malignancy risk is 25-30%
questions.explanation: In Swyer syndrome (46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis), mutation or deletion in SRY or related genes prevents testicular development. Consequently, the streak gonads produce neither anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) nor testosterone. In the absence of AMH, the Müllerian ducts develop into a normal uterus, fallopian tubes, and upper vagina; in the absence of testosterone, external genitalia are phenotypically female. The streak gonads carrying a Y chromosome carry a 25-30% lifetime risk of developing gonadoblastoma or dysgerminoma, necessitating prophylactic bilateral gonadectomy upon diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A phenotypic female infant with ambiguous genitalia is found to have a 46,XY karyotype. At puberty, she experiences marked virilization (deepening of voice, muscle mass, and phallic enlargement) without breast development. Which enzymatic defect explains this clinical picture?
questions.question: A phenotypic female infant with ambiguous genitalia is found to have a 46,XY karyotype. At puberty, she experiences marked virilization (deepening of voice, muscle mass, and phallic enlargement) without breast development. Which enzymatic defect explains this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: 5α-reductase type 2 (SRD5A2) deficiency impairs the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in target tissues. Since DHT is mandatory for external male virilization in utero, newborns present with ambiguous genitalia (pseudovaginal perineoscrotal hypospadias) or appear phenotypically female. However, at puberty, huge surges of LH and testicular testosterone act directly on testosterone-responsive receptors, causing dramatic virilization ('penis at 12' phenomenon) without gynecomastia.

questions.prompt: What is the classic cardiac anomaly and renal anomaly most commonly associated with Turner syndrome (45,X)?
questions.question: What is the classic cardiac anomaly and renal anomaly most commonly associated with Turner syndrome (45,X)?
options: Bicuspid aortic valve / Coarctation of the aorta; Horseshoe kidney
Tetralogy of Fallot; Polycystic kidney disease
Transposition of great vessels; Medullary sponge kidney
questions.answer: Bicuspid aortic valve / Coarctation of the aorta; Horseshoe kidney
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome (45,X or mosaicism) is the most common cause of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and primary amenorrhoea due to accelerated ovarian follicular atresia resulting in streak gonads. Cardinal cardiovascular anomalies include bicuspid aortic valve (30%) and coarctation of the aorta (10-15%), which carry high risk of aortic dissection. Renal anomalies are present in 30-40% of patients, classically horseshoe kidney and pelvic kidneys.

questions.prompt: What histological structure confirms the diagnosis of Ovotesticular DSD (true hermaphroditism)?
questions.question: What histological structure confirms the diagnosis of Ovotesticular DSD (true hermaphroditism)?
options: Coexistence of histologically confirmed ovarian follicles/stroma and testicular seminiferous tubules in the same individual
Presence of bilateral streak gonads containing fibrous tissue
Presence of Leydig cell hyperplasia with adrenal rests
Presence of an ovarian cyst with a rudimentary testis
questions.answer: Coexistence of histologically confirmed ovarian follicles/stroma and testicular seminiferous tubules in the same individual
questions.explanation: Ovotesticular DSD (formerly true hermaphroditism) is definitively defined by histological demonstration of both mature ovarian tissue (with primordial follicles) and testicular tissue (with seminiferous tubules) in the same individual. This may occur as a combined ovotestis (unilaterally or bilaterally) or as an ovary on one side and a testis on the other. The most common karyotype is 46,XX (~70%), followed by 46,XX/46,XY chimerism.

questions.prompt: According to the Prader clinical staging system for female virilization, which stage describes complete male-appearing external genitalia with a penile urethra at the tip of the phallus?
questions.question: According to the Prader clinical staging system for female virilization, which stage describes complete male-appearing external genitalia with a penile urethra at the tip of the phallus?
questions.explanation: The Prader staging system classifies ambiguous genitalia in virilized 46,XX females (such as in CAH): Stage 1 = mild clitoromegaly with normal vaginal orifice; Stage 2 = clitoromegaly with single urogenital sinus opening and posterior labial fusion; Stage 3 = marked clitoromegaly, complete labial fusion, single perineal opening; Stage 4 = phallic enlargement with hypospadias-like opening at the base; Stage 5 = complete penile urethra opening at the glans with complete scrotalization of labia (completely masculine external appearance).

questions.prompt: What is the optimal timing within the menstrual cycle for performing a Hysterosalpingography (HSG) in an infertility workup?
questions.question: What is the optimal timing within the menstrual cycle for performing a Hysterosalpingography (HSG) in an infertility workup?
options: In the early follicular phase, between days 7 and 10 of the cycle (after bleeding has ceased but before ovulation)
In the mid-luteal phase on day 21
questions.answer: In the early follicular phase, between days 7 and 10 of the cycle (after bleeding has ceased but before ovulation)
questions.explanation: HSG is ideally performed in the pre-ovulatory follicular phase, between cycle days 7 and 10. This window ensures: (1) Menstrual bleeding has completely ceased, preventing intravasation of contrast into open venous channels and retrograde dissemination of endometrium; (2) The endometrium is thin, minimizing false-positive filling defects; and (3) The patient is not pregnant, avoiding accidental radiation or disruption of an early conception.

questions.question: What is the gold standard diagnostic procedure for assessing tubal patency and pelvic peritoneal adhesions simultaneously?
options: Diagnostic laparoscopy with chromopertubation using dilute methylene blue
questions.answer: Diagnostic laparoscopy with chromopertubation using dilute methylene blue
questions.explanation: Diagnostic laparoscopy with chromopertubation (instillation of dilute methylene blue or indigo carmine via a cervical cannula) is the gold standard for evaluating tubal factor and peritoneal factor infertility. Unlike HSG, it provides direct 360-degree visualization of fimbrial architecture, peritubal and periovarian adhesions, pelvic endometriosis, and pelvic peritoneal anatomy.

questions.prompt: Which biomarker of ovarian reserve remains stable throughout the entire menstrual cycle and can be measured on any cycle day?
questions.question: Which biomarker of ovarian reserve remains stable throughout the entire menstrual cycle and can be measured on any cycle day?
questions.explanation: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) is secreted by granulosa cells of pre-antral and small antral follicles (< 8 mm). Because these small follicles develop continuously independent of gonadotropin cycles, serum AMH exhibits minimal intracycle variation and can be measured on any day of the menstrual cycle. FSH, estradiol, and inhibin B fluctuate widely and must be measured strictly on Day 2-3 of the cycle.

questions.prompt: What is the primary mechanism of action and first-line role of Letrozole in anovulatory infertility in women with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)?
questions.question: What is the primary mechanism of action and first-line role of Letrozole in anovulatory infertility in women with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)?
options: Aromatase inhibitor; Reversibly inhibits estrogen biosynthesis, reducing pituitary negative feedback to stimulate endogenous FSH release
Selective estrogen receptor modulator; Blocks estrogen receptors at the hypothalamus
Direct dopamine receptor agonist; Inhibits prolactin secretion
Insulin sensitizer; Directly activates ovarian LH receptors
questions.answer: Aromatase inhibitor; Reversibly inhibits estrogen biosynthesis, reducing pituitary negative feedback to stimulate endogenous FSH release
questions.explanation: Letrozole is a non-steroidal third-generation aromatase inhibitor. By blocking the conversion of androstenedione to estrone and testosterone to estradiol, it temporarily lowers circulating estrogens. This relieves hypothalamic-pituitary negative feedback, triggering endogenous pituitary FSH release to stimulate mono-follicular development. Unlike clomiphene, letrozole does not deplete endometrial or cervical estrogen receptors, achieving higher live birth and ovulation rates in PCOS women.

questions.prompt: In an infertility patient diagnosed with bilateral hydrosalpinx, what surgical intervention prior to In Vitro Fertilization (IVF) significantly doubles the clinical pregnancy rate?
questions.question: In an infertility patient diagnosed with bilateral hydrosalpinx, what surgical intervention prior to In Vitro Fertilization (IVF) significantly doubles the clinical pregnancy rate?
questions.explanation: Hydrosalpinx fluid is embryotoxic and exerts a mechanical wash-out effect, while downregulating endometrial receptivity markers (such as alpha-v beta-3 integrin and HOXA10). Meta-analyses demonstrate that hydrosalpinx halves IVF success rates and doubles spontaneous abortion rates. Prophylactic laparoscopic salpingectomy (or proximal tubal disconnection) before IVF eliminates reflux of toxic fluid, doubling clinical pregnancy and live birth rates.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended duration of regular unprotected intercourse before initiating an infertility evaluation in a woman aged 35 years or older?
questions.question: What is the recommended duration of regular unprotected intercourse before initiating an infertility evaluation in a woman aged 35 years or older?
questions.explanation: Infertility is defined as the inability to conceive after 12 months of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse in women under 35 years of age. However, in women aged 35 years and older, clinical evaluation and treatment should be initiated after 6 months of attempted conception due to age-related decline in ovarian reserve and oocyte quality. Immediate evaluation is indicated if there is a known history of oligo/amenorrhoea, advanced endometriosis, or pelvic inflammatory disease.

questions.prompt: What is the key clinical and physiological difference between In Vitro Fertilization (IVF) and Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection (ICSI)?
questions.question: What is the key clinical and physiological difference between In Vitro Fertilization (IVF) and Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection (ICSI)?
options: In IVF, thousands of motile sperm incubate with an oocyte allowing natural penetration; in ICSI, a single immobilized spermatozoon is microinjected directly into the ooplasm
IVF is used exclusively for azoospermia, whereas ICSI is used for tubal factor
In ICSI, fertilization occurs within the fallopian tube
In IVF, blastocyst biopsy is mandatory; in ICSI, cleavage biopsy is used
questions.answer: In IVF, thousands of motile sperm incubate with an oocyte allowing natural penetration; in ICSI, a single immobilized spermatozoon is microinjected directly into the ooplasm
questions.explanation: Conventional IVF involves co-incubating an unfertilized oocyte with approximately 50,000 to 100,000 motile spermatozoa in a dish, requiring the sperm to spontaneously penetrate the cumulus and zona pellucida. ICSI (developed by Palermo in 1992) involves mechanically stripping cumulus cells, selecting a single morphologically viable spermatozoon, breaking its tail to immobilize it, and directly injecting it through the zona pellucida into the ooplasm of a mature metaphase II oocyte. It is primarily indicated for severe male-factor subfertility.

questions.prompt: What is the primary strategy to prevent severe Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) in high-responder patients undergoing controlled ovarian hyperstimulation in a GnRH antagonist protocol?
questions.question: What is the primary strategy to prevent severe Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) in high-responder patients undergoing controlled ovarian hyperstimulation in a GnRH antagonist protocol?
options: Triggering final oocyte maturation with a GnRH agonist instead of hCG, combined with 'freeze-all' of embryos
Doubling the dose of urinary hCG trigger to 20,000 IU
Performing immediate fresh double blastocyst transfer
Administering high-dose intramuscular progesterone before oocyte pickup
questions.answer: Triggering final oocyte maturation with a GnRH agonist instead of hCG, combined with 'freeze-all' of embryos
questions.explanation: The pathophysiology of OHSS is driven by hCG-mediated secretion of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF) from multiple corpora lutea, causing marked third-space capillary leakage. In a GnRH antagonist stimulation cycle, substituting the traditional hCG trigger with a GnRH agonist trigger (e.g., triptorelin) induces an endogenous LH/FSH surge with a short half-life (~24-36 hours), completely preventing late OHSS. Cryopreserving all embryos ('freeze-all' protocol) and transferring in a subsequent natural/frozen cycle abolishes pregnancy-induced endogenous hCG production.

questions.prompt: What is the mathematical definition and formula for the 'Pearl Index' used to evaluate contraceptive failure rates?
questions.question: What is the mathematical definition and formula for the 'Pearl Index' used to evaluate contraceptive failure rates?
options: Number of accidental pregnancies per 100 woman-years of exposure (or per 1,200 woman-months of exposure)
Number of pregnancies divided by the total number of couples enrolled in a 10-year trial
Percentage of women experiencing irregular bleeding during the first 6 months of use
Ratio of ectopic pregnancies to normal intrauterine conceptions per 1,000 women
questions.answer: Number of accidental pregnancies per 100 woman-years of exposure (or per 1,200 woman-months of exposure)
questions.explanation: The Pearl Index is the standard epidemiological metric for contraceptive failure: Pearl Index = (Total number of accidental pregnancies * 1,200) / (Total months of exposure), representing the number of unintended pregnancies per 100 woman-years of contraceptive use. A lower Pearl Index indicates higher contraceptive efficacy (e.g., subdermal implant ~0.05, levonorgestrel IUD ~0.2, barrier condoms ~2-15).

questions.prompt: According to the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) for contraceptive use, what do Categories 1, 2, 3, and 4 represent?
questions.question: According to the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) for contraceptive use, what do Categories 1, 2, 3, and 4 represent?
options: Category 1: No restriction; Category 2: Advantages outweigh risks; Category 3: Risks outweigh advantages; Category 4: Unacceptable health risk (strictly contraindicated)
Category 1: Strictly contraindicated; Category 4: Completely safe without restriction
Category 1: Low efficacy; Category 4: Permanent sterilization
questions.answer: Category 1: No restriction; Category 2: Advantages outweigh risks; Category 3: Risks outweigh advantages; Category 4: Unacceptable health risk (strictly contraindicated)
questions.explanation: The WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC) uses a 4-tier classification: Category 1 = A condition for which there is no restriction for the use of the method; Category 2 = Advantages outweigh theoretical or proven risks; Category 3 = Theoretical or proven risks usually outweigh advantages (method not recommended unless alternatives unavailable); Category 4 = A condition that represents an unacceptable health risk (absolute contraindication, e.g., combined oral contraceptives in women aged >= 35 smoking >= 15 cigarettes/day).

questions.prompt: What is the primary contraceptive mechanism of action of the Levonorgestrel Intrauterine System (LNG-IUS, 52 mg)?
questions.question: What is the primary contraceptive mechanism of action of the Levonorgestrel Intrauterine System (LNG-IUS, 52 mg)?
options: Profound endometrial glandular atrophy and thick, impermeable cervical mucus plug that prevents sperm transit and penetration
Permanent suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis and inhibition of ovulation in 100% of cycles
Induction of a copper-ion sterile cytotoxic inflammatory reaction in the fallopian tube
Destruction of blastocyst cell membrane upon uterine contact
questions.answer: Profound endometrial glandular atrophy and thick, impermeable cervical mucus plug that prevents sperm transit and penetration
questions.explanation: The LNG-IUS (52 mg, e.g., Mirena) releases levonorgestrel directly into the uterine cavity at ~20 mcg/day initially. Its primary mechanisms of action are local: (1) marked endometrial suppression and decidualization with glandular atrophy, making the endometrium unreceptive to implantation; and (2) thickening and inspissation of cervical mucus, creating a formidable barrier to sperm transit and viability. The majority of women (> 75-85%) continue to have normal ovulatory ovarian cycles, demonstrating that systemic anovulation is not its primary mechanism.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: What is the most effective form of emergency contraception within 120 hours (5 days) of unprotected sexual intercourse?
questions.question: What is the most effective form of emergency contraception within 120 hours (5 days) of unprotected sexual intercourse?
options: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg single oral dose
questions.explanation: Insertion of a copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD) within 5 days (120 hours) of unprotected intercourse is the single most effective emergency contraceptive method, with a failure rate of < 0.1% (over 99.9% effective). Furthermore, it provides immediate long-term ongoing contraception for 10-12 years. If an oral agent is chosen, ulipristal acetate (selective progesterone receptor modulator) is more effective than levonorgestrel, particularly when taken 72-120 hours post-coitus or in overweight women.

questions.prompt: Which surgical female sterilization procedure involves grasping a loop of the mid-portion of the fallopian tube, crushing and ligating the base with absorbable chromic catgut, and excising a 1 cm segment of the loop?
questions.question: Which surgical female sterilization procedure involves grasping a loop of the mid-portion of the fallopian tube, crushing and ligating the base with absorbable chromic catgut, and excising a 1 cm segment of the loop?
questions.explanation: The Pomeroy technique is the most widely performed postpartum and interval tubal ligation method due to its simplicity, efficacy, and low failure rate. A loop of the mid-ampullary tube is elevated, its base is ligated with plain or chromic catgut (rapidly absorbable, avoiding tissue necrosis before separation), and the apex of the loop is excised. As the absorbable suture dissolves, the two cut ends retract and heal with a distinct fibrous gap. In contrast, the Madlener technique crushes the tube without excision, carrying higher recanalization rates.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended delay before a man can rely on vasectomy as a sole method of contraception, and how is sterility confirmed?
questions.question: What is the recommended delay before a man can rely on vasectomy as a sole method of contraception, and how is sterility confirmed?
options: At least 3 months and 20 ejaculations; Confirmed by azoospermia on post-vasectomy semen analysis (PVSA)
Immediate sterility following surgery; Confirmed by scrotal palpation
7 days; Confirmed by serum testosterone assay
12 months; Confirmed by negative urine analysis
questions.answer: At least 3 months and 20 ejaculations; Confirmed by azoospermia on post-vasectomy semen analysis (PVSA)
questions.explanation: Following vasectomy, residual viable spermatozoa remain stored in the ampullae of the vas deferens and seminal vesicles. Sterility is not instantaneous. An alternative contraceptive method must be used until post-vasectomy semen analysis (PVSA) confirms clearance. Guidelines mandate waiting at least 3 months and performing at least 20 ejaculations, with confirmation of azoospermia (or unmotile sperm < 100,000/mL) on a fresh semen sample.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: What non-contraceptive health benefit is conclusively associated with the long-term use of Combined Oral Contraceptive (COC) pills?
questions.question: What non-contraceptive health benefit is conclusively associated with the long-term use of Combined Oral Contraceptive (COC) pills?
options: Significant risk reduction for epithelial ovarian and endometrial adenocarcinoma
Significant risk reduction for cervical carcinoma and HPV infection
Elimination of deep vein thrombosis risk
questions.answer: Significant risk reduction for epithelial ovarian and endometrial adenocarcinoma
questions.explanation: Long-term use of combined oral contraceptives (COCs) provides robust, well-documented protection against both epithelial ovarian cancer (suppressing incessant ovulation and reducing risk by up to 50%) and endometrial adenocarcinoma (progestin-mediated antagonism of estrogenic mitogenesis). This protective effect persists for 15-30 years after discontinuation. Conversely, COCs slightly increase the relative risk of venous thromboembolism and cervical cancer (in persistent HPV-infected women).

questions.prompt: What is the standard WHO evidence-based medical abortion regimen for pregnancies up to 9-10 weeks (63-70 days) of gestation?
questions.question: What is the standard WHO evidence-based medical abortion regimen for pregnancies up to 9-10 weeks (63-70 days) of gestation?
options: Mifepristone 200 mg orally, followed 24-48 hours later by Misoprostol 800 mcg buccally, sublingually, or vaginally
Misoprostol 200 mcg orally alone as a single dose
Mifepristone 600 mg daily for 5 consecutive days
questions.answer: Mifepristone 200 mg orally, followed 24-48 hours later by Misoprostol 800 mcg buccally, sublingually, or vaginally
questions.explanation: The standard, highly effective regimen recommended by the WHO and international guidelines for early medical termination of pregnancy up to 63-70 days gestation is: Mifepristone 200 mg orally (a selective progesterone receptor antagonist that induces decidual breakdown and cervical softening), followed 24 to 48 hours later by Misoprostol 800 mcg administered buccally, sublingually, or vaginally (a prostaglandin E1 analogue that triggers strong myometrial contractions and cervical dilation). Complete abortion rates exceed 95-98%.

questions.prompt: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Amendment Act in India, up to what gestational age can a pregnancy be terminated with the opinion of one Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP)?
questions.question: Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Amendment Act in India, up to what gestational age can a pregnancy be terminated with the opinion of one Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP)?
questions.explanation: Under the amended MTP Act (2021) in India: (1) Termination of pregnancy up to 20 weeks requires the opinion of one Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP); (2) Termination between 20 and 24 weeks is permissible for specified categories of vulnerable women (survivors of sexual assault/rape, minors, change of marital status during pregnancy, severe physical disability, fetal malformations) and requires the opinion of two RMPs; (3) Beyond 24 weeks, termination is permitted for substantial fetal abnormalities diagnosed by a State-level Medical Board.

questions.prompt: What is the primary pharmacological action of Mifepristone (RU-486)?
questions.question: What is the primary pharmacological action of Mifepristone (RU-486)?
options: Competitive antagonism at progesterone receptors and glucocorticoid receptors
questions.answer: Competitive antagonism at progesterone receptors and glucocorticoid receptors
questions.explanation: Mifepristone is a synthetic 19-norsteroid compound that acts as a competitive antagonist at progesterone receptors (with higher affinity than endogenous progesterone) and glucocorticoid receptors. By blocking progesterone, it causes decidual degeneration, detachment of the blastocyst, decreased hCG secretion, and sensitization of the myometrium to prostaglandin-induced contractions. It also promotes cervical ripening through local collagen breakdown.

questions.prompt: What is the preferred surgical evacuation method for terminating early first-trimester pregnancy up to 12-14 weeks of gestation due to lower rates of uterine perforation and blood loss?
questions.question: What is the preferred surgical evacuation method for terminating early first-trimester pregnancy up to 12-14 weeks of gestation due to lower rates of uterine perforation and blood loss?
options: Manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) or electric suction curettage
Sharp metallic curettage alone without suction
questions.answer: Manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) or electric suction curettage
questions.explanation: Vacuum aspiration (either manual vacuum aspiration [MVA] with a handheld syringe generating 60 mmHg negative pressure, or electric suction curettage) is the gold standard surgical method for first-trimester abortion up to 12-14 weeks. Sharp metallic curettage alone is obsolete and condemned by the WHO because vacuum aspiration is faster, less painful, and associated with significantly lower rates of uterine perforation, cervical laceration, blood loss, and intrauterine adhesion formation (Asherman syndrome).

questions.prompt: A Rh-negative, non-sensitized woman undergoes surgical termination of pregnancy at 10 weeks gestation. What is the recommended dose and timing of anti-D immunoglobulin administration?
questions.question: A Rh-negative, non-sensitized woman undergoes surgical termination of pregnancy at 10 weeks gestation. What is the recommended dose and timing of anti-D immunoglobulin administration?
options: Anti-D immunoglobulin 50-100 mcg (or 300 mcg) within 72 hours of the procedure
Anti-D immunoglobulin 300 mcg at 28 weeks of a subsequent pregnancy only
Anti-D is not indicated for terminations before 20 weeks
Anti-D immunoglobulin 1,000 mcg intravenously within 2 hours
questions.answer: Anti-D immunoglobulin 50-100 mcg (or 300 mcg) within 72 hours of the procedure
questions.explanation: To prevent Rh isoimmunization in an unsensitized Rh-D negative woman undergoing any abortion (spontaneous or induced, surgical or medical beyond 10-12 weeks), anti-D immunoglobulin must be administered intramuscularly within 72 hours. For first-trimester events (<= 12 weeks), a dose of 50 to 100 mcg is protective (though 300 mcg is commonly administered if lower-dose vials are unavailable). Beyond 12 weeks, the full standard dose of 300 mcg (1,500 IU) is mandatory.

questions.prompt: Which organism is classically implicated in rapidly fatal, fulminant toxic shock syndrome without fever following medical abortion with mifepristone and misoprostol?
questions.question: Which organism is classically implicated in rapidly fatal, fulminant toxic shock syndrome without fever following medical abortion with mifepristone and misoprostol?
questions.explanation: Clostridium sordellii is an anaerobic, spore-forming, Gram-positive bacillus that can colonize the female genital tract. It is associated with rare, catastrophic fatal toxic shock syndrome following medical abortion or childbirth. The clinical hallmark is profound hypothermia (or absence of fever), severe refractory hypotension, marked third-spacing with hemoconcentration, and extreme leukemoid reaction (WBC count > 50,000 to 100,000/mcL) mediated by lethal and hemorrhagic exotoxins.

questions.prompt: When can an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUD) or subcutaneous contraceptive implant be safely inserted following an uncomplicated surgical or medical abortion?
questions.question: When can an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUD) or subcutaneous contraceptive implant be safely inserted following an uncomplicated surgical or medical abortion?
options: Immediately post-procedure (at the time of surgical evacuation, or once expulsion is confirmed)
Strictly 6 weeks post-procedure after the first normal menses
3 months after verifying negative serum beta-hCG
Only after completing 6 cycles of oral contraceptives
questions.answer: Immediately post-procedure (at the time of surgical evacuation, or once expulsion is confirmed)
questions.explanation: Post-abortion contraception can and should be initiated immediately. Following surgical evacuation (MVA or suction), an IUD (copper or levonorgestrel) or etonogestrel implant can be inserted immediately before the patient leaves the operating table, resulting in high continuation rates and significantly reducing repeat unintended pregnancies. In medical abortion, an implant can be placed on the day mifepristone is administered, and an IUD can be inserted as soon as complete expulsion is clinically or sonographically confirmed.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: What is the clinical definition of primary amenorrhoea according to international endocrine society guidelines?
questions.question: What is the clinical definition of primary amenorrhoea according to international endocrine society guidelines?
options: No menses by age 13 in the absence of secondary sexual characteristics, OR no menses by age 15 in the presence of normal secondary sexual characteristics
No menses by age 16 regardless of breast development
No menses by age 18 in all girls
No menses for 3 months after regular cycles have been established
questions.answer: No menses by age 13 in the absence of secondary sexual characteristics, OR no menses by age 15 in the presence of normal secondary sexual characteristics
questions.explanation: Primary amenorrhoea is clinically defined as: (1) Absence of menarche by age 13 years in the absence of normal secondary sexual development (thelarche/pubic hair); OR (2) Absence of menarche by age 15 years in the presence of normal secondary sexual development and linear growth (or > 3 years post-thelarche). Earlier evaluation is indicated if cyclic pelvic pain or obstructive anatomical signs are present.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: In the diagnostic evaluation of secondary amenorrhoea, what does a positive withdrawal bleed following a 10-day course of oral medroxyprogesterone acetate (10 mg/day) confirm?
questions.question: In the diagnostic evaluation of secondary amenorrhoea, what does a positive withdrawal bleed following a 10-day course of oral medroxyprogesterone acetate (10 mg/day) confirm?
options: Adequate endogenous estrogen priming of the endometrium and a patent, functional uterine outflow tract
questions.answer: Adequate endogenous estrogen priming of the endometrium and a patent, functional uterine outflow tract
questions.explanation: A positive progestin challenge test (occurrence of withdrawal bleeding within 2-7 days after completing a 5-10 day course of progesterone/medroxyprogesterone) confirms two critical physiological facts: (1) The ovaries are secreting sufficient endogenous estrogen to proliferate the endometrium (serum estradiol > 40-50 pg/mL), and (2) The uterine cavity and genital outflow tract are anatomically patent. This establishes anovulation (as seen in PCOS) as the etiology. A negative test mandates an estrogen-plus-progestin challenge to rule out outflow tract pathology (e.g., Asherman syndrome).
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: A 17-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhoea, absent secondary sexual characteristics, and complete anosmia (inability to smell). Serum LH and FSH are low. What is the diagnosis and its underlying pathogenesis?
questions.question: A 17-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhoea, absent secondary sexual characteristics, and complete anosmia (inability to smell). Serum LH and FSH are low. What is the diagnosis and its underlying pathogenesis?
options: Kallmann syndrome; Failure of embryonic GnRH-secreting neurons and olfactory axons to migrate from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus (KAL1 mutation)
Turner syndrome; Accelerated apoptosis of ovarian oocytes
Craniopharyngioma; Direct compression of the optic chiasm
Swyer syndrome; SRY gene deletion preventing gonadal differentiation
questions.answer: Kallmann syndrome; Failure of embryonic GnRH-secreting neurons and olfactory axons to migrate from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus (KAL1 mutation)
questions.explanation: Kallmann syndrome is an inherited form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism characterized by the combination of delayed/absent puberty (primary amenorrhoea) and anosmia/hyposmia. It is caused by defective embryonic migration of GnRH-synthesizing neuroendocrine cells and olfactory nerve fibers from the nasal olfactory placode through the cribriform plate into the forebrain/hypothalamus (associated with mutations in KAL1, FGFR1, PROKR2). Laboratory workup demonstrates inappropriately low/normal serum LH, FSH, and estradiol.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: What is the single most common cause of secondary amenorrhoea in women of reproductive age?
questions.question: What is the single most common cause of secondary amenorrhoea in women of reproductive age?
questions.explanation: In any woman of reproductive age presenting with secondary amenorrhoea (absence of menses for 3 months in a woman with previous regular cycles, or 6 months with oligomenorrhoea), pregnancy is statistically the single most common cause. A urine or serum beta-hCG pregnancy test is mandatory as the absolute first step in the diagnostic algorithm before pursuing endocrine investigations.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old woman develops secondary amenorrhoea following an emergency sharp curettage for severe postpartum hemorrhage. Cyclic hormonal replacement therapy fails to induce withdrawal bleeding. What is the gold standard diagnostic and therapeutic modality for this condition?
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman develops secondary amenorrhoea following an emergency sharp curettage for severe postpartum hemorrhage. Cyclic hormonal replacement therapy fails to induce withdrawal bleeding. What is the gold standard diagnostic and therapeutic modality for this condition?
options: Hysteroscopy with sharp/cold scissors adhesiolysis followed by estrogen therapy and an intrauterine stent
Blind repeat sharp curettage under general anesthesia
High-dose oral medroxyprogesterone acetate for 6 months
questions.answer: Hysteroscopy with sharp/cold scissors adhesiolysis followed by estrogen therapy and an intrauterine stent
questions.explanation: This patient has Asherman syndrome (intrauterine synechiae/adhesions), which develops when vigorous postpartum or postabortal curettage damages the basal layer of the endometrium (stratum basale), causing fibrous bridging and cavity obliteration. The failure to bleed after sequential estrogen and progestin confirms an end-organ outflow obstruction. Hysteroscopy is the gold standard for direct visualization and division of synechiae. Postoperatively, high-dose estrogen therapy (with a temporary intrauterine balloon or stent) promotes endometrial re-epithelialization.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: Which pituitary adenoma size defines a microprolactinoma versus a macroprolactinoma, and what is the first-line medical therapy?
questions.question: Which pituitary adenoma size defines a microprolactinoma versus a macroprolactinoma, and what is the first-line medical therapy?
options: Microprolactinoma < 10 mm; Macroprolactinoma >= 10 mm; First-line therapy is dopamine agonists (Cabergoline)
Microprolactinoma < 20 mm; Macroprolactinoma >= 20 mm; First-line therapy is transsphenoidal hypophysectomy
Microprolactinoma < 5 mm; Macroprolactinoma >= 5 mm; First-line therapy is radiotherapy
Microprolactinoma < 15 mm; Macroprolactinoma >= 15 mm; First-line therapy is octreotide
questions.answer: Microprolactinoma < 10 mm; Macroprolactinoma >= 10 mm; First-line therapy is dopamine agonists (Cabergoline)
questions.explanation: Prolactinomas are classified by diameter on contrast-enhanced pituitary MRI: Microprolactinomas measure < 10 mm (< 1 cm), whereas Macroprolactinomas measure >= 10 mm. Elevated prolactin suppresses hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility, causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, amenorrhoea, and galactorrhoea. First-line therapy for both micro- and macro-prolactinomas is medical with dopamine D2 receptor agonists, with Cabergoline being preferred over bromocriptine due to superior efficacy, higher tumor shrinkage rates, and fewer gastrointestinal side effects.

questions.prompt: What is the triad of symptoms characteristic of 'Female Athlete Triad' leading to functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea (FHA)?
questions.question: What is the triad of symptoms characteristic of 'Female Athlete Triad' leading to functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea (FHA)?
options: Low energy availability (with or without disordered eating), menstrual dysfunction (amenorrhoea), and low bone mineral density (osteopenia/osteoporosis)
Hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries, and insulin resistance
Severe dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, and cyclic pelvic pain
questions.answer: Low energy availability (with or without disordered eating), menstrual dysfunction (amenorrhoea), and low bone mineral density (osteopenia/osteoporosis)
questions.explanation: The Female Athlete Triad is an interrelated clinical entity comprising: (1) Low energy availability (caloric intake insufficient to support exercise energy expenditure), (2) Menstrual dysfunction (ranging from luteal phase defect to functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea caused by suppressed leptin, elevated ghrelin/cortisol, and suppressed kisspeptin/GnRH pulsatility), and (3) Impaired bone health (low bone mineral density, osteopenia, and stress fractures due to hypoestrogenism).

questions.prompt: What is the definitive medical reason why unopposed systemic estrogen replacement therapy must NEVER be administered to a postmenopausal woman with an intact uterus?
questions.question: What is the definitive medical reason why unopposed systemic estrogen replacement therapy must NEVER be administered to a postmenopausal woman with an intact uterus?
options: Unopposed estrogen dramatically increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial adenocarcinoma
Unopposed estrogen causes immediate severe hyperkalemia
Unopposed estrogen induces rapid pituitary gonadotropin-secreting adenomas
Unopposed estrogen causes irreversible ovarian torsion
questions.answer: Unopposed estrogen dramatically increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial adenocarcinoma
questions.explanation: Administration of systemic estrogen without an accompanying progestogen in a postmenopausal woman with an intact uterus stimulates continuous endometrial cellular proliferation and mitogenesis without cyclical secretory shedding, increasing the relative risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial adenocarcinoma by 4- to 8-fold. Therefore, a progestogen (e.g., micronized oral progesterone or medroxyprogesterone acetate) must always be co-prescribed to induce endometrial differentiation and protection. Only hysterectomized women can safely receive unopposed estrogen therapy.

questions.prompt: What is the 'window of opportunity' (timing hypothesis) for initiating menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) to maximize cardiovascular benefits and minimize risks?
questions.question: What is the 'window of opportunity' (timing hypothesis) for initiating menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) to maximize cardiovascular benefits and minimize risks?
options: Initiation within 10 years of menopause or before age 60 years
Initiation only after documented coronary artery calcification
questions.answer: Initiation within 10 years of menopause or before age 60 years
questions.explanation: Extensive re-analyses of the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) and international consensus guidelines establish the 'timing hypothesis' or 'window of opportunity': Initiating MHT in women who are within 10 years of menopause onset or under 60 years of age yields a favorable risk-to-benefit profile with significant reductions in vasomotor symptoms, osteoporotic fractures, and all-cause mortality, with neutral or beneficial effects on coronary atherosclerosis. Initiating MHT after age 60 or > 10 years postmenopause confers higher vascular and thromboembolic risks.

questions.prompt: Which Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) acts as an estrogen antagonist in breast and endometrium while acting as an agonist on bone, making it an excellent drug for postmenopausal osteoporosis without increasing endometrial cancer risk?
questions.question: Which Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) acts as an estrogen antagonist in breast and endometrium while acting as an agonist on bone, making it an excellent drug for postmenopausal osteoporosis without increasing endometrial cancer risk?
questions.explanation: Raloxifene is a second-generation SERM that acts as an estrogen agonist on bone (inhibiting osteoclast resorption and preserving bone mineral density) and lipid metabolism, while acting as an estrogen antagonist on breast tissue (reducing invasive ER-positive breast cancer risk) and on the endometrium (does NOT stimulate endometrial proliferation or increase endometrial cancer risk). In contrast, tamoxifen acts as an agonist on the endometrium, increasing the risk of endometrial polyps, hyperplasia, and adenocarcinoma.

questions.prompt: What synthetic steroid with weak estrogenic, progestogenic, and androgenic properties is used to treat postmenopausal vasomotor symptoms and preserve bone density with a low incidence of breast pain and vaginal bleeding?
questions.question: What synthetic steroid with weak estrogenic, progestogenic, and androgenic properties is used to treat postmenopausal vasomotor symptoms and preserve bone density with a low incidence of breast pain and vaginal bleeding?
questions.explanation: Tibolone is a synthetic steroid that is metabolized in vivo into three active compounds: 3α- and 3β-hydroxy-tibolone (which bind estrogen receptors in brain and bone, relieving hot flushes and preventing osteoporosis) and the Δ4-isomer of tibolone (which binds progesterone and androgen receptors, protecting the endometrium from hyperplasia and improving libido). In the breast and endometrium, tibolone also inhibits sulfatase and 17β-HSD type 1, preventing local active estradiol generation.

questions.prompt: Which route of menopausal estrogen administration bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism, does not increase clotting factor synthesis, and is therefore preferred in women with obesity, hypertension, or elevated VTE risk?
questions.question: Which route of menopausal estrogen administration bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism, does not increase clotting factor synthesis, and is therefore preferred in women with obesity, hypertension, or elevated VTE risk?
questions.explanation: Oral estrogens undergo extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism, which stimulates hepatic synthesis of coagulation factors (factors VII, VIII, X, prothrombin, and fibrinogen) and downregulates antithrombin, thereby elevating venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk. Transdermal administration of 17β-estradiol (via patch or topical gel) delivers the hormone directly into the systemic circulation, avoiding the hepatic first-pass effect. Transdermal estrogen does not significantly alter coagulation profiles and is the route of choice for women with BMI > 30, hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, or mild VTE risk factors.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended non-hormonal, neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptor antagonist recently approved for the treatment of moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes) in menopausal women with contraindications to estrogen?
questions.question: What is the recommended non-hormonal, neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptor antagonist recently approved for the treatment of moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes) in menopausal women with contraindications to estrogen?
questions.explanation: Fezolinetant is a first-in-class, non-hormonal, small-molecule neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptor antagonist. Menopausal estrogen deficiency leads to hypertrophy and hyperactivity of KNDy (kisspeptin, neurokinin B, dynorphin) neurons in the infundibular nucleus of the hypothalamus, which project to the thermoregulatory center and trigger vasomotor flush episodes. Fezolinetant blocks neurokinin B binding to the NK3 receptor, restoring thermal equilibrium without any hormonal or estrogenic stimulation.

questions.prompt: What is the absolute contraindication to the prescription of Menopausal Hormone Therapy (MHT)?
questions.question: What is the absolute contraindication to the prescription of Menopausal Hormone Therapy (MHT)?
options: Known, suspected, or past history of breast cancer and unexplained abnormal vaginal bleeding
Mild osteopenia with family history of hip fracture
History of uncomplicated bilateral laparoscopic tubal ligation
questions.answer: Known, suspected, or past history of breast cancer and unexplained abnormal vaginal bleeding
questions.explanation: Absolute contraindications to menopausal hormone therapy include: (1) Current, past, or suspected breast carcinoma; (2) Known or suspected estrogen-dependent malignant neoplasia (e.g., endometrial cancer); (3) Unexplained, undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding; (4) Active or recent venous thromboembolic disease (DVT/PE); (5) Active arterial thromboembolic disease (angina, myocardial infarction, stroke); (6) Severe active liver disease with abnormal liver function tests; and (7) Porphyria cutanea tarda.

Darkfield microscopy of ulcer exudate demonstrates motile spirochetes with regular tight spirals. What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?

Primary Syphilis (hard chancre); Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
Genital Herpes (HSV-2); oral Acyclovir 400 mg thrice daily
questions.answer: Primary Syphilis (hard chancre); Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.explanation: Primary syphilis characteristically presents with a single painless, indurated ulcer (Hunterian chancre) with clean granulating floor and non-suppurative rubbery lymphadenopathy. Treponema pallidum is identified on darkground microscopy. The drug of choice is Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose.

questions.question: A 22-year-old female presents with multiple painful, non-indurated, soft, ragged-edged ulcers with purulent bases on the vulva, and painful unilateral fluctuant inguinal lymphadenitis (suppurating bubo). Gram stain demonstrates Gram-negative coccobacilli in a 'school of fish' arrangement. What is the organism?

Gram stain demonstrates Gram-negative coccobacilli in parallel chains ('school of fish' or 'railroad track' pattern).

questions.question: In Donovanosis (Granuloma inguinale), what microscopic pathognomonic diagnostic feature is demonstrated within large mononuclear histiocytes on Giemsa or Leishman stain of tissue crush smears?
options: Donovan bodies (safety-pin appearing intracellular encapsulated bacteria)
questions.answer: Donovan bodies (safety-pin appearing intracellular encapsulated bacteria)
questions.explanation: Donovanosis (caused by Klebsiella granulomatis) produces painless, beefy-red, exuberant vascular granulomatous ulcers without true lymphadenopathy ('pseudobubo'). Tissue smear reveals pathognomonic Donovan bodies—pleomorphic rod-shaped bacilli exhibiting bipolar safety-pin staining inside large macrophages.

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old female presents with a thin, homogeneous, off-white, foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Vaginal pH is 5.2. Addition of 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) releases a pungent fishy amine odor (positive Whiff test). Saline wet mount reveals vaginal squamous epithelial cells with stippled borders obscured by adherent coccobacilli. What is the diagnosis?
questions.question: A 28-year-old female presents with a thin, homogeneous, off-white, foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Vaginal pH is 5.2. Addition of 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) releases a pungent fishy amine odor (positive Whiff test). Saline wet mount reveals vaginal squamous epithelial cells with stippled borders obscured by adherent coccobacilli. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bacterial vaginosis is diagnosed by Amsel's criteria (at least 3 of 4: homogeneous grey-white discharge, vaginal pH > 4.5, positive amine whiff test with 10% KOH, and presence of > 20% clue cells on wet mount). It represents an overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis and anaerobes replacing protective hydrogen peroxide-producing lactobacilli.

questions.question: A 30-year-old female presents with profuse, greenish-yellow, frothy, malodorous vaginal discharge and severe pruritus vulvae. Speculum examination reveals punctate mucosal hemorrhages on the ectocervix ('strawberry cervix' / colpitis macularis). Saline wet-mount microscopy demonstrates motile flagellated protozoa with jerky movement. What is the treatment?
options: Metronidazole 2 g single oral dose (or 400–500 mg twice daily for 7 days) with concurrent treatment of sexual partner
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days
questions.answer: Metronidazole 2 g single oral dose (or 400–500 mg twice daily for 7 days) with concurrent treatment of sexual partner
questions.explanation: Trichomonas vaginalis is a flagellated protozoan causing colpitis macularis ('strawberry cervix') and frothy yellow-green discharge. Metronidazole or tinidazole is curative. Because it is an STI, concurrent simultaneous treatment of the sexual partner is mandatory to prevent reinfection.

questions.prompt: A 24-year-old diabetic female complains of intense vulvar pruritus, burning, and thick, white, curdy ('cottage-cheese' like) vaginal discharge adhering to the vaginal walls. questions.question: A 24-year-old diabetic female complains of intense vulvar pruritus, burning, and thick, white, curdy ('cottage-cheese' like) vaginal discharge adhering to the vaginal walls. The vaginal pH is acidic (pH 4.0–4.5). Wet mount with 10% KOH demonstrates budding yeast and pseudohyphae. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Vulvovaginal candidiasis is characterized by intense vulvar erythema, curdy white discharge, normal acidic pH (< 4.5), and visualization of pseudohyphae and blastospores on 10% KOH preparation. First-line therapy includes oral fluconazole 150 mg or topical azole creams.

questions.prompt: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidelines, what are the three minimum clinical criteria that mandate empirical antibiotic therapy for Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) in sexually active young women presenting with lower abdominal pain?
questions.question: According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) guidelines, what are the three minimum clinical criteria that mandate empirical antibiotic therapy for Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) in sexually active young women presenting with lower abdominal pain?
options: Leukocytosis, high fever, and positive blood cultures
Cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, OR adnexal tenderness on bimanual pelvic examination
questions.answer: Cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, OR adnexal tenderness on bimanual pelvic examination
questions.explanation: To prevent permanent tubal scarring and infertility, empirical treatment for PID is initiated if a sexually active female has lower abdominal or pelvic pain and at least one of the three minimum clinical criteria on bimanual exam: cervical motion tenderness ('chandelier sign'), uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness.

questions.prompt: A 26-year-old female with acute Chlamydia trachomatis pelvic inflammatory disease develops acute right upper quadrant pain exacerbated by deep breathing, with tenderness over the liver edge. Laparoscopy demonstrates inflammatory perihepatic adhesions between the anterior liver capsule and abdominal wall ('violin-string' adhesions). What is this syndrome?
questions.question: A 26-year-old female with acute Chlamydia trachomatis pelvic inflammatory disease develops acute right upper quadrant pain exacerbated by deep breathing, with tenderness over the liver edge. Laparoscopy demonstrates inflammatory perihepatic adhesions between the anterior liver capsule and abdominal wall ('violin-string' adhesions). What is this syndrome?
questions.explanation: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is an extrapelvic complication of PID (most commonly Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae), resulting from ascending transperitoneal spread of exudate into the right paracolic gutter, causing localized fibrinous perihepatitis and pathognomonic 'violin-string' adhesions.

Ultrasound demonstrates a 7-cm complex, thick-walled multilocular adnexal mass with internal echoes, conforming to a Tubo-Ovarian Abscess (TOA). She is started on intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics (Ceftriaxone, Doxycycline, and Metronidazole). questions.question: A 28-year-old female is admitted with severe PID. Ultrasound demonstrates a 7-cm complex, thick-walled multilocular adnexal mass with internal echoes, conforming to a Tubo-Ovarian Abscess (TOA). She is started on intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics (Ceftriaxone, Doxycycline, and Metronidazole). What clinical finding indicates acute rupture of the TOA, mandating immediate emergency exploratory laparotomy?
options: Sudden development of generalized peritonitis, rigid board-like abdomen, and hemodynamic collapse / septic shock
Decrease in white blood cell count
questions.answer: Sudden development of generalized peritonitis, rigid board-like abdomen, and hemodynamic collapse / septic shock
questions.explanation: Rupture of a Tubo-Ovarian Abscess is a catastrophic gynaecological emergency. Sudden spillage of purulent fluid into the peritoneal cavity produces acute diffuse peritonitis, severe septic shock, and carries significant mortality unless managed by immediate resuscitation and emergent surgical exploration.

questions.explanation: In female genital tuberculosis (which is almost always secondary to hematogenous dissemination from a primary pulmonary or abdominal focus), the fallopian tubes are involved bilaterally in 90 to 100% of cases, followed by the endometrium (50–60%) and ovaries (20–30%).

questions.question: When scheduling an endometrial biopsy or diagnostic curettage to evaluate suspected endometrial tuberculosis in an infertile female, why is the biopsy specifically performed during the late premenstrual (secretory) phase of the menstrual cycle?
options: Because the endometrium is at its maximum thickness and tuberculous granulomas have had maximal time to develop before being shed with menstruation
Because Mycobacterium tuberculosis only multiplies during ovulation
questions.answer: Because the endometrium is at its maximum thickness and tuberculous granulomas have had maximal time to develop before being shed with menstruation
questions.explanation: Because the functional zone of the endometrium is shed every 28 days during menses, tuberculous granulomas are cast off monthly and must reform from the basal layer. An endometrial biopsy taken just prior to menstruation (days 22–26) provides the highest diagnostic yield for histopathological granulomas and GeneXpert PCR.

Extensive calcification of the round ligament only

More than 50% of the external anal sphincter (EAS) thickness is torn

Less than 50% of the external anal sphincter is torn

Incision of the hematoma under anaesthesia, thorough evacuation of clots, ligation of bleeding vessels, and obliteration of dead space with layered sutures

Standard management requires examination under anaesthesia, incision over the hematoma, evacuation of clots, identified bleeder ligation, and deep layered closure to obliterate dead space.

Leaving the muscle unsutured to heal by secondary intention

questions.explanation: Repair of full-thickness EAS lacerations (grade 3b/3c) utilizing an overlapping technique (or precise end-to-end approximation) using interrupted 3-0 delayed-absorbable sutures (PDS or Vicryl) restores the functional sphincter ring and provides superior fecal continence.

questions.question: During laparoscopic entry with a Veress needle at the umbilicus, bowel injury occurs. What is the single most common reason why electrosurgical thermal bowel injuries during laparoscopy carry a higher mortality than mechanical sharp trocar lacerations?
options: Thermal injuries often remain unrecognized intraoperatively, presenting insidiously with delayed perforation and feculent peritonitis on postoperative days 3 to 7
Electrosurgery immediately seals all bowel perforations
questions.answer: Thermal injuries often remain unrecognized intraoperatively, presenting insidiously with delayed perforation and feculent peritonitis on postoperative days 3 to 7
questions.explanation: Electrosurgical bowel injury causes delayed coagulation necrosis and lateral thermal tissue death that extends far beyond the visible burn. The bowel wall gradually sloughs over 72–96 hours, leading to delayed unrecognized fecal peritonitis, sepsis, and high mortality.

Two-layer primary closure performed transversely to the longitudinal axis of the bowel to avoid luminal stenosis
Leaving the perforation open with an external drain

On pelvic examination, a tender, fluctuant mass is palpable along the anterior vaginal wall, and compressing the mass expels purulent urine from the external urethral meatus. What is the diagnosis?
questions.question: A 35-year-old female presents with the classic 'three Ds' triad: Dysuria, Dyspareunia, and post-void Dribbling. On pelvic examination, a tender, fluctuant mass is palpable along the anterior vaginal wall, and compressing the mass expels purulent urine from the external urethral meatus. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic clinical triad of a suburethral diverticulum consists of dysuria, dyspareunia, and post-void dribbling (the 3 Ds). Palpation reveals an anterior suburethral cystic fullness, and gentle pressure 'milks' cloudy urine or pus from the urethral meatus. MRI pelvis is the gold standard diagnostic imaging.

Urine cultures are persistently sterile. Cystoscopy with hydrodistension reveals submucosal petechial hemorrhages (glomerulations) and a classic bleeding mucosal fissure ('Hunner's ulcer'). questions.question: A 40-year-old female presents with chronic suprapubic pain that increases as the bladder fills and is relieved by voiding, accompanied by extreme daytime and nighttime urinary frequency (voiding 20 times daily). Urine cultures are persistently sterile. Cystoscopy with hydrodistension reveals submucosal petechial hemorrhages (glomerulations) and a classic bleeding mucosal fissure ('Hunner's ulcer'). options: Carcinoma in situ of the bladder
questions.explanation: Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the bladder wall characterized by pelvic/suprapubic pain related to bladder filling, urinary urgency/frequency with sterile urine cultures, and cystoscopic findings of glomerulations or Hunner's ulcers.

questions.prompt: A 30-year-old female presents with continuous involuntary leaking of urine from the vagina following an obstructed labor 2 weeks ago. To differentiate a Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF) from a Ureterovaginal Fistula, the surgeon places three cotton swabs in the vagina and instills dilute methylene blue into the bladder via a transurethral catheter (Three-swab test). What result confirms a Vesicovaginal Fistula?
questions.question: A 30-year-old female presents with continuous involuntary leaking of urine from the vagina following an obstructed labor 2 weeks ago. To differentiate a Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF) from a Ureterovaginal Fistula, the surgeon places three cotton swabs in the vagina and instills dilute methylene blue into the bladder via a transurethral catheter (Three-swab test). What result confirms a Vesicovaginal Fistula?
options: All three swabs remain completely dry and unstained
The top swab is soaked with clear, unstained urine; the middle and bottom swabs remain dry
The middle or bottom swab is stained blue, while the top swab remains unstained
All three swabs are stained bright yellow
questions.answer: The middle or bottom swab is stained blue, while the top swab remains unstained
questions.explanation: In the three-swab test for VVF: blue dye in the bladder leaks through the fistulous tract, staining the lower or middle vaginal swab blue. In contrast, in a ureterovaginal fistula, methylene blue cannot reach the vagina, but the topmost swab is soaked with clear unstained urine from the upper urinary tract.

questions.prompt: What is the standard, time-honored waiting period before undertaking definitive surgical repair (Chassar Moir flap-splitting repair) of an obstetric vesicovaginal fistula caused by prolonged ischemic necrosis?
questions.question: What is the standard, time-honored waiting period before undertaking definitive surgical repair (Chassar Moir flap-splitting repair) of an obstetric vesicovaginal fistula caused by prolonged ischemic necrosis?
options: Immediate surgery within 24 hours of delivery
3 months, to allow ischemic sloughing, tissue edema, and active local inflammation to fully resolve
questions.answer: 3 months, to allow ischemic sloughing, tissue edema, and active local inflammation to fully resolve
questions.explanation: Obstetric VVF results from ischemic pressure necrosis of soft tissues crushed between the fetal presenting head and pubic symphysis. Surgical repair is deferred for approximately 3 months (8 to 12 weeks) until necrotic slough has separated, local inflammation has subsided, and tissues have vascularized.
