questions.question: A 48-year-old multiparous female complains of involuntary spurts of urine loss occurring exclusively during coughing, sneezing, laughing, or lifting heavy weights, with no urgency or nocturia. Urodynamic study shows involuntary leakage without detrusor contraction when intra-abdominal pressure rises. What is the gold-standard minimally invasive surgical procedure for genuine Stress Urinary Incontinence (SUI)?
options: Mid-urethral synthetic sling (Tension-free Vaginal Tape / TVT or Transobturator Tape / TOT)
questions.answer: Mid-urethral synthetic sling (Tension-free Vaginal Tape / TVT or Transobturator Tape / TOT)
questions.explanation: Mid-urethral synthetic slings (TVT or TOT) placed loosely beneath the mid-urethra provide a permanent suburethral backboard, restoring dynamic urethral kinking during increased intra-abdominal pressure, and represent the gold-standard surgical treatment for stress urinary incontinence with cure rates > 85-90%.

questions.prompt: In the standardized Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) staging system, what fixed anatomical landmark serves as the zero reference point (0 cm) against which all 6 points are measured in centimeters?
questions.question: In the standardized Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) staging system, what fixed anatomical landmark serves as the zero reference point (0 cm) against which all 6 points are measured in centimeters?
questions.explanation: The POP-Q system uses the plane of the hymen as the fixed zero reference point (0 cm). Prolapse points located proximal to (above) the hymen are designated by negative numbers (- cm), points at the hymen are 0, and points protruding distal to (outside) the hymen are designated by positive numbers (+ cm).

questions.prompt: A 34-year-old P2L2 female presents with second-degree uterine prolapse with marked elongation of the supravaginal cervix. She is keen to preserve her uterus and desires no further childbearing. What is the classic uterine-sparing surgical repair indicated for this condition?
questions.question: A 34-year-old P2L2 female presents with second-degree uterine prolapse with marked elongation of the supravaginal cervix. She is keen to preserve her uterus and desires no further childbearing. What is the classic uterine-sparing surgical repair indicated for this condition?
questions.explanation: The Manchester (Fothergill) repair is indicated for uterovaginal prolapse accompanied by marked supravaginal cervical elongation in women wishing to preserve the uterus. It involves amputation of the cervix, advancement and plication of the cardinal ligaments in front of the stump, and anterior colporrhaphy.

questions.question: A 78-year-old frail female with severe ischemic cardiomyopathy presents with complete procidentia (Stage IV prolapse) with decubitus ulceration. She is not sexually active and is considered a high-risk candidate for prolonged general anaesthesia. What simple, rapid, minimally invasive obliterative surgical option is appropriate under regional/local anaesthesia?
options: Le Fort partial colpocleisis (obliteration of the anterior and posterior vaginal walls with lateral drainage channels)
questions.answer: Le Fort partial colpocleisis (obliteration of the anterior and posterior vaginal walls with lateral drainage channels)
questions.explanation: Colpocleisis (Le Fort partial colpocleisis in women with a uterus, or total colpectomy in vault prolapse) is an obliterative procedure that surgically denudes and sutures the anterior and posterior vaginal walls together. It carries minimal morbidity, short operating time, and high success for non-sexually active elderly patients.

questions.prompt: What are the two normal physiological angles of orientation of the uterus in relation to the pelvic axis and vagina in an upright female?
questions.question: What are the two normal physiological angles of orientation of the uterus in relation to the pelvic axis and vagina in an upright female?
options: Anteversion (angle of ~90° between long axis of cervix and vagina) and Anteflexion (angle of ~120°–170° between long axis of uterine body and cervix)
questions.answer: Anteversion (angle of ~90° between long axis of cervix and vagina) and Anteflexion (angle of ~120°–170° between long axis of uterine body and cervix)
questions.explanation: In ~80% of women, the uterus is anteverted (cervical canal forms a forward angle of ~90° with the vaginal axis) and anteflexed (the corpus bends forward on the cervix at the level of the isthmus at an angle of ~120°–170°).

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old female presents with persistent pelvic aching, dyspareunia, and backache. Bimanual examination demonstrates a mobile retroverted uterus. To determine whether her symptoms are genuinely caused by retroversion rather than coincidental, the gynecologist manually corrects the uterus to an anteverted position and inserts a Hodge pessary for 4 weeks. What is this diagnostic evaluation termed?
questions.question: A 28-year-old female presents with persistent pelvic aching, dyspareunia, and backache. Bimanual examination demonstrates a mobile retroverted uterus. To determine whether her symptoms are genuinely caused by retroversion rather than coincidental, the gynecologist manually corrects the uterus to an anteverted position and inserts a Hodge pessary for 4 weeks. What is this diagnostic evaluation termed?
questions.explanation: Mobile retroversion is asymptomatic in most women. If symptoms (dyspareunia, backache) are suspected to arise from retroversion, the 'Pessary Test' is performed: the uterus is manually anteverted and supported by a Hodge or Smith pessary; if symptoms vanish completely and return after pessary removal, retroversion is considered clinically symptomatic.

questions.prompt: What is the primary etiology of non-puerperal (gynecological) chronic uterine inversion?
questions.question: What is the primary etiology of non-puerperal (gynecological) chronic uterine inversion?
options: Excessive traction on the umbilical cord
Extrusion of a fundal submucous leiomyoma (fibroid) or fundal endometrial polyp dragging the inverted uterine wall through the dilated cervical ring
Congenital weakness of the round ligaments
questions.answer: Extrusion of a fundal submucous leiomyoma (fibroid) or fundal endometrial polyp dragging the inverted uterine wall through the dilated cervical ring
questions.explanation: Non-puerperal chronic uterine inversion is rare (> 85% associated with uterine tumors). A pedunculated or sessile fundal submucous fibroid is expelled into the vagina by myometrial contractions, exerting traction that invaginates and pulls down the fundus into the cervical canal.

questions.prompt: A 22-year-old female presents on day 14 of a 28-day cycle with sudden-onset sharp lower quadrant abdominal pain lasting 12 hours, with no fever, vomiting, or abnormal bleeding. Urine pregnancy test is negative and pelvic ultrasound is unremarkable except for minimal physiologic fluid in the pouch of Douglas. What is this self-limiting ovulatory pain termed?
questions.question: A 22-year-old female presents on day 14 of a 28-day cycle with sudden-onset sharp lower quadrant abdominal pain lasting 12 hours, with no fever, vomiting, or abnormal bleeding. Urine pregnancy test is negative and pelvic ultrasound is unremarkable except for minimal physiologic fluid in the pouch of Douglas. What is this self-limiting ovulatory pain termed?
questions.explanation: Mittelschmerz is physiological midcycle pain occurring at the time of ovulation (day 14 of 28-day cycle), caused by follicular distension and peritoneal irritation by follicular fluid and minor bleeding following follicular rupture. It is brief (hours to 1 day) and resolves spontaneously.

questions.explanation: Chronic pelvic pain is defined as non-cyclical pain perceived in the pelvis, anterior abdominal wall, lumbosacral region, or buttocks lasting for 6 months or longer, leading to functional impairment or medical care.

Pelvic Doppler ultrasound and venography demonstrate tortuous, dilated pelvic and ovarian veins (> 6 mm diameter) with retrograde venous reflux. What is the diagnosis?
questions.question: A 32-year-old multiparous female complains of dull, aching chronic pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia, and post-coital aching that worsens markedly toward the end of the day and with prolonged standing. Pelvic Doppler ultrasound and venography demonstrate tortuous, dilated pelvic and ovarian veins (> 6 mm diameter) with retrograde venous reflux. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pelvic congestion syndrome is caused by incompetence and retrograde pooling in ovarian and internal iliac veins, producing chronic pelvic dull ache, positional exacerbation on prolonged standing, deep dyspareunia, and prominent perineal/vulvar varicosities.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended treatment of choice for early syphilis (primary, secondary, or early latent < 1 year duration)?
questions.question: What is the recommended treatment of choice for early syphilis (primary, secondary, or early latent < 1 year duration)?
options: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly as a single dose
Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18-24 million units IV daily for 14 days
Oral azithromycin 500 mg daily for 3 days
questions.answer: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly as a single dose
questions.explanation: CDC and international STI guidelines state that the treatment of choice for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis (< 1 year duration) is Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly in a single session. For late latent syphilis (> 1 year or unknown duration) or tertiary syphilis without neurosyphilis, the regimen is Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly for three consecutive weeks (total 7.2 million units). In non-pregnant penicillin-allergic patients, oral doxycycline (100 mg twice daily for 14 days) is the alternative.

questions.prompt: What is the pathognomonic microscopic finding on a tissue crush smear or Giemsa stain in Donovanosis (Granuloma Inguinale)?
questions.question: What is the pathognomonic microscopic finding on a tissue crush smear or Giemsa stain in Donovanosis (Granuloma Inguinale)?
options: Intracellular Donovan bodies (safety-pin appearing Gram-negative rods within large mononuclear histiocytes)
Intranuclear Cowdry A inclusion bodies with multinucleated giant cells
Gram-negative diplococci with a 'school of red fish' arrangement
Extracellular spirochetes with active corkscrew motility on darkfield microscopy
questions.answer: Intracellular Donovan bodies (safety-pin appearing Gram-negative rods within large mononuclear histiocytes)
questions.explanation: Donovanosis (Granuloma Inguinale), caused by Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis), produces painless, beefy-red, exuberant, bleed-on-contact vegetative granulomatous ulcers that lack true regional lymphadenopathy (pseudobuboes). The diagnostic hallmark on tissue smear or Giemsa/Wright stain is Donovan bodies: pleomorphic Gram-negative bacilli with polar condensation resembling closed safety pins within the cytoplasm of large vacuolated histiocytes.

questions.prompt: Which sexually transmitted genital ulcer is characteristically painful, soft, dirty-based with undermined edges, and caused by Haemophilus ducreyi?
questions.question: Which sexually transmitted genital ulcer is characteristically painful, soft, dirty-based with undermined edges, and caused by Haemophilus ducreyi?
questions.explanation: Genital ulcers can be differentiated clinically: (1) Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi): Exquisitely painful, soft base (soft sore), non-indurated, ragged undermined edges with purulent necrotic exudate, accompanied by painful unilateral suppurative inguinal buboes. (2) Primary syphilis (Chancre): Typically painless, single, indurated, clean base, non-tender rubbery lymphadenopathy. (3) LGV (Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3): Evanescent painless ulcer followed by painful matted lymphadenitis with the 'groove sign'.

questions.prompt: What is the updated CDC-recommended first-line regimen for uncomplicated urogenital, anorectal, or pharyngeal gonorrhoea in adults?
questions.question: What is the updated CDC-recommended first-line regimen for uncomplicated urogenital, anorectal, or pharyngeal gonorrhoea in adults?
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly as a single dose (or 1 g if body weight >= 150 kg)
Oral cefixime 400 mg single dose alone
questions.answer: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly as a single dose (or 1 g if body weight >= 150 kg)
questions.explanation: Due to widespread antimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the CDC guidelines recommend Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose for uncomplicated gonococcal infections of the cervix, urethra, rectum, and pharynx in patients weighing < 150 kg (1,000 mg IM if weight >= 150 kg). If chlamydial infection has not been ruled out by NAAT, oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days should be co-administered.

questions.prompt: What is the biological mechanism underlying the 'Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction' seen shortly after starting penicillin therapy for secondary syphilis?
questions.question: What is the biological mechanism underlying the 'Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction' seen shortly after starting penicillin therapy for secondary syphilis?
options: Massive release of endotoxin-like lipoproteins and cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-8) from dying spirochetes
Immediate IgE-mediated anaphylactic reaction against the beta-lactam ring
Rapid complement consumption causing immune-complex glomerulonephritis
questions.answer: Massive release of endotoxin-like lipoproteins and cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-8) from dying spirochetes
questions.explanation: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction occurs within 2 to 24 hours after initiating penicillin treatment for spirochetal infections (most prominently secondary syphilis). It is an acute systemic inflammatory response caused by the rapid lysis of abundant Treponema pallidum organisms, releasing massive quantities of treponemal lipoproteins and pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8). Clinical features include sudden chills, high fever, headache, tachycardia, flushing, and exacerbation of skin lesions. It is self-limiting and managed with antipyretics and reassurance (distinct from penicillin allergy).

questions.prompt: Which serological test for syphilis remains positive for life despite successful penicillin therapy and cure?
questions.question: Which serological test for syphilis remains positive for life despite successful penicillin therapy and cure?
questions.explanation: Serological tests for syphilis fall into two classes: (1) Non-treponemal tests (VDRL, RPR): Detect antibodies against cardiolipin-lecithin antigens. Their titers correlate with disease activity and decline (usually become non-reactive) with successful treatment, making them useful for tracking response to therapy. (2) Treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TP-PA, TPHA): Detect specific antibodies directed against Treponema pallidum proteins. In ~85-90% of individuals, once reactive, treponemal tests remain positive for life (serological scar) regardless of curative treatment.

questions.prompt: What is the classic 'Groove sign of Greenblatt' seen in Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV)?
questions.question: What is the classic 'Groove sign of Greenblatt' seen in Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV)?
options: Enlargement of inguinal and femoral lymph node groups separated by the fibrous Poupart's (inguinal) ligament
Linear ulceration extending from the fourchette to the anus
A transverse fissure across the mid-portion of the labia minora
Sulcus between an enlarged Bartholin gland and the pubic ramus
questions.answer: Enlargement of inguinal and femoral lymph node groups separated by the fibrous Poupart's (inguinal) ligament
questions.explanation: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, and L3, is characterized in its secondary stage by painful, suppurative inguinal and femoral lymphadenopathy. The 'Groove sign of Greenblatt' (pathognomonic for LGV in ~20% of cases) refers to a visible transverse depression or groove separating the enlarged upper inguinal nodes from the enlarged lower femoral nodes, formed by the unyielding inguinal ligament (Poupart's ligament) stretched between them.

questions.prompt: What are the four components of Amsel's diagnostic criteria for Bacterial Vaginosis (BV), and how many must be present for a clinical diagnosis?
questions.question: What are the four components of Amsel's diagnostic criteria for Bacterial Vaginosis (BV), and how many must be present for a clinical diagnosis?
options: Thin homogenous white-grey discharge, vaginal pH > 4.5, positive whiff test (fishy amine odor with 10% KOH), clue cells > 20% on wet mount; At least 3 of 4 required
Curdy white discharge, pseudohyphae on wet mount, vaginal pH < 4.0, severe pruritus; At least 2 required
Frothy green discharge, strawberry cervix, motile flagellates, pH > 6.0; All 4 required
Mucopurulent discharge, cervical friability, Gram-negative diplococci, dysuria; At least 1 required
questions.answer: Thin homogenous white-grey discharge, vaginal pH > 4.5, positive whiff test (fishy amine odor with 10% KOH), clue cells > 20% on wet mount; At least 3 of 4 required
questions.explanation: Amsel's criteria require the presence of at least 3 of the following 4 clinical indicators for the diagnosis of Bacterial Vaginosis (BV): (1) Homogeneous, thin, grayish-white vaginal discharge smoothly coating the vaginal walls; (2) Vaginal fluid pH > 4.5; (3) Positive 'Whiff test' (release of volatile amines producing a fishy odor upon adding a drop of 10% KOH); and (4) Presence of 'clue cells' (vaginal epithelial cells studded with adherent Gardnerella vaginalis and anaerobic coccobacilli obscuring cell margins) comprising > 20% of epithelial cells on saline wet mount.

questions.prompt: What is the Nugent scoring system cutoff for the definitive microbiological diagnosis of Bacterial Vaginosis on a Gram-stained vaginal smear?
questions.question: What is the Nugent scoring system cutoff for the definitive microbiological diagnosis of Bacterial Vaginosis on a Gram-stained vaginal smear?
questions.explanation: The Nugent score is the laboratory gold standard for diagnosing bacterial vaginosis. It quantifies three bacterial morphotypes under oil immersion (1000x): (1) Lactobacillus morphotypes (large Gram-positive rods, 0 to 4); (2) Gardnerella and Bacteroides morphotypes (small Gram-negative/variable rods, 0 to 4); and (3) Mobiluncus morphotypes (curved Gram-negative rods, 0 to 2). A total score of 0-3 is normal (Lactobacillus-predominant); 4-6 is intermediate; and 7-10 is definitive for Bacterial Vaginosis.

questions.prompt: A 26-year-old woman presents with severe vulvar itching, dysuria, and thick, curd-like white vaginal discharge. Speculum examination reveals normal vaginal pH of 4.0. Microscopy with 10% KOH demonstrates budding yeast and pseudohyphae. What is the standard first-line oral and topical treatment for uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis?
questions.question: A 26-year-old woman presents with severe vulvar itching, dysuria, and thick, curd-like white vaginal discharge. Speculum examination reveals normal vaginal pH of 4.0. Microscopy with 10% KOH demonstrates budding yeast and pseudohyphae. What is the standard first-line oral and topical treatment for uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis?
options: Oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose, OR topical clotrimazole 1% cream/pessary for 3-7 days
Oral metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days
Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days
Topical clindamycin 2% vaginal cream for 7 days
questions.answer: Oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose, OR topical clotrimazole 1% cream/pessary for 3-7 days
questions.explanation: Uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis (typically Candida albicans) characteristically occurs at an acidic vaginal pH (< 4.5). The diagnosis is confirmed by demonstration of budding blastospores and pseudohyphae on 10% KOH mount. Recommended first-line therapy is either a single oral dose of fluconazole 150 mg or short-course topical azoles (such as clotrimazole 100 mg vaginal tablets daily for 6 days or 500 mg single dose, or miconazole vaginal suppositories). In pregnant women, topical azoles for 7 days are strictly preferred over oral fluconazole.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended maintenance suppressive regimen for recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (RVVC, defined as >= 4 discrete episodes within 12 months)?
questions.question: What is the recommended maintenance suppressive regimen for recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (RVVC, defined as >= 4 discrete episodes within 12 months)?
options: Oral fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months, preceded by induction with 150 mg every 72 hours for 3 doses
Daily oral metronidazole 500 mg for 6 months
Single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin monthly
Continuous topical steroid cream daily for 1 year
questions.answer: Oral fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months, preceded by induction with 150 mg every 72 hours for 3 doses
questions.explanation: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (RVVC) is defined as 4 or more documented symptomatic episodes of candidiasis within a 12-month period. Management requires: (1) Induction therapy: Oral fluconazole 150 mg on Days 1, 4, and 7 to achieve mycological cure; followed by (2) Maintenance suppressive therapy: Oral fluconazole 150 mg once weekly for a duration of 6 months. Culture with species identification is mandatory because non-albicans species (e.g., Candida glabrata) may require topical boric acid or nystatin.

questions.prompt: What is the specific microscopic appearance and vaginal pH characteristic of Trichomonas vaginalis vaginitis?
questions.question: What is the specific microscopic appearance and vaginal pH characteristic of Trichomonas vaginalis vaginitis?
options: Motile, flagellated, pear-shaped protozoa with jerky, undulating movements; Vaginal pH > 5.0 to 6.0
Branching hyphae with right-angle branching; Vaginal pH 4.0
questions.answer: Motile, flagellated, pear-shaped protozoa with jerky, undulating movements; Vaginal pH > 5.0 to 6.0
questions.explanation: Trichomonas vaginalis is a flagellated, anaerobic protozoan. On fresh saline wet mount, it is identified by its pear-shaped morphology, 4 anterior flagella, and characteristic active jerky, tumbling, or undulating motility. The infection raises vaginal pH markedly (pH 5.0 to 6.5). The classic gross clinical picture includes a copious, frothy, malodorous greenish-yellow discharge and colposcopic punctate petechial mucosal hemorrhages ('strawberry cervix' or colpitis macularis).

questions.prompt: Why is concurrent treatment of sexual partners mandatory in Trichomoniasis but NOT routinely recommended in Bacterial Vaginosis or Candidiasis?
questions.question: Why is concurrent treatment of sexual partners mandatory in Trichomoniasis but NOT routinely recommended in Bacterial Vaginosis or Candidiasis?
options: Trichomoniasis is a true sexually transmitted infection with high rates of asymptomatic male carriage in the urethra and prostate; BV and Candidiasis are dysbioses
Bacterial Vaginosis cannot be transmitted sexually under any circumstances
Men are biologically immune to Trichomonas species
Metronidazole is toxic to male gametes
questions.answer: Trichomoniasis is a true sexually transmitted infection with high rates of asymptomatic male carriage in the urethra and prostate; BV and Candidiasis are dysbioses
questions.explanation: Trichomonas vaginalis is a sexually transmitted pathogen with partner concordance exceeding 70-80%; men frequently harbor asymptomatic colonization in the urethra and prostate. Without simultaneous partner treatment, the 'ping-pong' reinfection rate exceeds 20-30%. In contrast, Bacterial Vaginosis and Candidiasis represent endogenous disruptions of the normal vaginal microbial ecosystem (dysbiosis and yeast overgrowth), and randomized trials have demonstrated that treating male partners does not reduce female recurrence rates.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: What is the primary cellular mechanism by which Döderlein's lactobacilli maintain a healthy, acidic vaginal environment resistant to pathogenic colonization?
questions.question: What is the primary cellular mechanism by which Döderlein's lactobacilli maintain a healthy, acidic vaginal environment resistant to pathogenic colonization?
options: Fermentation of glycogen from exfoliated squamous cells into lactic acid (maintaining pH 3.8-4.5) and production of hydrogen peroxide and bacteriocins
Secretion of high concentrations of alkaline ammonia
Phagocytosis of pathogenic anaerobes by epithelial macrophages
Induction of local IgA secretion by stimulating the complement cascade
questions.answer: Fermentation of glycogen from exfoliated squamous cells into lactic acid (maintaining pH 3.8-4.5) and production of hydrogen peroxide and bacteriocins
questions.explanation: Normal vaginal homeostasis is mediated by Döderlein's lactobacilli (particularly Lactobacillus crispatus and L. jensenii). Estrogen stimulates vaginal squamous epithelial maturation and glycogen synthesis. Lactobacilli metabolize glycogen into lactic acid, maintaining a protective acidic microenvironment (pH 3.8 to 4.5). Furthermore, lactobacilli produce hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and antimicrobial peptides (bacteriocins) that directly inhibit anaerobes (Gardnerella, Prevotella), Candida, and STIs.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: According to the CDC guidelines, what are the three 'minimum clinical criteria' for the presumptive diagnosis of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) in a sexually active young woman?
questions.question: According to the CDC guidelines, what are the three 'minimum clinical criteria' for the presumptive diagnosis of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) in a sexually active young woman?
options: Cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness on bimanual pelvic examination
High fever > 38.3 C, purulent cervical discharge, and leukocytosis > 15,000/mcL
Positive NAAT for gonorrhoea, bilateral pelvic masses, and elevated ESR
Visible perihepatic violin-string adhesions on ultrasound
questions.answer: Cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness on bimanual pelvic examination
questions.explanation: To prevent delayed treatment and long-term sequelae (tubal factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain), the CDC guidelines recommend initiating empiric therapy for PID if a sexually active young woman or woman at risk for STIs has pelvic or lower abdominal pain and AT LEAST ONE of the following minimum clinical criteria on bimanual examination: (1) Cervical motion tenderness ('chandelier sign'), (2) Uterine tenderness, OR (3) Adnexal tenderness, in the absence of any other obvious cause.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: What is the CDC-recommended outpatient oral/intramuscular antimicrobial regimen for mild-to-moderate acute PID?
questions.question: What is the CDC-recommended outpatient oral/intramuscular antimicrobial regimen for mild-to-moderate acute PID?
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose PLUS Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days PLUS Metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 14 days
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days alone
Intramuscular gentamicin 80 mg daily for 5 days
questions.answer: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose PLUS Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days PLUS Metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 14 days
questions.explanation: The updated CDC-recommended outpatient regimen for acute PID is: (1) Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose (covers Neisseria gonorrhoeae and enteric Gram-negative rods); PLUS (2) Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days (covers Chlamydia trachomatis and Mycoplasma genitalium); PLUS (3) Metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 14 days (provides broad anaerobic coverage, treats concomitant bacterial vaginosis, and reduces pelvic abscess formation).

questions.prompt: What clinical syndrome is characterized by right upper quadrant pleuritic pain, friction rub, and laparoscopic 'violin-string' adhesions between the liver capsule and anterior abdominal wall following acute PID?
questions.question: What clinical syndrome is characterized by right upper quadrant pleuritic pain, friction rub, and laparoscopic 'violin-string' adhesions between the liver capsule and anterior abdominal wall following acute PID?
questions.explanation: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis) develops in 4-14% of women with acute PID, caused by direct peritoneal extension or lymphatic tracking of Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae into the paracolic gutters and subdiaphragmatic space. Patients present with acute right upper quadrant pleuritic pain, tenderness, and sometimes a liver friction rub, often mimicking acute cholecystitis. Laparoscopy characteristically demonstrates fine, fibrous, 'violin-string' adhesions between the anterior liver surface and the anterior abdominal wall/diaphragm.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: What are the definitive criteria mandating hospital admission and inpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy for a patient with acute PID?
questions.question: What are the definitive criteria mandating hospital admission and inpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy for a patient with acute PID?
options: Pregnancy, abscess, severe illness, oral intolerance, or failed outpatient therapy
Prior chlamydial infection, mild symptoms, and good tolerance of oral treatment
Age above 30 years, stable vital signs, and reliable outpatient follow-up
Unruptured nabothian cysts, mild symptoms, and no systemic illness
questions.answer: Pregnancy, abscess, severe illness, oral intolerance, or failed outpatient therapy
questions.explanation: CDC criteria for inpatient hospitalization and IV therapy in PID include: (1) Surgical emergencies (e.g., acute appendicitis) cannot be excluded; (2) Tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA); (3) Pregnancy; (4) Severe illness, high fever, intractable nausea/vomiting; (5) Inability to tolerate or comply with oral outpatient therapy; and (6) Lack of clinical response/worsening after 72 hours of oral antimicrobial therapy.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: In a hemodynamically stable patient diagnosed with an unruptured Tubo-Ovarian Abscess (TOA) measuring 6 cm on sonography, what is the initial standard management?
questions.question: In a hemodynamically stable patient diagnosed with an unruptured Tubo-Ovarian Abscess (TOA) measuring 6 cm on sonography, what is the initial standard management?
options: Hospitalization and inpatient broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic therapy with close observation for 48-72 hours
Immediate emergency total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
questions.answer: Hospitalization and inpatient broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic therapy with close observation for 48-72 hours
questions.explanation: In an intact, unruptured tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA) in a hemodynamically stable patient, initial management is medical: hospitalization and broad-spectrum parenteral IV antibiotics (e.g., Ampicillin/Sulbactam + Doxycycline, or Cefotetan + Doxycycline, or Gentamicin + Clindamycin) with strict bed rest. Medical therapy successfully resolves 70-85% of TOAs. Image-guided (ultrasound or CT) percutaneous aspiration/catheter drainage or laparoscopic intervention is reserved for abscesses that fail to improve after 48-72 hours or for uncontained acute rupture.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: What is the life-threatening surgical emergency that mandates immediate exploratory laparotomy in a patient with a known Tubo-Ovarian Abscess?
questions.question: What is the life-threatening surgical emergency that mandates immediate exploratory laparotomy in a patient with a known Tubo-Ovarian Abscess?
options: Acute rupture of the abscess with generalized peritonitis and septic shock
Persistent low-grade fever after 24 hours of antibiotics
Abscess size of 4 cm without peritonitis
questions.answer: Acute rupture of the abscess with generalized peritonitis and septic shock
questions.explanation: Acute rupture of a tubo-ovarian abscess is a surgical catastrophe with a historical mortality of 5-10%. Rupture spills gross purulent polymicrobial exudate into the peritoneal cavity, triggering rapid generalized peritonitis, bacteremia, endotoxemia, and septic shock with multi-organ failure. Immediate resuscitation followed by emergent exploratory laparotomy with peritoneal lavage, abscess debridement, and salpingo-oophorectomy is lifesaving.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: What is the approximate risk of tubal factor infertility following one, two, and three discrete episodes of acute pelvic inflammatory disease?
questions.question: What is the approximate risk of tubal factor infertility following one, two, and three discrete episodes of acute pelvic inflammatory disease?
options: ~12% after 1st episode, ~25% after 2nd episode, ~50% after 3rd episode
~1% after 1st episode, ~3% after 2nd episode, ~5% after 3rd episode
~50% after 1st episode, ~80% after 2nd episode, 100% after 3rd episode
Infertility risk is completely independent of the number of PID episodes
questions.answer: ~12% after 1st episode, ~25% after 2nd episode, ~50% after 3rd episode
questions.explanation: The landmark prospective studies by Weström demonstrated that post-PID tubal occlusive infertility doubles with each subsequent infection: the risk is approximately 11-12% after a single episode, rises to 23-25% after two episodes, and escalates to 54-55% (over half of women) after three or more episodes. Additionally, the risk of subsequent ectopic pregnancy increases 6- to 10-fold following PID due to deciliation and endosalpingeal fibrosis.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: What are the characteristic fluoroscopic appearances of the fallopian tubes on Hysterosalpingography (HSG) in chronic female genital tuberculosis?
questions.question: What are the characteristic fluoroscopic appearances of the fallopian tubes on Hysterosalpingography (HSG) in chronic female genital tuberculosis?
options: 'Lead-pipe' rigid tubes, 'tobacco-pouch' fimbria, and 'beaded' appearance of the ampulla
Marked bilateral hydrosalpinx with smooth normal rugae
Complete absence of contrast entry into the uterine cavity
Widely patent tortuous fallopian tubes with exuberant peritoneal spill
questions.answer: 'Lead-pipe' rigid tubes, 'tobacco-pouch' fimbria, and 'beaded' appearance of the ampulla
questions.explanation: Chronic tuberculosis endosalpingitis and perisalpingitis produce classic signs on HSG: (1) 'Lead-pipe' rigid tubes (fibrotic straight tubes lacking normal undulating peristalsis); (2) 'Beaded' or 'rosary-like' appearance caused by alternating strictures and segmentations; (3) 'Tobacco-pouch' sign (fimbrial phimosis with inverted fimbriae); and (4) 'Golf-club' or 'drum-stick' ampullary dilatation. Uterine findings include 'saw-tooth' irregular margins and asymmetric synechiae ('Netter's syndrome').
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: What is the primary mode of spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the female genital tract?
questions.question: What is the primary mode of spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis to the female genital tract?
options: Hematogenous dissemination from a primary pulmonary focus or lymph node
Direct ascending infection via sexual transmission
questions.answer: Hematogenous dissemination from a primary pulmonary focus or lymph node
questions.explanation: Female genital tuberculosis is almost invariably secondary to a primary infection elsewhere in the body (most commonly primary pulmonary tuberculosis or mesenteric/mediastinal lymph nodes). Transmission to the genital tract occurs predominantly via hematogenous dissemination (responsible for > 90% of cases), with bacilli depositing first in the mucosal lining of the fallopian tubes (involved in 90-100% of genital TB). From the tubes, direct endoluminal descent infects the endometrium in 50-60% of cases.

questions.prompt: Which anatomical structure separates an infralevator (vulvar/perineal) haematoma from a supralevator (broad ligament/pelvic) haematoma?
questions.question: Which anatomical structure separates an infralevator (vulvar/perineal) haematoma from a supralevator (broad ligament/pelvic) haematoma?
options: Perineal membrane (inferior fascia of urogenital diaphragm)
questions.explanation: Puerperal and traumatic genital haematomas are classified anatomically based on their relationship to the levator ani muscle: (1) Infralevator haematomas (vulval or perineal): Arise below the levator ani (branches of internal pudendal artery/veins), manifesting as visible, painful, tense purplish introital or labial swellings. (2) Supralevator haematomas: Arise above the levator ani (branches of uterine or hypogastric vessels), dissecting into the broad ligament and retroperitoneal space toward the kidney; they are invisible from the perineum but present with profound concealed hypovolemic shock.

questions.prompt: What is the management of choice for an expanding, severely painful vulvar haematoma > 5 cm in diameter following genital trauma?
questions.question: What is the management of choice for an expanding, severely painful vulvar haematoma > 5 cm in diameter following genital trauma?
options: Incision under anesthesia, evacuation of clot, identification and ligation of bleeding vessels, and obliteration of dead space (or packing)
Strict ice pack application and observation alone
Needle aspiration using a 22-gauge needle in the outpatient clinic
questions.answer: Incision under anesthesia, evacuation of clot, identification and ligation of bleeding vessels, and obliteration of dead space (or packing)
questions.explanation: Small, stable, non-expanding haematomas (< 4-5 cm) can be managed conservatively with ice packs, analgesics, and observation. However, an expanding, large (> 5 cm), or severely painful vulvar/vaginal haematoma requires surgical intervention under anesthesia: incising the overlying mucosa/skin, thorough evacuation of all hematoma clots, meticulous ligation of any bleeding vessels (often branches of the pudendal artery), and obliteration of dead space with figure-of-eight absorbable sutures, followed by tight vaginal packing and an indwelling urinary catheter.
questions.subject: Obstetrics and Gynaecology

questions.prompt: During a difficult laparoscopic adhesiolysis, an electrosurgical thermal injury to the rectosigmoid colon is unrecognized. On which postoperative day does fecal peritonitis typically manifest due to delayed sloughing of thermal necrosis?
questions.question: During a difficult laparoscopic adhesiolysis, an electrosurgical thermal injury to the rectosigmoid colon is unrecognized. On which postoperative day does fecal peritonitis typically manifest due to delayed sloughing of thermal necrosis?
questions.explanation: Unlike mechanical lacerations (sharp incisions/trocar punctures) that cause rapid contamination presenting within 24-48 hours, unappreciated thermal/electrosurgical injuries (monopolar diathermy arc/lateral thermal spread) produce coagulative tissue necrosis. The necrotic bowel wall thins and subsequently sloughs on postoperative day 4 to 7, leading to delayed bowel perforation, feculent peritonitis, leukopenia/leukocytosis, and insidious septic shock.

questions.prompt: What surgical flap procedure utilizes a pedicled fibrofatty flap from the labium majus to provide vascularization and tissue interposition during the repair of a recurrent rectovaginal fistula?
questions.question: What surgical flap procedure utilizes a pedicled fibrofatty flap from the labium majus to provide vascularization and tissue interposition during the repair of a recurrent rectovaginal fistula?
questions.explanation: The Martius labial fat pad flap (bulbocavernosus fibrofatty flap) mobilizes subcutaneous adipose tissue and bulbocavernosus muscle from the labium majus (pedicled on posterior labial vessels). It is tunneled beneath the vaginal mucosa and interposed between the repaired rectal wall and vaginal wall. It provides robust vascularity, prevents overlap of suture lines, and promotes healing in complex, recurrent, or radiation-induced rectovaginal and vesicovaginal fistulae.

questions.prompt: What is the microbiological criterion (Kass criterion) for defining 'significant bacteriuria' in a clean-catch midstream urine sample in an asymptomatic female?
questions.question: What is the microbiological criterion (Kass criterion) for defining 'significant bacteriuria' in a clean-catch midstream urine sample in an asymptomatic female?
options: >= 10^5 colony-forming units (CFU) per mL of a single uropathogen on two consecutive samples
questions.answer: >= 10^5 colony-forming units (CFU) per mL of a single uropathogen on two consecutive samples
questions.explanation: According to Edward Kass's classic criteria, significant asymptomatic bacteriuria in women is defined by the isolation of >= 10^5 (100,000) colony-forming units (CFU)/mL of a single uropathogen in two consecutive clean-catch midstream urine specimens (or a single catheterized specimen with >= 10^2 CFU/mL). In symptomatic acute uncomplicated cystitis, however, lower bacterial counts (>= 10^2 to 10^3 CFU/mL) are clinically diagnostic.

questions.prompt: What cystoscopic finding is pathognomonic for Interstitial Cystitis / Bladder Pain Syndrome (IC/BPS)?
questions.question: What cystoscopic finding is pathognomonic for Interstitial Cystitis / Bladder Pain Syndrome (IC/BPS)?
options: Hunner's ulcers (erythematous mucosal lesions with radiating vessels) and glomerulations on hydrodistension
Multiple papillary fronds over the trigone
Bullous edema around the ureteric orifices
questions.answer: Hunner's ulcers (erythematous mucosal lesions with radiating vessels) and glomerulations on hydrodistension
questions.explanation: Interstitial Cystitis / Bladder Pain Syndrome (IC/BPS) is a chronic, debilitating disorder presenting with pelvic/suprapubic pain related to bladder filling, severe urgency, and frequency in the absence of infection. The classic cystoscopic hallmark under general anesthesia with bladder hydrodistension is: (1) Hunner's ulcers (or lesions)—erythematous mucosal patches with small central vessels that bleed or crack with bladder filling (seen in 10-20% of patients); and (2) Glomerulations—diffuse punctate petechial mucosal hemorrhages after drainage.

questions.prompt: In the 'Three-Swab Test' (Moir's test) for distinguishing urinary fistulae, how are Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF) and Ureterovaginal Fistula (UVF) differentiated?
questions.question: In the 'Three-Swab Test' (Moir's test) for distinguishing urinary fistulae, how are Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF) and Ureterovaginal Fistula (UVF) differentiated?
options: VVF: Lowest swab is wet and blue (methylene blue instilled into bladder); UVF: Topmost swab is wet and colourless (or stained by oral/IV dye)
VVF: Topmost swab is dry; UVF: All swabs are stained dark blue
VVF: Middle swab is soaked with blood; UVF: No swab is wet
VVF: All swabs remain completely dry
questions.answer: VVF: Lowest swab is wet and blue (methylene blue instilled into bladder); UVF: Topmost swab is wet and colourless (or stained by oral/IV dye)
questions.explanation: In Moir's three-swab test, three cotton swabs are placed vertically in the vagina (top, middle, bottom), and the bladder is filled with 150-200 mL of dilute methylene blue: (1) Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF): Blue dye enters the vagina from the bladder, staining the middle or lowest swab blue. (2) Ureterovaginal fistula (UVF): Clear urine from the ureter trickles down from the vault, wetting the topmost swab while leaving all swabs uncoloured (unstained with blue). If oral phenazopyridine or IV indigo carmine is given, the topmost swab turns yellow/orange or blue.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended standard waiting time before attempting surgical repair of an obstetric vesicovaginal fistula?
questions.question: What is the recommended standard waiting time before attempting surgical repair of an obstetric vesicovaginal fistula?
options: 3 months (to allow inflammation, sloughing, and edema to completely subside)
Immediate emergency repair within 24 hours of labor
questions.answer: 3 months (to allow inflammation, sloughing, and edema to completely subside)
questions.explanation: Classical surgical teaching dictates that repair of an obstetric vesicovaginal fistula (caused by prolonged ischemic pressure necrosis of soft tissues between the fetal head and pubic symphysis) should be delayed for approximately 3 months (8 to 12 weeks). This interval allows necrotic slough to separate, acute sepsis and infection to resolve, edema to clear, and local tissues to regain vascularity, tensile strength, and mobility, which are mandatory for successful tension-free multilayered closure.

questions.prompt: What is the classic urodynamic finding that defines 'Overactive Bladder / Detrusor Overactivity' as the cause of urge urinary incontinence?
questions.question: What is the classic urodynamic finding that defines 'Overactive Bladder / Detrusor Overactivity' as the cause of urge urinary incontinence?
options: Involuntary detrusor muscle contractions during the bladder filling phase on cystometry
Abdominal leak point pressure (ALPP) < 60 cm H2O without detrusor pressure rise
Complete absence of post-void residual urine
questions.answer: Involuntary detrusor muscle contractions during the bladder filling phase on cystometry
questions.explanation: Detrusor overactivity is an urodynamic observation characterized by involuntary detrusor contractions during the filling phase, which may be spontaneous or provoked, while the patient is attempting to inhibit micturition. It is the underlying pathophysiological basis of urge urinary incontinence (overactive bladder). First-line therapies include bladder retraining, pelvic floor physical therapy, antimuscarinic agents (e.g., oxybutynin, solifenacin), or beta-3 adrenergic agonists (mirabegron).

questions.prompt: In the surgical management of pure stress urinary incontinence (SUI), what is the gold standard minimally invasive midurethral sling procedure?
questions.question: In the surgical management of pure stress urinary incontinence (SUI), what is the gold standard minimally invasive midurethral sling procedure?
options: Tension-free Vaginal Tape (TVT / retropubic) or Transobturator Tape (TOT)
Kelly plication of bladder neck alone
questions.answer: Tension-free Vaginal Tape (TVT / retropubic) or Transobturator Tape (TOT)
questions.explanation: Minimally invasive midurethral polypropylene mesh slings—specifically the retropubic tension-free vaginal tape (TVT, Ulmsten 1996) and the transobturator tape (TOT, Delorme 2001)—are the undisputed international gold standard surgical treatments for urodynamic stress urinary incontinence resulting from urethral hypermobility. They support the mid-urethra during increases in intra-abdominal pressure without tension. Kelly plication has high long-term recurrence rates and is no longer recommended as primary therapy for severe SUI.

questions.prompt: What is the Abdominal Leak Point Pressure (ALPP) threshold value on urodynamic testing that indicates 'Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency' (ISD)?
questions.question: What is the Abdominal Leak Point Pressure (ALPP) threshold value on urodynamic testing that indicates 'Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency' (ISD)?
questions.explanation: Abdominal Leak Point Pressure (ALPP) is the lowest intravesical pressure (induced by Valsalva or coughing) at which urinary leakage occurs across the external meatus: (1) ALPP < 60 cm H2O (or maximum urethral closure pressure MUCP < 20 cm H2O) defines severe Intrinsic Sphincter Deficiency (ISD)—a non-functioning 'lead-pipe' urethra. (2) ALPP > 90-100 cm H2O indicates pure urethral hypermobility. Patients with ISD respond poorly to simple anterior colporrhaphy and often require pubovaginal slings, retropubic midurethral slings (TVT), or periurethral bulking agents.

questions.prompt: What is the Q-tip (cotton swab) test used for in the physical examination of female urinary incontinence, and what angle defines urethral hypermobility?
questions.question: What is the Q-tip (cotton swab) test used for in the physical examination of female urinary incontinence, and what angle defines urethral hypermobility?
options: Measures the angle of urethral inclination from horizontal during maximum straining; An angle increase >= 30 degrees indicates urethral hypermobility
Detects urethral diverticulum; Swab insertion > 5 cm indicates hypermobility
Measures post-void residual volume; Angle > 90 degrees indicates urinary retention
Tests for detrusor sphincter dyssynergia; Rotation of swab clockwise indicates pathology
questions.answer: Measures the angle of urethral inclination from horizontal during maximum straining; An angle increase >= 30 degrees indicates urethral hypermobility
questions.explanation: The Q-tip test objectively assesses the anatomical support of the urethrovesical junction. A lubricated sterile cotton swab is inserted through the urethra into the bladder neck and then pulled back until resistance is met. The resting angle with the horizontal plane is noted. The patient is asked to perform a maximum Valsalva maneuver: a change or deflection angle >= 30 degrees from the horizontal indicates loss of pelvic floor support and anatomical urethral hypermobility.

questions.prompt: Which surgical technique for vesicovaginal fistula repair involves wide flap mobilization and closure in perpendicular layers (saucerization technique)?
questions.question: Which surgical technique for vesicovaginal fistula repair involves wide flap mobilization and closure in perpendicular layers (saucerization technique)?
options: Marion Sims / Chassar Moir flap-splitting technique
questions.answer: Marion Sims / Chassar Moir flap-splitting technique
questions.explanation: Chassar Moir popularized the flap-splitting technique for vaginal VVF repair: circumferential incision around the fistula tract, extensive sharp dissection to separate the bladder wall from the anterior vaginal wall for at least 1-2 cm, tension-free closure of the bladder muscularis with interrupted absorbable sutures (avoiding the bladder mucosa to prevent suture calculi), and closure of the vaginal mucosa in a perpendicular direction with non-overlapping suture lines.

questions.prompt: In the Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system, what is the anatomical reference line, and how are points proximal and distal to this line recorded?
questions.question: In the Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system, what is the anatomical reference line, and how are points proximal and distal to this line recorded?
options: The hymen is the reference line (plane 0); Points proximal (above) the hymen are expressed as negative centimeters (-), and points distal (beyond) the hymen are expressed as positive centimeters (+)
The external cervical os is the reference line (plane 0)
The ischial spines are the reference line; Proximal points are positive (+)
The perineal body is the reference line (plane 0)
questions.answer: The hymen is the reference line (plane 0); Points proximal (above) the hymen are expressed as negative centimeters (-), and points distal (beyond) the hymen are expressed as positive centimeters (+)
questions.explanation: The International Continence Society (ICS) POP-Q system uses the hymeneal ring as the fixed anatomical plane of reference (0 cm). Measurements are taken during maximum Valsalva: any anatomical landmark positioned proximal (cranial/inside) to the hymen is designated with a negative number (- cm), positions at the hymeneal plane are zero (0 cm), and any landmark projecting distal (caudal/protruding outside) to the hymen is designated with a positive number (+ cm).

questions.prompt: What are the exact definitions of Point Aa and Point Ba on the anterior vaginal wall in the POP-Q system?
questions.question: What are the exact definitions of Point Aa and Point Ba on the anterior vaginal wall in the POP-Q system?
options: Point Aa is fixed 3 cm proximal to the external urethral meatus on the anterior wall (range -3 to +3 cm); Point Ba represents the most dependent point of any remaining anterior vaginal wall between Aa and anterior fornix
Point Aa is the apex of the vagina; Point Ba is the posterior fornix
Point Aa is at the hymen; Point Ba is at the cervix
Point Aa is 5 cm proximal to the hymen; Point Ba is 1 cm proximal to the hymen
questions.answer: Point Aa is fixed 3 cm proximal to the external urethral meatus on the anterior wall (range -3 to +3 cm); Point Ba represents the most dependent point of any remaining anterior vaginal wall between Aa and anterior fornix
questions.explanation: In POP-Q anterior compartment quantification: (1) Point Aa: Located on the midline of the anterior vaginal wall exactly 3 cm proximal to the external urethral meatus (anatomically corresponds to the urethrovesical crease). In the absence of prolapse, Aa is -3 cm; its range is -3 to +3 cm. (2) Point Ba: Represents the most dependent or most prolapsed point of the anterior vaginal wall anywhere from Point Aa to the anterior vaginal fornix/cervix (Point C). In normal anatomy, Ba is -3 cm.

questions.prompt: What defines Stage III pelvic organ prolapse according to the POP-Q staging system?
questions.question: What defines Stage III pelvic organ prolapse according to the POP-Q staging system?
options: The most dependent portion of the prolapse is > 1 cm beyond the hymen (+1 cm), but protrudes no further than 2 cm less than the total vaginal length (tvl - 2 cm)
The most dependent portion of the prolapse is between -1 cm and +1 cm relative to the hymen
Complete eversion of the entire vaginal length (procidentia)
questions.answer: The most dependent portion of the prolapse is > 1 cm beyond the hymen (+1 cm), but protrudes no further than 2 cm less than the total vaginal length (tvl - 2 cm)
questions.explanation: POP-Q staging criteria: Stage 0: No prolapse (Aa, Ap, Ba, Bp = -3 cm; C/D between -tvl and -(tvl-2) cm); Stage I: Most distal portion of prolapse is > 1 cm above the hymen (< -1 cm); Stage II: Most distal portion of prolapse is between -1 cm and +1 cm (inclusive) of the hymen; Stage III: Most distal portion of prolapse extends > +1 cm beyond the hymen, but not further than (tvl - 2) cm; Stage IV: Complete procidentia / eversion of the lower genital tract (most distal point >= tvl - 2 cm).

questions.question: Which surgical operation is indicated for genital prolapse in a young woman desiring uterine preservation who has supravaginal elongation of the cervix?
options: Total vaginal hysterectomy with pelvic floor repair
questions.explanation: The Manchester (Fothergill) operation is an uterine-conserving procedure for uterine prolapse accompanied by hypertrophic supravaginal elongation of the cervix in women who wish to retain their uterus (or who have completed childbearing but decline hysterectomy). The four essential steps are: (1) Dilatation and curettage, (2) Amputation of the elongated cervix, (3) Anterior colporrhaphy, and (4) Plication of the cardinal (Mackenrodt's) ligaments in front of the cervical stump (Fothergill stitch) to pull the cervix backward and tilt the fundus forward.

questions.question: What is the primary surgical suspension site in a Sacrospinous Ligament Fixation (SSLF) for post-hysterectomy vaginal vault prolapse?
options: Right sacrospinous ligament (1.5 to 2 cm medial to the ischial spine)
Anterior longitudinal ligament of the sacral promontory (S1)
questions.answer: Right sacrospinous ligament (1.5 to 2 cm medial to the ischial spine)
questions.explanation: Sacrospinous ligament fixation (SSLF) is a classic transvaginal extraperitoneal suspension procedure for apical vault prolapse. The apex of the vagina is sutured to the right sacrospinous ligament (unilateral right-sided fixation is standard to avoid the sigmoid colon on the left). Sutures must be placed at least 1.5 to 2 cm medial to the ischial spine to avoid injury to the internal pudendal neurovascular bundle and sciatic nerve traversing the greater sciatic foramen.

questions.prompt: What is the definitive obliterative surgical procedure for severe pelvic organ prolapse in an elderly, frail woman with multiple medical comorbidities who is no longer sexually active?
questions.question: What is the definitive obliterative surgical procedure for severe pelvic organ prolapse in an elderly, frail woman with multiple medical comorbidities who is no longer sexually active?
questions.explanation: Colpocleisis (such as the Le Fort partial colpocleisis in patients with an intact uterus, or total colpocleisis in post-hysterectomy patients) is an obliterative procedure with success rates > 95-98%, extremely low surgical morbidity, short operating time, and can even be performed under local/regional anesthesia. Rectangular strips of anterior and posterior vaginal epithelium are denuded and the underlying muscular walls are sutured together, obliterating the vaginal canal while leaving lateral drainage channels for uterine secretions. It is reserved strictly for frail elderly women who are no longer sexually active.

questions.prompt: What is the primary anatomical etiology of an enterocoele (herniation of the pouch of Douglas into the rectovaginal septum)?
questions.question: What is the primary anatomical etiology of an enterocoele (herniation of the pouch of Douglas into the rectovaginal septum)?
options: Defect in the rectovaginal fascia (Denonvilliers' fascia) with separation of uterosacral ligaments allowing small bowel herniation
Detachment of pubocervical fascia from the arcus tendineus fasciae pelvis
Avulsion of the bulbospongiosus muscle from the perineal body
Hypertrophy of the superficial transverse perineal muscle
questions.answer: Defect in the rectovaginal fascia (Denonvilliers' fascia) with separation of uterosacral ligaments allowing small bowel herniation
questions.explanation: An enterocoele is a true pelvic hernia where peritoneal sac (containing loops of small bowel or sigmoid colon and omentum) herniates downward through the pouch of Douglas between the anterior wall of the rectum and the posterior wall of the vagina. It results from attenuation, stretching, or detachment of the endopelvic fascia (rectovaginal fascia) and diastasis of the uterosacral ligaments, often following hysterectomy if the cul-de-sac was not obliterated (McCall culdoplasty).

questions.prompt: What are the four clinical degrees of acute uterine inversion?
questions.question: What are the four clinical degrees of acute uterine inversion?
options: First degree: Fundus indented but remains above external os; Second degree: Inverted fundus protrudes through external os into vagina; Third degree: Fundus protrudes outside the introitus; Fourth degree: Complete inversion involving vagina (procidentia uteri)
First degree: Cervix dilated 2 cm; Fourth degree: Ruptured lower uterine segment
First degree: Asymptomatic; Fourth degree: Neurogenic shock only
First degree: Partial prolapse; Fourth degree: Complete hysterectomy required
questions.answer: First degree: Fundus indented but remains above external os; Second degree: Inverted fundus protrudes through external os into vagina; Third degree: Fundus protrudes outside the introitus; Fourth degree: Complete inversion involving vagina (procidentia uteri)
questions.explanation: Uterine inversion is clinically staged into four degrees: (1) First degree (Incomplete): The inverted uterine fundus indents the cavity but does not pass through the cervical os; (2) Second degree (Complete): The inverted fundus passes through the cervix into the vaginal canal; (3) Third degree (Prolapsed): The inverted fundus extends outside the vaginal introitus; (4) Fourth degree (Total): Both the entire uterus and the vaginal walls are completely turned inside out.

questions.prompt: What abdominal surgical procedure for chronic or irreducible uterine inversion involves incising the constricting cervical ring posteriorly to reposition the fundus?
questions.question: What abdominal surgical procedure for chronic or irreducible uterine inversion involves incising the constricting cervical ring posteriorly to reposition the fundus?
questions.explanation: When acute or subacute uterine inversion cannot be repositioned manually (Johnson's maneuver) or with hydrostatic pressure (O'Sullivan's technique), surgical correction is necessary: (1) Huntington procedure: Gradual upward traction on the round ligaments and fundus using Allis clamps through a laparotomy; (2) Haultain operation: If a tight cervical ring resists traction, an incision is made through the posterior wall of the constricting cervical ring, relieving the obstruction and enabling upward repositioning of the fundus, followed by repair of the uterine incision in layers.

questions.prompt: What is the diagnostic gold standard for confirming Pelvic Congestion Syndrome (PCS) associated with ovarian vein incompetence?
questions.question: What is the diagnostic gold standard for confirming Pelvic Congestion Syndrome (PCS) associated with ovarian vein incompetence?
options: Transcatheter retrograde ovarian and internal iliac venography
questions.answer: Transcatheter retrograde ovarian and internal iliac venography
questions.explanation: Pelvic Congestion Syndrome (PCS) is characterized by chronic dull aching pelvic pain exacerbated by prolonged standing, coitus (post-coital ache), and premenstrually, accompanied by vulvar and perineal varicosities. The definitive diagnostic gold standard is retrograde transcatheter ovarian venography, which demonstrates retrograde flow, delayed clearance of contrast (> 20 seconds), marked ovarian vein dilatation (> 6-10 mm), and engorged tortuous pelvic venous plexuses. Transcatheter coil embolization is the treatment of choice.

questions.prompt: What are the clinical characteristics that differentiate superficial (introital) dyspareunia from deep dyspareunia?
questions.question: What are the clinical characteristics that differentiate superficial (introital) dyspareunia from deep dyspareunia?
options: Superficial: Pain at the vaginal orifice upon attempted initial penetration (e.g., provoked vestibulodynia, vaginismus); Deep: Pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis with deep penile thrusting (e.g., endometriosis, PID, fixed retroverted uterus)
Superficial is purely psychological; Deep is purely anatomical
Superficial is seen only in multiparas; Deep is seen only in nulliparas
Superficial requires laparotomy; Deep is treated with topical estrogen
questions.answer: Superficial: Pain at the vaginal orifice upon attempted initial penetration (e.g., provoked vestibulodynia, vaginismus); Deep: Pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis with deep penile thrusting (e.g., endometriosis, PID, fixed retroverted uterus)
questions.explanation: Dyspareunia is anatomically categorized as: (1) Superficial (introital): Pain experienced at the introitus or lower vagina during entry/attempted penetration. Etiologies include provoked vestibulodynia, vulvovaginal atrophy (GSM), hymeneal rigidities, vulvovaginitis, and vaginismus (involuntary pelvic floor spasm). (2) Deep dyspareunia: Pain triggered by deep vaginal thrusting impacting pelvic viscera. Etiologies include endometriosis (uterosacral/pouch of Douglas nodules), chronic PID, fixed retroverted uterus, adenomyosis, and chronic pelvic congestion.

questions.prompt: What is the single most common anatomical site of ectopic tubal gestation, accounting for approximately 70–80% of all tubal pregnancies?
questions.question: What is the single most common anatomical site of ectopic tubal gestation, accounting for approximately 70–80% of all tubal pregnancies?
questions.explanation: Over 95% of ectopic pregnancies occur in the fallopian tube. Among tubal implantations, the ampulla is the widest and most common site (70–80%), followed by the isthmus (12%), fimbria (5%), and interstitial/cornual segment (2–3%).

questions.prompt: What is the 'discriminatory zone' of serum beta-hCG on high-resolution Transvaginal Sonography (TVS), above which an intrauterine gestational sac MUST reliably be visualized if a normal intrauterine pregnancy exists?
questions.question: What is the 'discriminatory zone' of serum beta-hCG on high-resolution Transvaginal Sonography (TVS), above which an intrauterine gestational sac MUST reliably be visualized if a normal intrauterine pregnancy exists?
questions.explanation: The discriminatory zone is the serum quantitative beta-hCG level (usually 1500–2000 mIU/mL on TVS) above which a normal singleton intrauterine gestational sac should always be seen. An empty uterine cavity with beta-hCG above this threshold strongly indicates an ectopic pregnancy or non-viable gestation.

questions.question: A 26-year-old stable female is diagnosed with an unruptured ampullary ectopic pregnancy. Serum beta-hCG is 2200 mIU/mL, ultrasound shows an ectopic mass measuring 2.8 cm with no embryonic cardiac activity, and minimal free fluid. What is the evidence-based medical therapy of choice?

questions.answer: Systemic single-dose Intramuscular Methotrexate (50 mg/m2 body surface area) with monitoring of beta-hCG on days 4 and 7
questions.explanation: Eligibility criteria for medical management of ectopic pregnancy with single-dose IM methotrexate (50 mg/m2): hemodynamically stable patient, serum beta-hCG < 5000 mIU/mL, unruptured ectopic mass < 3.5 cm, absence of embryonic cardiac motion, and normal renal/hepatic profiles.

questions.prompt: In contrast to a partial hydatidiform mole, what cytogenetic karyotype and fertilization event characterizes a Complete Hydatidiform Mole in > 90% of cases?
questions.question: In contrast to a partial hydatidiform mole, what cytogenetic karyotype and fertilization event characterizes a Complete Hydatidiform Mole in > 90% of cases?
options: Triploid 69,XXY resulting from dispermic fertilization of a normal haploid ovum
Diploid 46,XX androgenetic in origin, resulting from fertilization of an 'empty' enucleate ovum by a single haploid sperm that duplicates its chromosomes (homozygous)
questions.answer: Diploid 46,XX androgenetic in origin, resulting from fertilization of an 'empty' enucleate ovum by a single haploid sperm that duplicates its chromosomes (homozygous)
questions.explanation: Complete hydatidiform mole is completely androgenetic (paternal origin): > 90% are 46,XX resulting from endoreduplication of a 23,X sperm in an empty anuclear ovum. There is diffuse villous swelling, circumferential trophoblastic hyperplasia, and zero fetal tissue.

questions.question: A 24-year-old female presents with 10 weeks of amenorrhea, severe hyperemesis, dark prune-juice vaginal bleeding, and a uterus enlarged to 18 weeks' size. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrates a diffuse vesicular intrauterine pattern with multiple cystic spaces and absence of a fetus ('snowstorm' or 'bunch of grapes' appearance), with bilateral multilocular 8-cm ovarian cysts. What are the ovarian cysts?
options: Theca Lutein Cysts induced by excessively high circulating beta-hCG levels
questions.answer: Theca Lutein Cysts induced by excessively high circulating beta-hCG levels
questions.explanation: In complete molar pregnancy, massive production of beta-hCG (which shares an identical alpha-subunit with LH and FSH) causes extensive ovarian hyperstimulation, producing large, bilateral, multilocular Theca Lutein Cysts. They regress spontaneously following molar evacuation.

questions.prompt: What is the primary definitive surgical treatment for evacuating a diagnosed hydatidiform mole in a patient wishing to preserve future fertility?
questions.question: What is the primary definitive surgical treatment for evacuating a diagnosed hydatidiform mole in a patient wishing to preserve future fertility?
options: Medical induction with high-dose oxytocin alone
Suction evacuation and curettage under ultrasound guidance with concurrent oxytocin infusion started after evacuation begins
questions.answer: Suction evacuation and curettage under ultrasound guidance with concurrent oxytocin infusion started after evacuation begins
questions.explanation: Suction curettage with a large-bore cannula under ultrasound guidance is the gold-standard treatment for hydatidiform mole. Oxytocin infusion is initiated only as suction begins (to prevent embolization of trophoblastic tissue into the uterine venous sinuses).

questions.question: A 58-year-old postmenopausal female presents with chronic, intractable vulvar pruritus. Physical examination shows parchment-like, atrophic, crinkled porcelain-white plaques affecting the labia majora, labia minora, and perianal skin in a symmetrical 'figure-of-eight' or keyhole distribution, with resorption of the labia minora and burying of the clitoris. What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?
options: Lichen Sclerosus; ultra-potent topical corticosteroids (e.g., Clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment)
Extramammary Paget's disease; wide local excision
questions.answer: Lichen Sclerosus; ultra-potent topical corticosteroids (e.g., Clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment)
questions.explanation: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic autoimmune dermatosis featuring thin, white, parchment-like skin in a classic figure-of-eight distribution around the vulva and anus, with loss of labial architecture. The first-line medical therapy is ultra-potent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol propionate 0.05%).

questions.question: A 28-year-old female presents with acute throbbing pain and swelling on the posterolateral aspect of the vaginal introitus at the 4 o'clock position, causing difficulty sitting and walking. Examination reveals a 4-cm fluctuant, hot, exquisitely tender mass in the lower third of the labium majus. What is the standard office-based or minor surgical procedure providing drainage while preserving glandular function?
options: Complete radical excision of the gland under general anaesthesia
Incision and drainage with placement of a Word catheter (or Marsupialization)
questions.answer: Incision and drainage with placement of a Word catheter (or Marsupialization)
questions.explanation: Acute Bartholin abscess management requires drainage and creation of a permanent tract to prevent recurrence. A small incision with insertion of a Word catheter (balloon inflated with 2-3 mL saline and left for 4-6 weeks for epithelialization) or surgical marsupialization preserves gland secretory function.

questions.question: Why is an incisional punch biopsy mandatory in postmenopausal women presenting with newly diagnosed vulvar dystrophies, leukoplakia, or chronic non-healing ulcers?
options: To rule out differentiated Vulvar Intraepithelial Neoplasia (dVIN) and invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma
questions.answer: To rule out differentiated Vulvar Intraepithelial Neoplasia (dVIN) and invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma
questions.explanation: Long-standing lichen sclerosus and leukoplakic vulvar dystrophies carry a 3–5% lifetime risk of transforming into HPV-independent invasive squamous cell carcinoma (often via dVIN). Biopsy of suspicious, indurated, or refractory areas is essential to rule out malignancy.

questions.question: A 25-year-old female presents with a painless, smooth, cystic swelling located in the anterolateral wall of the upper vagina. Histology of the cyst wall demonstrates non-mucinous cuboidal or low columnar epithelium without cilia. What is the embryological origin of a Gartner's Duct Cyst?
options: Inclusion of squamous epithelium following perineal laceration
questions.explanation: Gartner's duct cysts develop from vestigial caudal remnants of the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct. They are characteristically located along the anterolateral wall of the upper vagina.

questions.question: What is the single most common benign cystic lesion of the vagina overall, typically located on the posterior or lateral wall at the site of a prior episiotomy or obstetric laceration?
questions.explanation: Epidermal inclusion cysts are the most common vaginal cysts, arising when fragments of stratified squamous epithelium are buried beneath the vaginal mucosa during repair of an episiotomy, obstetric tear, or vaginal surgery.

questions.prompt: In in-utero exposure to Diethylstilbestrol (DES), what benign vaginal anomaly is characteristically seen in young women, which also carries an increased risk of Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma of the vagina?
questions.question: In in-utero exposure to Diethylstilbestrol (DES), what benign vaginal anomaly is characteristically seen in young women, which also carries an increased risk of Clear Cell Adenocarcinoma of the vagina?
questions.explanation: Maternal ingestion of diethylstilbestrol (DES) during early pregnancy interferes with the replacement of Müllerian columnar epithelium by squamoid urogenital sinus cells, leading to vaginal adenosis, cockscomb cervix, and a risk of clear cell adenocarcinoma.

questions.question: According to the FIGO leiomyoma subclassification system, what is a 'Type 0' and 'Type 2' submucous uterine leiomyoma?
options: Type 0 is subserosal; Type 2 is transmural
Type 0 is 100% intracavitary pedunculated; Type 2 is intramural with < 50% intracavitary protrusion
Type 0 is intramural; Type 2 is cervical
Type 0 is parasitic; Type 2 is subserosal
questions.answer: Type 0 is 100% intracavitary pedunculated; Type 2 is intramural with < 50% intracavitary protrusion
questions.explanation: FIGO classifies submucous fibroids as: Type 0 = 100% intracavitary pedunculated; Type 1 = submucous with >= 50% of diameter protruding into the endometrial cavity; Type 2 = intramural with < 50% protruding into the cavity.

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old primigravida at 20 weeks' gestation presents with acute, localized, severe abdominal pain over a pre-existing 6-cm intramural uterine fibroid, low-grade fever, and focal tenderness, without vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows heterogeneous central cystic changes within the myoma. What acute aseptic degenerative process is occurring?
questions.question: A 28-year-old primigravida at 20 weeks' gestation presents with acute, localized, severe abdominal pain over a pre-existing 6-cm intramural uterine fibroid, low-grade fever, and focal tenderness, without vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows heterogeneous central cystic changes within the myoma. What acute aseptic degenerative process is occurring?
questions.explanation: Red (carneous) degeneration occurs predominantly during the mid-trimester of pregnancy or puerperium. Rapid estrogen-driven tumor growth outgrows its vascular supply, leading to venous thrombosis, extensive extravasation of blood into the whorled tumor tissue, and hemolysis. Management is strictly conservative with analgesics and hydration.

questions.prompt: During abdominal myomectomy for a large symptomatic intramural leiomyoma in a nulliparous female wishing to conceive, what surgical principle minimizes blood loss and future risk of uterine rupture during pregnancy?
questions.question: During abdominal myomectomy for a large symptomatic intramural leiomyoma in a nulliparous female wishing to conceive, what surgical principle minimizes blood loss and future risk of uterine rupture during pregnancy?
options: Making multiple transverse incisions across the uterine corpus

Infiltration of vasopressin (20 units in 100 mL saline) into the myoma pseudocapsule, a single anterior midline vertical uterine incision, enucleation along the pseudocapsule, and multi-layer myometrial closure
Leaving the myometrial defect open to drain
questions.answer: Infiltration of vasopressin (20 units in 100 mL saline) into the myoma pseudocapsule, a single anterior midline vertical uterine incision, enucleation along the pseudocapsule, and multi-layer myometrial closure
questions.explanation: Standard myomectomy principles: inject dilute vasopressin or use a tourniquet for hemostasis, make minimal uterine incisions (preferring an anterior midline incision to access multiple fibroids), shell out within the avascular plane of the pseudocapsule, and meticulously close the myometrium in layers without dead space.

questions.prompt: What is the single most common anatomical site of ectopic endometrial implant localization in pelvic endometriosis?
questions.question: What is the single most common anatomical site of ectopic endometrial implant localization in pelvic endometriosis?
questions.explanation: The ovary is the most common site of pelvic endometriosis (involved in > 60% of cases), followed by the pouch of Douglas, posterior broad ligament, and uterosacral ligaments. Repeated cyclical bleeding produces an endometrioma filled with thick, chocolate-brown fluid.

questions.prompt: On bimanual examination of a 30-year-old female presenting with severe deep dyspareunia, progressive dysmenorrhea, and subfertility, what physical examination finding is characteristic of deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE)?
questions.question: On bimanual examination of a 30-year-old female presenting with severe deep dyspareunia, progressive dysmenorrhea, and subfertility, what physical examination finding is characteristic of deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE)?
options: Fixed retroverted uterus with exquisitely tender, nodular induration in the uterosacral ligaments and pouch of Douglas
Smooth, painless cystic mass at the introitus
questions.answer: Fixed retroverted uterus with exquisitely tender, nodular induration in the uterosacral ligaments and pouch of Douglas
questions.explanation: Deep infiltrating endometriosis forms dense scarring and fibrosis in the cul-de-sac, fixing the uterus in retroversion and producing tender, palpable 'shotty' nodules along the uterosacral ligaments and posterior fornix, accounting for severe deep dyspareunia and dyschezia.

questions.question: A 44-year-old multiparous female presents with progressive heavy menstrual bleeding and severe, deep dysmenorrhea. On bimanual examination, the uterus is symmetrically and globally enlarged (12–14 weeks' size), soft to boggy, and globally tender during menstruation. Pelvic ultrasound reveals diffuse myometrial heterogeneity, subendometrial echogenic linear striations, and myometrial anterior-posterior asymmetry without discrete encapsulated masses. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Adenomyosis is the benign invasion of endometrial glands and stroma into the myometrium, accompanied by reactive myometrial smooth muscle hyperplasia. The uterus is characteristically uniformly enlarged, soft/boggy, and exquisitely tender on premenstrual/menstrual examination.
