questions.prompt: Which gastrointestinal disease frequently manifests in childhood as unexplained linear growth failure and delayed puberty months to years before overt gastrointestinal symptoms appear?
questions.question: Which gastrointestinal disease frequently manifests in childhood as unexplained linear growth failure and delayed puberty months to years before overt gastrointestinal symptoms appear?
questions.explanation: Celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy) can present atypically in school-age children and adolescents without classic chronic diarrhea or abdominal distension. The presenting complaint is often isolated short stature, poor growth velocity, pubertal delay, or refractory iron deficiency anemia. Screening with anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) IgA antibodies (along with total serum IgA) is a mandatory component of any short stature diagnostic workup.

questions.prompt: What statistical cutoff defines Microcephaly in an infant?
questions.question: What statistical cutoff defines Microcephaly in an infant?
options: Occipitofrontal head circumference < -2 Standard Deviations (< -2 SD) or below the 3rd percentile for age and sex
Head circumference < 35 cm at any age
Head circumference smaller than the chest circumference after 1 year
questions.answer: Occipitofrontal head circumference < -2 Standard Deviations (< -2 SD) or below the 3rd percentile for age and sex
questions.explanation: Microcephaly is defined as an occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) measuring more than 2 standard deviations below the mean (< -2 SD) for age and sex. Severe microcephaly is defined as OFC < -3 SD, which correlates strongly with severe structural brain anomalies, neurodevelopmental impairment, and microencephaly (e.g., congenital cytomegalovirus, Zika virus, chromosomal aneuploidies).

questions.prompt: What is the single most common form of primary craniosynostosis, and what head shape deformity does it produce?
questions.question: What is the single most common form of primary craniosynostosis, and what head shape deformity does it produce?
options: Sagittal suture synostosis; Produces an elongated, narrow skull (Scaphocephaly / Dolichocephaly)
Coronal suture synostosis; Produces a pointed skull (Oxycephaly)
Metopic suture synostosis; Produces a flat skull (Plagiocephaly)
Lambdoid suture synostosis; Produces cloverleaf skull (Kleeblattschädel)
questions.answer: Sagittal suture synostosis; Produces an elongated, narrow skull (Scaphocephaly / Dolichocephaly)
questions.explanation: Craniosynostosis is the premature pathological fusion of one or more cranial sutures. Sagittal synostosis accounts for ~50-60% of all single-suture cases. Because the skull cannot expand perpendicular to the fused sagittal suture, compensatory growth occurs parallel to it (Virchow's law), creating an elongated, boat-shaped, narrow cranium termed scaphocephaly (or dolichocephaly). Coronal synostosis produces brachycephaly (short, wide head) or plagiocephaly (asymmetrical head).
questions.subject: Pediatrics

questions.prompt: What is the key clinical sign that distinguishes benign deformational (positional) posterior plagiocephaly from true lambdoid craniosynostosis on vertex examination?
questions.question: What is the key clinical sign that distinguishes benign deformational (positional) posterior plagiocephaly from true lambdoid craniosynostosis on vertex examination?
options: In deformational plagiocephaly, the ipsilateral ear is shifted forward (parallelogram-shaped head); in lambdoid synostosis, the ipsilateral ear is displaced posteriorly (trapezoid-shaped head)
Deformational plagiocephaly occurs exclusively in preterm infants
Lambdoid synostosis has no palpable bony ridge
Deformational plagiocephaly causes rapid optic atrophy
questions.answer: In deformational plagiocephaly, the ipsilateral ear is shifted forward (parallelogram-shaped head); in lambdoid synostosis, the ipsilateral ear is displaced posteriorly (trapezoid-shaped head)
questions.explanation: Viewing the head from above (vertex view) distinguishes positional plagiocephaly from true synostosis: In positional plagiocephaly (non-synostotic flattening from supine positioning), the flattened occiput pushes the ipsilateral ear and frontal bone forward, giving the skull a parallelogram configuration. In true unilateral lambdoid craniosynostosis, the fused suture pulls the ipsilateral ear and skull base posteriorly and inferiorly, giving a trapezoid configuration with a prominent mastoid bulge and contralateral parietal bossing.

questions.prompt: What classic physical sign on ocular examination indicates elevated intracranial pressure in an infant with progressive hydrocephalus?
questions.question: What classic physical sign on ocular examination indicates elevated intracranial pressure in an infant with progressive hydrocephalus?
options: 'Setting sun' sign (downward gaze paresis with sclera visible above the iris)
questions.answer: 'Setting sun' sign (downward gaze paresis with sclera visible above the iris)
questions.explanation: In infants with hydrocephalus and markedly elevated intracranial pressure, the 'setting sun' sign (sunset phenomenon) is seen: the eyes are persistently deviated downward, exposing the white sclera between the upper eyelid and the superior limbus of the iris. It is caused by pressure on the midbrain tectum and periaqueductal gray matter affecting upward vertical conjugate gaze (Parinaud syndrome).

questions.prompt: What is the definitive initial diagnostic imaging modality of choice for evaluating macrocephaly in an infant with an open anterior fontanelle?
questions.question: What is the definitive initial diagnostic imaging modality of choice for evaluating macrocephaly in an infant with an open anterior fontanelle?
options: Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) of the head
questions.explanation: In an infant with an open anterior fontanelle presenting with macrocephaly (OFC > +2 SD) or a rapidly crossing head circumference percentile, transfontanellar cranial ultrasonography is the ideal first-line imaging modality. It requires no sedation, emits zero ionizing radiation, and reliably visualizes the ventricular size (ruling out hydrocephalus, Dandy-Walker malformation, intraventricular hemorrhage) and extra-axial spaces (benign enlargement of subarachnoid space / BESS).

questions.prompt: At what age does a normal infant achieve: (1) Complete neck holding without head lag, and (2) Sitting without support with a straight back?
questions.question: At what age does a normal infant achieve: (1) Complete neck holding without head lag, and (2) Sitting without support with a straight back?
options: Neck holding: 3 to 4 months; Sitting without support: 8 months
Neck holding: 1 month; Sitting without support: 4 months
Neck holding: 6 months; Sitting without support: 12 months
Neck holding: 8 months; Sitting without support: 15 months
questions.answer: Neck holding: 3 to 4 months; Sitting without support: 8 months
questions.explanation: Gross motor milestones: (1) Complete neck holding with no head lag when pulled to sit is attained by 3 to 4 months; (2) Rolling over from prone to supine at 5 months, and supine to prone at 6 months; (3) Sitting with trunk support (triad posture, propping on hands) at 6 months; (4) Sitting steadily without any support with a straight back at 8 months; (5) Standing with support at 9 months; (6) Standing independently at 12 months; (7) Walking independently at 12-15 months.

questions.prompt: At what age does an infant achieve a mature 'fine pincer grasp' (picking up a small pellet using the tips of the index finger and thumb)?
questions.question: At what age does an infant achieve a mature 'fine pincer grasp' (picking up a small pellet using the tips of the index finger and thumb)?
questions.explanation: Fine motor development follows a precise sequence: (1) Bidextrous reaching for objects at 4 months; (2) Unidextrous reach at 6 months; (3) Palmar grasp (ulnar-palmar) at 5-6 months; (4) Transfer of objects hand-to-hand at 6-7 months; (5) Immature (crude/inferior) pincer grasp (using the pads of thumb and index finger) at 9-10 months; and (6) Mature (fine) pincer grasp (neat opposition of the tips of distal phalanges of the thumb and index finger) at 12 months.

questions.prompt: At what age does a child normally: (1) Speak a single word with specific meaning (e.g., 'mama', 'dada'), and (2) Speak two-word phrases (e.g., 'give milk', 'go car')?
questions.question: At what age does a child normally: (1) Speak a single word with specific meaning (e.g., 'mama', 'dada'), and (2) Speak two-word phrases (e.g., 'give milk', 'go car')?
options: Single meaningful word: 12 months; Two-word phrases: 24 months (2 years)
Single meaningful word: 6 months; Two-word phrases: 12 months
Single meaningful word: 18 months; Two-word phrases: 36 months
Single meaningful word: 9 months; Two-word phrases: 15 months
questions.answer: Single meaningful word: 12 months; Two-word phrases: 24 months (2 years)
questions.explanation: Language development milestones: (1) Cooing (musical vowels) at 3 months; (2) Monosyllabic babbling ('ba', 'da') at 6 months; (3) Bisimilar babbling ('ba-ba', 'ma-ma' non-specific) at 9 months; (4) 1-2 words with specific meaning at 12 months; (5) Vocabulary of 6-10 words at 18 months; (6) 2-word meaningful telegraphic phrases at 24 months (2 years); (7) 3-word sentences and stating own name and gender at 36 months (3 years).

questions.prompt: What social-personal milestone is achieved at 2 months of age, and what milestone is achieved at 6 to 8 months?
questions.question: What social-personal milestone is achieved at 2 months of age, and what milestone is achieved at 6 to 8 months?
options: 2 months: Social smile (smiles responsively to vocal/visual stimulation); 6-8 months: Stranger anxiety (fears unfamiliar persons)
2 months: Waving bye-bye; 6 months: Parallel play
2 months: Toilet training; 6 months: Social smile
2 months: Stranger anxiety; 6 months: Separation anxiety
questions.answer: 2 months: Social smile (smiles responsively to vocal/visual stimulation); 6-8 months: Stranger anxiety (fears unfamiliar persons)
questions.explanation: Social and personal milestones: (1) Spontaneous non-social reflex smile at birth/neonatal; (2) Social smile (smiling in response to a smiling face or maternal voice) at 6-8 weeks (2 months); (3) Recognizes mother at 3 months; (4) Enjoys mirror at 6 months; (5) Stranger anxiety (distress and withdrawal when approached by an unfamiliar person) at 6 to 8 months; (6) Waves 'bye-bye' and plays peek-a-boo at 9 months; (7) Cooperates in dressing at 12 months.

questions.prompt: At what age can a child successfully build a tower of: (1) 3 cubes, (2) 6 cubes, and (3) 9 cubes?
questions.question: At what age can a child successfully build a tower of: (1) 3 cubes, (2) 6 cubes, and (3) 9 cubes?
options: 3 cubes: 18 months; 6 cubes: 24 months (2 years); 9 cubes: 36 months (3 years)
3 cubes: 12 months; 6 cubes: 18 months; 9 cubes: 24 months
3 cubes: 24 months; 6 cubes: 36 months; 9 cubes: 48 months
3 cubes: 6 months; 6 cubes: 12 months; 9 cubes: 18 months
questions.answer: 3 cubes: 18 months; 6 cubes: 24 months (2 years); 9 cubes: 36 months (3 years)
questions.explanation: Block building milestones: (1) 15 months: Tower of 2 cubes; (2) 18 months: Tower of 3 cubes; (3) 24 months (2 years): Tower of 6 cubes; (4) 30 months: Tower of 8 cubes; (5) 36 months (3 years): Tower of 9-10 cubes, and can copy a 3-cube bridge; (6) 48 months (4 years): Builds a 6-cube gate.

questions.prompt: What is the chronological sequence and age at which a child can copy geometrical figures: Circle, Cross, Square, and Triangle?
questions.question: What is the chronological sequence and age at which a child can copy geometrical figures: Circle, Cross, Square, and Triangle?
options: Circle: 3 years; Cross: 4 years; Square: 4.5 years; Triangle: 5 years
Circle: 2 years; Cross: 3 years; Square: 4 years; Triangle: 5 years
Triangle: 3 years; Square: 4 years; Circle: 5 years; Cross: 6 years
Circle: 1 year; Square: 2 years; Triangle: 3 years; Diamond: 4 years
questions.answer: Circle: 3 years; Cross: 4 years; Square: 4.5 years; Triangle: 5 years
questions.explanation: Drawing/copying milestones proceed in an orderly visual-motor sequence: (1) Scribbles spontaneously: 15-18 months; (2) Copies a vertical stroke: 2 years (24 months); (3) Copies a horizontal stroke: 2.5 years (30 months); (4) Copies a Circle: 3 years (36 months); (5) Copies a Cross (+): 4 years; (6) Copies a Square: 4.5 years; (7) Copies a Triangle: 5 years; (8) Copies a Diamond: 6-7 years.

questions.prompt: At what age does a child normally master: (1) Running stiffly and walking backward, and (2) Riding a tricycle?
questions.question: At what age does a child normally master: (1) Running stiffly and walking backward, and (2) Riding a tricycle?
options: Running and walking backward: 18-24 months; Riding a tricycle: 36 months (3 years)
Running: 12 months; Riding a tricycle: 24 months
Running: 36 months; Riding a tricycle: 5 years
Running: 9 months; Riding a tricycle: 18 months
questions.answer: Running and walking backward: 18-24 months; Riding a tricycle: 36 months (3 years)
questions.explanation: Advanced gross motor milestones: (1) 18 months: Walks backward, runs stiffly, pulls a toy while walking; (2) 24 months (2 years): Walks up and down stairs 2 feet per step, kicks a ball without falling; (3) 36 months (3 years): Rides a tricycle, pedals well, walks up stairs alternating feet (1 foot per step), stands momentarily on one foot; (4) 48 months (4 years): Hops on one foot, skips, walks down stairs alternating feet.
questions.subject: Pediatrics

questions.prompt: At what age do the primitive neonatal reflexes: (1) Moro reflex, and (2) Asymmetric Tonic Neck Reflex (ATNR) normally disappear?
questions.question: At what age do the primitive neonatal reflexes: (1) Moro reflex, and (2) Asymmetric Tonic Neck Reflex (ATNR) normally disappear?
options: Moro reflex: Disappears by 4 to 6 months; ATNR: Disappears by 4 to 6 months
Moro reflex: Disappears at 12 months; ATNR: Disappears at 18 months
Both disappear within 48 hours of birth
Both persist normally throughout the first 2 years of life
questions.answer: Moro reflex: Disappears by 4 to 6 months; ATNR: Disappears by 4 to 6 months
questions.explanation: Primitive neonatal reflexes are mediated by brainstem/spinal cord centers and become integrated as the cerebral cortex matures: (1) Moro reflex (abduction and extension of arms followed by adduction and crying in response to sudden head drop): appears at 28-32 wks gestation, complete at term, and normally disappears by 4 to 6 months; (2) ATNR ('fencing posture'): appears at 2-4 wks, peaks at 2 months, and disappears by 4 to 6 months; (3) Palmar grasp disappears by 3 to 4 months; (4) Plantar grasp disappears by 9 to 12 months. Persistence of primitive reflexes beyond 6 months is an ominous sign of cerebral palsy.
questions.subject: Pediatrics

questions.prompt: What is considered a developmental 'Red Flag Sign' in an infant that warrants immediate comprehensive neurodevelopmental evaluation?
questions.question: What is considered a developmental 'Red Flag Sign' in an infant that warrants immediate comprehensive neurodevelopmental evaluation?
options: Inability to sit independently without support by 9-10 months of age, or no babbling by 9 months
Inability to write cursive letters at 3 years
Inability to hop on one foot at 2 years
Absence of secondary teeth eruption at 12 months
questions.answer: Inability to sit independently without support by 9-10 months of age, or no babbling by 9 months
questions.explanation: Critical developmental red flags include: (1) No social smile by 2-3 months; (2) Persistent fisting or lack of visual tracking by 3-4 months; (3) Significant head lag on pull-to-sit by 4-5 months; (4) Inability to sit steadily without support by 9-10 months; (5) Absence of babbling or reciprocal gestures by 9-12 months; (6) Not walking independently by 18 months; (7) Fewer than 6 meaningful words by 18 months; and (8) ANY loss of previously acquired motor, social, or language milestones at any age (developmental regression).
questions.subject: Pediatrics

questions.prompt: At what age does a child normally achieve daytime bladder control, and when is nighttime urinary continence established?
questions.question: At what age does a child normally achieve daytime bladder control, and when is nighttime urinary continence established?
options: Daytime continence: 2.5 to 3 years; Nighttime continence: 4 to 5 years
Daytime continence: 12 months; Nighttime continence: 18 months
Daytime continence: 5 years; Nighttime continence: 8 years
Both are established simultaneously at 18 months
questions.answer: Daytime continence: 2.5 to 3 years; Nighttime continence: 4 to 5 years
questions.explanation: Bladder control develops sequentially: (1) By 18 months: child indicates wet pants; (2) By 2 years: child shows readiness for toilet training and communicates urge to void; (3) By 2.5 to 3 years: daytime bladder control is achieved; (4) By 4 to 5 years: nighttime urinary continence is established. Involuntary voiding during sleep (nocturnal enuresis) is considered abnormal only beyond 5 years of age.
questions.subject: Pediatrics

questions.prompt: What is the clinical definition of 'Global Developmental Delay' (GDD)?
questions.question: What is the clinical definition of 'Global Developmental Delay' (GDD)?
options: Significant delay (>= 2 standard deviations below the mean) in two or more developmental domains in a child under 5 years of age
Isolated speech delay in a child aged 3 years with normal motor skills
IQ < 70 measured on a formalized psychometric test in a child over 10 years
Motor impairment resulting strictly from muscular dystrophy
questions.answer: Significant delay (>= 2 standard deviations below the mean) in two or more developmental domains in a child under 5 years of age
questions.explanation: Global Developmental Delay (GDD) is defined as a significant delay in two or more of the following developmental domains in a child under 5 years of age: (1) Gross/fine motor, (2) Speech/language, (3) Cognition, (4) Social/personal, and (5) Activities of daily living. 'Significant delay' is defined as performance >= 2 standard deviations below the mean on age-appropriate standardized norm-referenced testing. In children older than 5 years who can undergo psychometric testing, the condition is reclassified as Intellectual Disability (ID) if IQ is < 70 with adaptive deficits.
questions.subject: Pediatrics

questions.prompt: According to DSM-5 criteria, what are the two core diagnostic symptom domains for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)?
questions.question: According to DSM-5 criteria, what are the two core diagnostic symptom domains for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)?
options: Persistent deficits in social communication/interaction, and restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities
Severe isolated expressive language impairment with normal social reciprocity
Progressive intellectual regression following normal development for 3 years
questions.answer: Persistent deficits in social communication/interaction, and restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities
questions.explanation: DSM-5 defines Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) by two core behavioral domains presenting in early childhood: (1) Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts (e.g., deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, nonverbal communicative behaviors like eye contact and pointing, and developing/understanding relationships); and (2) Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities (e.g., stereotyped motor movements/hand flapping, insistence on sameness/inflexible adherence to routines, highly fixated interests, and hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input).
questions.subject: Pediatrics

questions.prompt: What is the single most common inherited monogenic cause of intellectual disability and autism in males?
questions.question: What is the single most common inherited monogenic cause of intellectual disability and autism in males?
options: Fragile X syndrome (FMR1 trinucleotide CGG repeat expansion)
questions.answer: Fragile X syndrome (FMR1 trinucleotide CGG repeat expansion)
questions.explanation: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is the most common chromosomal (genetic) cause of intellectual disability overall. However, Fragile X syndrome is the most common INHERITED monogenic cause of intellectual disability and the leading known monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder. It is caused by an unstable expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat (> 200 repeats, full mutation) in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR1 gene on chromosome Xq27.3, leading to hypermethylation and transcriptional silencing of the fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP). Features include long narrow face, large everted ears, high-arched palate, and post-pubertal macroorchidism.
questions.subject: Pediatrics

questions.prompt: A 2-year-old girl who had normal motor and social development until 14 months experiences rapid regression of purposeful hand skills, loss of spoken words, development of stereotypic midline 'hand-wringing' movements, and episodic hyperventilation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.question: A 2-year-old girl who had normal motor and social development until 14 months experiences rapid regression of purposeful hand skills, loss of spoken words, development of stereotypic midline 'hand-wringing' movements, and episodic hyperventilation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rett syndrome is an X-linked dominant neurodevelopmental disorder affecting almost exclusively females (lethal in hemizygous males in utero), caused by de novo mutations in the MECP2 (methyl-CpG-binding protein 2) gene. After an apparently normal initial 6 to 18 months of development, affected girls enter a period of developmental stagnation followed by rapid regression: loss of purposeful hand movements and expressive speech, development of stereotypic repetitive hand movements (classic midline hand-wringing or washing), deceleration of head growth (acquired microcephaly), gait ataxia, breathing irregularities (apnea/hyperventilation), and seizures.
questions.subject: Pediatrics

questions.prompt: What is the recommended first-line non-pharmacological behavioral therapy of choice for young children diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder?
questions.question: What is the recommended first-line non-pharmacological behavioral therapy of choice for young children diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder?
options: Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) / Early Intensive Behavioral Intervention (EIBI)
Chemo-sensory integration diet without behavioral therapy
questions.answer: Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) / Early Intensive Behavioral Intervention (EIBI)
questions.explanation: Early Intensive Behavioral Intervention (EIBI) based on the principles of Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) is the gold standard, evidence-based therapy for young children with ASD. ABA systematically breaks down skills into small, teachable steps, using positive reinforcement to enhance functional communication, joint attention, social engagement, and adaptive behaviors while reducing disruptive behaviors. Co-therapies include speech and language therapy and occupational therapy.

questions.prompt: In boys, what is the earliest physical manifestation of normal puberty, and at what testicular volume using a Prader orchidometer is it defined?
questions.question: In boys, what is the earliest physical manifestation of normal puberty, and at what testicular volume using a Prader orchidometer is it defined?
options: Testicular enlargement; Defined by testicular volume >= 4 mL
Appearance of coarse pubic hair at the base of the penis; Volume >= 8 mL
Peak height growth spurt; Volume >= 6 mL
questions.answer: Testicular enlargement; Defined by testicular volume >= 4 mL
questions.explanation: The first physical sign of puberty in boys is testicular enlargement (growth of the testes and scrotum with thinning and reddening of the scrotal skin, Tanner Stage G2). A testicular volume >= 4 mL (measured with a Prader orchidometer) or maximum testicular length >= 2.5 cm indicates activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis (gonadarche), occurring on average at 11.5 to 12 years of age. In contrast, pubarche (pubic hair) typically follows months later.

questions.prompt: At which Tanner stage of breast development in girls does Peak Height Velocity (the adolescent growth spurt) occur?
questions.question: At which Tanner stage of breast development in girls does Peak Height Velocity (the adolescent growth spurt) occur?
options: Tanner Stage B2 to B3 (prior to menarche)
Tanner Stage B5 (after complete breast maturation)
questions.answer: Tanner Stage B2 to B3 (prior to menarche)
questions.explanation: In girls, peak height velocity (PHV) occurs relatively early in the pubertal sequence, typically during Tanner breast stages B2 to B3 (average age 11.5 to 12 years; growth velocity ~8-9 cm/year), well before menarche. Menarche occurs late in puberty (Tanner B4, ~2-2.5 years after thelarche), by which time growth velocity has already decelerated significantly; girls grow only an additional 5-7 cm total after menarche. In boys, PHV occurs later (Tanner G4, age 13.5-14 years).

questions.prompt: What is the defining anatomical characteristic of Tanner Stage 4 (B4) in female breast development?
questions.question: What is the defining anatomical characteristic of Tanner Stage 4 (B4) in female breast development?
options: Projection of the areola and papilla to form a secondary mound above the level of the breast contour
Enlargement of breast and areola with no separation of their contours
Breast bud with elevation of breast and papilla as a small mound
Mature breast with recession of areola into general breast contour
questions.answer: Projection of the areola and papilla to form a secondary mound above the level of the breast contour
questions.explanation: Tanner staging of female breast development (Sexual Maturity Rating): Stage B1: Preadolescent (elevation of papilla only); Stage B2: Breast bud stage (small mound under areola with areolar widening); Stage B3: Further enlargement of breast and areola with continuous single contour; Stage B4: Projection of the areola and papilla above the level of the surrounding breast parenchyma to form a distinct secondary mound; Stage B5: Mature adult configuration with recession of areola into the general breast contour leaving only the papilla projecting.

questions.prompt: What is the clinical management of asymptomatic, bilateral, tender subareolar breast enlargement (adolescent gynecomastia, Tanner G3) in a healthy 14-year-old male?
questions.question: What is the clinical management of asymptomatic, bilateral, tender subareolar breast enlargement (adolescent gynecomastia, Tanner G3) in a healthy 14-year-old male?
options: Reassurance and observation, as it spontaneously regresses within 1 to 2 years in > 90% of cases
questions.answer: Reassurance and observation, as it spontaneously regresses within 1 to 2 years in > 90% of cases
questions.explanation: Physiological pubertal gynecomastia occurs in up to 50-65% of healthy adolescent boys, typically peaking at Tanner stages G3-G4 (ages 13-14). It results from a transient physiological imbalance between circulating free estradiol and testosterone, with high aromatase activity. In the vast majority (> 90%) of cases, the subareolar glandular tissue spontaneously regresses completely within 12 to 24 months. The management of choice is thorough reassurance, education, and observation.

questions.prompt: What is the total body water (TBW) content as a percentage of body weight in a preterm neonate, a full-term neonate, and an older child, respectively?
questions.question: What is the total body water (TBW) content as a percentage of body weight in a preterm neonate, a full-term neonate, and an older child, respectively?
questions.explanation: Total body water (TBW) decreases progressively with age: In preterm infants, TBW accounts for 80-85% of body weight (with extracellular fluid [ECF] being the largest component at ~50%). In full-term neonates, TBW is ~75% (ECF ~40-45%, ICF ~30-35%). By 1 year of age, TBW drops to ~65%, and stabilizes at adult levels (~60% of body weight, with ICF ~40% and ECF ~20%) by late childhood. Because infants possess a larger ECF compartment and higher surface-area-to-weight ratio, they are exceptionally prone to rapid dehydration.

questions.prompt: According to the WHO classification of dehydration in acute diarrhea, which clinical signs categorize a child as having 'Severe Dehydration'?
questions.question: According to the WHO classification of dehydration in acute diarrhea, which clinical signs categorize a child as having 'Severe Dehydration'?
options: At least two of: Lethargic or unconscious, sunken eyes, unable to drink or drinking poorly, skin pinch goes back very slowly (> 2 seconds)
Restless and irritable, drinking eagerly/thirsty, skin pinch goes back slowly (< 2 seconds)
Active and alert, normal eyes, drinks normally, skin pinch goes back immediately
Mild tachycardia with dry lips alone
questions.answer: At least two of: Lethargic or unconscious, sunken eyes, unable to drink or drinking poorly, skin pinch goes back very slowly (> 2 seconds)
questions.explanation: The WHO guidelines classify dehydration into three clinical categories based on 4 cardinal signs (general condition, eyes, thirst/drinking, and skin pinch): (1) Severe Dehydration (>= 10% fluid deficit): Presence of >= 2 signs: Lethargic or unconscious; Sunken eyes; Unable to drink or drinking poorly; Skin pinch retracts very slowly (> 2 seconds). Requires immediate IV therapy (Plan C). (2) Some Dehydration (5-9% fluid deficit): >= 2 signs: Restless/irritable; Sunken eyes; Drinks eagerly/thirsty; Skin pinch goes back slowly (< 2 seconds). Managed with oral rehydration solution (Plan B). (3) No Dehydration (< 5% deficit): None of these signs; managed at home with extra fluids (Plan A).

The child is reassessed after 4 hours to classify into No, Some, or Severe Dehydration.

questions.explanation: The revised WHO/UNICEF reduced-osmolarity ORS formulation has a total osmolarity of 245 mOsm/L. Its precise constituent concentrations are: Sodium: 75 mEq/L (mmol/L); Chloride: 65 mEq/L; Anhydrous Glucose: 75 mmol/L (13.5 g/L); Potassium: 20 mEq/L (1.5 g/L KCl); Trisodium citrate dihydrate: 10 mmol/L (2.9 g/L). Compared to original high-sodium ORS (311 mOsm/L), reduced-osmolarity ORS shortens diarrhea duration, decreases stool output by ~25%, and reduces the need for unscheduled IV therapy by 33%.

questions.prompt: Using the Holliday-Segar method, what is the daily maintenance fluid requirement for a 16 kg child?
questions.question: Using the Holliday-Segar method, what is the daily maintenance fluid requirement for a 16 kg child?
questions.explanation: The Holliday-Segar formula calculates 24-hour maintenance water based on weight: (1) First 10 kg: 100 mL/kg = 1,000 mL; (2) Next 10 kg (11-20 kg): 50 mL/kg for each kg above 10 kg; (3) Each kg above 20 kg: 20 mL/kg. For a 16 kg child: (10 kg * 100) + (6 kg * 50) = 1,000 + 300 = 1,300 mL/24 hours (Hourly 4-2-1 rule: 4 mL/kg/hr for first 10 kg [40] + 2 mL/kg/hr for next 6 kg [12] + 1 mL/kg/hr thereafter = 52-54 mL/hr).

questions.answer: Sodium: 2 to 3 mEq/kg/day; Potassium: 1 to 2 mEq/kg/day
questions.explanation: Normal baseline maintenance electrolyte requirements for children are: Sodium (Na+): 2 to 3 mEq/100 mL of maintenance water (or 2-3 mEq/kg/day); Potassium (K+): 1 to 2 mEq/100 mL of maintenance water (or 1-2 mEq/kg/day); Chloride (Cl-): 2 to 3 mEq/100 mL. Potassium should only be added to IV fluids AFTER the child has documented adequate urine output (voided) to prevent fatal hyperkalemia in anuric renal failure.

questions.prompt: Why is the use of hypotonic intravenous maintenance solutions (such as 0.18% saline in 5% dextrose / 'N/5') discouraged in hospitalized sick pediatric patients in modern clinical practice?
questions.question: Why is the use of hypotonic intravenous maintenance solutions (such as 0.18% saline in 5% dextrose / 'N/5') discouraged in hospitalized sick pediatric patients in modern clinical practice?
options: High risk of hospital-acquired acute hyponatremia and fatal hyponatremic encephalopathy caused by elevated non-osmotic ADH secretion
questions.answer: High risk of hospital-acquired acute hyponatremia and fatal hyponatremic encephalopathy caused by elevated non-osmotic ADH secretion
questions.explanation: Hospitalized pediatric patients frequently experience non-osmotic release of Arginine Vasopressin (ADH / SIADH-like state) triggered by pain, nausea, fever, stress, anesthesia, and pulmonary/CNS infections. Administering hypotonic fluids (e.g., 0.18% or 0.2% NaCl in dextrose) provides free water in the presence of impaired water excretion, rapidly leading to dilutional hyponatremia, acute cerebral edema, brain herniation, and death. Modern pediatric guidelines mandate using isotonic or near-isotonic solutions (such as 0.9% NaCl in 5% dextrose or Plasmalyte) for maintenance IV therapy.

questions.explanation: WHO and IAP guidelines universally recommend oral zinc supplementation for all children with acute watery diarrhea: (1) Infants aged 2 to 6 months: 10 mg elemental zinc daily for 14 days; (2) Children aged > 6 months: 20 mg elemental zinc daily for 14 days. Zinc promotes mucosal regeneration, brush border enzyme activity, and local intestinal cell-mediated immunity, significantly reducing the duration and severity of the current diarrheal episode and protecting against repeat episodes for the subsequent 2-3 months.

50 mL/kg of half-normal saline over 2 hours
questions.answer: 20 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid (Ringer's Lactate or 0.9% Normal Saline) administered as a rapid push over 10 to 15 minutes
questions.explanation: Hypovolemic shock (tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill > 3 seconds, cold clammy extremities, weak/absent peripheral pulses, and hypotension) requires immediate restoration of effective circulating intravascular volume. The standard emergency bolus is 20 mL/kg of an isotonic crystalloid (balanced crystalloid like Ringer's Lactate or 0.9% Normal Saline) administered rapidly via a large-bore peripheral cannula or intraosseous needle over 10-15 minutes, repeated up to 40-60 mL/kg in the first hour while monitoring for signs of fluid overload.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum safe rate of correcting chronic hypernatremic dehydration (serum Na+ > 150 mEq/L) to prevent cerebral edema, brain herniation, and seizures?
questions.question: What is the maximum safe rate of correcting chronic hypernatremic dehydration (serum Na+ > 150 mEq/L) to prevent cerebral edema, brain herniation, and seizures?
options: Not faster than 0.5 mEq/L/hour (maximum 10 to 12 mEq/L drop per 24 hours), correcting slowly over 48 to 72 hours
Rapid correction of 2 mEq/L/hour over 6 hours
Immediate bolus of sterile distilled water intravenously
Drop serum sodium by 30 mEq/L in the first 12 hours
questions.answer: Not faster than 0.5 mEq/L/hour (maximum 10 to 12 mEq/L drop per 24 hours), correcting slowly over 48 to 72 hours
questions.explanation: In hypernatremic dehydration, brain cells adapt to hyperosmolar stress over 24-48 hours by generating intracellular 'idiogenic osmoles' (e.g., taurine, myoinositol, glutamine) to maintain intracellular volume. If hypernatremia is corrected rapidly with hypotonic fluids, the extracellular osmolality plummets while brain cells retain these idiogenic osmoles, driving massive free water movement into cerebral neurons. This produces acute cerebral edema, seizures, permanent neurological injury, and death. Serum sodium must decrease slowly at a rate <= 0.5 mEq/L/hour (<= 10-12 mEq/L per 24 hours), typically replacing the fluid deficit over 48 to 72 hours.

questions.prompt: What catastrophic neurological complication occurs when chronic severe hyponatremia is corrected too rapidly (> 12 mEq/L per 24 hours)?
questions.question: What catastrophic neurological complication occurs when chronic severe hyponatremia is corrected too rapidly (> 12 mEq/L per 24 hours)?
questions.explanation: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia (> 10-12 mEq/L in 24 hours or > 18 mEq/L in 48 hours) dehydrates brain glial cells and oligodendrocytes because brain cells cannot re-accumulate intracellular organic osmoles fast enough. The resulting rapid intracellular dehydration causes demyelination of pontine and extrapontine white matter tracts (Central Pontine Myelinolysis / Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome). It manifests 2-6 days after correction with pseudobulbar palsy, spastic quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and 'locked-in' syndrome.

questions.prompt: A 9-month-old infant with rotavirus gastroenteritis presents with active generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Point-of-care serum sodium is 114 mEq/L. What is the immediate treatment of choice for acute symptomatic hyponatremic seizures?
questions.question: A 9-month-old infant with rotavirus gastroenteritis presents with active generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Point-of-care serum sodium is 114 mEq/L. What is the immediate treatment of choice for acute symptomatic hyponatremic seizures?
options: 3% Hypertonic Saline (NaCl): 3 to 5 mL/kg IV over 10 to 15 minutes
Oral rehydration salts solution via nasogastric tube
questions.answer: 3% Hypertonic Saline (NaCl): 3 to 5 mL/kg IV over 10 to 15 minutes
questions.explanation: Acute symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma, status epilepticus, usually with Na+ < 120 mEq/L) is a medical emergency caused by acute cerebral edema. The goal is to rapidly raise serum sodium by 4 to 6 mEq/L to halt cerebral herniation and seizures. The treatment of choice is 3% hypertonic saline administered at 3 to 5 mL/kg IV over 10 to 15 minutes (or 2 mL/kg repeated up to twice). Once seizures terminate, further correction should proceed slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.

questions.prompt: What is the characteristic clinical presentation of 'doughy skin' and hyperirritability in a dehydrated infant indicative of?
questions.question: What is the characteristic clinical presentation of 'doughy skin' and hyperirritability in a dehydrated infant indicative of?
questions.explanation: In hypernatremic dehydration (serum Na+ > 150 mEq/L), the hypertonic extracellular fluid draws water out of intracellular compartments, relatively preserving intravascular circulating volume while shrinking intracellular space. As a result, classic signs of shock and circulatory collapse appear late. Instead, the subcutaneous fat and skin feel thickened, velvety, and 'doughy' (the skin pinch retracts with a characteristic sluggishness rather than remaining tented). The infant is characteristically lethargic yet hyperirritable, exhibiting a high-pitched cry, marked thirst, hyperreflexia, and fever.

questions.prompt: What are the sequential electrocardiographic (ECG) changes observed in progressive Hyperkalemia (serum K+ > 6.0 mEq/L)?
questions.question: What are the sequential electrocardiographic (ECG) changes observed in progressive Hyperkalemia (serum K+ > 6.0 mEq/L)?
options: Tall peaked symmetrical T waves -> Prolonged PR interval & flattened P waves -> Widened QRS complex -> Sine-wave pattern and ventricular fibrillation / asystole
Prominent U waves -> ST segment depression -> Inverted T waves
Shortened QT interval -> Delta waves -> Complete heart block
questions.answer: Tall peaked symmetrical T waves -> Prolonged PR interval & flattened P waves -> Widened QRS complex -> Sine-wave pattern and ventricular fibrillation / asystole
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia alters myocardial resting membrane potential with predictable progressive ECG stages: (1) Serum K+ 5.5-6.5 mEq/L: Tall, peaked, narrow-based, symmetrical T waves (best seen in precordial leads V2-V4); (2) Serum K+ 6.5-7.5 mEq/L: Prolongation of PR interval, progressive flattening and disappearance of P waves; (3) Serum K+ 7.5-8.0 mEq/L: Widening of QRS complex, blending with the ST segment; (4) Serum K+ > 8.0 mEq/L: Formation of a classic 'sine-wave' pattern, rapidly deteriorating into ventricular flutter/fibrillation or asystole.

questions.prompt: What is the immediate, life-saving first-line medication administered to stabilize the cardiac myocyte membrane in a child with severe hyperkalemia and ECG changes?
questions.question: What is the immediate, life-saving first-line medication administered to stabilize the cardiac myocyte membrane in a child with severe hyperkalemia and ECG changes?
options: 10% Calcium Gluconate: 0.5 mL/kg (50 mg/kg) IV slow push over 5 to 10 minutes under cardiac monitoring
questions.answer: 10% Calcium Gluconate: 0.5 mL/kg (50 mg/kg) IV slow push over 5 to 10 minutes under cardiac monitoring
questions.explanation: In severe hyperkalemia with widening QRS or loss of P waves, intravenous calcium (10% Calcium Gluconate 0.5 mL/kg, or Calcium Chloride in cardiac arrest) is the mandatory first drug. Calcium does NOT lower serum potassium; rather, it directly antagonizes the membrane actions of hyperkalemia by raising the cardiac threshold potential, stabilizing the myocyte membrane within 1-3 minutes and averting fatal arrhythmias. Its protective effect lasts 30-60 minutes, during which definitive potassium-lowering agents (insulin-glucose, salbutamol, sodium bicarbonate, and dialysis) are initiated.

questions.prompt: What are the classic ECG features and neurological manifestations of severe Hypokalemia (serum K+ < 2.5 mEq/L)?
questions.question: What are the classic ECG features and neurological manifestations of severe Hypokalemia (serum K+ < 2.5 mEq/L)?
options: ECG: Flattened/inverted T waves, ST depression, prominent U waves, prolonged QT interval; Clinical: Muscle weakness, hyporeflexia, and paralytic ileus
ECG: Peaked T waves and shortened QT; Clinical: Hyperreflexia and tetany
ECG: Sine wave pattern; Clinical: Chvostek sign
questions.answer: ECG: Flattened/inverted T waves, ST depression, prominent U waves, prolonged QT interval; Clinical: Muscle weakness, hyporeflexia, and paralytic ileus
questions.explanation: Severe hypokalemia hyperpolarizes cell membranes, causing muscular and cardiac excitability changes: (1) ECG features: Flattening or inversion of T waves, ST segment depression, prominent U waves (appearing after the T wave), and apparent prolongation of the QT interval (QU interval); (2) Neuromuscular features: Ascending symmetrical muscle weakness, hypotonia, diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, and paralytic ileus (abdominal distension and absent bowel sounds due to smooth muscle paralysis).

questions.prompt: What is the maximum safe concentration and infusion rate of Potassium Chloride (KCl) administered via a peripheral intravenous line in a child?
questions.question: What is the maximum safe concentration and infusion rate of Potassium Chloride (KCl) administered via a peripheral intravenous line in a child?
options: Maximum concentration: 40 mEq/L; Maximum rate: 0.3 to 0.5 mEq/kg/hour
Maximum concentration: 100 mEq/L; Maximum rate: 2.0 mEq/kg/hour
Maximum concentration: 10 mEq/L; Maximum rate: 0.05 mEq/kg/hour
Potassium should be given as a rapid undiluted IV push
questions.answer: Maximum concentration: 40 mEq/L; Maximum rate: 0.3 to 0.5 mEq/kg/hour
questions.explanation: Potassium must NEVER be administered as an IV bolus or push (which triggers immediate cardiac arrest). For peripheral venous infusion, the maximum concentration of KCl is 40 mEq/L (concentrations up to 60-80 mEq/L require a central venous catheter to prevent chemical phlebitis and sclerosis). The maximum safe intravenous infusion rate of potassium is 0.3 to 0.5 mEq/kg/hour under continuous cardiac monitoring.

questions.prompt: What is the physiological mechanism of action of nebulized Salbutamol (albuterol) in lowering serum potassium during acute hyperkalemia?
questions.question: What is the physiological mechanism of action of nebulized Salbutamol (albuterol) in lowering serum potassium during acute hyperkalemia?
options: Stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, activating Na+/K+-ATPase to drive potassium from extracellular fluid into cells
Increases renal tubular excretion of potassium by inhibiting aldosterone
Binds potassium directly in the alveolar capillary membrane
Stimulates parathyroid hormone to exchange calcium for potassium
questions.answer: Stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, activating Na+/K+-ATPase to drive potassium from extracellular fluid into cells
questions.explanation: Beta-2 adrenergic agonists (e.g., nebulized salbutamol at 2.5-5 mg for children < 25 kg, 10-20 mg for older children) stimulate cell-surface beta-2 receptors, activating adenylyl cyclase and increasing intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP). This directly activates the membrane-bound Na+/K+-ATPase pump, shifting potassium rapidly from the extracellular compartment into skeletal muscle and liver cells. The onset of action is 15-30 minutes, lowering serum potassium by 0.5 to 1.5 mEq/L for 2 to 4 hours.

questions.prompt: What clinical syndrome is characterized by hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and profound salt-wasting shock in a 2-week-old infant?
questions.question: What clinical syndrome is characterized by hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and profound salt-wasting shock in a 2-week-old infant?
options: Classic salt-wasting Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency)
questions.answer: Classic salt-wasting Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency)
questions.explanation: Classic salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents in the 2nd to 3rd week of life with acute adrenal crisis: severe hyponatremia, marked hyperkalemia, normal-to-low blood pressure or shock, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, and failure to regain birth weight with vomiting and dehydration. Cortisol and aldosterone deficiency prevent renal distal tubule sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion. Measurement of markedly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) is diagnostic.

questions.prompt: What are Chvostek's sign and Trousseau's sign in the physical diagnosis of pediatric hypocalcemia?
questions.question: What are Chvostek's sign and Trousseau's sign in the physical diagnosis of pediatric hypocalcemia?
options: Chvostek: Tapping the facial nerve produces ipsilateral twitching of facial muscles; Trousseau: Inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure for 3 minutes produces carpopedal spasm
Chvostek: Dorsiflexion of big toe on stroking sole; Trousseau: Contraction of biceps
Chvostek: Carpopedal spasm on hyperventilation; Trousseau: Tapping the patellar tendon
Both represent involuntary tonic spasms of the vocal cords
questions.answer: Chvostek: Tapping the facial nerve produces ipsilateral twitching of facial muscles; Trousseau: Inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure for 3 minutes produces carpopedal spasm
questions.explanation: Latent tetany in hypocalcemia is elicited by two classic neurological signs: (1) Chvostek's sign: Tapping the facial nerve over the parotid gland 2 cm anterior to the ear tragus triggers involuntary ipsilateral contraction/twitching of the facial muscles (orbicularis oris, corner of mouth, or eyelid); (2) Trousseau's sign: Inflating a sphygmomanometer cuff on the upper arm to 20 mmHg above systolic blood pressure for 3 minutes triggers ischemia-induced neuromuscular excitability manifesting as carpopedal spasm (flexion of wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints, extension of interphalangeal joints, and adduction of the thumb—'main d'accoucheur'). Trousseau's sign is significantly more sensitive and specific.

questions.prompt: Why does concurrent Hypomagnesemia (serum Mg2+ < 1.5 mg/dL) cause severe, refractory hypocalcemia that fails to respond to calcium therapy alone?
questions.question: Why does concurrent Hypomagnesemia (serum Mg2+ < 1.5 mg/dL) cause severe, refractory hypocalcemia that fails to respond to calcium therapy alone?
options: Severe magnesium depletion inhibits parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion and induces skeletal end-organ resistance to PTH
Magnesium directly chelates calcium in the blood
Magnesium deficiency increases renal calcium excretion tenfold
Magnesium binds to vitamin D receptors blocking calcitriol synthesis
questions.answer: Severe magnesium depletion inhibits parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion and induces skeletal end-organ resistance to PTH
questions.explanation: Magnesium is a critical cofactor for adenylate cyclase and intracellular second-messenger signaling. Severe hypomagnesemia (< 1.0-1.5 mg/dL) impairs parathyroid gland function by paradoxically inhibiting the secretion and release of Parathyroid Hormone (PTH), while concurrently inducing end-organ peripheral resistance to PTH in target bone and renal tubules. Consequently, hypocalcemia secondary to hypomagnesemia is refractory to calcium and vitamin D supplementation until the underlying magnesium deficit is actively corrected with intravenous or oral magnesium sulfate.

questions.prompt: What is the formula for calculating the Serum Anion Gap, and what is its normal reference range in children?
questions.question: What is the formula for calculating the Serum Anion Gap, and what is its normal reference range in children?
options: Anion Gap = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-); Normal range is 8 to 12 mEq/L (up to 16 if potassium included)
Anion Gap = (Na+ + K+) - (Cl- - HCO3-); Normal range is 20 to 25 mEq/L
Anion Gap = Cl- - HCO3-; Normal range is 4 to 6 mEq/L
Anion Gap = Na+ / (BUN + Glucose); Normal range is 280 to 295 mOsm/L
questions.answer: Anion Gap = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-); Normal range is 8 to 12 mEq/L (up to 16 if potassium included)
questions.explanation: The Serum Anion Gap represents unmeasured anions in plasma (primarily albumin, phosphate, and sulfate): Anion Gap = [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]). The normal reference range is 8 to 12 mEq/L (or 10-14 mEq/L). Metabolic acidosis is classified into: (1) High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (HAGMA, > 12 mEq/L): Caused by unmeasured fixed acids—DKA (ketoacids), Lactic acidosis (sepsis/hypoxia), Inborn errors of metabolism (organic acidemias), and Toxins (salicylates, methanol, ethylene glycol); (2) Normal Anion Gap (Hyperchloremic) Metabolic Acidosis: Diarrhea (loss of HCO3-), Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA), or excessive 0.9% normal saline infusion.

questions.prompt: What is the definitive medical treatment for acute symptomatic hypocalcemia presenting with carpopedal spasm, stridor, or seizures?
questions.question: What is the definitive medical treatment for acute symptomatic hypocalcemia presenting with carpopedal spasm, stridor, or seizures?
options: 10% Calcium Gluconate: 1 to 2 mL/kg (100-200 mg/kg) IV diluted 1:1 with 5% dextrose, given slowly over 10 to 15 minutes under continuous ECG monitoring
Oral calcium carbonate tablets crushed with water
Rapid intravenous push of 10% Calcium Chloride via scalp vein
questions.answer: 10% Calcium Gluconate: 1 to 2 mL/kg (100-200 mg/kg) IV diluted 1:1 with 5% dextrose, given slowly over 10 to 15 minutes under continuous ECG monitoring
questions.explanation: Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, laryngospasm/stridor, prolonged QTc interval, seizures) mandates immediate intravenous calcium: 10% Calcium Gluconate is administered at 1 to 2 mL/kg (equivalent to 100-200 mg/kg or 9-18 mg/kg elemental calcium). It should be diluted in an equal volume of 5% dextrose or saline and infused slowly over 10 to 15 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring (stop infusion if bradycardia develops). Peripheral extravasation must be strictly avoided to prevent tissue necrosis.

questions.prompt: A 3-week-old male infant presents with projectile, non-bilious vomiting after every feed, visible peristaltic waves, and a palpable olive-sized mass in the epigastrium. What classic acid-base and electrolyte disturbance is expected on arterial blood gas analysis?
questions.question: A 3-week-old male infant presents with projectile, non-bilious vomiting after every feed, visible peristaltic waves, and a palpable olive-sized mass in the epigastrium. What classic acid-base and electrolyte disturbance is expected on arterial blood gas analysis?
options: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia
Hyperchloremic normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis with compensatory metabolic alkalosis
questions.answer: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
questions.explanation: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes persistent loss of gastric secretions containing hydrochloric acid (HCl), potassium, and water. This produces: (1) Hypochloremia (loss of Cl-); (2) Metabolic alkalosis (loss of H+ with elevated serum HCO3-); (3) Hypokalemia (due to secondary hyperaldosteronism driving renal K+ excretion to conserve volume and Na+); (4) Paradoxical aciduria: as potassium depletion worsens, the renal cortical collecting tubules exchange H+ instead of K+ for Na+, resulting in acidic urine despite severe systemic alkalemia. Surgery (Ramstedt pyloromyotomy) must be delayed until electrolytes and alkalosis are completely normalized.

questions.prompt: How do the whey-to-casein protein ratios compare between human breastmilk and unmodified cow's milk?
questions.question: How do the whey-to-casein protein ratios compare between human breastmilk and unmodified cow's milk?
options: Human breastmilk is whey-predominant (60:40 to 80:20); Cow's milk is casein-predominant (20:80)
Human milk is 100% casein; Cow's milk is 100% whey
Human milk is casein-predominant (10:90); Cow's milk is whey-predominant (70:30)
questions.answer: Human breastmilk is whey-predominant (60:40 to 80:20); Cow's milk is casein-predominant (20:80)
questions.explanation: Human milk contains a whey-to-casein ratio of approximately 60:40 in mature milk (and up to 80:20 in colostrum), making it easy to digest and forming soft, flocculent, rapidly emptying curds in the infant stomach. Major whey proteins in human milk are alpha-lactalbumin and lactoferrin (beta-lactoglobulin is absent). In contrast, cow's milk is heavily casein-predominant (20:80 whey:casein ratio), forming tough, dense, rubbery curds that are difficult for an infant to digest, and containing high concentrations of allergenic beta-lactoglobulin.

questions.prompt: What is the caloric energy density and fat content of mature human breastmilk?
questions.question: What is the caloric energy density and fat content of mature human breastmilk?
options: Energy density: approximately 67 kcal/dL (0.67 kcal/mL); Fat: 3.5 to 4.0 g/dL
questions.answer: Energy density: approximately 67 kcal/dL (0.67 kcal/mL); Fat: 3.5 to 4.0 g/dL
questions.explanation: Mature human breastmilk provides approximately 65 to 67 kcal/dL (0.67 kcal/mL or ~20 kcal/oz). Carbohydrates (primarily lactose, 7.0 g/dL) provide ~40% of calories; Fats (3.5-4.0 g/dL, rich in long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids DHA and ARA) provide ~50% of total calories; and Protein (0.9-1.1 g/dL) provides ~10% of calories. Colostrum has a lower energy density (~55 kcal/dL) but higher protein (up to 2-3 g/dL, rich in secretory IgA) and lower fat content.

questions.prompt: At what age should complementary feeding (weaning) be initiated alongside continued breastfeeding according to WHO and national guidelines?
questions.question: At what age should complementary feeding (weaning) be initiated alongside continued breastfeeding according to WHO and national guidelines?
options: At 6 completed months (180 days) of age
questions.answer: At 6 completed months (180 days) of age
questions.explanation: WHO and national pediatric guidelines universally recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 completed months of life (180 days). At 6 months, an infant's gastrointestinal tract, kidney function, and neuromuscular swallowing mechanisms (loss of extrusion reflex) are mature, while nutritional requirements for energy, iron, zinc, and micronutrients begin to exceed what breastmilk alone can provide. Complementary feeding with nutrient-dense, hygienic family foods should be introduced at 6 months while continuing breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond.

questions.prompt: What is the primary immunological factor in human breastmilk that provides mucosal protection by binding bacterial and viral surface antigens in the infant's gut?
questions.question: What is the primary immunological factor in human breastmilk that provides mucosal protection by binding bacterial and viral surface antigens in the infant's gut?
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA (sIgA) is the predominant immunoglobulin in human colostrum and mature milk. It consists of a dimeric IgA molecule joined by a J-chain and linked to a secretory component that protects it from proteolytic degradation by infant gastric pepsin and intestinal proteases. sIgA coats the intestinal mucosa, agglutinating pathogens, neutralizing enterotoxins, and preventing bacterial adhesion and translocation without inducing inflammatory tissue damage.

questions.prompt: What is the daily recommended energy (calorie) intake per kilogram for a healthy infant during the first 6 months of life?
questions.question: What is the daily recommended energy (calorie) intake per kilogram for a healthy infant during the first 6 months of life?
questions.explanation: During early infancy, rapid growth and high metabolic rate demand substantial energy: (1) 0-6 months: ~100 to 110 kcal/kg/day (protein ~1.5-1.8 g/kg/day); (2) 6-12 months: ~90 to 100 kcal/kg/day; (3) 1-3 years: ~80 to 90 kcal/kg/day; (4) Older children: ~1,000 kcal for the first year + 100 kcal for each additional year of age.
