questions.prompt: A 9-month-old male infant presents with recurrent pyogenic sinopulmonary infections (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) and chronic otitis media starting around 6 months of age. Examination reveals a complete absence of tonsillar tissue and palpable peripheral lymph nodes. Flow cytometry shows < 1% circulating CD19+/CD20+ B cells with markedly reduced levels of IgG, IgA, and IgM, but normal numbers of CD3+ T cells. What is the underlying molecular diagnosis?
questions.question: A 9-month-old male infant presents with recurrent pyogenic sinopulmonary infections (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) and chronic otitis media starting around 6 months of age. Examination reveals a complete absence of tonsillar tissue and palpable peripheral lymph nodes. Flow cytometry shows < 1% circulating CD19+/CD20+ B cells with markedly reduced levels of IgG, IgA, and IgM, but normal numbers of CD3+ T cells. What is the underlying molecular diagnosis?
options: X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (Bruton disease / BTK gene mutation)
questions.answer: X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (Bruton disease / BTK gene mutation)
questions.explanation: X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA, Bruton disease) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the Bruton Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) gene on the X chromosome (Xq22). BTK is essential for B-cell signal transduction; its absence halts B-cell differentiation at the pre-B cell stage in bone marrow. Infants remain healthy until ~6 months of age due to protection by maternal transplacental IgG. As maternal antibodies wane, they develop recurrent infections with encapsulated pyogenic bacteria and enteroviruses. Characteristic findings include absent tonsils/germinal centers, near-total absence of mature B cells (CD19+/CD20+ < 1-2%), and pan-hypogammaglobulinemia with intact T-cell numbers and function. Treatment is lifelong monthly IVIG replacement.

questions.prompt: A 2-month-old male infant develops severe failure to thrive, persistent oral candidiasis refractory to nystatin, protracted intractable diarrhea, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Following BCG vaccination at birth, the infant developed disseminated cutaneous nodules and ulceration. Chest radiograph shows an absent thymic shadow, and absolute lymphocyte count is 800/mm^3. What is the diagnosis, and what is the definitive curative therapy?
questions.question: A 2-month-old male infant develops severe failure to thrive, persistent oral candidiasis refractory to nystatin, protracted intractable diarrhea, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Following BCG vaccination at birth, the infant developed disseminated cutaneous nodules and ulceration. Chest radiograph shows an absent thymic shadow, and absolute lymphocyte count is 800/mm^3. What is the diagnosis, and what is the definitive curative therapy?
options: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID); Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)
Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome; Monthly intravenous immunoglobulin alone
Chronic Granulomatous Disease; Lifelong interferon-gamma injections
questions.answer: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID); Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)
questions.explanation: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a pediatric medical emergency characterized by profound defects in cellular (T-cell) and humoral (B-cell) immunity. It presents in early infancy (< 3 months) with failure to thrive, persistent opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, CMV), intractable diarrhea, and life-threatening disseminated disease from live vaccines (disseminated BCGitis). Laboratory hallmarks are profound absolute lymphopenia (< 2,500-3,000/mm^3 in an infant), absent thymic shadow, and absent T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) on newborn screening. All live vaccines are strictly contraindicated. The definitive curative treatment is allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT) or gene therapy.

questions.prompt: A 4-year-old boy presents with recurrent suppurative lymphadenitis, hepatic abscesses, and osteomyelitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia marcescens, and Aspergillus fumigatus. A dihydrorhodamine-123 (DHR) flow cytometry assay reveals absent generation of reactive oxygen species during the neutrophil respiratory burst. What is the diagnosis, and which enzyme complex is defective?
questions.question: A 4-year-old boy presents with recurrent suppurative lymphadenitis, hepatic abscesses, and osteomyelitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia marcescens, and Aspergillus fumigatus. A dihydrorhodamine-123 (DHR) flow cytometry assay reveals absent generation of reactive oxygen species during the neutrophil respiratory burst. What is the diagnosis, and which enzyme complex is defective?
options: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD); Defect in phagocyte NADPH oxidase enzyme complex
Chediak-Higashi syndrome; Defect in LYST lysosomal trafficking regulator
Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency type 1; Defect in CD18 beta-2 integrin
Myeloperoxidase (MPO) deficiency; Defect in halide oxidation
questions.answer: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD); Defect in phagocyte NADPH oxidase enzyme complex
questions.explanation: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) is an inherited immunodeficiency (most commonly X-linked mutation in the CYBB gene encoding gp91phox) causing dysfunction of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex. Phagocytes can engulf bacteria normally but are unable to generate superoxide radicals, hydrogen peroxide, and reactive oxygen species during the respiratory burst. Consequently, patients are uniquely susceptible to catalase-positive microorganisms (which break down their own endogenous H2O2): Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, and Aspergillus species. The gold-standard diagnostic test is DHR-123 flow cytometry (or nitroblue tetrazolium [NBT] reduction test). Lifelong prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, itraconazole, and recombinant IFN-gamma is standard.

questions.prompt: A 1-year-old male infant presents with petechial hemorrhages, severe flexural eczema, and recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections. Complete blood count reveals marked thrombocytopenia (platelet count 28,000/mm^3) with significantly reduced Mean Platelet Volume (micro-thrombocytes). What is the classic syndrome, and what is the underlying genetic defect?
questions.question: A 1-year-old male infant presents with petechial hemorrhages, severe flexural eczema, and recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections. Complete blood count reveals marked thrombocytopenia (platelet count 28,000/mm^3) with significantly reduced Mean Platelet Volume (micro-thrombocytes). What is the classic syndrome, and what is the underlying genetic defect?
options: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS); Mutation in WAS gene affecting actin cytoskeleton regulation
Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP); Autoantibodies against GpIIb/IIIa
Bernard-Soulier syndrome; Deficiency of glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex
Ataxia-Telangiectasia; Mutation in ATM serine/threonine kinase
questions.answer: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS); Mutation in WAS gene affecting actin cytoskeleton regulation
questions.explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS) is an X-linked recessive immunodeficiency characterized by the classic clinical triad of: (1) Micro-thrombocytopenia (petechiae, purpura, bloody diarrhea, with characteristically SMALL platelets having reduced mean platelet volume [MPV]); (2) Severe atopic eczema; and (3) Recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections due to progressive combined immunodeficiency. It is caused by mutations in the WAS gene, which encodes the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP), an essential regulator of actin cytoskeleton remodeling in hematopoietic and lymphoid cells. Immunoglobulin profile shows low IgM, elevated IgA and IgE, and normal/variable IgG.
questions.subject: Pediatrics

questions.prompt: A 2-day-old male infant presents with hypocalcemic tetanic seizures, truncus arteriosus on echocardiography, low-set ears, micrognathia, and an absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph. Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) confirms a microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2. What embryonic developmental defect is responsible for this condition?
questions.question: A 2-day-old male infant presents with hypocalcemic tetanic seizures, truncus arteriosus on echocardiography, low-set ears, micrognathia, and an absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph. Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) confirms a microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2. What embryonic developmental defect is responsible for this condition?
options: Dysmorphogenesis of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches (DiGeorge Syndrome)
Failure of closure of the first branchial cleft
Arrest in migration of cranial neural crest cells into the 1st pharyngeal arch only
Premature obliteration of the thyroglossal duct
questions.answer: Dysmorphogenesis of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches (DiGeorge Syndrome)
questions.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (Catch-22: Cardiac anomalies, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia) is caused by a heterozygous microdeletion of chromosome 22q11.2 (TBX1 gene). This disrupts the embryonic development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal (branchial) pouches, which normally give rise to the thymus gland and inferior parathyroid glands (from the 3rd pouch) and superior parathyroid glands (from the 4th pouch). Parathyroid hypoplasia leads to severe neonatal hypocalcemia and tetany; thymic hypoplasia/aplasia causes T-cell lymphopenia and opportunistic infections. Conotruncal cardiac anomalies (truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch) are characteristic.
questions.subject: Pediatrics

questions.prompt: A 32-year-old construction worker is brought to the casualty following a high-velocity motor vehicle crash. Examination reveals an open tibial fracture with an 11-cm laceration, extensive soft-tissue stripping, and exposed cortical bone. Periosteal coverage is preserved, and local soft-tissue coverage of the bone is achievable without a free flap. Distal neurovascular status is intact. According to the Gustilo-Anderson classification, this fracture is categorized as:
questions.explanation: Gustilo-Anderson Type IIIA fractures involve high-energy trauma with an open wound > 10 cm and extensive soft-tissue laceration or flaps, but adequate soft-tissue coverage of bone is present. Type IIIB involves extensive periosteal stripping and bone exposure requiring reconstructive flap coverage. Type IIIC includes an open fracture associated with an arterial injury requiring repair.

questions.prompt: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman with known metastatic adenocarcinoma presents with sudden severe right thigh pain while walking, without antecedent trauma. Radiographs reveal an osteolytic lesion with a transverse cortical break in the subtrochanteric region of the right femur. Which pathogenetic mechanism defines this fracture?
options: Failure through bone weakened by pre-existing focal pathology
Cyclic fatigue failure of normal bone under repetitive strain
Microtrabecular insufficiency failure from acute periosteal avulsion
Stress concentration at the insertion of normal tendon
questions.answer: Failure through bone weakened by pre-existing focal pathology
questions.explanation: A pathological fracture occurs through bone weakened by pre-existing disease (such as metastases, multiple myeloma, bone cysts, or osteomyelitis) under normal physiological stress. In contrast, stress/fatigue fractures result from cyclic, repetitive subthreshold loading on structurally normal bone.

questions.prompt: In an acute trauma patient who fell from a height, radiographs show a fracture where two bony fragments are firmly driven into each other without abnormal mobility at the fracture site. What is the clinical hallmark of this impacted fracture?
options: Absence of abnormal mobility and crepitus despite localized bony tenderness
Presence of a visible flail segment with false joint motion
Audible crepitus upon gentle limb rotation
Immediate distal sensory loss from nerve tethering
questions.answer: Absence of abnormal mobility and crepitus despite localized bony tenderness
questions.explanation: In impacted fractures, the fractured bone fragments are driven into each other, providing intrinsic temporary stability. Consequently, the classical signs of fracture like abnormal mobility and bone crepitus are absent, making diagnosis dependent on localized tenderness, loss of function, and radiographic demonstration.

questions.prompt: A 42-year-old mechanic sustains an isolated, displaced intra-articular fracture of the radial styloid process following a rotational blow to the dorsoradial wrist. What is the eponym for this injury?
questions.explanation: Chauffeur's (Hutchinson's) fracture is an intra-articular fracture of the radial styloid process, historically caused by the backfire of an automobile starting crank handle hitting the dorsum of the wrist. Barton's is an intra-articular fracture-subluxation of the radiocarpal joint, Smith's is a reverse Colles' fracture, and Galeazzi's is a distal radius fracture with distal radioulnar joint dislocation.

questions.prompt: A collegiate athlete suffers a severe inversion injury of the ankle. Clinical examination reveals marked diffuse swelling, severe ecchymosis, complete loss of ligamentous restraint with wide joint opening on stress testing, and an inability to bear weight. This ligament injury is classified as:
questions.explanation: Ligament injuries are graded based on tissue disruption: Grade I is a mild stretch with microscopic fiber tearing, no joint laxity, and minimal swelling; Grade II is a partial or incomplete tear with moderate laxity and preserved endpoint; Grade III is a complete ligament rupture with gross joint instability, wide joint opening, and severe loss of function.

questions.topic: Anatomy of Bone and Fracture Healing
questions.topicTitle: Anatomy of Bone and Fracture Healing
questions.prompt: During physiological secondary fracture healing in a tubular long bone, what is the correct chronological sequence of reparative stages?
options: Hematoma -> Granulation tissue -> Callus formation -> Consolidation -> Remodeling
Hematoma -> Callus formation -> Granulation tissue -> Remodeling -> Consolidation
Granulation tissue -> Hematoma -> Consolidation -> Callus formation -> Remodeling
Hematoma -> Primary osteon bridging -> Fibrous sleeve -> Medullary remodeling
questions.answer: Hematoma -> Granulation tissue -> Callus formation -> Consolidation -> Remodeling
questions.explanation: Secondary (indirect) bone healing occurs in 5 classical stages: 1. Stage of hematoma (hours to days); 2. Stage of granulation tissue (soft tissue procallus, ~2 weeks); 3. Stage of callus (cartilaginous soft callus transforming to hard woven bone callus by endochondral ossification, ~4-12 weeks); 4. Stage of consolidation (woven bone replaced by mature lamellar bone); 5. Stage of remodeling (restoration of original cortical architecture).

questions.topic: Anatomy of Bone and Fracture Healing
questions.topicTitle: Anatomy of Bone and Fracture Healing
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old athlete undergoes anatomical reduction and absolute rigid internal fixation of a transverse radial shaft fracture using a compression plate with zero interfragmentary strain. Postoperative radiographs show progressive disappearance of the fracture line without any visible external callus. What type of bone healing has occurred?
options: Secondary bone healing with delayed union
Endochondral ossification within the medullary canal
questions.explanation: Primary (direct) bone healing occurs when a fracture is anatomically reduced with absolute rigidity and interfragmentary compression (strain < 2%). Under these biomechanical conditions, no external callus forms; instead, osteoclasts create longitudinal cutting cones across the fracture interface, immediately followed by osteoblasts depositing secondary osteons directly bridging the fracture gap.

questions.topic: Anatomy of Bone and Fracture Healing
questions.topicTitle: Anatomy of Bone and Fracture Healing
questions.prompt: Under normal physiological conditions in the adult skeleton, what is the anatomical distribution of arterial blood supply to the diaphysis of a long bone?
options: Nutrient artery supplies inner two-thirds; periosteal vessels supply outer one-third
Periosteal vessels supply inner two-thirds; nutrient artery supplies outer one-third
Nutrient artery supplies the entire cortex under centripetal flow
Metaphyseal anastomoses supply 80% of the mid-diaphyseal cortex
questions.answer: Nutrient artery supplies inner two-thirds; periosteal vessels supply outer one-third
questions.explanation: The diaphysis of a tubular long bone receives a centrifugal arterial supply: the nutrient artery enters the nutrient canal, divides into ascending and descending medullary branches, and supplies the bone marrow and inner two-thirds of the cortex under high hydrostatic pressure. The periosteal capillary network provides the outer one-third of the cortex under lower pressure.

questions.topic: Anatomy of Bone and Fracture Healing
questions.topicTitle: Anatomy of Bone and Fracture Healing
questions.prompt: Why does a fracture of cancellous bone (such as the calcaneum or vertebral body) heal substantially faster than a fracture through cortical bone?
options: Abundant osteogenic trabecular surface area with direct internal callus union
Absence of endosteal capillary networks allowing rapid fibrous bridging
Higher hydroxyapatite density resisting local shear strain
Greater dependence on external periosteal cartilaginous sleeve formation
questions.answer: Abundant osteogenic trabecular surface area with direct internal callus union
questions.explanation: Cancellous bone has a broad contact area, highly vascular marrow, and abundant trabecular surfaces lined by active osteoblasts. Fracture healing in cancellous bone occurs by direct internal callus and trabecular bridging without the intermediate large external periosteal cartilaginous callus phase required in cortical bone.

questions.topic: Anatomy of Bone and Fracture Healing
questions.topicTitle: Anatomy of Bone and Fracture Healing
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old chronic heavy smoker on long-term systemic corticosteroids sustains a closed distal tibial shaft fracture. At 6 months, he exhibits persistent mobility and absence of bridging callus. Which combination of mechanisms is primarily responsible for impaired union in this patient?
options: Microvascular vasoconstriction and suppressed osteoblast differentiation
Elevated calcitonin levels and excessive bone resorption
Accelerated osteoid matrix synthesis with fibrous capping
Increased vascular endothelial growth factor with premature remodeling
questions.answer: Microvascular vasoconstriction and suppressed osteoblast differentiation
questions.explanation: Smoking causes peripheral vasoconstriction, tissue hypoxia, and downregulates osteoblast function through nicotine and carbon monoxide toxicity. Systemic corticosteroids inhibit osteoblast differentiation, downregulate type I collagen synthesis, and impair local angiogenesis, dramatically predisposing the fracture to delayed union or non-union.

questions.prompt: A 24-year-old motorcyclist arrives in the emergency department with a contaminated Gustilo Type IIIB open tibial fracture 2 hours after a crash. Following ABCDE resuscitation, what is the mandatory immediate local management step?
options: Sterile dressing, intravenous antibiotics, splinting, and urgent operative debridement
Immediate primary wound closure in the emergency room under local anesthesia
Vigorous mechanical scrub with povidone-iodine and definitive plate fixation
Wound packing with topical antibiotic powder and delayed cast immobilization
questions.answer: Sterile dressing, intravenous antibiotics, splinting, and urgent operative debridement
questions.explanation: Management of open fractures prioritizes prevention of sepsis: after initial ATLS stabilization, the wound is photographed, covered with a sterile saline-soaked dressing (no probing in the ER), IV antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis are administered immediately, the limb is splinted, and the patient is taken to the operating room for formal debridement, copious saline irrigation, and skeletal stabilization.

questions.prompt: What chemical reaction occurs during the setting of Plaster of Paris (POP) bandages used for orthopaedic cast immobilization?
options: Exothermic conversion of calcium sulfate hemihydrate to calcium sulfate dihydrate
Endothermic polymerization of anhydrous calcium phosphate into hydroxyapatite
Non-thermal evaporation of ethyl silicate leaving a rigid silica matrix
Oxidation of hydrated calcium carbonate catalyzed by ambient oxygen
questions.answer: Exothermic conversion of calcium sulfate hemihydrate to calcium sulfate dihydrate
questions.explanation: Plaster of Paris consists of gypsum (calcium sulfate dihydrate) that has been heated to drive off part of its water of crystallization, forming calcium sulfate hemihydrate: (CaSO4)2.H2O. When mixed with water, it rehydrates to form calcium sulfate dihydrate [CaSO4.2H2O] in an exothermic reaction that generates palpable heat during setting.

questions.prompt: Why is anatomical reduction with rigid internal fixation mandatory in intra-articular fractures, whereas minor axial displacement can be accepted in extra-articular diaphyseal fractures?
options: Articular step-off alters contact stresses and leads to rapid post-traumatic osteoarthritis
Intra-articular fractures heal exclusively through extensive periosteal bridging callus
Synovial fluid degrades any metal implant that lacks interfragmentary compression
Articular cartilage contains abundant blood supply that triggers heterotopic ossification
questions.answer: Articular step-off alters contact stresses and leads to rapid post-traumatic osteoarthritis
questions.explanation: Articular cartilage has virtually no regenerative capacity. Any residual intra-articular step-off or gap greater than 1-2 mm causes concentrated contact stresses across opposing cartilage surfaces during joint motion, producing accelerated cartilage wear and debilitating post-traumatic osteoarthritis.

questions.prompt: When immobilizing a fractured long bone in a plaster cast, what is the standard joint immobilization rule to achieve rotational and angular stability?
options: Immobilize the joint immediately proximal and the joint immediately distal to the fracture
Encompass all joints of the entire affected extremity up to the trunk
Immobilize only the fracture zone, leaving both adjacent joints completely mobile
Immobilize the proximal joint only, while keeping the distal joint free
questions.answer: Immobilize the joint immediately proximal and the joint immediately distal to the fracture
questions.explanation: To prevent angular displacement and especially rotational shearing forces exerted by muscles traversing the fracture site, a rigid cast must immobilize the joint immediately above and the joint immediately below the fractured long bone (e.g., above-knee cast for tibia fracture, above-elbow cast for forearm bones fracture).

questions.prompt: A 35-year-old male with an isolated closed midshaft transverse femoral fracture is hemodynamically stable. What is the definitive treatment of choice?
options: Closed reamed locked intramedullary interlocking nailing
Open reduction and broad dynamic compression plate (DCP) fixation
Skeletal traction on a Bohler-Braun frame for 12 weeks
External ring fixator with tensioned transfixion wires
questions.answer: Closed reamed locked intramedullary interlocking nailing
questions.explanation: Closed reamed locked intramedullary interlocking nailing is the gold standard for diaphyseal femoral fractures: it provides load-sharing biomechanical stability, preserves the fracture hematoma and periosteal biology, allows early mobilization and weight-bearing, and achieves union rates exceeding 95-98%.

questions.prompt: A 26-year-old male sustains an isolated closed midshaft femur fracture in a rural area. Which emergency splint should be applied to provide immediate pain relief, align fragments, and minimize bleeding during ambulance transport?
options: Cramer wire splint bent at 90 degrees
Denis Browne splint with bilateral footplates
questions.explanation: The Thomas splint is the standard emergency splint for femur shaft fractures. It utilizes the padded ring seated against the ischial tuberosity as a counter-traction point while fixed traction is applied to the foot/ankle, aligning the bone, reducing muscle spasm, minimizing bleeding, and preventing bone ends from piercing the femoral neurovascular bundle.

questions.prompt: When setting up skeletal traction on a Bohler-Braun frame for a femoral fracture, how many pulleys are present on the frame and what is the primary role of the middle pulley?
options: Three pulleys; the middle pulley maintains traction in the longitudinal axis of the femur
Two pulleys; the middle pulley suspends the foot to prevent foot drop
Four pulleys; the middle pulley controls lateral tilt of the patella
One pulley; it redirects both counter-traction and limb elevation
questions.answer: Three pulleys; the middle pulley maintains traction in the longitudinal axis of the femur
questions.explanation: The Bohler-Braun frame has three pulleys: the distal/inferior pulley prevents foot drop by suspending the foot, the middle pulley carries the primary traction cord aligned with the axis of the femur, and the proximal/superior pulley is used for supracondylar or vertical traction when needed.

questions.prompt: A surgeon plans to insert a Steinmann pin through the proximal tibia for skeletal traction in a distal femoral fracture. To avoid iatrogenic injury to the common peroneal nerve, what is the safe anatomical entry site and direction of pin insertion?
options: 2 cm posterior and 2 cm inferior to the tibial tuberosity, driven from lateral to medial
1 cm anterior to the fibular head, driven from lateral to medial
3 cm directly distal to the medial joint line, driven from medial to lateral
Directly through the tibial tuberosity crest, driven from anterior to posterior
questions.answer: 2 cm posterior and 2 cm inferior to the tibial tuberosity, driven from lateral to medial
questions.explanation: The safe entry point for proximal tibial skeletal traction is 2 cm posterior and 2 cm inferior to the tibial tuberosity. It must be inserted from the lateral side to the medial side because inserting from lateral to medial pushes the pin away from the common peroneal nerve winding around the fibular neck.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum safe weight permissible when applying skin traction to an adult lower limb?
options: 4 to 5 kg (or roughly 10% of body weight)
questions.answer: 4 to 5 kg (or roughly 10% of body weight)
questions.explanation: Skin traction relies on adhesive strapping applied to the skin and subcutaneous tissues. The maximum safe weight that can be applied is 4 to 5 kg (approximately 10% of body weight). Exceeding this limit leads to shearing forces that tear epidermis from the dermis, causing severe friction blisters, skin sloughing, and ulceration.

questions.prompt: One week after insertion of a distal femoral skeletal traction pin, a patient develops high fever, severe knee pain, and a tense knee effusion. Arthrocentesis confirms septic arthritis. What technical error during pin insertion caused this complication?
options: Pin inserted too distal, violating the suprapatellar synovial pouch
Pin inserted through the adductor tubercle, injuring the saphenous nerve
Pin driven from medial to lateral, piercing the femoral artery
Pin placed through the popliteus tendon groove on the lateral condyle
questions.answer: Pin inserted too distal, violating the suprapatellar synovial pouch
questions.explanation: The suprapatellar pouch of the knee joint extends up to 5 cm proximal to the superior pole of the patella beneath the quadriceps tendon. If a distal femoral traction pin is placed too distal (within 2-3 cm of the joint line), it penetrates the synovial pouch; pin track infection can then track directly into the joint space, producing septic arthritis.

questions.topic: Recent Advances in the Treatment of Fractures
questions.topicTitle: Recent Advances in the Treatment of Fractures
questions.prompt: In elderly patients with severe osteoporotic comminuted metaphyseal fractures, how does a Locking Compression Plate (LCP) achieve mechanical stability compared to a conventional Dynamic Compression Plate (DCP)?
options: Threaded screw heads lock into the plate, forming a fixed-angle internal fixator independent of bone friction
Screws compress the plate tightly against periosteum to maximize frictional grip
The plate undergoes thermal memory contraction to compress fracture fragments
The plate delivers piezoelectric micro-currents to stimulate periosteal osteogenesis
questions.answer: Threaded screw heads lock into the plate, forming a fixed-angle internal fixator independent of bone friction
questions.explanation: In conventional DCP, stability depends on friction generated by pressing the plate tightly against the bone surface, which requires strong bone screw purchase and strips periosteal blood supply. In an LCP, threaded screw heads lock rigidly into the plate, forming a fixed-angle 'internal fixator' construct where stability depends on the screw-plate interface rather than bone-plate friction, protecting periosteal vascularity.

questions.topic: Recent Advances in the Treatment of Fractures
questions.topicTitle: Recent Advances in the Treatment of Fractures
questions.prompt: Which fundamental biological principle forms the basis of distraction osteogenesis in the Ilizarov method?
options: Law of tension-stress: gradual controlled mechanical distraction stimulates active tissue regeneration
Wolff's law of bone remodeling under compressive piezoelectric polarity
Pauwels' law of shear-force suppression in intra-articular fractures
Heuter-Volkmann law of epiphyseal growth retardation under compression
questions.answer: Law of tension-stress: gradual controlled mechanical distraction stimulates active tissue regeneration
questions.explanation: Ilizarov's Law of Tension-Stress states that gradual, continuous mechanical traction applied to living tissues creates a state of active metabolic stimulation that induces tissue regeneration and histogenesis of bone, vessels, nerves, skin, and muscle. In cortical bone, distraction at a rate of 1 mm per day in 4 divided increments produces robust new bone.

questions.topic: Recent Advances in the Treatment of Fractures
questions.topicTitle: Recent Advances in the Treatment of Fractures
questions.prompt: A 36-year-old male sustains a comminuted distal tibial fracture with significant soft-tissue contusion. The surgeon chooses Minimally Invasive Percutaneous Plate Osteosynthesis (MIPPO). What is the main biological advantage of this technique?
options: Submuscular extra-periosteal plate tunneling preserves fracture hematoma and periosteal blood supply
Direct anatomical reduction and rigid compression of every small comminuted fragment
Elimination of intraoperative fluoroscopy and radiation exposure
Production of absolute rigid stability with primary direct bone healing
questions.answer: Submuscular extra-periosteal plate tunneling preserves fracture hematoma and periosteal blood supply
questions.explanation: MIPPO is a biological fixation method: rather than opening the fracture site (which evacuates osteogenic fracture hematoma and strips periosteal blood vessels), a plate is inserted percutaneously through small proximal and distal incisions and bridged across the comminuted zone. This preserves the biological osteogenic envelope and promotes rapid secondary healing via robust bridging callus.

questions.topic: Recent Advances in the Treatment of Fractures
questions.topicTitle: Recent Advances in the Treatment of Fractures
questions.prompt: How has the modern philosophy of AO fracture fixation evolved regarding the treatment of comminuted diaphyseal fractures?
options: Shifted from anatomical rigidity and direct healing to biological flexible fixation and secondary callus union
Shifted from closed intramedullary nailing to routine open anatomical plating of all fragments
Shifted from functional mobilization to prolonged cast immobilization after plate fixation
Shifted to exclusive conservative management with skeletal traction for 12 weeks
questions.answer: Shifted from anatomical rigidity and direct healing to biological flexible fixation and secondary callus union
questions.explanation: The original AO concept emphasized anatomical reduction, absolute rigid fixation, interfragmentary compression, and primary direct bone healing without callus. Over time, extensive periosteal stripping caused high rates of non-union and infection in comminuted fractures. The modern AO philosophy emphasizes 'biological fixation'—preserving vascularity and soft tissues, achieving functional alignment, and encouraging secondary healing with robust bridging callus.

questions.topic: Recent Advances in the Treatment of Fractures
questions.topicTitle: Recent Advances in the Treatment of Fractures
questions.prompt: What is the mechanical mechanism by which a Sarmiento functional brace stabilizes a midshaft humeral or tibial fracture during limb movement?
options: Compression of surrounding musculature creates hydrostatic fluid pressure that maintains axial alignment
Rigid metallic hinge locks eliminate all adjacent joint rotation and motion
Absolute suppression of interfragmentary micro-motion allowing direct primary union
Continuous transcutaneous electrical stimulation of deep compartment flexors
questions.answer: Compression of surrounding musculature creates hydrostatic fluid pressure that maintains axial alignment
questions.explanation: Sarmiento functional bracing utilizes hydrostatic pressure: rigid or semi-rigid shells conform tightly to the thigh, leg, or arm, compressing the fluid-filled muscular envelope. When the muscles contract during active joint motion, the enclosed fluid/soft tissues act as an incompressible hydraulic cylinder that resists angular and shortening displacement while allowing beneficial axial micro-motion.

questions.topic: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.topicTitle: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.prompt: A 29-year-old driver involved in a high-speed roll-over crash arrives with a deformed right thigh and hypotension (BP 85/55 mmHg). In accordance with ATLS primary survey resuscitation protocols, what three screening radiographs are routinely obtained in the trauma bay?
options: Cervical spine lateral (or CT), Chest AP, and Pelvis AP
Skull AP/Lateral, Femur AP/Lateral, and Abdomen erect
Pelvis AP, Bilateral knees AP, and Thoracolumbar spine AP
Chest PA erect, Right femur AP/Lateral, and Forearm AP
questions.answer: Cervical spine lateral (or CT), Chest AP, and Pelvis AP
questions.explanation: During the ATLS primary survey resuscitation phase, after managing Airway, Breathing, and Circulation, the three standard screening radiographs for an unconscious or severely injured polytrauma patient are: 1. Cervical spine lateral (or rapid pan-scan CT); 2. Chest anteroposterior (AP); and 3. Pelvis AP (to rapidly identify life-threatening hemorrhage from pelvic ring disruption). Individual extremity radiographs are performed during the secondary survey.

questions.topic: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.topicTitle: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.prompt: In standard orthopaedic radiography, what are the components of the clinical 'Rule of Twos'?
options: Two views (AP/Lateral), Two joints (above/below), Two limbs (in children), and Two occasions (pre/post-reduction)
Two surgeons, Two assistants, Two tourniquets, and Two hours maximum operating time
Two radiographs per hour, Two splints per limb, Two weeks traction, and Two months casting
Two skin incisions, Two cortical screws, Two locking plates, and Two suction drains
questions.answer: Two views (AP/Lateral), Two joints (above/below), Two limbs (in children), and Two occasions (pre/post-reduction)
questions.explanation: The 'Rule of Twos' in orthopaedic radiology consists of: 1. Two views: Anteroposterior (AP) and lateral, as a fracture visible in one projection may be completely concealed in the other; 2. Two joints: Must include the joint above and joint below the fractured bone; 3. Two limbs: In pediatric patients with open growth plates, compare with the uninjured opposite limb; 4. Two occasions: Repeat radiograph immediately after reduction, and after 1-2 weeks if an undisplaced or stress fracture is suspected.

questions.topic: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.topicTitle: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.prompt: A 6-year-old child presents with elbow pain and swelling following a fall from monkey bars. Why is a comparative radiograph of the contralateral uninjured elbow essential before ruling out a fracture?
options: Multiple unossified cartilaginous centers and normal physes can simulate or conceal fractures
Pediatric elbow injuries are obligatorily bilateral due to symmetrical force transmission
Contralateral comparison is required to determine systemic osteoid mineralization status
Physeal closure occurs prematurely within 24 hours of contralateral injury
questions.answer: Multiple unossified cartilaginous centers and normal physes can simulate or conceal fractures
questions.explanation: The pediatric elbow has six secondary ossification centers that appear and fuse at predictable ages (CRITOE: Capitulum 1y, Radial head 3y, Internal/medial epicondyle 5y, Trochlea 7y, Olecranon 9y, External/lateral epicondyle 11y). Non-ossified cartilage is radiolucent, and normal physeal lines can be misdiagnosed as fractures, or displaced avulsion fragments misdiagnosed as normal centers. A comparative film of the normal elbow prevents catastrophic errors.

questions.topic: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.topicTitle: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.prompt: In orthopaedic clinical practice, after what time interval is an untreated or neglected fracture formally classified as an 'old fracture'?
questions.explanation: According to standard orthopaedic definitions, an untreated fracture presenting more than 3 weeks after trauma is categorized as an 'old fracture'. By 3 weeks, early soft callus and fibrous tissue have organized between the fragments, making simple closed reduction impossible without formal open mobilization, osteoclasis, or osteotomy.

questions.topic: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.topicTitle: Approach to a Patient with Limb Injury
questions.prompt: A 34-year-old male with an open distal femoral fracture presents with an expanding pulsatile hematoma in the popliteal fossa, absent distal pedal pulses, and a cold, pale foot. What is the immediate management requirement?
options: Immediate emergency surgical exploration in the operating room without delaying for CT angiography
Urgent non-contrast CT scan of the brain followed by CT angiography of the lower limb
Application of an elastic compression bandage and observation for 6 hours
Immediate reduction of the fracture in the emergency room under local hematoma block
questions.answer: Immediate emergency surgical exploration in the operating room without delaying for CT angiography
questions.explanation: 'Hard signs' of arterial injury include: 1. Active, pulsatile arterial bleeding; 2. Expanding or pulsatile hematoma; 3. Palpable thrill or audible bruit; 4. Absent distal pulses; 5. Obvious signs of distal limb ischemia (pale, cold, mottled, pulseless extremity). The presence of hard signs mandates immediate emergency surgical exploration and vascular repair without wasting precious warm ischemia time on non-invasive imaging.

questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male with a closed midshaft tibial fracture in an above-knee cast develops excruciating leg pain 8 hours post-injury. The pain is refractory to IV morphine and is exacerbated by passive extension of the toes. The anterolateral compartment is tense and woody. Distal pedal pulses are palpable. What is the immediate management step?
options: Bivalve the cast and split all padding to the skin, and prepare for urgent four-compartment fasciotomy
Administer intravenous mannitol and elevate the leg 45 degrees above the heart
Apply an ice pack, increase the analgesic dose, and re-examine in 4 hours
Perform an immediate closed reduction under regional block to relieve bony pressure
questions.answer: Bivalve the cast and split all padding to the skin, and prepare for urgent four-compartment fasciotomy
questions.explanation: Pain out of proportion to injury and pain elicited by passive stretching of compartment muscles are the earliest and most reliable signs of acute compartment syndrome. The presence of palpable peripheral pulses does NOT rule out compartment syndrome (pulses disappear only in late/terminal stages). The immediate intervention is to remove all constricting dressings (split cast and padding down to skin) and prepare for emergent surgical fasciotomy.

questions.prompt: When assessing compartment syndrome using needle manometry, what delta-P threshold (diastolic blood pressure minus intracompartmental pressure) mandates emergency surgical fasciotomy?
options: Delta P of 30 mmHg or less
Delta P of 50 mmHg or less
Delta P of 70 mmHg or less
Delta P of 15 mmHg or less
questions.answer: Delta P of 30 mmHg or less
questions.explanation: Tissue perfusion is determined by the pressure gradient between microvascular perfusion pressure and tissue pressure. An absolute compartment pressure > 30-40 mmHg or, more accurately, a delta-P (diastolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure) of 30 mmHg or less indicates critical tissue ischemia and mandates emergency decompression by fasciotomy.

questions.prompt: A 22-year-old male sustains closed bilateral femoral fractures. Thirty-six hours after admission, he develops acute confusion, tachypnea (respiratory rate 34/min), PaO2 of 54 mmHg on room air, and petechial hemorrhages across the anterior chest and conjunctivae. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fat Embolism Syndrome typically presents 24 to 72 hours following closed long-bone (especially femur) or pelvic fractures. Gurd's diagnostic criteria require at least one major sign and four minor signs, or two major signs. Major signs include: 1. Respiratory insufficiency (tachypnea, PaO2 < 60 mmHg); 2. Neurological depression/confusion; 3. Subconjunctival and axillary/chest petechial rash (pathognomonic, caused by fat emboli occluding dermal capillaries).

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental biological distinction between delayed union and non-union of a fracture?
options: In delayed union, reparative osteogenesis remains active; in non-union, reparative processes have ceased completely
Delayed union requires immediate bone grafting; non-union heals with simple splinting
Delayed union is declared at 6 weeks; non-union is strictly defined at 12 weeks for all bones
Delayed union is always infected; non-union is always aseptic
questions.answer: In delayed union, reparative osteogenesis remains active; in non-union, reparative processes have ceased completely
questions.explanation: Delayed union means the fracture is taking longer than the expected average time to unite for that specific bone, but the fracture gap remains open, vascularity is preserved, and union can still be achieved with continued immobilization. Non-union implies that all reparative processes have ceased, the bone ends have become rounded and sclerotic (or atrophic/tapered), the medullary canal is sealed by bone, and a false joint (pseudoarthrosis) has formed.

questions.prompt: A 40-year-old male with an isolated midshaft tibial fracture presents 8 months post-injury with persistent pain on weight-bearing and demonstrable mobility. Radiographs show a persistent radiolucent gap flanked by flared, dense, sclerotic bone ends resembling an 'elephant's foot'. What is the diagnosis and surgical treatment principle?
options: Hypertrophic non-union; requires rigid mechanical stabilization without mandatory bone grafting
Atrophic non-union; requires massive autologous cancellous bone grafting with cast immobilization
Infected non-union; requires radical bone resection and long-term antibiotic beads
Oligotrophic non-union; requires low-intensity pulsed ultrasound without internal fixation
questions.answer: Hypertrophic non-union; requires rigid mechanical stabilization without mandatory bone grafting
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic non-union (vascular/elephant-foot) occurs when biological healing potential and blood supply are excellent, but mechanical stability is inadequate (excessive interfragmentary motion). Abundant fibrocartilage forms, producing flared sclerotic ends. Treatment focuses strictly on restoring rigid mechanical stability (e.g., reamed interlocking intramedullary nailing); bone grafting is generally unnecessary.

questions.prompt: A 35-year-old female presents 9 months after an open, severely stripped forearm fracture with painless abnormal mobility. Radiographs show pencil-thin, tapered, osteopenic bone ends separated by a wide radiolucent gap with no visible callus. What is the fundamental surgical requirement for this atrophic non-union?
options: Excision of intervening fibrous tissue, opening sclerosed canals, autologous cancellous bone grafting, and rigid plate fixation
Application of a tight plaster cast for an additional 6 months to allow osteonal bridging
Percutaneous injection of bone marrow aspirate without opening the non-union site
External immobilization and high-frequency ultrasound therapy alone
questions.answer: Excision of intervening fibrous tissue, opening sclerosed canals, autologous cancellous bone grafting, and rigid plate fixation
questions.explanation: Atrophic non-union is characterized by a complete failure of biological osteogenesis and poor vascularity. The bone ends are tapered, rounded, and avascular ('pencil-in-cup' or 'horse's foot'). Treatment requires both biological stimulation (freshening bone ends, opening sclerosed medullary canals, decortication, and autologous cancellous bone grafting) and mechanical stability with rigid plate fixation.

questions.prompt: A 48-year-old woman sustains a distal radius fracture treated in a tight cast for 6 weeks. Two weeks after cast removal, she presents with severe burning pain in the hand out of proportion to the original trauma, diffuse hand edema, hyperesthesia, warmth, and finger stiffness. Radiographs show patchy, spotty osteopenia ('ground-glass' osteoporosis). What is the diagnosis?
options: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I (Sudeck's atrophy)
questions.answer: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I (Sudeck's atrophy)
questions.explanation: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I (CRPS I), historically known as Sudeck's atrophy or reflex sympathetic dystrophy, is an exaggerated neurovascular and autonomic response to trauma (often minor or following tight cast immobilization). It presents with burning pain, allodynia, hyperpathia, autonomic dysregulation (edema, color and temperature changes), and progressive joint stiffness. Radiographs classically reveal spotty, patchy juxta-articular osteoporosis.

questions.prompt: A 14-year-old boy sustains an elbow dislocation that is successfully reduced. His parents take him for vigorous daily massage and forced passive extension exercises. Three weeks later, the elbow is tender and stiff, and radiographs reveal a cloudy mass of new bone forming within the brachialis muscle anterior to the elbow joint. What is the diagnosis and immediate management?
options: Myositis ossificans traumatica; stop all massage and passive stretching, splint the elbow, and allow the bone mass to mature
Osteosarcoma of the distal humerus; proceed with emergency wide-margin limb-salvage resection
Chronic septic arthritis; perform emergency arthrotomy and open synovectomy
Early Volkmann's contracture; perform emergency forearm flexor fasciotomy
questions.answer: Myositis ossificans traumatica; stop all massage and passive stretching, splint the elbow, and allow the bone mass to mature
questions.explanation: Myositis ossificans traumatica is heterotopic bone formation within muscle or periarticular soft tissues following trauma, classically occurring in the brachialis muscle after elbow injuries subjected to vigorous massage or forceful passive manipulation. Management requires immediate cessation of massage/passive stretching, resting the joint in a splint until the acute inflammatory phase subsides, followed by active gentle mobilization. Premature excision causes severe recurrence; excision is considered only after the mass has fully matured on radiograph (6-12 months).

questions.prompt: What is the earliest and most sensitive imaging modality for detecting avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head following an intracapsular fracture, before plain radiographs show any changes?
options: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) demonstrating a low-signal T1 band and 'double-line sign' on T2
High-resolution CT scan showing subchondral trabecular condensation
Contrast-enhanced ultrasound showing joint capsule thickening
Standing pelvic radiograph measuring the acetabular roof index
questions.answer: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) demonstrating a low-signal T1 band and 'double-line sign' on T2
questions.explanation: MRI is the gold standard and most sensitive diagnostic tool for detecting early avascular necrosis (Ficat-Arlet Stage 0/I), detecting microvascular ischemia weeks to months before plain radiographs show osteopenia, sclerosis, or the 'crescent sign' of subchondral collapse. Classically, MRI demonstrates a serpentine band of low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and the pathognomonic 'double-line sign' on T2-weighted images.

questions.prompt: In established Volkmann's Ischaemic Contracture (VIC) of the forearm, what is the classic deformity of the wrist and fingers, and which muscle group is primarily fibrosed?
options: Wrist flexion, MCP hyperextension, and IP flexion; caused by fibrosis of the deep volar flexors (FDP and FPL)
Wrist extension, MCP flexion, and IP extension; caused by fibrosis of the extensor digitorum communis
Radial deviation with thumb adduction contracture; caused by fibrosis of abductor pollicis longus
Isolated intrinsic hand muscle clawing with completely normal wrist motion
questions.answer: Wrist flexion, MCP hyperextension, and IP flexion; caused by fibrosis of the deep volar flexors (FDP and FPL)
questions.explanation: Volkmann's Ischaemic Contracture is the end-stage cicatricial sequela of untreated compartment syndrome of the forearm. The deep flexor compartment—chiefly Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP) and Flexor Pollicis Longus (FPL)—suffers ischemic infarction and turns into inelastic fibrous scar tissue. This produces the classic deformity: wrist flexion, MCP hyperextension, and severe IP flexion. A key sign is that finger extension can be increased only by simultaneously flexing the wrist (Volkmann's sign).

questions.topic: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.topicTitle: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.prompt: What is the anatomical distinction between a joint dislocation and a subluxation?
options: Dislocation is complete loss of articular contact; subluxation is partial loss of contact with some articular apposition remaining
Dislocation involves an associated bone avulsion; subluxation involves ligamentous sprain only
Dislocation occurs only in ball-and-socket joints; subluxation occurs only in hinge joints
Dislocation is congenital in origin; subluxation is exclusively acquired from trauma
questions.answer: Dislocation is complete loss of articular contact; subluxation is partial loss of contact with some articular apposition remaining
questions.explanation: According to standard orthopaedic definitions, a dislocation (luxation) represents complete, total disruption of joint congruity such that the articulating bone surfaces lose all anatomical contact with each other. In a subluxation, there is partial displacement and incongruity, but a portion of the opposing articular cartilages remains in contact.

questions.topic: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.topicTitle: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.prompt: Why is an acute dislocation of a major joint (such as the hip or knee) an orthopaedic emergency requiring immediate reduction?
options: Displaced articular ends compress, stretch, or kink adjacent vessels, risking irreversible avascular necrosis or limb ischemia
Synovial fluid decomposes within 4 hours, causing irreversible chemical chondrolysis
Periarticular ligaments undergo acute ossification if displaced for more than 6 hours
The joint capsule closes permanently by primary intention within 12 hours
questions.answer: Displaced articular ends compress, stretch, or kink adjacent vessels, risking irreversible avascular necrosis or limb ischemia
questions.explanation: Acute joint dislocation is an emergency because the displaced skeletal ends exert direct tension, compression, or kinking on vital periarticular neurovascular structures. For example, in hip dislocation, the retinacular vessels supplying the femoral head are stretched, risking avascular necrosis (the risk escalates dramatically if reduction is delayed > 6 hours); in knee dislocation, popliteal artery occlusion risks limb amputation.

questions.topic: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.topicTitle: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.prompt: A 20-year-old collegiate gymnast sustains an acute posterolateral elbow dislocation. Following prompt, uncomplicated closed reduction under procedural sedation, what is the mandatory immediate clinical step?
options: Perform a neurovascular assessment of brachial artery and median/ulnar/radial nerves, followed by post-reduction radiographs
Apply a circular plaster cast from shoulder to palm for 8 weeks without checking pulses
Schedule the patient for immediate open capsular reconstruction and ligament repair
Place the patient in continuous skeletal traction via an olecranon pin for 3 weeks
questions.answer: Perform a neurovascular assessment of brachial artery and median/ulnar/radial nerves, followed by post-reduction radiographs
questions.explanation: Immediately after reducing any dislocation, the surgeon must: 1. Re-evaluate and document neurovascular integrity (e.g., in elbow dislocation, assess radial pulse, capillary refill, and motor/sensory function of median, radial, and ulnar nerves); 2. Obtain orthogonal post-reduction radiographs to confirm concentric reduction and exclude previously obscured fractures; 3. Gently assess range of motion and joint stability to determine the safe arc of movement.

questions.topic: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.topicTitle: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.prompt: In recurrent anterior dislocation of the shoulder, what pathological lesion consists of an avulsion of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum with the attached inferior glenohumeral ligament?
questions.explanation: A Bankart lesion is the primary essential lesion predisposing to recurrent anterior shoulder instability: it is an avulsion of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum from the glenoid rim, typically accompanied by disruption of the anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament complex (IGHLC). A Hill-Sachs lesion is a compression fracture of the posterolateral humeral head caused by impaction against the hard anterior glenoid rim.

questions.topic: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.topicTitle: Injury to Joints: Dislocation and Subluxation
questions.prompt: What clinical feature distinguishes recurrent dislocation of the patella from habitual dislocation of the patella in adolescents?
options: Recurrent dislocation is episodic following trauma or laxity; habitual dislocation occurs obligatorily every time the knee flexes due to vastus lateralis contracture
Recurrent dislocation dislocates medially; habitual dislocation dislocates laterally
Recurrent dislocation affects males only; habitual dislocation affects females after skeletal maturity
Recurrent dislocation is managed by quadriceps release; habitual dislocation requires patellectomy
questions.answer: Recurrent dislocation is episodic following trauma or laxity; habitual dislocation occurs obligatorily every time the knee flexes due to vastus lateralis contracture
questions.explanation: Recurrent patellar dislocation is episodic, often starting after an initial traumatic subluxation and recurring during pivoting or twisting movements in patients with underlying predisposing factors (e.g., high Q angle, patella alta, trochlear dysplasia). Habitual patellar dislocation occurs obligatorily and painlessly every time the knee flexes, almost always caused by an abnormal fibrous band or tight contracture of the vastus lateralis / iliotibial band tethering the patella laterally during flexion.

questions.prompt: An 8-year-old girl falls from a swing onto her outstretched hand. Radiographs of the distal radius reveal a fracture line passing across the growth plate and traversing vertically through the epiphysis into the articular joint space. According to the Salter-Harris classification, this is classified as:
questions.explanation: Salter-Harris Type III is an intra-articular physeal injury where the fracture runs along the physis and exits through the epiphysis into the joint. Type I is a pure transverse separation through the physis. Type II passes through the physis and exits through the metaphysis (creating a triangular Thurston-Holland sign). Type IV crosses through the metaphysis, physis, and epiphysis in continuity.

questions.prompt: Which Salter-Harris physeal injury pattern is statistically the most common, accounting for approximately 75% of all growth plate fractures?
options: Salter-Harris Type II (physis fracture with metaphyseal Thurston-Holland fragment)
Salter-Harris Type I (pure cleavage separation through hypertrophic zone)
Salter-Harris Type III (intra-articular fracture traversing physis and epiphysis)
Salter-Harris Type V (crush injury of physeal germinal cells)
questions.answer: Salter-Harris Type II (physis fracture with metaphyseal Thurston-Holland fragment)
questions.explanation: Salter-Harris Type II is by far the most frequent physeal fracture (~75%). The shear force cleaves the weak hypertrophic zone of the physis and directs obliquely into the metaphysis, producing a characteristic triangular metaphyseal fragment known as the Thurston-Holland sign. The periosteal hinge remains intact on the metaphyseal side, facilitating stable closed reduction.

questions.prompt: A 9-year-old boy sustains a displaced Salter-Harris Type IV fracture of the distal femoral physis. What surgical principle is essential to prevent progressive angular deformity, bone bridging (physeal bar), and leg-length discrepancy?
options: Anatomical open reduction and internal fixation with smooth wires placed parallel to the physis
Closed reduction and loose circular casting allowing minor displacement
Prolonged skeletal traction for 8 weeks until bridging callus forms
Immediate open resection of the entire growth plate with early arthrodesis
questions.answer: Anatomical open reduction and internal fixation with smooth wires placed parallel to the physis
questions.explanation: Salter-Harris Type IV is an intra-articular fracture crossing metaphysis, physis, and epiphysis. If reduced with any step-off or gap, endochondral ossification forms an osseous bridge across the physis (physeal bar), resulting in asymmetric tethering, severe angular deformity, and limb shortening. Anatomic reduction and stabilization using smooth K-wires (or screws placed strictly within the epiphysis and metaphysis without traversing the physis) are mandatory.

questions.prompt: Why do incomplete greenstick fractures occur almost exclusively in growing children rather than in mature adult bone?
options: Thick vascular periosteum combined with elastic, porous, compliant cortical bone
Higher concentration of insoluble crystalline hydroxyapatite in pediatric bone
Continuous plastic deformation occurring under low torsional forces in adult bone
Complete absence of Haversian canals in immature pediatric skeletons
questions.answer: Thick vascular periosteum combined with elastic, porous, compliant cortical bone
questions.explanation: Greenstick fractures reflect the unique biomechanical properties of immature pediatric bone: the bone has high water and collagen content, lower mineral density, and greater elasticity. Under bending forces, the bone behaves like a green twig—the cortex on the convex (tension) side breaks while the cortex on the concave (compression) side buckles without complete fracture, held securely by a thick, tough periosteal sleeve.

questions.prompt: When evaluating the spontaneous remodeling potential of malunited pediatric long-bone fractures, which deformity has the LEAST capacity for spontaneous correction by skeletal growth?
options: Angular deformity in the plane of adjacent hinge joint movement
Metaphyseal angular deformity near an active growth plate
Appositional bayonet displacement with mild shortening in a child under 8 years
questions.explanation: Pediatric bone remodels based on the Heuter-Volkmann law and Wolff's law. Remodeling is greatest for: 1. Younger children with significant remaining growth; 2. Fractures near an active growth plate (metaphyseal); 3. Angular deformities in the plane of joint motion (flexion-extension). In contrast, rotational (torsional) deformities do NOT correct spontaneously with growth and persist into adult life unless surgically realigned.

questions.prompt: A 5-year-old girl sustains a closed midshaft femoral fracture. The surgeon deliberately accepts 1.0 to 1.5 cm of bayonet appositional shortening during closed reduction and spica casting. What physiological phenomenon justifies this decision?
options: Post-traumatic hyperemic overgrowth of the fractured femur over the next 1 to 2 years
Spontaneous elastic recoil of the iliotibial band pulling bone fragments apart
Rapid chondrolysis of the contralateral femoral physis equalizing limb length
Permanent arrest of distal femoral physeal growth on the injured side
questions.answer: Post-traumatic hyperemic overgrowth of the fractured femur over the next 1 to 2 years
questions.explanation: In children aged 2 to 10 years, femoral fractures stimulate increased regional vascularity and hyperemia during fracture healing, accelerating physeal growth plates. This causes 1 to 2 cm of longitudinal overgrowth of the injured femur over the next 18 to 24 months. Therefore, an initial 1 cm of bayonet apposition and shortening is desirable to prevent long-term limb length inequality (overlengthening).

questions.prompt: A 7-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with unexplained swelling and irritability. Skeletal survey reveals multiple fractures at varying stages of healing, including metaphyseal bucket-handle avulsions and posterior rib fractures near the costovertebral junctions. What condition must be suspected?
options: Non-accidental injury (Battered baby syndrome / physical abuse)
questions.answer: Non-accidental injury (Battered baby syndrome / physical abuse)
questions.explanation: The radiological constellation of fractures of different healing ages, metaphyseal corner/bucket-handle fractures (caused by violent twisting or shaking), posterior rib fractures (caused by thoracic squeezing), and spinous process fractures is pathognomonic for non-accidental injury (battered baby syndrome / physical abuse). It demands immediate hospitalization, child protection notification, and a full multidisciplinary forensic evaluation.

questions.prompt: What is the mechanical mechanism of a pediatric torus (buckle) fracture commonly seen in the distal radius?
options: Axial compressive loading causing impaction and wrinkling of the porous metaphyseal cortex
High-velocity torsional stress causing longitudinal cleavage of the diaphysis
Direct transverse shear force slicing through the epiphysis
Avulsion of the periosteal cuff by sudden extensor tendon contraction
questions.answer: Axial compressive loading causing impaction and wrinkling of the porous metaphyseal cortex
questions.explanation: A torus or buckle fracture is a classic pediatric compressive injury. Axial load (e.g., fall on an outstretched hand) compresses the porous, compliant trabecular bone of the distal radial metaphysis, producing acute buckling or bulging of the cortex. There is no true cortical disruption, no displacement, and it heals reliably within 3 weeks in a simple splint or cast.

questions.prompt: A 6-year-old boy presents with a malunited supracondylar fracture of the humerus resulting in a severe gunstock deformity (cubitus varus). What is the primary anatomical component of the malunion responsible for this deformity?
options: Medial tilting (coronal collapse) and internal rotation of the distal fragment
Complete premature growth arrest of the lateral condylar physis
Avascular necrosis of the trochlea and capitulum
Lateral translocation of the olecranon process
questions.answer: Medial tilting (coronal collapse) and internal rotation of the distal fragment
questions.explanation: Cubitus varus ('gunstock deformity') following supracondylar fractures is caused by mechanical malunion of the distal fragment, specifically medial tilt, medial translation, and internal rotation. Contrary to historical belief, it is NOT due to asymmetric physeal growth arrest. The distal humeral physis contributes only 15-20% to humerus growth and does not correct the coronal plane malunion.

questions.prompt: In Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE), through which specific histological zone of the proximal femoral physis does mechanical displacement characteristically occur?
options: Zone of hypertrophy (maturation and provisional calcification)
Zone of primary bone deposition in the metaphysis
questions.answer: Zone of hypertrophy (maturation and provisional calcification)
questions.explanation: In SCFE, the mechanical shearing separation occurs precisely through the zone of hypertrophy (specifically the cell hypertrophy and provisional calcification layers) of the growth plate. This zone has the lowest matrix-to-cell ratio and lacks structural collagen cross-linking, making it vulnerable to shear stresses during the adolescent growth spurt under hormonal influences.

questions.prompt: A 32-year-old man awakens after a deep sleep with his right upper arm draped over a hard chair. On examination, he has complete wrist drop and finger drop, loss of sensation over the first dorsal web space, but normal triceps strength and an intact triceps jerk. What is the diagnosis and site of compression?
options: Saturday night palsy; compression of radial nerve in the spiral groove
Crutch palsy; compression of radial nerve high in the axilla
Posterior interosseous nerve syndrome; entrapment at the Arcade of Frohse
Pronator teres syndrome; median nerve compression in the forearm
questions.answer: Saturday night palsy; compression of radial nerve in the spiral groove
questions.explanation: Saturday night palsy is a compression injury of the radial nerve in the spiral (radial) groove of the mid-shaft humerus. Because the motor branches to the triceps and anconeus arise proximal to the spiral groove (in the axilla), triceps power and elbow extension are fully preserved, but all wrist and finger extensors innervated distally (BR, ECRL, ECRB, EDC, ECU, EPL, etc.) are paralyzed, accompanied by numbness over the first dorsal web space.

questions.prompt: According to the nerve injury classifications of Seddon and Sunderland, which grade represents complete anatomical transection of the nerve trunk (axon, endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium)?
questions.explanation: Seddon's Neurotmesis corresponds to Sunderland Grade V: the nerve trunk is completely divided, with disruption of axons, endoneurial tubes, perineurium, and the external epineurium. Complete Wallerian degeneration occurs, and spontaneous recovery is impossible. Accurate surgical realignment and microscopic end-to-end neurorrhaphy (or nerve grafting) are obligatory.

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old kitchen worker suffers a deep glass laceration on the volar wrist proximal to the flexor retinaculum. Examination reveals loss of finger abduction/adduction, a positive Froment's sign, and sensory loss over the hypothenar eminence and little finger. Which nerve is severed?
options: Ulnar nerve (low ulnar nerve injury at the wrist)
High radial nerve in the spiral groove
Median nerve at the pronator canal
Anterior interosseous nerve at the fibrous arch of FDS
questions.answer: Ulnar nerve (low ulnar nerve injury at the wrist)
questions.explanation: This presentation reflects low ulnar nerve palsy at the wrist: denervation of intrinsic hand muscles (interossei, medial two lumbricals, hypothenar muscles, and adductor pollicis). Loss of adductor pollicis causes a positive Froment's sign (patient flexes thumb IP joint via FPL, innervated by AIN, to hold paper). Sensation over the hypothenar area and little finger is lost.

questions.prompt: What physiological phenomenon underlies Tinel's sign in a regenerating peripheral nerve, and at what approximate rate does axonal regeneration advance?
options: Percussion over regenerating unmyelinated axonal sprouts elicits paresthesias; advances at ~1 mm/day
Electrical discharge from demyelinated Schwann cells; advances at 5 mm/day
Microvascular spasms within the endoneurium; advances at 3 cm/week
Retrograde motor unit firing; advances at 10 mm/day
questions.answer: Percussion over regenerating unmyelinated axonal sprouts elicits paresthesias; advances at ~1 mm/day
questions.explanation: Tinel's sign is elicited by gently tapping along the path of a damaged nerve from distal to proximal. When the percussion reaches the tips of regenerating, unmyelinated axonal sprouts (growth cones), tingling sensations (paresthesias) shoot into the cutaneous distribution of the nerve. A progressive distally advancing Tinel's sign indicates active axonal regeneration, which occurs at the rate of ~1 mm/day (or 1 mm per 24 hours, ~1 inch per month).

questions.prompt: A patient sustains a high median nerve transection at the elbow. When asked to make a tight fist, the index and middle fingers remain extended while the ring and little fingers flex into the palm. What is this clinical posture termed?
questions.explanation: In high median nerve palsy, the patient cannot flex the thumb, index, or middle fingers when attempting to make a fist because of paralysis of the FPL, FDS, and the radial half of FDP (innervating digits 2 and 3). The ring and little fingers flex normally because the ulnar half of FDP is innervated by the intact ulnar nerve. This resulting posture resembles a priest giving a papal blessing ('Benediction sign' or 'pointing sign').

questions.prompt: What is the anatomical basis for the Ulnar Paradox in peripheral nerve injuries?
options: Clawing of ring and little fingers is more severe in low ulnar nerve palsy than in high ulnar nerve palsy
Sensory loss is greater in high lesions, but motor loss is restricted to low lesions
The nerve regenerates twice as fast following high lesions compared to low lesions
Intrinsic muscles are paralyzed in high lesions but completely spared in low lesions
questions.answer: Clawing of ring and little fingers is more severe in low ulnar nerve palsy than in high ulnar nerve palsy
questions.explanation: The Ulnar Paradox states: 'the higher the lesion, the less severe the clawing.' In a low ulnar lesion (at the wrist), the intrinsic muscles (interossei, lumbricals 3 and 4) are paralyzed, but the extrinsic muscle Flexor Digitorum Profundus (FDP) to digits 4 and 5 is intact; active FDP flexion unopposed by lumbricals produces severe clawing. In a high ulnar lesion (above elbow), FDP to digits 4 and 5 is also paralyzed, removing the primary flexor force at the IP joints, resulting in markedly less conspicuous clawing.

questions.prompt: A 25-year-old motorcyclist sustains a fracture of the neck of the fibula. On examination, he is unable to dorsiflex or evert his foot, walks with a steppage gait, and has numbness over the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is injured?
options: Tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa
Saphenous nerve at the adductor canal
Deep femoral nerve in the obturator groove
questions.explanation: The common peroneal nerve winds tightly around the neck of the fibula in a subcutaneous, vulnerable position where it can be crushed by direct blows or fibular neck fractures. Division causes loss of both deep peroneal (foot and toe dorsiflexors) and superficial peroneal (peroneus longus and brevis evertors) branches, causing classic foot drop, loss of eversion, equinovarus attitude during swing phase (steppage gait), and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.

questions.prompt: How does clinical examination reliably differentiate Pronator Teres Syndrome from Carpal Tunnel Syndrome?
options: Sensation over the thenar eminence is preserved in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome but diminished in Pronator Teres Syndrome
Phalen's maneuver is positive in Pronator Teres Syndrome but negative in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
Abductor pollicis brevis power is completely normal in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
Nocturnal paresthesias are exclusively present in Pronator Teres Syndrome
questions.answer: Sensation over the thenar eminence is preserved in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome but diminished in Pronator Teres Syndrome
questions.explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises approximately 5 to 6 cm proximal to the wrist and travels superficial to the flexor retinaculum into the palm. Therefore, in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (compression inside the carpal tunnel under the retinaculum), sensation over the base of the thenar eminence is characteristically spared. In contrast, in proximal median nerve entrapment (Pronator Teres Syndrome), the palmar cutaneous branch is compressed, resulting in sensory loss over the thenar eminence.

questions.prompt: A patient with an open infected midshaft humeral fracture sustains an irreparable 8-cm gap in the radial nerve. One year later, with all extensor muscles completely denervated, what is the classic tendon transfer of choice to restore wrist extension?
options: Transfer of Pronator Teres (PT) to Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis (ECRB)
Transfer of Flexor Carpi Ulnaris (FCU) to Biceps brachii
Transfer of Brachioradialis to Flexor Digitorum Profundus
Transfer of Palmaris longus directly to Triceps tendon
questions.answer: Transfer of Pronator Teres (PT) to Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis (ECRB)
questions.explanation: For permanent, irreparable radial nerve palsy, standard tendon transfer (the Robert Jones or modified transfer) restores function: 1. Pronator Teres (PT) transferred to Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis (ECRB) to restore wrist extension; 2. Flexor Carpi Radialis (FCR) or Flexor Carpi Ulnaris (FCU) transferred to Extensor Digitorum Communis (EDC) to restore finger extension; 3. Palmaris Longus (PL) transferred to Extensor Pollicis Longus (EPL) to restore thumb extension.

questions.prompt: In electrodiagnostic testing following acute peripheral nerve transection, how many days after injury do denervation changes (fibrillations and positive sharp waves) first appear on needle EMG?
questions.explanation: Following complete nerve division, distal axons conduct normally for up to 48-72 hours. Wallerian degeneration then begins and takes 2 to 3 weeks (14-21 days) to complete down the entire length of the distal nerve segment. Spontaneous denervation potentials (fibrillations and positive sharp waves) indicating loss of neural control over muscle membrane potentials appear on EMG only after Wallerian degeneration reaches the motor endplate, usually at 2-3 weeks.

questions.prompt: A 6-year-old child presents with knock-knees. On examination with medial femoral condyles in contact, the intermalleolar distance (IMD) measures 9 cm. Beyond what threshold is genu valgum considered pathological in a child older than 7 years?
options: Any degree of knee valgus at any age
questions.explanation: Physiological genu valgum is normal between ages 3 and 6 years, with spontaneous resolution expected by age 7 (normal adult valgus is 5-7 degrees). An intermalleolar distance (IMD) exceeding 8 cm in a child older than 7 years, or unilateral/progressive valgus, is considered pathological and requires workup (rickets, trauma, skeletal dysplasia) and possible surgical correction.

questions.prompt: A 10-year-old child with post-traumatic cubitus varus following a malunited supracondylar fracture is scheduled for corrective osteotomy. Which procedure is the classic standard technique described by French?
options: Lateral closing-wedge osteotomy of the distal humerus
Medial opening-wedge distraction osteotomy with fibular graft
Dome-shaped derotation osteotomy of the radial neck
Resection of the lateral epicondyle with annular ligament release
questions.answer: Lateral closing-wedge osteotomy of the distal humerus
questions.explanation: The classic French osteotomy for cubitus varus is a lateral closing-wedge osteotomy of the supracondylar distal humerus. The medial cortical hinge is preserved, a predetermined triangular wedge of bone is excised from the lateral cortex, the osteotomy is closed to restore the carrying angle, and stability is maintained using crossed screws or K-wires.

questions.prompt: What is the primary mechanical advantage of an opening-wedge osteotomy compared to a closing-wedge osteotomy?
options: Opening-wedge preserves or gains bone length, whereas closing-wedge causes limb shortening
Opening-wedge eliminates any need for bone grafting or plate fixation
Opening-wedge permits immediate full weight-bearing without hardware
Opening-wedge never places tension on adjacent neurovascular structures
questions.answer: Opening-wedge preserves or gains bone length, whereas closing-wedge causes limb shortening
questions.explanation: An opening-wedge osteotomy corrects angular deformity while increasing overall bone length (beneficial when the injured limb is already short), but creates a structural gap requiring autologous/allograft bone grafting and rigid plate fixation. In contrast, a closing-wedge osteotomy achieves direct bone-on-bone contact with faster union, but inherently shortens the limb.

questions.prompt: What fundamental clinical feature distinguishes a structural deformity from a postural (functional) deformity?
options: A structural deformity is fixed by permanent tissue contractures; a postural deformity is passively fully correctable
A structural deformity always involves a fracture; a postural deformity is confined to skin
A structural deformity occurs only in geriatrics; a postural deformity occurs only in neonates
A structural deformity has absent reflexes; a postural deformity has brisk reflexes
