Hangman's fracture; high incidence of esophageal rupture
Clay-shoveler's fracture; high incidence of apical lung puncture
questions.answer: Chance fracture; high incidence of intra-abdominal hollow viscus perforation
questions.explanation: A Chance fracture is a flexion-distraction injury classically caused by a lap seatbelt: the axis of flexion rotates around an anterior fulcrum (the seatbelt over the anterior abdominal wall). Tensile distraction forces rip horizontally through the posterior bony arch/ligaments and middle column, with compression/splitting of the anterior vertebral body. Up to 50% of patients have associated intra-abdominal injuries (bowel perforation, mesenteric tears, pancreatic/splenic lacerations).

questions.prompt: What is the key pathological difference between a burst fracture and a simple wedge compression fracture?
options: Burst fractures disrupt both anterior and middle columns with retropulsion; compression fractures involve only the anterior column
Burst fractures occur only in cervical spine; compression fractures occur only in sacrum
Burst fractures never cause neurological deficit; compression fractures cause total paraplegia
Burst fractures are purely ligamentous injuries without bony fracture
questions.answer: Burst fractures disrupt both anterior and middle columns with retropulsion; compression fractures involve only the anterior column
questions.explanation: Both injuries result from axial loading. In a simple wedge compression fracture, failure is restricted to the anterior column (anterior cortex collapses into a wedge), while the middle column remains intact and acts as a hinge, preventing posterior retropulsion and preserving the spinal canal. In a burst fracture, the axial force crushes the middle column as well as the anterior column, retropulsing posterosuperior bone fragments into the spinal canal, risking neurological injury.

questions.prompt: A male dives into shallow water and strikes his head. CT reveals a four-part burst fracture involving bilateral fractures of both the anterior and posterior arches of C1. What eponymic injury is this?
questions.explanation: A Jefferson fracture is an axial-loading compressive burst fracture of the atlas (C1). The axial force drives the wedge-shaped occipital condyles downward into the lateral masses of C1, bursting the ring outward into bilateral fractures of the anterior and posterior arches (producing 4 distinct fractures). On an open-mouth odontoid radiograph, lateral displacement (overhang) of both C1 lateral masses relative to C2 exceeding a combined total of 7 mm indicates rupture of the transverse atlantal ligament.

questions.prompt: What anatomical lesion defines a Hangman's fracture of the cervical spine?
options: Bilateral fractures through the pars interarticularis (neural arch) of C2
Fracture through the waist of the dens with anterior atlantoaxial subluxation
Complete avulsion of the transverse atlantal ligament without bony fracture
Compression burst fracture of the body of C3 with retropulsion
questions.answer: Bilateral fractures through the pars interarticularis (neural arch) of C2
questions.explanation: A Hangman's fracture (traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2) is caused by hyperextension and distraction (historically seen in judicial hanging; today seen in motor vehicle crashes when the forehead strikes the windshield). The bilateral pars interarticularis (isthmus) of C2 fractures, dissociating the anterior body of C2 from its posterior neural arch. Because the neural canal expands at this level, cord compression is surprisingly infrequent unless severe displacement occurs.

questions.prompt: In the Anderson and D'Alonzo classification of odontoid fractures, which type traverses the waist (base) of the dens and has the highest non-union rate?
questions.explanation: Anderson and D'Alonzo classified odontoid fractures into 3 types: Type I: Avulsion fracture of the apex/tip of the dens (stable); Type II: Fracture through the base/waist of the dens where it joins the body of C2 (most common, highly unstable, and prone to non-union due to poor blood supply and high shear); Type III: Fracture extending down into the vascular cancellous body of C2 (unites readily with halo-vest or cervical collar).

questions.prompt: A road worker feels sudden sharp interscapular pain while vigorously shoveling gravel. Radiographs show an isolated avulsion fracture of the C7 spinous process. What is this fracture termed?
questions.explanation: A Clay-shoveler's fracture is an isolated avulsion fracture of the spinous process of a lower cervical or upper thoracic vertebra (most commonly C7, followed by C6 and T1). It is caused by violent, sudden contraction of the trapezius, rhomboid, and serratus posterior superior muscles pulling against the supraspinous ligament during heavy lifting or shoveling. It is a stable injury managed conservatively with analgesia and a soft collar.

questions.prompt: According to the ASIA Impairment Scale, how is an ASIA Grade B injury defined?
options: Sensory but no motor function preserved below the neurological level, including sacral segments S4-S5
Complete absence of all motor and sensory function in sacral segments S4-S5
Motor function preserved with more than half of key muscles having grade >= 3/5
Normal motor and sensory function throughout all dermatomes and myotomes
questions.answer: Sensory but no motor function preserved below the neurological level, including sacral segments S4-S5
questions.explanation: ASIA Impairment Scale grades spinal cord injury: Grade A (Complete): No motor or sensory function preserved in sacral segments S4-S5; Grade B (Sensory Incomplete): Sensory but NO motor function preserved below the neurological level, including sacral segments S4-S5; Grade C (Motor Incomplete): Motor function preserved below level, with more than half of key muscles having a muscle grade < 3/5; Grade D (Motor Incomplete): At least half of key muscles have a grade >= 3/5; Grade E: Normal.

questions.prompt: According to the NEXUS criteria, what five findings allow safe clinical clearance of the cervical spine without imaging?
options: No midline cervical tenderness, no focal neurological deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, and no distracting injury
Normal blood pressure, absence of skull fracture, reactive pupils, age under 40, and negative toxicology
Patient able to walk, no facial laceration, heart rate < 100, normal hemoglobin, and normal chest X-ray
Cervical flexion to 90 degrees, negative Hoffman sign, intact gag reflex, normal gait, and no ear bleeding
questions.answer: No midline cervical tenderness, no focal neurological deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, and no distracting injury
questions.explanation: The NEXUS low-risk criteria allow safe clinical clearance of the cervical spine without imaging if the patient meets ALL 5 criteria: 1. No posterior midline cervical spine tenderness; 2. No focal neurological deficits; 3. Normal alertness (GCS 15); 4. No evidence of alcohol or drug intoxication; 5. No painful distracting injuries (e.g., long bone fractures, large burns, visceral injuries) that could mask neck pain. If any criterion is failed, imaging is mandatory.

questions.prompt: A trauma patient with a T6 cord injury has complete flaccid motor paralysis, total anesthesia below T6, absent deep tendon reflexes, and an absent bulbocavernosus reflex. What physiological state is this?
questions.explanation: Spinal shock is the immediate, transient physiological cessation of all spinal cord reflex activity below the level of a severe acute cord transection or contusion. Hallmarks: complete flaccid paralysis, total anesthesia, loss of autonomic tone, absent deep tendon reflexes, and loss of visceral reflexes (areflexic neurogenic bladder, loss of bulbocavernosus reflex and anal wink). It typically lasts from 24 to 48 hours up to several weeks.

questions.prompt: What physiological event and reflex recovery officially marks the termination of spinal shock?
options: Spontaneous recovery of voluntary great toe extension
Return of the patellar tendon jerk alone
questions.explanation: The termination of spinal shock is officially defined by the return of the bulbocavernosus reflex (elicited by squeezing the glans penis or tugging on the Foley catheter while feeling for reflex contraction of the external anal sphincter via digital rectal examination). Once the bulbocavernosus reflex returns, any persistent absence of motor and sensory function indicates a true, permanent 'complete' spinal cord injury (ASIA A).

questions.prompt: A patient with acute C5 cervical trauma presents with hypotension (BP 75/45 mmHg), bradycardia (HR 46 bpm), and warm, dry skin. What is the diagnosis and mechanism?
options: Neurogenic shock; disruption of descending sympathetic pathways causing unopposed vagal tone and vasodilation
Spinal shock; direct traumatic loss of reflex arc motor neurons
Hypovolemic shock; occult internal hemorrhage into the retroperitoneum
Cardiogenic shock; direct blunt traumatic myocardial contusion
questions.answer: Neurogenic shock; disruption of descending sympathetic pathways causing unopposed vagal tone and vasodilation
questions.explanation: Neurogenic shock (a form of distributive shock) occurs in acute spinal cord injuries at or above T6. Interruption of the descending sympathetic pathways from the brainstem leaves parasympathetic (vagal) innervation to the heart unopposed, producing the classic combination of profound hypotension (arteriolar and venous vasodilation with peripheral blood pooling) AND bradycardia. Unlike hypovolemic shock (cold, clammy, tachycardic), the skin in neurogenic shock is warm, dry, and flushed.

questions.prompt: A 68-year-old male with cervical spondylosis falls forward striking his forehead (hyperextension injury). He has severe motor weakness in both arms and hands (Grade 1/5) but preserved leg strength (Grade 4/5). What syndrome is this?
questions.explanation: Central Cord Syndrome is the most common incomplete cervical cord injury. It classically occurs in elderly individuals with pre-existing cervical spondylosis following a hyperextension injury: the cord is pinched anteriorly by osteophytes and posteriorly by the buckled ligamentum flavum. Because the cervical somatotopic fibers of the lateral corticospinal tracts lie centrally while sacral and lumbar fibers lie peripherally, the upper extremities (especially the hands) suffer severe motor deficit while lower extremity motor function is largely spared.

questions.prompt: A patient sustains a penetrating stab wound causing hemisection of the right thoracic spinal cord (T8). What pattern of deficits defines Brown-Séquard syndrome below the lesion?
options: Ipsilateral motor paralysis and proprioception loss, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature
Bilateral total motor paralysis with complete preservation of pain and temperature
Contralateral motor paralysis with ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature
Bilateral loss of all sensory modalities with preserved voluntary motor power
questions.answer: Ipsilateral motor paralysis and proprioception loss, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature
questions.explanation: Brown-Séquard syndrome (spinal cord hemisection): 1. Ipsilateral to lesion: Loss of voluntary motor function below lesion (corticospinal tract crosses at medulla); loss of proprioception, vibration, and fine touch (dorsal columns ascend uncrossed to medulla); 2. Contralateral to lesion: Loss of pain and temperature sensation beginning 1-2 segments below the lesion (spinothalamic tract fibers cross the midline 1-2 segments above their entry).

questions.prompt: In Anterior Spinal Artery Syndrome resulting from retropulsion of a burst fracture, which sensory modalities are classically PRESERVED below the lesion?
options: Proprioception, vibration sensation, and deep light touch (posterior columns)
questions.answer: Proprioception, vibration sensation, and deep light touch (posterior columns)
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord (anterior horns, corticospinal tracts, and spinothalamic tracts). Occlusion or compression produces complete bilateral motor paralysis below the lesion and total loss of pain and temperature sensation. However, the posterior one-third of the cord (dorsal columns: fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) is supplied by the paired posterior spinal arteries, completely preserving proprioception, vibration, and deep light touch.

questions.prompt: A patient with chronic T4 paraplegia develops pounding headache, facial sweating/flushing, severe hypertension (BP 210/110 mmHg), and bradycardia (HR 48 bpm). What is this condition and its most common trigger?
options: Autonomic dysreflexia; most commonly triggered by acute bladder distension or fecal impaction
Addisonian adrenal crisis; triggered by corticosteroid withdrawal
Pheochromocytoma crisis; triggered by abdominal palpation
Acute pulmonary embolism; triggered by deep vein thrombosis
questions.answer: Autonomic dysreflexia; most commonly triggered by acute bladder distension or fecal impaction
questions.explanation: Autonomic dysreflexia occurs in patients with spinal cord lesions at or above T6. Noxious visceral stimuli below the lesion (overwhelmingly a distended, blocked urinary bladder in >80%, or fecal impaction) trigger massive, uninhibited sympathetic discharge from isolated thoracolumbar splanchnic nerves, causing severe vasoconstriction and life-threatening hypertension. Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus detect the hypertension and stimulate vagal bradycardia, but the descending inhibitory impulses cannot cross the cord lesion.

questions.prompt: What has historically been the most common cause of long-term mortality in chronic traumatic paraplegia?
options: Renal failure and urosepsis secondary to chronic neurogenic bladder dysfunction
Secondary osteosarcoma at the fracture site
Congestive heart failure from lower limb disuse
questions.answer: Renal failure and urosepsis secondary to chronic neurogenic bladder dysfunction
questions.explanation: Chronic neurogenic bladder (spastic reflexic or flaccid) leads to high intravesical pressures, vesicoureteral reflux, staghorn calculi, chronic pyelonephritis, renal amyloidosis, and lethal urosepsis. The introduction of clean intermittent catheterization (CIC), urodynamic monitoring, anticholinergics, and strict urinary surveillance revolutionized paraplegic life expectancy, shifting mortality towards respiratory and cardiovascular causes.

questions.prompt: During the acute spinal shock stage, what is the standard method for managing the neurogenic bladder to prevent detrusor overstretching?
options: Clean Intermittent Catheterization (CIC) maintaining bladder volume below 400 to 500 mL
Suprapubic cystostomy without monitoring bladder filling volumes
Credé manual compression of the lower abdomen every 2 hours
Continuous irrigation with normal saline through a three-way catheter at 500 mL/hr
questions.answer: Clean Intermittent Catheterization (CIC) maintaining bladder volume below 400 to 500 mL
questions.explanation: During spinal shock, the bladder is completely flaccid and acontractile; failure to decompress results in painless overdistension, stretching the detrusor muscle beyond its elastic limit, causing permanent myogenic damage and bladder rupture. Clean Intermittent Catheterization (CIC) every 4-6 hours (maintaining bladder volumes < 400-500 mL) is the standard method, minimizing infection rates compared to long-term indwelling catheters.

questions.prompt: What clinical finding constitutes 'Sacral Sparing' in acute spinal cord trauma, and why is it of major prognostic importance?
options: Preservation of perianal sensation, voluntary anal contraction, or toe flexion; proves incomplete injury with higher recovery potential
Presence of normal deep tendon knee reflexes with absent sensation
Return of the cremasteric reflex within 1 hour of trauma
Intact motor power in the upper extremities only
questions.answer: Preservation of perianal sensation, voluntary anal contraction, or toe flexion; proves incomplete injury with higher recovery potential
questions.explanation: Sacral sparing is the hallmark of an incomplete spinal cord injury. Because sacral motor and sensory tracts (corticospinal and spinothalamic) run in the most peripheral, superficial rim of the spinal cord, they are the last to be damaged by central or expanding lesions. The presence of any sacral sparing (perianal sensation, voluntary anal sphincter contraction, deep anal sensation) proves axonal continuity across the injury site and predicts a favorable prognosis for walking recovery.

questions.prompt: A 13-year-old girl is noted by her mother to have uneven shoulder levels and a prominent right scapula. During the clinical examination, the patient is asked to bend forward at the waist with knees straight and arms hanging freely (Adam's forward bend test). A prominent rotational rib hump is immediately accentuated on the right thoracic region. What is the diagnostic significance of this test?
questions.explanation: Adam's forward bend test is the cardinal clinical screening test for structural scoliosis. In a postural (functional) scoliosis, the spinal curvature straightens out on forward bending. In a structural scoliosis, the vertebral bodies are fixed in rotation (spinous processes rotated toward the concavity, vertebral bodies and ribs pushed toward the convexity), producing an asymmetric rib prominence or 'rib hump' on the convex side that accentuates during forward flexion.

questions.prompt: How is the Cobb angle formally measured on a standing whole-spine anteroposterior radiograph to quantify the severity of a scoliotic curve?
options: Angle between perpendiculars of upper and lower endplate lines of end-vertebrae
Distance between C7 plumb line and gluteal cleft
Angle connecting transverse process tips on convexity
Angle between L1 superior endplate and sacral promontory
questions.answer: Angle between perpendiculars of upper and lower endplate lines of end-vertebrae
questions.explanation: To measure Cobb's angle: 1. Identify the 'end-vertebrae' (the most tilted vertebrae at the upper and lower limits of the curve, whose endplates tilt most severely toward the concavity of the curve); 2. Draw a line along the superior endplate of the upper end-vertebra; 3. Draw a line along the inferior endplate of the lower end-vertebra; 4. The angle formed at the intersection of these lines (or perpendiculars drawn from them) is the Cobb angle.

questions.prompt: What skeletal maturity parameter is assessed by the Risser sign on a standing pelvic radiograph, and why is a Risser Grade 0 or 1 associated with high clinical concern in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis?
options: Iliac crest apophysis ossification; indicates significant remaining spinal growth
Ischial tuberosity fusion; marks completion of all spinal growth
Triradiate cartilage closure; marks cessation of curve progression
Greater trochanter ossification; marks need for halo traction
questions.answer: Iliac crest apophysis ossification; indicates significant remaining spinal growth
questions.explanation: The Risser sign grades the progressive ossification of the iliac apophysis across 4 quadrants from anterolateral to posteromedial: Grade 0 (no ossification); Grade 1 (first 25% ossified); Grade 2 (50%); Grade 3 (75%); Grade 4 (100% excursion across iliac crest); Grade 5 (complete bony fusion to the ilium). A Risser grade of 0 or 1 during the adolescent growth spurt indicates substantial remaining spinal growth and a very high risk of rapid curve progression.

questions.prompt: According to standard orthopaedic guidelines, what is the management threshold for an adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) curve based on Cobb angle in a skeletally immature patient (Risser 0-2)?
options: Observation for <20 degrees; bracing for 20-40 degrees; surgery for >45-50 degrees
Surgery for <20 degrees; observation for >40 degrees
Bed rest for <30 degrees; plaster cast for >40 degrees
Electrical stimulation alone for all curve magnitudes
questions.answer: Observation for <20 degrees; bracing for 20-40 degrees; surgery for >45-50 degrees
questions.explanation: Management of AIS depends on Cobb angle and skeletal maturity: 1. Curves < 20 degrees: Observation with serial radiographs every 4-6 months; 2. Curves 20 to 40 degrees in a growing child (Risser 0-2): Rigid spinal orthosis/bracing (e.g., Boston thoracolumbosacral orthosis or Milwaukee brace worn 18-23 hours/day) to prevent further progression; 3. Curves exceeding 45-50 degrees: Surgical correction with posterior spinal instrumentation and fusion.

questions.prompt: In Meyerding's classification of spondylolisthesis (forward slip of one vertebra over the one below), what percentage of anterior displacement of the L5 vertebral body on the S1 sacral base defines a 'Grade II' slip?
questions.explanation: Meyerding classified spondylolisthesis by dividing the superior sacral plateau into 4 quarters: Grade I: 0% to 25% forward slip of the superior vertebra; Grade II: 26% to 50% forward slip; Grade III: 51% to 75% forward slip; Grade IV: 76% to 100% forward slip; Grade V (Spondyloptosis): Complete displacement (>100%), where the L5 vertebra slips completely off the sacral promontory into the pelvic cavity.

questions.prompt: A 36-year-old female presents with persistent, symmetrical pain and swelling in both hands, wrists, and knees for 4 months. She suffers from profound morning stiffness lasting over 90 minutes. Examination reveals tender, spongy synovitis involving the Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and Proximal Interphalangeal (PIP) joints, but the Distal Interphalangeal (DIP) joints are completely spared. Laboratory testing reveals high-titer anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic, systemic autoimmune inflammatory polyarthritis characterized by bilateral, symmetrical synovitis classically targeting the small joints of the hands and feet (MCP, PIP, MTP joints and wrists) while characteristically SPARING the DIP joints (unlike osteoarthritis and psoriatic arthritis). Prolonged morning stiffness (>1 hour) is a hallmark. Anti-CCP antibodies possess >95% specificity for RA.

questions.prompt: What is the underlying pathomechanics differentiating a 'Swan-neck deformity' from a 'Boutonnière deformity' of the fingers in chronic rheumatoid arthritis?
options: Swan-neck: PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion; Boutonnière: PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension
Swan-neck: DIP hyperextension with PIP flexion; Boutonnière: MCP dislocation
Swan-neck: FDP tendon rupture; Boutonnière: Lumbrical contracture
Swan-neck: FDS tendon avulsion; Boutonnière: Extensor hood avulsion
questions.answer: Swan-neck: PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion; Boutonnière: PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension
questions.explanation: In RA hand deformities: 1. Swan-neck deformity: Laxity or rupture of the volar plate at the PIP joint allows the lateral bands to subluxate dorsally, producing PIP hyperextension; the tight FDP then pulls the DIP into secondary flexion; 2. Boutonnière deformity: Synovitis distends the PIP joint, causing rupture or stretching of the central slip of the extensor tendon; the lateral bands slip volarly below the axis of the PIP joint, acting as flexors of the PIP joint while hyperextending the DIP joint.

questions.prompt: A 24-year-old man presents with chronic, insidious low back pain and morning stiffness for 8 months that improves with exercise and worsens with rest. He has alternating buttock pain and reduced chest expansion measuring only 1.8 cm. Radiographs reveal bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis and squaring of the lumbar vertebral bodies. HLA-B27 is strongly positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory seronegative spondyloarthropathy strongly associated with HLA-B27 (>90%). It characteristically affects young adult males (peak 20-30 years). Cardinal features: bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis (earliest and mandatory diagnostic feature), inflammatory back pain, diminished chest expansion (<2.5 cm at the 4th intercostal space due to costovertebral joint ankylosis), vertebral squaring, and ascending spinal fusion.

questions.prompt: What classic radiological features characterize advanced, 'end-stage' Ankylosing Spondylitis on anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the spine?
options: Bamboo spine, dagger sign, and trolley-track sign
Diffuse punched-out lytic lesions with vertebral collapse
Flowing anterior hyperostosis preserving disc heights
Multiple Schmorl nodes with anterior wedging
questions.answer: Bamboo spine, dagger sign, and trolley-track sign
questions.explanation: In advanced ankylosing spondylitis: 1. Marginal syndesmophytes (calcification/ossification of the outer fibers of the annulus fibrosus) bridge vertebral margins vertically, creating the classic smooth undulating 'bamboo spine'; 2. Ossification of the central supraspinous and interspinous ligaments appears as a single dense central radiodense line on AP view ('dagger sign'); 3. Combined ossification of the central ligaments and bilateral apophyseal joint capsules forms three parallel longitudinal dense lines ('trolley-track sign').

questions.prompt: Why is pre-operative cervical spine radiography (specifically dynamic flexion-extension lateral views) mandatory in all rheumatoid arthritis patients scheduled for elective orthopaedic or general surgery under endotracheal intubation?
options: Detects atlantoaxial subluxation risking fatal spinal cord compression
Precludes endotracheal tube placement in all cases
questions.answer: Detects atlantoaxial subluxation risking fatal spinal cord compression
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid synovial pannus frequently invades and destroys the synovial bursa between the anterior arch of C1, the odontoid process (dens), and the transverse atlantal ligament. The resulting atlantoaxial subluxation (AAS) is present in up to 30-50% of RA patients (anterior atlantodens interval > 3 mm in adults on flexion view). Neck manipulation during laryngoscopy and endotracheal intubation can produce catastrophic, fatal displacement of C1 on C2 with acute cervicomedullary cord compression.

questions.prompt: What clinical triad defines Felty's syndrome, an uncommon extra-articular manifestation of severe, long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and xerostomia
Rheumatoid arthritis, glomerulonephritis, and alveolar hemorrhage
Rheumatoid arthritis, aortic regurgitation, and complete heart block
questions.explanation: Felty's syndrome is a serious systemic manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis characterized by the triad of: 1. Long-standing, destructive, seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis; 2. Splenomegaly; 3. Neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count < 1500/mm3). Patients have an extraordinarily high risk of recurrent, life-threatening bacterial infections (especially skin and pulmonary infections) and chronic lower extremity ulcers.

questions.prompt: A 42-year-old male with plaque psoriasis presents with severe, asymmetrical pain and swelling in the DIP joints of both hands, diffuse sausage-like swelling of the entire right middle finger (dactylitis), and pitted, dystrophic fingernails. Radiographs of the DIP joints show erosion of the distal phalanx base and sharpening of the middle phalanx head, producing a classic 'pencil-in-cup' deformity. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy affecting 10-30% of patients with psoriasis. Hallmarks: asymmetric oligoarthritis or DIP-predominant polyarthritis, dactylitis ('sausage digit' caused by simultaneous tenosynovitis and arthritis), nail pitting and onycholysis, and destructive osteolysis leading to arthritis mutilans and the classic 'pencil-in-cup' appearance (tapered proximal phalanx head fitting into an expanded, cup-shaped distal phalanx base).

questions.prompt: What is the classical clinical triad that characterizes Reactive Arthritis (historically known as Reiter's syndrome), and what are the most common triggering antecedent infections?
options: Urethritis, conjunctivitis, and oligoarthritis following Chlamydia or enteric infection
Jaundice, ascites, and encephalopathy following Hepatitis B
Hematuria, flank pain, and palpable mass following E. coli
Dysphagia, glossitis, and anemia following H. pylori
questions.answer: Urethritis, conjunctivitis, and oligoarthritis following Chlamydia or enteric infection
questions.explanation: Reactive arthritis is an autoimmune, seronegative spondyloarthropathy occurring 1-4 weeks following a mucosal infection. The classic aphorism 'can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree' summarizes the triad: 1. Aseptic urethritis/cervicitis; 2. Conjunctivitis or uveitis; 3. Asymmetric, additive oligoarthritis (predominantly lower extremity joints, enthesitis of Achilles tendon/plantar fascia). Common triggers: Chlamydia trachomatis (venereal) or Shigella/Salmonella/Campylobacter (dysenteric).

questions.prompt: A 52-year-old male awakens at 2 AM with excruciating, sudden-onset pain, violent erythema, warmth, and marked swelling of his right first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint (podagra). Synovial fluid aspiration examined under compensated polarized light microscopy reveals needle-shaped, intracellular crystals displaying strongly NEGATIVE birefringence (yellow when parallel to the slow axis). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by precipitation of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid when serum urate exceeds solubility. The 1st MTP joint is the site of first presentation in >50-70% of patients (podagra). Polarized light microscopy of joint aspirate is diagnostic: MSU crystals are needle-shaped and show strong NEGATIVE birefringence (appear bright yellow when aligned parallel to the compensator axis and blue when perpendicular).

questions.prompt: How do the synovial fluid crystals and radiographic findings in Pseudogout (Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate - CPPD deposition disease) differ from those in true Gout?
options: Rhomboid crystals with weak positive birefringence and chondrocalcinosis
Needle-shaped crystals with strong negative birefringence and tophi
Spherical crystals with zero birefringence and osteolytic lesions
Envelope-shaped crystals with negative birefringence and osteopenia
questions.answer: Rhomboid crystals with weak positive birefringence and chondrocalcinosis
questions.explanation: In Calcium Pyrophosphate Dihydrate (CPPD) crystal deposition disease (pseudogout): 1. Crystals: Rhomboid or rod-shaped with weak POSITIVE birefringence (appear blue when aligned parallel to the compensator axis); 2. Radiographs: Show pathognomonic chondrocalcinosis—delicate, punctate, or linear radio-opacities within fibrocartilage (menisci of knee, triangular fibrocartilage of wrist) and hyaline articular cartilage.

questions.prompt: A 64-year-old overweight woman presents with bilateral knee pain for 3 years, worse after prolonged walking, standing, and descending stairs. She reports morning stiffness that lasts only 10 to 15 minutes. On physical examination, there is coarse joint crepitus on passive flexion, mild medial joint-line tenderness, and a varus deformity. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Primary osteoarthritis is a degenerative 'wear and tear' joint disorder characterized by progressive loss of articular cartilage, subchondral sclerosis, and osteophyte formation. Hallmarks: age > 50 years, mechanical pain (worse with weight-bearing, walking down stairs, relieved by rest), brief morning stiffness (<30 minutes, unlike RA), joint crepitus, and gradual varus deformity due to preferential wear of the medial compartment.

questions.prompt: According to the classic Kellgren-Lawrence radiographic grading system for Osteoarthritis, what specific features define 'Grade 3' severity?
options: Moderate osteophytes with definite joint space narrowing and sclerosis
Doubtful joint space narrowing with minute osteophytic specks
Definite osteophytes with completely preserved joint space
Severe joint space obliteration with marked bone contour deformity
questions.answer: Moderate osteophytes with definite joint space narrowing and sclerosis
questions.explanation: The Kellgren-Lawrence radiographic classification of OA: Grade 0: Normal; Grade 1 (Doubtful): Doubtful narrowing of joint space and possible osteophytic lipping; Grade 2 (Minimal): Definite osteophytes and possible joint space narrowing; Grade 3 (Moderate): Moderate multiple osteophytes, definite joint space narrowing, some sclerosis, and possible deformity of bone ends; Grade 4 (Severe): Large osteophytes, marked joint space narrowing, severe sclerosis, and definite bone contour deformity.

questions.prompt: In nodal primary generalized osteoarthritis of the hands, what anatomical interphalangeal joints do Heberden's nodes and Bouchard's nodes specifically involve?
options: Heberden nodes at DIP joints; Bouchard nodes at PIP joints
Heberden nodes at MCP joints; Bouchard nodes at wrist joints
Heberden nodes at PIP joints; Bouchard nodes at DIP joints
Heberden nodes at thumb CMC joint; Bouchard nodes at DIP joints
questions.answer: Heberden nodes at DIP joints; Bouchard nodes at PIP joints
questions.explanation: Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes are prominent, firm, knobby osteophytic enlargements characteristic of primary nodal osteoarthritis of the hands: 1. Heberden's nodes occur at the Distal Interphalangeal (DIP) joints (far more common, strong familial female predilection); 2. Bouchard's nodes occur at the Proximal Interphalangeal (PIP) joints.

questions.prompt: What are the four cardinal radiographic hallmarks of primary Osteoarthritis on plain orthogonal radiographs?
options: Asymmetric joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, and subchondral cysts
Symmetric joint space narrowing, periarticular osteopenia, erosions, and ankylosis
Punched-out lytic lesions, sunburst reaction, sequestrum, and involucrum
Widened joint space, loose bodies, cortical destruction, and Codman triangle
questions.answer: Asymmetric joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, and subchondral cysts
questions.explanation: The four pathognomonic radiological signs of osteoarthritis: 1. Non-uniform, asymmetrical joint space narrowing (reflecting focal mechanical cartilage loss in weight-bearing zones); 2. Subchondral bone sclerosis/eburnation (thickening of subchondral bone in response to concentrated stress); 3. Marginal osteophytes (bony spurs formed by endochondral ossification at joint margins); 4. Subchondral radiolucent cysts (geodes, formed by synovial fluid micro-intrusion through trabecular microfractures).

questions.prompt: A 60-year-old male presents with clumsy, numb hands, difficulty buttoning his shirt, and a broad-based, unsteady, stiff gait. Neurological examination reveals brisk hyperreflexia in both lower extremities, sustained ankle clonus, bilateral positive Babinski signs, and a positive Hoffman's sign. What degenerative spinal condition is this?
questions.explanation: Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy (CSM) is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction in older adults (>55 years). Degenerative cervical disc bulging, facet hypertrophy, osteophytes, and buckling of the ligamentum flavum compress the cervical spinal cord. Symptoms: insidious loss of fine motor dexterity in the hands ('numb clumsy hands') combined with an upper motor neuron (UMN) spastic gait, hyperreflexia, clonus, extensor plantars, and positive Hoffman's sign.

questions.prompt: A 32-year-old nursing mother presents with severe pain over the radial aspect of her right wrist that worsens when lifting her baby. On examination, there is localized tenderness and swelling over the radial styloid process. When the patient tucks her thumb into her palm, curls her fingers over it, and the examiner gently deviates the wrist ulnarly, sharp excruciating pain is reproduced over the radial styloid. What is the diagnosis, and which specific tendon sheaths are inflamed?
options: De Quervain tenosynovitis (APL and EPB tendons)
Trigger thumb (FPL tendon at A1 pulley)
questions.answer: De Quervain tenosynovitis (APL and EPB tendons)
questions.explanation: De Quervain's tenosynovitis is a stenosing tenovaginitis of the first dorsal extensor compartment of the wrist, which contains the Abductor Pollicis Longus (APL) and Extensor Pollicis Brevis (EPB) tendons. It is classically seen in mothers lifting infants ('baby wrist') or repetitive thumb abduction/wrist deviation. The physical maneuver described is Finkelstein's test (Eichhoff's maneuver), which stretches the inflamed tendons within the tight osteofibrous canal, reproducing sharp localized pain.

questions.prompt: What precise anatomical structures form the boundaries of the Carpal Tunnel, and what ten structures pass through it beneath the flexor retinaculum?
options: Carpal arch and flexor retinaculum; transmits 9 flexor tendons and median nerve
Radius and ulna; transmits radial nerve, ulnar nerve, and 8 extensor tendons
Palmar fascia; transmits ulnar artery, ulnar nerve, and 4 lumbrical tendons
Thenar fascia; transmits radial artery, median nerve, and abductor pollicis
questions.answer: Carpal arch and flexor retinaculum; transmits 9 flexor tendons and median nerve
questions.explanation: The carpal tunnel is an inelastic fibro-osseous conduit: its floor and lateral walls are formed by the concavity of the carpal bones (scaphoid, trapezium laterally; pisiform, hook of hamate medially), and its roof is the dense transverse carpal ligament (flexor retinaculum). Exactly 10 structures pass through: the Median Nerve, 4 tendons of Flexor Digitorum Superficialis, 4 tendons of Flexor Digitorum Profundus, and 1 tendon of Flexor Pollicis Longus.

questions.prompt: A 48-year-old female computer programmer presents with nocturnal tingling, burning numbness, and pain in the thumb, index, and middle fingers of her right hand that awakens her from sleep, relieved by shaking her hand ('flick sign'). On examination, there is thenar muscle atrophy and weakness of thumb abduction (Abductor Pollicis Brevis). Phalen's test reproduces numbness within 45 seconds. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome is the most common entrapment neuropathy, caused by compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel. Classic presentation: nocturnal paresthesias in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, and radial half of ring finger), positive Phalen's wrist-flexion test, positive Tinel's percussion sign, and relief on shaking the hand ('flick sign'). Motor weakness and atrophy of the Abductor Pollicis Brevis (thenar wasting) indicate severe, advanced nerve compression.

questions.prompt: In lateral epicondylitis of the humerus (Tennis Elbow), which specific tendon origin is primarily degenerate and micro-torn at the lateral humeral epicondyle?
questions.explanation: Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis / lateral epicondylalgia) is NOT an acute inflammatory condition; rather, it is an angiofibroblastic tendinosis (repetitive micro-tearing, failed biological healing response, and fibrovascular hyperplasia) originating primarily at the origin of the Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis (ECRB) tendon from the lateral epicondyle (with or without EDC involvement). Pain is aggravated by resisted active wrist extension with the elbow in extension (Cozen's test).

questions.prompt: A 56-year-old male with a history of alcohol use presents with nodular, cord-like thickening of the palmar fascia of both hands. Over 2 years, he has developed progressive, irreversible flexion contractures of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of his ring and little fingers, preventing him from placing his hand flat on a tabletop (positive Hueston tabletop test). What is the diagnosis?
options: Claw hand secondary to ulnar nerve palsy
questions.explanation: Dupuytren's contracture is a benign, proliferative fibroplastic disorder of the palmar aponeurosis. Myofibroblasts proliferate within the pretendinous bands, forming nodules that mature into dense, collagen-rich, inelastic cords that contract longitudinally, drawing the MCP and PIP joints into fixed flexion deformities (ring and little fingers most commonly involved). The inability to place the palm flat on a table is Hueston's tabletop test, an indication for surgical fasciotomy or fasciectomy.

questions.prompt: In stenosing tenosynovitis producing a 'Trigger Finger' or 'Trigger Thumb', at which specific anatomical pulley does the primary mechanical discrepancy and nodular tendon entrapment occur?
options: A1 (first annular) pulley at the metacarpal head
A2 pulley on the proximal phalanx
A3 pulley at the PIP joint
A4 pulley on the middle phalanx
questions.answer: A1 (first annular) pulley at the metacarpal head
questions.explanation: Trigger finger (stenosing tenovaginitis) is caused by repetitive friction and mismatch between the flexor tendon (which develops a reactive intratendinous nodule) and the tight first annular (A1) pulley at the level of the metacarpal head (distal palmar crease). As the digit flexes, the nodule is pulled into the sheath; on attempted extension, the nodule becomes mechanically trapped beneath the proximal edge of the A1 pulley, producing painful snapping, clicking, or locking in flexion.

questions.prompt: A 52-year-old diabetic woman presents with gradual-onset, severe shoulder pain followed by progressive, global restriction of both active AND passive movements of the glenohumeral joint in all planes, with external rotation being the earliest and most severely restricted motion. Radiographs are normal. What condition is this, and what is its primary pathology?
questions.explanation: Frozen shoulder (Adhesive Capsulitis) is characterized by insidious painful stiffening of the shoulder with profound global restriction of BOTH active and passive glenohumeral motion (external rotation restricted first and most severely, followed by abduction and internal rotation). Pathology shows progressive inflammatory capsular fibrosis, dense contracture of the coracohumeral ligament, obliteration of the inferior axillary fold, and loss of intra-articular volume (reduced from 15-20 mL to <5 mL).

questions.prompt: A 42-year-old nurse complains of severe, sharp, stabbing heel pain on the plantar aspect of her foot that is excruciating during the first few steps after getting out of bed in the morning, gradually easing with walking, but recurring after prolonged rest. On examination, exquisite tenderness is elicited by pressing directly over the medial calcaneal tuberosity. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Plantar fasciitis is a traction-overload enthesopathy/degenerative tear of the origin of the thick plantar aponeurosis at the medial tubercle of the calcaneus. Hallmark symptom: 'start-up' heel pain—severe pain upon taking the first few steps in the morning (the fascia contracts overnight in plantarflexion; taking weight suddenly stretches the tight, inflamed enthesis). Tenderness is precisely localized to the anteromedial border of the plantar calcaneal tuberosity.

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old obese male who wears a tight police duty belt presents with persistent burning dysesthesia, tingling, and numbness localized to the anterolateral aspect of his right thigh. Motor power, knee reflexes, and straight leg raising are completely normal. What is the diagnosis, and which nerve is compressed?
options: Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve compression)
questions.answer: Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve compression)
questions.explanation: Meralgia paraesthetica (Bernhardt-Roth syndrome) is an isolated sensory entrapment neuropathy of the Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve (LFCN) of the thigh (derived from L2-L3). The nerve is compressed where it pierces or passes beneath the lateral attachment of the inguinal ligament just medial to the Anterior Superior Iliac Spine (ASIS). Because the LFCN is a PURELY SENSORY nerve, there is burning pain, numbness, and hyperesthesia over the anterolateral thigh with completely normal motor power and reflexes.

questions.prompt: What is the most common anatomical site of origin and internal composition of a simple Ganglion Cyst of the wrist?
options: Dorsal scapholunate ligament; viscous mucinous fluid rich in hyaluronic acid
Volar radial artery sheath; serosanguinous synovial fluid
Flexor tendon sheath; purulent bacterial exudate
First dorsal compartment; calcified osteoid tissue
questions.answer: Dorsal scapholunate ligament; viscous mucinous fluid rich in hyaluronic acid
questions.explanation: A ganglion cyst is the most common benign soft-tissue tumor-like swelling of the hand and wrist (>60-70%). Approximately 70% arise on the dorsal aspect of the wrist, pedicled to the underlying scapholunate ligament or capsule. It is a true cystic degeneration of periarticular fibrous tissue (not lined by true synoviocytes, but by flattened cells) filled with thick, clear, viscous, mucin-rich fluid containing high concentrations of hyaluronic acid and glucosamine.

questions.prompt: A 20-month-old toddler presents with delayed walking, frontal bossing, craniotabes, pigeon-chest deformity (pectus carinatum), symmetrical bead-like enlargements along the costochondral junctions ('rachitic rosary'), and marked widening of the wrists. Anteroposterior radiograph of the wrists shows widening, cupping, splaying, and ragged fraying of the distal radial and ulnar metaphyses with widening of the radiolucent physeal gap. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rickets is a disease of growing children caused by deficiency of vitamin D (or calcium/phosphate metabolism) leading to failure of mineralization of newly formed osteoid matrix and growth plate cartilaginous matrix. Hallmarks: frontal bossing, craniotabes, rachitic rosary, Harrison's sulcus, widening of epiphyses (wrists/ankles), and bowlegs/knock-knees. Radiographs show cupping (concave metaphysis), fraying (ragged margins), splaying (flared metaphysis), and widened growth plates.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental histological and biochemical distinction between Osteoporosis and Osteomalacia?
options: Osteoporosis: decreased bone mass with normal mineralisation; Osteomalacia: defective mineralisation of osteoid matrix
Osteoporosis: hypermineralisation; Osteomalacia: complete loss of matrix
Osteoporosis: occurs exclusively in men; Osteomalacia: occurs only in children
Osteoporosis: elevated alkaline phosphatase; Osteomalacia: normal alkaline phosphatase
questions.answer: Osteoporosis: decreased bone mass with normal mineralisation; Osteomalacia: defective mineralisation of osteoid matrix
questions.explanation: Osteoporosis is a quantitative defect: there is decreased bone volume and mass, but whatever bone is present is normally mineralized (normal ratio of mineral to collagen matrix; normal calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase). Osteomalacia is a qualitative defect occurring in the mature adult skeleton: organic osteoid matrix is deposited at normal or elevated rates by osteoblasts, but mineralization fails, leading to unmineralized wide osteoid seams, bone softening, low/normal calcium, low phosphate, and markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase.

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old multiparous woman with poor nutritional intake and chronic lack of sunlight exposure presents with generalized bone pain, severe proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from a chair, waddling gait), and bone tenderness. Plain radiographs reveal symmetrical, transverse, radiolucent bands perpendicular to the cortex on the medial femoral neck, superior pubic rami, and axillary borders of the scapulae. What are these pathognomonic radiological lesions termed?
questions.explanation: Looser's zones (pseudofractures, Milkman's lines, or Umbauzonen) are the radiological hallmark of osteomalacia. They are narrow, ribbon-like radiolucent bands traversing the cortex (usually perpendicular to the long axis, with sclerotic margins) representing cortical microstress fractures repaired with unmineralized fibrous osteoid tissue. They are classically bilateral, symmetrical, and found in the axillary border of the scapula, femoral neck, pubic rami, ribs, and proximal ulna.

questions.prompt: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) diagnostic criteria based on Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) measurement of the lumbar spine or femoral neck, what T-score threshold defines 'Osteoporosis'?
questions.explanation: WHO DEXA scan criteria (comparing patient's bone mineral density to a young adult sex-matched reference population): 1. Normal: T-score >= -1.0 SD; 2. Osteopenia: T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 SD; 3. Osteoporosis: T-score <= -2.5 SD; 4. Severe (established) Osteoporosis: T-score <= -2.5 SD in the presence of one or more documented fragility fractures.

questions.prompt: A 54-year-old female presents with recurrent calcium nephrolithiasis, generalized lethargy, abdominal constipation, and diffuse bone aches. Radiographs show generalized osteopenia, subperiosteal cortical resorption on the radial aspect of the middle phalanges of the fingers, 'salt-and-pepper' skull degranulation, and multiple cystic expansile osteolytic lesions in the mandible and clavicle. Serum calcium is 11.8 mg/dL, phosphate is 2.1 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) is markedly elevated. What is the diagnosis?
options: Primary hyperparathyroidism with osteitis fibrosa cystica
questions.answer: Primary hyperparathyroidism with osteitis fibrosa cystica
questions.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism (most commonly due to a solitary parathyroid adenoma) produces excess PTH, stimulating osteoclastic bone resorption. Skeletal manifestations (Osteitis Fibrosa Cystica / von Recklinghausen's disease of bone): 1. Subperiosteal cortical bone resorption (most specific sign, seen on radial borders of middle phalanges); 2. Salt-and-pepper demineralization of skull; 3. Loss of lamina dura around teeth; 4. Brown tumors (cystic fibrous accumulations filled with osteoclasts, macrophages, and hemosiderin).

questions.prompt: What histological architectural hallmark characterizes the sclerotic, 'burned-out' phase of Paget's disease of bone (Osteitis Deformans) under light microscopy?
options: Disorganized mosaic pattern with thick, irregular cement lines
Uniform Haversian canals with concentric lamellae
Continuous unmineralized osteoid seams lining trabeculae
Sheets of small round blue cells with glycogen granules
questions.answer: Disorganized mosaic pattern with thick, irregular cement lines
questions.explanation: Paget's disease progresses through 3 phases: 1. Osteolytic (resorptive) phase; 2. Mixed osteolytic-osteoblastic phase; 3. Sclerotic (quiescent / burned-out) phase. In the sclerotic phase, rapid, chaotic, disorganized bone formation and resorption produce an abnormal 'mosaic' or 'jigsaw puzzle' architectural pattern: irregularly shaped fragments of lamellar bone are joined by prominent, thick, wavy, dark blue cement lines, resulting in bone that is structurally enlarged, weak, and brittle.

questions.prompt: A 68-year-old elderly man complains that his hat size has progressively increased over the past 5 years and that he has developed progressive bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and deep, dull aching pain in his bowed left tibia. Plain radiographs reveal cortical thickening, coarsened trabeculae, expansion of the skull bones ('cotton-wool' appearance), and bowing of the tibia. Serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated at 850 IU/L, but serum calcium and phosphate are normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Paget's disease typically affects elderly patients (>60 years). Hallmarks: progressive enlargement of the cranium ('increasing hat size'), cranial nerve impingement (sensorineural deafness due to eighth nerve compression in the auditory canal), bone expansion, and anterolateral bowing of the femur/tibia with microfractures ('banana fractures'). Laboratory profile: isolated, massive elevation of serum Alkaline Phosphatase (reflecting exuberant osteoblastic activity) with completely normal serum calcium and phosphate.

questions.prompt: In an elderly patient with long-standing, multi-focal Paget's disease of bone, what rare (<1%) but catastrophic complication must be suspected if the patient presents with a sudden onset of severe, localized, unrelenting bone pain, a rapidly enlarging warm soft-tissue mass, and an aggressive osteolytic cortical breakthrough on radiograph?
questions.explanation: The most dreaded complication of Paget's disease is malignant degeneration into secondary osteosarcoma (Pagetic sarcoma), occurring in <1% of patients. It typically arises in long-standing polyostotic disease in individuals over 60 years. Hallmark: sudden onset of severe localized bone pain, rapid enlargement of a mass, pathological fracture, and permeative osteolytic cortical destruction. Pagetic osteosarcoma is highly aggressive with a dismal 5-year survival (<10%).

questions.prompt: A 40-year-old male living in an endemic rural region with high well-water fluoride concentrations presents with joint stiffness, neck pain, and inability to bend his spine. Plain radiographs show marked, uniform osteosclerosis of the axial skeleton (vertebrae resembling 'chalk'), ossification of the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments, and dense periosteal outgrowths. Teeth show dark brown mottling of the enamel. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Endemic skeletal fluorosis occurs from chronic ingestion of high-fluoride drinking water (>3-5 ppm). Fluoride incorporates into hydroxyapatite forming fluoroapatite crystals, stimulating chaotic osteoblastic bone formation. Hallmarks: mottled dental enamel (fluorosis), progressive joint stiffness, diffuse chalky osteosclerosis of the axial spine and pelvis, calcification/ossification of ligaments (sacrotuberous, sacrospinous, interosseous membrane, ligamentum flavum), and dense periosteal hyperostosis.

questions.prompt: What is the first-line pharmacological class of antiresorptive agents of choice for treating postmenopausal osteoporosis to reduce the risk of vertebral and hip fragility fractures, and what is their cellular mechanism of action?
options: Bisphosphonates; inhibit osteoclastic farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthase
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; stimulate calcitonin secretion
Calcium channel blockers; promote direct osteoid crystallization
Loop diuretics; inhibit renal calcium excretion
questions.answer: Bisphosphonates; inhibit osteoclastic farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthase
questions.explanation: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (oral Alendronate, Risedronate, or annual IV Zoledronic acid) are the first-line antiresorptive therapy for osteoporosis. They bind with high affinity to hydroxyapatite crystals in bone; when internalized by resorbing osteoclasts, they inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthase in the mevalonate pathway, preventing prenylation of small GTP-binding proteins (Rho, Rac), leading to osteoclast inactivation and apoptosis, increasing bone mineral density and reducing fractures by 40-70%.

questions.prompt: A 6-year-old boy presents with a 4-month history of a painless limp and vague, dull aching pain in the right groin referred to the anteromedial knee. On physical examination, internal rotation and abduction of the right hip in flexion are markedly restricted. Plain radiograph reveals increased radiodensity (sclerosis), widening of the joint space, and slight flattening of the capital femoral epiphysis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis (osteochondritis) of the femoral head epiphysis affecting growing children (peak 4-8 years, 4:1 male predominance). Symptoms begin insidiously with an antalgic limp and mild groin/knee pain (referred via obturator nerve). Physical hallmark: early, preferential loss of internal rotation and abduction in flexion. Radiographs demonstrate the classic avascular changes (increased density, subchondral lucency, flattening, fragmentation).

questions.prompt: According to Waldenström's classic chronological staging of Perthes disease on serial plain radiographs, what are the four sequential stages in order of progression?
questions.explanation: Waldenström's radiographic stages of Perthes disease: 1. Initial/Condensation stage (6-12 months): Epiphysis stops growing, appears smaller and homogeneously radiodense; subchondral fracture ('crescent sign') appears; 2. Fragmentation stage (1-2 years): Necrotic bone is resorbed by vascular granulation tissue; epiphysis breaks into fragments; 3. Reossification stage (healing, 2-3 years): New bone is deposited from periphery; 4. Residual stage: Final mature femoral head contour remains (spherical, oval, or flat/coxa plana).

questions.prompt: In Herring's lateral pillar classification of Perthes disease assessed on the anteroposterior pelvic radiograph during the fragmentation stage, what defines 'Herring Group B' severity?
options: Lateral pillar maintains >50% of its normal height
Lateral pillar maintains 100% height with no radiolucency
Lateral pillar collapses to <50% of normal height
Complete resorption of all three pillars with dislocation
questions.answer: Lateral pillar maintains >50% of its normal height
questions.explanation: Herring's lateral pillar classification evaluates the height of the lateral 15-30% of the femoral head (the lateral pillar, which bears the brunt of acetabular contact stresses): Group A: No loss of height in the lateral pillar (normal height, excellent prognosis); Group B: Lateral pillar maintains >50% of its normal height (moderate prognosis; surgical containment beneficial if age > 8 years); Group C: Lateral pillar collapses to <50% of normal height (poor prognosis, head deforms severely).

questions.prompt: What clinical and radiological indicators comprise Catterall's classic 'Head-at-Risk' signs in Perthes disease, warning of impending severe femoral head deformity and extrusion?
options: Gage sign, lateral calcification, lateral subluxation, and horizontal physis
Absence of knee pain with normal internal rotation
Normal abduction of 60 degrees with symmetric skin folds
Preserved lateral pillar height with negative Trendelenburg
questions.answer: Gage sign, lateral calcification, lateral subluxation, and horizontal physis
questions.explanation: Catterall's 'Head-at-Risk' signs indicate a high risk of permanent femoral head deformity and uncontainment: 1. Gage's sign (small radiolucent V-shaped defect at the lateral margin of the epiphysis/adjacent metaphysis); 2. Calcification lateral to the epiphysis; 3. Lateral subluxation/extrusion of the femoral head from the acetabulum; 4. Horizontalization of the physis; 5. Diffuse metaphyseal radiolucent cysts/reactions.

questions.prompt: An 18-year-old male athlete presents with intermittent aching knee pain, joint swelling, and a sensation of sudden knee 'giving way' and locking. Plain radiographs demonstrate a well-demarcated, crescentic subchondral radiolucent line separating a partially detached oval bone fragment on the lateral, non-weight-bearing aspect of the MEDIAL femoral condyle. What is the diagnosis?
options: Giant cell tumour of distal femur
questions.explanation: Osteochondritis Dissecans (OCD) is an idiopathic focal avascular necrosis of subchondral bone leading to demarcation and potential detachment of an articular cartilage and bone fragment into the joint space. It classically affects the lateral aspect of the MEDIAL femoral condyle (>75% of cases; area of lateral intercondylar notch impingement by the tibial spine). As the fragment loosens, it causes effusion, aching pain, and true mechanical locking when it drops into the joint as a loose body ('joint mouse').

questions.prompt: According to the Ficat and Arlet classification of Avascular Necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head, what pathognomonic radiological finding on the lateral or frog-leg radiograph marks the transition from Stage II to Stage III?
options: Complete obliteration of acetabular joint space
Normal plain radiograph with marrow edema on MRI
questions.explanation: Ficat-Arlet staging of femoral head AVN: Stage 0: Pre-clinical, pre-radiographic (normal X-ray and MRI); Stage 1: Normal plain radiograph, diagnostic changes on MRI (marrow edema, band); Stage 2: Diffuse sclerosis, osteopenia, and cystic changes on X-ray, but normal spherical contour with NO collapse; Stage 3: Subchondral collapse manifested as the pathognomonic 'crescent sign' (subchondral radiolucent fracture line) and flattening; Stage 4: Joint space narrowing and secondary osteoarthritis.

questions.prompt: A 14-year-old adolescent athlete presents with localized pain, tenderness, and a prominent, firm swelling over the tibial tuberosity that is exacerbated by running, jumping, and direct kneeling. Radiographs reveal fragmentation and irregular soft-tissue swelling at the tibial tuberosity apophysis. What is the diagnosis, and what is the underlying pathoetiology?
options: Brodie abscess of proximal tibial metaphysis
questions.explanation: Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity occurring in active adolescents (10-15 years, especially running/jumping sports). Repetitive tensile pull of the quadriceps muscle through the patellar tendon on the secondary ossification center (apophysis) of the tibial tubercle causes micro-avulsions, inflammation, fragmentation, and reactive heterotopic bone formation. It is benign, self-limiting upon physeal fusion, and treated with rest, ice, and activity modification.

questions.prompt: A 10-year-old soccer player presents with bilateral, burning posterior heel pain aggravated by running. On examination, there is exquisite tenderness when compressing the medial and lateral aspects of the posterior calcaneus simultaneously ('calcaneal squeeze test'). Radiographs show patchy sclerotic condensation and fragmentation of the posterior calcaneal apophysis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sever's disease (calcaneal apophysitis) is a common, self-limiting traction apophysitis at the insertion of the Achilles tendon into the secondary ossification center of the calcaneal tuberosity in active children aged 8-12 years. Repetitive microtrauma from the tight gastrosoleus complex during the growth spurt creates pain. The clinical pathognomonic test is the 'squeeze test' (mediolateral compression of the posterior calcaneus elicits sharp pain).

questions.prompt: What specific tarsal and metatarsal bones are affected in Köhler's disease versus Freiberg's infraction in pediatric osteochondrosis?
options: Köhler: Tarsal navicular; Freiberg: Second metatarsal head
Köhler: First metatarsal head; Freiberg: Cuboid
Köhler: Medial cuneiform; Freiberg: Fifth metatarsal base
questions.answer: Köhler: Tarsal navicular; Freiberg: Second metatarsal head
questions.explanation: In juvenile osteochondroses: 1. Köhler's disease is avascular necrosis/osteochondritis of the tarsal navicular bone, typically presenting in boys aged 3-7 years with a painful limp and navicular tenderness (X-ray shows wafer-thin, sclerotic, fragmented navicular; self-limiting with complete reconstitution); 2. Freiberg's disease (infraction) is avascular necrosis of the head of the second (or third) metatarsal, classically affecting adolescent girls, producing collapse and flattening of the metatarsal head.

questions.prompt: In the core decompression procedure for early (Ficat Stage I or II) avascular necrosis of the femoral head, what is the fundamental biological and mechanical goal of drilling into the necrotic zone?
options: Relieves intraosseous venous hypertension and promotes vascular ingrowth
Arthrodeses femoral head to acetabular socket
Excises articular cartilage to stimulate fibrous scarring
questions.answer: Relieves intraosseous venous hypertension and promotes vascular ingrowth
questions.explanation: In early avascular necrosis, microvascular ischemia leads to intraosseous venous stasis, marrow edema, and extremely high intraosseous compartment pressures (>30 mmHg, normal <10 mmHg), which perpetuate ischemia. Core decompression (drilling a 3-8 mm track from the lateral cortex through the femoral neck into the center of the necrotic head lesion) relieves this intraosseous hypertension, provides immediate pain relief, and creates a vascular conduit for creeping substitution and neovascularization.

questions.prompt: A 6-week-old female infant is brought to the clinic because her head is constantly tilted toward the right shoulder with the chin rotated pointing toward the left. On palpation, a firm, non-tender, olive-shaped, mobile mass is felt within the lower third of the right sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle. What is the diagnosis and its classic histological basis?
options: Congenital muscular torticollis (fibrous contracture of sternocleidomastoid)
questions.answer: Congenital muscular torticollis (fibrous contracture of sternocleidomastoid)
questions.explanation: Congenital muscular torticollis (fibromatosis colli / sternomastoid tumor) typically presents in infants aged 2-8 weeks (often following breech extraction or birth trauma). Muscle ischemia or intrauterine compression results in fibrous replacement and contracture of the SCM: the tight muscle pulls the mastoid toward the clavicle (lateral head tilt to the IPSILATERAL side) and rotates the chin toward the CONTRALATERAL shoulder. >90% resolve with early passive stretching exercises.

questions.prompt: A 28-year-old female presents with pain, numbness, and tingling along the medial border of her forearm and hypothenar hand (C8-T1 distribution) and coldness of her hand, exacerbated by carrying heavy grocery bags. Adson's maneuver reproduces paresthesias and obliterates the radial pulse. What anatomical anomaly is the underlying cause, and which structures are compressed?
options: Cervical rib compressing C8-T1 lower trunk and subclavian artery
Carpal tunnel syndrome compressing median nerve
Cubital tunnel syndrome compressing ulnar nerve
questions.answer: Cervical rib compressing C8-T1 lower trunk and subclavian artery
questions.explanation: A cervical rib is a congenital supernumerary rib arising from the C7 vertebra. As it curves downward and forward toward the first thoracic rib, it (or its fibrous band) elevates and compresses the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1 fibers -> tingling in ulnar digits, weakness of intrinsics) and the subclavian artery (ischemia, pallor, weak pulse, post-stenotic aneurysm). In Adson's test, neck extension, head rotation toward affected side, and deep inspiration obliterate the radial pulse.

questions.prompt: A 5-year-old boy presents with an acute limp and hip pain 10 days following a mild viral upper respiratory infection. He is afebrile (temperature 37.1 C), comfortable at rest, but resists extreme internal rotation. Serum WBC, ESR, and CRP are within normal limits. Ultrasound reveals a small, transient, clear hip effusion. Following 5 days of bed rest and oral ibuprofen, the child is completely asymptomatic with full normal motion. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Transient synovitis ('observation hip') is the most common cause of acute painful limp in young children (aged 3-8 years). It is a benign, self-limiting, non-specific reactive synovitis that classically develops 1-2 weeks after a viral upper respiratory illness. Unlike septic arthritis (high fever, severe pain, inability to bear weight, ESR > 40, Kocher criteria positive), transient synovitis patients are afebrile or low-grade, have normal/mild inflammatory markers, and recover fully within 7-10 days with simple rest and NSAIDs.

questions.prompt: What is the quantitative anatomical definition of 'Coxa Vara' of the hip, and what is the normal adult femoral neck-shaft (CCD) angle?
options: Neck-shaft angle <120 degrees; normal adult angle is 125-135 degrees
Neck-shaft angle >145 degrees; normal adult angle is 110 degrees
Acetabular anteversion <5 degrees; normal adult angle is 45 degrees
questions.answer: Neck-shaft angle <120 degrees; normal adult angle is 125-135 degrees
questions.explanation: The collodiaphyseal angle (neck-shaft angle) is formed by the axis of the femoral neck and the axis of the femoral shaft: Normal in infants is 140-150 degrees; in normal adults it is 125 to 135 degrees. Coxa vara is defined as a pathological reduction of the neck-shaft angle to < 120 degrees (congenital, developmental, or acquired secondary to rickets, fibrous dysplasia, or malunited trochanteric fracture). In contrast, coxa valga is an angle > 135-140 degrees.

questions.prompt: An overweight, rapidly growing 13-year-old boy presents with dull pain in his left knee and an antalgic limp for 6 weeks. On examination, when the examiner passively flexes the left hip, the thigh obligatorily rotates into external rotation and abduction (positive Drehmann sign). Anteroposterior pelvic radiograph shows that a line drawn along the superior cortex of the femoral neck (Klein's line) fails to intersect the lateral capital femoral epiphysis (Trethowan's sign). What is the diagnosis?
options: Avulsion fracture of anterior inferior iliac spine
questions.explanation: SCFE is the most common adolescent hip disorder, characteristically affecting obese adolescent boys (11-15 years). The capital femoral epiphysis slips posteriorly and inferiorly through the hypertrophic physeal zone. Hallmark: Drehmann sign (obligatory external rotation during hip flexion). On AP radiograph, Klein's line normally cuts through the lateral third of the epiphysis; in SCFE, it passes completely outside the head (Trethowan's sign). Immediate in-situ single cannulated screw fixation is mandatory.

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old male presents with a painless, smooth, fluctuant, oval swelling in the popliteal fossa that becomes tense and prominent when the knee is fully extended, and soft and less prominent when the knee is flexed to 45 degrees (Foucher's sign). What is the diagnosis, and between which two muscle tendons does this synovial cyst characteristically arise?
options: Baker cyst (between semimembranosus and medial gastrocnemius)
Meniscal cyst (between biceps femoris and popliteus)
questions.answer: Baker cyst (between semimembranosus and medial gastrocnemius)
questions.explanation: A Baker's cyst (popliteal synovial cyst) is a chronic distension of the gastrocnemio-semimembranosus bursa located in the posteromedial popliteal fossa. It communicates with the knee joint via a slit-like opening. In adults, it is almost always secondary to underlying intra-articular pathology (meniscal tear, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis) causing chronic effusion. Foucher's sign (cyst hard/prominent in extension, soft in flexion) is pathognomonic.

questions.prompt: What are the four most common etiologies responsible for producing intra-articular 'loose bodies' ('joint mice') in the knee joint?
options: Osteochondritis dissecans, synovial chondromatosis, osteochondral fractures, and osteophytes
Gouty tophi, tuberculous sequestra, calcaneal spurs, and Brodie abscesses
Cruciate ligament tears, fabella subluxation, prepatellar bursitis, and xanthomas
Spondylolisthesis, ganglion cysts, fibrous dysplasia, and myositis ossificans
questions.answer: Osteochondritis dissecans, synovial chondromatosis, osteochondral fractures, and osteophytes
questions.explanation: Intra-articular loose bodies ('joint mice') are small, unattached fragments of bone, cartilage, or fibrous tissue floating freely within a synovial cavity: 1. Osteochondritis dissecans (detached osteochondral flake, most common in young patients); 2. Synovial chondromatosis (synovial metaplasia forming hundreds of cartilaginous nodules); 3. Osteoarthritis (detached marginal osteophytes or fragmented fibrillated cartilage); 4. Traumatic osteochondral shear fractures.

questions.prompt: In evaluating a patient with Flatfoot (Pes Planus), what simple clinical examination maneuver (Jack's toe-raise test) definitively differentiates a flexible flatfoot from a rigid flatfoot?
options: Passive great toe hyperextension reconstitutes arch in flexible flatfoot
Active ankle dorsiflexion reconstitutes arch in rigid flatfoot
Mediolateral calcaneal compression reconstitutes arch in flexible flatfoot
questions.answer: Passive great toe hyperextension reconstitutes arch in flexible flatfoot
questions.explanation: Jack's test (Great Toe Extension test) utilizes the Windlass mechanism: When the great toe is passively dorsiflexed, the plantar fascia is pulled taut around the first metatarsal head, which naturally elevates the medial longitudinal arch and inverts the calcaneus. If the arch reconstitutes, it is a normal/supple flexible flatfoot. If the arch remains completely flat, rigid, and locked, it indicates a rigid flatfoot (most commonly due to tarsal coalition or congenital vertical talus).

questions.prompt: A 15-year-old adolescent presents with a rigid, severely painful, non-correctable flatfoot and recurrent ankle sprains. Peroneal muscle spasm is demonstrable on forced inversion. Plain oblique radiographs of the foot demonstrate an abnormal fibro-osseous bridge between the calcaneus and the navicular bone ('anteater nose' sign). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tarsal coalition is an abnormal congenital failure of segmentation producing a fibrous, cartilaginous, or bony connection between two or more tarsal bones. The two most common varieties are Calcaneonavicular coalition (~50%) and Talocalcaneal (subtalar) coalition (~45%). Symptoms manifest in adolescence (12-16 years) as the coalition ossifies, producing rigid flatfoot, loss of subtalar motion, and peroneal spasticity. The elongated anterior process of calcaneus on oblique view resembles an 'anteater nose'.

questions.prompt: In foot deformities, what are the precise anatomical alignment definitions of 'Hallux Valgus', and what radiographic cutoff angles define a moderate-to-severe deformity requiring surgical correction?
options: Hallux valgus angle >15-20 degrees and intermetatarsal angle >9-10 degrees
Hallux valgus angle <5 degrees and intermetatarsal angle <5 degrees
Fixed plantarflexion with intermetatarsal angle >45 degrees
Dorsal toe subluxation with Bohler angle <10 degrees
questions.answer: Hallux valgus angle >15-20 degrees and intermetatarsal angle >9-10 degrees
questions.explanation: Hallux valgus is a complex deformity characterized by lateral deviation of the hallux (great toe) and medial deviation of the first metatarsal, resulting in a prominent, painful bunion over the medial first metatarsal head. Normal radiographic angles: Hallux Valgus Angle (HVA, angle between first metatarsal and proximal phalanx) is < 15 degrees; Intermetatarsal Angle (IMA, angle between first and second metatarsals) is < 9 degrees. Angles exceeding these cutoffs indicate hallux valgus.

questions.prompt: In a 62-year-old diabetic patient with non-reconstructable peripheral arterial dry gangrene involving all five toes, what is the ideal anatomical level for an elective Transtibial (Below-Knee) Amputation to provide the most optimal stump for prosthetic fitting?
options: 12 to 15 cm below knee joint line with posterior flap (Burgess)
Through mid-patellar tendon at the joint line
2 cm above medial malleolus to preserve maximal length
Immediately distal to tibial tuberosity within 3 cm
questions.answer: 12 to 15 cm below knee joint line with posterior flap (Burgess)
questions.explanation: The ideal below-knee (transtibial) amputation stump is 12 to 15 cm below the knee joint line (or at the junction of the upper and middle thirds of the leg). Stumps shorter than 7-8 cm lack adequate lever arm to control a prosthesis, while stumps longer than 15-18 cm have poor distal blood supply and inadequate clearance for modern dynamic prosthetic foot components. The Burgess technique utilizes a well-vascularized long posterior flap rich in sural artery supply.

questions.prompt: What is the precise anatomical level of bone transection in a classic 'Syme's Amputation' of the foot, and what unique weight-bearing feature does it offer?
options: Ankle disarticulation with malleolar shaving; provides end-bearing heel pad
Calcaneal excision with talar preservation; requires crutches
questions.answer: Ankle disarticulation with malleolar shaving; provides end-bearing heel pad
questions.explanation: Syme's amputation is an ankle disarticulation where the distal articular surfaces of the tibia and fibula (including both malleoli) are shaved off flush with the joint line. The specialized, thick, fibrofatty heel pad (which has durable shock-absorbing fibrous septa) is preserved and anchored over the flat cut end of the tibia, providing a true end-bearing stump that allows the patient to walk short distances even without a prosthesis.

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old male who underwent an above-knee amputation 3 weeks ago complains of intense, burning, and crushing pain perceived as originating from the absent toes and foot of the amputated limb. The surgical stump is completely healed with no signs of infection or neuroma. What is this neuropathic phenomenon termed, and what is the first-line medical therapy?
options: Phantom limb pain (treated with gabapentinoids and mirror therapy)
Phantom limb sensation (managed with immediate revision surgery)
Complex regional pain syndrome Type II (treated with sympathectomy)
questions.answer: Phantom limb pain (treated with gabapentinoids and mirror therapy)
questions.explanation: Phantom limb pain is severe, painful neuropathic dysesthesia perceived in the missing, amputated portion of the limb (present in up to 60-80% of amputees). It must be distinguished from benign 'phantom limb sensation' (painless awareness of the missing limb, which is universal and harmless). Phantom pain is central/neuropathic in origin; first-line management involves neuropathic pain medications (gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine) combined with psychological mirror-box therapy.

questions.prompt: What critical physiological feature distinguishes lower-extremity amputations in growing children from adult amputations, and how does it influence surgical technique?
options: Appositional terminal bone spike overgrowth; disarticulation is preferred
Complete failure of stump wound healing; transfixion is avoided
Inability to fit prostheses before age 18; amputation is delayed
Immediate premature closure of all proximal physes within 24 hours
questions.answer: Appositional terminal bone spike overgrowth; disarticulation is preferred
questions.explanation: In children, transecting a long bone diaphysis triggers vigorous, continuous appositional bone overgrowth from the periosteum and cut medullary canal, producing a sharp, conical bone spike that pushes through the distal skin flap. This is NOT due to physeal growth, but appositional osteogenesis. Consequently, in pediatric orthopaedics, joint disarticulations (e.g., knee or ankle disarticulation) that preserve intact epiphyseal cartilaginous caps are strongly preferred over diaphyseal amputations.
