Because humans are accidental hosts, the larvae lack collagenases to breach the basement membrane and wander aimlessly within the epidermis, producing an intensely pruritic, creeping, serpiginous inflammatory track. Treatment is oral albendazole or ivermectin.

questions.question: A traveler returning from rural sub-Saharan Africa presents with a painful, swollen, white papule with a central dark punctum on the periungual border of her great toe. Dermoscopy reveals a central black opening surrounded by a whitish halo (the posterior abdomen of an embedded gravid flea). What is this infestation termed?
questions.prompt: A traveler returning from rural sub-Saharan Africa presents with a painful, swollen, white papule with a central dark punctum on the periungual border of her great toe. Dermoscopy reveals a central black opening surrounded by a whitish halo (the posterior abdomen of an embedded gravid flea). What is this infestation termed?
questions.explanation: Tungiasis is an ectoparasitosis caused by the burrowing flea Tunga penetrans (jigger / chigoe flea). The fertilized female flea burrows into the periungual epidermis of the toes or soles, swelling to the size of a pea as its abdomen distends with eggs. It presents as a white papulonodule with a central black dot (the flea's respiratory spiracles and anus) through which eggs are expelled.

questions.question: A 32-year-old field biologist presents with two tender, furuncle-like erythematous nodules on his scalp. He reports a bizarre sensation of localized crawling and squirming beneath the skin. On close examination, each nodule exhibits a central pore with serosanguinous discharge through which a respiratory spiracle occasionally protrudes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old field biologist presents with two tender, furuncle-like erythematous nodules on his scalp. He reports a bizarre sensation of localized crawling and squirming beneath the skin. On close examination, each nodule exhibits a central pore with serosanguinous discharge through which a respiratory spiracle occasionally protrudes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Furuncular cutaneous myiasis is an infestation of viable human skin by dipterous fly larvae (maggots), most commonly Dermatobia hominis (human botfly, Central/South America) or Cordylobia anthropophaga (tumbu fly, Africa). The larva develops inside a tender, boil-like subcutaneous cavity with a central respiratory spiracle hole that discharges serous fluid.

questions.question: A 22-year-old male complains of intense, unrelenting itching that is excruciatingly worse at night in bed. Physical examination reveals erythematous excoriated papules in the finger web spaces, flexor wrists, axillae, anterior axillary folds, periumbilical area, and buttocks, with prominent pruritic nodules on the shaft of the penis and scrotum. What is this classic anatomical distribution termed?
questions.prompt: A 22-year-old male complains of intense, unrelenting itching that is excruciatingly worse at night in bed. Physical examination reveals erythematous excoriated papules in the finger web spaces, flexor wrists, axillae, anterior axillary folds, periumbilical area, and buttocks, with prominent pruritic nodules on the shaft of the penis and scrotum. What is this classic anatomical distribution termed?
questions.explanation: The classic anatomical distribution of scabies lesions is known as the 'Circle of Hebra': it spares the head, neck, and upper back in immunocompetent adults, preferentially targeting thin stratum corneum regions: interdigital web spaces of fingers, flexor aspects of wrists, elbows, axillary folds, umbilicus, belt-line, genitalia (penis/scrotum in men, areolae in women), and buttocks.

questions.question: A 64-year-old bedridden patient with advanced Parkinson's disease residing in a nursing facility presents with generalized, thick, psoriasiform, yellow-gray, fissured, hyperkeratotic crusts over the hands, palms, soles, and scalp with minimal pruritus. Skin scraping under light microscopy reveals thousands of live mites and ova per high-power field. What is this condition termed?
questions.prompt: A 64-year-old bedridden patient with advanced Parkinson's disease residing in a nursing facility presents with generalized, thick, psoriasiform, yellow-gray, fissured, hyperkeratotic crusts over the hands, palms, soles, and scalp with minimal pruritus. Skin scraping under light microscopy reveals thousands of live mites and ova per high-power field. What is this condition termed?
questions.explanation: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies is a rare, hyper-infestation occurring in immunocompromised, neurologically impaired, or institutionalized patients who cannot mount a normal cell-mediated hypersensitivity response or cannot scratch. The skin is colonized by millions of Sarcoptes scabiei mites, producing thick, warty, asbestos-like, malodorous hyperkeratotic crusts. Because itching is absent or minimal, diagnosis is frequently delayed, triggering devastating institutional epidemics.

questions.question: What microscopic structures identified on a mineral oil preparation from an unroofed skin burrow definitively establish the microbiological diagnosis of Scabies?
questions.prompt: What microscopic structures identified on a mineral oil preparation from an unroofed skin burrow definitively establish the microbiological diagnosis of Scabies?
options: Sarcoptes scabiei female mite, oval eggs, and scybala
questions.answer: Sarcoptes scabiei female mite, oval eggs, and scybala
questions.explanation: Definitive microscopic confirmation of scabies is made by placing a drop of mineral oil over a fresh, intact burrow, scraping the lesion vigorously with a sterile scalpel blade down to the stratum basale, and examining under low power (10x-40x) light microscopy. Visualizing the eight-legged adult female mite (with anterior suckers and dorsal spines), oval translucent eggs, or characteristic brownish fecal pellets (scybala) confirms the diagnosis.

questions.question: What is the first-line topical drug of choice for the treatment of classic Scabies in adults, and what is the proper application protocol?
questions.prompt: What is the first-line topical drug of choice for the treatment of classic Scabies in adults, and what is the proper application protocol?
options: 5% Permethrin cream applied overnight, repeated in 7-14 days
1% Lindane lotion applied daily for 14 days
questions.answer: 5% Permethrin cream applied overnight, repeated in 7-14 days
questions.explanation: Permethrin 5% cream is the topical gold standard for scabies. It acts by disrupting sodium channel conductance, causing neurotoxic paralysis and death of the mite. Protocol: applied thoroughly to all skin surfaces from the chin/jawline down to the toes (including under fingernails, umbilicus, and genitalia), left on overnight for 8-14 hours before washing off, and repeated after 7 to 14 days to eliminate newly hatched nymphs. All close household contacts must be treated simultaneously.

questions.question: What is the recommended oral dosage and scheduling of Ivermectin for the management of Scabies, and in which patient populations is its use strictly contraindicated?
questions.prompt: What is the recommended oral dosage and scheduling of Ivermectin for the management of Scabies, and in which patient populations is its use strictly contraindicated?
options: Oral Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg repeated at 14 days; avoid in pregnancy/<15 kg
Oral Ivermectin 50 mcg/kg daily for 7 days; avoid in renal failure
Oral Ivermectin 12 mg single dose without repetition; avoid in elderly
Oral Ivermectin 400 mcg/kg monthly; avoid in hypertension
questions.answer: Oral Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg repeated at 14 days; avoid in pregnancy/<15 kg
questions.explanation: Oral Ivermectin is dosed at 200 micrograms/kg taken with a fatty meal, and a second dose MUST be repeated 10-14 days later because ivermectin is not ovicidal (it does not kill mite eggs; the second dose catches newly hatched larvae before they reach sexual maturity). It is contraindicated during pregnancy, lactation, and in young children weighing less than 15 kg due to the risk of crossing the immature blood-brain barrier.

questions.question: A 19-year-old male was successfully treated for scabies with two courses of 5% permethrin cream 6 weeks ago. Repeated skin scrapings are negative for mites. However, he presents with intensely pruritic, firm, persistent, reddish-brown nodules on the shaft of his penis and scrotum. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 19-year-old male was successfully treated for scabies with two courses of 5% permethrin cream 6 weeks ago. Repeated skin scrapings are negative for mites. However, he presents with intensely pruritic, firm, persistent, reddish-brown nodules on the shaft of his penis and scrotum. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Post-scabetic nodules (nodular scabies) develop in 7-10% of patients and can persist for months after the active scabies infestation has been completely eradicated. They represent a sterile, localized, cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to retained, dead mite parts and antigens in the dermis. They are not contagious and are best managed with potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids.

questions.question: An 8-year-old schoolgirl presents with intense occipital scalp itching and localized cervical lymphadenopathy. Examination reveals oval, white, gleaming operculated nits firmly cemented to the hair shafts near the scalp that cannot be detached by sliding with fingers. What is the diagnosis and organism?
questions.prompt: An 8-year-old schoolgirl presents with intense occipital scalp itching and localized cervical lymphadenopathy. Examination reveals oval, white, gleaming operculated nits firmly cemented to the hair shafts near the scalp that cannot be detached by sliding with fingers. What is the diagnosis and organism?
questions.explanation: Pediculosis capitis (head lice infestation) is caused by Pediculus humanus capitis. Nits (eggs) are glued firmly to hair shafts by a chitinous cement secreted by the female louse, distinguishing them from dandruff or hair casts which slide easily along the shaft. Nits located within 6 mm of the scalp indicate active, viable infestation. Standard treatment is 1% permethrin lotion or 0.5% malathion lotion.

questions.question: A homeless male presents with diffuse excoriations, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and lichenification on his trunk and shoulders ('vagabond disease'). Lice and nits are found clustered within the seams of his clothing rather than on his skin. Which three major systemic infectious diseases are vector-borne transmitted by this parasite?
questions.prompt: A homeless male presents with diffuse excoriations, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and lichenification on his trunk and shoulders ('vagabond disease'). Lice and nits are found clustered within the seams of his clothing rather than on his skin. Which three major systemic infectious diseases are vector-borne transmitted by this parasite?
options: Epidemic typhus, trench fever, and relapsing fever
Scrub typhus, Q fever, and Lyme disease
Rocky Mountain spotted fever, tularemia, and ehrlichiosis
Plague, murine typhus, and Chagas disease
questions.answer: Epidemic typhus, trench fever, and relapsing fever
questions.explanation: Pediculus humanus corporis (the body louse) lives in the seams of clothing and visits the human skin only to feed. Chronic infestation causes the dry, thickened, hyperpigmented 'vagabond's skin'. The body louse is a medically dangerous vector transmitting three life-threatening epidemic diseases: 1. Epidemic typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii); 2. Trench fever (Bartonella quintana); 3. Louse-borne relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis).

questions.question: A 24-year-old sexually active male presents with intense pubic pruritus. Examination reveals rust-colored specks on his underwear and multiple asymptomatic, discrete, non-blanching, slate-gray or bluish macules (3 to 10 mm) scattered across the lower abdomen and thighs. What are these characteristic macules termed, and what produces them?
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old sexually active male presents with intense pubic pruritus. Examination reveals rust-colored specks on his underwear and multiple asymptomatic, discrete, non-blanching, slate-gray or bluish macules (3 to 10 mm) scattered across the lower abdomen and thighs. What are these characteristic macules termed, and what produces them?
options: Maculae caeruleae; caused by louse saliva enzymes altering host hemoglobin to biliverdin
Koplik spots; caused by viral endothelial necrosis
Janeway lesions; caused by septic micro-emboli
Osler nodes; caused by immune complex vasculitis
questions.answer: Maculae caeruleae; caused by louse saliva enzymes altering host hemoglobin to biliverdin
questions.explanation: Maculae caeruleae (taches bleues) are pathognomonic, slate-gray, bluish, non-tender, non-blanching macules seen in Phthiriasis (Pediculosis pubis / crab louse infestation). They are produced by the action of an anticoagulant salivary enzyme secreted by Phthirus pubis during feeding, which enzymatically degrades host heme/bilirubin into biliverdin in the subcutaneous fat.

questions.question: A hotel guest awakens with rows of intensely pruritic, erythematous, edematous papules arranged in linear groups of three along her exposed arm and neck ('breakfast, lunch, and dinner' sign). What arthropod is responsible for this distinct biting pattern?
questions.prompt: A hotel guest awakens with rows of intensely pruritic, erythematous, edematous papules arranged in linear groups of three along her exposed arm and neck ('breakfast, lunch, and dinner' sign). What arthropod is responsible for this distinct biting pattern?
questions.explanation: Cimex lectularius (the human bedbug) feeds nocturnally on exposed skin surfaces while the host sleeps. The bites classically present in a linear, consecutive grouping of three or four lesions, historically termed the 'breakfast, lunch, and dinner' sign, corresponding to sequential test bites along a capillary bed by a feeding bug.

questions.question: A 34-year-old male presents with sharply demarcated, salmon-pink erythematous plaques covered by thick, layered, silvery-white micaceous scales over both extensor elbows, knees, and presacral region. Skin biopsy demonstrates regular epidermal acanthosis with uniform clubbed elongation of rete ridges, absence of the stratum granulosum, confluent parakeratosis, and focal intracorneal collections of neutrophils. What are these diagnostic neutrophil aggregates termed?
questions.prompt: A 34-year-old male presents with sharply demarcated, salmon-pink erythematous plaques covered by thick, layered, silvery-white micaceous scales over both extensor elbows, knees, and presacral region. Skin biopsy demonstrates regular epidermal acanthosis with uniform clubbed elongation of rete ridges, absence of the stratum granulosum, confluent parakeratosis, and focal intracorneal collections of neutrophils. What are these diagnostic neutrophil aggregates termed?
questions.explanation: Munro microabscesses are collections of degenerated neutrophils migrating through the epidermis and trapped within parakeratotic stratum corneum, representing a cardinal histological hallmark of psoriasis vulgaris. Neutrophil collections within the spinous layer with surrounding spongiosis are termed spongiform pustules of Kogoj. Pautrier microabscesses contain atypical CD4+ T-lymphocytes in Mycosis Fungoides.

questions.question: What precise microvascular and epidermal architecture explains the elicitation of Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding droplets upon peeling the membrane of Bulkeley) in plaque psoriasis?
questions.prompt: What precise microvascular and epidermal architecture explains the elicitation of Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding droplets upon peeling the membrane of Bulkeley) in plaque psoriasis?
options: Thinning of suprapapillary plates over dilated capillaries
Necrosis and rupture of large subcutaneous arterioles
questions.answer: Thinning of suprapapillary plates over dilated capillaries
questions.explanation: In psoriasis, the suprapapillary epidermal plate (the epidermis overlying dermal papillae) is dramatically thinned to just a few cell layers. The dermal papillae are elongated and house dilated, tortuous, hyperpermeable capillary loops. When the overlying silvery scales and the glistening basement layer (membrane of Bulkeley) are removed, the roof of these superficial papillary capillary loops is torn, producing punctate pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign).

questions.question: A 16-year-old high school student suddenly develops an acute, widespread eruption of hundreds of small, drop-like (2 to 8 mm), scaly, salmon-colored papules and plaques across his trunk and proximal extremities, 2 weeks after recovering from severe exudative pharyngitis. Serum antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer is markedly elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 16-year-old high school student suddenly develops an acute, widespread eruption of hundreds of small, drop-like (2 to 8 mm), scaly, salmon-colored papules and plaques across his trunk and proximal extremities, 2 weeks after recovering from severe exudative pharyngitis. Serum antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer is markedly elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Guttate psoriasis characteristically erupts in children and adolescents 1 to 3 weeks following an acute Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis or perianal streptococcal infection. It manifests as a sudden 'rain shower' eruption of small, droplet-like (gutta = drop) erythematous scaly papules on the trunk and limbs, strongly linked to HLA-Cw*0602.

questions.question: A 42-year-old female with long-standing plaque psoriasis was inappropriately treated with a 2-week course of high-dose systemic oral prednisolone. Three days after abruptly stopping the steroids, she develops high spiking fever, rigors, leukocytosis, and an acute eruption of sheets of hundreds of pinpoint sterile yellow pustules coalescing into 'lakes of pus' on a generalized fiery erythroderma. What life-threatening condition is this?
questions.prompt: A 42-year-old female with long-standing plaque psoriasis was inappropriately treated with a 2-week course of high-dose systemic oral prednisolone. Three days after abruptly stopping the steroids, she develops high spiking fever, rigors, leukocytosis, and an acute eruption of sheets of hundreds of pinpoint sterile yellow pustules coalescing into 'lakes of pus' on a generalized fiery erythroderma. What life-threatening condition is this?
options: Generalized pustular psoriasis of von Zumbusch
questions.answer: Generalized pustular psoriasis of von Zumbusch
questions.explanation: Generalized Pustular Psoriasis of von Zumbusch is an acute, life-threatening form of psoriasis that is classically triggered by the abrupt withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids. Patients experience profound systemic toxicity, high fever, circulatory instability, and rapid eruption of waves of sterile, superficial pustules that coalesce into extensive 'lakes of pus' on fiery erythematous skin.

questions.question: Which combination of nail changes is considered the most specific and characteristic for Psoriatic Nail Disease?
questions.prompt: Which combination of nail changes is considered the most specific and characteristic for Psoriatic Nail Disease?
options: Deep irregular pits, 'oil drop' (salmon patch) discoloration, and subungual hyperkeratosis
Splinter hemorrhages alone with pterygium inversum
questions.answer: Deep irregular pits, 'oil drop' (salmon patch) discoloration, and subungual hyperkeratosis
questions.explanation: Psoriatic nail dystrophy occurs in up to 50% of psoriasis patients and 80% of psoriatic arthritis patients. Hallmarks: 1. Nail matrix psoriasis: deep, irregular, randomly distributed punctate pits (due to focal parakeratosis of the proximal matrix), leukonychia, and red spots in the lunula; 2. Nail bed psoriasis: pathognomonic 'oil-drop' or 'salmon patch' (translucent yellowish-red discoloration from bed parakeratosis), subungual hyperkeratosis, and distal onycholysis.

questions.question: A 55-year-old male presents with generalized erythema and scaling involving over 92% of his total body surface area, accompanied by severe peripheral edema, shivering from impaired thermoregulation, and high-output cardiac decompensation. What percentage of cutaneous involvement defines Erythroderma?
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old male presents with generalized erythema and scaling involving over 92% of his total body surface area, accompanied by severe peripheral edema, shivering from impaired thermoregulation, and high-output cardiac decompensation. What percentage of cutaneous involvement defines Erythroderma?
options: Greater than 90% body surface area involvement
Greater than 50% body surface area involvement
Greater than 30% body surface area involvement
Greater than 75% body surface area involvement
questions.answer: Greater than 90% body surface area involvement
questions.explanation: Erythroderma (exfoliative dermatitis) is defined as generalized, confluent erythema and scaling affecting at least 90% of the total body surface area. It represents a dermatological emergency causing profound metabolic and hemodynamic complications: hypothermia (from cutaneous vasodilation), high-output cardiac failure, massive protein loss from exfoliated scale, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances. Pre-existing psoriasis is the single most common cause.

questions.question: What is the specific immunological molecular target of Ustekinumab, a human monoclonal antibody approved for the treatment of moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis?
questions.prompt: What is the specific immunological molecular target of Ustekinumab, a human monoclonal antibody approved for the treatment of moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis?
options: Shared p40 subunit of interleukin-12 (IL-12) and interleukin-23 (IL-23)
questions.answer: Shared p40 subunit of interleukin-12 (IL-12) and interleukin-23 (IL-23)
questions.explanation: Ustekinumab is a fully human IgG1kappa monoclonal antibody that binds with high affinity to the common shared p40 protein subunit of both interleukin-12 (IL-12) and interleukin-23 (IL-23). By preventing p40 from interacting with the IL-12Rbeta1 receptor, it blocks both the Th1 (IL-12 driven) and Th17 (IL-23 driven) inflammatory cascades. In contrast, Guselkumab and Risankizumab selectively target the p19 subunit of IL-23 alone.

questions.question: A 48-year-old male with severe recalcitrant psoriasis is treated with oral Methotrexate (15 mg/week). What serious chronic parenchymal organ toxicity requires serial non-invasive screening (such as transient elastography / FibroScan or serum procollagen III amino-terminal peptide [P3NP]) after cumulative doses exceed 1.5 grams?
questions.prompt: A 48-year-old male with severe recalcitrant psoriasis is treated with oral Methotrexate (15 mg/week). What serious chronic parenchymal organ toxicity requires serial non-invasive screening (such as transient elastography / FibroScan or serum procollagen III amino-terminal peptide [P3NP]) after cumulative doses exceed 1.5 grams?
questions.explanation: Methotrexate is a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor widely used in severe psoriasis. Long-term cumulative use (>1.5 to 3.0 grams) carries a significant risk of cumulative hepatic steatosis, progressive fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Current guidelines recommend non-invasive monitoring using serum Procollagen III N-terminal peptide (P3NP) assays or hepatic transient elastography (FibroScan) to minimize the need for routine surveillance liver biopsies.

questions.question: Why must a 28-year-old female patient treated with oral Acitretin for severe plaque psoriasis strictly maintain effective contraception during therapy and for a full three years AFTER completing the course?
questions.prompt: Why must a 28-year-old female patient treated with oral Acitretin for severe plaque psoriasis strictly maintain effective contraception during therapy and for a full three years AFTER completing the course?
options: Transesterification into etretinate with prolonged 120-day half-life
Accelerated hepatic clearance causing therapeutic failure
Synergistic induction of acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis
Competitive inhibition of intestinal retinoid absorption
questions.answer: Transesterification into etretinate with prolonged 120-day half-life
questions.explanation: Acitretin (an oral second-generation aromatic retinoid) has an elimination half-life of ~50 hours. However, in the presence of even minuscule amounts of dietary ethanol/alcohol, acitretin undergoes reverse metabolic transesterification into its parent compound, Etretinate. Etretinate is lipophilic, stored in adipose tissue, has an extremely prolonged elimination half-life (120 days), and is notoriously teratogenic (craniofacial, cardiac, and CNS malformations), necessitating strict contraception for 3 years post-therapy.

questions.question: What histopathological pattern of the dermo-epidermal junction and epidermal rete pegs is classically described in fully established, mature Psoriasis vulgaris?
questions.prompt: What histopathological pattern of the dermo-epidermal junction and epidermal rete pegs is classically described in fully established, mature Psoriasis vulgaris?
options: Regular, uniform elongation and clubbing of rete ridges ('test-tubes in a rack')
Saw-toothed irregular rete pegs with basal liquefaction
Complete atrophy and flattening of all rete pegs
questions.answer: Regular, uniform elongation and clubbing of rete ridges ('test-tubes in a rack')
questions.explanation: The histopathology of mature psoriasis vulgaris is characterized by: 1. Regular, uniform elongation of rete ridges with club-shaped thickened lower portions, famously likened to 'test-tubes in a rack'; 2. Marked thinning of suprapapillary plates; 3. Dilated, tortuous capillaries in edematous dermal papillae; 4. Confluent parakeratosis with absent stratum granulosum; 5. Munro microabscesses and Kogoj pustules.

questions.question: A 36-year-old female presents with an intensely itchy eruption on the flexor surfaces of both wrists, forearms, and medial ankles. Examination reveals shiny, flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules crossed by a delicate, fine, lacy network of whitish lines on their surface. What are these diagnostic white surface lines termed, and what is the underlying condition?
questions.prompt: A 36-year-old female presents with an intensely itchy eruption on the flexor surfaces of both wrists, forearms, and medial ankles. Examination reveals shiny, flat-topped, polygonal, violaceous papules crossed by a delicate, fine, lacy network of whitish lines on their surface. What are these diagnostic white surface lines termed, and what is the underlying condition?
questions.explanation: Lichen planus is a chronic T-cell-mediated autoimmune mucocutaneous disorder summarized by the '6 Ps': Pruritic, Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped), Purple (violaceous), Papules and Plaques. The characteristic fine, white, reticular, lacy lines on the surface of papules and oral mucosal lesions are known as Wickham's striae, produced histologically by focal, localized thickening of the stratum granulosum (focal hypergranulosis).

questions.question: Which constellation of histopathological findings on a punch biopsy of an active cutaneous lesion is pathognomonic for Lichen Planus?
questions.prompt: Which constellation of histopathological findings on a punch biopsy of an active cutaneous lesion is pathognomonic for Lichen Planus?
options: Band-like interface infiltrate, basal liquefaction, and saw-toothed rete
Elongated rete ridges with Munro microabscesses
questions.answer: Band-like interface infiltrate, basal liquefaction, and saw-toothed rete
questions.explanation: The classic histopathological tetrad of Lichen Planus: 1. Compact orthokeratosis without parakeratosis; 2. Wedge-shaped hypergranulosis; 3. Irregular 'saw-toothed' acanthosis of rete ridges; 4. Basal layer liquefactive degeneration (hydropic vacuolization); 5. Band-like (lichenoid) lymphocytic infiltrate hugging the dermo-epidermal junction; 6. Civatte bodies (colloid/cytoid bodies—apoptotic basal keratinocytes).

questions.question: What are 'Max Joseph spaces' observed on histopathological examination of Lichen Planus?
questions.prompt: What are 'Max Joseph spaces' observed on histopathological examination of Lichen Planus?
options: Subepidermal clefts due to extensive basal cell liquefaction
questions.answer: Subepidermal clefts due to extensive basal cell liquefaction
questions.explanation: In lichen planus, severe, widespread liquefactive hydropic degeneration of basal keratinocytes destroys the mechanical continuity of the dermo-epidermal junction. During histological tissue processing, this weakened junction separates focally, forming small, artifactual clefts between the basal epidermis and papillary dermis termed 'Max Joseph spaces'. When this separation becomes extensive clinically, it produces the rare variant 'Bullous Lichen Planus'.

questions.question: A 45-year-old male presents with persistent, painful, ulcerated, and eroded lesions on the bilateral buccal mucosa that have failed to respond to topical antiseptics for 18 months. Biopsy confirms erosive (ulcerative) oral lichen planus. Why is long-term clinical surveillance mandatory in this specific patient?
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old male presents with persistent, painful, ulcerated, and eroded lesions on the bilateral buccal mucosa that have failed to respond to topical antiseptics for 18 months. Biopsy confirms erosive (ulcerative) oral lichen planus. Why is long-term clinical surveillance mandatory in this specific patient?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma transformation risk in erosive oral variant
Adenocarcinoma transformation risk in reticular variant
Systemic B-cell lymphoma risk in hypertrophic variant
Basal cell carcinoma transformation risk in bullous variant
questions.answer: Squamous cell carcinoma transformation risk in erosive oral variant
questions.explanation: While reticular oral lichen planus (characterized by asymptomatic bilateral lacy Wickham striae) is typically benign, the chronic erosive (ulcerative) and atrophic subtypes of oral lichen planus are officially classified as oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs). They carry an estimated 1% to 2% lifetime risk of malignant transformation into oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC), mandating regular long-term follow-up and biopsy of suspicious non-healing ulcers.

questions.question: A 40-year-old female presents with progressive, patchy hair loss on the crown and vertex of her scalp. Examination reveals perifollicular erythema, violaceous scaling around emerging hair shafts ('perifollicular collarettes'), and scarring loss of follicular ostia. Biopsy reveals a dense lymphocytic infiltrate destroying the follicular infundibulum and isthmus with permanent scarring. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old female presents with progressive, patchy hair loss on the crown and vertex of her scalp. Examination reveals perifollicular erythema, violaceous scaling around emerging hair shafts ('perifollicular collarettes'), and scarring loss of follicular ostia. Biopsy reveals a dense lymphocytic infiltrate destroying the follicular infundibulum and isthmus with permanent scarring. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lichen planopilaris (LPP) is the follicular variant of lichen planus, representing a primary cicatricial (scarring) alopecia. It preferentially targets the stem-cell-rich bulge region of hair follicles (infundibulum and isthmus). Hallmarks: active violaceous follicular papules and scaling at the advancing perimeter of smooth, shiny, atrophic bald patches where follicular openings are permanently obliterated.

questions.question: What classic clinical triad defines the Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome?
questions.prompt: What classic clinical triad defines the Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome?
options: Cicatricial scalp alopecia, non-scarring axillary alopecia, and spinous papules
Patchy alopecia areata, leukonychia, and vitiligo
Scarring eyebrow loss, keratoderma, and ichthyosis
Total scalp atrichia, anhidrosis, and conical incisors
questions.answer: Cicatricial scalp alopecia, non-scarring axillary alopecia, and spinous papules
questions.explanation: Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome is an uncommon variant of lichen planus characterized by the pathognomonic triad of: 1. Multifocal primary cicatricial (scarring) alopecia of the scalp; 2. Non-cicatricial hair loss involving the axillae and pubic hair; 3. Disseminated follicular hyperkeratotic, spinous papules on the trunk and limbs resembling lichen spinulosus.

questions.question: A 52-year-old postmenopausal female presents with severe vulvar pruritus, dyspareunia, and burning. Physical examination reveals porcelain-white, ivory-colored, atrophic plaques with a wrinkled 'cigarette-paper' texture surrounding the vulva and perianal region in a classic 'figure-of-eight' or 'hourglass' configuration, with resorption and fusion of the labia minora. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old postmenopausal female presents with severe vulvar pruritus, dyspareunia, and burning. Physical examination reveals porcelain-white, ivory-colored, atrophic plaques with a wrinkled 'cigarette-paper' texture surrounding the vulva and perianal region in a classic 'figure-of-eight' or 'hourglass' configuration, with resorption and fusion of the labia minora. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lichen sclerosus (historically kraurosis vulvae) is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis with a predilection for the anogenital region in postmenopausal women. Classic appearance: porcelain-white, shiny, polygonal papules and atrophic plaques with follicular plugging, wrinkling ('cigarette-paper skin'), and fusion of the labia minora ('architectural obliteration') in an anogenital 'figure-of-eight' distribution. Patients have an increased risk (4-5%) of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.question: A 50-year-old male presents with thick, hyperkeratotic, verrucous, brownish-violaceous plaques covered by fine adherent scales on the anterior aspect of both shins. Pruritus is extraordinarily intense and intractable. Biopsy confirms Hypertrophic Lichen Planus. What malignant transformation can rarely complicate long-standing neglected lesions on the shins?
questions.prompt: A 50-year-old male presents with thick, hyperkeratotic, verrucous, brownish-violaceous plaques covered by fine adherent scales on the anterior aspect of both shins. Pruritus is extraordinarily intense and intractable. Biopsy confirms Hypertrophic Lichen Planus. What malignant transformation can rarely complicate long-standing neglected lesions on the shins?
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic (verrucous) lichen planus is the most pruritic variant of lichen planus, characteristically targeting the pretibial surfaces (shins) and dorsal feet as symmetric, thick, purplish, warty plaques with follicular plugging. Chronic, neglected, long-standing hypertrophic LP carries an elevated risk of malignant transformation into invasive well-differentiated Squamous Cell Carcinoma.

questions.question: Which clinical and histopathological feature most reliably distinguishes a Lichenoid Drug Eruption from idiopathic Lichen Planus?
questions.prompt: Which clinical and histopathological feature most reliably distinguishes a Lichenoid Drug Eruption from idiopathic Lichen Planus?
options: Parakeratosis, tissue eosinophils, and absence of Wickham striae
Absent basal liquefaction and absent pruritus
questions.answer: Parakeratosis, tissue eosinophils, and absence of Wickham striae
questions.explanation: Lichenoid drug eruptions (triggered by beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, thiazides, antimalarials, and gold) clinically mimic idiopathic LP but have distinguishing features: lesions are often more eczematous, psoriasiform, or photo-distributed, and Wickham striae are usually absent. On biopsy, the presence of focal parakeratosis, apoptotic Civatte bodies in the upper spinous/granular layers, and dermal infiltrate containing eosinophils and plasma cells distinguishes it from idiopathic LP.

questions.question: What is the classical diagnostic phenomenon termed when cutaneous lichen planus papules erupt within linear surgical scars, scratch marks, or areas of friction?
questions.prompt: What is the classical diagnostic phenomenon termed when cutaneous lichen planus papules erupt within linear surgical scars, scratch marks, or areas of friction?
questions.explanation: The Koebner phenomenon (isomorphic response) is characteristically positive in active Lichen Planus (along with psoriasis and vitiligo). Traumatizing normal-appearing skin via scratches, surgical incisions, or constant friction stimulates keratinocyte release of cytokines (IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha) that recruit autoreactive cytotoxic T cells, precipitating identical violaceous polygonal flat-topped papules along the linear path of injury within 7 to 14 days.

questions.question: A 42-year-old male presents with an orange-red erythroderma that characteristically spares sharp, well-demarcated 'islands of normal skin' within the diffuse erythema. The dorsa of his fingers show follicular hyperkeratotic papules resembling a 'nutmeg grater', and his palms and soles display a thick, waxy, yellow-orange keratoderma ('PRP sandals'). What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 42-year-old male presents with an orange-red erythroderma that characteristically spares sharp, well-demarcated 'islands of normal skin' within the diffuse erythema. The dorsa of his fingers show follicular hyperkeratotic papules resembling a 'nutmeg grater', and his palms and soles display a thick, waxy, yellow-orange keratoderma ('PRP sandals'). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris (PRP, particularly classical adult Type I) is characterized by: 1. Rapidly spreading orange-red (salmon-colored) plaques with pathognomonic, sharply defined 'islands of normal skin' (nappes claires); 2. Follicular hyperkeratotic plug-like papules on the dorsal proximal phalanges ('nutmeg-grater sign'); 3. Waxy, yellow-orange, thickened palmoplantar keratoderma resembling a sandal ('PRP sandal'); 4. Alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis ('checkerboard pattern') on histology.

questions.question: What clinical triad characterizes Sézary Syndrome, the leukemic and erythrodermic variant of Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma (Mycosis Fungoides)?
questions.prompt: What clinical triad characterizes Sézary Syndrome, the leukemic and erythrodermic variant of Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma (Mycosis Fungoides)?
options: Erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, and circulating cerebriform Sézary cells
Erythroderma, hepatomegaly, and peripheral Reed-Sternberg cells
Exfoliative dermatitis, nephrotic proteinuria, and smudge cells
Ichthyosiform erythroderma, sensorineural deafness, and keratitis
questions.answer: Erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, and circulating cerebriform Sézary cells
questions.explanation: Sézary syndrome is the leukemic, aggressive form of Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma (CTCL). Diagnostic triad: 1. Pruritic, generalized, exfoliative erythroderma; 2. Generalized lymphadenopathy; 3. Demonstration of circulating clonally expanded CD4+ T-helper cells with grooved, folded, hyperconvoluted 'cerebriform' nuclei (Sézary cells) exceeding 1,000/mcL in peripheral blood or a CD4/CD8 ratio >10.

questions.question: What are the four most frequent underlying dermatological dermatoses that account for over 75% of all cases of secondary adult Erythroderma?
questions.prompt: What are the four most frequent underlying dermatological dermatoses that account for over 75% of all cases of secondary adult Erythroderma?
options: Psoriasis, Eczema (atopic/contact), Adverse drug reactions, and Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma
Lichen planus, Pemphigus vulgaris, Vitiligo, and Alopecia areata
Basal cell carcinoma, Melanoma, Histiocytosis, and Leprosy
Impetigo, Scabies, Tinea corporis, and Molluscum contagiosum
questions.answer: Psoriasis, Eczema (atopic/contact), Adverse drug reactions, and Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphoma
questions.explanation: The leading etiologies of erythroderma (exfoliative dermatitis) in adults: 1. Preexisting dermatoses (Psoriasis is #1, followed by Atopic, Seborrheic, and Allergic Contact Eczemas); 2. Adverse drug eruptions (anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides); 3. Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Sézary syndrome / Mycosis fungoides); 4. Idiopathic ('red man syndrome').

questions.question: A 52-year-old male presents with multiple, large (>5 cm), irregularly shaped, atrophic, dusky-red patches exhibiting cigarette-paper wrinkling, telangiectasias, and reticulate pigmentation (poikiloderma) distributed across his 'bathing-trunk' area. Biopsy reveals atypical lymphoid cells along the dermo-epidermal junction. What condition is this, and what malignancy does it portend?
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old male presents with multiple, large (>5 cm), irregularly shaped, atrophic, dusky-red patches exhibiting cigarette-paper wrinkling, telangiectasias, and reticulate pigmentation (poikiloderma) distributed across his 'bathing-trunk' area. Biopsy reveals atypical lymphoid cells along the dermo-epidermal junction. What condition is this, and what malignancy does it portend?
options: Large-plaque parapsoriasis; high propensity to progress into Mycosis Fungoides
Guttate parapsoriasis; progression into B-cell lymphoma
Pityriasis rosea; progression into systemic lupus erythematosus
Eczema craquelé; progression into basal cell carcinoma
questions.answer: Large-plaque parapsoriasis; high propensity to progress into Mycosis Fungoides
questions.explanation: Large-plaque parapsoriasis is a chronic clonal T-cell dermatosis presenting with large (>5 cm), yellowish-fawn to dusky-erythematous patches characteristically distributed in 'bathing-trunk' or sun-shielded areas, often demonstrating poikiloderma (mottled atrophy, telangiectasia, pigmentation). It represents a form of pre-Mycosis Fungoides or patch-stage Mycosis Fungoides with a high rate of malignant progression (up to 30-40% over decades).

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy presents with an acute, self-limiting eruption of recurrent crops of erythematous macules and papules that rapidly evolve into hemorrhagic vesicles, central crusts, and varioliform (pockmark-like) scars, accompanied by low-grade fever. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 14-year-old boy presents with an acute, self-limiting eruption of recurrent crops of erythematous macules and papules that rapidly evolve into hemorrhagic vesicles, central crusts, and varioliform (pockmark-like) scars, accompanied by low-grade fever. What is the diagnosis?
options: Pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta (PLEVA / Mucha-Habermann disease)
questions.answer: Pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta (PLEVA / Mucha-Habermann disease)
questions.explanation: Pityriasis Lichenoides et Varioliformis Acuta (PLEVA, also known as Mucha-Habermann disease) is an acute clonal T-cell-mediated reactive papulosquamous disorder. It presents in children and young adults with recurrent crops of inflammatory papules that develop central purpura, blister formation, ulceration, and necrosis, characteristically healing with depressed, varioliform (pockmark-like) scars.

questions.question: According to the classic Hanifin and Rajka diagnostic criteria for Atopic Dermatitis, a patient must fulfill at least three of four Major Criteria. What are these four Major Criteria?
questions.prompt: According to the classic Hanifin and Rajka diagnostic criteria for Atopic Dermatitis, a patient must fulfill at least three of four Major Criteria. What are these four Major Criteria?
options: Pruritus, typical flexural/facial morphology, chronicity, and atopic history
Xerosis, palmar hyperlinearity, pityriasis alba, and elevated IgE
Dennie-Morgan fold, keratosis pilaris, and cataracts
Recurrent skin infections, cheilitis, and nipple eczema
questions.answer: Pruritus, typical flexural/facial morphology, chronicity, and atopic history
questions.explanation: The 4 Major Hanifin-Rajka Criteria for Atopic Dermatitis: 1. Pruritus (cardinal symptom); 2. Typical morphology and distribution: facial/extensor involvement in infants; flexural lichenification and linearity in adults; 3. Chronic or chronically-relapsing course; 4. Personal or family history of atopic diathesis (asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis). Minor criteria include xerosis, ichthyosis, Dennie-Morgan infraorbital fold, hyperlinear palms, and elevated serum IgE.

questions.question: What epidermal structural protein gene undergoes loss-of-function mutations in up to 50% of patients with moderate-to-severe Atopic Dermatitis, predisposing to defective stratum corneum hydration and transepidermal allergen penetration?
questions.prompt: What epidermal structural protein gene undergoes loss-of-function mutations in up to 50% of patients with moderate-to-severe Atopic Dermatitis, predisposing to defective stratum corneum hydration and transepidermal allergen penetration?
questions.explanation: Loss-of-function mutations in the Filaggrin (FLG) gene (located on chromosome 1q21 in the Epidermal Differentiation Complex) represent the strongest known genetic risk factor for Atopic Dermatitis (and Ichthyosis Vulgaris). Filaggrin deficiency disrupts keratohyalin packing, impairs natural moisturizing factor (NMF) generation, raises stratum corneum pH, and leads to defective barrier function, allowing percutaneous allergen penetration and triggering Th2 immune cascades.

questions.question: What is the precise molecular target and mechanism of action of Dupilumab, a breakthrough fully human monoclonal antibody approved for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis?
questions.prompt: What is the precise molecular target and mechanism of action of Dupilumab, a breakthrough fully human monoclonal antibody approved for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis?
options: IL-4 receptor alpha subunit, inhibiting IL-4 and IL-13
TNF-alpha soluble ligand, inhibiting receptor binding
IL-23 p19 subunit, blocking Th17 differentiation
questions.answer: IL-4 receptor alpha subunit, inhibiting IL-4 and IL-13
questions.explanation: Dupilumab is a recombinant human IgG4 monoclonal antibody directed against the shared alpha subunit of the interleukin-4 receptor complex (IL-4R-alpha). Because IL-4R-alpha is a component of both the Type I receptor (IL-4 specific) and Type II receptor (utilized by both IL-4 and IL-13), Dupilumab potently blocks the dual downstream signaling of IL-4 and IL-13, the two master Th2 cytokines driving atopic dermatitis.

questions.question: A 25-year-old female develops a pruritic, vesicular, weeping erythematous eruption exactly underlying the metal buckle of her belt and metal studs of her jeans. Which metal is the single most common contact allergen worldwide, and what immunologic mechanism mediates this reaction?
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old female develops a pruritic, vesicular, weeping erythematous eruption exactly underlying the metal buckle of her belt and metal studs of her jeans. Which metal is the single most common contact allergen worldwide, and what immunologic mechanism mediates this reaction?
options: Nickel sulfate; Type IV (delayed-type) cell-mediated hypersensitivity
Cobalt chloride; Type I IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity
Gold sodium thiomalate; Type III immune complex deposition
questions.answer: Nickel sulfate; Type IV (delayed-type) cell-mediated hypersensitivity
questions.explanation: Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD) to Nickel is the most frequent contact allergy in the world (>15% of women). It is a classic Type IV (delayed-type) cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction: Nickel acts as a hapten, binding to epidermal self-proteins, processed by epidermal Langerhans cells, and presented to CD4+ T-helper 1 (Th1) memory cells. Re-exposure triggers cytokine release (IFN-gamma, IL-2), producing spongiotic dermatitis 48 to 72 hours later. Patch testing with 5% nickel sulfate confirms the diagnosis.

questions.question: Which key pathophysiological and clinical features distinguish Irritant Contact Dermatitis (ICD) from Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD)?
questions.prompt: Which key pathophysiological and clinical features distinguish Irritant Contact Dermatitis (ICD) from Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD)?
options: Non-immunologic direct cytotoxicity, burning sensation, and sharp borders
Type IV hypersensitivity requiring sensitization and spreading beyond borders
IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity causing evanescent wheals
Clonal T-cell memory proliferation with positive patch test
questions.answer: Non-immunologic direct cytotoxicity, burning sensation, and sharp borders
questions.explanation: Irritant Contact Dermatitis (accounting for 80% of all contact dermatitis, commonly seen in wet-workers / dishwashers): 1. Non-immunologic: direct chemical or physical injury to keratinocyte cell membranes and skin barrier; 2. No sensitization phase required: occurs on first exposure if concentration is high enough; 3. Burning and pain dominate over itching; 4. Strictly limited to the anatomical area of contact; 5. Negative patch test.

questions.question: A 32-year-old male presents with greasy, yellowish, greasy scales overlying poorly defined erythematous patches on his scalp, eyebrows, glabella, nasolabial folds, and presternal region. What commensal lipid-dependent fungal organism plays a central pathogenic role in triggering this inflammation?
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old male presents with greasy, yellowish, greasy scales overlying poorly defined erythematous patches on his scalp, eyebrows, glabella, nasolabial folds, and presternal region. What commensal lipid-dependent fungal organism plays a central pathogenic role in triggering this inflammation?
options: Malassezia species (M. restricta and M. globosa)
questions.answer: Malassezia species (M. restricta and M. globosa)
questions.explanation: Seborrheic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory disorder localized to sebum-rich anatomical regions (scalp, face, chest, retroauricular folds). Lipophilic Malassezia yeasts (especially M. restricta and M. globosa) metabolize sebum triglycerides using fungal lipases, releasing irritant free fatty acids (oleic acid, arachidonic acid) that breach the epidermal barrier and incite secondary inflammation in susceptible hosts. Topical ketoconazole and zinc pyrithione are first-line treatments.

questions.question: A 45-year-old male with dry skin presents with multiple discrete, coin-shaped (nummular), intensely pruritic, erythematous plaques studded with tiny vesicles, oozing, and crusts on the extensor aspects of his lower legs and forearms. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old male with dry skin presents with multiple discrete, coin-shaped (nummular), intensely pruritic, erythematous plaques studded with tiny vesicles, oozing, and crusts on the extensor aspects of his lower legs and forearms. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Nummular eczema (discoid dermatitis) is characterized by strikingly discrete, coin-shaped (nummular = coin-like), round or oval plaques ranging from 1 to 5 cm in diameter. Lesions classically develop on the lower legs and arms of middle-aged and elderly individuals with underlying xerosis, presenting with clustered papules, microvesicles, confluent serous weeping, and honey-colored crusting.

questions.question: A 26-year-old female complains of recurrent, intensely pruritic crops of deep-seated, tense, clear, non-erythematous vesicles located symmetrically along the lateral borders of her fingers and on her palms, resembling 'tapioca pudding'. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 26-year-old female complains of recurrent, intensely pruritic crops of deep-seated, tense, clear, non-erythematous vesicles located symmetrically along the lateral borders of her fingers and on her palms, resembling 'tapioca pudding'. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pompholyx (dyshidrotic eczema / vesicular palmoplantar dermatitis) is an acute or recurrent episodic eruption characterized by deep-seated, tense, pruritic vesicles likened to 'tapioca pudding grains' on the lateral margins of the fingers, palms, and soles. Despite its historical name 'dyshidrosis', it has no relationship to eccrine sweat gland dysfunction, but represents an intense spongiotic reaction triggered by contact allergens, sweating, or atopy.

questions.question: A 60-year-old female with chronic varicose veins presents with pitting edema, brawny brownish-orange pigmentation, and itchy eczematous scaling over the medial aspect of both lower legs. What microvascular pathology and biochemical breakdown product cause this characteristic discoloration?
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old female with chronic varicose veins presents with pitting edema, brawny brownish-orange pigmentation, and itchy eczematous scaling over the medial aspect of both lower legs. What microvascular pathology and biochemical breakdown product cause this characteristic discoloration?
options: Chronic venous hypertension causing extravasation of erythrocytes and dermal hemosiderin deposition
questions.answer: Chronic venous hypertension causing extravasation of erythrocytes and dermal hemosiderin deposition
questions.explanation: Stasis dermatitis is a direct consequence of chronic venous insufficiency and ambulatory venous hypertension: incompetent valves in the saphenous and perforator veins transmit elevated hydrostatic pressures to dermal capillary beds. Capillaries distend, become permeable, and extravasate erythrocytes into the dermis. Macrophages phagocytose the red cells, degrading hemoglobin into hemosiderin pigment, which produces the characteristic indelible golden-brown or brawny staining.

questions.question: An 80-year-old male residing in a heated nursing facility during winter presents with dry, itchy, polygonal plates of skin separated by superficial red fissures on his anterior shins, giving the appearance of 'cracked porcelain' or 'dry riverbed'. What is this entity termed?
questions.prompt: An 80-year-old male residing in a heated nursing facility during winter presents with dry, itchy, polygonal plates of skin separated by superficial red fissures on his anterior shins, giving the appearance of 'cracked porcelain' or 'dry riverbed'. What is this entity termed?
questions.explanation: Asteatotic eczema (eczema craquelé) is caused by severe cutaneous dehydration, lipid depletion, and loss of epidermal barrier integrity in elderly individuals, aggravated by low humidity, dry indoor heating, and frequent hot soapy baths. It characteristically affects the pretibial shins as a network of fine red fissures crisscrossing polygonal keratin plates, resembling cracked china, dried mud, or crazy paving.

questions.question: What clinical duration threshold strictly differentiates Acute Urticaria from Chronic Urticaria, and how long does an individual wheal characteristically persist at a single anatomical spot?
questions.prompt: What clinical duration threshold strictly differentiates Acute Urticaria from Chronic Urticaria, and how long does an individual wheal characteristically persist at a single anatomical spot?
options: 6 weeks duration; individual wheals resolve within 24 hours
2 weeks duration; individual wheals persist over 48 hours
12 weeks duration; individual lesions persist over several days
4 weeks duration; individual lesions persist over 72 hours
questions.answer: 6 weeks duration; individual wheals resolve within 24 hours
questions.explanation: Urticaria is categorized chronologically into Acute (<6 weeks duration, frequently triggered by infections, foods, or medications) and Chronic (spontaneous or inducible wheals occurring almost daily for >=6 weeks). Cardinal diagnostic feature: an individual urticarial wheal (edematous, pruritic plaque with surrounding erythema) is evanescent, developing rapidly and completely resolving within 2 to 24 hours without leaving any residual ecchymosis, purpura, or pigmentation.

questions.question: A 32-year-old female presents with persistent urticarial wheals that burn and sting rather than itch. Unlike classic hives, each individual lesion remains fixed at the exact same site for 48 to 72 hours and resolves leaving behind localized purpura and faint brown post-inflammatory staining. Biopsy demonstrates leukocytoclastic vasculitis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old female presents with persistent urticarial wheals that burn and sting rather than itch. Unlike classic hives, each individual lesion remains fixed at the exact same site for 48 to 72 hours and resolves leaving behind localized purpura and faint brown post-inflammatory staining. Biopsy demonstrates leukocytoclastic vasculitis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Urticarial vasculitis is a Type III immune complex-mediated small vessel vasculitis that clinically mimics urticaria. Critical distinguishing features: 1. Lesions persist for >24 hours at the exact same anatomical location (classic urticaria resolves <24 hours); 2. Burning, tender, or painful rather than purely pruritic; 3. Resolves with palpable purpura or post-inflammatory hemosiderin hyperpigmentation; 4. Biopsy confirms true leukocytoclastic vasculitis (fibrinoid necrosis, nuclear dust).

questions.question: A 20-year-old collegiate athlete develops intense itching and an eruption of tiny (1 to 3 mm), punctate, highly pruritic wheals surrounded by large, intense erythematous flares across his trunk and neck within 10 minutes of beginning a vigorous run, taking a hot shower, or eating spicy soup. What type of physical urticaria is this?
questions.prompt: A 20-year-old collegiate athlete develops intense itching and an eruption of tiny (1 to 3 mm), punctate, highly pruritic wheals surrounded by large, intense erythematous flares across his trunk and neck within 10 minutes of beginning a vigorous run, taking a hot shower, or eating spicy soup. What type of physical urticaria is this?
questions.explanation: Cholinergic urticaria is a distinctive physical inducible urticaria triggered by any factor that raises core body temperature by >=0.5 to 1.0 C (vigorous physical exertion, hot baths, emotional stress, spicy food). Sympathetic postganglionic cholinergic nerve fibers stimulate sweat glands and mast cells, producing classic monomorphic, tiny (1-3 mm) follicular wheals surrounded by widespread, axon-reflex flare erythema.

questions.question: A 24-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of non-pruritic, painless swelling of his lips, eyelids, laryngeal airway, and severe crampy abdominal pain without any cutaneous hives or wheals. Laboratory workup reveals severely reduced serum C4 levels and a quantitative deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH). What is the primary mediator driving this angioedema?
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of non-pruritic, painless swelling of his lips, eyelids, laryngeal airway, and severe crampy abdominal pain without any cutaneous hives or wheals. Laboratory workup reveals severely reduced serum C4 levels and a quantitative deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH). What is the primary mediator driving this angioedema?
questions.explanation: Hereditary Angioedema (HAE Types I and II) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the SERPING1 gene, leading to deficiency (Type I, 85%) or functional dysfunction (Type II, 15%) of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH). Unchecked activation of the plasma kallikrein-kinin system results in excessive production of Bradykinin, a potent non-histaminergic vasodilator that increases vascular permeability, causing swelling of the face, bowel wall (colic), and fatal laryngeal asphyxiation.

questions.question: A 22-year-old male presents with an acute, symmetrical eruption of asymptomatic, concentric, three-zoned 'target' or 'iris' lesions on the dorsa of his hands, palms, and extensor forearms, 8 days after an episode of recurrent herpes labialis. What is the diagnosis, and what defines a true classic target lesion?
questions.prompt: A 22-year-old male presents with an acute, symmetrical eruption of asymptomatic, concentric, three-zoned 'target' or 'iris' lesions on the dorsa of his hands, palms, and extensor forearms, 8 days after an episode of recurrent herpes labialis. What is the diagnosis, and what defines a true classic target lesion?
options: Erythema multiforme minor; concentric target lesions with dusky center
Fixed drug eruption; solitary bullous hyperpigmented plaque
Granuloma annulare; annular erythematous beaded plaque
Urticarial vasculitis; fixed wheals persisting over 48 hours
questions.answer: Erythema multiforme minor; concentric target lesions with dusky center
questions.explanation: Erythema Multiforme (EM) is an acute, immune-mediated mucocutaneous reactive condition triggered primarily by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1 and HSV-2 in >70-80% of recurrent cases). The pathognomonic lesion is the 'classic target' (iris lesion), which has THREE concentric zones: 1. A central dusky, dark, purpuric or blistering zone; 2. An intermediate pale, edematous, raised ring; 3. A sharply defined, outer bright erythematous border.

questions.question: A 24-year-old female presents with multiple exquisitely tender, warm, painful, non-ulcerating, bright red subcutaneous nodules on the anterior surfaces of both shins, accompanied by ankle arthralgia and malaise, 10 days after a streptococcal sore throat. Over 3 weeks, the nodules evolve from red to purplish and yellowish-green, resembling resolving bruises ('erythema contusiformis'). What is the diagnosis and its primary histological classification?
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old female presents with multiple exquisitely tender, warm, painful, non-ulcerating, bright red subcutaneous nodules on the anterior surfaces of both shins, accompanied by ankle arthralgia and malaise, 10 days after a streptococcal sore throat. Over 3 weeks, the nodules evolve from red to purplish and yellowish-green, resembling resolving bruises ('erythema contusiformis'). What is the diagnosis and its primary histological classification?
options: Erythema nodosum; septal panniculitis without vasculitis
Erythema induratum; lobular panniculitis with vasculitis
questions.answer: Erythema nodosum; septal panniculitis without vasculitis
questions.explanation: Erythema nodosum (EN) is the most common form of panniculitis. It is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to various systemic antigenic triggers (Streptococcal pharyngitis, sarcoidosis, primary tuberculosis, IBD, drugs like sulfonamides and OCPs). Hallmarks: tender subcutaneous nodules on anterior shins that never ulcerate and resolve like a bruise (erythema contusiformis). Histologically, it is the prototype of Septal Panniculitis WITHOUT Vasculitis.

questions.question: What pathognomonic microscopic histopathological structure located within the thickened subcutaneous interlobular septa confirms the diagnosis of early Erythema Nodosum?
questions.prompt: What pathognomonic microscopic histopathological structure located within the thickened subcutaneous interlobular septa confirms the diagnosis of early Erythema Nodosum?
questions.explanation: Miescher's radial granulomas are the pathognomonic histopathological hallmark of early erythema nodosum. They are small, well-defined nodular aggregates of histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells arranged radially around a tiny central star-shaped or cleft-like central space within the thickened interlobular septa of the subcutaneous fat.

questions.question: A 28-year-old female presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest radiography, acute bilateral ankle arthritis, and painful erythema nodosum on both shins. What is this clinical triad termed, and what is its prognosis in Sarcoidosis?
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old female presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest radiography, acute bilateral ankle arthritis, and painful erythema nodosum on both shins. What is this clinical triad termed, and what is its prognosis in Sarcoidosis?
options: Löfgren syndrome; acute benign sarcoidosis with high spontaneous remission
Heerfordt syndrome; progressive sarcoidosis with facial palsy
Mikulicz syndrome; chronic dacryosialoadenitis requiring immunosuppression
Sweet syndrome; acute neutrophilic dermatosis with leukemia
questions.answer: Löfgren syndrome; acute benign sarcoidosis with high spontaneous remission
questions.explanation: Löfgren syndrome is an acute, self-limiting clinical phenotype of Sarcoidosis characterized by the classic triad of: 1. Erythema nodosum; 2. Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) on chest X-ray; 3. Migratory polyarthritis/periarthritis (predominantly involving the ankles). It has an extraordinarily favorable prognosis, with spontaneous complete resolution in >80-90% of patients within 1 to 2 years, requiring only symptomatic treatment with NSAIDs.

questions.question: A 56-year-old chronic alcoholic male presents with acute severe epigastric pain radiating to his back, accompanied by multiple tender, erythematous, subcutaneous nodules on his lower legs. Biopsy reveals enzymatic fat necrosis with pathognomonic 'ghost adipocytes' (anucleated adipocytes with thick, shadowy basophilic walls and calcium saponification). What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 56-year-old chronic alcoholic male presents with acute severe epigastric pain radiating to his back, accompanied by multiple tender, erythematous, subcutaneous nodules on his lower legs. Biopsy reveals enzymatic fat necrosis with pathognomonic 'ghost adipocytes' (anucleated adipocytes with thick, shadowy basophilic walls and calcium saponification). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic panniculitis (pancreatitis-associated subcutaneous fat necrosis) occurs in 2-3% of patients with acute/chronic pancreatitis or acinar cell carcinoma of the pancreas. Massive release of pancreatic enzymes (lipase and amylase) into the systemic circulation causes distant enzymatic digestion of peri-articular and subcutaneous fat. Histology shows pathognomonic 'ghost cells' (necrotic adipocytes lacking nuclei with shadowy basophilic borders) and calcium deposition (saponification).

questions.question: A 34-year-old female with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with deep, firm, non-tender subcutaneous nodules and plaques on her cheeks, upper arms, and buttocks. As the lesions slowly regress over several months, they leave behind disfiguring, deep, punched-out, saucer-like lipoatrophic depressions. What is this variant termed?
questions.prompt: A 34-year-old female with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with deep, firm, non-tender subcutaneous nodules and plaques on her cheeks, upper arms, and buttocks. As the lesions slowly regress over several months, they leave behind disfiguring, deep, punched-out, saucer-like lipoatrophic depressions. What is this variant termed?
questions.explanation: Lupus erythematosus profundus (lupus panniculitis) is a chronic inflammatory disorder of subcutaneous fat occurring in 2-3% of patients with SLE or discoid lupus. It characteristically affects fatty areas (cheeks, shoulders, upper arms, breasts, buttocks) as deep indurated plaques that heal with marked subcutaneous atrophy, producing permanent, unsightly cup-shaped or saucer-like depressions. Biopsy shows lobular panniculitis with hyaline fat necrosis and lymphoid follicles.

questions.question: A 28-year-old male takes an oral tablet of Cotrimoxazole for a urinary tract infection. Twelve hours later, a solitary, well-demarcated, rounded, dusky-violaceous, burning plaque with an edematous border erupts on the glans penis. The lesion heals over 2 weeks with dense slate-gray hyperpigmentation. Six months later, he takes the same drug and the plaque flares up at the EXACT SAME anatomical site. What is the diagnosis and its immunopathogenesis?
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old male takes an oral tablet of Cotrimoxazole for a urinary tract infection. Twelve hours later, a solitary, well-demarcated, rounded, dusky-violaceous, burning plaque with an edematous border erupts on the glans penis. The lesion heals over 2 weeks with dense slate-gray hyperpigmentation. Six months later, he takes the same drug and the plaque flares up at the EXACT SAME anatomical site. What is the diagnosis and its immunopathogenesis?
options: Fixed drug eruption; mediated by intraepidermal resident CD8+ T-cells
Erythema multiforme; dermal perivascular immune complex deposition
Drug-induced urticaria; IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation
questions.answer: Fixed drug eruption; mediated by intraepidermal resident CD8+ T-cells
questions.explanation: Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE) is characterized by well-demarcated, solitary or few, dusky-erythematous or violaceous round plaques that recur precisely at the same anatomical site upon re-exposure to the culprit drug (common drugs: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, NSAIDs, paracetamol, tetracyclines). Pathogenesis involves quiescent intraepidermal CD8+ effector memory T cells permanently stationed in the basal epidermis at the site; upon drug re-challenge, they rapidly reactivate and release IFN-gamma and granzyme B, inducing localized basal cell apoptosis.

questions.question: According to the Bastuji-Garin consensus classification, what threshold percentage of detached Body Surface Area (BSA) differentiates Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS), SJS/TEN Overlap, and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)?
questions.prompt: According to the Bastuji-Garin consensus classification, what threshold percentage of detached Body Surface Area (BSA) differentiates Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS), SJS/TEN Overlap, and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)?
options: SJS: <10% BSA; Overlap: 10-30% BSA; TEN: >30% BSA
SJS: <20% BSA; Overlap: 20-50% BSA; TEN: >50% BSA
SJS: mucosal only; Overlap: trunk only; TEN: generalized
SJS: <5% BSA; Overlap: 5-15% BSA; TEN: >15% BSA
questions.answer: SJS: <10% BSA; Overlap: 10-30% BSA; TEN: >30% BSA
questions.explanation: SJS and TEN represent points on a clinical severity spectrum of drug-induced epidermal necrolysis characterized by full-thickness epidermal necrosis and extensive mucosal detachments: 1. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS): <10% of total body surface area (BSA) epidermal detachment; 2. SJS/TEN Overlap: 10% to 30% BSA epidermal detachment; 3. Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN / Lyell syndrome): >30% BSA epidermal detachment. Nikolsky sign is positive on erythematous areas.

questions.question: What seven clinical and biochemical prognostic parameters assessed within the first 24 hours of hospital admission constitute the validated SCORTEN score for predicting mortality in Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis?
questions.prompt: What seven clinical and biochemical prognostic parameters assessed within the first 24 hours of hospital admission constitute the validated SCORTEN score for predicting mortality in Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis?
options: Age ≥40, heart rate ≥120, malignancy, BSA ≥10%, urea, glucose, bicarbonate
Fever, leukocytosis, elevated CRP, hypotension, thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, hypoalbuminemia
Male sex, obesity, previous allergy, anemia, elevated ESR, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia
Hypothermia, neutropenia, procalcitonin, acute renal failure, hypokalemia, hyperkalemia
questions.answer: Age ≥40, heart rate ≥120, malignancy, BSA ≥10%, urea, glucose, bicarbonate
questions.explanation: The SCORTEN prognostic score assigns 1 point for each of 7 independent risk factors measured within 24 hours of admission: 1. Age >= 40 years; 2. Heart rate >= 120 beats/min; 3. Presence of underlying malignancy/cancer; 4. Body surface area detached >= 10%; 5. Serum urea (BUN) > 28 mg/dL (10 mmol/L); 6. Serum glucose > 252 mg/dL (14 mmol/L); 7. Serum bicarbonate < 20 mEq/L (20 mmol/L). A score of 0-1 predicts 3% mortality, whereas a score >= 5 predicts >90% mortality.

questions.question: Which human leukocyte antigen (HLA) allele is strongly associated with Carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis in Han Chinese and Southeast Asian populations, making pre-treatment genetic screening mandatory?
questions.prompt: Which human leukocyte antigen (HLA) allele is strongly associated with Carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis in Han Chinese and Southeast Asian populations, making pre-treatment genetic screening mandatory?
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN is extraordinarily linked to the HLA-B*15:02 allele in Southeast Asian populations (odds ratio >1000 in Han Chinese, Thai, and Malaysian patients). The FDA and international guidelines mandate genetic screening for HLA-B*15:02 prior to initiating carbamazepine in these ethnic groups. In comparison, HLA-B*58:01 is associated with Allopurinol-induced SJS/TEN, and HLA-B*57:01 with Abacavir hypersensitivity.

questions.question: A 38-year-old male develops high remittent fever, facial edema, diffuse morbilliform exanthem, tender generalized lymphadenopathy, marked peripheral eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count 2800/mcL), and marked hepatic transaminitis (ALT 650 IU/L), 4 weeks after initiating Carbamazepine for seizures. Serology demonstrates reactivation of Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6). What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 38-year-old male develops high remittent fever, facial edema, diffuse morbilliform exanthem, tender generalized lymphadenopathy, marked peripheral eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count 2800/mcL), and marked hepatic transaminitis (ALT 650 IU/L), 4 weeks after initiating Carbamazepine for seizures. Serology demonstrates reactivation of Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6). What is the diagnosis?
options: DRESS syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms)
questions.answer: DRESS syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms)
questions.explanation: DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms / Drug-Induced Hypersensitivity Syndrome - DIHS) is a severe, life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction. Hallmark features: prolonged latency (2 to 8 weeks after starting the drug; high-risk drugs: aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfasalazine, dapsone), severe facial edema, diffuse maculopapular exanthem, atypical lymphocytosis, prominent eosinophilia, visceral organ damage (hepatitis in >70%, nephritis, pneumonitis), and frequent reactivation of latent HHV-6 and EBV.

questions.question: A 45-year-old female presents with acute high fever, leukocytosis with marked neutrophilia, and the sudden eruption of hundreds of small (<5 mm), non-follicular, sterile pustules arising on a widespread edematous, fiery erythematous background, 36 hours after initiating oral Amoxicillin. Skin biopsy demonstrates subcorneal spongiform pustules packed with neutrophils and dermal edema. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old female presents with acute high fever, leukocytosis with marked neutrophilia, and the sudden eruption of hundreds of small (<5 mm), non-follicular, sterile pustules arising on a widespread edematous, fiery erythematous background, 36 hours after initiating oral Amoxicillin. Skin biopsy demonstrates subcorneal spongiform pustules packed with neutrophils and dermal edema. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute Generalized Exanthematous Pustulosis (AGEP) is a severe cutaneous adverse reaction typically triggered by antibiotics (beta-lactams, macrolides, quinolones) in >80% of cases. Distinctive features: very short latency period (less than 24 to 48 hours post-ingestion), sudden onset of high fever, marked peripheral blood neutrophilia (>7000/mcL), and hundreds of tiny, discrete, non-follicular sterile pustules coalescing over flexural and intertriginous folds, rapidly resolving with desquamation within 10-14 days.

questions.question: A 24-year-old patient taking long-term oral Minocycline for cystic acne develops a distinct blue-gray to bluish-black pigmentation localized to the anterior shins and ankles, sclerae, and mucosal alveolar ridges of the mouth. What is the mechanism of this drug-induced hyperpigmentation?
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old patient taking long-term oral Minocycline for cystic acne develops a distinct blue-gray to bluish-black pigmentation localized to the anterior shins and ankles, sclerae, and mucosal alveolar ridges of the mouth. What is the mechanism of this drug-induced hyperpigmentation?
options: Dermal accumulation of insoluble complexes of minocycline metabolites and iron/hemosiderin within macrophages
Stimulation of epidermal melanogenesis via MSH receptor upregulation
Permanent covalent binding of minocycline to keratinocyte nuclei
Direct extravasation of bile pigments into the stratum basale
questions.answer: Dermal accumulation of insoluble complexes of minocycline metabolites and iron/hemosiderin within macrophages
questions.explanation: Minocycline causes three types of cutaneous pigmentation: Type I (blue-black pigment in scars/acne lesions); Type II (blue-gray pigmentation of the anterior shins, ankles, and forearms); Type III (diffuse muddy-brown pigmentation in sun-exposed areas). Type II pigmentation is caused by dermal deposition of minocycline-iron chelates and hemosiderin-like pigment complexes engulfed by dermal macrophages and perivascular histiocytes.

questions.question: A 62-year-old male with atrial fibrillation on long-term Amiodarone therapy complains that his skin has turned a striking slate-gray to bluish-violaceous hue on sun-exposed areas of his face and hands ('smurf skin'). What is the underlying pathology of this amiodarone-induced pigmentation?
questions.prompt: A 62-year-old male with atrial fibrillation on long-term Amiodarone therapy complains that his skin has turned a striking slate-gray to bluish-violaceous hue on sun-exposed areas of his face and hands ('smurf skin'). What is the underlying pathology of this amiodarone-induced pigmentation?
options: Lipofuscin and drug metabolites within lysosomal inclusion bodies
Melanin hyperproduction stimulated by alpha-MSH in basal layer
Hemosiderin extravasation surrounding subcutaneous eccrine coils
Silver nanoparticle precipitation along elastic fibers
questions.answer: Lipofuscin and drug metabolites within lysosomal inclusion bodies
questions.explanation: Amiodarone (which contains iodine) causes two distinct dermatological side effects: acute phototoxicity (erythema, burning) in up to 50% of patients, and distinctive slate-gray to bluish-violaceous pigmentation of photo-exposed facial skin in 1-2% of patients taking high doses (>400 mg/day for >1-2 years). Histology and electron microscopy reveal yellow-brown lipofuscin granules and membrane-bound electron-dense lysosomal inclusions (myeloid bodies) within dermal macrophages.

questions.question: A 45-year-old male receiving Phenytoin for post-traumatic epilepsy develops DRESS syndrome. Why must aromatic anticonvulsants (Phenytoin, Carbamazepine, and Phenobarbital) ALL be permanently avoided in this patient?
