questions.prompt: What biological tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) inhibitor is officially approved for the systemic treatment of moderate-to-severe, treatment-refractory Hidradenitis Suppurativa (Hurley Stage II and III)?
questions.explanation: Adalimumab (a fully human monoclonal anti-TNF-alpha IgG1 antibody) was the first biologic approved for moderate-to-severe Hidradenitis Suppurativa. Massive overexpression of TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, and IL-17 in HS lesions drives chronic follicular occlusion, suppurative inflammation, and tissue destruction. Weekly maintenance dosing of Adalimumab significantly reduces inflammatory nodule and abscess counts (HiSCR response).

questions.question: A 24-year-old female presents with intensely pruritic, monomorphic, flesh-colored to yellowish, dome-shaped follicular papules confined strictly to both axillae, areolae of the breasts, and pubic area, which become much more pruritic during emotional stress and hot weather. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old female presents with intensely pruritic, monomorphic, flesh-colored to yellowish, dome-shaped follicular papules confined strictly to both axillae, areolae of the breasts, and pubic area, which become much more pruritic during emotional stress and hot weather. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fox-Fordyce disease (apocrine miliaria) is a chronic inflammatory disorder occurring almost exclusively in post-pubertal females (aged 13-35 years). It is caused by keratinous plugging of the apocrine duct infundibulum, causing sweat retention, rupture of the intraepidermal duct, and intense spongiotic microvesiculation. Hallmarks: intensely pruritic, monomorphic, dome-shaped follicular papules localized strictly to apocrine-bearing areas (axillae, areolae, umbilicus, pubic region).

questions.question: What neurochemical mechanism explains why intradermal injections of Botulinum Toxin Type A provide prolonged, profound relief (6 to 9 months) in severe Primary Focal Palmar and Axillary Hyperhidrosis?
questions.prompt: What neurochemical mechanism explains why intradermal injections of Botulinum Toxin Type A provide prolonged, profound relief (6 to 9 months) in severe Primary Focal Palmar and Axillary Hyperhidrosis?
options: Cleaves SNAP-25, blocking presynaptic acetylcholine release at eccrine glands
Competitive antagonist at postjunctional muscarinic M3 receptors
Destroys sympathetic chain ganglia through coagulative necrosis
Blocks apical membrane voltage-gated chloride channels in coils
questions.answer: Cleaves SNAP-25, blocking presynaptic acetylcholine release at eccrine glands
questions.explanation: Eccrine sweat glands are anatomically innervated by postganglionic sympathetic fibers that are uniquely CHOLINERGIC (releasing acetylcholine, not norepinephrine). Botulinum toxin Type A enters presynaptic nerve endings and enzymatically cleaves SNAP-25 (a core SNARE protein), preventing the docking and fusion of acetylcholine vesicles with the presynaptic membrane, thereby abolishing neuroglandular stimulation and sweat secretion for 6 to 9 months.

questions.question: In the normal human hair growth cycle, what are the three sequential physiological phases of a follicular unit, their average durations, and the percentage of scalp hairs normally residing in each phase?
questions.prompt: In the normal human hair growth cycle, what are the three sequential physiological phases of a follicular unit, their average durations, and the percentage of scalp hairs normally residing in each phase?
options: Anagen: 2-6 years (85-90%); Catagen: 2-3 weeks (1-2%); Telogen: 3 months (10-15%)
Anagen: 1 year (50%); Catagen: 5 years (40%); Telogen: 1 week (10%)
Anagen: 3 months (90%); Catagen: 6 months (5%); Telogen: 1 year (5%)
Anagen: 2 weeks (80%); Catagen: 10 years (15%); Telogen: 2 years (5%)
questions.answer: Anagen: 2-6 years (85-90%); Catagen: 2-3 weeks (1-2%); Telogen: 3 months (10-15%)
questions.explanation: The hair cycle consists of: 1. Anagen (active growth phase): lasts 2 to 6 years, determines hair length, accounts for 85-90% of scalp hairs; 2. Catagen (transition/regression phase): apoptosis-driven involution of the lower two-thirds of the follicle, lasts 2 to 3 weeks, accounts for 1-2% of hairs; 3. Telogen (resting phase): club hair forms, lasts ~3 months (100 days), accounts for 10-15% of hairs, culminating in exogen (shedding).

questions.question: A 24-year-old male presents with the sudden appearance of a completely smooth, round, well-circumscribed, non-scarring patch of hair loss on his beard and scalp. Trichoscopic examination at the active advancing border demonstrates short, fractured hairs whose proximal shaft near the scalp is thin and hypopigmented while the distal end is dark and expanded ('exclamation-mark hairs'). What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male presents with the sudden appearance of a completely smooth, round, well-circumscribed, non-scarring patch of hair loss on his beard and scalp. Trichoscopic examination at the active advancing border demonstrates short, fractured hairs whose proximal shaft near the scalp is thin and hypopigmented while the distal end is dark and expanded ('exclamation-mark hairs'). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition caused by collapse of hair follicle immune privilege in the anagen bulb driven by CD8+ NKG2D+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes. Hallmark: round, smooth, non-scarring bald patches. Pathognomonic dermoscopic/trichoscopic feature at the active perimeter: 'exclamation-mark hairs' (micro-attenuation of the hair shaft near the scalp due to transient inflammation of the matrix, snapping as it emerges).

questions.question: What clinical pattern of Alopecia Areata is characterized by a wave of band-like hair loss running along the lower posterior occipital and temporal margins of the scalp, and is notoriously refractory to conventional therapy?
questions.prompt: What clinical pattern of Alopecia Areata is characterized by a wave of band-like hair loss running along the lower posterior occipital and temporal margins of the scalp, and is notoriously refractory to conventional therapy?
questions.explanation: Ophiasis (derived from the Greek 'ophis' = snake, describing its serpentine distribution) is a distinct clinical variant of alopecia areata where hair loss follows a winding, band-like track along the temporal and lower occipital scalp margins. It is strongly associated with atopic diathesis, carries a poor prognosis for spontaneous regrowth, and is notoriously resistant to standard intralesional corticosteroids and systemic therapy.

questions.question: What class of targeted small-molecule oral therapeutics (such as Baricitinib and Ritlecitinib) has been approved for severe Alopecia Areata, acting by disrupting the interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) and interleukin-15 (IL-15) signaling cascades to restore follicular immune privilege?
questions.prompt: What class of targeted small-molecule oral therapeutics (such as Baricitinib and Ritlecitinib) has been approved for severe Alopecia Areata, acting by disrupting the interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) and interleukin-15 (IL-15) signaling cascades to restore follicular immune privilege?
questions.explanation: In alopecia areata, CD8+ T cells secrete IFN-gamma, which signals through the JAK1/JAK2 pathway to induce follicular epithelial cells to secrete IL-15. IL-15 then binds IL-15R on CD8+ T cells (signaling through JAK1/JAK3) to promote cytotoxic granzyme and perforin release. Oral JAK inhibitors (such as Baricitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, and Ritlecitinib, a JAK3/TEC inhibitor) interrupt this feed-forward loop, suppressing follicular inflammation and restoring anagen hair regrowth.

questions.question: Which validated clinical classification scales are used to grade the progressive severity of Male-Pattern Hair Loss versus Female-Pattern Hair Loss, respectively?
questions.prompt: Which validated clinical classification scales are used to grade the progressive severity of Male-Pattern Hair Loss versus Female-Pattern Hair Loss, respectively?
options: Hamilton-Norwood scale for males; Ludwig scale (or Sinclair scale) for females
Hunt-Hess scale for males; Glasgow scale for females
Enneking scale for males; Mankin scale for females
Risser scale for males; Tanner scale for females
questions.answer: Hamilton-Norwood scale for males; Ludwig scale (or Sinclair scale) for females
questions.explanation: Androgenetic alopecia severity is graded using standardized morphological scales: 1. Hamilton-Norwood classification for males: grades frontotemporal recession (Types I-III) progressing to vertex thinning (Type IV-V) and confluence leaving only an occipitotemporal rim (Types VI-VII); 2. Ludwig scale for females: evaluates progressive, diffuse centrifugal thinning over the crown and vertex with strict preservation of the frontal hairline (Grades I, II, and III).

questions.question: What is the precise enzymatic mechanism and hormonal metabolite responsible for driving follicular miniaturization in Androgenetic Alopecia (pattern hair loss)?
questions.prompt: What is the precise enzymatic mechanism and hormonal metabolite responsible for driving follicular miniaturization in Androgenetic Alopecia (pattern hair loss)?
options: Type II 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to DHT, miniaturizing hairs
Aromatase converts androstenedione to estradiol, inducing premature teloptosis
17-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase converts DHEA to cortisol, destroying bulges
Steroid sulfatase hydrolyzes DHEA-S, triggering lymphocytic follicular scarring
questions.answer: Type II 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to DHT, miniaturizing hairs
questions.explanation: In androgenetic alopecia, genetically susceptible dermal papillae hair follicles express high levels of the intracellular enzyme Type II 5-alpha reductase. This enzyme converts circulating Testosterone into Dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which has a 5-fold higher binding affinity for the androgen receptor. DHT-receptor complexes alter gene expression, shortening the anagen growth phase from years to months and progressively transforming large, pigmented terminal hairs into microscopic, non-pigmented vellus hairs.

questions.question: What is the pharmacological mechanism of action of oral Finasteride in the treatment of Male Androgenetic Alopecia, and why is its handling strictly prohibited by women who are pregnant or may become pregnant?
questions.prompt: What is the pharmacological mechanism of action of oral Finasteride in the treatment of Male Androgenetic Alopecia, and why is its handling strictly prohibited by women who are pregnant or may become pregnant?
options: Type II 5-alpha reductase inhibitor; causes male fetal feminization
Androgen receptor antagonist; induces maternal ventricular arrhythmias
Lanosterol demethylase inhibitor; induces fatal fetal aplasia cutis
Dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor; triggers severe maternal megaloblastic anemia
questions.answer: Type II 5-alpha reductase inhibitor; causes male fetal feminization
questions.explanation: Finasteride is a synthetic 4-azasteroid that acts as a potent, competitive, selective inhibitor of the Type II 5-alpha reductase isoenzyme, suppressing serum and scalp DHT concentrations by >70%. Because DHT is absolutely essential for the normal differentiation of external male genitalia during fetal organogenesis, pregnant women must never ingest or even handle crushed/broken finasteride tablets due to transdermal absorption risking severe pseudohermaphroditism and hypospadias in a male fetus.

questions.question: A 28-year-old female presents with acute, diffuse shedding of hair across her entire scalp that began abruptly 10 weeks after a severe bout of high-grade dengue fever and hospitalization. A gentle hair pull test extracts over 15 hairs, all of which exhibit uniform, non-dystrophic, club-shaped bulbs without root sheaths under light microscopy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old female presents with acute, diffuse shedding of hair across her entire scalp that began abruptly 10 weeks after a severe bout of high-grade dengue fever and hospitalization. A gentle hair pull test extracts over 15 hairs, all of which exhibit uniform, non-dystrophic, club-shaped bulbs without root sheaths under light microscopy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute Telogen Effluvium is a non-scarring, diffuse alopecia occurring characteristically 2 to 3 months (the duration of the normal telogen phase) after a major systemic physiological or metabolic insult (high fever, severe infection, major surgery, hemorrhage, childbirth [telogen gravidarum], or crash dieting). The stress prematurely precipitates up to 30-50% of growing anagen hairs into catagen and telogen, resulting in massive, synchronous club hair shedding 100 days later.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman undergoing systemic intravenous chemotherapy with Doxorubicin and Cyclophosphamide for breast cancer presents with dramatic, near-complete hair loss that began just 10 days after her first chemotherapy infusion. Microscopic examination of shed hairs reveals fractured, tapered, pencil-point proximal hair shafts. What is the mechanism of this hair loss?
questions.prompt: A 42-year-old woman undergoing systemic intravenous chemotherapy with Doxorubicin and Cyclophosphamide for breast cancer presents with dramatic, near-complete hair loss that began just 10 days after her first chemotherapy infusion. Microscopic examination of shed hairs reveals fractured, tapered, pencil-point proximal hair shafts. What is the mechanism of this hair loss?
options: Anagen effluvium; acute mitotic arrest of matrix keratinocytes
Telogen effluvium; synchronized premature entry into resting telogen
Alopecia areata; autoimmune CD8+ attack against hair bulb
Trichotillomania; mechanical fracture of shafts with trichomalacia
questions.answer: Anagen effluvium; acute mitotic arrest of matrix keratinocytes
questions.explanation: Anagen effluvium is caused by an acute, catastrophic insult to the rapidly dividing keratinocytes in the anagen hair bulb (matrix cells, which have the highest mitotic rate in the human body). Cytotoxic chemotherapy or ionizing radiation abruptly halts DNA synthesis and mitosis: the hair shaft thins acutely, narrows, and fractures inside the follicular canal or at the skin surface within 1 to 2 weeks of exposure. The hair roots show characteristic tapered, pencil-point, dysplastic proximal ends.

questions.question: An 11-year-old girl is brought by her parents with an irregular, bizarre-shaped, asymmetrical patch of hair loss on her right frontoparietal scalp. Trichoscopy demonstrates hairs fractured at varying, uneven lengths from the scalp surface, coiled/corkscrew hairs, broom hairs, and black dots, with completely healthy, non-inflamed underlying scalp skin. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: An 11-year-old girl is brought by her parents with an irregular, bizarre-shaped, asymmetrical patch of hair loss on her right frontoparietal scalp. Trichoscopy demonstrates hairs fractured at varying, uneven lengths from the scalp surface, coiled/corkscrew hairs, broom hairs, and black dots, with completely healthy, non-inflamed underlying scalp skin. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Trichotillomania is an obsessive-compulsive related disorder characterized by repetitive, compulsive manual pulling of one's own hair. Clinical hallmarks: irregular, geometric, bizarrely contoured patches of incomplete baldness (usually on the side of the dominant hand); hairs are broken at varying lengths; exclamation-mark hairs are absent; the scalp skin is normal and non-scarred. Trichoscopy shows fractured shafts, trichoptilosis (split ends), flame hairs, and coiled hair remnants.

questions.question: Which clinical presentation of onychomycosis is recognized as a specific, highly sensitive clinical cutaneous marker of severe immunosuppression and advanced HIV infection?
questions.prompt: Which clinical presentation of onychomycosis is recognized as a specific, highly sensitive clinical cutaneous marker of severe immunosuppression and advanced HIV infection?
questions.explanation: While Distal and Lateral Subungual Onychomycosis (DLSO) is by far the most common pattern in immunocompetent hosts, Proximal Subungual Onychomycosis (PSO)—where the fungus penetrates directly into the proximal nail fold and invades the newly formed nail plate from the matrix—is exceedingly rare in healthy individuals. It is considered an important clinical cutaneous hallmark of advanced HIV/AIDS (CD4 count <200 cells/mcL) and profound immunosuppression.

questions.question: A 35-year-old male presents with transverse, horizontal, band-like depressions running across all twenty nail plates at exactly the same distance from the proximal nail fold. History reveals he suffered a life-threatening episode of septic shock requiring intensive care 3 months ago. What are these diagnostic grooves termed?
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old male presents with transverse, horizontal, band-like depressions running across all twenty nail plates at exactly the same distance from the proximal nail fold. History reveals he suffered a life-threatening episode of septic shock requiring intensive care 3 months ago. What are these diagnostic grooves termed?
questions.explanation: Beau's lines are transverse, horizontal linear depressions traversing the entire width of the nail plate. They reflect a temporary, acute, reversible arrest of mitotic division in the proximal nail matrix caused by severe systemic physiological stress (high fever, sepsis, myocardial infarction, chemotherapy). Because normal fingernails grow at ~3 mm/month (0.1 mm/day), the exact distance of the groove from the cuticle allows dating of the antecedent illness.

questions.question: A 28-year-old female presents with severe fatigue, pallor, and spoon-shaped fingernails characterized by central concavity and everted, upturned lateral and distal edges capable of holding a drop of water without spilling ('koilonychia'). What is the most common underlying hematological etiology?
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old female presents with severe fatigue, pallor, and spoon-shaped fingernails characterized by central concavity and everted, upturned lateral and distal edges capable of holding a drop of water without spilling ('koilonychia'). What is the most common underlying hematological etiology?
options: Severe chronic iron deficiency anemia (with or without Plummer-Vinson syndrome)
questions.answer: Severe chronic iron deficiency anemia (with or without Plummer-Vinson syndrome)
questions.explanation: Koilonychia (spoon nails) is an abnormal nail plate dystrophy where the normal convex curvature is inverted, forming a saucer-like or spoon-like central depression. The classic physical examination test is the 'water-drop test' (a drop of water placed on the nail plate remains pooled without rolling off). Severe, chronic iron deficiency anemia is by far the most frequent systemic cause (also seen in hemochromatosis and Plummer-Vinson syndrome).

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy presents with uniform, severe dystrophic changes affecting all twenty fingernails and toenails. Every nail plate appears dull, opaque, lusterless, fragile, and marked by excessive fine longitudinal striations and superficial scaling, giving a rough 'sandpaper' texture. What is this entity termed, and with which three dermatoses is it classically associated?
questions.prompt: An 8-year-old boy presents with uniform, severe dystrophic changes affecting all twenty fingernails and toenails. Every nail plate appears dull, opaque, lusterless, fragile, and marked by excessive fine longitudinal striations and superficial scaling, giving a rough 'sandpaper' texture. What is this entity termed, and with which three dermatoses is it classically associated?
options: Trachyonychia (Twenty-Nail Dystrophy); Alopecia areata, Lichen planus, and Psoriasis
Pachyonychia congenita; Epidermolysis bullosa, Darier disease, and Hailey-Hailey disease
questions.answer: Trachyonychia (Twenty-Nail Dystrophy); Alopecia areata, Lichen planus, and Psoriasis
questions.explanation: Trachyonychia (Twenty-Nail Dystrophy / sandpaper nails) is a benign inflammatory matrix dystrophy affecting children and young adults. All 20 nails (or a subset) become uniformly rough, dull, grayish, brittle, and covered by prominent longitudinal ridging likened to rough sandpaper. Nail matrix biopsy reveals that trachyonychia is not a distinct disease, but an idiopathic phenotypic expression of Lichen Planus (spongiotic or lichenoid matrix inflammation), Alopecia Areata, or Psoriasis.

questions.question: What classic clinical triad defines Yellow Nail Syndrome, a rare systemic disorder characterized by complete cessation of nail plate growth?
questions.prompt: What classic clinical triad defines Yellow Nail Syndrome, a rare systemic disorder characterized by complete cessation of nail plate growth?
options: Yellow nails, primary lymphedema, and chronic respiratory disease
Yellow nails, chronic renal failure, and hepatosplenomegaly
Yellow nails, sensory peripheral neuropathy, and corneal opacities
Yellow nails, multiple endocrine neoplasia, and cutaneous neurofibromas
questions.answer: Yellow nails, primary lymphedema, and chronic respiratory disease
questions.explanation: Yellow Nail Syndrome is a rare clinical entity defined by the classic triad of: 1. Characteristic nail changes: nail growth slows to <0.1 mm/week, nails become thickened, pale yellow-to-green, excessively curved transversely, with loss of the lunula and cuticle; 2. Chronic lymphedema (present in 80%, typically bilateral lower limbs); 3. Chronic respiratory tract manifestations (exudative pleural effusions, bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis). The underlying defect is congenital or acquired lymphatic microangiopathy.

questions.question: Which anatomical landmark feature definitively distinguishes the classic acute Malar 'Butterfly' Rash of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) from the facial eruptions of Rosacea and Seborrheic Dermatitis?
questions.prompt: Which anatomical landmark feature definitively distinguishes the classic acute Malar 'Butterfly' Rash of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) from the facial eruptions of Rosacea and Seborrheic Dermatitis?
options: Strict sparing of the nasolabial folds
Involvement of the upper eyelids with violaceous edema
Presence of central comedones and purulent pustules
Greasy, yellowish scales confined to the eyebrows
questions.answer: Strict sparing of the nasolabial folds
questions.explanation: The classic acute cutaneous lupus erythematous rash is the malar ('butterfly') rash: an erythematous, edematous plaque distributed symmetrically across the bridge of the nose and both malar eminences. Its cardinal, pathognomonic diagnostic feature is the strict SPARING of the nasolabial folds (due to anatomical shadowing from UV light). In contrast, seborrheic dermatitis and rosacea characteristically involve the nasolabial folds.

questions.question: A 36-year-old male presents with chronic, scarring, well-demarcated, coin-shaped erythematous plaques on his scalp and face with adherent hyperkeratotic scales. When the scale is peeled back, small horny keratotic plugs are seen projecting from the undersurface, corresponding to patent follicular orifices ('carpet-tack sign' / tin-tack sign). As lesions resolve, they produce permanent cicatricial alopecia and depigmentation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 36-year-old male presents with chronic, scarring, well-demarcated, coin-shaped erythematous plaques on his scalp and face with adherent hyperkeratotic scales. When the scale is peeled back, small horny keratotic plugs are seen projecting from the undersurface, corresponding to patent follicular orifices ('carpet-tack sign' / tin-tack sign). As lesions resolve, they produce permanent cicatricial alopecia and depigmentation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE) is the most common form of chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Triad of progression: 1. Inflammatory active erythema with adherent hyperkeratotic scale; 2. Follicular plugging (carpet-tack or tin-tack sign, where keratotic spicules project from the underside of peeled scale); 3. End-stage central atrophic scarring, telangiectasia, follicular obliteration (permanent cicatricial alopecia), and hyperpigmented margins with central depigmentation.

questions.question: A 30-year-old female presents with a non-scarring, non-indurated, widespread annular and polycyclic erythematous eruption over her shoulders, upper back, and V-neck area triggered by sun exposure. Serological evaluation demonstrates high-titer anti-Ro/SSA antibodies. What variant of cutaneous lupus is this, and what fetal complication is associated if she becomes pregnant?
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old female presents with a non-scarring, non-indurated, widespread annular and polycyclic erythematous eruption over her shoulders, upper back, and V-neck area triggered by sun exposure. Serological evaluation demonstrates high-titer anti-Ro/SSA antibodies. What variant of cutaneous lupus is this, and what fetal complication is associated if she becomes pregnant?
options: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE); complete congenital fetal heart block
Systemic sclerosis; fetal limb reduction defects
Lupus profundus; neonatal polycystic kidney disease
questions.answer: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE); complete congenital fetal heart block
questions.explanation: Subacute Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (SCLE) presents with non-scarring annular/polycyclic or papulosquamous plaques on sun-exposed upper trunk and arms. It is extraordinarily linked to anti-Ro/SSA antibodies (>80%) and HLA-DR3. Transplacental crossing of maternal anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB IgG antibodies between weeks 16-24 of gestation can attack the fetal cardiac conduction system, producing irreversible congenital complete heart block (Neonatal Lupus Erythematosus).

questions.question: What critical diagnostic and prognostic distinction is established by the 'Lupus Band Test' on Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF)?
questions.prompt: What critical diagnostic and prognostic distinction is established by the 'Lupus Band Test' on Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF)?
options: Granular band in normal sun-protected skin confirms systemic lupus
Band positivity in oral mucosa confirms Behçet disease
Linear band of IgA along the basement membrane confirms Pemphigus
Deposition of IgE along dermal papillae confirms Atopic dermatitis
questions.answer: Granular band in normal sun-protected skin confirms systemic lupus
questions.explanation: The Lupus Band Test (LBT) is Direct Immunofluorescence demonstrating a continuous, granular band of immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM) and complement (C3) along the basement membrane zone: 1. Positive in LESIONAL skin: seen in >90% of Discoid Lupus (DLE) and SLE; 2. Positive in SUN-EXPOSED normal-appearing skin: suggests lupus; 3. Positive in NON-LESIONAL, SUN-PROTECTED skin (e.g., inner arm or buttocks): highly specific for active, severe Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) with high risk of lupus nephritis.

questions.question: A 46-year-old female presents with symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, difficulty climbing stairs, and a violaceous, dusky-erythematous periorbital edema involving both upper eyelids ('heliotrope rash'). Physical examination of the hands reveals pathognomonic violaceous, flat-topped, lichenoid papules and plaques overlying the dorsal aspect of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and interphalangeal (IP) joints. What are these joint papules termed, and what is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 46-year-old female presents with symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, difficulty climbing stairs, and a violaceous, dusky-erythematous periorbital edema involving both upper eyelids ('heliotrope rash'). Physical examination of the hands reveals pathognomonic violaceous, flat-topped, lichenoid papules and plaques overlying the dorsal aspect of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and interphalangeal (IP) joints. What are these joint papules termed, and what is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dermatomyositis is an idiopathic autoimmune inflammatory myopathy with distinct cutaneous features. Gottron papules are pathognomonic: violaceous, flat-topped lichenoid papules symmetrically overlying the dorsal MCP, PIP, and DIP joints (in contrast to SLE, which preferentially targets the interphalangeal spaces between joints, SPARING the knuckles). The Heliotrope rash (violaceous periorbital edema resembling the heliotrope flower) is also pathognomonic.

questions.question: A 52-year-old female presents with clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis, rapidly progressive fatal interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD), and painful, refractory cutaneous vasculitic ulcers over the digital pulp and palmar creases. Which specific myositis-specific autoantibody is strongly linked to this lethal phenotype?
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old female presents with clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis, rapidly progressive fatal interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD), and painful, refractory cutaneous vasculitic ulcers over the digital pulp and palmar creases. Which specific myositis-specific autoantibody is strongly linked to this lethal phenotype?
questions.explanation: Anti-MDA5 (melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5) autoantibodies define a clinically distinct and aggressive subgroup of dermatomyositis, characterized by: 1. Little or no muscle weakness (clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis - CADM); 2. Painful cutaneous ulcerations (digital pulp, knuckles, elbows); 3. Palmar violaceous papules; 4. High incidence of rapidly progressive, treatment-resistant interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD) with a catastrophic 6-month mortality rate.

questions.question: A 45-year-old female presents with cold-induced triphasic color changes of her fingers (white to blue to red), sclerodactyly with skin bound down to underlying tissue, beaked facies with microstomia and radial furrowing around the lips, telangiectasias on her face, and subcutaneous calcific nodules over her elbows. Systemic workup confirms the CREST syndrome variant of Limited Systemic Sclerosis. Which circulating autoantibody is highly specific for this limited cutaneous form?
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old female presents with cold-induced triphasic color changes of her fingers (white to blue to red), sclerodactyly with skin bound down to underlying tissue, beaked facies with microstomia and radial furrowing around the lips, telangiectasias on her face, and subcutaneous calcific nodules over her elbows. Systemic workup confirms the CREST syndrome variant of Limited Systemic Sclerosis. Which circulating autoantibody is highly specific for this limited cutaneous form?
questions.explanation: CREST syndrome is the classic clinical manifestation of Limited Cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis (lcSSc): Calcinosis cutis, Raynaud's phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, and Telangiectasia. Skin thickening is restricted to the face and distal extremities below the elbows and knees. Anti-Centromere Antibodies (ACA) are positive in >70-80% of patients with limited disease (predicting isolated pulmonary arterial hypertension), whereas Anti-Scl-70 associates with Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

questions.question: A 50-year-old male with Diffuse Cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis (dcSSc) positive for Anti-RNA Polymerase III antibodies is treated with high-dose systemic oral Prednisolone (40 mg/day) for severe inflammatory joint pain. Within 3 weeks, he develops acute malignant hypertension (BP 220/120 mmHg), encephalopathy, and oliguric acute renal failure with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. What catastrophic iatrogenic complication has been triggered?
questions.prompt: A 50-year-old male with Diffuse Cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis (dcSSc) positive for Anti-RNA Polymerase III antibodies is treated with high-dose systemic oral Prednisolone (40 mg/day) for severe inflammatory joint pain. Within 3 weeks, he develops acute malignant hypertension (BP 220/120 mmHg), encephalopathy, and oliguric acute renal failure with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. What catastrophic iatrogenic complication has been triggered?
questions.explanation: Scleroderma Renal Crisis (SRC) occurs in 10-15% of patients with diffuse systemic sclerosis, characterized by acute abrupt malignant hypertension, oliguric acute kidney injury, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. High-dose corticosteroids (>15 mg/day of prednisone) and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are the two strongest recognized risk factors precipitating SRC. ACE inhibitors (specifically captopril) are the life-saving treatment of choice.

questions.question: A 9-year-old girl presents with a solitary, linear, indurated, ivory-white, scar-like sclerotic band extending vertically down her forehead and frontoparietal scalp, with underlying localized depression and permanent loss of hair along the band ('en coup de sabre'). What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 9-year-old girl presents with a solitary, linear, indurated, ivory-white, scar-like sclerotic band extending vertically down her forehead and frontoparietal scalp, with underlying localized depression and permanent loss of hair along the band ('en coup de sabre'). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Morphea (localized scleroderma) is characterized by sclerosis confined to the skin and subcutaneous tissue without internal organ involvement or Raynaud's phenomenon. Linear Morphea 'en coup de sabre' (resembling the blow of a sabre or sword) typically arises in children on the frontoparietal scalp and paramedian forehead, presenting as an indurated gutter-like groove with cicatricial alopecia, which may be associated with hemifacial atrophy (Parry-Romberg syndrome).

questions.question: A 32-year-old female presents with severe Raynaud's phenomenon, swollen 'puffy' hands with tapering sausage digits, proximal muscle weakness, and polyarthritis, demonstrating overlapping features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis. Serum antinuclear antibody (ANA) shows a high-titer speckled pattern. Which specific autoantibody is pathognomonic for Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD)?
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old female presents with severe Raynaud's phenomenon, swollen 'puffy' hands with tapering sausage digits, proximal muscle weakness, and polyarthritis, demonstrating overlapping features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis. Serum antinuclear antibody (ANA) shows a high-titer speckled pattern. Which specific autoantibody is pathognomonic for Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD)?
questions.explanation: Mixed Connective Tissue Disease (MCTD / Sharp syndrome) is an overlap connective tissue disorder combining clinical hallmarks of systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis/dermatomyositis. The hallmark serological requirement in all diagnostic criteria sets (Alarcón-Segovia, Kasukawa) is the presence of high-titer circulating antibodies directed against U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (U1-RNP), usually in the absence of anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies.

questions.question: A 24-year-old obese male presents with symmetrical, velvety, papillomatous, hyperpigmented, brown-black plaques on the posterior and lateral folds of his neck, axillae, and groins. Skin tags (acrochordons) are scattered throughout the plaques. What is the diagnosis and its primary endocrine pathophysiology?
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old obese male presents with symmetrical, velvety, papillomatous, hyperpigmented, brown-black plaques on the posterior and lateral folds of his neck, axillae, and groins. Skin tags (acrochordons) are scattered throughout the plaques. What is the diagnosis and its primary endocrine pathophysiology?
options: Acanthosis nigricans; hyperinsulinemia stimulating IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes
Hemochromatosis; iron overload stimulating tyrosinase in epidermal basal cells
Addison disease; ACTH stimulating melanocortin-1 receptors directly
Cushing disease; excess cortisol inducing epidermal thinning and lipid synthesis
questions.answer: Acanthosis nigricans; hyperinsulinemia stimulating IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes
questions.explanation: Acanthosis nigricans is characterized by hyperpigmented, velvety, verrucous plaques in intertriginous skin folds (posterior neck, axillae). In benign forms (associated with obesity, Type 2 diabetes mellitus, insulin resistance, and PCOS), severe hyperinsulinemia leads to supra-physiological insulin concentrations that cross-react with and activate Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1) receptors on epidermal keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts, stimulating excessive proliferation.

questions.question: A 38-year-old female with long-standing Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus presents with multiple, shiny, well-demarcated, atrophic, waxy yellowish-brown plaques with prominent surface telangiectasias and violaceous borders on the anterior pretibial shins. Skin biopsy reveals palisading granulomas surrounding degenerated collagen ('necrobiosis') arranged in horizontal parallel tiers throughout the full dermis ('sandwich pattern'). What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 38-year-old female with long-standing Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus presents with multiple, shiny, well-demarcated, atrophic, waxy yellowish-brown plaques with prominent surface telangiectasias and violaceous borders on the anterior pretibial shins. Skin biopsy reveals palisading granulomas surrounding degenerated collagen ('necrobiosis') arranged in horizontal parallel tiers throughout the full dermis ('sandwich pattern'). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Necrobiosis Lipoidica (NL / NLD) is a chronic granulomatous disorder occurring in 0.3-1.2% of diabetic patients, with a 3:1 female predominance. Hallmarks: yellow-brown, waxy, atrophic pretibial plaques where the epidermis thins to allow dermal blood vessels to shine through as prominent telangiectasias. Classic histopathology: alternating horizontal tiers of granulomatous inflammation and degenerated collagen necrosis (necrobiosis) extending from the superficial dermis into the subcutis.

questions.question: A 42-year-old male with severe familial hypertriglyceridemia presents with the explosive, sudden eruption of crops of small (1 to 4 mm), dome-shaped, firm, yellowish-orange papules surrounded by an inflammatory erythematous halo over his buttocks, shoulders, and extensor surfaces of his arms. Serum triglycerides are measured at 2400 mg/dL. What type of xanthoma is this, and what acute medical complication is he at imminent risk of developing?
questions.prompt: A 42-year-old male with severe familial hypertriglyceridemia presents with the explosive, sudden eruption of crops of small (1 to 4 mm), dome-shaped, firm, yellowish-orange papules surrounded by an inflammatory erythematous halo over his buttocks, shoulders, and extensor surfaces of his arms. Serum triglycerides are measured at 2400 mg/dL. What type of xanthoma is this, and what acute medical complication is he at imminent risk of developing?
questions.explanation: Eruptive xanthomas are cutaneous hallmarks of severe chylomicronemia and hypertriglyceridemia (serum triglycerides typically >1000 to 2000 mg/dL; Fredrickson Types I, IV, and V). They present as crops of tiny, tender, yellow-orange papules on an erythematous base on the buttocks, thighs, and extensor limbs. The presence of eruptive xanthomas signals an imminent, life-threatening risk of Acute Pancreatitis, mandating immediate dietary fat restriction and lipid-lowering therapy.

questions.question: A 45-year-old female with severe Graves' ophthalmopathy presents with bilateral, non-pitting, indurated, shiny, purplish-brown plaques and nodules with prominent follicular orifices resembling an 'orange peel' (peau d'orange) on her anterior lower legs and dorsa of feet. What is the diagnosis, and what glycosaminoglycan is massively deposited within the reticular dermis?
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old female with severe Graves' ophthalmopathy presents with bilateral, non-pitting, indurated, shiny, purplish-brown plaques and nodules with prominent follicular orifices resembling an 'orange peel' (peau d'orange) on her anterior lower legs and dorsa of feet. What is the diagnosis, and what glycosaminoglycan is massively deposited within the reticular dermis?
options: Pretibial myxedema (Thyroid dermopathy); Hyaluronic acid (and chondroitin sulfate)
questions.answer: Pretibial myxedema (Thyroid dermopathy); Hyaluronic acid (and chondroitin sulfate)
questions.explanation: Pretibial myxedema (thyroid dermopathy) occurs in 1-5% of patients with Graves' disease, almost always in the presence of severe exophthalmos and high-titer TSH-receptor autoantibodies (TRAb). Stimulated by TRAb, orbital and pretibial dermal fibroblasts proliferate and synthesize colossal amounts of hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans (predominantly hyaluronic acid). The mucin accumulates in the reticular dermis, producing woody, non-pitting, peau d'orange plaques on the pretibial shins.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy fulfills the National Institutes of Health (NIH) consensus diagnostic criteria for Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1 / von Recklinghausen disease). Which specific constellation of cutaneous and ocular signs fulfills these criteria?
questions.prompt: A 7-year-old boy fulfills the National Institutes of Health (NIH) consensus diagnostic criteria for Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1 / von Recklinghausen disease). Which specific constellation of cutaneous and ocular signs fulfills these criteria?
options: ≥6 café-au-lait macules, Crowe sign, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules
Three café-au-lait macules, facial angiofibromas, and shagreen patch
Ash-leaf macules, periungual fibromas, optic glioma, and hypopigmented streaks
Port-wine stain, facial asymmetry, glaucoma, and leptomeningeal angioma
questions.answer: ≥6 café-au-lait macules, Crowe sign, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules
questions.explanation: NIH diagnostic criteria for NF1 require >=2 of the following 7 features: 1. >=6 Café-au-lait macules (>5 mm in prepubertal; >15 mm in postpubertal individuals); 2. >=2 Neurofibromas of any type or 1 plexiform neurofibroma; 3. Crowe sign: axillary or inguinal intertriginous freckling; 4. Optic pathway glioma; 5. >=2 Lisch nodules (melanocytic iris hamartomas on slit-lamp); 6. Distinctive osseous lesion (sphenoid dysplasia or anterolateral bowing/pseudarthrosis of tibia); 7. First-degree relative with NF1.

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy presents with dry, rough skin with fine, polygonal, light gray-to-brown adherent scales on his extensor extremities and back, which began during early infancy. Physical examination demonstrates striking, absolute SPARING of the flexural creases (antecubital and popliteal fossae), hyperlinear palms and soles, and keratosis pilaris on his arms. What is the diagnosis and its inheritance pattern?
questions.prompt: A 14-year-old boy presents with dry, rough skin with fine, polygonal, light gray-to-brown adherent scales on his extensor extremities and back, which began during early infancy. Physical examination demonstrates striking, absolute SPARING of the flexural creases (antecubital and popliteal fossae), hyperlinear palms and soles, and keratosis pilaris on his arms. What is the diagnosis and its inheritance pattern?
options: Ichthyosis vulgaris; Autosomal semidominant (Filaggrin gene mutation)
X-linked recessive ichthyosis; X-linked recessive (Steroid sulfatase deficiency)
questions.answer: Ichthyosis vulgaris; Autosomal semidominant (Filaggrin gene mutation)
questions.explanation: Ichthyosis vulgaris is the most common disorder of cornification (1 in 250 individuals), inherited in an autosomal semidominant pattern with incomplete penetrance, caused by loss-of-function mutations in the Filaggrin (FLG) gene on chromosome 1q21. Hallmark: fine, polygonal, white-to-gray scales with free edges on extensor surfaces with classic, strict SPARING of flexural creases (antecubital, popliteal, axillary vaults), associated with palmar hyperlinearity, keratosis pilaris, and atopy.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy presents with prominent, generalized, thick, dark brown, adherent, polygonal scales over his neck, trunk, and extensor limbs, giving a distinctive 'dirty neck' appearance. The flexural creases are involved, but palms and soles are normal. Corneal examination reveals asymptomatic deep comma-shaped stromal opacities. His mother had an obstetric history of failure of labor progression requiring cesarean delivery. What is the diagnosis and enzymatic deficiency?
questions.prompt: A 12-year-old boy presents with prominent, generalized, thick, dark brown, adherent, polygonal scales over his neck, trunk, and extensor limbs, giving a distinctive 'dirty neck' appearance. The flexural creases are involved, but palms and soles are normal. Corneal examination reveals asymptomatic deep comma-shaped stromal opacities. His mother had an obstetric history of failure of labor progression requiring cesarean delivery. What is the diagnosis and enzymatic deficiency?
options: X-linked recessive ichthyosis; Steroid sulfatase (arylsulfatase C) deficiency
questions.answer: X-linked recessive ichthyosis; Steroid sulfatase (arylsulfatase C) deficiency
questions.explanation: X-linked Recessive Ichthyosis (XLI) affects 1 in 6000 males, caused by deletions or mutations in the STS gene encoding Steroid Sulfatase (arylsulfatase C). Deficiency leads to cholesterol sulfate accumulation in the stratum corneum, inhibiting desquamation. Hallmarks: prominent, dirty-brown, large adherent scales ('dirty neck' sign); asymptomatic deep comma-shaped stromal corneal opacities; cryptorchidism in 20%; and maternal failure of labor progression due to placental steroid sulfatase deficiency.

questions.question: What is the precise ultrastructural cleavage level and molecular target in Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (Hallopeau-Siemens type), an agonizing mechanobullous genodermatosis characterized by severe mucosal strictures, pseudosyndactyly ('mitten-hand' deformities), and aggressive Squamous Cell Carcinoma?
questions.prompt: What is the precise ultrastructural cleavage level and molecular target in Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (Hallopeau-Siemens type), an agonizing mechanobullous genodermatosis characterized by severe mucosal strictures, pseudosyndactyly ('mitten-hand' deformities), and aggressive Squamous Cell Carcinoma?
options: Sublamina densa split with absent type VII collagen fibrils
Intraepidermal basal cell cytolysis; Keratin 14 gene mutation
Intra-lamina lucida split; Laminin-332 gene mutation
Subcorneal granular cell split; Desmoglein 1 mutation
questions.answer: Sublamina densa split with absent type VII collagen fibrils
questions.explanation: Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (RDEB, Hallopeau-Siemens) is caused by biallelic null mutations in the COL7A1 gene encoding Type VII collagen, the primary component of anchoring fibrils that secure the lamina densa to the papillary dermis. Complete loss of anchoring fibrils results in blister cleavage in the SUBLAMINA DENSA zone below the basement membrane. Blisters heal with relentless, mutilating dermal fibrosis, leading to fusion of digits ('mitten hands'), microstomia, esophageal webs, and fatal metastatic SCC.

questions.question: A 3-year-old child presents with multiple ash-leaf-shaped hypopigmented macules on the trunk visualized under Wood's lamp, facial angiofibromas across the malar area, and infantile spasms with cortical tubers on brain MRI. What autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome is this, and which tumor suppressor genes are mutated?
questions.prompt: A 3-year-old child presents with multiple ash-leaf-shaped hypopigmented macules on the trunk visualized under Wood's lamp, facial angiofibromas across the malar area, and infantile spasms with cortical tubers on brain MRI. What autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome is this, and which tumor suppressor genes are mutated?
options: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (Bourneville disease); TSC1 and TSC2 genes
questions.answer: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (Bourneville disease); TSC1 and TSC2 genes
questions.explanation: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC / epiloia) is an autosomal dominant hamartomatous multi-organ phakomatosis caused by mutations in TSC1 (chromosome 9q34, encoding Hamartin) or TSC2 (chromosome 16p13, encoding Tuberin), which form a complex that normally inhibits the mTOR pathway. Cutaneous hallmarks: 1. Ash-leaf hypomelanotic macules (earliest sign, present at birth); 2. Facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum, appearing at 3-5 years); 3. Shagreen patch (connective tissue nevus); 4. Periungual fibromas (Koenen tumors).

questions.question: An 8-year-old girl born to consanguineous parents presents with extreme solar sensitivity resulting in severe sunburns upon minimal UV exposure in infancy, widespread dense freckling, xerosis, poikiloderma on sun-exposed facial skin, and bilateral corneal clouding. By age 7, she has developed multiple primary Basal Cell Carcinomas and invasive Squamous Cell Carcinomas. What DNA repair mechanism is defective in Xeroderma Pigmentosum?
questions.prompt: An 8-year-old girl born to consanguineous parents presents with extreme solar sensitivity resulting in severe sunburns upon minimal UV exposure in infancy, widespread dense freckling, xerosis, poikiloderma on sun-exposed facial skin, and bilateral corneal clouding. By age 7, she has developed multiple primary Basal Cell Carcinomas and invasive Squamous Cell Carcinomas. What DNA repair mechanism is defective in Xeroderma Pigmentosum?
options: Nucleotide excision repair defect failing to excise pyrimidine dimers
Mismatch repair (MMR) pathway, causing microsatellite instability
Base excision repair (BER) pathway, causing 8-hydroxyguanine accumulation
Homologous recombination repair, leading to chromosome fragility
questions.answer: Nucleotide excision repair defect failing to excise pyrimidine dimers
questions.explanation: Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP, complementation groups XPA through XPG) is an autosomal recessive genodermatosis characterized by severe impairment of the Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) multi-enzyme machinery. Cells are completely unable to recognize and excise bulky DNA photoproducts induced by ultraviolet light (such as cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers [CPDs] and 6-4 photoproducts). This produces a >1000-fold to 10,000-fold increase in the incidence of non-melanoma skin cancer and cutaneous melanoma before age 10.

questions.question: A 24-year-old female presents every spring with an intensely itchy, symmetrical eruption of monomorphic erythematous papules, papulovesicles, and plaques on sun-exposed areas (V-neck of chest and dorsal forearms) developing 8 to 24 hours after her first significant seasonal sun exposure. As summer progresses, the eruption gradually decreases in severity despite continued sun exposure ('hardening phenomenon'). What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old female presents every spring with an intensely itchy, symmetrical eruption of monomorphic erythematous papules, papulovesicles, and plaques on sun-exposed areas (V-neck of chest and dorsal forearms) developing 8 to 24 hours after her first significant seasonal sun exposure. As summer progresses, the eruption gradually decreases in severity despite continued sun exposure ('hardening phenomenon'). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Polymorphous Light Eruption (PMLE) is the most common acquired idiopathic photodermatosis worldwide (>10-20% of fair-skinned individuals). It represents a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to a photo-induced cutaneous neoantigen triggered by UVA (and UVB). Hallmarks: delayed onset (hours to days post-exposure), pruritic papules or papulovesicles on exposed skin (sparing the face due to habitual exposure), and the pathognomonic 'hardening' phenomenon (tolerance develops through repetitive sun exposure by late summer).

questions.question: A 52-year-old male with chronic Hepatitis C infection and alcohol use presents with extreme skin fragility and tense bullae on the dorsa of his hands that rupture upon trivial friction, healing with milia, pigment changes, and atrophic scars. Examination reveals dark brown facial hyperpigmentation and prominent hypertrichosis on his temples and cheeks. Urine examined under Wood's light emits a brilliant coral-pink to red fluorescence. What is the diagnosis and the defective enzyme?
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old male with chronic Hepatitis C infection and alcohol use presents with extreme skin fragility and tense bullae on the dorsa of his hands that rupture upon trivial friction, healing with milia, pigment changes, and atrophic scars. Examination reveals dark brown facial hyperpigmentation and prominent hypertrichosis on his temples and cheeks. Urine examined under Wood's light emits a brilliant coral-pink to red fluorescence. What is the diagnosis and the defective enzyme?
options: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT); Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) deficiency
Acute intermittent porphyria; Porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency
questions.answer: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT); Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) deficiency
questions.explanation: Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT) is the most common porphyria, caused by acquired or hereditary deficiency of hepatic Uroporphyrinogen Decarboxylase (UROD). Uroporphyrins accumulate in the blood and deposit in skin, where absorption of Soret band light (400-410 nm) generates reactive oxygen species. Hallmarks: mechanobullous skin fragility on dorsal hands with milia, facial hypertrichosis, and dark tea-colored urine that fluoresces brilliant coral-pink under Wood's lamp (365 nm UVA). High association with Hepatitis C virus.

questions.question: Which clinical and immunological characteristics distinguish a Phototoxic Drug Eruption from a Photoallergic Drug Eruption?
questions.prompt: Which clinical and immunological characteristics distinguish a Phototoxic Drug Eruption from a Photoallergic Drug Eruption?
options: Phototoxicity is dose-dependent non-immunologic sunburn; Photoallergy is type IV eczematous allergy
Phototoxicity requires 2 weeks sensitization; Photoallergy occurs on first exposure
Phototoxicity is mediated by circulating IgE antibodies causing urticarial wheals
Photoallergy is universal dose-dependent toxicity resolving within 2 hours
questions.answer: Phototoxicity is dose-dependent non-immunologic sunburn; Photoallergy is type IV eczematous allergy
questions.explanation: Phototoxicity: 1. Non-immunologic direct cellular damage by photoactivated drug radicals; 2. Dose-dependent (occurs in anyone given sufficient drug + UV dose); 3. Rapid onset (minutes to hours); 4. Morphologically resembles an exaggerated, severe sunburn (erythema, edema, bullae); 5. Strictly delimited to exposed skin (sharp cutoffs at clothing lines); common drugs: Doxycycline, amiodarone, thiazides. Photoallergy: Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity; eczematous; spreads beyond exposed skin; requires prior sensitization.

questions.question: A 28-year-old female develops intensely pruritic, erythematous, edematous wheals and flares across all uncovered skin within 5 to 10 minutes of direct sunlight exposure, which completely vanish within 1 to 2 hours after she steps into indoor shade. Phototesting with visible light and UVA reproduces identical hives. What is this physical photodermatosis termed?
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old female develops intensely pruritic, erythematous, edematous wheals and flares across all uncovered skin within 5 to 10 minutes of direct sunlight exposure, which completely vanish within 1 to 2 hours after she steps into indoor shade. Phototesting with visible light and UVA reproduces identical hives. What is this physical photodermatosis termed?
questions.explanation: Solar urticaria is an uncommon, chronic physical inducible urticaria where direct exposure to sunlight (UVA, UVB, or visible light) triggers wheal-and-flare formation within 5 to 10 minutes. It is mediated by a Type I (immediate) IgE-dependent hypersensitivity reaction: a light-induced chromophore in the skin acts as a photoallergen that binds circulating IgE, triggering immediate mast cell degranulation. Wheals resolve rapidly (<1-2 hours) after UV exposure ceases.

questions.question: A 24-year-old male bartender squeezed dozens of fresh limes for cocktails at an outdoor beach party on a sunny afternoon. Two days later, he develops painless, linear, streaked, bizarre-shaped erythematous macules and bullae on the dorsa of his hands, which heal leaving behind dense, dark brown hyperpigmentation that persists for months ('margarita photodermatitis'). What is the diagnosis and the responsible photochemical?
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male bartender squeezed dozens of fresh limes for cocktails at an outdoor beach party on a sunny afternoon. Two days later, he develops painless, linear, streaked, bizarre-shaped erythematous macules and bullae on the dorsa of his hands, which heal leaving behind dense, dark brown hyperpigmentation that persists for months ('margarita photodermatitis'). What is the diagnosis and the responsible photochemical?
options: Phytophotodermatitis; Furocoumarins (Psoralens like 5-methoxypsoralen) interacting with UVA light
questions.answer: Phytophotodermatitis; Furocoumarins (Psoralens like 5-methoxypsoralen) interacting with UVA light
questions.explanation: Phytophotodermatitis (Berloque dermatitis / lime-induced photodermatitis) is a non-immunologic phototoxic reaction caused by skin contact with plants containing phototoxic furocoumarins (psoralens, especially 5-MOP and 8-MOP in limes, celery, parsnips, figs) followed by exposure to solar Ultraviolet A (UVA, 320-400 nm). The activated psoralen intercalates into DNA and generates singlet oxygen, causing epidermal necrosis, bizarre linear/splattered blister patterns, and intense, long-lasting hyperpigmentation.

questions.question: A 36-year-old HIV-infected male presents with an intensely pruritic, symmetrical eruption of numerous discrete, 2 to 5 mm, firm, hyperpigmented, urticarial papules distributed across the extensor surfaces of his extremities and trunk, without excoriated burrows or web space lesions. What is this dermatosis termed, and of what CD4 threshold is it a recognized clinical marker?
questions.prompt: A 36-year-old HIV-infected male presents with an intensely pruritic, symmetrical eruption of numerous discrete, 2 to 5 mm, firm, hyperpigmented, urticarial papules distributed across the extensor surfaces of his extremities and trunk, without excoriated burrows or web space lesions. What is this dermatosis termed, and of what CD4 threshold is it a recognized clinical marker?
options: Pruritic Papular Eruption (PPE) of HIV; CD4 count <200 cells/mcL
questions.answer: Pruritic Papular Eruption (PPE) of HIV; CD4 count <200 cells/mcL
questions.explanation: Pruritic Papular Eruption (PPE) of HIV is one of the most common and characteristic cutaneous manifestations of advanced HIV disease in tropical regions. It presents as intensely pruritic, chronic, symmetric, monomorphic papules on the extensor limbs and trunk. Histology reveals perivascular and perifollicular lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrates. PPE serves as an established clinical surrogate marker for severe immunosuppression (CD4 count <200 cells/mcL).

questions.question: An HIV-seropositive male with a CD4 count of 150 cells/mcL presents with asymptomatic, corrugated, vertically folded, white, plaque-like lesions along the lateral borders of his tongue that CANNOT be scraped or wiped off with a wooden tongue depressor. What is the diagnosis and its viral etiology?
questions.prompt: An HIV-seropositive male with a CD4 count of 150 cells/mcL presents with asymptomatic, corrugated, vertically folded, white, plaque-like lesions along the lateral borders of his tongue that CANNOT be scraped or wiped off with a wooden tongue depressor. What is the diagnosis and its viral etiology?
options: Oral lichen planus; Hepatitis C virus
questions.explanation: Oral Hairy Leukoplakia (OHL) is an opportunistic intraepithelial mucocutaneous manifestation of severe HIV immunosuppression (and other immunocompromised states). It is caused by productive, opportunistic replication of the Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV / HHV-4) within lingual epithelial cells. Hallmark: vertically corrugated, white, adherent, non-scrapable plaques strictly localized to the lateral borders of the tongue, differentiating it from oral candidal thrush.

questions.question: A 40-year-old male with AIDS (CD4 count 45 cells/mcL) presents with fever, night sweats, and multiple rapidly growing, vascular, red-to-violaceous, friable, dome-shaped papules and subcutaneous nodules resembling pyogenic granulomas on his face and limbs. Warthin-Starry silver stain of biopsy tissue demonstrates clusters of tangled, granular, dark silver-staining bacilli in an edematous vascular stroma. What is the diagnosis and organism?
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old male with AIDS (CD4 count 45 cells/mcL) presents with fever, night sweats, and multiple rapidly growing, vascular, red-to-violaceous, friable, dome-shaped papules and subcutaneous nodules resembling pyogenic granulomas on his face and limbs. Warthin-Starry silver stain of biopsy tissue demonstrates clusters of tangled, granular, dark silver-staining bacilli in an edematous vascular stroma. What is the diagnosis and organism?
options: Bacillary angiomatosis; Bartonella henselae (or Bartonella quintana)
questions.answer: Bacillary angiomatosis; Bartonella henselae (or Bartonella quintana)
questions.explanation: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferative zoonosis occurring almost exclusively in severely immunocompromised individuals (CD4 <100 cells/mcL). It is caused by Gram-negative fastidious bacilli: Bartonella henselae (transmitted by domestic cat scratches or cat fleas) or Bartonella quintana (transmitted by the human body louse). Warthin-Starry silver stain or Steiner stain reveals clumps of purple-black bacilli. Oral Erythromycin or Doxycycline is the definitive treatment.

questions.question: A 32-year-old HIV-infected male presents with an intensely pruritic, recurring eruption of sterile, dome-shaped, follicular papules and pustules across the face, neck, and upper chest, with prominent absolute peripheral eosinophilia. Biopsy demonstrates a dense eosinophilic infiltrate centered on the sebaceous gland and follicular infundibulum. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old HIV-infected male presents with an intensely pruritic, recurring eruption of sterile, dome-shaped, follicular papules and pustules across the face, neck, and upper chest, with prominent absolute peripheral eosinophilia. Biopsy demonstrates a dense eosinophilic infiltrate centered on the sebaceous gland and follicular infundibulum. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: HIV-associated Eosinophilic Pustular Folliculitis (EPF / Ofuji-like disease) is an intensely pruritic dermatosis occurring typically when CD4 counts fall below 250-300 cells/mcL. Hallmarks: urticarial follicular papules and sterile pustules favoring the face, neck, and upper trunk, accompanied by prominent blood and tissue eosinophilia. Treatment involves initiation of Antiretroviral Therapy (ART), high-potency topical corticosteroids, oral indomethacin, or phototherapy (UVB).

questions.question: A 38-year-old HIV-infected male with a baseline CD4 count of 35 cells/mcL begins combination Antiretroviral Therapy (ART). Four weeks later, while his viral load plummets and his CD4 count surges to 220 cells/mcL, he suddenly develops an explosive, severe, necrotic, multi-dermatomal eruption of Herpes Zoster and severe worsening of previously stable Kaposi Sarcoma lesions. What immunological phenomenon explains this paradoxical deterioration?
questions.prompt: A 38-year-old HIV-infected male with a baseline CD4 count of 35 cells/mcL begins combination Antiretroviral Therapy (ART). Four weeks later, while his viral load plummets and his CD4 count surges to 220 cells/mcL, he suddenly develops an explosive, severe, necrotic, multi-dermatomal eruption of Herpes Zoster and severe worsening of previously stable Kaposi Sarcoma lesions. What immunological phenomenon explains this paradoxical deterioration?
options: Secondary treatment failure due to viral resistance
questions.explanation: Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS) is an exuberant, dysregulated inflammatory reaction occurring in 10-25% of HIV patients initiating effective ART. Rapid quantitative recovery of CD4+ T-lymphocytes and antigen-specific memory immunity restores the host's capacity to mount intense inflammatory attacks against preexisting, subclinical, or occult infectious pathogens (such as VZV, mycobacteria, CMV, Cryptococcus, or HHV-8). ART should be continued while managing the infection.

questions.question: A 26-year-old male presents with a solitary, painless, indurated ulcer on the coronal sulcus of his penis that developed 3 weeks after unprotected intercourse. On examination, the ulcer has clean, sharply defined, elevated margins, a red serous base, cartilage-like indurated margins, and is accompanied by bilateral, painless, rubbery, discrete, non-matted inguinal lymphadenopathy. Darkfield microscopy of ulcer exudate demonstrates motile, slender, corkscrew-shaped spirochetes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 26-year-old male presents with a solitary, painless, indurated ulcer on the coronal sulcus of his penis that developed 3 weeks after unprotected intercourse. On examination, the ulcer has clean, sharply defined, elevated margins, a red serous base, cartilage-like indurated margins, and is accompanied by bilateral, painless, rubbery, discrete, non-matted inguinal lymphadenopathy. Darkfield microscopy of ulcer exudate demonstrates motile, slender, corkscrew-shaped spirochetes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The hard chancre (Hunterian chancre) of Primary Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum (incubation period 9-90 days, average 21 days). Cardinal hallmarks: 1. Usually solitary; 2. Exquisitely PAINLESS; 3. Pronounced cartilage-like ('button-like') induration at the base and margins; 4. Clean, beefy-red base discharging clear serous fluid; 5. Accompanied by bilateral, painless, discrete, firm, non-suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy ('shotty nodes').

questions.question: A 28-year-old male presents with a non-pruritic, generalized, symmetrical eruption of copper-colored, ham-colored macules and scaly papules prominently involving the palms and soles, each surrounded by a delicate collarette of scale (Biett's collarette). Examination of the perianal area reveals flat, moist, broad-based, highly infectious hypertrophic plaques. What is the diagnosis, and what are the perianal plaques termed?
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old male presents with a non-pruritic, generalized, symmetrical eruption of copper-colored, ham-colored macules and scaly papules prominently involving the palms and soles, each surrounded by a delicate collarette of scale (Biett's collarette). Examination of the perianal area reveals flat, moist, broad-based, highly infectious hypertrophic plaques. What is the diagnosis, and what are the perianal plaques termed?
questions.explanation: Secondary Syphilis develops 4 to 10 weeks after the primary chancre, caused by systemic treponemal bacteremia. Cutaneous hallmarks: 1. Non-pruritic, ham-colored or coppery papulosquamous eruption typically involving the PALMS and SOLES, with a pathognomonic peripheral fringe of scale (Biett's sign); 2. Condylomata lata: soft, flat-topped, moist, velvety, grayish-white hypertrophic papules in warm intertriginous folds (anogenital region) that teem with infectious spirochetes; 3. 'Moth-eaten' non-scarring alopecia.

questions.question: A 50-year-old male with untreated syphilis for 15 years presents with a solitary, painless, deep-seated subcutaneous nodule on his upper leg that slowly broke down to form a chronic, punched-out ulcer with vertical borders and a central, adherent, yellowish-gray necrotic slough resembling 'wash-leather'. Biopsy demonstrates endarteritis obliterans and granulomas. What is this tertiary syphilitic lesion termed?
questions.prompt: A 50-year-old male with untreated syphilis for 15 years presents with a solitary, painless, deep-seated subcutaneous nodule on his upper leg that slowly broke down to form a chronic, punched-out ulcer with vertical borders and a central, adherent, yellowish-gray necrotic slough resembling 'wash-leather'. Biopsy demonstrates endarteritis obliterans and granulomas. What is this tertiary syphilitic lesion termed?
questions.explanation: A gumma is the hallmark lesion of Tertiary (Late Benign) Syphilis. It begins in the dermis, subcutaneous tissue, or bone as a painless, rubbery granulomatous nodule that undergoes ischemic central necrosis, ulcerating into a characteristic 'punched-out' ulcer with punched-out vertical margins and a pathognomonic, tough, adherent, yellowish necrotic base likened to 'wash-leather'. Gummas contain very few spirochetes, representing a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.question: What is the first-line, gold-standard antimicrobial regimen of choice for an adult diagnosed with early syphilis (primary, secondary, or early latent of less than one year duration)?
questions.prompt: What is the first-line, gold-standard antimicrobial regimen of choice for an adult diagnosed with early syphilis (primary, secondary, or early latent of less than one year duration)?
options: Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
Procaine Penicillin 1.2 million units IM daily for 30 days
Oral Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 3 days
questions.answer: Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.explanation: Benzathine Penicillin G (2.4 million units IM administered as a single dose, often divided into two 1.2 million unit injections in each buttock) is the definitive, globally established treatment of choice for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis (<1 year duration). Penicillin maintains treponemicidal serum levels (>0.03 mcg/mL) for over 2 to 3 weeks, eradicating the slowly dividing spirochetes.

questions.question: A patient receiving his first intramuscular injection of Benzathine Penicillin G for secondary syphilis suddenly develops shaking rigors, high fever (39.5 C), headache, tachycardia, flushing, and transient accentuation of his cutaneous rash 4 hours after the injection. What is this acute reaction, and what is its appropriate management?
questions.prompt: A patient receiving his first intramuscular injection of Benzathine Penicillin G for secondary syphilis suddenly develops shaking rigors, high fever (39.5 C), headache, tachycardia, flushing, and transient accentuation of his cutaneous rash 4 hours after the injection. What is this acute reaction, and what is its appropriate management?
options: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction; manage supportively without stopping penicillin
Type I anaphylactic IgE reaction; administer immediate intramuscular epinephrine
Serum sickness; administer high-dose systemic steroids
Toxic epidermal necrolysis; discontinue penicillin permanently
questions.answer: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction; manage supportively without stopping penicillin
questions.explanation: The Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction is an acute, benign, self-limiting systemic reaction occurring in up to 50-75% of patients with early syphilis within 2 to 12 hours of initiating antimicrobial therapy (most commonly penicillin). Massive lysis of treponemes releases massive quantities of lipoproteins, endotoxins, and inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-8). It is NOT an allergic drug reaction: management consists of reassurance, bed rest, and antipyretics (paracetamol), and penicillin must NEVER be discontinued.

questions.question: A 24-year-old male presents with four excruciatingly painful, soft, non-indurated, deep ulcers on his prepuce with ragged, undermined, irregular borders and a necrotic, purulent, foul-smelling yellow-gray base. Two days later, a painful, fluctuant, inflammatory unilateral inguinal lymph node (bubo) develops, threatening to rupture spontaneously through a single sinus. Gram stain of the ulcer exudate reveals Gram-negative coccobacilli arranged in parallel chains resembling a 'school of fish' or 'railroad tracks'. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male presents with four excruciatingly painful, soft, non-indurated, deep ulcers on his prepuce with ragged, undermined, irregular borders and a necrotic, purulent, foul-smelling yellow-gray base. Two days later, a painful, fluctuant, inflammatory unilateral inguinal lymph node (bubo) develops, threatening to rupture spontaneously through a single sinus. Gram stain of the ulcer exudate reveals Gram-negative coccobacilli arranged in parallel chains resembling a 'school of fish' or 'railroad tracks'. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chancroid is an acute, sexually transmitted ulcerative infection caused by Haemophilus ducreyi (a fastidious Gram-negative coccobacillus). Cardinal distinguishing features from primary syphilis: 1. Multiple, soft, NON-INDURATED ulcers ('soft sore'); 2. Exquisitely PAINFUL; 3. Ragged, undermined margins with foul-smelling purulent base; 4. Unilateral, painful, suppurative bubo that characteristically uniloculates and ruptures through a SINGLE sinus; 5. Gram stain shows 'school-of-fish' or 'railroad-track' morphology.

questions.question: A 30-year-old male presents with massive, painful, matted inguinal and femoral lymphadenopathy in his right groin that is visibly divided into upper and lower groups by Poupart's inguinal ligament, producing the pathognomonic 'Groove sign of Greenblatt'. The buboes become multilocular and discharge purulent fluid through multiple sinus tracts. History reveals an evanescent, painless herpetiform papule on his coronal sulcus that healed spontaneously 3 weeks ago. What is the diagnosis and organism?
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old male presents with massive, painful, matted inguinal and femoral lymphadenopathy in his right groin that is visibly divided into upper and lower groups by Poupart's inguinal ligament, producing the pathognomonic 'Groove sign of Greenblatt'. The buboes become multilocular and discharge purulent fluid through multiple sinus tracts. History reveals an evanescent, painless herpetiform papule on his coronal sulcus that healed spontaneously 3 weeks ago. What is the diagnosis and organism?
options: Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV); Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, and L3
questions.answer: Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV); Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, and L3
questions.explanation: Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV) is an invasive systemic STI caused by the lymphotropic serovars L1, L2, and L3 of Chlamydia trachomatis. Stages: Primary stage: a small, painless, transient, non-indurated papule/erosion that heals rapidly; Secondary stage (2-6 weeks later): acute suppurative lymphadenitis (buboes) of inguinal and femoral nodes separated by the inguinal ligament, producing the pathognomonic 'Groove sign of Greenblatt', discharging through MULTIPLE fistulous sinus tracts ('watering-can groin').

questions.question: A 32-year-old male presents with a slowly spreading, painless, beefy-red, velvety, exuberant, granulomatous, friable ulcer with elevated, rolled, everted margins on his penile shaft and scrotum that bleeds copiously upon touch. There is total ABSENCE of true regional lymphadenopathy, though fluctuant subcutaneous granulomas ('pseudobuboes') are palpable in the groin. Giemsa stain of a tissue crush preparation reveals large mononuclear histiocytes stuffed with diagnostic, closed safety-pin-shaped, bipolar-staining intracellular bacilli. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old male presents with a slowly spreading, painless, beefy-red, velvety, exuberant, granulomatous, friable ulcer with elevated, rolled, everted margins on his penile shaft and scrotum that bleeds copiously upon touch. There is total ABSENCE of true regional lymphadenopathy, though fluctuant subcutaneous granulomas ('pseudobuboes') are palpable in the groin. Giemsa stain of a tissue crush preparation reveals large mononuclear histiocytes stuffed with diagnostic, closed safety-pin-shaped, bipolar-staining intracellular bacilli. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Donovanosis (Granuloma Inguinale) is a chronic, progressively destructive STI caused by the intracellular Gram-negative bacillus Klebsiella granulomatis. Cardinal hallmarks: 1. PAINLESS, beefy-red, friable, velvety, exuberant granulomatous ulcer that bleeds readily; 2. Complete absence of true inguinal lymphadenopathy (true buboes do not occur; instead, subcutaneous granulomas in the groin form 'pseudobuboes'); 3. Diagnostic Giemsa/Wright stain demonstration of 'Donovan bodies' (safety-pin-shaped bacilli in large histiocytes).

questions.question: A 22-year-old sexually active female presents with sudden onset of severe vulvar pain, burning upon micturition, fever, and bilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Examination reveals crops of tiny, clustered, thin-walled vesicles on an erythematous base across both labia majora that rapidly rupture into exquisitely tender, shallow, polycyclic, punched-out erosions. Tzanck smear demonstrates multinucleated giant cells with nuclear molding. What is the diagnosis?
questions.prompt: A 22-year-old sexually active female presents with sudden onset of severe vulvar pain, burning upon micturition, fever, and bilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Examination reveals crops of tiny, clustered, thin-walled vesicles on an erythematous base across both labia majora that rapidly rupture into exquisitely tender, shallow, polycyclic, punched-out erosions. Tzanck smear demonstrates multinucleated giant cells with nuclear molding. What is the diagnosis?
options: Primary genital herpes; herpes simplex virus type 2
questions.answer: Primary genital herpes; herpes simplex virus type 2
questions.explanation: Genital herpes is the most common cause of genital ulcer disease worldwide, caused predominantly by HSV-2 (and increasingly HSV-1). Primary genital herpes presents 2-14 days post-exposure with severe pain, dysuria, systemic fever, and crops of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base that erode into painful, scalloped, shallow ulcers with crusting and tender bilateral adenopathy. Episodes recur due to viral latency within sacral dorsal root ganglia.

questions.question: Which clinical diagnostic summary correctly differentiates the five classical causes of Genital Ulcer Disease (GUD)?
questions.prompt: Which clinical diagnostic summary correctly differentiates the five classical causes of Genital Ulcer Disease (GUD)?
options: Syphilis: indurated/painless; Chancroid: purulent/painful; Donovanosis: beefy-red; LGV: groove sign
Syphilis: painful multiple pustules; Chancroid: painless indurated; Donovanosis: purulent; LGV: vesicles
Syphilis: beefy-red pseudobuboes; Chancroid: painless erosion; Donovanosis: vesicles; LGV: soft chancre
