Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is incorrect because the interventricular foramina of Monro connect the lateral ventricles to the third ventricle. Option B is incorrect because the median foramen of Magendie allows CSF to exit the fourth ventricle into the cisterna magna. Option D is incorrect because the lateral foramina of Luschka allow CSF to exit the fourth ventricle into the cerebellopontine angle cisterns.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Normal brain and spinal anatomy on imaging
questions.topicTitle: Normal brain and spinal anatomy on imaging
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old man undergoes MRI of the brain. On sagittal T1-weighted images, the cerebellar tonsils are identified 2 mm below the level of the foramen magnum (drawn along the basion-opisthion line). He is completely asymptomatic. What is the clinical significance of this finding?
options: Chiari I malformation requiring urgent surgical decompression
Chiari II malformation associated with myelomeningocele
questions.explanation: Why correct: Cerebellar tonsillar descent of up to 3 to 5 mm below the foramen magnum can be seen as an incidental, benign anatomical variant in asymptomatic individuals. Pathological Chiari I is usually diagnosed when descent exceeds 5 mm (often >6 mm) with crowding of the foramen magnum and associated symptoms or syrinx. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is incorrect because 2 mm of ectopia in an asymptomatic patient does not meet the diagnostic threshold for Chiari I and does not require surgery. Option C is incorrect because Chiari II involves severe caudal herniation of the vermis, fourth ventricle, and medulla, invariably linked with myelomeningocele. Option D is incorrect because acute downward herniation presents with coma, pupillary abnormalities, and effacement of basal cisterns, not isolated 2 mm tonsillar position.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Normal brain and spinal anatomy on imaging
questions.topicTitle: Normal brain and spinal anatomy on imaging
questions.prompt: Which cerebrospinal fluid cistern lies immediately anterior to the pons on midline sagittal imaging?
questions.explanation: Why correct: The prepontine cistern is located anterior to the pons, separating it from the clivus; it contains the basilar artery and abducens nerves (CN VI). Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is incorrect because the quadrigeminal (superior) cistern lies posterior to the midbrain colliculi. Option C is incorrect because the interpeduncular cistern lies anterior to the midbrain between the two cerebral peduncles. Option D is incorrect because the cisterna magna (cerebellomedullary cistern) is located posteroinferior to the cerebellum and dorsal to the medulla.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Normal brain and spinal anatomy on imaging
questions.topicTitle: Normal brain and spinal anatomy on imaging
questions.prompt: Which ligament lines the posterior surface of the vertebral bodies inside the anterior aspect of the spinal canal?
questions.explanation: Why correct: The posterior longitudinal ligament (PLL) runs along the posterior aspects of the vertebral bodies and intervening intervertebral discs, lining the anterior boundary of the spinal canal. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is incorrect because the anterior longitudinal ligament (ALL) runs along the anterior surfaces of the vertebral bodies. Option C is incorrect because the ligamentum flavum interconnects the laminae of adjacent vertebrae along the posterior spinal canal. Option D is incorrect because the supraspinous ligament connects the tips of the spinous processes from C7 to the sacrum.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Normal brain and spinal anatomy on imaging
questions.topicTitle: Normal brain and spinal anatomy on imaging
questions.prompt: An MRI of the lumbar spine is performed for back pain. On axial T2-weighted images at the L4-L5 level, which spinal nerve roots are located within the lateral recesses before exiting under the L5 pedicles?
questions.explanation: Why correct: In the lumbar spine, a paracentral/lateral recess disc herniation at L4-L5 compresses the traversing L5 nerve root (which exits at the level below, under the L5 pedicle). Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is incorrect because the L4 root is the exiting root at L4-L5, which courses through the superior neural foramen under the L4 pedicle. Option C is incorrect because S1 roots traverse at the L5-S1 disc level. Option D is incorrect because L3 roots exit at the L3-L4 level superiorly.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Normal brain and spinal anatomy on imaging
questions.topicTitle: Normal brain and spinal anatomy on imaging
questions.prompt: In the Circle of Willis, which vessel connects the anterior cerebral circulations across the midline?
questions.explanation: Why correct: The anterior communicating artery (ACom) links the left and right anterior cerebral arteries (A1 segments), completing the anterior aspect of the arterial circle of Willis. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is incorrect because the posterior communicating artery connects the internal carotid artery to the posterior cerebral artery. Option B is incorrect because the basilar artery is formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries in the posterior circulation. Option D is incorrect because the middle cerebral arteries are lateral branches of the internal carotids and do not participate in the circle of Willis ring itself.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.topicTitle: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.prompt: What is the primary neuroimaging modality of choice for the initial emergency evaluation of acute closed head injury?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Non-contrast CT is rapid, universally available, highly sensitive for acute hemorrhage and skull fractures, and compatible with ICU ventilators and life-support monitoring equipment. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is incorrect because MRI is time-consuming, less available acutely, sensitive to motion artifact, and problematic with non-MRI compatible life-support equipment. Option C is incorrect because plain radiographs miss intracranial hematomas and brain contusions in up to 50% of significant trauma cases. Option D is an invasive vascular procedure indicated for vascular dissection or aneurysm, not general head trauma screening.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.topicTitle: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.prompt: Which of the following is considered an absolute contraindication to standard Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Non-MRI conditional cardiac pacemakers can experience lead heating, pacing inhibition, or induced lethal arrhythmias in the strong magnetic field, making them an absolute contraindication unless specially evaluated in designated MRI-safety protocols with conditional devices. Why distractors are incorrect: Options A, C, and D are incorrect because titanium implants, copper IUDs, and dental amalgams are non-ferromagnetic and safe for MRI (though they may produce local susceptibility artifacts).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.topicTitle: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old woman presents with optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, and paresthesias. A neurological condition of demyelination is suspected. Why is MRI vastly superior to CT in this clinical setting?
options: CT causes radiation necrosis in demyelinating plaques
CT has poor soft-tissue contrast and dense beam-hardening artifacts in the posterior fossa and spinal cord
MRI uses ionizing radiation that selectively highlights myelin breakdown
MRI requires lumbar puncture prior to image acquisition
questions.answer: CT has poor soft-tissue contrast and dense beam-hardening artifacts in the posterior fossa and spinal cord
questions.explanation: Why correct: CT has relatively low intrinsic soft-tissue contrast resolution and suffers from severe beam-hardening artifacts near dense bone (such as the skull base, posterior fossa, and spinal canal), rendering multiple sclerosis plaques invisible. MRI (T2/FLAIR) has exceptional soft-tissue resolution and detects periventricular and infratentorial demyelinating lesions clearly. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is false; diagnostic CT doses never cause radiation necrosis. Option C is false; MRI uses non-ionizing radiofrequency pulses and magnetic fields. Option D is false; lumbar puncture is a separate diagnostic test and is not required for MRI.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.topicTitle: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.prompt: On which MRI pulse sequence does normal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) appear bright (hyperintense)?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Pure fluid, such as CSF, has a long T2 relaxation time and therefore appears bright (hyperintense) on T2-weighted sequences. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is incorrect because fluid has a long T1 relaxation time and appears dark (hypointense) on T1-weighted sequences. Option C is incorrect because FLAIR specifically suppresses free water/CSF signal to make it dark, highlighting periventricular pathology. Option D is incorrect because normal free-flowing CSF has high diffusivity and appears dark or suppressed on standard trace DWI.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.topicTitle: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.prompt: A 58-year-old man presents with sudden severe headache. A non-contrast head CT performed within 4 hours is completely negative for subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). What is the mandatory next step in management according to standard emergency neuroimaging algorithms?
options: Perform a diagnostic lumbar puncture (LP) to test for xanthochromia/erythrocytes
questions.answer: Perform a diagnostic lumbar puncture (LP) to test for xanthochromia/erythrocytes
questions.explanation: Why correct: Although modern 3rd-generation CT within 6 hours has high sensitivity (>98-99%), false negatives still occur. If clinical suspicion for aneurysmal SAH remains high and CT is negative, lumbar puncture (performed >6-12 hours from ictus to allow bilirubin formation) is the definitive gold standard to evaluate for xanthochromia and exclude SAH. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is dangerous and could result in untreated aneurysmal rebleeding and death. Option C is irrelevant for intracranial SAH. Option D is an extreme, invasive procedure completely inappropriate for SAH workup.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.topicTitle: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.prompt: Which MRI sequence is most sensitive for detecting cytotoxic edema in hyperacute ischemic stroke within minutes of onset?
questions.explanation: Why correct: DWI detects restricted Brownian motion of water molecules caused by Na+/K+ ATPase pump failure and intracellular cytotoxic edema, demonstrating hyperintensity within 15-30 minutes of arterial occlusion. Why distractors are incorrect: Options B and D are conventional anatomical sequences that often remain normal for the first 6-12 hours of acute infarction. Option C is primarily sensitive to magnetic susceptibility from blood products and calcifications, not acute cellular ischemia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.topicTitle: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.prompt: A patient with suspected cerebellar stroke undergoes a non-contrast CT. The image quality in the posterior fossa is degraded by thick, alternating dark and light streaking artifacts between the petrous temporal bones. What is the name of this artifact?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Beam-hardening artifact occurs in CT when lower-energy X-ray photons are absorbed preferentially as the polychromatic beam traverses dense cortical bone (such as the petrous ridges), causing dark streaks that obscure posterior fossa structures. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is an MRI artifact due to the resonant frequency difference between fat and water. Option C is an MRI artifact occurring when the field of view is smaller than the imaged body part. Option D is an MRI artifact seen as parallel lines near sharp high-contrast interfaces due to finite Fourier sampling.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.topicTitle: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.prompt: What is the primary clinical advantage of FLAIR (Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery) over standard T2-weighted MRI in brain imaging?
options: It suppresses fat signal from the scalp
It nulls high signal from free CSF, making periventricular and subarachnoid lesions conspicuously hyperintense
It eliminates the need for intravenous contrast in brain abscesses
It acquires images in under 1 second to eliminate motion artifact
questions.answer: It nulls high signal from free CSF, making periventricular and subarachnoid lesions conspicuously hyperintense
questions.explanation: Why correct: FLAIR utilizes an inversion time (TI) chosen to null signal from pure, freely moving fluid (CSF). As a result, ventricular and sulcal CSF appears black, while pathological hyperintense lesions (e.g., demyelination, edema, subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis) stand out without being masked by bright CSF. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A describes STIR or fat saturation techniques, not FLAIR. Option C is incorrect because contrast is still needed to evaluate ring enhancement in abscesses. Option D is incorrect; FLAIR sequences take several minutes to acquire.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.topicTitle: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.prompt: A patient with suspected cauda equina syndrome undergoes emergency imaging. In an institution where both CT and MRI are available 24/7, which modality is the gold standard investigation of choice, and why?
options: Non-contrast CT because it shows bony spinal architecture faster
MRI of the lumbosacral spine because it provides superior visualization of soft tissue, discs, thecal sac, and individual nerve roots
CT myelography because MRI cannot depict the spinal canal
Digital subtraction angiography to assess the artery of Adamkiewicz
questions.answer: MRI of the lumbosacral spine because it provides superior visualization of soft tissue, discs, thecal sac, and individual nerve roots
questions.explanation: Why correct: Urgent MRI is the gold standard for cauda equina syndrome because of its unmatched soft-tissue contrast, allowing direct visualization of herniated disc fragments, hematoma, tumor, the degree of thecal sac effacement, and compression of cauda equina nerve roots. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is incorrect because CT alone cannot clearly resolve individual soft-tissue nerve roots or uncalcified disc fragments inside the spinal canal. Option C is an invasive backup when MRI is contraindicated (e.g., non-compatible pacemaker). Option D is used for spinal vascular malformations, not cauda equina mechanical compression.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.topicTitle: CT versus MRI in neurological conditions
questions.prompt: Which MRI sequence is specifically designed to exploit magnetic susceptibility effects to detect microhemorrhages, cavernomas, and blood breakdown products like hemosiderin?
options: Gradient Recalled Echo (GRE) or Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging (SWI)
questions.answer: Gradient Recalled Echo (GRE) or Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging (SWI)
questions.explanation: Why correct: GRE and SWI lack the 180-degree refocusing pulse of spin-echo sequences, making them exquisitely sensitive to local magnetic field inhomogeneities caused by paramagnetic blood degradation products (deoxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin, hemosiderin), which show up as profound signal loss ('blooming'). Why distractors are incorrect: Options B and C are spin-echo based sequences that actively refocus magnetic field inhomogeneities, diminishing susceptibility artifacts. Option D is a fat-suppressed sequence optimized for detecting marrow edema and soft tissue inflammation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 22-year-old cyclist falls, sustaining a blow to the pterion, suffers brief loss of consciousness, wakes up feeling lucid for two hours, then rapidly deteriorates into a coma. Emergency CT reveals a biconvex (lentiform), hyperdense extra-axial collection that does not cross cranial sutures. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Why correct: The classic presentation (lucid interval following temporal trauma) combined with the hallmark CT appearance (biconvex/lentiform hyperdense extra-axial mass confined by cranial sutures where dura is tightly adherent to bone) is diagnostic of an epidural (extradural) hematoma, usually caused by middle meningeal artery rupture. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B presents as a crescent-shaped collection that crosses suture lines. Option C appears as high attenuation filling the sulci and basal cisterns. Option D represents parenchymal brain injury, typically involving the gyral crests of the inferior frontal and anterior temporal lobes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which vessel is most commonly lacerated in the pathogenesis of an acute epidural hematoma?
questions.explanation: Why correct: The middle meningeal artery (running in the epidural space beneath the pterion) is lacerated in ~85-90% of epidural hematomas, frequently associated with a fracture of the squamosal temporal bone. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is incorrect because bridging cortical veins traversing the subdural space are torn in subdural hematomas. Options C and D are large basal arteries whose rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage, dissection, or massive ischemic/hemorrhagic stroke.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: An 82-year-old male with cerebral atrophy on warfarin presents with insidious confusion, progressive lethargy, and mild hemiparesis following a minor fall three weeks ago. Head CT reveals a crescent-shaped extra-axial collection over the cerebral hemisphere that is hypodense relative to cortex and crosses suture lines. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Chronic subdural hematoma typically occurs in elderly patients or anticoagulated individuals with brain atrophy (stretching bridging veins). Over weeks, the hematoma liquefies and becomes hypodense (<30 HU) compared to brain parenchyma, maintaining its characteristic crescentic shape crossing sutures. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is hyperdense, biconvex, and restricted by sutures. Option C is hyperdense within sulci and basal cisterns, presenting with sudden thunderclap headache. Option D is hemorrhage confined within the ventricular chambers.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Why do acute subdural hematomas characteristically cross cranial suture lines but do NOT cross the midline across the dural reflections?
options: They lie beneath the pia mater and are bounded by the falx
They lie in the potential space between the dura mater and arachnoid, freely traversing sutures, but are restricted by the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli
They are confined to the subperiosteal space of the inner table
They only accumulate inside the Virchow-Robin perivascular spaces
questions.answer: They lie in the potential space between the dura mater and arachnoid, freely traversing sutures, but are restricted by the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli
questions.explanation: Why correct: Subdural hematomas occupy the space deep to the dura and superficial to the arachnoid; because the outer dura's adherence to sutures does not restrict this internal space, subdural blood tracks freely over the convexity across sutures. However, it cannot cross the midline or tentorial notch because it is bounded by the rigid dural reflections (falx cerebri and tentorium). Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is incorrect because blood beneath the pia is intraparenchymal, not subdural. Option C describes the epidural space (specifically cephalohematoma or extradural). Option D describes microscopic fluid around penetrating vessels.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 19-year-old unrestrained driver involved in a high-speed rollover collision has a Glasgow Coma Scale of 4 at the scene. Initial non-contrast head CT shows only subtle punctate hyperdensities at the grey-white matter junction of the frontal lobes and in the splenium of the corpus callosum, disproportionate to his severe neurological deficit. What is the underlying pathology?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) results from violent rotational acceleration/deceleration shear forces. CT is notoriously insensitive, showing only subtle microhemorrhages (or normal findings) at classic predilection sites: grey-white matter junction, corpus callosum (splenium), and dorsolateral midbrain/brainstem. MRI (especially GRE/SWI) is much more sensitive. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B typically presents 24-72 hours after long-bone fractures with hypoxia, petechial rash, and a 'starfield' pattern on brain MRI. Option C presents with ventriculomegaly, not shear hemorrhages. Option D ignores the punctate shear hemorrhages in classic DAI locations.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: In non-contrast CT evaluation of acute head trauma, what does the 'swirl sign' within an acute epidural or subdural hematoma signify?
options: Active, ongoing bleeding (unclotted, lower-attenuation blood surrounded by clotted hyperdense blood)
Chronic complete liquefaction of the clot
questions.answer: Active, ongoing bleeding (unclotted, lower-attenuation blood surrounded by clotted hyperdense blood)
questions.explanation: Why correct: The 'swirl sign' represents areas of low attenuation (unclotted, fresh extravasated blood) swirling within a hyperdense clot, indicating hyperacute active bleeding and impending rapid hematoma expansion—a neurosurgical emergency. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B describes homogeneous hypodensity of chronic hematomas. Option C is false; swirl sign indicates rapid progression, not healing. Option D is incorrect; gas appears as marked negative attenuation (~ -1000 HU), not swirl sign.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old unrestrained driver suffers severe head injury. CT reveals bilateral cortical hyperdense areas surrounded by edema in the inferior frontal poles and anterior temporal lobes abutting the inner table of the skull. What is the term for this traumatic parenchymal lesion?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Cerebral contusions represent bruised brain parenchyma caused by coup and contrecoup impacts against irregular internal bony surfaces (orbital roofs, sphenoid wings, petrous ridges). They characteristically involve the inferior frontal and anterior/inferior temporal lobes, appearing as patchy hyperdensities that may 'blossom' (expand) over the first 24-48 hours. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is vascular, typically at arterial bifurcations. Option C is an incidental congenital vascular malformation with a 'popcorn' appearance on MRI. Option D is an aggressive infiltrative neoplasm, not an acute post-traumatic lesion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 70-year-old male on aspirin falls down stairs. Head CT shows an extra-axial collection over the right hemisphere. The collection has a dependent high-attenuation layer and a nondependent low-attenuation layer, resembling a 'hematocrit effect'. What does this indicate?
options: Acute-on-chronic subdural hematoma (recurrent hemorrhage into a pre-existing chronic subdural)
Pure epidural hematoma with suture diastasis
questions.answer: Acute-on-chronic subdural hematoma (recurrent hemorrhage into a pre-existing chronic subdural)
questions.explanation: Why correct: An acute-on-chronic subdural hematoma occurs when fragile neocapillaries within the membranes of a chronic subdural rupture, producing fresh acute blood (dense, sedimenting dependently) mixed with liquefied chronic subdural fluid (nondependent, lower density), creating a fluid-fluid or 'hematocrit' level. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is biconvex and homogeneous acutely. Option C is an infection characterized by rim-enhancing fluid and fever. Option D is intracranial air appearing pitch black (-1000 HU).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the typical attenuation (in Hounsfield Units) of fresh, coagulated blood in an acute intracranial hematoma on non-contrast CT?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Acute clotted blood has a characteristic attenuation of +60 to +80 HU due to the high protein concentration of globin molecules in packed red blood cells. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A represents fat attenuation (-50 to -100 HU). Option B represents water or pure CSF attenuation (0 to +10 HU). Option D represents cortical bone (>1000 HU).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On non-contrast head CT following trauma, hyperdense blood is identified tracing into the interhemispheric fissure and outlining the cerebral sulci over the convexities. No skull fracture or biconvex mass is identified. What type of hemorrhage is present?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage is the most common traumatic intracranial hemorrhage, appearing as hyperdense blood filling the subarachnoid space (sulci, sylvian fissures, and basal cisterns). Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is a focal biconvex extra-axial mass outside the brain. Option C is a collection of clear CSF (hypodense) in the subdural space resulting from an arachnoid tear. Option D is an extracranial subperiosteal collection of blood over the skull in neonates.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the earliest reliable sign of acute middle cerebral artery (MCA) ischemic infarction visible on non-contrast CT within the first 1 to 2 hours of onset?
options: Massive midline shift with uncal herniation
Hyperdense middle cerebral artery sign ('dense MCA sign')
questions.answer: Hyperdense middle cerebral artery sign ('dense MCA sign')
questions.explanation: Why correct: The 'dense MCA sign' represents direct visualization of acute intraluminal thrombus or thromboembolus within the M1 segment of the MCA, appearing hyperdense (+70-80 HU) compared to other vessels due to packed RBCs and clot. It can be seen immediately upon occlusion. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A develops later (typically at 24-72 hours) as vasogenic edema peaks. Option C represents chronic, established tissue loss seen months later. Option D is a late subacute imaging finding resulting from selective neuronal necrosis in vulnerable cortical layers.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 64-year-old male presents with acute onset right hemiplegia and expressive aphasia 90 minutes ago. Non-contrast head CT demonstrates loss of the normal grey-white differentiation at the lateral margin of the basal ganglia on the left. What is this early CT ischemic sign called?
options: Loss of the insular ribbon sign
questions.answer: Loss of the insular ribbon sign
questions.explanation: Why correct: The 'loss of the insular ribbon' refers to effacement and hypodensity of the insular cortex, causing loss of the normal sharp grey-white boundary between the insular ribbon and the underlying external/extreme capsule. Because the insular cortex is supplied by the MCA and has minimal collateral supply, it is exceptionally vulnerable to early ischemia. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is a non-specific sign of general swelling. Option C refers to basilar artery thrombosis in the posterior circulation. Option D is an imaging finding seen in vascular malformations or abscesses.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: In the Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score (ASPECTS) system used to quantify early ischemic changes in the middle cerebral artery territory, what is the maximum normal baseline score?
questions.explanation: Why correct: The ASPECTS system divides the MCA territory into 10 defined regions (caudate, lentiform nucleus, internal capsule, insular ribbon, M1-M6 cortical zones). A normal non-contrast CT receives a baseline score of 10. For each region showing distinct early ischemic change, 1 point is subtracted. An ASPECTS score ≤ 6 indicates extensive infarction and correlates with poorer prognosis and higher hemorrhage risk with reperfusion therapy. Why distractors are incorrect: Options A, B, and D are incorrect score scales; the maximum normal ASPECTS score is 10.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 71-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with left-sided hemiplegia. An urgent MRI brain is performed. Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI) demonstrates bright hyperintensity in the right frontoparietal cortex, while the corresponding Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC) map shows dark hypointensity ('restricted diffusion'). What does this mismatch confirm?
options: T2 shine-through artifact from an old chronic infarct
Acute cytotoxic edema from acute ischemic infarction
Vasogenic edema from a metastatic brain lesion
questions.answer: Acute cytotoxic edema from acute ischemic infarction
questions.explanation: Why correct: In acute ischemia, failure of cellular energy pumps leads to intracellular water accumulation (cytotoxic edema). This restricts the Brownian motion of water molecules, producing high signal on trace DWI and low signal (darkness) on the quantitative ADC map. True restricted diffusion requires this pairing (bright DWI + dark ADC). Why distractors are incorrect: Option A ('T2 shine-through') occurs when a chronic lesion is bright on DWI but also bright (or normal) on ADC due to high T2 signal, not true diffusion restriction. Option B is incorrect because vasogenic edema causes increased extracellular water and elevated (bright) ADC. Option D is incorrect as these findings represent definite acute tissue infarction.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: In multimodal CT or MR perfusion imaging for acute stroke, how is the 'ischemic penumbra' defined?
options: Tissue with irreversible infarction where both CBF and CBV are profoundly reduced
Potentially salvageable tissue characterized by delayed transit time (increased Tmax/MTT) with preserved or slightly elevated cerebral blood volume (CBV)
Tissue that has undergone hemorrhagic transformation with blood-fluid levels
Tissue showing complete loss of blood-brain barrier integrity on post-contrast imaging
questions.answer: Potentially salvageable tissue characterized by delayed transit time (increased Tmax/MTT) with preserved or slightly elevated cerebral blood volume (CBV)
questions.explanation: Why correct: The ischemic penumbra represents hypoperfused tissue at risk of dying but still viable due to collateral flow. Autoregulation causes local vasodilation, maintaining cerebral blood volume (CBV) despite prolonged mean transit time (MTT) or delayed time-to-peak (Tmax). If CBV collapses along with cerebral blood flow (CBF), the tissue is part of the non-viable ischemic core. The mismatch between penumbra and core is the target for endovascular thrombectomy. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A defines the non-salvageable ischemic core. Option C defines secondary hemorrhage. Option D describes late blood-brain barrier disruption.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 56-year-old hypertensive diabetic smoker develops sudden pure motor hemiparesis of the right face, arm, and leg without sensory loss or cortical signs (no aphasia or visual field cut). Non-contrast CT is initially normal. Repeat imaging identifies a 9 mm focal cavity in the posterior limb of the left internal capsule. What type of stroke is this?
options: Major territorial MCA bifurcation embolic infarct
questions.explanation: Why correct: Lacunar infarcts are small (<15-20 mm) subcortical strokes caused by lipohyalinosis or microatheroma of small penetrating lenticulostriate or thalamoperforator arteries. The classic lacunar syndrome of pure motor hemiparesis results from an infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B produces cortical deficits (aphasia, gaze deviation, hemineglect). Option C typically produces 'man-in-a-barrel' syndrome or bilateral visual disturbances along ACA-MCA or MCA-PCA boundary zones. Option D produces parasagittal or temporal hemorrhagic infarctions crossing arterial territories.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary role of emergency non-contrast head CT prior to administering intravenous recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA) in suspected acute stroke?
options: To accurately measure the penumbra size
To definitively rule out intracranial hemorrhage
To assess cerebral venous collateral capacity
To verify the presence of intracranial atherosclerosis
questions.answer: To definitively rule out intracranial hemorrhage
questions.explanation: Why correct: The immediate, non-negotiable prerequisite before administering thrombolytic therapy (rtPA) is to exclude intracranial hemorrhage, which is an absolute contraindication to thrombolysis. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A requires CT perfusion or MRI, not standard NCCT. Option C requires CT venography. Option D requires CT angiography or DSA.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 68-year-old male with severe internal carotid artery stenosis suffers profound intraoperative hypotension during bypass surgery. Postoperatively, brain MRI reveals linear, band-like infarctions located at the junction between the anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery territories. What is the pathophysiological mechanism of this infarct?
options: Cardioembolic occlusion of the main trunk
Watershed (borderzone) infarction due to global hypoperfusion
Direct mechanical transection of perforating arteries
questions.answer: Watershed (borderzone) infarction due to global hypoperfusion
questions.explanation: Why correct: Watershed or borderzone infarcts occur in the most distal territories between adjacent major arterial distributions (e.g., ACA-MCA or MCA-PCA junctions). They are caused by severe hemodynamic failure/hypoperfusion, particularly in the setting of proximal high-grade carotid stenosis or systemic hypotension. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A leads to territorial branch or trunk infarcts rather than specific borderzone distributions. Option C presents with intracranial hemorrhage. Option D occurs with direct trauma or surgical laceration.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old man undergoes repeat CT 48 hours after a large territorial ischemic stroke. The repeat scan shows petechial and confluent hyperdensities within the previously hypodense infarcted cortex. What is this phenomenon called?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Hemorrhagic transformation is a frequent complication of ischemic stroke, occurring when reperfusion (either spontaneous or post-thrombolysis) delivers blood under systemic pressure to capillaries whose endothelial walls have suffered ischemic breakdown and necrosis. It ranges from asymptomatic petechiae (HI-1, HI-2) to parenchymal hematoma (PH-1, PH-2). Why distractors are incorrect: Option B occurs primarily in the sulcal spaces, not in the necrotic brain parenchyma. Option C is a diffuse glial neoplasm. Option D is an intraluminal clot within the dural venous sinuses.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which vascular territory is infarcted when a patient presents with contralateral lower-limb weakness greater than upper-limb weakness, abulia, and urinary incontinence?
questions.explanation: Why correct: The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the motor and sensory homunculus representation for the contralateral leg/foot, the supplementary motor area, and parasagittal micturition centers. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A supplies the occipital lobe and inferior temporal lobe; infarction causes homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Option C supplies the brainstem and leads to 'locked-in' syndrome, coma, or cranial nerve palsies. Option D supplies the superior cerebellum, causing gait ataxia and dysmetria.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the single most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Glioblastoma (WHO Grade 4) is the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults, accounting for approximately 50% of all malignant intrinsic brain neoplasms. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is the most common primary brain tumor overall, but it is typically benign (WHO Grade 1) and extra-axial. Option C is the most common malignant brain tumor in children, not adults. Option D is a benign (WHO Grade 1) cystic tumor primarily affecting pediatric posterior fossae.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 65-year-old male presents with headache, cognitive slowing, and left-sided weakness. Contrast-enhanced MRI reveals an irregular, thick-walled, heterogeneously ring-enhancing necrotic mass centered in the deep white matter of the right hemisphere, crossing the corpus callosum into the left hemisphere ('butterfly' pattern), surrounded by profound vasogenic edema. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Glioblastoma typically presents as a large, necrotic mass with irregular, shaggy, thick ring enhancement and significant vasogenic edema, characteristically tracking across the corpus callosum white matter tracts into the contralateral hemisphere ('butterfly glioma'). Why distractors are incorrect: Option B usually demonstrates solid, homogeneous, non-necrotic enhancement in immunocompetent patients, with marked diffusion restriction. Option C typically has a smooth, thin, uniform enhancing rim with the medial wall thinner than the lateral wall, and intense central restricted diffusion. Option D typically displays an open (incomplete) C-shaped ring of enhancement facing the cortical grey matter.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old female presents with focal seizures. Contrast-enhanced MRI reveals a sharply circumscribed, extra-axial, homogeneously enhancing mass abutting the inner table of the parietal calvarium with an adjacent thickened, enhancing dura ('dural tail sign') and hyperostosis of the overlying bone. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Meningiomas are slow-growing extra-axial tumors originating from arachnoid cap cells. Classic neuroimaging findings include a well-defined extra-axial mass with broad dural base, intense homogeneous enhancement, a reactive 'dural tail', and adjacent bony hyperostosis. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is an aggressive infiltrative intra-axial necrotic malignancy. Option C is an intraventricular or spinal cord tumor. Option D is an intra-axial lesion, typically located at the grey-white matter junction with out-of-proportion vasogenic edema.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Overall, what is the most common intracranial neoplasm found in adults?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Metastases from systemic malignancies (lung, breast, melanoma, renal, colon) represent the most frequent intracranial tumors in adults, outnumbering primary brain tumors by at least 2:1 to 4:1. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is a relatively rare primary glial neoplasm. Option C is a common benign sellar neoplasm, but far less frequent than secondary metastatic disease. Option D is a benign dysontogenetic sellar/suprasellar tumor mostly seen in children and older adults.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 62-year-old heavy smoker presents with sudden seizure. Brain MRI reveals multiple well-circumscribed, solid-and-cystic enhancing nodules distributed precisely at the grey-white matter junctions of both cerebral hemispheres, surrounded by disproportionately extensive digitating vasogenic edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Multiple enhancing spherical lesions located at the arterial watershed/grey-white matter junctions (where blood-borne emboli lodge in narrowing arterioles) with extensive vasogenic edema in a smoker are pathognomonic for hematogenous brain metastases, most frequently from bronchogenic carcinoma. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B typically presents as non-enhancing or perivenular oval lesions along the callososeptal interface. Option C is a single infiltrative, poorly enhancing mass. Option D causes recurrent lobar intracerebral hemorrhages, not multiple enhancing masses.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 48-year-old male presents with progressive right-sided sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance disturbance. Contrast-enhanced MRI reveals a smoothly marginated, intensely enhancing mass centered within the right internal auditory canal (IAC) that flares out into the cerebellopontine angle, resembling an 'ice cream cone'. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Vestibular schwannoma arises from Schwann cells of the superior or inferior vestibular branch of CN VIII. The classic appearance is an avidly enhancing mass with its 'cone' inside the internal auditory canal and its 'scoop of ice cream' protruding into the cerebellopontine angle cistern. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B does not enhance avidly and restricts on DWI (bright on DWI). Option C follows pure CSF signal on all sequences (dark on T1, bright on T2, suppresses on FLAIR, no diffusion restriction, no enhancement). Option D is located within the sella turcica, not the CPA.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 7-year-old child presents with morning vomiting, headache, and truncal ataxia. MRI demonstrates a well-circumscribed cerebellar hemispheric mass with a large cystic component and a brightly enhancing mural nodule. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO Grade 1) is the most common pediatric posterior fossa tumor, classic for its 'cyst with an enhancing mural nodule' appearance within the cerebellar hemisphere. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B (medulloblastoma) is a hypercellular solid mass arising from the cerebellar vermis in the roof of the fourth ventricle with marked restricted diffusion. Option C is exceptionally rare in young children and presents as a necrotic infiltrative mass. Option D is an adult cortical tumor characterized by coarse clumped calcifications.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old man presents with new-onset seizures. Non-contrast CT reveals a cortical/subcortical mass in the frontal lobe with dense, clumped, 'popcorn-like' calcifications. MRI shows cortical expansion with high signal on T2 and faint heterogenous enhancement. 1p/19q codeletion is confirmed on subsequent genetics. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Oligodendrogliomas are defined by IDH mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion. On neuroimaging, they classicially present as superficial frontal lobe cortical/subcortical masses that contain dense calcifications (in up to 90% of cases) and cause cortical remodeling/calvarial thinning. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is an intraventricular tumor attached to the septum pellucidum. Option C rarely calcifies and presents as a deep periventricular densely enhancing mass. Option D is an extra-axial peripheral nerve sheath tumor.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What type of brain edema is characteristically associated with malignant brain neoplasms, resulting from breakdown of the blood-brain barrier?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Vasogenic edema results from disruption of tight junctions in tumor capillaries (breakdown of the blood-brain barrier). Fluid leaks into the extracellular spaces, tracking selectively along white matter tracts and sparing cortical grey matter (yielding a 'finger-like' or digitating pattern on T2/FLAIR). Why distractors are incorrect: Option A is intracellular swelling caused by energy pump failure in acute ischemia, involving both grey and white matter. Option C results from transependymal flow of CSF in acute obstructive hydrocephalus. Option D results from acute hyponatremia or dialysis disequilibrium.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old female presents with amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and bitemporal hemianopsia. Sagittal and coronal T1 contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrates an avidly enhancing 18 mm mass arising within the sella turcica, extending superiorly through the diaphragma sellae to compress the optic chiasm ('figure-of-eight' or snowman appearance). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Why correct: A pituitary adenoma >10 mm is classified as a macroadenoma. As it expands superiorly out of the expanded sella turcica, it is cinched by the diaphragma sellae, producing a waist-like constriction ('figure-of-eight' or snowman appearance) and compresses the overlying optic chiasm, causing classic bitemporal hemianopsia. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is primarily suprasellar, typically cystic and calcified, not purely sellar in origin. Option C is a benign non-enhancing non-neoplastic cyst between anterior and posterior pituitary lobes. Option D arises from the tuberculum sellae or planum sphenoidale with a distinct dural tail, maintaining a separate normal pituitary gland below.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: How is 'non-communicating' (obstructive) hydrocephalus fundamentally differentiated from 'communicating' hydrocephalus?
options: Non-communicating hydrocephalus has a physical structural blockage to CSF flow within the ventricular system, whereas communicating hydrocephalus has patent ventricles with impaired resorption at the arachnoid granulations
Non-communicating hydrocephalus causes brain atrophy, whereas communicating hydrocephalus increases intracranial pressure
Non-communicating hydrocephalus only occurs in elderly adults, whereas communicating hydrocephalus occurs only in neonates
Non-communicating hydrocephalus spares the lateral ventricles
questions.answer: Non-communicating hydrocephalus has a physical structural blockage to CSF flow within the ventricular system, whereas communicating hydrocephalus has patent ventricles with impaired resorption at the arachnoid granulations
questions.explanation: Why correct: Non-communicating (intraventricular obstructive) hydrocephalus occurs when an obstruction within the ventricular system (e.g., aqueductal stenosis, colloid cyst, tumor) prevents CSF from exiting into the subarachnoid space. Communicating (extraventricular) hydrocephalus occurs when CSF flows out of the fourth ventricle but cannot be absorbed by the arachnoid villi (e.g., post-meningitis, post-SAH) or, rarely, is overproduced (choroid plexus papilloma). Why distractors are incorrect: Option B describes hydrocephalus ex vacuo (atrophy), not communicating hydrocephalus. Option C is false; both forms can occur at any age. Option D is false; non-communicating hydrocephalus typically produces dramatic dilatation of the lateral ventricles.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 74-year-old male presents with the classic clinical triad of gait disturbance, progressive cognitive impairment, and urinary incontinence ('wet, wacky, and wobbly'). MRI reveals marked ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal enlargement, with narrow, crowded sulci at the high cerebral convexities and effacement of the callosal angle. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) presents with Hakim's triad (gait ataxia, dementia, urinary incontinence) and characteristic neuroimaging: disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus (DESH), marked ventriculomegaly disproportionate to cortical atrophy, tight parasagittal high-convexity sulci, and an acute callosal angle (<90 degrees on coronal T1). Why distractors are incorrect: Option B features prominent cerebral and hippocampal atrophy with enlarged convex sulci and compensatory ex vacuo ventricular dilation. Option C typically presents in younger individuals with an obstructed aqueduct and normal fourth ventricle. Option D presents in young, overweight women with headaches, papilledema, and slit-like ventricles.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the key imaging feature on T2/FLAIR MRI that signifies acute, active intraventricular hypertension in obstructive hydrocephalus?
questions.explanation: Why correct: When intraventricular pressure exceeds ependymal resistance, CSF is driven across the disrupted ependymal lining into the surrounding periventricular deep white matter, producing smooth, halo-like hyperintensity on T2/FLAIR known as transependymal CSF permeation or periventricular edema. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is a sign of diffuse cerebral atrophy (hydrocephalus ex vacuo). Option C is a post-traumatic or post-shunting collection. Option D is seen in chronic shunting or microcephaly, not acute hypertension.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which index is classically measured on axial brain CT/MRI to assess ventriculomegaly, defined as the ratio of the maximum frontal horn diameter to the maximum internal transverse skull diameter (where >0.30 indicates hydrocephalus)?
questions.explanation: Why correct: The Evans index is the maximal frontal horn width divided by the maximal inner biparietal diameter at the same axial level; a ratio greater than 0.30 indicates ventriculomegaly. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is an ischemic stroke score. Option C is a subarachnoid hemorrhage vasospasm risk scale. Option D refers to CT attenuation units.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old male presents with sudden severe positional headaches that resolve upon lying down, accompanied by episodic drop attacks. Brain CT reveals an isolated, well-circumscribed, hyperdense round mass in the anterosuperior third ventricle causing acute bilateral dilation of the lateral ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle. What is the diagnosis?
options: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle
questions.answer: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle
questions.explanation: Why correct: Colloid cysts classicially arise at the roof of the third ventricle immediately adjacent to the bilateral foramina of Monro. They can cause intermittent 'ball-valve' obstruction of the foramina of Monro, precipitating acute bilateral lateral ventriculomegaly, sudden thunderclap positional headaches, acute herniation, or sudden death. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is located in the posterior third ventricle / pineal region. Option C is located in the fourth ventricle. Option D involves acute hemorrhage within the sella turcica.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A non-contrast CT in an 85-year-old female with Alzheimer disease shows prominent enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles alongside prominent, diffuse widening of all cerebral sulci and sylvian fissures throughout the brain. There is no periventricular halo. What is the correct radiological diagnosis?
options: Hydrocephalus ex vacuo (compensatory ventriculomegaly due to brain atrophy)
Communicating hydrocephalus secondary to acute meningitis
questions.answer: Hydrocephalus ex vacuo (compensatory ventriculomegaly due to brain atrophy)
questions.explanation: Why correct: Hydrocephalus ex vacuo is physiological enlargement of the ventricular system and subarachnoid spaces in response to parenchymal volume loss (generalized cerebral atrophy). Intracranial pressure is normal, sulci are widened (not effaced), and there is no transependymal edema. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B features effaced sulci, high ICP, and periventricular edema. Option C causes isolated lateral ventriculomegaly. Option D presents with fever, meningismus, and sulcal exudates.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On neuroimaging of a neonate with rapidly increasing head circumference, MRI reveals severe dilation of the lateral and third ventricles, while the fourth ventricle remains completely normal in caliber. What is the most likely etiology?
options: Obstruction of the foramina of Luschka and Magendie
Choroid plexus carcinoma of the fourth ventricle
questions.explanation: Why correct: Congenital aqueductal stenosis (the most common cause of congenital obstructive hydrocephalus) blocks the cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius between the third and fourth ventricles. Consequently, the lateral and third ventricles dilate, while the downstream fourth ventricle remains normal in size. Why distractors are incorrect: Options B and C cause massive dilatation of the fourth ventricle (e.g., giant posterior fossa cyst in Dandy-Walker). Option D causes fourth ventricular enlargement and mass effect.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 26-year-old female with obesity presents with chronic daily headaches, transient visual obscurations, pulse-synchronous tinnitus, and bilateral papilledema. Lumbar puncture demonstrates an elevated opening pressure of 32 cm H2O with normal CSF composition. Brain MRI reveals empty sella, flattened posterior sclerae, and tortuous optic nerves with distended perioptic subarachnoid spaces, but normal-to-small ventricles. What is the diagnosis?
options: Obstructive hydrocephalus due to tectal glioma
questions.explanation: Why correct: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) features elevated intracranial pressure without a mass or ventricular dilation. Hallmark neuroimaging findings include an partially empty sella, flattening of the posterior globes, prominent CSF in the perioptic nerve sheaths, intraocular protrusion of the optic nerve heads (papilledema), and bilateral transverse sinus stenosis. Ventricles are typically normal or slit-like. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B causes severe trilventricular hydrocephalus. Option C causes ventriculomegaly in elderly patients without papilledema. Option D presents with focal pontine/medullary expansion and cranial nerve palsies.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 5-year-old boy with a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placed for hydrocephalus presents to the emergency department with nausea, lethargy, and headache. What initial imaging workup is recommended to evaluate for shunt malfunction?
options: Emergency non-contrast head CT and a plain radiographic shunt series (skull, neck, chest, abdomen)
questions.answer: Emergency non-contrast head CT and a plain radiographic shunt series (skull, neck, chest, abdomen)
questions.explanation: Why correct: Suspected shunt malfunction is evaluated by combining a non-contrast head CT (to compare ventricular size with prior baseline scans) and a plain X-ray 'shunt series' from skull to abdomen (to inspect for catheter disconnection, kinking, fracturing, or migration). Why distractors are incorrect: Option B involves high unnecessary radiation without mechanical structural detail. Option C is hazardous in acute shunt failure with high ICP due to herniation risk. Option D is an invasive vascular study unrelated to CSF shunts.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the radiological term for downward displacement and bowing of the optic chiasm, stretching of the floor of the third ventricle, and elevation and thinning of the corpus callosum seen on sagittal MRI in severe chronic hydrocephalus?
options: Ventricular diverticulum and corpus callosal thinning
questions.answer: Ventricular diverticulum and corpus callosal thinning
questions.explanation: Why correct: Progressive chronically elevated ventricular pressure exerts mechanical tension on surrounding structures, leading to outward ballooning and thinning of the corpus callosum and downward bowing/depression of the third ventricular floor. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B refers specifically to herniation of CSF into the sella turcica compressing the pituitary gland. Option C is a benign enlargement of the posteroinferior retrocerebellar cistern with an intact vermis. Option D refers to venous vessel dilatation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What CT image reconstruction algorithm and window display setting is mandatory for detecting subtle, non-displaced calvarial and skull base fractures?
options: Bone window (width ~2000-3000 HU, level ~500-700 HU) with sharp high-frequency kernel
Brain window (width ~80 HU, level ~40 HU) with smooth soft-tissue kernel
questions.answer: Bone window (width ~2000-3000 HU, level ~500-700 HU) with sharp high-frequency kernel
questions.explanation: Why correct: Bone windows with wide window width and high window level, paired with a sharp, high-spatial-resolution bone reconstruction kernel, maximize cortical edge definition and suppress soft tissue, allowing fine linear fracture lucencies to be detected. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B ('brain window') is designed for soft tissue contrast to evaluate grey-white differentiation and hematomas; dense bone appears completely saturated (pure white), obscuring fractures. Option C is optimized for distinguishing acute extra-axial collections from the inner table. Option D is optimized for pulmonary parenchyma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male presents with clear, watery fluid draining from his right nostril after blunt facial trauma. High-resolution CT of the skull base confirms a fracture of the cribriform plate with small bubbles of intracranial air (pneumocephalus). What is the fluid, and what is the primary risk?
options: CSF rhinorrhea; risk of bacterial meningitis
Allergic rhinitis; risk of sinus mucopyocele
Lacrimal duct fluid; risk of orbital cellulitis
questions.answer: CSF rhinorrhea; risk of bacterial meningitis
questions.explanation: Why correct: Fractures of the cribriform plate or ethmoid roof tear the adherent dura and arachnoid mater, establishing a direct fistulous tract between the subarachnoid space and the nasal cavity (CSF rhinorrhea). This creates a direct route for nasopharyngeal bacteria to enter the intracranial vault, causing recurrent or fatal bacterial meningitis (most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae). Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is incorrect as watery drainage containing beta-2 transferrin with intracranial air is traumatic CSF leak, not allergy. Options C and D are anatomically and clinically incorrect.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient involved in a motor vehicle crash presents with bilateral periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes') and retroauricular ecchymosis ('Battle sign'). Head CT is most likely to reveal a fracture involving which anatomical structure?
options: Basilar skull (petrous temporal bone and/or anterior cranial fossa skull base)
questions.answer: Basilar skull (petrous temporal bone and/or anterior cranial fossa skull base)
questions.explanation: Why correct: Raccoon eyes (periorbital ecchymosis from anterior fossa/orbital roof fractures) and Battle sign (mastoid ecchymosis from petrous temporal bone fractures) are classic clinical hallmarks of basilar skull fractures. Why distractors are incorrect: Options B and C are facial fractures that produce local facial swelling/malocclusion without Battle sign. Option D is a vault fracture that does not produce skull base tracking of blood into the periorbital or mastoid tissues.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: How are fractures of the petrous temporal bone traditionally classified based on the orientation of the fracture line relative to the long axis of the petrous pyramid, and which type has a higher incidence of sensorineural hearing loss and facial nerve transection?
options: Longitudinal vs. Transverse; Transverse fractures carry higher rates of facial nerve transection and sensorineural hearing loss
Depressed vs. Linear; Depressed fractures carry higher rates of sensorineural hearing loss
Longitudinal vs. Transverse; Longitudinal fractures carry higher rates of sensorineural hearing loss
Compound vs. Closed; Closed fractures carry higher rates of facial nerve injury
questions.answer: Longitudinal vs. Transverse; Transverse fractures carry higher rates of facial nerve transection and sensorineural hearing loss
questions.explanation: Why correct: Petrous fractures are classified as longitudinal (~70-80%, running parallel to the petrous ridge) or transverse (~10-20%, running perpendicular to the ridge). Transverse fractures cross the otic capsule and internal auditory canal, causing direct damage to the cochlea/vestibule (sensorineural hearing loss and severe vertigo) and facial nerve transection in up to 50% of cases (compared to ~20% in longitudinal fractures, which more often cause conductive hearing loss from ossicular disruption or hemotympanum). Why distractors are incorrect: Option C is reversed; transverse fractures cause far higher rates of otic capsule injury. Options B and D are inappropriate classification schemes for petrous bone trauma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the defining imaging feature of a 'depressed skull fracture' on head CT?
options: The fractured outer table of the calvarium is displaced inward beyond the inner table of the adjacent intact skull
The fracture line runs strictly along a cranial suture without bone displacement
The fracture is associated with scalp hematoma only without calvarial break
There are multiple linear fractures radiating from a central point without displacement
questions.answer: The fractured outer table of the calvarium is displaced inward beyond the inner table of the adjacent intact skull
questions.explanation: Why correct: A skull fracture is considered significantly depressed when the outer table of the depressed segment is displaced inward by more than the thickness of the adjacent inner table (calvarial width, typically >5-10 mm). Such fractures often tear the underlying dura and lacerate cortex, frequently necessitating surgical elevation. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B describes suture diastasis. Option C describes a simple subgaleal hematoma. Option D describes a stellate non-depressed fracture.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 10-year-old child presents after blunt head trauma. Skull radiography demonstrates separation of the coronal suture exceeding 3 mm compared to the contralateral side. What is the specific diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Why correct: A diastatic fracture is a traumatic separation of cranial bones along a suture line (most common in children under 12 whose cranial sutures are not yet fully interdigitated or fused), defined by widened suture gap (>2-3 mm). Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is a pediatric long-bone fracture pattern, not a cranial suture separation. Option C (leptomeningeal cyst) is a delayed complication of pediatric skull fracture where dura tears and pulsating leptomeninges erode and widen the fracture margins over months. Option D is premature congenital closure of cranial sutures.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 3-year-old falls from a porch, sustaining a linear parietal skull fracture. Four months later, the parents bring the child back noticing a pulsating, enlarging soft swelling along the old fracture line. Repeat CT reveals erosion and scalloping of the calvarial margins with widening of the fracture defect. What is this entity?
options: Osteomyelitis of the calvarium (Pott puffy tumor)
questions.explanation: Why correct: A 'growing skull fracture' (post-traumatic leptomeningeal cyst) occurs almost exclusively in children under 3 years old when a linear fracture is accompanied by an unrecognized tear in the underlying dura. Continuous CSF pulsations cause leptomeninges (and sometimes brain parenchyma) to herniate into the fracture line, progressively resorbing bone edges and widening the gap over weeks to months. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is an osteolytic lesion without prior trauma history. Option C is calvarial osteomyelitis secondary to frontal sinusitis. Option D is a rare benign myofibroblastic scalp tumor.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the crucial differentiator on CT between a true linear skull fracture and a normal cranial suture?
options: Fractures are sharply marginated, straight or jagged lucent lines lacking sclerotic corticated borders and do not occur in anatomical suture distributions
Sutures always cross cranial sutures at right angles
Fractures always have dense sclerotic borders
Fractures are isodense to white matter
questions.answer: Fractures are sharply marginated, straight or jagged lucent lines lacking sclerotic corticated borders and do not occur in anatomical suture distributions
questions.explanation: Why correct: Normal cranial sutures have interdigitating, serpiginous margins with well-defined, smooth cortical sclerotic borders and follow well-known anatomical paths. In contrast, linear fractures are sharp, lucent, non-sclerotic lines with straight or branching jagged paths that often traverse suture lines or vascular grooves. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is false; sutures demarcate bones, not cross them. Option C describes chronic healing fractures or sutures, not acute fractures. Option D is completely incorrect attenuation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On non-contrast CT, the presence of intracranial gas bubbles within the subdural, subarachnoid, or ventricular spaces after trauma is termed:
questions.explanation: Why correct: Pneumocephalus refers to the presence of air or gas within the cranial cavity, which in the setting of trauma implies a breach of the skull base, paranasal sinuses, mastoid air cells, or calvarium with an associated dural laceration. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B refers to air in the pleural space. Option C refers to excess CSF in the ventricles. Option D refers to free air in the abdominal peritoneal cavity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old male presents with severe facial trauma following an assault. High-resolution coronal CT shows bilateral fractures traversing the pterygomaxillary junction, medial and lateral walls of the maxillary sinuses, and the nasal septum, completely separating the hard palate and alveolar process from the midface. Which Le Fort fracture is this?
options: Le Fort I fracture (transmaxillary / floating palate)
questions.answer: Le Fort I fracture (transmaxillary / floating palate)
questions.explanation: Why correct: A Le Fort I fracture is a horizontal maxillary fracture separating the maxillary teeth and alveolar arch from the upper midface ('floating palate'). Hallmark fractures involve the pterygoid plates and the anterolateral and medial walls of the maxillary sinus. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B (Le Fort II) is pyramidal, extending through the nasal bridge, lacrimal bones, and infraorbital rims. Option C (Le Fort III) is complete craniofacial disjunction running through the zygomatic arches, lateral orbital walls, and nasofrontal suture. Option D is a tetrapod fracture of the zygoma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: According to the Denis Three-Column model of the spine, which anatomical structures constitute the 'middle column'?
options: Posterior half of the vertebral body, posterior aspect of the intervertebral disc, and the posterior longitudinal ligament (PLL)
Anterior longitudinal ligament, anterior two-thirds of the vertebral body, and anterior annulus fibrosus
Pedicles, facet joints, laminae, ligamentum flavum, and spinous processes
Spinal cord and thecal sac only
questions.answer: Posterior half of the vertebral body, posterior aspect of the intervertebral disc, and the posterior longitudinal ligament (PLL)
questions.explanation: Why correct: In Denis' three-column spine model, the middle column is formed by the posterior half of the vertebral body, the posterior annulus fibrosus/disc, and the posterior longitudinal ligament. Disruption of the middle column (as in burst fractures) almost always renders the spinal fracture unstable. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B defines the anterior column. Option C defines the posterior column. Option D is neural tissue, not a biomechanical spinal column component.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 50-year-old man dives headfirst into shallow water. CT of the cervical spine reveals four-point fractures involving both the anterior and posterior arches of C1 (atlas) with lateral displacement of the lateral masses beyond the articular margins of the C2 superior facets (total lateral displacement >7 mm on coronal view). What is the specific fracture?
questions.explanation: Why correct: A Jefferson fracture is a burst fracture of the C1 atlas ring caused by axial loading (e.g., diving into shallow water). The wedge-shaped occipital condyles drive down into the C1 lateral masses, fracturing both the anterior and posterior arches. Summed lateral displacement of the lateral masses >7 mm indicates transverse atlantal ligament rupture, indicating instability. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B (Hangman) is bilateral pars interarticularis fractures of C2. Option C (Clay-shoveler) is an avulsion of the C6/C7 spinous process. Option D is a devastating flexion or extension injury with an anterior vertebral body fragment.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 42-year-old unrestrained driver sustains hyperextension of the neck in a high-speed frontal collision. Sagittal CT of the cervical spine demonstrates bilateral traumatic spondylolysis (fracture through the pars interarticularis / pedicles of C2) with anterior subluxation of the C2 vertebral body on C3. What is this fracture called?
options: Hangman fracture (traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis)
questions.answer: Hangman fracture (traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis)
questions.explanation: Why correct: A Hangman fracture is traumatic spondylolisthesis of C2, characterized by bilateral fractures of the pars interarticularis of the axis with variable anterior displacement of C2 on C3, caused by forceful hyperextension and distraction/axial loading. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is a C1 burst ring fracture. Option C is a fracture through the base/waist of the odontoid process. Option D is a flexion-distraction injury through all three columns in the thoracolumbar spine (seatbelt injury).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: In the Anderson and D'Alonzo classification of odontoid (dens) fractures, which type involves the base/waist of the dens and has the highest rate of nonunion due to watershed vascularity?
options: Type II (fracture through the base/waist of the dens)
Type III (fracture extending deep into the C2 vertebral body)
Type IV (longitudinal split of the dens)
questions.answer: Type II (fracture through the base/waist of the dens)
questions.explanation: Why correct: Type II odontoid fractures occur at the junction of the dens with the C2 vertebral body (the waist). Because this junction has a tenuous arterial watershed supply and limited cancellous surface contact, it has a high propensity for nonunion or fibrous union (~30-40%), often requiring surgical fixation. Why distractors are incorrect: Option A (Type I) is a stable avulsion of the apex by the alar ligament. Option C (Type III) extends into the vascular cancellous bone of the C2 vertebral body and has a high union rate with conservative immobilization. Option D is not part of the standard Anderson-D'Alonzo classification.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old male wearing a lap-only seatbelt is involved in a head-on collision. CT of the lumbar spine demonstrates a horizontal fracture line passing through the spinous process, laminae, pedicles, and extending completely across the L2 vertebral body. What is the specific name of this flexion-distraction injury?
questions.explanation: Why correct: A Chance fracture is a classic flexion-distraction injury (classically caused by a lap-only seatbelt pivoting anterior to the spine), resulting in tensile failure that splits all three columns horizontally across the bony and/or ligamentous elements. It is frequently associated with intra-abdominal visceral injuries (e.g., bowel perforation, mesenteric tears). Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is an axial loading failure causing comminution of the vertebral body with retropulsion of middle column bone. Option C involves isolated anterior column failure without middle column disruption. Option D is isolated avulsion of a cervical spinous process.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 23-year-old rugby player sustains severe hyperflexion-compression of the cervical spine. CT shows a triangular bone fragment sheared off the anteroinferior margin of the C5 vertebral body with retropulsion of the posterior body into the canal, kyphotic angulation, and widening of the posterior interspinous distance. What is this devastating injury?
questions.explanation: Why correct: A flexion teardrop fracture is one of the most severe cervical spine injuries, caused by violent hyperflexion and compression. It features a triangular 'teardrop' fragment off the anteroinferior vertebral body, posterior displacement of the remainder of the body into the spinal cord, disruption of all anterior and posterior columns/ligaments, and catastrophic acute anterior cord syndrome (quadriplegia and loss of pain/temperature). Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is an avulsion of the anteroinferior border by the anterior longitudinal ligament during hyperextension, generally stable in flexion. Option C is a stable spinous process avulsion. Option D shows a 'jumped' facet with rotatory subluxation but no anterior body teardrop fragment.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What primary imaging feature differentiates an unstable thoracolumbar 'burst fracture' from a stable 'wedge compression fracture' on CT?
options: Involvement of the middle column with retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal in burst fractures
Burst fractures only occur in the coccyx
Wedge compression fractures always transect the spinal cord
Wedge compression fractures show loss of posterior column integrity
questions.answer: Involvement of the middle column with retropulsion of bone fragments into the spinal canal in burst fractures
questions.explanation: Why correct: In a simple wedge compression fracture, failure is restricted to the anterior column (anterior body height loss), leaving the middle column intact. In contrast, a burst fracture is caused by severe axial load that shatters both the anterior and middle columns, characteristically driving retropulsed bone fragments into the spinal canal with risk of cord/thecal sac compression. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B is false; burst fractures are most common at the thoracolumbar junction (T11-L2). Option C is false; wedge compression fractures are typically stable and rarely cause cord injury. Option D is false; posterior columns are intact in simple wedge compression fractures.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A lateral cervical spine radiograph shows anterior displacement of the C5 vertebral body over C6 by approximately 50% of the vertebral body width. Both the inferior articular facets of C5 lie completely anterior to the superior articular facets of C6 ('jumped facets'). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Why correct: Bilateral facet dislocation is an extremely unstable injury caused by severe hyperflexion. Both inferior facets dislocate anteriorly over the superior facets of the vertebra below, producing ≥50% anterior subluxation on the lateral view and high risk of complete spinal cord transection. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B (unilateral facet dislocation) produces ~25% anterior translation with rotation and a 'bow-tie' or 'bat-wing' appearance of articular pillars. Option C is grossly incorrect. Option D involves C2 pars fractures, not C5/C6 facet dislocation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 78-year-old female with known multiple myeloma presents with severe mid-back pain. Spinal MRI reveals a collapsed T8 vertebral body. Which of the following MRI features strongly favors a malignant/metastatic pathological fracture over a benign osteoporotic compression fracture?
options: Complete replacement of the normal fatty bone marrow with convex posterior cortical bulging into the spinal canal, pedicle marrow involvement, and an epidural soft-tissue mass
Preservation of normal fatty marrow signal on non-contrast T1, a horizontal low-signal fracture line, and retropulsion of an intact posterosuperior bone fragment
Absence of enhancement after intravenous gadolinium
Presence of intravertebral vacuum cleft phenomenon (Kummel disease)
questions.answer: Complete replacement of the normal fatty bone marrow with convex posterior cortical bulging into the spinal canal, pedicle marrow involvement, and an epidural soft-tissue mass
questions.explanation: Why correct: Malignant vertebral fractures typically demonstrate complete diffuse replacement of normal marrow signal (low on T1, high on T2/STIR), convex posterior vertebral contour bulging into the epidural space, destruction of the pedicles/posterior elements, and associated extraosseous epidural soft-tissue masses. Why distractors are incorrect: Option B describes typical features of acute benign osteoporotic fractures (retropulsed posterosuperior bone fragment, spared marrow fat elsewhere in the body). Option C is false; tumors enhance avidly. Option D (intravertebral vacuum cleft/Kummel disease) represents ischemic osteonecrosis, a classic sign of benign osteoporotic collapse.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the radiologist measuring when evaluating the 'predental space' (atlantodental interval, ADI) on a lateral cervical radiograph to assess for transverse ligament rupture in adults?
options: The distance between the posterior cortex of the anterior arch of C1 and the anterior cortex of the dens (normal ≤3 mm in adults)
The width of the spinal canal at C7
The height of the dens above the foramen magnum
The vertical gap between C1 spinous process and C2 lamina
questions.answer: The distance between the posterior cortex of the anterior arch of C1 and the anterior cortex of the dens (normal ≤3 mm in adults)
questions.explanation: Why correct: The atlantodental interval (ADI) is the distance between the anterior arch of C1 and the odontoid process. Normal ADI is ≤3 mm in adults (and ≤5 mm in children). An increased ADI signifies rupture or incompetence of the transverse atlantal ligament (seen in trauma, rheumatoid arthritis, or Down syndrome), representing atlantoaxial instability.
