questions.prompt: A 19-year-old post-laparotomy patient on shallow breathing due to incisional pain demonstrates fine horizontal linear opacities 1 to 3 mm thick and several centimeters long at both lung bases, without fissure displacement. What is this radiographic finding?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Subsegmental atelectasis (also called plate-like or Fleischner's atelectasis) appears as thin horizontal linear bands parallel to the diaphragm in the lung bases. It commonly occurs in post-operative patients, splinting from pain, or pulmonary embolism due to shallow respiration and focal surfactant depletion. Distractor rationales: B are diagonal lines extending from the hila toward the periphery caused by distended interlobular lymphatics. C are benign solitary pulmonary nodules often containing popcorn calcification. D are focal pleural thickenings along the posterolateral chest wall or diaphragmatic domes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A complete 'white-out' of the entire right hemithorax is noted on a portable radiograph of an intubated patient. The trachea and mediastinal structures are markedly shifted TOWARD the right side. What is the diagnosis?
options: Total right lung collapse (e.g., from an obstructing mucus plug or left mainstem malposition of the endotracheal tube)
Severe right sided consolidation without airway obstruction
questions.answer: Total right lung collapse (e.g., from an obstructing mucus plug or left mainstem malposition of the endotracheal tube)
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A completely opacified hemithorax (white-out) with ipsilateral mediastinal shift (shift TOWARD the opacity) is diagnostic of massive volume loss, namely total lung collapse (e.g., right mainstem mucus plug or endotracheal tube positioned selectively into the left main bronchus). Distractor rationales: B and C cause mass effect and shift the mediastinum AWAY from the opacified hemithorax (contralateral shift). D typically causes little to no mediastinal shift because lobar volume is preserved.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the minimum volume of pleural fluid typically required to cause blunting of the posterior costophrenic sulcus on an upright lateral chest radiograph?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The posterior costophrenic sulcus is the most dependent portion of the pleural space in the upright thorax. A small volume of 25 to 50 mL of pleural fluid is sufficient to cause blunting on a lateral upright radiograph. In contrast, 150 to 200 mL is generally required to blunt the lateral costophrenic sulcus on a standard frontal (PA) radiograph. Distractor rationales: B is the threshold for detection on the frontal (PA) view. C and D represent moderate-to-large effusions easily visible on all upright projections.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old male presents with dyspnea. An upright PA chest radiograph demonstrates blunting of the right lateral costophrenic angle with a curvilinear opacity that rises laterally along the chest wall. What is this classic radiographic sign?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The meniscus sign is the classic radiographic appearance of a free-flowing pleural effusion on an upright radiograph. Capillary action and negative intrapleural pressure cause the fluid to rise higher along the lateral chest wall and axilla than medially, creating a concave upper border with the apex pointing toward the axilla. Distractor rationales: B is a wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity in pulmonary infarction. C is the loss of anatomical borders when two densities abut. D occurs in tracheobronchial rupture where the collapsed lung falls into the dependent pleural space.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 58-year-old woman with cirrhosis has a chest radiograph that appears to show an elevated right hemidiaphragm with lateral displacement of the diaphragmatic apex ('peak shifted laterally'). On expiration or lateral decubitus positioning, fluid layers freely. What was the initial finding on the upright film?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A subpulmonic effusion occurs when pleural fluid accumulates between the inferior surface of the lower lobe and the superior surface of the diaphragm without filling the costophrenic sulcus. Characteristic signs include lateral displacement of the dome (peak) of the apparent hemidiaphragm, a steep lateral descent, and on the left side, increased distance between the gastric bubble and the lung base (>1.5-2 cm). Distractor rationales: B would demonstrate herniation of abdominal viscera into the thorax with disruption of the diaphragmatic contour. C is congenital thinning/weakness of the diaphragm producing a smooth localized bulge. D causes true elevation of the hemidiaphragm with normal apex contour and paradoxical motion on sniff test under fluoroscopy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A portable AP supine chest radiograph is obtained for an ICU patient after abdominal surgery. Which radiographic appearance is most characteristic of a moderate pleural effusion in this positioning?
options: A diffuse, veiled, ground-glass increased radiodensity across the entire hemithorax with vascular markings still visible
A sharp, horizontal air-fluid level across the middle third of the thorax
A dense triangular retrocardiac opacity with depression of the hilum
Blunting of the sharp anterior cardiophrenic angle only
questions.answer: A diffuse, veiled, ground-glass increased radiodensity across the entire hemithorax with vascular markings still visible
questions.explanation: Correct: A. In the supine position, free-flowing pleural fluid distributes along the dependent posterior pleural space, creating a diffuse, homogeneous, veiled increase in radiodensity over the entire hemithorax while underlying pulmonary vascular markings usually remain discernable. Sharp menisci are typically absent. Distractor rationales: B requires both air and fluid in the pleural space (hydropneumothorax) on an erect or horizontal beam film, not a standard supine effusion. C describes left lower lobe atelectasis. D is not a typical sign of supine pleural effusion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary role of a lateral decubitus chest radiograph with a horizontal X-ray beam in the evaluation of pleural fluid?
options: To differentiate free-flowing from loculated pleural effusion and detect small amounts (as little as 5 mL)
To measure pulmonary arterial pressure non-invasively
To differentiate between right and left ventricular enlargement
To confirm whether an endotracheal tube is positioned above the carina
questions.answer: To differentiate free-flowing from loculated pleural effusion and detect small amounts (as little as 5 mL)
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A lateral decubitus film (with the suspect side down) allows gravity-dependent layering of free pleural fluid along the lateral thoracic wall. It confirms whether an effusion is free-flowing versus loculated and can detect very small volumes of fluid (as little as 5 to 10 mL). Distractor rationales: B requires echocardiography or catheterization. C is evaluated on echocardiography or CT/MRI. D is assessed on standard frontal radiographs.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 65-year-old male with congestive heart failure has an oval-shaped, well-circumscribed radiopacity located within the horizontal fissure on frontal and lateral chest radiographs. After 3 days of aggressive intravenous diuretic therapy, the opacity completely resolves. What is this entity?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A 'pseudotumor' (or 'phantom tumor' / 'vanishing tumor') is a loculated pleural effusion within an interlobar fissure (most commonly the minor fissure), often secondary to congestive heart failure. Its biconvex, spindle, or lenticular shape resembles a lung mass, but it rapidly disappears or shrinks following diuretic therapy. Distractor rationales: B does not resolve rapidly with diuretics. C is a benign parenchymal neoplasm that is stable over time and often calcified. D is a mobile fungal ball in a pre-existing cavity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following radiological characteristics best distinguishes a loculated pleural empyema from a peripheral intrapulmonary lung abscess on contrast-enhanced chest CT?
options: Empyema demonstrates the 'split pleura sign' with obtuse angles to the chest wall, while lung abscess is spherical with acute angles and interrupts vessels
Empyema is always perfectly spherical with acute margins to the chest wall
Lung abscess shows thickening of both visceral and parietal pleura separated by fluid
Empyema causes destruction of adjacent pulmonary parenchyma and crosses fissures freely
questions.answer: Empyema demonstrates the 'split pleura sign' with obtuse angles to the chest wall, while lung abscess is spherical with acute angles and interrupts vessels
questions.explanation: Correct: A. On contrast CT, an empyema is lenticular/biconvex in the pleural space, forms obtuse angles with the adjacent chest wall, compresses adjacent lung, and characteristically exhibits the 'split pleura sign' (thickened, enhancing visceral and parietal pleural layers separated by fluid). In contrast, a lung abscess is intraparenchymal, round/spherical, forms acute angles with the pleura, and destroys lung tissue and vessels. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D confuse the classical distinguishing features.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 70-year-old patient presents with massive right hemithoracic opacification ('white-out'). The trachea and mediastinum are markedly displaced to the LEFT (contralateral side). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A massive pleural effusion adds volume to the hemithorax, acting as a space-occupying lesion that exerts mass effect, pushing mediastinal structures and the trachea away from the side of the opacity (contralateral mediastinal shift). Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are volume-loss entities where mediastinal structures shift TOWARD the side of the opacified hemithorax (ipsilateral shift).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What finding on an upright chest radiograph indicates the presence of BOTH air and fluid within the pleural space (hydropneumothorax)?
options: A dead-straight, horizontal fluid line extending to the chest wall
A concave upward meniscus along the axillary chest wall
Diffuse hazy veiled opacity over the hemithorax
Convex bulging of the horizontal fissure
questions.answer: A dead-straight, horizontal fluid line extending to the chest wall
questions.explanation: Correct: A. In a hydropneumothorax, the presence of air eliminates the negative intrathoracic surface tension that normally pulls fluid upward along the pleura to create a meniscus. Consequently, the air-fluid interface forms an absolute straight, perfectly horizontal line across the hemithorax on an upright or decubitus view. Distractor rationales: B is the normal meniscus of fluid alone without air. C is seen in supine fluid layering. D is the bulging fissure sign of lobar pneumonia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting minimal volumes of pleural fluid (as little as 5 to 10 mL) at the bedside?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Thoracic ultrasound is extremely sensitive for pleural effusion, capable of detecting as little as 5 to 10 mL of fluid. It can be performed rapidly at the bedside, distinguishes fluid from pleural thickening, and provides real-time guidance for thoracentesis. Distractor rationales: B requires 150-200 mL. C requires several hundred milliliters and lacks sensitivity. D is cumbersome and delivers unnecessary radiation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the fundamental radiographic finding of a pneumothorax on an upright frontal chest radiograph?
options: A thin, sharp white visceral pleural line separated from the chest wall by peripheral lucency devoid of lung markings
A concave opacity rising along the lateral chest wall
An air-filled bronchus surrounded by consolidated lung
Inward bowing of the intercostal spaces
questions.answer: A thin, sharp white visceral pleural line separated from the chest wall by peripheral lucency devoid of lung markings
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A pneumothorax is identified on an upright chest radiograph by the visceral pleural line—a thin, crisp white line formed by the visceral pleura separating the collapsed lung from the radiolucent pleural space, which is completely devoid of bronchovascular markings. Distractor rationales: B is the meniscus sign of a pleural effusion. C is an air bronchogram. D is an indirect sign of atelectasis/volume loss; pneumothorax typically expands intercostal spaces.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old intubated ICU patient is supine. The clinician notices a strikingly deep, hyperlucent, and sharp costophrenic angle on the right side extending toward the right upper quadrant. No apical visceral pleural line is identified. What is this sign?
options: Deep sulcus sign, indicating pneumothorax in the supine patient
questions.answer: Deep sulcus sign, indicating pneumothorax in the supine patient
questions.explanation: Correct: A. In a supine patient, pleural air rises to the least dependent (anterior and inferior) portions of the hemithorax, particularly the anterior costophrenic sulcus. This produces the 'deep sulcus sign,' characterized by an abnormally deep, lucent, and sharp costophrenic angle on the affected side. Distractor rationales: B is free air outlining the entire central diaphragm in pneumomediastinum. C is visualization of both inner and outer walls of the bowel in pneumoperitoneum. D is non-pathological interposition of the colon between the liver and right hemidiaphragm.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 22-year-old tall, slender male presents with sudden-onset sharp right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath while resting. Upright chest radiograph reveals a 2.5 cm apical pneumothorax without mediastinal shift. What is the underlying pathology of this primary spontaneous pneumothorax?
options: Rupture of small subpleural apical blebs or bullae
Cavitation of an underlying squamous cell carcinoma
Erosion of a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation
Necrotizing pneumonia caused by anaerobic oral flora
questions.answer: Rupture of small subpleural apical blebs or bullae
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically occurs in young, tall, thin males due to the spontaneous rupture of apical subpleural blebs or bullae, thought to arise from high negative transpulmonary pressure gradients at the lung apices. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are secondary causes seen in older or diseased populations, not primary spontaneous pneumothorax in young healthy individuals.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old unrestrained driver involved in a motor vehicle collision arrives hypotensive (BP 75/40 mmHg), tachycardic (HR 145 bpm), with distended neck veins and absent left-sided breath sounds. A stat portable radiograph shows total collapse of the left lung, depression and inversion of the left hemidiaphragm, and marked deviation of the trachea and heart to the RIGHT. What is the immediate management?
options: Immediate needle decompression or finger thoracostomy of the left hemithorax without waiting for further imaging
Emergent contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to rule out aortic transection
Left-sided thoracentesis using an 18G needle directed posteroinferiorly
High-dose intravenous inotropes and fluid resuscitation alone
questions.answer: Immediate needle decompression or finger thoracostomy of the left hemithorax without waiting for further imaging
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening medical emergency. Accumulating pleural pressure exceeds atmospheric pressure, compressing the vena cava and right atrium, collapsing venous return, and causing obstructive shock. The hallmark signs on imaging are ipsilateral lung collapse, diaphragmatic depression/inversion, and contralateral mediastinal/tracheal shift. Management is immediate clinical decompression (needle decompression or finger thoracostomy) followed by chest tube placement. Distractor rationales: B delays life-saving decompression and risks cardiac arrest. C is the treatment for pleural effusion. D fails to treat the underlying mechanical obstructive shock.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: How does an expiratory chest radiograph assist in the detection of a subtle, suspected pneumothorax?
options: Lung volume decreases while the volume of pleural air remains constant, making the relative pneumothorax larger and more radiolucent compared to denser lung tissue
Expiration forces pleural air into the major fissure where it is easier to see
Expiratory films significantly lower radiation exposure
Expiration causes bronchovascular markings to disappear completely
questions.answer: Lung volume decreases while the volume of pleural air remains constant, making the relative pneumothorax larger and more radiolucent compared to denser lung tissue
questions.explanation: Correct: A. On expiration, the volume of the lung parenchyma decreases and its radiodensity increases as air is expelled. However, the volume of air trapped in the pleural space remains unchanged, so the pneumothorax occupies a relatively larger proportion of the hemithorax and stands out in sharper contrast against the opacified lung. Distractor rationales: B is incorrect because pleural air does not selectively enter fissures. C and D are factually inaccurate.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On an upright chest radiograph, a curved linear opacity is seen projecting over the right hemithorax. Closer inspection reveals that bronchovascular markings extend beyond this line all the way to the peripheral chest wall. What is this artifact/mimic?
options: Pleural adhesion binding down the lung
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A skin fold is a common mimic of a pneumothorax on portable radiographs. It creates an edge or Mach band, but unlike a true visceral pleural line, pulmonary vessels and lung markings can be traced clearly beyond the skin fold to the thoracic wall. Furthermore, a skin fold typically appears as a broad, dark-to-light boundary rather than a discrete thin white line. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are incorrect because in a true pneumothorax, no bronchovascular markings are seen in the pleural space peripheral to the visceral pleura.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 65-year-old patient with severe COPD has a large, thin-walled gas-filled lucency in the right upper zone. The clinician is trying to differentiate a large bulla from a pneumothorax on a chest radiograph. Which feature favors a large bulla over a pneumothorax?
options: Its inner border is concave toward the chest wall, and lung parenchyma is absent only within its discrete thin circular wall
Its inner border is convex toward the chest wall, outlining the entire lung contour
It is associated with deep sulcus sign and inversion of the diaphragm
It resolves completely within 24 hours of oxygen therapy
questions.answer: Its inner border is concave toward the chest wall, and lung parenchyma is absent only within its discrete thin circular wall
questions.explanation: Correct: A. An emphysematous bulla has a wall whose curvature is typically concave toward the chest wall, whereas the visceral pleural line in a pneumothorax is convex toward the lateral chest wall, paralleling the thoracic contour. Additionally, lung markings are seen outside the bulla's margin. Distractor rationales: B describes the visceral pleura of a pneumothorax. C is characteristic of tension pneumothorax. D is incorrect; bullae do not resolve with oxygen therapy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary hemodynamic consequence of tension pneumothorax that leads to cardiovascular collapse?
options: Compression of the inferior and superior vena cava leading to decreased venous return and cardiac output
Direct rupture of the ascending aorta
Coronary artery spasm caused by vagal overactivity
questions.answer: Compression of the inferior and superior vena cava leading to decreased venous return and cardiac output
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Positive intrapleural pressure in a tension pneumothorax shifts the mediastinum contralaterally, kinking and compressing the superior and inferior venae cavae. This abruptly impedes systemic venous return to the right heart, precipitating a dramatic reduction in cardiac output and obstructive shock. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are not the mechanical mechanisms of hemodynamic collapse in tension pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On lung point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), which of the following findings is 100% SPECIFIC for ruling in a pneumothorax?
options: Identification of a 'lung point' (the boundary where normal lung sliding alternates with absent sliding in real-time)
Presence of multiple vertical B-lines (lung rockets)
questions.answer: Identification of a 'lung point' (the boundary where normal lung sliding alternates with absent sliding in real-time)
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The 'lung point' on thoracic ultrasound represents the physical transition zone where normal pleural sliding (and B-lines) alternates with the absent sliding and barcode/stratosphere sign of a pneumothorax. When present, the lung point has virtually 100% specificity for confirming a pneumothorax. Distractor rationales: B (B-lines) and C (sea-shore sign) confirm normal lung sliding and RULE OUT a pneumothorax at that probe location. D confirms pleural effusion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient with acute asthma exacerbation develops chest pain and neck swelling. Chest radiography shows thin radiolucent vertical streaks outlining the cardiac silhouette and aorta, extending into the soft tissues of the neck. No pleural line is seen along the thoracic cage. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The Macklin effect involves alveolar rupture due to high intra-alveolar pressures (e.g., severe asthma, barotrauma, Valsalva), with air dissecting along bronchovascular sheaths into the mediastinum (pneumomediastinum) and tracking superiorly into cervical subcutaneous tissues (subcutaneous emphysema). Radiographically, air outlines the heart, aortic knob, and mediastinal pleura. Distractor rationales: B would show a pleural line and lung collapse in the hemithorax. C would enlarge the water-bottle cardiac silhouette without linear gas streaks. D causes mediastinal widening without free mediastinal or subcutaneous gas.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the classical anatomical distribution of parenchymal cavitary lesions in post-primary (reactivation) pulmonary tuberculosis?
options: Apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes, and superior segments of the lower lobes
Anterior segments of the upper lobes and middle lobe
Basal segments of both lower lobes exclusively
Lingular segments and anterior cardiophrenic angles
questions.answer: Apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes, and superior segments of the lower lobes
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Post-primary (reactivation or adult-type) tuberculosis classically has a predilection for lung regions with high ventilation-perfusion ratios and high oxygen tension (PaO2), specifically the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes (85%) and the superior segments of the lower lobes (10-15%). Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are less oxygenated and are infrequent sites for post-primary cavitary reactivation; anterior upper lobe involvement alone is more typical of bacterial aspiration or malignancy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What radiological components constitute the classic 'Ghon complex' in primary pulmonary tuberculosis?
options: A calcified subpleural parenchymal granuloma (Ghon focus) combined with ipsilateral calcified hilar/mediastinal lymph nodes
A thick-walled apical cavity with an internal mobile aspergilloma
Diffuse 1 to 2 mm micronodules scattered symmetrically throughout both lungs
Consolidation of the right middle lobe with an air bronchogram
questions.answer: A calcified subpleural parenchymal granuloma (Ghon focus) combined with ipsilateral calcified hilar/mediastinal lymph nodes
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The Ghon complex (or Ranke complex when calcified) consists of the initial parenchymal site of tuberculous infection (Ghon focus, typically mid-to-lower lung subpleural) associated with infected and subsequently calcified ipsilateral hilar or paratracheal lymph nodes. Distractor rationales: B describes a secondary mycetoma in a tuberculous cavity. C describes miliary tuberculosis. D describes standard bacterial lobar pneumonia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 29-year-old immigrant from an endemic region presents with chronic fever, night sweats, weight loss, and severe dyspnea. A chest radiograph demonstrates countless, uniform, sharp 1 to 2 mm micronodules distributed diffusely and randomly throughout both lungs from apices to bases. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Miliary tuberculosis is caused by hematogenous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis throughout the pulmonary and systemic circulation. Radiographically, it is characterized by innumerable, tiny (1-2 mm), discrete, uniform, millet seed-like micronodules distributed evenly and randomly across all lung zones. Distractor rationales: B shows small nodules predominantly in the upper lobes associated with egg-shell calcification of hilar nodes. C presents with diffuse ground-glass or cystic perihilar opacities without discrete 1-2 mm nodules. D presents with subpleural, basilar-predominant reticulation and honeycombing.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old male with active post-primary tuberculosis has high-resolution CT of the chest. The scan reveals small branching centrilobular nodular opacities resembling budding branches. What is this sign and what does it signify?
options: Tree-in-bud sign, indicating active endobronchial spread of infection with impaction of small airways
Halo sign, indicating angioinvasive fungal infection
Galaxy sign, indicating chronic pulmonary sarcoidosis
Crazy paving sign, indicating pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
questions.answer: Tree-in-bud sign, indicating active endobronchial spread of infection with impaction of small airways
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The 'tree-in-bud' pattern on HRCT represents dilated centrilobular branching bronchioles impacted with mucus, pus, or granulomatous inflammation, characteristic of active endobronchial dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Distractor rationales: B is a nodule with surrounding ground-glass hemorrhage seen in angioinvasive aspergillosis. C is a large granulomatous mass surrounded by satellite nodules seen in sarcoidosis. D is thickened interlobular septa superimposed on ground-glass opacification seen in PAP or severe edema.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which radiographic projection is particularly useful for demonstrating subtle apical tuberculous infiltrate or cavitation obscured by overlying clavicles and first ribs?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The apical lordotic view projects the clavicles and anterior first ribs superior to the thoracic cage, allowing unobstructed visualization of the lung apices where early or minimal post-primary tuberculous infiltration and cavitation reside. Distractor rationales: B is used to detect small pleural effusions or pneumothorax. C is used to evaluate air trapping or small pneumothoraces. D is used to evaluate cardiac chambers or rib fractures.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old male with a history of treated cavitary tuberculosis presents with massive hemoptysis. Contrast-enhanced CT shows a pseudoaneurysm arising from a branch of the pulmonary artery along the wall of a chronic tuberculous cavity. What is this life-threatening vascular lesion called?
options: Mycotic aneurysm of the descending aorta
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A Rasmussen aneurysm is an inflammatory pseudoaneurysm of a branch of the pulmonary artery adjacent to or within the wall of a tuberculous cavity. Rupture of a Rasmussen aneurysm causes massive, potentially fatal hemoptysis. Distractor rationales: B is a rare tortuous mucosal submucosal artery in the bronchus. C is a bacterial infection of the aortic wall. D is a congenital direct communication between pulmonary artery and vein.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 58-year-old patient with an old, healed tuberculous cavity in the left apex now presents with recurrent minor hemoptysis. A chest radiograph demonstrates a mobile, rounded soft tissue mass inside the cavity, separated from the superior cavity wall by a crescent of air (Monod sign). What is this lesion?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. An aspergilloma (mycetoma or fungal ball) is composed of Aspergillus hyphae, mucus, and cellular debris that colonizes a pre-existing epithelialized pulmonary cavity (most commonly from healed TB). On imaging, it appears as a dependent, mobile rounded mass surrounded by a crescent of air (the Monod sign or air-crescent sign) that shifts position when the patient changes from supine to prone. Distractor rationales: B is an irregular, non-mobile wall thickening without positional shifting. C is an Echinococcus infection with floating membranes (water-lily sign). D is a benign lung parenchymal nodule.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: How does the radiographic presentation of pulmonary tuberculosis differ in an advanced HIV/AIDS patient (CD4 < 100 cells/microL) compared to an immunocompetent adult?
options: Severe HIV patients typically show adenopathy, lower lobe opacities, and lack cavitation, resembling primary TB
Severe HIV patients develop massive apical cavitation and extensive pleural fibrosis
Severe HIV patients always present with normal chest radiographs
Severe HIV patients exclusively develop calcified Ghon complexes
questions.answer: Severe HIV patients typically show adenopathy, lower lobe opacities, and lack cavitation, resembling primary TB
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Cell-mediated immunity is required to form caseating granulomas, tissue necrosis, and cavitary lesions characteristic of post-primary TB. In severely immunosuppressed patients (e.g., CD4 < 100), the host cannot mount this response; hence, cavitation is rare, and the disease resembles primary tuberculosis, presenting with prominent mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy, lower or middle lobe consolidation, and high rates of miliary dissemination. Distractor rationales: B describes immunocompetent post-primary reactivation. C is incorrect; chest radiographs are usually abnormal (though subtle). D requires robust delayed-type hypersensitivity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 34-year-old male with untreated primary tuberculosis presents with unilateral chest pain and dullness. A chest radiograph reveals a large unilateral pleural effusion without visible parenchymal consolidation. Pleural fluid analysis shows an exudate with high protein, lymphocytic predominance, and elevated adenosine deaminase (ADA). What is the pathogenesis of this tuberculous pleurisy?
options: Delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to tuberculous antigens entering the pleural space from rupture of a subpleural caseous focus
Direct hematogenous seeding of billions of actively multiplying organisms throughout the pleura
Secondary bacterial superinfection by Staphylococcus aureus
Lymphatic obstruction by massive subdiaphragmatic metastases
questions.answer: Delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to tuberculous antigens entering the pleural space from rupture of a subpleural caseous focus
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Tuberculous pleural effusion in primary TB is predominantly a delayed-type hypersensitivity response triggered by the rupture of a tiny, often radiographically occult subpleural caseous focus into the pleural space. This produces a lymphocyte-rich, exudative effusion with high ADA levels, and acid-fast bacilli smears of the fluid are typically negative due to the paucibacillary immune nature. Distractor rationales: B describes tuberculous empyema (rare, grossly purulent with high bacilli load). C and D are incorrect etiologies.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the characteristic appearance of healed, remote tuberculosis on a routine chest radiograph in an asymptomatic person?
options: Dense calcified apical parenchymal nodules and calcified hilar lymph nodes with apical pleural thickening
Bilateral fluffy alveolar opacities with air bronchograms
Kerley B lines and enlarged central pulmonary arteries
questions.answer: Dense calcified apical parenchymal nodules and calcified hilar lymph nodes with apical pleural thickening
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Healed, remote, inactive tuberculosis characteristically demonstrates calcified granulomas (calcified Ghon foci), calcified hilar/mediastinal lymph nodes, apical pleural capping (thickening), and fibrous apical scarring with architectural distortion and volume loss. Distractor rationales: B represents acute alveolar pneumonia or pulmonary edema. C represents pulmonary venous or arterial hypertension. D represents chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: By definition in thoracic radiology, what size threshold differentiates a solitary pulmonary nodule (SPN) from a pulmonary mass?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. In radiology, a solitary pulmonary nodule (SPN) is defined as a well-circumscribed, rounded opacity measuring up to 3 cm (30 mm) in maximum diameter, surrounded by aerated lung, without associated atelectasis or adenopathy. Lesions greater than 3 cm are termed 'pulmonary masses' and are presumed malignant until proven otherwise. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are incorrect dimensional thresholds.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 64-year-old male with a 45 pack-year smoking history undergoes a CT of the chest. A 2.2 cm non-calcified nodule is identified in the left upper lobe. Which of the following morphological features most strongly increases the likelihood of malignancy?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Spiculated margins (corona radiata) reflect malignant cellular infiltration into surrounding interlobular septa or desmoplastic host reaction, carrying a positive predictive value for malignancy of >85-90%. Distractor rationales: B is typical of benign lesions like hamartomas or granulomas (though up to 20% of malignancies can have smooth borders). C and D are classic benign patterns of calcification (along with laminated and 'popcorn' calcification).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which histological subtype of lung cancer has the strongest association with peripheral lung location and often arises within areas of pre-existing parenchymal scars?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Adenocarcinoma is the most common primary lung cancer in both smokers and non-smokers. It characteristically arises in the peripheral lung zones, subpleurally, and frequently develops at sites of prior scar or chronic inflammation ('scar carcinoma'). Distractor rationales: B (squamous cell) and C (small cell) characteristically arise centrally in major bronchi, producing hilar masses and atelectasis. D (typical carcinoid) arises centrally from neuroendocrine cells in main/lobar bronchi.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 58-year-old male with severe shoulder pain, Horner syndrome (ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), and weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles has a chest radiograph. An apical opacity is seen invading the right first and second ribs and transverse processes. What is this clinical-radiological entity?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A Pancoast tumor (superior sulcus tumor) is a primary lung neoplasm (most commonly non-small cell, such as squamous cell or adenocarcinoma) located at the extreme thoracic inlet/apex. It invades the brachial plexus (C8-T1 nerve roots causing hand weakness/shoulder pain), the sympathetic chain/stellate ganglion (causing Horner syndrome), and adjacent ribs/vertebrae. Distractor rationales: B is in the anterior mediastinum. C is a benign intraparenchymal lung nodule. D is in the posterior mediastinum without invading the apex or creating Horner syndrome.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 62-year-old male smoker has a 5 cm solitary mass in the right lung with central cavitation on CT. The cavity wall is thick and irregular, measuring 18 mm at its thickest point, with nodular internal margins. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
questions.answer: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Squamous cell carcinoma is the lung malignancy that most frequently undergoes central necrosis and cavitation (up to 10-15% of cases). A cavity wall thickness > 15 mm, especially with nodular, irregular inner borders, strongly indicates malignancy (95% likelihood). Distractor rationales: B has a hairline-thin wall (< 1 mm). C is a thin-walled, avascular air space without soft tissue walls. D is a thin-walled, transient gas-filled space that develops after trauma or staphylococcal pneumonia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following patterns of calcification within a solitary pulmonary nodule is considered diagnostic of a benign pulmonary hamartoma?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. 'Popcorn' calcification—multiple chondroid calcific rings and arcs resembling popped kernels of corn—is pathognomonic for a pulmonary hamartoma. The presence of internal fat attenuation (-40 to -120 HU) on CT further confirms this benign diagnosis. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are indeterminate or suspicious calcification patterns that do not guarantee benignity and can be seen in scar carcinomas or mucinous adenocarcinomas.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 50-year-old woman with a history of treated invasive breast cancer 3 years ago has a routine chest radiograph demonstrating multiple bilateral, well-defined, rounded soft-tissue nodules of varying sizes scattered throughout both lower lung zones. What classic radiological appearance does this represent?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Hematogenous dissemination of malignancies (such as breast, colorectal, renal cell, choriocarcinoma, or osteosarcoma) classically produces multiple, bilateral, well-circumscribed, rounded masses of varying sizes predominantly in the lower lung zones (reflecting greater blood flow), commonly termed 'cannonball metastases.' Distractor rationales: B typically presents as persistent subsolid or ground-glass nodules. C presents as millions of tiny, uniform, 1-2 mm micronodules. D are rare and almost always solitary.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old male with a history of occupational exposure to shipyard insulation and asbestos presents with progressive breathlessness and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Chest CT demonstrates diffuse, nodular, circumferential thickening of the right pleura with contraction of the hemithorax and extension into the fissures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Malignant pleural mesothelioma is strongly associated with asbestos exposure (latency 30-45 years). Characteristic CT features include circumferential, nodular, rind-like pleural thickening (> 1 cm), volume loss of the affected hemithorax, and invasion into interlobar fissures, the mediastinum, or chest wall. Distractor rationales: B are bilateral, discrete, flat, calcified or non-calcified plaques along the posterolateral mid-chest and diaphragm that do not cause circumferential rind or volume loss. C is acute alveolar consolidation. D is a congenital anomaly of non-functioning lung tissue with systemic arterial supply.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary role of 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography / Computed Tomography (FDG-PET/CT) in the evaluation of a solitary pulmonary nodule?
options: Assessing glucose metabolic activity (standardized uptake value, SUV) to differentiate hypermetabolic malignancy from benign lesions and stage mediastinal nodes
Providing microscopic histological proof of cancer subtypes without biopsy
Distinguishing pure bacterial pneumonia from fungal infection
questions.answer: Assessing glucose metabolic activity (standardized uptake value, SUV) to differentiate hypermetabolic malignancy from benign lesions and stage mediastinal nodes
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Malignant tumors exhibit increased glycolysis (Warburg effect). 18F-FDG PET/CT detects areas of elevated glucose metabolism; an SUVmax > 2.5 in a non-calcified nodule > 8-10 mm is highly suspicious for malignancy and also allows accurate staging of regional lymph nodes and distant metastases. Distractor rationales: B is incorrect because PET/CT cannot provide histopathological confirmation (tissue biopsy is required). C is incorrect because both active infections and active granulomas take up FDG (false positives). D is performed by high-resolution CT, not PET.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On high-resolution CT, a persistent 1.5 cm pulmonary nodule is identified that is hazy and does not obscure the underlying bronchial and vascular margins. What is this nodule type, and what is its clinical significance?
options: Pure ground-glass nodule (subsolid nodule), with a high likelihood of being an adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) or minimally invasive adenocarcinoma
Solid nodule, with high certainty of being a completely benign hamartoma
Calcified granuloma, requiring no further follow-up
questions.answer: Pure ground-glass nodule (subsolid nodule), with a high likelihood of being an adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) or minimally invasive adenocarcinoma
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A ground-glass nodule (nonsolid or subsolid nodule) is defined on CT as hazy increased attenuation that permits visualization of underlying parenchymal vessels and bronchial walls. Persistent pure ground-glass nodules > 6 mm have a high probability of representing pre-invasive or early invasive adenocarcinoma (e.g., adenocarcinoma in situ, minimally invasive adenocarcinoma) and require systematic CT follow-up. Distractor rationales: B is incorrect because solid nodules completely obscure parenchymal margins. C completely obscures vessels and has dense calcification (>100 HU). D has an identifiable feeding artery and draining vein.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What radiological sign on high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) is the definitive hallmark of macroscopic end-stage pulmonary fibrosis in usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Honeycombing is characterized on HRCT by clustered, thick-walled, cystic air spaces measuring 3 to 10 mm arranged in stacked rows along the subpleural lung regions, typically sharing common walls. It is the defining feature of a definite UIP pattern and indicates irreversible, end-stage fibrotic lung destruction. Distractor rationales: B represents infectious bronchiolitis. C represents air-space consolidation. D represents angioinvasive fungal infection or organizing pneumonia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 66-year-old male smoker presents with insidious onset of progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, and digital clubbing. Auscultation reveals fine, dry, 'Velcro-like' crackles at both lung bases. HRCT demonstrates subpleural, basal-predominant reticular opacities, traction bronchiectasis, and subpleural honeycombing without significant ground-glass opacity. What is the diagnosis?
options: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Usual Interstitial Pneumonia pattern)
questions.answer: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Usual Interstitial Pneumonia pattern)
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The clinical triad of progressive dyspnea, dry cough, and velcro crackles in an older adult combined with the HRCT pattern of subpleural, basilar-predominant reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, and honeycombing without prominent ground glass is diagnostic of Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP), which in the absence of an identifiable cause constitutes Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF). Distractor rationales: B (NSIP) is characterized by prominent ground-glass opacity, subpleural sparing, and absence or rarity of honeycombing. C is an acute non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema with diffuse dependent consolidation. D presents with smooth interlobular septal thickening superimposed on ground-glass opacities ('crazy paving') without honeycombing.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old African American female presents with erythema nodosum, bilateral ankle arthralgias, and fatigue. A routine chest radiograph demonstrates symmetric, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and right paratracheal lymphadenopathy without parenchymal infiltrates. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The classic triad of bilateral hilar and right paratracheal lymphadenopathy ('Garland triad' or '1-2-3 sign') on chest radiography in a young woman presenting with erythema nodosum, polyarthralgias, and fever constitutes Löfgren syndrome, a classic acute presentation of Stage I sarcoidosis. Distractor rationales: B presents with diffuse 1-2 mm parenchymal micronodules. C usually presents with asymmetric, anterior mediastinal or paratracheal nodal enlargement and systemic B-symptoms. D requires occupational exposure to silica and features upper-lobe nodules with egg-shell calcification.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What anatomical structure do Kerley B lines represent on a chest radiograph?
options: Distended main bronchi filled with mucus
Subpleural blebs within the visceral pleura
Fibrous pleural plaques along the ribs
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Kerley B lines are short (1 to 2 cm long), thin (1 mm wide) horizontal lines located perpendicular to the lateral pleural surface at the lung bases. They represent edema, cellular infiltration, or fibrosis expanding the interlobular septa of the secondary pulmonary lobules (most commonly seen in pulmonary venous hypertension/left heart failure or lymphangitic carcinomatosis). Distractor rationales: B are bronchial walls (peribronchial cuffing). C are subpleural emphysematous spaces. D are pleural plaques.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 48-year-old female with systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) develops progressive shortness of breath. HRCT demonstrates symmetric ground-glass opacities and fine reticulation located predominantly in the lower lung zones, with noticeable preservation of a narrow strip of subpleural parenchyma immediately beneath the pleura (subpleural sparing). Honeycombing is absent. What is the most likely pattern?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) is the most frequent pulmonary manifestation of connective tissue diseases (especially systemic sclerosis). Its key HRCT hallmarks are basilar-predominant ground-glass opacities, fine reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, and characteristic subpleural sparing, with an absence of extensive honeycombing. Distractor rationales: B (UIP) features direct subpleural involvement and prominent honeycombing without subpleural sparing. C (DIP) is almost exclusively found in active heavy cigarette smokers. D (LIP) presents with diffuse thin-walled pulmonary cysts and ground-glass opacities, commonly associated with Sjögren syndrome.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old avid bird breeder presents with recurrent episodes of chills, cough, and dyspnea several hours after cleaning pigeon coops. Expiratory HRCT demonstrates areas of decreased attenuation and vascular caliber that fail to increase in density on expiration ('air trapping'), interspersed with normal and ground-glass lung ('headcheese sign'). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) is an immune-mediated interstitial disease caused by inhaling organic antigens (e.g., avian proteins). The 'headcheese sign' (three-density sign) reflects a mixed infiltrative and bronchiolar obstructive process: areas of ground-glass attenuation (interstitial infiltration), normal lung attenuation, and mosaic hypodensity/air trapping from small-airway bronchiolitis on expiratory CT. Distractor rationales: B has no expiratory air trapping or ground-glass three-density pattern. C presents with diffuse sand-like calcifications obscuring heart borders. D is an occupational granulomatous disease in aerospace/electronics workers mimicking sarcoidosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary anatomical unit of the lung evaluated on high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The secondary pulmonary lobule is the fundamental anatomical and physiological unit of lung architecture visualized on HRCT. Measuring 1 to 2.5 cm, it is bounded by fibrous interlobular septa containing pulmonary veins and lymphatics, and supplied centrally by a core centrilobular bronchiole and pulmonary artery. Distractor rationales: B is a subdivision of the secondary lobule (each lobule contains 3-12 acini). C is a gross anatomical subdivision of a lobe. D is a microscopic terminal airway component.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 59-year-old male stone-cutter with 25 years of silica dust exposure has a chest radiograph showing numerous small rounded nodules in the upper lobes. In addition, the hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes exhibit peripheral, rim-like calcification. What is this classic nodal pattern called?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. 'Eggshell calcification' refers to thin, well-defined peripheral rim-like calcification along the outer margin of enlarged hilar or mediastinal lymph nodes. It is classically associated with silicosis and coal workers' pneumoconiosis (and occasionally sarcoidosis, treated lymphoma, or histoplasmosis). Distractor rationales: B is pathognomonic of pulmonary hamartoma. C is characteristic of benign granulomas (e.g., histoplasmosis). D is non-specific calcification seen in old necrotic or infarcted tissue.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is 'traction bronchiectasis' and why does it occur in interstitial lung disease?
options: Irregular dilatation of bronchial airways caused by mechanical pulling (retraction) by adjacent fibrotic lung parenchyma
Congenital failure of bronchial cartilage development
Bronchial dilatation caused by high bacterial mucus plugging
Spasmodic dilation of smooth muscle caused by sympathetic overdrive
questions.answer: Irregular dilatation of bronchial airways caused by mechanical pulling (retraction) by adjacent fibrotic lung parenchyma
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Traction bronchiectasis (and bronchiolectasis) is the mechanical pulling outward and irreversible distortion of bronchi and bronchioles caused by the retractile fibrous force of surrounding architectural distortion and fibrosis in interstitial lung disease. Distractor rationales: B is Williams-Campbell syndrome. C describes cystic bronchiectasis secondary to chronic necrotizing infections (e.g., CF). D is a non-existent physiological mechanism.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old female presents with recurrent spontaneous pneumothoraces and exertional dyspnea. HRCT reveals multiple bilateral, thin-walled, uniformly round air-filled cysts distributed diffusely throughout the lungs, with completely normal intervening lung parenchyma. Serum VEGF-D is markedly elevated. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) occurs almost exclusively in women of childbearing age (sporadic or associated with tuberous sclerosis). Characteristic HRCT findings are innumerable, symmetric, thin-walled, round cysts evenly distributed throughout all lung zones with completely normal intervening parenchyma. Chylothorax, pneumothorax, and elevated VEGF-D are classic. Distractor rationales: B (PLCH) occurs in young cigarette smokers and features bizarre, irregularly shaped, bilobed cysts and nodules that spare the lung bases. C shows lucencies without perceptible walls and predominates in upper lobes of smokers. D presents with ground-glass opacities.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is considered the most reliable radiographic sign of pulmonary hyperinflation on a lateral chest radiograph?
options: Flattening or depression of the diaphragmatic domes
questions.answer: Flattening or depression of the diaphragmatic domes
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Flattening or downward depression (loss of the normal cranial convexity) of the hemidiaphragms on the lateral and frontal views is the single most sensitive and specific sign of severe hyperinflation in pulmonary emphysema/COPD. Distractor rationales: B is incorrect because hyperinflation widens and increases the retrosternal clear space (> 2.5 cm behind the sternum). C is incorrect; hyperinflation pulls the mediastinum down and elongates it. D is incorrect; hyperinflation spreads bronchovascular markings apart (attenuation).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a standard frontal chest radiograph of an adult with severe COPD, how many posterior ribs are typically visible above the right hemidiaphragm?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. In normal individuals, 9 to 10 posterior ribs are visible. In patients with severe hyperinflation due to air trapping in COPD or asthma, 11 to 12 posterior ribs (or >7 anterior ribs) are projected above the diaphragm. Distractor rationales: B and D represent poor inspiratory effort (underinflation). C is the normal inspiratory rib count.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 68-year-old male with a 50 pack-year smoking history presents with worsening dyspnea. A frontal chest radiograph shows flattened hemidiaphragms, an elongated and narrowed cardiac silhouette ('tubular' or 'vertical' heart), widening of intercostal spaces, and overall pulmonary hyperlucency. What is the physiological cause of the narrow cardiac appearance?
options: Depression of the diaphragm pulling the heart vertically, combined with hyperinflated lungs compressing the mediastinum
Left ventricular atrophy due to starvation
Severe volume loss of the lingula
questions.answer: Depression of the diaphragm pulling the heart vertically, combined with hyperinflated lungs compressing the mediastinum
questions.explanation: Correct: A. In severe pulmonary emphysema, low, flattened diaphragms pull the mediastinum and pericardium inferiorly, elongating the cardiac silhouette. Simultaneously, expanding, hyperinflated lungs physically compress the heart laterally, giving it a classic long, narrow, 'tubular' or 'droplet' appearance. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D do not account for the classic radiological tubular heart of COPD.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which subtype of emphysema is most strongly associated with cigarette smoking and classically demonstrates a predilection for the upper lobes and apical segments?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Centrilobular (centriacinar) emphysema is strongly linked to cigarette smoking. It selectively destroys the respiratory bronchioles in the center of the secondary pulmonary lobule, with classic predilection for the upper lobes (apical and posterior segments). Distractor rationales: B (panlobular) involves the entire lobule uniformly, affects predominantly the lower lobes, and is classic for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. C (paraseptal) affects peripheral subpleural alveoli and is associated with spontaneous pneumothoraces in young adults. D is scar-related.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 36-year-old non-smoker with early-onset severe shortness of breath and elevated liver enzymes has a chest radiograph and CT scan. Imaging demonstrates severe, diffuse pulmonary emphysema with marked architectural destruction predominantly affecting the lower lobes (bases). What is the underlying genetic condition?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic disorder resulting in uninhibited neutrophil elastase activity, leading to panlobular (panacinar) emphysema. Unlike smoking-induced centrilobular emphysema (which is upper lobe predominant), alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency classically destroys the lower lung zones and bases and presents at an early age in non-smokers. Distractor rationales: B causes upper lobe-predominant cystic bronchiectasis and mucus plugging. C causes bronchiectasis, sinusitis, and situs inversus. D causes aortic root dilation, apical blebs, and pectus deformities without basilar panacinar emphysema.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the radiological definition of an emphysematous bulla?
options: A sharply demarcated, air-filled thin-walled space measuring greater than 1 cm in diameter, formed by alveolar wall destruction
A dilated main bronchus filled with fluid
A subpleural collection of air measuring less than 1 mm
questions.answer: A sharply demarcated, air-filled thin-walled space measuring greater than 1 cm in diameter, formed by alveolar wall destruction
questions.explanation: Correct: A. An emphysematous bulla is an area of emphysematous lung destruction measuring greater than 1 cm (10 mm) in diameter, bounded by a thin, hairline wall (<1 mm). Subpleural air collections < 1 cm are termed 'blebs.' When bullae occupy more than one-third of a hemithorax, it is termed 'giant bullous emphysema' (vanishing lung syndrome). Distractor rationales: B defines a bronchocele or mucoid impaction. C describes tiny blebs. D is a lung abscess or aspergilloma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 64-year-old male with severe COPD develops worsening peripheral edema and jugular venous distention. A chest radiograph demonstrates marked enlargement of the descending right pulmonary artery (transverse diameter > 16 mm), rapid tapering of peripheral vessels ('pruning'), and cardiomegaly with fullness of the retrosternal clear space. What hemodynamic complication has developed?
options: Pulmonary arterial hypertension and cor pulmonale
questions.answer: Pulmonary arterial hypertension and cor pulmonale
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Longstanding hypoxic vasoconstriction and capillary bed destruction in COPD leads to pulmonary arterial hypertension and subsequent right ventricular failure (cor pulmonale). Classic radiographic signs include enlargement of central pulmonary arteries (descending RPA > 16 mm in men, > 15 mm in women) with rapid peripheral caliber reduction ('pruning'), and right ventricular enlargement encroaching on the retrosternal clear space. Distractor rationales: B features cephalization, pulmonary venous congestion, and Kerley B lines. C causes massive symmetric globular enlargement without central pulmonary artery pruning. D features pericardial calcification without isolated central pulmonary artery dilation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a lateral chest radiograph, what measurement of the retrosternal clear space (measured horizontally from the posterior sternal cortex to the anterior margin of the ascending aorta) is diagnostic of hyperinflation?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. On an adult lateral chest radiograph, the retrosternal clear space is normally less than 2.5 cm. In hyperinflation and emphysema, the expanding anterior lung segments push deeper behind the sternum, increasing the retrosternal clear space to > 2.5 cm. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are normal or narrowed (narrowed retrosternal space is seen in right ventricular hypertrophy or anterior mediastinal masses).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 70-year-old patient with chronic bronchitis presents with acute respiratory distress. The frontal radiograph shows thickened, parallel line densities seen end-on ('tram-track sign') and thickened circular rings ('peribronchial cuffing') near the hila. What do these signs represent?
options: Inflammatory bronchial wall thickening and peribronchial edema
questions.answer: Inflammatory bronchial wall thickening and peribronchial edema
questions.explanation: Correct: A. 'Tram-tracks' (parallel linear opacities of thickened bronchial walls seen in profile) and 'peribronchial cuffing' (thick-walled circular rings seen end-on) reflect inflammatory mucosal hypertrophy and peribronchial fluid or edema, frequently seen in chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, asthma, and viral bronchiolitis. Distractor rationales: B is pleural, peripheral, and calcified. C are nodular vascular structures with feeding arteries. D are horizontal basilar lines without lumina.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On an inspiratory-expiratory HRCT protocol performed for a patient with persistent dyspnea, what is the significance of areas of low attenuation that remain radiolucent and fail to increase in density during expiration?
options: Air trapping secondary to small airway (bronchiolar) obstruction
questions.answer: Air trapping secondary to small airway (bronchiolar) obstruction
questions.explanation: Correct: A. During normal expiration, healthy lung parenchyma expels air, increasing in density and appearing whiter on CT. In obstructive small airway diseases (e.g., constrictive bronchiolitis, asthma, COPD), obstructed bronchiolar segments cannot expel gas; hence, they remain hyperlucent and show no volume change—a hallmark sign known as 'air trapping.' Distractor rationales: B shows diffuse increase in attenuation. C causes high-density calcium deposition. D causes increased opacity, not persistent lucency.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the imaging modality of choice (gold standard clinical diagnostic test) for the evaluation of suspected acute pulmonary embolism?
options: Standard posteroanterior and lateral chest radiography
questions.explanation: Correct: A. CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the primary, first-line diagnostic modality of choice for suspected acute pulmonary embolism (PE). It allows direct visualization of intraluminal filling defects in the pulmonary arterial tree from main pulmonary arteries down to subsegmental branches, while simultaneously evaluating alternative lung and mediastinal diagnoses. Distractor rationales: B has low sensitivity and specificity for PE (often normal or non-specifically abnormal). C can assess right ventricular strain but cannot reliably visualize pulmonary arterial thrombi directly. D cannot differentiate intraluminal blood from thrombus without intravenous contrast.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the most common radiographic finding on a standard chest radiograph in a patient with an acute pulmonary embolism?
options: A completely normal chest radiograph (or non-specific subsegmental atelectasis)
questions.answer: A completely normal chest radiograph (or non-specific subsegmental atelectasis)
questions.explanation: Correct: A. In the majority of patients with acute pulmonary embolism, the chest radiograph is completely normal or demonstrates non-specific abnormalities such as minimal subsegmental atelectasis or small pleural effusions. A normal chest radiograph in a patient with severe acute dyspnea and hypoxia should strongly heighten clinical suspicion for PE. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are classic and highly specific radiographic signs of PE, but they are relatively rare (< 5-10% of cases).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old woman develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis 5 days after undergoing total knee arthroplasty. A chest radiograph demonstrates a peripheral, pleural-based, wedge-shaped opacity with its rounded apex directed toward the hilum at the right costophrenic angle. What is this sign?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Hampton's hump is a classic radiographic sign of pulmonary infarction secondary to pulmonary embolism. It is a wedge-shaped, pleural-based consolidation with a convex apex pointing toward the hilum, representing alveolar hemorrhage and ischemic necrosis in a devascularized peripheral segment. Distractor rationales: B is focal regional oligemia distal to an occluded vessel. C is enlargement of the central pulmonary artery due to an impacted large thrombus. D is a crescent of aerated lung in left upper lobe collapse.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the 'Westermark sign' in pulmonary embolism?
options: Focal regional oligemia (hyperlucency) of the lung distal to an occluded pulmonary artery
Enlargement of the descending right interlobar pulmonary artery
questions.answer: Focal regional oligemia (hyperlucency) of the lung distal to an occluded pulmonary artery
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The Westermark sign represents focal regional oligemia (diminished pulmonary vascular markings and corresponding hyperlucency) in the lung parenchyma supplied by an occluded pulmonary artery. Distractor rationales: B is Hampton's hump. C is Fleischner's sign (or Palla's sign). D is an indirect non-specific sign of atelectasis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old male presents with sudden syncope, hypotension, and cyanosis. On CTPA, an extensive non-occlusive filling defect is identified that straddles the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery, extending into both right and left main pulmonary arteries. What is this specific finding?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A saddle pulmonary embolus is a large thrombus lodged precisely at the bifurcation of the main pulmonary trunk, extending into both the right and left main pulmonary arteries. It carries high mortality due to acute right ventricular strain and obstructive shock. Distractor rationales: B is an intimal tear in the ascending aorta. C is obstruction of systemic venous drainage from the head/upper extremities. D is reversal of a left-to-right intracardiac shunt due to severe pulmonary vascular resistance.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following CTPA findings is an objective sign of acute right ventricular strain (dysfunction) indicating high-risk/submassive pulmonary embolism?
options: Right ventricular (RV) to left ventricular (LV) diameter ratio greater than 1.0 (measured in the axial four-chamber view)
Decreased diameter of the inferior vena cava with collapse
questions.answer: Right ventricular (RV) to left ventricular (LV) diameter ratio greater than 1.0 (measured in the axial four-chamber view)
questions.explanation: Correct: A. On CTPA, an RV/LV diameter ratio > 1.0 (or > 0.9) measured in the transverse axial reconstructed four-chamber plane is an established, validated imaging marker of acute right ventricular dilatation and strain. Other signs include flattening or leftward bowing of the interventricular septum and contrast reflux into the inferior vena cava and hepatic veins. Distractor rationales: B is seen in hypovolemic shock; acute RV strain causes distention and IVC reflux. C is an unrelated pleural finding. D indicates chronic systemic hypertension or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old pregnant female at 14 weeks gestation with normal baseline chest radiography presents with suspected acute pulmonary embolism. She has a severe documented anaphylactic allergy to iodinated intravenous contrast media. What is the most appropriate next imaging test?
options: Standard invasive pulmonary catheter angiography with full contrast load
questions.explanation: Correct: A. In pregnant patients with suspected PE who have normal chest radiographs, or patients with severe anaphylactic contrast allergies or renal impairment, Ventilation-Perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy is the preferred diagnostic modality. It avoids iodinated contrast and delivers very low radiation doses to the fetus. Distractor rationales: B cannot evaluate pulmonary arterial lumen filling defects. C uses large loads of the very iodinated contrast to which she has a life-threatening allergy. D evaluates esophageal anatomy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan, what finding constitutes a 'high probability' result for pulmonary embolism according to PIOPED criteria?
options: Two or more large (>75% of a segment) wedge-shaped perfusion defects with completely normal ventilation (V/Q mismatch)
Matched perfusion and ventilation defects with corresponding radiographic consolidation
A single subsegmental perfusion defect with matching ventilation defect
Diffuse, symmetric perfusion to both lungs with delayed xenon washout
questions.answer: Two or more large (>75% of a segment) wedge-shaped perfusion defects with completely normal ventilation (V/Q mismatch)
questions.explanation: Correct: A. By PIOPED criteria, a high probability scan for PE requires two or more large (or equivalent moderate) segmental wedge-shaped perfusion defects with normal preserved ventilation (V/Q mismatch), in the absence of corresponding radiographic abnormalities. This scenario carries a >85-90% positive predictive value for PE. Distractor rationales: B and C represent V/Q matches (low/intermediate probability), often seen in pneumonia, atelectasis, or COPD. D is typical of obstructive airway disease without PE.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the direct imaging appearance of an acute pulmonary thrombus on contrast-enhanced CT pulmonary angiography?
options: A central intraluminal filling defect surrounded by contrast, forming acute angles with the arterial wall
A dense, completely calcified mass obliterating the carina
Extravasation of contrast into the pleural space
An air-filled cavity with fluid levels
questions.answer: A central intraluminal filling defect surrounded by contrast, forming acute angles with the arterial wall
questions.explanation: Correct: A. An acute pulmonary embolism appears directly on CTPA as a central or eccentric intraluminal filling defect that does not enhance with contrast, often surrounded by a rim of contrast ('polo mint sign' on cross-section), forming acute angles with the vessel wall. Distractor rationales: B describes calcified lymph nodes or granulomas. C represents vascular rupture. D represents a lung abscess or cavity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 58-year-old male with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) undergoes chest CT. Which imaging feature differentiates chronic pulmonary thromboembolism from acute pulmonary embolism?
options: Eccentric filling defects adhering to the vessel wall at obtuse angles, recanalization channels, webs, and arterial calcification
Central filling defects forming acute angles with the arterial wall
Rapid complete resolution of thrombus within 48 hours
Uniform, severe bronchiectasis in the upper lobes
questions.answer: Eccentric filling defects adhering to the vessel wall at obtuse angles, recanalization channels, webs, and arterial calcification
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Chronic pulmonary thromboembolism is distinguished on CT by organized eccentric thrombi forming obtuse angles with the vessel wall, intraluminal webs, bands, narrow recanalized channels, vessel retraction, and hypertrophied bronchial collateral arteries. Distractor rationales: B is the hallmark of acute PE. C is seen only in fresh acute clot following thrombolysis or anticoagulation. D is cystic fibrosis or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What are the classic '4 Ts' of anterior mediastinal masses?
options: Thymoma, Teratoma (germ cell tumor), Thyroid (substernal goiter), 'Terrible' lymphoma
Thoracic duct cyst, Thymoma, Tanycytic ependymoma, Teratoma
questions.answer: Thymoma, Teratoma (germ cell tumor), Thyroid (substernal goiter), 'Terrible' lymphoma
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The classic mnemonic '4 Ts' for anterior mediastinal masses encompasses: 1) Thymic lesions (thymoma, thymic carcinoma, thymic cyst), 2) Teratoma / germ cell tumors, 3) Thyroid goiter (substernal extension), and 4) 'Terrible' lymphoma (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin). Distractor rationales: B, C, and D contain non-anterior or incorrect clinical entities.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 42-year-old female presents with bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and progressive muscle fatigue that worsens toward the evening. A chest radiograph reveals fullness of the retrosternal clear space, and CT demonstrates a 4 cm homogeneous, well-encapsulated soft-tissue mass in the anterior mediastinum. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Thymoma is the most common anterior mediastinal mass in middle-aged adults. Approximately 30-50% of patients with thymoma have myasthenia gravis (characterized by fatigable weakness, ptosis, and anti-AChR antibodies), and 10-15% of myasthenia gravis patients have a thymoma. Distractor rationales: B is located in the posterior paravertebral gutter. C is a middle mediastinal congenital foregut duplication cyst. D is a continuous downward extension from the cervical thyroid, typically showing high iodine attenuation and displacing the trachea.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 22-year-old male presents with acute anterior chest pain. Contrast-enhanced CT reveals a large anterior mediastinal mass containing areas of soft tissue, fluid attenuation, fat (-70 HU), and coarse dental-like calcifications. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Mature cystic teratoma is a germ cell neoplasm containing elements from multiple germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm). The pathognomonic CT appearance is an anterior mediastinal mass containing fluid, soft tissue, macroscopic fat (fat-fluid levels), and calcification/ossification (often tooth or bone-like). Distractor rationales: B does not contain teeth or macroscopic fat-fluid levels. C (pure seminoma) is typically a homogeneous, lobulated soft-tissue mass without calcification or fat. D is a soft-tissue nodal mass without macroscopic fat or teeth.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which anatomical compartment of the mediastinum is the most common location for neurogenic tumors (e.g., schwannoma, neurofibroma, ganglioneuroma)?
options: Superior mediastinum above the sternal angle only
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Neurogenic tumors account for 75-90% of all posterior mediastinal masses. They arise from peripheral nerves, spinal nerve roots, or the sympathetic chain in the paravertebral sulcus. Distractor rationales: B is the site for the '4 Ts' (thymoma, teratoma, thyroid, lymphoma). C is the site for lymphadenopathy, vascular aneurysms, and foregut cysts (bronchogenic and pericardial cysts). D is not the primary site for neurogenic tumors.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the 'hilum overlay sign' and what diagnostic information does it provide?
options: Pulmonary hilar vessels are seen clearly through a mass on the frontal radiograph, confirming that the mass is located in the anterior or posterior mediastinum and does NOT arise from the hilum itself
Hilar vessels are completely obliterated, confirming an anterior mediastinal mass
The minor fissure is pulled over the right hilum
The descending aorta crosses anterior to the pulmonary artery
questions.answer: Pulmonary hilar vessels are seen clearly through a mass on the frontal radiograph, confirming that the mass is located in the anterior or posterior mediastinum and does NOT arise from the hilum itself
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The hilum overlay sign, described by Benjamin Felson, occurs when the branches of the pulmonary artery are clearly seen through the cardiomediastinal mass. This proves that the mass is not in the middle mediastinum (hilum) itself, but either anterior or posterior to it (usually anterior, e.g., thymoma or teratoma). Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are incorrect definitions.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 26-year-old woman presents with persistent dry cough, night sweats, and painless cervical lymphadenopathy. A chest radiograph demonstrates massive, lobulated anterior mediastinal and bilateral paratracheal widening with an enlarged cardiomediastinal ratio (>0.33). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common lymphoma of the mediastinum, characteristically affecting young adults in their 20s. It typically presents as a large, lobulated, multi-station anterior mediastinal and paratracheal mass, often with systemic B-symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss). Distractor rationales: B is located in the posterior paravertebral gutter without bilateral paratracheal widening. C is a benign, water-density cyst at the right cardiophrenic angle. D is in the posterior or middle mediastinum adjacent to the esophagus.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old asymptomatic male has a routine chest radiograph demonstrating a smooth, sharply demarcated round opacity at the right cardiophrenic angle. CT reveals a thin-walled, non-enhancing mass with uniform water attenuation (0 to 10 HU). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Pericardial cysts are benign congenital cysts occurring in the middle mediastinum, classically located at the cardiophrenic angle (70% on the right, 25-30% on the left). On CT, they present as unilocular, smooth, thin-walled lesions with homogeneous fluid attenuation (0-20 HU) and no contrast enhancement. Distractor rationales: B is an anterior mediastinal soft-tissue mass with solid enhancement. C is posterior in the paravertebral gutter. D is an aggressive pleural-based malignant rind.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old male with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1) has a chest radiograph showing a posterior mediastinal mass. CT demonstrates smooth expansion and remodeling of an adjacent neural foramen with erosion of the adjacent vertebral pedicle and rib head ('dumbbell tumor'). What is this neoplasm?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Schwannomas and neurofibromas arising from spinal nerve roots can grow both within the spinal canal and extradural posterior mediastinum, forming a classic hourglass or 'dumbbell' configuration. They cause smooth, pressure-erosion and remodeling of the adjacent neural exit foramen, pedicle, and posterior rib. NF-1 is strongly associated with plexiform neurofibromas. Distractor rationales: B is anterior mediastinal. C is a benign foregut cyst without neural foramen erosion. D is a diffuse lymphatic malformation in the neck/anterior chest.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the 'cervicothoracic sign' and how does it localize an upper thoracic mass?
