options: If a mass extends above the clavicles and its borders remain visible, it is located posteriorly; if its borders disappear above the clavicle, it is located anteriorly (in the neck/anterior mediastinum)
If a mass is visible above the clavicle, it must be an aortic aneurysm
Obscuration of the first rib confirms a middle mediastinal lymph node
Any mass above the clavicle is within the thyroid gland
questions.answer: If a mass extends above the clavicles and its borders remain visible, it is located posteriorly; if its borders disappear above the clavicle, it is located anteriorly (in the neck/anterior mediastinum)
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The cervicothoracic sign utilizes the silhouette sign at the thoracic inlet. Because the lung extends higher posteriorly than anteriorly, an anterior mass entering the soft tissues of the neck loses its anatomical interface with aerated lung above the clavicles and its upper border disappears. In contrast, a posterior mediastinal mass continues to be surrounded by apical lung above the clavicles, keeping its borders sharp and well-defined. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are incorrect applications of this principle.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old woman presents with fullness in the lower neck and progressive stridor. A chest radiograph demonstrates a superior mediastinal mass displacing the trachea to the right. On contrast CT, the mass exhibits high non-contrast attenuation, intense prolonged contrast enhancement, and continuity with the cervical thyroid gland. What is this mass?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A substernal thyroid goiter represents caudad extension of a cervical multinodular goiter into the anterior/superior mediastinum. Classic CT characteristics include direct anatomical continuity with the cervical thyroid, high baseline attenuation (due to intrinsic iodine content, 70-120 HU), prolonged vivid enhancement, coarse calcifications, and tracheal displacement/compression. Distractor rationales: B contains fat and teeth. C is fluid density at the cardiophrenic angle. D enhances dynamically with the aortic lumen and is vascular.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the clinical and radiological definition of a 'flail chest'?
options: Fracture of three or more contiguous ribs in two or more places each, creating a free-floating chest wall segment
Fracture of any two ribs with an associated pneumothorax
Fracture of the first rib combined with clavicular dislocation
Bilateral sternal fractures accompanied by flail diaphragm
questions.answer: Fracture of three or more contiguous ribs in two or more places each, creating a free-floating chest wall segment
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A flail chest is defined as fractures of three or more adjacent ribs in two or more locations along each rib, resulting in a mechanically unstable, free-floating thoracic segment that moves paradoxically during respiration (inward on inspiration, outward on expiration). Distractor rationales: B, C, and D do not satisfy the anatomical criteria for flail chest.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male arrives at the emergency department 1 hour after a high-speed motorcycle crash. A portable AP chest radiograph shows patchy, non-segmental, geographic alveolar opacities in the right mid- and lower lung zones underlying multiple rib fractures. The opacities do not follow lobar fissures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Pulmonary contusion is the most common lung injury in blunt chest trauma, caused by blunt deceleration forces rupturing pulmonary capillaries and filling alveoli with blood and edema. Radiographically, it appears rapidly (within 6 hours of injury) as patchy, non-segmental alveolar consolidation that does not respect lobar anatomy and is directly adjacent to thoracic trauma/fractures. Distractor rationales: B typically takes 24-48 hours to manifest radiographically and has a dependent distribution. C appears as a round air- or blood-filled cavity (traumatic pneumatocele or hematoma). D typically presents with a normal radiograph or focal oligemia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old driver was involved in a severe frontal deceleration motor vehicle collision. A supine chest radiograph shows mediastinal widening (> 8 cm at the aortic knob), obscuration of the aortic knob contour, depression of the left main bronchus (> 40 degrees), and deviation of the nasogastric tube to the right. What catastrophic injury must be suspected immediately?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Traumatic aortic injury (typically occurring at the aortic isthmus just distal to the left subclavian artery due to tethering by the ligamentum arteriosum) presents with classic indirect signs of mediastinal hematoma: mediastinal widening (>8 cm on supine AP film), loss/obscuration of the aortic knob, depression of the left mainstem bronchus, deviation of the trachea/NG tube to the right, and an apical pleural cap. Immediate CT angiography of the chest is mandatory. Distractor rationales: B shows total lung collapse and contralateral mediastinal shift without mediastinal hematoma. C causes pneumomediastinum and pleural effusion after forceful emesis. D causes intrathoracic herniation of the liver.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the most common anatomical site of traumatic thoracic aortic injury in blunt deceleration trauma?
options: Aortic isthmus (just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery)
Aortic root immediately above the coronary ostia
questions.answer: Aortic isthmus (just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery)
questions.explanation: Correct: A. More than 90% of blunt traumatic aortic injuries occur at the aortic isthmus, which is the transition zone between the mobile aortic arch and the fixed descending thoracic aorta, anchored by the ligamentum arteriosum. Rapid deceleration creates severe shearing and torsion forces at this junction. Distractor rationales: B is the second most common site (8-10%) and is usually immediately fatal. C and D are rare sites for blunt deceleration shear injury.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A trauma patient with blunt chest injury undergoes CT. A focal oval, gas- and fluid-filled cavity measuring 3 cm is identified within an area of pulmonary contusion. Over subsequent days, the surrounding contusion clears, leaving a persistent thin-walled cyst. What is this lesion?
options: Lung abscess from secondary bacterial infection
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A pulmonary laceration occurs when blunt compressive trauma tears lung parenchyma. Elastic recoil of adjacent lung causes the lacerated space to pull open into a round or oval cavity. Initially filled with blood (traumatic hematocele) or air (traumatic pneumatocele), it is often masked by surrounding contusion, becoming conspicuous as the contusion resolves over 48-72 hours. Distractor rationales: B is a congenital unilocular water-attenuation cyst without trauma history. C is an infected necrotic cavity with fever and purulent sputum. D is a neonatal overinflation anomaly.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old male presents following severe blunt chest trauma. A portable radiograph shows a large right pneumothorax. Despite the placement of two large-bore chest tubes connected to continuous suction, there is a massive persistent air leak and the right lung fails to re-expand. What severe airway injury should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A massive continuous air leak and failure of the lung to re-expand despite multiple functioning chest tubes is the classic presentation of a major tracheobronchial rupture (typically within 2-3 cm of the carina). In complete bronchial transection, the collapsed lung falls away from the hilum toward the dependent posterior costophrenic angle ('fallen lung sign'). Distractor rationales: B causes a small simple pneumothorax that re-expands rapidly with tube thoracostomy. C herniates abdominal contents. D has no airway communication.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old female presents after a high-speed collision. Chest radiograph demonstrates the tip of a nasogastric tube curling in the lower left hemithorax above the diaphragm, accompanied by focal constriction of the stomach at the level of the left hemidiaphragm ('collar sign'). What is the diagnosis?
options: Traumatic diaphragmatic rupture with gastric herniation
questions.answer: Traumatic diaphragmatic rupture with gastric herniation
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Traumatic diaphragmatic rupture (much more common on the left side due to protective cushioning of the liver on the right) permits abdominal viscera (stomach, colon, spleen) to herniate into the negative-pressure thoracic cavity. The 'collar sign' is focal waist-like constriction of the herniated hollow viscus as it passes through the tear in the muscular diaphragm. Visualizing the NG tube in the left thorax confirms intrathoracic herniation of the stomach. Distractor rationales: B has the stomach sliding through the esophageal hiatus without traumatic diaphragmatic tear or acute collar sign. C is congenital thinning with intact diaphragmatic continuation. D causes pneumomediastinum without the stomach entering the pleural space.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Fractures of the first and second ribs are clinically significant primarily because:
options: They require immense force and are frequently associated with life-threatening injuries to adjacent subclavian vessels, brachial plexus, and aorta
They inevitably cause tension pneumothorax within 10 minutes
They are the most common cause of diaphragmatic rupture
They always require emergent open reduction and internal fixation
questions.answer: They require immense force and are frequently associated with life-threatening injuries to adjacent subclavian vessels, brachial plexus, and aorta
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The 1st and 2nd ribs are broad, thick, and well-protected by the clavicle, scapula, and shoulder girdle muscles. Fractures of these ribs require high-energy impact and are associated in up to 30% of cases with catastrophic vascular (subclavian artery/vein, aorta) and neurological (brachial plexus) injuries, as well as severe tracheobronchial or cardiac trauma. Distractor rationales: B is false; many do not cause tension pneumothorax. C is false; lower rib (8th-12th) fractures are associated with diaphragmatic, splenic, or liver tears. D is false; non-displaced rib fractures are managed conservatively unless flail or reconstructing.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A trauma patient sustains multiple lower left rib (9th to 11th) fractures. In addition to assessing the chest, which subdiaphragmatic organ must be evaluated with high priority on contrast-enhanced CT?
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The spleen lies directly beneath the left 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs in the left upper quadrant. Fractures of these lower left ribs are strongly associated with traumatic splenic laceration, subcapsular hematoma, and life-threatening intra-abdominal hemorrhage. (Conversely, lower right rib fractures injure the liver). Distractor rationales: B is protected by the right lower ribs. C is in the right upper quadrant. D is in the right lower quadrant.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is a 'hemothorax' and how does it appear on an upright chest radiograph compared to a simple pleural effusion?
options: Blood within the pleural space, presenting with an identical meniscus sign and costophrenic angle blunting as any other pleural fluid
Blood inside the alveoli, appearing as diffuse air bronchograms
A calcified hematoma strictly confined to the rib cortex
questions.answer: Blood within the pleural space, presenting with an identical meniscus sign and costophrenic angle blunting as any other pleural fluid
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A hemothorax is the presence of blood within the pleural cavity (hematocrit >= 50% of peripheral blood). On plain radiography, blood has the exact same radiodensity (water density) as transudative or exudative fluid, presenting identically with blunting of the costophrenic angle and a lateral meniscus sign on upright radiographs. Distractor rationales: B describes alveolar hemorrhage or contusion. C describes pneumopericardium. D describes calcified subperiosteal hematoma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.topicTitle: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.prompt: On a neutral-position frontal chest radiograph of an adult patient, where should the radio-opaque tip of an endotracheal tube (ETT) ideally be located?
options: Approximately 3 to 5 cm above the carina (at the level of T2 to T4 vertebral bodies)
At the exact level of the vocal cords
1 to 2 cm into the right mainstem bronchus
At the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium
questions.answer: Approximately 3 to 5 cm above the carina (at the level of T2 to T4 vertebral bodies)
questions.explanation: Correct: A. In an adult with the head in neutral position, the tip of the endotracheal tube should ideally reside in the mid-trachea, approximately 3 to 5 cm (or roughly 5 cm) above the carina (corresponding to the T2-T4 vertebral level). This allows 2 cm of safety margin for neck flexion and extension without risk of extubation or bronchial intubation. Distractor rationales: B is too high (risk of vocal cord trauma and accidental extubation). C represents an endobronchial intubation. D is the target location for a central venous catheter tip, not an ETT.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.topicTitle: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.prompt: A post-intubation portable chest radiograph reveals that the ETT tip has advanced into the right mainstem bronchus. What immediate radiographic consequence is most likely to be seen in the left lung?
options: Total or partial left lung atelectasis (collapse) with mediastinal shift to the left
Severe left pulmonary edema with Kerley B lines
Hyperlucency of the entire left hemithorax
questions.answer: Total or partial left lung atelectasis (collapse) with mediastinal shift to the left
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Because the right mainstem bronchus is wider and branches more vertically from the trachea than the left, an over-inserted ETT almost invariably enters the right mainstem bronchus. This completely occludes ventilation to the left lung, leading to rapid resorption atelectasis (complete left lung collapse) with volume loss and leftward mediastinal shift. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are not the standard immediate mechanical consequences of selective right mainstem intubation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.topicTitle: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.prompt: How does physiological movement of the patient's head affect the position of the endotracheal tube tip on a chest radiograph?
options: Neck flexion pushes the tube tip approximately 2 cm toward the carina; neck extension pulls the tip approximately 2 cm upward toward the larynx
Neck flexion pulls the tube upward toward the vocal cords
Neck extension advances the tube deeper into the right mainstem bronchus
Head movement has zero effect on the tip position
questions.answer: Neck flexion pushes the tube tip approximately 2 cm toward the carina; neck extension pulls the tip approximately 2 cm upward toward the larynx
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The mnemonic 'the tube goes where the chin goes' describes ETT displacement with neck movement. Neck flexion (chin down toward chest) pushes the carina and trachea upward relative to the fixed tube, causing the ETT tip to advance deeper toward the carina (by ~2 cm). Conversely, neck extension (chin up) pulls the ETT tip cephalad away from the carina toward the vocal cords (by ~2 cm). Distractor rationales: B and C invert these physiological relationships. D is false.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.topicTitle: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.prompt: Where is the ideal anatomical position for the tip of a central venous catheter (CVC) placed via the internal jugular or subclavian vein?
options: In the lower third of the superior vena cava near the cavoatrial junction
Deep within the inferior vena cava
In the right ventricle crossing the tricuspid valve
questions.answer: In the lower third of the superior vena cava near the cavoatrial junction
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The optimal position for the tip of a central venous catheter (CVC) or peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) is in the lower superior vena cava at or just above the cavoatrial junction (often projected at the level of the right tracheobronchial angle or 1 to 2 vertebral bodies below the carina). This minimizes risks of vessel thrombosis, vascular erosion, and cardiac arrhythmias. Distractor rationales: B is too high, carrying increased risk of venous thrombosis and catheter malfunction. C is too deep and indicates migration into the IVC. D is dangerous, risking tricuspid valve damage, ventricular arrhythmias, and myocardial perforation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.topicTitle: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.prompt: Following the placement of a left subclavian vein central venous catheter, a post-procedure chest radiograph demonstrates the catheter tip descending vertically along the left lateral border of the aortic arch and left mediastinum, rather than crossing the midline. What anatomical variant or malposition has occurred?
options: Persistent left superior vena cava (PLSVC) or accidental cannulation of the left internal mammary/pleural vein
Normal course through the azygos vein
questions.answer: Persistent left superior vena cava (PLSVC) or accidental cannulation of the left internal mammary/pleural vein
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A catheter placed via the left subclavian or jugular vein normally courses through the left brachiocephalic vein, crossing the midline from left to right to enter the right-sided SVC. If the catheter runs straight down the left mediastinal border, it is either positioned within a congenital persistent left superior vena cava (PLSVC, draining into the coronary sinus) or has cannulated the left internal thoracic (mammary) vein or left superior intercostal vein. Distractor rationales: B is on the right side. C would cross the midline and enter the heart chambers. D crosses the midline obliquely.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.topicTitle: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.prompt: A right subclavian central line is placed in an ICU patient. The post-procedure chest radiograph demonstrates a small apical pneumothorax (1 cm rim of air). What is the underlying anatomical reason for this common complication?
options: The apical pleural cupola (dome of the pleura) extends 2 to 3 cm above the medial third of the clavicle
The right lung apex is devoid of visceral pleura
The right subclavian artery lies anterior to the vein
The phrenic nerve pierces the apical pleura
questions.answer: The apical pleural cupola (dome of the pleura) extends 2 to 3 cm above the medial third of the clavicle
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The cervical dome of the pleura (pleural cupola) and lung apex normally project approximately 2 to 3 cm above the medial third of the clavicle and first rib into the root of the neck. During subclavian vein catheterization, an inadvertent inferior or posterior needle pass can easily puncture this apical pleura, resulting in a pneumothorax (1-3% incidence). Distractor rationales: B is false; the apex is covered by visceral and parietal pleura. C is false; the subclavian vein lies anterior to the scalenus anterior muscle, while the artery lies posterior. D is false.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.topicTitle: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.prompt: A post-procedural chest radiograph for a newly placed nasogastric (NG) tube demonstrates the tube tracking down the mid-trachea and curving into the right lower lobe bronchus. The patient is non-verbal and not coughing. What is the appropriate immediate action?
options: Immediately remove the tube without administering any feeds, medications, or flushes
Inject 50 mL of sterile water and auscultate over the epigastrium
Advance the tube by an additional 15 cm to enter the stomach
Commence tube feedings at a low rate
questions.answer: Immediately remove the tube without administering any feeds, medications, or flushes
questions.explanation: Correct: A. Inadvertent tracheobronchial intubation by a nasogastric or feeding tube is a potentially fatal complication (risking pneumothorax, bronchopleural fistula, pulmonary laceration, and catastrophic chemical aspiration). In critically ill or obtunded patients, the cough reflex may be completely absent. The tube must be removed immediately without flushing or feeding. Auscultation is notoriously unreliable and must never be used to confirm NG tube position. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are extremely dangerous and can cause fatal pulmonary aspiration or tension pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.topicTitle: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.prompt: On a chest radiograph, what is the correct radiological appearance and position of a properly sited nasogastric (NG) tube?
options: The tube descends in the midline, bisects the carina, crosses the diaphragm, and its side hole and tip lie at least 10 cm within the stomach below the gastroesophageal junction
The tip terminates precisely at the carina
The tube curves sharply to the right into the middle lobe bronchus
The tip lies within the distal third of the esophagus above the diaphragm
questions.answer: The tube descends in the midline, bisects the carina, crosses the diaphragm, and its side hole and tip lie at least 10 cm within the stomach below the gastroesophageal junction
questions.explanation: Correct: A. A properly placed NG tube must: 1) remain in the midline, 2) bisect the carina (following the esophagus behind the trachea), 3) cross the diaphragm in the midline/left, and 4) have its side hole and tip positioned deep inside the stomach (at least 10 cm below the gastroesophageal junction, projecting over the gastric air bubble). Distractor rationales: B and C represent dangerous bronchial intubations. D is intraesophageal, where feeding leads to fatal pulmonary aspiration.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.topicTitle: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.prompt: A tube thoracostomy (chest tube) is inserted for a large right-sided pneumothorax. On the post-procedure radiograph, the clinician notices that the 'sentinel hole' (the interruption in the radiopaque line along the tube) is located outside the thoracic cage within the subcutaneous tissues of the chest wall. What is the clinical consequence?
options: The drainage system will entrain atmospheric air or subcutaneous gas, causing failure of lung re-expansion and extensive subcutaneous emphysema
Immediate cardiac arrest due to phrenic nerve transection
The tube will deliver hyperbaric suction to the lung
No consequence, as the sentinel hole is purely cosmetic
questions.answer: The drainage system will entrain atmospheric air or subcutaneous gas, causing failure of lung re-expansion and extensive subcutaneous emphysema
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The chest tube has a side hole (sentinel hole) marked by a break in its radiopaque stripe. All drainage holes, especially the sentinel hole, must reside completely within the pleural space. If the sentinel hole is outside the rib cage in the subcutaneous tissue, it cannot evacuate pleural air/fluid, causes massive subcutaneous emphysema, and allows external air to enter the pleural space. Distractor rationales: B, C, and D are incorrect.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.topicTitle: Endotracheal tube and central line positioning
questions.prompt: A pulmonary artery catheter (Swan-Ganz catheter) is placed in an ICU patient. On the morning portable chest radiograph, the catheter tip is noted to be wedged > 5 cm beyond the right interlobar pulmonary artery into the extreme lateral periphery of the right lower lobe. What catastrophic complication is the patient at high risk of developing if the catheter is not withdrawn immediately?
options: Pulmonary artery rupture and pseudoaneurysm formation, leading to fatal hemoptysis
questions.answer: Pulmonary artery rupture and pseudoaneurysm formation, leading to fatal hemoptysis
questions.explanation: Correct: A. The tip of a pulmonary artery catheter should remain in a proximal main lobar pulmonary artery (within 2 to 3 cm of the hilum, not extending beyond the medial third of the hemithorax). A peripherally wedged catheter tip or prolonged balloon inflation in a small segmental artery can cause pulmonary artery rupture or pulmonary infarction, presenting with massive, catastrophic hemoptysis (mortality > 50%). The catheter must be immediately deflated and pulled back. Distractor rationales: B is impossible because the catheter traverses the venous/right heart circulation (RA, RV, PA), not the left-sided aortic valve. C and D are anatomically unrelated.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following retroperitoneal structures crosses the midline anterior to the aorta and posterior to the superior mesenteric artery?
questions.explanation: Correct: The left renal vein courses transversely from the left kidney hilum across the midline to empty into the inferior vena cava (IVC), passing through the vascular 'nutcracker' angle between the superior mesenteric artery (anteriorly) and the abdominal aorta (posteriorly).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old male undergoes a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen for non-specific abdominal discomfort. The radiologist notes normal anatomy of the peritoneal recesses. Which of the following potential spaces represents the most dependent portion of the peritoneal cavity in a supine patient?
questions.explanation: Correct: In the supine patient, the hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch) is the lowest, most dependent potential space in the upper abdomen (and superior peritoneal cavity), where pathological fluid such as blood, ascites, or pus preferentially accumulates.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: According to the Couinaud classification of hepatic segmental anatomy, which anatomical landmark separates the right hepatic lobe into anterior and posterior segments?
questions.explanation: Correct: The right hepatic vein courses within the right intersegmental fissure and divides the functional right liver into anterior segments (V and VIII) and posterior segments (VI and VII).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following gastrointestinal structures is primarily located in an entirely retroperitoneal position?
questions.explanation: Correct: The second (descending), third (horizontal), and fourth (ascending) parts of the duodenum are classic secondary retroperitoneal structures, fixed to the posterior abdominal wall.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old woman is evaluated for right upper quadrant pain. CT shows an anomaly where the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct join more than 15 mm proximal to the ampulla of Vater outside the duodenal wall. What is the clinical significance of this anomalous pancreaticobiliary ductal union?
options: Predisposition to choledochal cysts and gallbladder carcinoma due to reflux of pancreatic enzymes
Higher incidence of annular pancreas and duodenal web
Direct progression to splenic vein thrombosis
Congenital absence of the cystic duct
questions.answer: Predisposition to choledochal cysts and gallbladder carcinoma due to reflux of pancreatic enzymes
questions.explanation: Correct: Anomalous pancreaticobiliary duct junction (APBDJ) occurs when the pancreatic and bile ducts unite outside the duodenal wall, creating an abnormally long common channel. This bypasses the sphincter of Oddi, allowing reciprocal reflux of pancreatic secretions into the biliary tree, leading to mucosal hyperplasia, choledochal cysts, and a significantly increased risk of biliary tract malignancy (especially gallbladder carcinoma).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the standard radiographic '3-6-9 rule' used to estimate the normal upper limit of luminal diameter of the gastrointestinal tract on a supine abdominal radiograph?
options: Small bowel 3 cm, Colon 6 cm, Cecum 9 cm
Duodenum 3 cm, Jejunum 6 cm, Ileum 9 cm
Appendix 3 mm, Common bile duct 6 mm, Pancreatic duct 9 mm
Small bowel 3 cm, Cecum 6 cm, Sigmoid colon 9 cm
questions.answer: Small bowel 3 cm, Colon 6 cm, Cecum 9 cm
questions.explanation: Correct: The '3-6-9 rule' is a widely utilized radiological mnemonic: normal maximum luminal diameters on plain radiographs are 3 cm for the small intestine, 6 cm for the large bowel/colon, and 9 cm for the cecum.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 72-year-old nursing home resident presents with massive abdominal distension and obstipation. An abdominal plain radiograph demonstrates an inverted U-shaped dilated loop of large bowel extending from the pelvis toward the right upper quadrant, resembling a 'coffee bean'. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: Sigmoid volvulus classic radiographic appearance is the 'coffee bean sign' or inverted U-tube sign, with the apex pointing toward the right upper quadrant and lack of haustral markings in the twisted loop, arising from the pelvis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which anatomical feature best distinguishes dilated jejunum from dilated colon on a plain abdominal radiograph?
options: Valvulae conniventes (plicae circulares) completely traversing the luminal width
Haustral folds extending across the entire diameter of the lumen
Location strictly confined to the peripheral margins of the peritoneal cavity
Presence of mottled gas-fluid contents representing formed stool
questions.answer: Valvulae conniventes (plicae circulares) completely traversing the luminal width
questions.explanation: Correct: Valvulae conniventes (plicae circulares) are thin, closely spaced mucosal folds characteristic of the jejunum that cross the entire transverse diameter of the bowel lumen from wall to wall. In contrast, colonic haustra extend only partially across the lumen.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 50-year-old male presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to his back. A supine abdominal radiograph demonstrates localized gaseous distension of a proximal jejunal loop in the left upper quadrant, with absence of gas in the distal small bowel and colon. This finding is best termed a:
questions.explanation: Correct: A 'sentinel loop' represents localized adynamic ileus of an isolated bowel loop adjacent to an acute inflammatory focus (such as a dilated jejunal loop adjacent to acute pancreatitis or an ileal loop in acute appendicitis).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A plain abdominal radiograph in an elderly patient demonstrates marked gaseous distension of the ascending and transverse colon terminating abruptly at the splenic flexure, with complete collapse of the descending colon. This sign is known as:
questions.explanation: Correct: The 'colon cut-off sign' is characterized by gaseous distension of the colon up to the splenic flexure with abrupt absence of gas distally, reflecting functional spasm of the descending colon caused by retroperitoneal inflammatory spread from acute pancreatitis (or occasionally mechanical obstruction by a splenic flexure tumor).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old trauma victim who is immobilized on a spine board cannot stand for an erect chest or abdominal radiograph. To evaluate for suspected pneumoperitoneum, which plain radiographic projection is the most sensitive alternative?
options: Left lateral decubitus abdominal radiograph with horizontal beam
Right lateral decubitus abdominal radiograph with horizontal beam
questions.answer: Left lateral decubitus abdominal radiograph with horizontal beam
questions.explanation: Correct: The left lateral decubitus view with a horizontal X-ray beam is the gold standard alternative to an erect chest radiograph. In this position, free intraperitoneal air rises and accumulates over the lateral margin of the liver and right paracolic gutter, where it is easily distinguished from gastric fundic and colonic gas bubbles.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following densities has the LOWEST radiographic attenuation (appears most radiolucent/black) on a conventional plain abdominal film?
questions.explanation: Correct: The five fundamental radiographic densities in order of increasing attenuation (from blackest/most radiolucent to whitest/most radio-opaque) are: Gas/Air < Fat < Soft tissue/Fluid < Bone/Calcium < Metal.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: An erect chest radiograph of an asymptomatic 68-year-old male reveals interposition of a loop of large intestine between the superior surface of the liver and the right hemidiaphragm, mimicking free subdiaphragmatic air. Haustral markings are clearly identified within the gas collection. This benign entity is known as:
questions.explanation: Correct: Chilaiditi sign refers to the asymptomatic hepatodiaphragmatic interposition of bowel (usually colon, occasionally small bowel) between the liver and diaphragm; when accompanied by clinical symptoms like pain or constipation, it is called Chilaiditi syndrome. The presence of haustral or plical folds rules out pneumoperitoneum.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary diagnostic utility of visualizing the preperitoneal (properitoneal) fat stripe on a normal supine abdominal radiograph?
options: Assessing retroperitoneal or lateral peritoneal inflammation, hematoma, or free fluid causing stripe effacement
Measuring the thickness of the transverse abdominis muscle
questions.answer: Assessing retroperitoneal or lateral peritoneal inflammation, hematoma, or free fluid causing stripe effacement
questions.explanation: Correct: The properitoneal fat stripes (flank stripes) are radiolucent bands of fat between the transversalis fascia and peritoneum on both lateral abdominal walls. Blurring, widening, or effacement of these fat stripes indicates adjacent fluid, edema, hematoma, or peritonitis in the paracolic gutters.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What percentage of urinary tract calculi and gallstones, respectively, are typically radio-opaque and visible on an unenhanced plain abdominal radiograph?
questions.explanation: Correct: Approximately 85% to 90% of renal and ureteral stones contain sufficient calcium (calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate) to be radio-opaque on X-rays, whereas only about 10% to 15% of gallstones are sufficiently calcified to be visible on plain radiographs (the majority being radiolucent cholesterol stones).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the most common cause of mechanical small bowel obstruction (SBO) in adults with a history of prior abdominopelvic surgery?
questions.explanation: Correct: Postoperative peritoneal adhesions account for approximately 60% to 75% of all cases of mechanical small bowel obstruction in adults with prior abdominal surgery.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 58-year-old woman presents with crampy central abdominal pain, vomiting, and obstipation. An erect abdominal radiograph shows multiple dilated central bowel loops (>3 cm) with multiple air-fluid levels arranged in a 'stepladder' pattern and a 'string of pearls' sign. Colon and rectum are devoid of gas. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: The radiographic presence of central dilated small bowel loops (>3 cm), a 'stepladder' configuration of air-fluid levels on erect films, the 'string of pearls' (or beads) sign (small bubbles of gas trapped between valvulae conniventes in predominantly fluid-filled loops), and paucity of distal colonic/rectal gas are hallmark findings of mechanical small bowel obstruction.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 64-year-old male presents with acute severe abdominal pain out of proportion to exam. Contrast-enhanced CT shows a C-shaped loop of fluid-filled small bowel with converging mesenteric vessels, radial distribution of stretched mesenteric vessels pointing to a single point, engorged mesenteric veins, and high attenuation of the bowel wall on non-contrast imaging. What urgent condition do these findings indicate?
options: Closed-loop small bowel obstruction with strangulation / ischemia
Uncomplicated simple adhesive small bowel obstruction
questions.answer: Closed-loop small bowel obstruction with strangulation / ischemia
questions.explanation: Correct: A closed-loop obstruction occurs when a segment of bowel is obstructed at two adjacent points (e.g., by a single adhesive band or internal hernia). CT features include a U-shaped or C-shaped fluid-filled loop, radial mesenteric vessel convergence, mesenteric swirling, and signs of strangulation/ischemia such as wall thickening, high unenhanced wall attenuation (hemorrhagic infarction), mesenteric fluid/haze, and delayed or absent wall enhancement. This is a surgical emergency.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On contrast-enhanced abdominal CT, which cross-sectional finding is considered the most reliable indicator for identifying the exact site of mechanical bowel obstruction?
options: Transition point showing caliber change from dilated proximal bowel to collapsed distal bowel
Presence of a small bowel feces sign
Paucity of gas within the ascending colon
questions.answer: Transition point showing caliber change from dilated proximal bowel to collapsed distal bowel
questions.explanation: Correct: The transition point—defined by an abrupt change in luminal diameter from dilated bowel proximally (>3 cm for small bowel) to collapsed/decompressed bowel distally—is the most reliable CT sign for identifying the precise anatomical location and underlying etiology of mechanical bowel obstruction.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the most common etiology of large bowel obstruction (LBO) in adults in developed countries?
questions.explanation: Correct: Colorectal adenocarcinoma (particularly of the rectosigmoid and left colon) accounts for approximately 60% of all cases of large bowel obstruction in adults.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 78-year-old male with an obstructing adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon has an incompetent ileocecal valve. Which of the following radiographic consequences is most expected on his abdominal imaging?
options: Decompression of the colon into the small bowel, producing dilated small bowel loops and decreasing cecal perforation risk
Rapid, massive cecal distension (>10 cm) without any small bowel gas, creating a closed-loop phenomenon
Spontaneous volvulus of the transverse colon
questions.answer: Decompression of the colon into the small bowel, producing dilated small bowel loops and decreasing cecal perforation risk
questions.explanation: Correct: When the ileocecal valve is incompetent (occurring in ~20-30% of people), colonic gas and fluid can decompress retrogradely into the small intestine. This results in dilated small bowel loops mimicking small bowel obstruction and relieves intraluminal tension in the cecum, lowering the immediate risk of cecal rupture.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: An 80-year-old female presents with subacute small bowel obstruction. Abdominal CT demonstrates: (1) marked dilatation of jejunal loops, (2) branching gas within the biliary tree (pneumobilia), and (3) an ectopic, calcified, laminated 3.5 cm mass obstructing the distal ileum. What is the clinical eponym for this constellation of findings?
questions.explanation: Correct: Rigler's triad refers to the diagnostic triad of gallstone ileus: (1) mechanical small bowel obstruction, (2) pneumobilia, and (3) an ectopic radiodense gallstone (most commonly impacted in the narrow terminal ileum) following a cholecystoenteric fistula.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 4-year-old boy presents with intermittent colicky abdominal pain, drawing his legs to his chest, and passage of dark red 'currant jelly' stool. Abdominal ultrasound reveals a multilayered target (doughnut) lesion on transverse view and a 'pseudokidney' appearance on longitudinal view in the right abdomen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: Ileocolic intussusception is the most common cause of bowel obstruction in infants and toddlers (ages 3 months to 3 years). Ultrasound is the diagnostic gold standard, demonstrating concentric alternating rings of bowel mucosa, bowel wall, and invaginated mesenteric fat ('target' or 'doughnut' sign on transverse view, and 'pseudokidney' sign longitudinally).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the critical cecal diameter threshold on plain radiography or CT beyond which the risk of impending ischemic gangrene and perforation escalates dramatically in acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome)?
questions.explanation: Correct: In Ogilvie syndrome (acute colonic pseudo-obstruction), a cecal diameter greater than 10 to 12 cm on plain radiography or CT represents a critical threshold where Laplace's law (wall tension = pressure x radius / wall thickness) places the thin-walled cecum at high risk for ischemia and spontaneous diastatic perforation, often prompting pharmacological (neostigmine) or endoscopic decompression.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 3-day-old full-term neonate presents with persistent bilious emesis. An upper GI series with water-soluble contrast is performed. Which of the following findings on fluoroscopy is diagnostic of midgut malrotation with volvulus?
options: The duodenojejunal (DJ) junction is located to the right of the spine and inferior to the duodenal bulb, with a corkscrew appearance of the proximal jejunum
The DJ junction is located to the left of the left vertebral pedicle and level with the duodenal bulb
Reflux of contrast from the stomach into the distal esophagus
A double bubble sign with absence of distal bowel gas
questions.answer: The duodenojejunal (DJ) junction is located to the right of the spine and inferior to the duodenal bulb, with a corkscrew appearance of the proximal jejunum
questions.explanation: Correct: In normal gut rotation, the duodenojejunal (DJ) junction (ligament of Treitz) lies to the left of the spine at the level of the duodenal bulb. In malrotation with midgut volvulus, the DJ junction is displaced inferiorly and to the right of the vertebral column, and the twisted descending duodenum and proximal jejunum assume a pathognomonic 'corkscrew' configuration.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the single most sensitive plain radiographic examination for detecting small volumes of free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum)?
options: Erect (upright) chest radiograph including the diaphragms
Lateral view of the lumbar spine
questions.answer: Erect (upright) chest radiograph including the diaphragms
questions.explanation: Correct: An erect chest radiograph centered on the diaphragms is the most sensitive plain film for pneumoperitoneum because the X-ray beam is tangential to the highest point of the peritoneal cavity (the diaphragmatic domes), allowing detection of as little as 1 to 2 mL of subdiaphragmatic free gas.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old male with a history of peptic ulcer disease presents with sudden-onset, agonizing epigastric pain and abdominal rigidity. An erect chest X-ray shows crescentic lucencies under both diaphragmatic domes. What is the most likely source of the pneumoperitoneum?
questions.explanation: Correct: Perforation of an anterior duodenal (or gastric) peptic ulcer is the classic cause of acute peritonitis and pneumoperitoneum, readily recognized on upright chest radiographs as free subdiaphragmatic air.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Rigler's sign (also known as the 'double-wall sign') on a supine abdominal radiograph is caused by:
options: Gas present on both the mucosal (luminal) and serosal (peritoneal) surfaces of the bowel wall
Hypertrophic muscular wall thickening seen in Crohn's disease
Submucosal edema and intramural gas tracking within the bowel wall
Gas trapped between the two layers of the greater omentum
questions.answer: Gas present on both the mucosal (luminal) and serosal (peritoneal) surfaces of the bowel wall
questions.explanation: Correct: Rigler's sign (double-wall sign) occurs when pneumoperitoneum results in free gas in the peritoneal cavity outlining the outer serosal margin of the bowel wall, while normal intraluminal gas outlines the inner mucosal surface. This makes the bowel wall sharply visible as a distinct stripe.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A supine abdominal radiograph in an infant with suspected necrotizing enterocolitis reveals a distinct linear vertical radiolucency in the upper right abdomen running along the anterior abdominal wall. This finding is the:
questions.explanation: Correct: The falciform ligament sign is seen on supine radiographs when large-volume pneumoperitoneum outlines both sides of the falciform ligament with free gas, causing it to appear as a well-defined vertical soft-tissue stripe in the right upper quadrant/midline.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 42-year-old female presents with severe back and flank pain 6 hours following a difficult endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with biliary sphincterotomy. A supine abdominal CT demonstrates air outlining the right kidney, tracking along the psoas muscle, and surrounding the second portion of the duodenum, but NO free air over the liver dome or under the diaphragm. What is the diagnosis?
options: Free peritoneal rupture of the gallbladder
questions.explanation: Correct: During ERCP sphincterotomy, duodenal or periampullary perforation enters the anterior pararenal space of the retroperitoneum because the descending duodenum (D2) is a retroperitoneal structure. On CT, this presents as retroperitoneal air (pneumoretroperitoneum) outlining the duodenum, right kidney, and psoas margin, without free intraperitoneal air under the diaphragm.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: The 'continuous diaphragm sign' on an AP chest or abdominal radiograph indicates:
options: Pneumoperitoneum or pneumomediastinum allowing the central diaphragmatic tendon beneath the cardiac silhouette to be visualized
Complete rupture of the left hemidiaphragmatic dome with herniation of stomach
questions.answer: Pneumoperitoneum or pneumomediastinum allowing the central diaphragmatic tendon beneath the cardiac silhouette to be visualized
questions.explanation: Correct: Normally, the central portion of the diaphragm is obscured by the cardiac silhouette due to silhouette sign (isodense contact). When free gas accumulates either below the diaphragm in the peritoneal cavity or above it in the pericardium/mediastinum, gas interfaces with the central diaphragm, making the entire diaphragm visible as a single continuous line from flank to flank.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: The 'football sign' on a supine pediatric abdominal radiograph is pathognomonic for:
options: Massive pneumoperitoneum outlining the entire peritoneal cavity
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis with gastric overdistension
Ileocolic intussusception mass in the right flank
questions.answer: Massive pneumoperitoneum outlining the entire peritoneal cavity
questions.explanation: Correct: The football sign describes a large, oval-shaped lucency resembling an American football occupying the central abdomen on a supine radiograph, produced by massive pneumoperitoneum that distends the peritoneal cavity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 65-year-old patient who underwent uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy 48 hours ago has mild port-site tenderness. An erect chest X-ray shows a 5 mm sliver of subdiaphragmatic gas. What is the most appropriate radiological interpretation?
options: Expected post-laparoscopic pneumoperitoneum, which can normally persist for several days (up to 7-10 days)
Definitive evidence of postoperative iatrogenic bowel perforation requiring immediate re-exploration
Diaphragmatic rupture secondary to trocar placement
questions.answer: Expected post-laparoscopic pneumoperitoneum, which can normally persist for several days (up to 7-10 days)
questions.explanation: Correct: Pneumoperitoneum is an expected benign finding following laparotomy or laparoscopy (due to CO2 insufflation). Residual free air typically absorbs within 24 to 72 hours following laparoscopy and up to 7-10 days after open laparotomy; in the absence of signs of peritonitis, fever, or increasing gas volume, small residual gas is physiological.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old female presents with acute severe right lower quadrant pain, high fever, and rebound tenderness. Unenhanced CT reveals focal extraluminal gas bubbles, thickened cecal/appendiceal wall, and marked inflammatory fat stranding in the right lower quadrant. Which of the following is the most definitive CT sign of gastrointestinal perforation?
options: Extraluminal free gas bubbles adjacent to the inflamed bowel segment
Mucosal hyperenhancement of adjacent ileal loops
Absence of gas within the rectum
questions.answer: Extraluminal free gas bubbles adjacent to the inflamed bowel segment
questions.explanation: Correct: The presence of extraluminal free gas (either clustered focal microbubbles in the mesentery or free peritoneal gas) is the most specific and definitive cross-sectional sign of bowel wall perforation on CT.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On an erect chest or abdominal radiograph, which anatomical structure normally prevents free subdiaphragmatic gas from crossing directly from the right subphrenic space into the left subphrenic space across the anterior midline?
questions.explanation: Correct: The falciform ligament attaches the anterosuperior surface of the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm in the midline, creating a vertical anatomical barrier that separates the right and left subphrenic spaces anteriorly.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the standard outer-wall-to-outer-wall diameter threshold on graded-compression ultrasonography or CT used as a primary diagnostic criterion for acute appendicitis?
questions.explanation: Correct: An outer diameter of greater than 6 mm (measured from external serosa to external serosa) of a non-compressible, blind-ending tubular structure in the right lower quadrant is the classic diagnostic threshold for acute appendicitis on both ultrasound and CT.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 9-year-old boy presents with right lower quadrant pain, low-grade fever, and anorexia for 18 hours. According to standard pediatric imaging guidelines, what is the initial diagnostic imaging modality of choice?
options: Standard supine and upright abdominal radiographs
questions.explanation: Correct: Graded-compression ultrasonography is the first-line imaging modality for pediatric patients and pregnant women presenting with suspected acute appendicitis because it avoids ionizing radiation (ALARA principle) and has high sensitivity and specificity in children with thin body habitus.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following sonographic features is characteristically demonstrated in uncomplicated acute appendicitis?
options: Blind-ending, non-compressible tubular structure with increased wall hyperemia on color Doppler
Compressible tubular structure exhibiting active peristalsis
Thin wall (<1 mm) with a luminal caliber of 4 mm
Extensive pericecal gas with collapse of the appendiceal lumen
questions.answer: Blind-ending, non-compressible tubular structure with increased wall hyperemia on color Doppler
questions.explanation: Correct: Sonographic hallmarks of acute appendicitis include: a blind-ending tubular structure originating from the cecal base, non-compressibility under graded transducer pressure, outer diameter > 6 mm, wall thickening (> 2-3 mm), lack of peristalsis, and increased vascularity (hyperemia/ring of fire) on color Doppler.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old pregnant woman in her second trimester presents with right upper quadrant and flank pain. Point-of-care ultrasound is inconclusive due to maternal body habitus. Which imaging modality is the preferred next step for suspected acute appendicitis?
options: Abdominal and pelvic MRI without intravenous gadolinium
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT with iodinated IV contrast
Abdominal and pelvic MRI with gadolinium contrast
questions.answer: Abdominal and pelvic MRI without intravenous gadolinium
questions.explanation: Correct: In pregnant patients where ultrasound is equivocal or non-visualized, MRI without intravenous gadolinium is the recommended imaging modality of choice. It provides excellent soft-tissue resolution, avoids ionizing radiation, and accurately visualizes the appendix (which is often displaced superiorly by the gravid uterus).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old male undergoes IV contrast-enhanced abdominal CT for acute right lower quadrant pain. A calcified density measuring 8 mm is seen impacted at the appendiceal base, with distal appendiceal dilation (9 mm) and periappendiceal fat stranding. This calcified density is called an:
questions.explanation: Correct: An appendicolith (fecalith) is a calcified concretion of inspissated fecal material, mucus, and calcium salts. When lodged at the appendiceal orifice, it causes luminal obstruction, leading to acute appendicitis. Its presence on CT is associated with an increased risk of gangrene and perforation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old male presents with right lower quadrant pain and fever. CT reveals a 4 cm rim-enhancing fluid collection containing several gas bubbles centered in the right iliac fossa adjacent to a defect in the appendiceal wall, with surrounding intense fat stranding. What is the diagnosis and appropriate management?
options: Perforated appendicitis with periappendiceal abscess; typically managed with percutaneous catheter drainage and IV antibiotics
Uncomplicated acute catarrhal appendicitis; immediate outpatient discharge
Epiploic appendagitis; conservative oral analgesia alone
questions.answer: Perforated appendicitis with periappendiceal abscess; typically managed with percutaneous catheter drainage and IV antibiotics
questions.explanation: Correct: The presence of a focal wall defect, extraluminal gas bubbles, and a rim-enhancing fluid collection indicates perforated appendicitis complicated by an organized periappendiceal abscess. Stable patients are typically managed with IV antibiotics and ultrasound- or CT-guided percutaneous drainage, followed by interval appendectomy if indicated.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: The 'arrowhead sign' on an oral or rectal contrast-enhanced CT of the cecum in suspected appendicitis refers to:
options: Focal symmetric thickening of the cecal apex pointing directly toward the obstructed appendiceal orifice
Extravasation of barium into the peritoneal cavity pointing toward the flank
A triangle of free gas adjacent to the liver margin
Displacement of the terminal ileum superiorly by an ovarian cyst
questions.answer: Focal symmetric thickening of the cecal apex pointing directly toward the obstructed appendiceal orifice
questions.explanation: Correct: The arrowhead sign (or cecal bar sign) is produced on CT when contrast in the cecum funnels into the thickened, inflamed, and edematous cecal apex, forming an arrowhead-shaped configuration whose apex points directly at the obstructed appendiceal orifice.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 12-year-old girl is evaluated for right lower quadrant abdominal pain and fever. Ultrasound demonstrates multiple enlarged, hypervascular mesenteric lymph nodes (>8 mm short axis) clustered in the ileocecal region, with normal caliber (4 mm), compressible appendix with preserved wall layering. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: Mesenteric adenitis is a common benign self-limiting mimic of appendicitis in children, characterized by three or more enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes (often >= 8 mm in short axis) clustered in the right lower quadrant, with a completely normal, compressible, non-dilated appendix.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old male presents with acute focal left lower quadrant pain. Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrates an oval, 2 cm, fat-density lesion abutting the serosal surface of the descending colon, surrounded by an inflammatory hyperattenuating ring with a central hyperdense punctate dot (thrombosed central vein). The adjacent colonic wall is of normal caliber. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: Epiploic appendagitis is a benign self-limiting inflammation caused by torsion or venous thrombosis of an appendiceal epiploica. CT shows a pathognomonic 1-4 cm oval, fat-attenuating mass abutting the colonic serosa, surrounded by an hyperattenuating rim ('hyperattenuating ring sign') and often containing a central high-density punctate dot representing a thrombosed central vessel, without significant colonic wall thickening.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 62-year-old woman is incidentally found on pelvic CT to have a 3.5 cm cystic, tubular mass in the right lower quadrant with thin, curvilinear mural calcifications and no surrounding fat stranding. The patient is asymptomatic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Appendiceal mucocele (e.g., low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm - LAMN)
questions.answer: Appendiceal mucocele (e.g., low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm - LAMN)
questions.explanation: Correct: An appendiceal mucocele represents chronic mucinous distension of the appendiceal lumen, most commonly due to a low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm (LAMN) or retention cyst. Classic CT features are a well-circumscribed, low-attenuation (cystic) tubular/round mass in the RLQ, often with curvi-linear mural (eggshell) calcifications and an absence of periappendiceal fat stranding (unless superinfected or ruptured).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the optimal timing for performing a contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) to accurately detect and stage pancreatic parenchymal necrosis in acute pancreatitis?
options: At least 72 to 96 hours after symptom onset
Within the first 6 hours of symptom onset
Immediately upon arrival in the emergency room regardless of duration
questions.answer: At least 72 to 96 hours after symptom onset
questions.explanation: Correct: Contrast-enhanced CT performed during the first 48 to 72 hours frequently underestimates the presence and extent of pancreatic necrosis because microvascular ischemia and complete non-enhancement require 72 to 96 hours to demarcate. Performing CT at 72-96 hours provides the most reliable evaluation of parenchymal necrosis according to international guidelines.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: According to the Revised Atlanta Classification, how is an acute fluid collection developing within the first 4 weeks of interstitial edematous pancreatitis (IEP) without necrosis defined?
questions.explanation: Correct: Under the Revised Atlanta Classification, an acute peripancreatic fluid collection (APFC) occurs in interstitial edematous pancreatitis (IEP) within the first 4 weeks, lacks a defined non-epithelial wall, and contains homogeneous fluid without solid necrotic debris.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Under the Revised Atlanta Classification, what collection type develops after 4 weeks in a patient with necrotizing pancreatitis, characterized by a well-defined inflammatory capsule containing both fluid and non-liquefied necrotic debris?
questions.explanation: Correct: Walled-off necrosis (WON) is defined as a mature, encapsulated collection of non-liquefied pancreatic and/or peripancreatic necrotic tissue and fluid surrounded by a well-defined fibrous capsule, occurring typically 4 or more weeks after the onset of necrotizing pancreatitis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 54-year-old male with severe acute necrotizing pancreatitis undergoes CT on day 14 due to spiking fevers, chills, and refractory leukocytosis. The scan reveals an unencapsulated pancreatic bed collection with multiple dispersed pockets of gas bubbles. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: The presence of extraluminal gas bubbles within a necrotic pancreatic or peripancreatic collection on CT (in the absence of prior instrumentation or a fistula to adjacent bowel) is the most specific radiological sign of infected pancreatic necrosis, which carries high mortality and requires antibiotics and step-up intervention.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 48-year-old woman with a history of alcohol use disorder presents with upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Endoscopy reveals isolated bleeding gastric fundic varices without esophageal varices. CT confirms thrombosis of the splenic vein. This clinical entity is known as:
questions.explanation: Correct: Splenic vein thrombosis (often secondary to pancreatitis, as the splenic vein runs directly along the posterior pancreatic border) leads to isolated venous congestion of the spleen and short gastric/left gastroepiploic veins, causing sinistral (left-sided) portal hypertension manifested by isolated gastric fundal varices with normal portal vein pressure and absent esophageal varices.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 56-year-old male with necrotizing pancreatitis suddenly develops severe hypotension and a dropping hematocrit on day 21. Dynamic CT angiography reveals a 2.5 cm intensely enhancing, rounded vascular structure arising from the splenic artery within a peripancreatic fluid collection. What is the diagnosis and preferred emergency treatment?
options: Arterial pseudoaneurysm; urgent transcatheter coil embolization
Simple pancreatic pseudocyst; percutaneous pigtail drainage
Splenic vein thrombosis; immediate systemic anticoagulation
questions.answer: Arterial pseudoaneurysm; urgent transcatheter coil embolization
questions.explanation: Correct: Digestive pancreatic elastases and inflammatory enzymes can erode adjacent arterial walls (most commonly the splenic artery, followed by gastroduodenal and pancreaticoduodenal arteries), forming an arterial pseudoaneurysm. CT angiography reveals intense contrast enhancement matching the arterial blood pool. Because of high rupture risk, emergency treatment is endovascular transcatheter coil embolization or covered stent placement.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the defining CT criterion for diagnosing pancreatic parenchymal necrosis on contrast-enhanced CT?
options: Focal or diffuse non-enhancement of the pancreatic parenchyma (attenuation <30-50 HU during the pancreatic parenchymal phase)
Diffuse enlargement of the pancreatic head with hyperenhancement (>150 HU)
Normal homogenous parenchymal enhancement with surrounding ascites
questions.answer: Focal or diffuse non-enhancement of the pancreatic parenchyma (attenuation <30-50 HU during the pancreatic parenchymal phase)
questions.explanation: Correct: Pancreatic necrosis is defined on contrast-enhanced CT as an area of non-enhancement of pancreatic glandular tissue (typically measuring less than 30 to 50 HU in the arterial/parenchymal phase, compared to normal enhancing gland >100 HU).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 58-year-old male presents with painless jaundice, weight loss, and new-onset diabetes. Abdominal CT shows diffuse, featureless, 'sausage-shaped' enlargement of the pancreas with loss of lobular architecture, a thin hypoattenuating capsule-like rim, and irregular main pancreatic duct narrowing. Laboratory testing demonstrates elevated serum IgG4. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP, specifically Type 1 IgG4-related systemic disease) classically presents on CT/MRI as diffuse 'sausage-like' enlargement of the pancreas with effacement of normal parenchymal clefts, a distinct hypoattenuating peripheral halo/capsule-like rim, diffuse or multifocal stricturing of the main pancreatic duct, and elevated serum IgG4. It shows dramatic clinical and radiological response to corticosteroid therapy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the classic radiographic and CT appearance of advanced chronic pancreatitis?
options: Coarse parenchymal calcifications, irregular pancreatic ductal dilatation with intraductal calculi, and glandular atrophy
Smooth diffuse parenchymal hypertrophy with hypervascular blush
Diffuse replacement of the entire gland by low-attenuation fluid cysts (>10 cm)
questions.answer: Coarse parenchymal calcifications, irregular pancreatic ductal dilatation with intraductal calculi, and glandular atrophy
questions.explanation: Correct: The pathognomonic triad of advanced chronic pancreatitis on imaging (CT or plain abdominal films) consists of: (1) coarse pancreatic parenchymal calcifications, (2) irregular 'chain-of-lakes' dilatation of the main pancreatic duct with intraductal calculi, and (3) progressive parenchymal atrophy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 43-year-old female presents with acute severe epigastric pain and elevated amylase and lipase. On transabdominal ultrasound, the pancreas is poorly visualized due to overlying transverse colon gas. However, the gallbladder shows multiple mobile hyperechoic foci with acoustic shadowing, and the common bile duct is dilated to 9 mm. What is the most likely etiology of her acute pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Correct: Gallstones are the leading cause of acute pancreatitis worldwide (responsible for ~40-50% of cases). The sonographic identification of cholelithiasis and common bile duct dilatation in the setting of acute pancreatitis strongly indicates gallstone migration through the ampulla of Vater (gallstone/biliary pancreatitis).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the characteristic enhancement pattern of a cavernous hepatic hemangioma on multi-phase contrast-enhanced CT or MRI?
options: Peripheral, nodular, discontinuous enhancement in the arterial phase with progressive centripetal fill-in on portal venous and delayed phases
Rapid, intense, homogeneous arterial hyperenhancement with early washout in the portal venous phase
Peripheral rim enhancement with central non-enhancing necrosis on all phases
Progressive, delayed, concentric hyperenhancement peaking at 15 minutes with capsular retraction
questions.answer: Peripheral, nodular, discontinuous enhancement in the arterial phase with progressive centripetal fill-in on portal venous and delayed phases
questions.explanation: Correct: Cavernous hemangiomas characteristically demonstrate peripheral, globular/nodular, discontinuous enhancement during the early hepatic arterial phase, followed by progressive centripetal (inward) fill-in on portal venous and delayed phases, matching the attenuation/intensity of the blood pool (aorta and veins).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old asymptomatic woman undergoes an ultrasound showing an incidental well-circumscribed liver mass. Dynamic MRI demonstrates brisk, homogeneous arterial phase hyperenhancement, isointensity to background liver on portal venous phase, and a central stellate non-enhancing scar that shows delayed hyperenhancement on 10-minute delayed images. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) is a benign hyperplastic response to a congenital vascular malformation. Its classic imaging features are: rapid, intense, homogeneous arterial hyperenhancement, near-isointensity on portal venous phase, and a pathognomonic central stellate fibrous scar that enhances characteristically on delayed phases (due to myxoid/fibrous stroma).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old woman with a 10-year history of oral contraceptive pill (OCP) use presents with acute right upper quadrant pain. MRI demonstrates a 6 cm heterogeneously hypervascular liver lesion with areas of T1 hyperintensity (internal hemorrhage) and microscopic fat on chemical-shift imaging (drop in signal on out-of-phase imaging). What is the diagnosis and its primary clinical risk?
options: Hepatic adenoma; risk of spontaneous rupture with hemoperitoneum and malignant transformation
Focal nodular hyperplasia; risk of fatal biliary obstruction
Cavernous hemangioma; risk of malignant degeneration into angiosarcoma
Simple hepatic cyst; risk of secondary infection
questions.answer: Hepatic adenoma; risk of spontaneous rupture with hemoperitoneum and malignant transformation
questions.explanation: Correct: Hepatic adenomas are benign, hormone-driven neoplasms strongly associated with oral contraceptive pill use and anabolic steroids. They frequently contain intracellular lipid (signal drop on out-of-phase T1 MRI) and are prone to spontaneous acute intratumoral or intraperitoneal hemorrhage (hemoperitoneum). Larger adenomas (>5 cm) and the beta-catenin mutated subtype also harbor a risk of malignant transformation to HCC.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Under the Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS), which two imaging features on multiphasic contrast-enhanced CT or MRI are considered the primary diagnostic hallmarks of Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) in a patient with cirrhosis?
options: Non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement (APHE) and portal venous/delayed phase 'washout'
Peripheral nodular puddle enhancement and centripetal fill-in
Persistent delayed capsular enhancement without arterial enhancement
Complete absence of enhancement across all phases with central calcification
questions.answer: Non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement (APHE) and portal venous/delayed phase 'washout'
questions.explanation: Correct: In at-risk patients (cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B), the combination of non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement (APHE) followed by 'washout' appearance on the portal venous or delayed phases is the pathognomonic vascular hallmark of Hepatocellular Carcinoma (LI-RADS 5), reflecting neovascularization supplied by abnormal unpaired hepatic arteries and diminished portal venous supply.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 64-year-old male with hepatitis C cirrhosis undergoes a routine surveillance ultrasound, which reveals a new 2.4 cm solid, hypoechoic hepatic nodule in segment VI. Four-phase liver CT confirms non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement, clear delayed 'washout', and an enhancing peripheral capsule. What is the appropriate LI-RADS category?
questions.explanation: Correct: According to LI-RADS CT/MRI criteria, a lesion >= 20 mm in a cirrhotic liver that exhibits non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement (APHE) plus at least one major feature (such as 'washout' or enhancing capsule) is categorized as LR-5: Definitely HCC, which allows definitive non-invasive diagnosis without requiring biopsy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 68-year-old male with a history of sigmoid colon resection for adenocarcinoma presents with elevated CEA levels. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen shows multiple liver lesions with peripheral rim-like enhancement in the portal venous phase and central hypodensity ('target' or 'bull's-eye' sign). These lesions represent:
questions.explanation: Correct: Colorectal carcinoma liver metastases are classically hypovascular. On contrast-enhanced CT (most apparent in the portal venous phase when normal hepatic parenchyma enhances brightly), they appear as hypoattenuating masses with an enhancing peripheral viable tumor rim and central necrosis/edema, producing the classic 'target' or 'bull's-eye' sign.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following primary malignancies is most characteristically associated with HYPERVASCULAR hepatic metastases demonstrating avid arterial-phase enhancement on multiphasic CT/MRI?
options: Neuroendocrine tumors (e.g., carcinoid or islet cell tumors)
Infiltrating ductal carcinoma of the breast
questions.answer: Neuroendocrine tumors (e.g., carcinoid or islet cell tumors)
questions.explanation: Correct: Hypervascular liver metastases enhance avidly during the early hepatic arterial phase and are typically derived from neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), renal cell carcinoma (RCC), thyroid carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, and malignant melanoma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old male presents with high fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice. CT reveals a 5 cm complex low-attenuation hepatic collection with an enhancing peripheral wall and a surrounding outer zone of hypodensity representing perilesional edema (the 'double target' sign). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A pyogenic liver abscess typically presents on contrast-enhanced CT as a well-defined fluid collection (10-30 HU) with the 'double target sign': an inner hyperdense enhancing ring (the hyperemic collagenous abscess capsule) surrounded by an outer hypodense non-enhancing concentric zone (edematous hepatic parenchyma).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 65-year-old female presents with malaise and weight loss. CT demonstrates an infiltrative, poorly enhancing mass in the peripheral right hepatic lobe associated with marked focal retraction of the overlying hepatic capsule, peripheral bile duct dilatation, and progressive delayed contrast enhancement. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (peripheral cholangiocarcinoma) is a desmoplastic tumor characterized by abundant dense fibrous stroma. Its classic imaging features are: peripheral hypovascularity, progressive delayed contrast enhancement (fibrous pooling), capsular retraction (due to cicatricial fibrosis), and satellite nodules with peripheral biliary duct dilatation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following ultrasound criteria is essential for diagnosing a benign simple hepatic cyst?
options: Anechoic lumen, imperceptible thin wall, well-defined back wall, and posterior acoustic enhancement
Internal echogenic layering debris with dirty acoustic shadowing
Thick irregular septations with central vascularity on color Doppler
Hyperechoic solid mass with posterior edge shadowing
questions.answer: Anechoic lumen, imperceptible thin wall, well-defined back wall, and posterior acoustic enhancement
questions.explanation: Correct: The classic ultrasound criteria for a benign simple epithelial hepatic cyst are: (1) completely anechoic (echo-free) internal lumen, (2) sharply demarcated, imperceptible thin smooth walls, (3) round or oval shape, and (4) marked posterior acoustic enhancement (increased through-transmission).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What morphological hepatic volume redistribution is classically observed in advanced macronodular or micronodular liver cirrhosis on cross-sectional imaging?
options: Hypertrophy of the caudate lobe and lateral segments (II/III), with atrophy of the right lobe and medial segment (IV)
Symmetric, uniform pan-hepatic enlargement without focal atrophy
Atrophy of the caudate lobe with massive compensatory hypertrophy of the right posterior segments
Selective hypertrophy of the quadrate lobe (segment IV) with normal remaining liver
questions.answer: Hypertrophy of the caudate lobe and lateral segments (II/III), with atrophy of the right lobe and medial segment (IV)
questions.explanation: Correct: In chronic cirrhosis, hepatic fibrosis and altered vascular perfusion lead to progressive atrophy of the right hepatic lobe (segments V-VIII) and medial segment of the left lobe (segment IV), accompanied by compensatory hypertrophy of the caudate lobe (segment I) and lateral segments of the left lobe (segments II and III).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the normal upper limit of the main portal vein diameter on transabdominal ultrasound or contrast-enhanced CT in a healthy adult?
questions.explanation: Correct: The normal caliber of the main portal vein in adults is up to 13 mm (measured anterior to the IVC in quiet respiration). A diameter exceeding 13 mm is a recognized, sensitive indicator of portal hypertension (although caliber may paradoxically normalize when extensive portosystemic collaterals decompress the portal bed).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 56-year-old male with alcoholic cirrhosis presents with progressive abdominal distension. Ultrasound of the liver demonstrates a patent, tubular vascular channel originating from the left portal vein, traversing through the ligamentum teres along the anterior abdominal wall toward the umbilicus, with continuous hepatofugal flow on color Doppler. This finding represents:
questions.explanation: Correct: A recanalized paraumbilical vein opens in portal hypertension as an important portosystemic collateral pathway. It arises from the umbilical segment of the left portal vein and courses inferiorly within the falciform ligament / ligamentum teres to anastomose with systemic epigastric veins at the anterior abdominal wall (manifesting clinically as caput medusae / Cruveilhier-Baumgarten syndrome).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On spectral Doppler ultrasound of the main portal vein, which flow pattern indicates severe, decompensated portal hypertension?
options: Hepatofugal (retrograde) flow directed away from the liver
Hepatopetal (antegrade) continuous flow directed toward the liver
Monophasic gentle undulating flow toward the liver with mean velocity 25 cm/s
Pulsatile triphasic waveform matching the cardiac cycle
questions.answer: Hepatofugal (retrograde) flow directed away from the liver
questions.explanation: Correct: Normal portal venous flow is hepatopetal (toward the liver) with a gently undulating continuous waveform.
