options: Nuchal translucency measurement with an otherwise limited survey
Spinal imaging in two planes with cranial lemon/banana sign assessment
Maternal serum AFP measurement without structural spinal assessment
Routine fetal spinal MRI without an initial ultrasound examination
questions.answer: Spinal imaging in two planes with cranial lemon/banana sign assessment
questions.explanation: Open neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly) are screened with ultrasound by visualizing the spine and looking for cranial signs: the 'lemon sign' (frontal bone scalloping) and 'banana sign' (curved cerebellum/Arnold-Chiari malformation). A: NT measurement screens for chromosomal anomalies, not NTDs, at 11–14 weeks. C: Serum AFP is a screening adjunct but not the definitive anatomical assessment. D: MRI is a problem-solving tool, not primary screening.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Polyhydramnios is defined as an amniotic fluid index (AFI) of greater than:
questions.explanation: Polyhydramnios is defined as AFI >20 cm (or single deepest vertical pocket >8 cm). It is associated with fetal swallowing anomalies (esophageal atresia, neuromuscular conditions), diabetes, twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, and fetal anemia. A: 15 cm is the upper limit of normal. B: 18 cm is within the borderline range. D: 25 cm indicates severe polyhydramnios.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 20-week fetus is found to have bilateral choroid plexus cysts (CPCs). What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Reassure — isolated CPCs are a normal variant at all gestational ages
Perform detailed anatomic survey; offer genetic counseling and consider aneuploidy screening (trisomy 18) if other markers are present
Immediate cesarean section to deliver the fetus
questions.answer: Perform detailed anatomic survey; offer genetic counseling and consider aneuploidy screening (trisomy 18) if other markers are present
questions.explanation: Isolated CPCs are generally benign and resolve by 26–28 weeks. However, they are soft markers for trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome). A detailed anatomy survey for other structural abnormalities is essential. If other markers are present (cardiac defects, overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet), genetic counseling and amniocentesis/cfDNA testing should be offered. A: Isolated CPCs are generally benign, but not if combined with other anomalies. C & D: These interventions are not appropriate based on CPCs alone.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On fetal ultrasound, dangling of the cerebellum into the foramen magnum with obliteration of the cisterna magna is characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation: Chiari II malformation involves herniation of the cerebellar vermis and brainstem through the foramen magnum (the 'banana sign'), obliteration of the cisterna magna, and is always associated with open spina bifida (myelomeningocele). The 'lemon sign' (frontal bone scalloping) is also present. A: Dandy-Walker shows posterior fossa cyst with absent or hypoplastic vermis and enlarged posterior fossa. C: Holoprosencephaly involves failure of prosencephalon division. D: Isolated ventriculomegaly does not cause these posterior fossa findings.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which biometric parameter is MOST accurate for fetal weight estimation in the second and third trimesters?
options: A combination of BPD, HC, abdominal circumference (AC), and femur length (FL)
questions.answer: A combination of BPD, HC, abdominal circumference (AC), and femur length (FL)
questions.explanation: Estimated fetal weight (EFW) using Hadlock's formula combines BPD, HC, AC, and FL, providing the most accurate weight estimation (±15%). AC is particularly important as it reflects fetal liver size and nutritional status. A, B, D: Single parameters are less accurate for weight estimation than multiparameter formulas.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A fetus at 22 weeks is found to have a single umbilical artery (SUA). What is the recommended follow-up?
options: No further action needed — SUA is a normal variant
Detailed anatomy scan to exclude associated structural anomalies; offer aneuploidy screening if anomalies identified
questions.answer: Detailed anatomy scan to exclude associated structural anomalies; offer aneuploidy screening if anomalies identified
questions.explanation: SUA (two-vessel cord) is associated with structural anomalies (especially renal and cardiac) and chromosomal abnormalities. A detailed anatomy survey is essential. If the SUA is isolated, the prognosis is generally good, but growth scans are recommended. A: SUA is not a 'normal variant' — it requires evaluation. C: Immediate delivery is not indicated. D: Follow-up at 38 weeks is insufficient — early detailed assessment is needed.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On prenatal ultrasound, bilateral renal agenesis is associated with which sequence of findings?
options: Oligohydramnios, absent fetal bladder, pulmonary hypoplasia — Potter sequence
Normal amniotic fluid, absent renal pelves
Echogenic kidneys with enlarged renal cortex
questions.answer: Oligohydramnios, absent fetal bladder, pulmonary hypoplasia — Potter sequence
questions.explanation: Bilateral renal agenesis leads to absence of fetal urine production, resulting in severe oligohydramnios, absence of the fetal bladder (no urine to fill it), pulmonary hypoplasia (amniotic fluid is essential for lung development), and classic Potter facies. This is Potter sequence. A: Polyhydramnios and macrosomia are associated with diabetic macrosomia. C: Normal fluid cannot persist without fetal urinary contribution from ~18 weeks. D: Echogenic kidneys suggest dysplastic kidneys, not agenesis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Gastroschisis on fetal ultrasound is distinguished from omphalocele by:
options: Presence of a covering membrane and associated chromosomal anomalies
Herniation through the umbilical ring with liver involvement
Defect to the right of the umbilical cord insertion with free-floating bowel loops and no covering membrane
Central defect containing only small bowel
questions.answer: Defect to the right of the umbilical cord insertion with free-floating bowel loops and no covering membrane
questions.explanation: Gastroschisis: paraumbilical defect (usually right side), no covering membrane, herniated bowel loops floating freely in amniotic fluid, no liver involvement, low association with chromosomal anomalies. Omphalocele: central umbilical defect, covered by a membrane, may contain liver, high association with chromosomal anomalies (trisomy 18, 13). A: Covering membrane and chromosomal risk describe omphalocele. B: Liver involvement and umbilical ring herniation describe omphalocele. D: Central defect without membrane description still fits omphalocele.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A biophysical profile (BPP) score of 2/10 at 35 weeks in a growth-restricted fetus indicates:
options: Significant fetal compromise — prompt delivery should be considered
questions.answer: Significant fetal compromise — prompt delivery should be considered
questions.explanation: A BPP score of 0–2/10 (or ≤4/10 in many protocols) indicates significant fetal compromise with high risk of perinatal asphyxia. Prompt delivery is generally recommended, weighing gestational age and maturity. The BPP assesses: fetal breathing movements, gross body movements, tone, amniotic fluid volume, and NST. A: 2/10 is critically low. B: Equivocal is 6/10. D: Expectant management is inappropriate at this score in a compromised fetus.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old woman presents with acute pelvic pain at mid-cycle. Ultrasound reveals a 4 cm anechoic, thin-walled, unilocular cyst in the right ovary with posterior acoustic enhancement and no internal Doppler flow. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: A simple follicular cyst is anechoic, thin-walled, unilocular, <10 cm, with posterior enhancement and no internal vascularity. In a reproductive-age woman, this is the most common adnexal cyst, often physiological. A: Endometrioma has a characteristic ground-glass (low-level echoes) appearance. B: Dermoid cysts have echogenic components (hair, fat), shadowing, and the 'tip of the iceberg' sign. D: Serous cystadenoma is typically larger and may be multilocular.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: The sonographic hallmark of an endometrioma on transvaginal ultrasound is:
options: A unilocular anechoic cyst with thin walls
Homogeneous low-level ('ground glass') internal echogenicity with a thick wall
A complex cyst with thick septations and papillary projections
A hyperechoic mass with posterior acoustic shadowing
questions.answer: Homogeneous low-level ('ground glass') internal echogenicity with a thick wall
questions.explanation: Endometriomas have a characteristic 'ground glass' (homogeneous low-level internal echogenicity) appearance due to old hemorrhagic blood products, with a thick wall and sometimes dependent debris. The appearance is highly specific (>95%). A: This describes a simple cyst. C: Thick septations and papillary projections raise concern for malignancy. D: Posterior shadowing is characteristic of dermoids.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which scoring system is commonly used to stratify the risk of malignancy in adnexal masses on ultrasound?
questions.explanation: O-RADS (developed from the IOTA group research) is the standardized scoring system for classifying adnexal mass risk of malignancy on ultrasound (1–5 scale), analogous to BI-RADS for breast and TI-RADS for thyroid. A: BI-RADS is for breast imaging. B: PI-RADS is for prostate MRI. D: TI-RADS is for thyroid nodules.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman is incidentally found to have a 2 cm simple-appearing unilocular ovarian cyst with no internal flow. Based on current guidelines, the most appropriate management is:
options: Immediate surgical excision — all ovarian cysts in postmenopausal women require surgery
Reassurance and annual follow-up ultrasound for up to 2 years
Repeat ultrasound in 6 weeks only if symptomatic
questions.answer: Reassurance and annual follow-up ultrasound for up to 2 years
questions.explanation: Current guidelines (SRU, ACR, IOTA) indicate that simple unilocular cysts ≤10 cm in postmenopausal women have very low malignancy risk (<1%). Annual follow-up ultrasound for 1–2 years is recommended. A: Surgery is not required for all simple cysts in postmenopausal women. C: CA-125 and CT are not indicated for simple cysts — they may cause unnecessary cascade of investigations. D: Follow-up should be structured (annual), not symptom-driven alone.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On ultrasound, a 'tip of the iceberg' sign with echogenic material and posterior acoustic shadowing within an adnexal mass is MOST consistent with:
questions.explanation: The 'tip of the iceberg' sign in dermoid cysts occurs because the hyperechoic contents (hair, fat, sebum) reflect sound, leaving the posterior portion in acoustic shadow. The echogenic material is the 'iceberg' — the full extent of the cyst is hidden. A: Serous cystadenocarcinoma has complex features but not this specific appearance. B: Mucinous cystadenoma typically has multiple thin locules with mucinous (slightly echogenic) fluid. D: TOA has complex, heterogeneous features with thick walls.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old woman presents with acute severe left pelvic pain. Ultrasound shows an enlarged left ovary measuring 6 × 5 cm with absent Doppler flow. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Ovarian torsion presents with sudden severe unilateral pain, enlarged ovary (often with a lead point mass), and absent or reduced Doppler flow. This is a surgical emergency. Absent Doppler flow with ovarian enlargement is highly suggestive. A: Ruptured cyst may cause free fluid but ovary is not enlarged with absent flow. C: Endometrioma does not cause acute absent Doppler. D: TOA has complex cystic features with thick walls and is treated medically first.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which ultrasound feature of an adnexal mass has the HIGHEST specificity for malignancy?
options: Solid papillary projections with internal vascularity (color Doppler flow)
questions.answer: Solid papillary projections with internal vascularity (color Doppler flow)
questions.explanation: Solid papillary projections with internal color Doppler vascularity within a cystic adnexal mass are the most specific ultrasound features for ovarian malignancy. These indicate solid vascularized tissue projecting from the cyst wall. A: Unilocular simple cysts, even when large, have very low malignancy risk. C: Ground-glass echogenicity is specific for endometrioma. D: Bilaterality can be seen in endometriomas, metastases, or synchronous primary tumors — not specific for malignancy alone.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) on ultrasound is characterized by:
options: A single large follicle (>3 cm) per ovary
≥20 follicles per ovary measuring 2–9 mm ('string of pearls') with increased ovarian volume (>10 mL)
questions.answer: ≥20 follicles per ovary measuring 2–9 mm ('string of pearls') with increased ovarian volume (>10 mL)
questions.explanation: PCOS on ultrasound (per Rotterdam criteria, updated 2023 threshold): ≥20 follicles per ovary measuring 2–9 mm (arranged peripherally — 'string of pearls') and/or ovarian volume >10 mL on either ovary. A: A dominant follicle is normal in the follicular phase — PCOS features multiple small follicles, not a single dominant one. C: Large simple cysts >5 cm are not PCOS features. D: Dermoids are unrelated to PCOS.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A multilocular cyst with mucinous content (variable low-level echogenicity in multiple locules) in a 45-year-old woman most likely represents:
questions.explanation: Mucinous cystadenomas are typically multilocular with multiple locules of varying echogenicity due to mucinous content. They can grow to large sizes. A: Serous cystadenomas are often unilocular with serous (anechoic) fluid. C: Endometriomas are typically unilocular with ground-glass echogenicity. D: Follicular cysts are simple and unilocular.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A hemorrhagic ovarian cyst on ultrasound characteristically shows:
options: Anechoic fluid with no internal architecture
Fishnet/lace-like (reticular) internal echogenic pattern with no Doppler flow
Hyperechoic solid nodule within the cyst
questions.answer: Fishnet/lace-like (reticular) internal echogenic pattern with no Doppler flow
questions.explanation: Hemorrhagic ovarian cysts have a distinctive 'fishnet' or 'lace-like' (reticular) internal echogenicity due to fibrin strands and retracting clot. Crucially, no internal Doppler flow is detected (distinguishing it from solid vascularized tissue). A: Anechoic fluid is a simple cyst. C: Thick septations with projections suggest malignancy. D: A hyperechoic solid nodule with no Doppler retraction/fibrin pattern suggests different pathology.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) on ultrasound most commonly appear as:
options: Anechoic masses with posterior acoustic enhancement
Well-defined, hypoechoic to isoechoic solid masses that may cause uterine contour deformity and posterior acoustic shadowing
Hyperechoic masses replacing the entire uterus
questions.answer: Well-defined, hypoechoic to isoechoic solid masses that may cause uterine contour deformity and posterior acoustic shadowing
questions.explanation: Fibroids are benign smooth muscle tumors appearing as well-circumscribed solid masses, typically hypoechoic to isoechoic relative to myometrium, often causing uterine contour irregularity. Calcification causes posterior shadowing. A: Anechoic masses with posterior enhancement describe cysts. C: Hyperechoic replacement of the uterus can occur with extensive adenomyosis or molar pregnancy. D: Fibroids are solid, not cystic.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which location of uterine fibroid is MOST associated with abnormal uterine bleeding and subfertility?
options: Subserosal fibroid projecting from the outer uterine surface
Submucosal fibroid distorting the endometrial cavity
questions.answer: Submucosal fibroid distorting the endometrial cavity
questions.explanation: Submucosal fibroids are most strongly associated with abnormal uterine bleeding (heavy menstrual bleeding) and subfertility because they distort the endometrial cavity, impair implantation, and disrupt endometrial vascularity. A: Subserosal fibroids have least effect on bleeding and fertility. C: Intramural fibroids may cause bleeding if they distort the cavity but less than submucosal. D: Cervical fibroids are rare and can obstruct the cervical canal.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 38-year-old woman with menorrhagia has a saline infusion sonography (SIS) showing a broad-based, hyperechoic polypoid structure arising from the posterior endometrial wall that does not move with fluid instillation. This is MOST consistent with:
questions.explanation: A submucosal fibroid on SIS appears as a broad-based, hypoechoic (or isoechoic to myometrium), sessile mass that does not move freely with fluid. Its echogenicity matches myometrium. An endometrial polyp is typically hyperechoic to the endometrium, pedunculated, and has a feeding vessel on Doppler. A: Endometrial polyps are hyperechoic, pedunculated, and move more freely. C: RPOC would be in the context of recent pregnancy. D: Carcinoma appears as irregular endometrial thickening with heterogeneous echogenicity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On MRI, uterine leiomyomas classically appear as:
options: Isointense to endometrium on all sequences
questions.explanation: Leiomyomas are composed of densely packed smooth muscle cells with a collagenous stroma, resulting in low signal intensity (dark) on T2-weighted MRI. This is the characteristic appearance. Degeneration (e.g., red degeneration = hemorrhage, cystic change) can alter this appearance. A: T2 hyperintensity in a fibroid suggests degeneration or leiomyosarcoma. C: T1 high signal occurs in hemorrhagic (red) degeneration. D: Fibroids are clearly distinct from endometrium.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A pregnant woman at 16 weeks presents with severe localized uterine tenderness. Ultrasound shows a large fibroid with central heterogeneous echotexture and cystic areas. What complication of fibroids is most likely?
questions.explanation: Red (carneous) degeneration is the most common type of fibroid degeneration in pregnancy, caused by rapid growth outpacing blood supply → hemorrhagic infarction. It presents with acute localized pain and tenderness overlying the fibroid, with heterogeneous/cystic ultrasound appearance. A: Sarcomatous transformation is rare and not typically pregnancy-related. C: Calcification is a chronic degenerative change, usually painless, in postmenopausal women. D: Torsion occurs with pedunculated subserosal fibroids but would present differently.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: The FIGO classification of uterine fibroids classifies fibroids primarily based on:
options: Location and relationship to the myometrium and endometrium (types 0–8)
Histological grade of smooth muscle differentiation
questions.answer: Location and relationship to the myometrium and endometrium (types 0–8)
questions.explanation: The FIGO PALM-COEIN leiomyoma classification (types 0–8) categorizes fibroids by their anatomical relationship: 0 (pedunculated intracavitary), 1 (<50% intramural), 2 (≥50% intramural), 3 (contacts endometrium), 4 (intramural), 5, 6 (subserosal), 7 (subserosal pedunculated), 8 (other). This guides clinical management. A: Size and number are noted but are not the primary classification basis. C: Histological classification is separate (surgical pathology). D: Vascularity is not part of FIGO classification.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which imaging modality is BEST for pre-procedural mapping of uterine fibroids before uterine fibroid embolization (UFE) or myomectomy?
questions.explanation: MRI with contrast (gadolinium) is the gold standard for fibroid mapping before UFE or myomectomy. It accurately delineates fibroid number, size, location, vascularity, and degree of enhancement (viable vs. infarcted tissue), essential for procedural planning. A: Ultrasound may miss small or numerous fibroids and cannot reliably assess vascularity for embolization planning. B: CT involves radiation and has inferior soft-tissue contrast. D: Hysteroscopy only evaluates intracavitary fibroids.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On ultrasound, calcification within a fibroid appears as:
options: Hyperechoic foci or rim with posterior acoustic shadowing
questions.answer: Hyperechoic foci or rim with posterior acoustic shadowing
questions.explanation: Calcification within fibroids appears as hyperechoic foci or a hyperechoic peripheral rim ('eggshell' calcification) with posterior acoustic shadowing — the same appearance as calcification elsewhere. A: Low-level internal echoes suggest cystic/myxoid degeneration, not calcification. C: Anechoic areas with enhancement suggest cystic degeneration. D: Irregular hyperechoic areas without shadowing could represent other degenerative changes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old woman with multiple large fibroids undergoes MRI. One fibroid shows T1 hyperintensity and T2 hypointensity. What type of degeneration does this indicate?
questions.explanation: T1 high signal within a fibroid indicates the presence of blood products (methemoglobin in subacute hemorrhage), consistent with hemorrhagic/red degeneration. Fibroid remains T2 hypointense overall as the dense smooth muscle stroma is preserved. A: Hyaline degeneration shows no T1 signal change. C: Cystic degeneration shows T2 high signal (fluid) and T1 low signal. D: Myxoid degeneration shows T2 heterogeneous high signal.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A feature on MRI that should raise concern for leiomyosarcoma rather than a benign leiomyoma is:
options: T2 dark (hypointense) signal with well-defined margins
Irregular margins, T2 heterogeneous high signal, necrosis, and rapid growth on serial imaging
Multiple fibroids in a premenopausal woman
questions.answer: Irregular margins, T2 heterogeneous high signal, necrosis, and rapid growth on serial imaging
questions.explanation: Leiomyosarcoma is rare but suspected when MRI shows: irregular/ill-defined margins, heterogeneous T2 signal (not uniformly dark), central necrosis/hemorrhage, and rapid growth on serial imaging, particularly in a postmenopausal woman or in a growing 'fibroid' after menopause. A: Typical features of a benign fibroid. C: Calcification is a benign degenerative feature. D: Multiple fibroids in a premenopausal woman is typical benign leiomyomatosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a thickened endometrium of 8 mm with heterogeneous echogenicity. The MOST appropriate next step is:
options: Reassure — 8 mm is within normal postmenopausal range
Endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy to evaluate for endometrial carcinoma
questions.answer: Endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy to evaluate for endometrial carcinoma
questions.explanation: In a postmenopausal woman with bleeding, endometrial thickness >4–5 mm requires histological evaluation (biopsy or hysteroscopy with directed biopsy) to exclude endometrial carcinoma. The threshold for biopsy in symptomatic women is lower than in asymptomatic women. A: 8 mm in a symptomatic postmenopausal woman exceeds the threshold. C: Delay in evaluation is inappropriate in the context of postmenopausal bleeding. D: HRT is contraindicated until malignancy is excluded.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On saline infusion sonography (SIS), an endometrial polyp is BEST characterized by:
options: A broad-based submucosal mass with echogenicity matching the myometrium
A pedunculated, hyperechoic (relative to myometrium) intracavitary mass with a feeding vessel on Doppler
Diffuse irregular endometrial thickening without a focal mass
questions.answer: A pedunculated, hyperechoic (relative to myometrium) intracavitary mass with a feeding vessel on Doppler
questions.explanation: Endometrial polyps on SIS appear as pedunculated or sessile, hyperechoic intracavitary masses with a single feeding vessel ('stalk vessel') on Doppler. They are smooth-bordered. A: Broad-based with myometrial echogenicity describes a submucosal fibroid. C: Diffuse irregular thickening raises concern for hyperplasia or carcinoma. D: An anechoic collection suggests hematometra or fluid in the cavity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On MRI, endometrial carcinoma most commonly appears as:
options: A T2 hypointense mass within the endometrium
A T2 intermediate-to-high signal mass expanding the endometrial cavity with disruption of the junctional zone
A T1 hyperintense mass within the myometrium
A T2 homogeneous hypointense mass with well-defined margins
questions.answer: A T2 intermediate-to-high signal mass expanding the endometrial cavity with disruption of the junctional zone
questions.explanation: Endometrial carcinoma on T2-weighted MRI typically appears as an intermediate-to-hyperintense mass expanding the endometrial cavity. Assessment of junctional zone integrity is critical for staging — disruption indicates myometrial invasion (stage I A vs. I B). A & D: Low signal is characteristic of fibroids. C: T1 hyperintensity suggests hemorrhage, not the typical carcinoma appearance.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Adenomyosis on MRI is defined by:
options: A T2 hypointense intramural mass with a capsule
Thickening of the junctional zone >12 mm (diffuse) or focal T2 dark myometrial thickening with small T2-bright foci
T2 hyperintense myometrial mass replacing the junctional zone
Normal junctional zone with T1-bright endometrial thickening
questions.answer: Thickening of the junctional zone >12 mm (diffuse) or focal T2 dark myometrial thickening with small T2-bright foci
questions.explanation: Adenomyosis is ectopic endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium. MRI criteria: junctional zone thickness ≥12 mm (diffuse adenomyosis) or focal junctional zone thickening with embedded T2-bright foci (representing trapped endometrial glands/hemorrhage). A: A T2 hypointense mass with capsule describes a fibroid. C: T2 hyperintense mass replacing junctional zone is not typical of adenomyosis. D: T1-bright endometrial thickening without junctional zone change is not adenomyosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Tamoxifen use in breast cancer survivors is associated with which endometrial finding on ultrasound?
options: Uniform endometrial thinning with an atrophic appearance
Heterogeneous endometrial thickening with cystic spaces
Isolated submucosal fibroids with a normal endometrial stripe
Cervical canal stenosis with a uniformly thin endometrium
questions.answer: Heterogeneous endometrial thickening with cystic spaces
questions.explanation: Tamoxifen (a selective estrogen receptor modulator) has estrogenic effects on the endometrium, causing irregular thickening, cystic changes, polyp formation, and increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma. Endometrial surveillance is recommended. A: Atrophy is the opposite — tamoxifen stimulates the endometrium. C: Fibroids are not specifically a tamoxifen complication. D: Cervical stenosis is not associated with tamoxifen.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Asherman syndrome (intrauterine adhesions) on saline infusion sonography (SIS) appears as:
options: A uniformly distensible uterine cavity with thin endometrium
Irregular filling defects, bridging bands across the cavity, and restricted cavity distension
questions.answer: Irregular filling defects, bridging bands across the cavity, and restricted cavity distension
questions.explanation: Asherman syndrome (intrauterine synechia) is characterized on SIS by irregular filling defects, bridging fibrous bands crossing the uterine cavity, and a cavity that cannot be fully distended by saline. The endometrium appears thin and irregular. A: A distensible cavity with thin endometrium is normal or atrophic. C: A large polyp is a focal finding without the bridging bands. D: Diffuse hyperechogenicity is non-specific.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On ultrasound, which feature of endometrial thickening is MOST concerning for malignancy?
options: Symmetrical, homogeneous hyperechoic stripe of 10 mm in the secretory phase
Irregular, heterogeneous endometrial thickening with Doppler vascularity and disruption of the endometrial-myometrial interface
Hyperechoic stripe of 6 mm in a premenopausal woman
Thin echogenic endometrium of 3 mm in a postmenopausal woman
questions.answer: Irregular, heterogeneous endometrial thickening with Doppler vascularity and disruption of the endometrial-myometrial interface
questions.explanation: Features most concerning for endometrial carcinoma on ultrasound include: irregular/heterogeneous thickening, disruption of the endometrial-myometrial interface (myometrial invasion), and abnormal vascularity on Doppler. A: Symmetrical thick endometrium in secretory phase is normal. C: 6 mm in a premenopausal woman is within normal range. D: 3 mm in a postmenopausal woman is reassuringly thin.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: The primary role of MRI in staging endometrial carcinoma is to assess:
options: The histological grade of the tumor
Depth of myometrial invasion and cervical stromal involvement
The primary diagnosis — MRI is used to detect, not stage, endometrial cancer
questions.answer: Depth of myometrial invasion and cervical stromal involvement
questions.explanation: MRI is the preferred modality for staging endometrial carcinoma because it accurately assesses depth of myometrial invasion (<50% vs. ≥50% — stage IA vs. IB) and cervical stromal involvement (stage II). These determine surgical approach (simple vs. radical hysterectomy, nodal sampling). A: Histological grading requires tissue biopsy, not imaging. C: Polyp counting is a diagnostic role, not staging. D: MRI can aid diagnosis but is primarily used for staging.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which condition is MOST commonly associated with endometrial hyperplasia?
options: Unopposed estrogen stimulation (PCOS, obesity, anovulation, estrogen-secreting tumors)
questions.answer: Unopposed estrogen stimulation (PCOS, obesity, anovulation, estrogen-secreting tumors)
questions.explanation: Endometrial hyperplasia results from chronic unopposed estrogen stimulation without progesterone opposition. Risk factors include PCOS (anovulation), obesity (peripheral estrogen conversion), estrogen-only HRT, granulosa cell tumors, and nulliparity. A: Hypoestrogen causes endometrial atrophy, not hyperplasia. C & D: Prior curettage and Asherman syndrome cause adhesions and atrophy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Hematometra (blood in the uterine cavity) on ultrasound appears as:
options: Anechoic fluid in the endometrial cavity
Echogenic or heterogeneous fluid distending the endometrial cavity
Thin endometrial stripe with no fluid
questions.answer: Echogenic or heterogeneous fluid distending the endometrial cavity
questions.explanation: Hematometra (uterine blood accumulation, typically due to cervical stenosis/obstruction) appears as echogenic or complex (heterogeneous) fluid distending the endometrial cavity, reflecting blood products in various stages of clotting. A: Simple anechoic fluid (hydrometra) indicates serous fluid, not blood. C: Polyps are focal solid structures. D: A thin stripe indicates a normal or atrophic endometrium without cavity distension.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On transvaginal ultrasound, a tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA) is BEST characterized by:
options: A simple anechoic ovarian cyst with thin walls
A complex multiloculated adnexal mass with thick walls, internal echoes, and no color Doppler flow
A complex thick-walled adnexal mass merging with the ovary, with internal echoes and peripheral hypervascularity on Doppler
A tubular fluid-filled structure separate from the ovary
questions.answer: A complex thick-walled adnexal mass merging with the ovary, with internal echoes and peripheral hypervascularity on Doppler
questions.explanation: TOA appears as a complex, heterogeneous, thick-walled adnexal mass merging with or incorporating the ovary, with internal echoes (debris/pus), and peripheral hypervascular flow on Doppler indicating the inflammatory response. B: Absent Doppler flow would suggest a non-inflammatory mass. A: Simple cysts are not TOA. D: A tubular fluid-filled structure alone describes hydrosalpinx.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Hydrosalpinx on ultrasound is characterized by:
options: A thick-walled tubular structure with internal echoes and Doppler flow
A thin-walled, tortuous, fluid-filled tubular adnexal structure separate from the ovary, with incomplete septa ('cogwheel' sign in cross-section)
A complex ovarian mass with solid components
A pelvic fluid collection posterior to the uterus
questions.answer: A thin-walled, tortuous, fluid-filled tubular adnexal structure separate from the ovary, with incomplete septa ('cogwheel' sign in cross-section)
questions.explanation: Hydrosalpinx is a dilated, fluid-filled fallopian tube due to distal obstruction. It appears as a thin-walled, tortuous tubular structure separate from the ovary, with anechoic fluid and incomplete septa (incomplete separation = 'cogwheel' appearance in cross-section; 'waist sign' where the lumen appears constricted). A: Thick walls with echoes and flow suggest TOA. C: This describes an ovarian mass. D: Free pelvic fluid is not hydrosalpinx.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the MOST common organism associated with pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)?
questions.explanation: PID is most commonly caused by sexually transmitted organisms, primarily Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, often in a polymicrobial infection including anaerobes. A: Staph. aureus is not typically associated with PID (more skin/surgical infections). C: Group B Strep is associated with neonatal infection, not PID. D: E. coli can be part of polymicrobial TOA but is not the primary causative organism.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On MRI, which feature of a TOA helps distinguish it from ovarian malignancy?
options: T2-bright fluid within an isolated ovarian lesion
A merged tubo-ovarian complex with pus and no enhancing solid nodules
Enhancing solid papillary projections within a cystic lesion
Absent Doppler flow within the entire affected ovary
questions.answer: A merged tubo-ovarian complex with pus and no enhancing solid nodules
questions.explanation: TOA is distinguished from malignancy by: bilateral involvement (75%), clinical signs of infection, T1-bright pus/blood content, and absence of solid enhancing nodular components. Malignancy tends to show papillary projections or solid enhancing nodes. A: T2 high signal fluid is seen in both. C: Papillary projections favor malignancy, not TOA. D: Doppler is not available on MRI; it is not a distinguishing MRI feature.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is a complication of PID characterized by:
options: Perihepatitis — inflammation of the liver capsule causing right upper quadrant pain
Pelvic abscess extending into the psoas muscle
questions.answer: Perihepatitis — inflammation of the liver capsule causing right upper quadrant pain
questions.explanation: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is perihepatitis (inflammation of the liver capsule and peritoneum) occurring as a complication of PID, when organisms ascend to the right upper quadrant, causing adhesions between the anterior liver surface and abdominal wall ('violin string' adhesions at laparoscopy). It presents as right upper quadrant pain in a patient with PID. A: Tubal scarring is a consequence of PID but not Fitz-Hugh-Curtis. C & D: These are other complications of pelvic infection.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Ultrasound versus MRI in pelvic disease
questions.topicTitle: Ultrasound versus MRI in pelvic disease
questions.prompt: In the evaluation of deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE), which imaging modality has superior sensitivity for detecting posterior compartment involvement (rectovaginal septum, uterosacral ligaments)?
options: MRI with systematic protocol (T2, T1 fat-saturated)
questions.answer: MRI with systematic protocol (T2, T1 fat-saturated)
questions.explanation: MRI with a dedicated pelvic protocol (T2 and T1 fat-saturated sequences) is superior for detecting DIE, particularly in the posterior compartment. It delineates involvement of the rectovaginal septum, uterosacral ligaments, bowel, and bladder — essential for surgical planning. A: Transabdominal ultrasound is limited by bowel gas and depth. B: CT has poor soft tissue contrast for DIE. D: Plain X-ray has no role in endometriosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Ultrasound versus MRI in pelvic disease
questions.topicTitle: Ultrasound versus MRI in pelvic disease
questions.prompt: For initial evaluation of a pelvic mass in a reproductive-age woman, which modality is the recommended FIRST-LINE imaging?
questions.explanation: Transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality for pelvic mass evaluation — it is widely available, lacks ionizing radiation, has high resolution for pelvic organs, and can characterize most adnexal masses. MRI is the second-line modality for problem-solving when ultrasound is equivocal. A: MRI is second-line (not first-line). B: CT uses radiation and has inferior soft tissue resolution compared to TVS for pelvic organs. D: PET-CT is used for staging known malignancy, not initial pelvic mass evaluation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Ultrasound versus MRI in pelvic disease
questions.topicTitle: Ultrasound versus MRI in pelvic disease
questions.prompt: MRI is PREFERRED over ultrasound for which of the following pelvic conditions?
options: Staging of cervical and endometrial carcinoma
Ovarian torsion in the emergency setting
questions.answer: Staging of cervical and endometrial carcinoma
questions.explanation: MRI is the preferred modality for staging cervical and endometrial carcinoma due to its superior soft tissue contrast and ability to assess parametrial involvement, cervical stromal invasion, myometrial depth, and lymph node involvement. A: Simple cysts are adequately characterized by ultrasound. B: First-trimester viability is assessed with ultrasound (no radiation, real-time, Doppler). D: Torsion is initially assessed with ultrasound in the emergency setting.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Ultrasound versus MRI in pelvic disease
questions.topicTitle: Ultrasound versus MRI in pelvic disease
questions.prompt: Which advantage does transvaginal ultrasound have over MRI for pelvic imaging?
options: Superior characterization of deep infiltrating endometriosis
Ability to perform real-time dynamic assessment, Doppler evaluation, and immediate clinical correlation with a reproducible examination
questions.answer: Ability to perform real-time dynamic assessment, Doppler evaluation, and immediate clinical correlation with a reproducible examination
questions.explanation: TVS advantages over MRI: real-time dynamic imaging (watching cyst movement, tender site identification), immediate Doppler assessment, no claustrophobia, widely available, cost-effective, and direct clinical correlation with the patient's symptoms. A: MRI is superior for DIE. C: MRI is better for retroperitoneal structures. D: TVS is highly operator-dependent — this is a limitation, not an advantage.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Ultrasound versus MRI in pelvic disease
questions.topicTitle: Ultrasound versus MRI in pelvic disease
questions.prompt: A 72-year-old woman with known endometrial carcinoma has an equivocal CT showing possible bladder wall thickening. Which modality should be used next for optimal staging?
options: Repeat CT with different contrast phase
MRI of the pelvis with contrast
questions.answer: MRI of the pelvis with contrast
questions.explanation: MRI with gadolinium contrast provides superior soft tissue resolution for assessing bladder wall invasion, myometrial depth, and local extension of endometrial carcinoma. For local staging (T stage), MRI is superior to CT. A: CT with different phases would not improve soft tissue contrast. C: Transabdominal ultrasound has insufficient depth and resolution for staging in this context. D: PET-CT is used for distant metastatic staging, not local invasion assessment.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On CT of the skull, the inner table, diploe, and outer table of the calvarium are best demonstrated on which window setting?
questions.explanation: Bone windows use a wide window width and high window level to differentiate the dense cortical bone of the inner and outer tables from the less dense trabecular bone of the diploe. A: Soft tissue window is used for brain parenchyma and soft tissue structures. C: Lung window is for pulmonary structures. D: Brain window is optimized for intracranial structures, not calvarium detail.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: The pterion is a clinically important cranial landmark because it marks the thinnest part of the calvarium and overlies the:
questions.explanation: The pterion (junction of frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones) is the thinnest part of the skull and overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery. Trauma here commonly causes epidural hematoma from arterial rupture. A: Superior sagittal sinus is at the midline (vertex). C: Anterior cerebral artery is intracranial near the frontal lobes. D: Cavernous sinus is at the skull base.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a lateral skull X-ray, the 'vascular grooves' of the middle meningeal artery must be distinguished from fractures. Which feature helps differentiate them?
options: Fractures are broader than vascular grooves
Vascular grooves have sclerotic (white) margins, branch in a regular arborizing pattern, and have predictable anatomical locations; fractures are sharper, non-branching, and cross vascular grooves
Fractures are always curved, vascular grooves are straight
Vascular grooves always show soft tissue swelling externally
questions.answer: Vascular grooves have sclerotic (white) margins, branch in a regular arborizing pattern, and have predictable anatomical locations; fractures are sharper, non-branching, and cross vascular grooves
questions.explanation: Vascular grooves have sclerotic margins (white, smooth edges), follow predictable courses, and branch in the expected arborizing pattern of meningeal vessels. Fractures have sharper, non-sclerotic margins, don't follow predictable vessel paths, and may cross vascular grooves. A: Width is not a reliable distinguishing feature. C: Fractures can be linear or curved. D: Scalp soft tissue swelling relates to the point of impact, not vascular grooves.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which cranial suture is responsible for most craniofacial growth in the anteroposterior direction and closes last (around 22–30 years)?
questions.explanation: The sagittal suture (between the two parietal bones) is responsible for lateral expansion of the skull and closes between ages 22–30 years. Premature sagittal fusion causes scaphocephaly. The coronal suture closes at ~24 years, lambdoid at ~26 years. The metopic suture (frontal) closes earliest at 2–3 years. A: Coronal suture governs frontal-parietal growth. B: Lambdoid suture governs occipital growth. D: Metopic closes earliest in childhood.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On CT of the paranasal sinuses in coronal plane, the ostiomeatal complex (OMC) is composed of all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The ostiomeatal complex includes the middle meatus, uncinate process, ethmoid infundibulum, maxillary sinus ostium, and anterior ethmoid cells. It is the critical drainage pathway for the maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoid sinuses. The superior turbinate and superior meatus drain the posterior ethmoid cells and sphenoid sinus — separate from the OMC.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old man is involved in a motor vehicle accident. CT head shows a biconvex (lenticular) hyperdense extradural collection temporally, with an overlying temporal bone fracture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An epidural (extradural) hematoma is biconvex/lenticular in shape, hyperdense on CT, typically temporal in location, caused by middle meningeal artery rupture (80%) from an overlying temporal bone fracture. It does not cross suture lines. A: Subdural hematoma is crescent-shaped and crosses suture lines. C: Contrecoup contusion is cerebral parenchymal damage at the opposite pole. D: SAH appears as hyperdensity in the cisterns/sulci.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A Le Fort II fracture of the facial bones on CT characteristically involves:
options: Bilateral horizontal fractures through the pterygoid plates and maxilla only
A pyramidal fracture through the nasal bones, medial orbital walls/floors, and maxilla, with the nasal complex forming the apex
Fractures extending through the zygomatic arches and lateral orbital walls
questions.answer: A pyramidal fracture through the nasal bones, medial orbital walls/floors, and maxilla, with the nasal complex forming the apex
questions.explanation: Le Fort II is a pyramidal fracture involving: nasal bones, medial orbital walls (lacrimal), orbital floors, inferior orbital rims, and maxilla — separating the central face as a pyramid from the skull base. A: Le Fort I is a horizontal maxillary fracture. C: Le Fort III involves the zygomatic arches and is a craniofacial separation. D: Isolated nasal fracture is not a Le Fort fracture.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 'blowout fracture' of the orbit occurs when:
options: Direct impact on the orbital rim causes rim fracture
Sudden rise in intraorbital pressure from a blunt force transmits force to the weakest wall (orbital floor/medial wall), causing it to fracture inward without rim fracture
The zygomatic arch is fractured and transmits force to the orbital walls
A penetrating injury perforates the orbital walls
questions.answer: Sudden rise in intraorbital pressure from a blunt force transmits force to the weakest wall (orbital floor/medial wall), causing it to fracture inward without rim fracture
questions.explanation: A blowout fracture occurs when a blunt force (e.g., a fist, ball) suddenly increases intraorbital pressure, which is transmitted to the weakest orbital walls — the floor (into the maxillary sinus) and medial wall (into the ethmoid sinuses) — causing fracture without orbital rim fracture. Orbital contents (fat, inferior rectus muscle) may herniate into the sinus. A: Rim fracture is an 'impure' blowout. C: Zygoma fractures are different. D: Penetrating injury is not a blowout mechanism.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On CT, a 'teardrop sign' in the context of orbital trauma refers to:
options: Intraocular hemorrhage shaped like a teardrop
Herniation of orbital fat and/or inferior rectus muscle through an orbital floor blowout fracture into the maxillary sinus, appearing as a teardrop-shaped density hanging from the orbital floor
A teardrop-shaped hematoma adjacent to the optic nerve
questions.answer: Herniation of orbital fat and/or inferior rectus muscle through an orbital floor blowout fracture into the maxillary sinus, appearing as a teardrop-shaped density hanging from the orbital floor
questions.explanation: The 'teardrop sign' on coronal CT images of the sinuses shows a teardrop-shaped soft tissue density (orbital fat ± inferior rectus muscle) prolapsing through an orbital floor blowout fracture into the maxillary sinus roof. This indicates orbital content herniation. A: Intraocular hemorrhage has a different appearance. C: No such optic nerve finding. D: Lacrimal gland enlargement is not a trauma sign.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which fracture is known as a 'tripod' or 'trimalar' fracture?
options: Fracture of the zygomatic bone at three sites: zygomatic arch, zygomaticofrontal suture, and inferior orbital rim/zygomaticomaxillary junction
Fracture of all three bones forming the orbital rim
Fracture of the three nasal bones
questions.answer: Fracture of the zygomatic bone at three sites: zygomatic arch, zygomaticofrontal suture, and inferior orbital rim/zygomaticomaxillary junction
questions.explanation: A tripod (trimalar/zygomaticomaxillary complex) fracture involves the zygoma at three points: (1) zygomatic arch, (2) zygomaticofrontal suture (lateral orbital wall), and (3) zygomaticomaxillary suture (inferior orbital rim/floor). It is the most common major facial fracture after nasal fractures. B: Not a defined entity. C: Le Fort III is craniofacial disjunction. D: Nasal fractures are separate.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 6-year-old child presents with periorbital bruising ('raccoon eyes'), CSF rhinorrhea, and anosmia following head trauma. These findings are MOST consistent with:
options: Epidural hematoma with temporal bone fracture
Anterior cranial fossa fracture involving the cribriform plate
questions.answer: Anterior cranial fossa fracture involving the cribriform plate
questions.explanation: Anterior cranial fossa fractures (especially involving the cribriform plate of the ethmoid) cause: bilateral periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'), CSF rhinorrhea (CSF leaking through nose), and anosmia (olfactory nerve damage). Epidural hematoma from temporal fracture causes unilateral Battle's sign (post-auricular bruising). A: Temporal bone fracture causes Battle's sign. C: Subdural hematoma doesn't cause rhinorrhea or anosmia. D: Nasal fracture alone doesn't cause CSF leak.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: CT is the preferred imaging for acute facial fractures primarily because:
options: It provides rapid, comprehensive multiplanar bone and soft tissue evaluation and is readily available in the emergency setting
CT avoids the need for patient cooperation
questions.answer: It provides rapid, comprehensive multiplanar bone and soft tissue evaluation and is readily available in the emergency setting
questions.explanation: CT is the gold standard for facial fractures: rapid acquisition, excellent bone detail with multiplanar reformations (axial, coronal, sagittal, 3D), simultaneous evaluation of intracranial injuries and soft tissue, and wide availability in emergency settings. A: CT uses ionizing radiation (a disadvantage). C: MRI is not contraindicated per se but is slower and less practical in acute trauma. D: Both require some degree of patient cooperation; sedation may be needed for both.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A depressed skull fracture is defined as one where:
options: The fracture extends across a suture line
The inner table is displaced inward by more than the thickness of the adjacent calvarium
The fracture involves the skull base
The fracture has a 'ping-pong ball' appearance in adults
questions.answer: The inner table is displaced inward by more than the thickness of the adjacent calvarium
questions.explanation: A depressed skull fracture is defined as inward displacement of the inner table of the skull by a distance greater than the thickness of the adjacent calvarium (i.e., depressed by more than the full skull thickness). This is a surgical threshold indicator. A: Crossing a suture (diastatic fracture) is a different type. C: Skull base fractures are a different category. D: 'Ping-pong' fractures are greenstick fractures seen in neonates/infants, not the adult definition.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On CT, a longitudinal temporal bone fracture (most common type) characteristically runs:
options: Perpendicular to the long axis of the petrous ridge, often damaging the ossicular chain
Parallel to the long axis of the petrous ridge, typically involving the external auditory canal and middle ear without inner ear damage
Through the cochlea causing sensorineural hearing loss
Through the mastoid air cells only
questions.answer: Parallel to the long axis of the petrous ridge, typically involving the external auditory canal and middle ear without inner ear damage
questions.explanation: Longitudinal temporal bone fractures (80% of temporal fractures) run parallel to the petrous ridge, usually involving the EAC, tympanic membrane, and middle ear (ossicular chain). They cause conductive hearing loss. Longitudinal rarely damages the inner ear. A: Transverse fractures run perpendicular to the petrous ridge, damaging the otic capsule/inner ear → sensorineural loss, facial nerve palsy. C: Cochlear damage is seen in transverse fractures. D: Isolated mastoid involvement is uncommon.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient with a temporal bone fracture develops facial nerve palsy immediately after trauma. Which fracture type is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Transverse temporal bone fractures (running perpendicular to the petrous ridge) have a high rate of facial nerve injury (50%) because the fracture line crosses the labyrinthine segment of the facial nerve canal and the otic capsule. Longitudinal fractures cause facial palsy in only 20% (usually delayed, from edema). A: Longitudinal fractures cause less severe/delayed facial palsy. C: Parietal fractures don't involve the facial nerve. D: Occipital condyle fractures can injure CN XII, not typically CN VII.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On coronal CT of the sinuses, which sinus drains into the superior meatus?
questions.explanation: The posterior ethmoid cells (and the sphenoid sinus via the sphenoethmoid recess) drain into the superior meatus, which lies above the superior turbinate. The maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoid sinuses drain via the ostiomeatal complex into the middle meatus. A, B, D: These all drain into the middle meatus via the ostiomeatal complex.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 'Haller cell' (infraorbital ethmoid cell) is clinically significant because it can:
options: Compress the olfactory nerves causing anosmia
Narrow the maxillary sinus ostium/infundibulum predisposing to recurrent maxillary sinusitis
questions.answer: Narrow the maxillary sinus ostium/infundibulum predisposing to recurrent maxillary sinusitis
questions.explanation: A Haller cell is an anatomical variant — an ethmoid air cell that extends laterally into the floor of the orbit above the maxillary sinus ostium. When enlarged, it can narrow the infundibulum and maxillary sinus ostium, predisposing to recurrent maxillary sinusitis and is important for pre-FESS (functional endoscopic sinus surgery) planning. A: Olfactory nerves are in the olfactory cleft, not affected by Haller cells. C: Orbital apex syndrome involves optic nerve/muscle compression. D: Haller cells are anterior — not near the sphenoethmoid recess.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On CT of the sinuses, the ostiomeatal complex (OMC) is BEST evaluated in which plane?
questions.explanation: The coronal plane CT of the sinuses optimally demonstrates the ostiomeatal complex — the middle meatus, uncinate process, ethmoid infundibulum, and maxillary sinus ostium — and their anatomical relationships. This is the standard projection for pre-FESS planning. A: Axial plane is used for anterior-posterior relationships but not optimal for OMC. C & D: These planes are not standard for OMC evaluation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 'concha bullosa' is defined as:
options: Mucosal thickening of the inferior turbinate
Pneumatization (air cell) within the middle turbinate
A polyp arising from the middle turbinate
Bone hypertrophy of the superior turbinate
questions.answer: Pneumatization (air cell) within the middle turbinate
questions.explanation: A concha bullosa is the most common anatomical variant of the paranasal sinuses — pneumatization of the middle turbinate. When large, it can narrow the OMC and middle meatus, contributing to sinusitis and obstruction. It is important to identify before FESS. A: Inferior turbinate hypertrophy is a different (and common) entity. C: A polyp is a soft tissue lesion, not aeration. D: Superior turbinate hypertrophy is a different variant.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the MOST common benign tumor of the paranasal sinuses?
questions.explanation: Osteoma is the most common benign tumor of the paranasal sinuses (and skull), most frequently arising from the frontal sinus. It appears as a hyperdense, well-defined bony mass on CT. B: Inverted papilloma is the most important benign sinonasal tumor due to its malignant transformation potential (~10%) and recurrence tendency — but it is not the most common. C: Chondroma is rare. D: Antrochoanal polyp is the most common polyp arising from the maxillary sinus antrum extending into the choana.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On CT, an antrochoanal polyp is characterized by:
options: A hyperdense mass filling the maxillary sinus and choanae
A hypodense (soft tissue) mass originating from the maxillary sinus antrum, extending through an enlarged maxillary sinus ostium into the posterior nasal cavity and nasopharynx
A calcified mass within the sphenoid sinus
questions.answer: A hypodense (soft tissue) mass originating from the maxillary sinus antrum, extending through an enlarged maxillary sinus ostium into the posterior nasal cavity and nasopharynx
questions.explanation: An antrochoanal polyp is a single large polyp arising from the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus, extending through a widened ostium into the middle meatus and posterior nasal cavity/nasopharynx. It is typically unilateral and appears as a homogeneous soft tissue mass. A: Hyperdense masses suggest different pathology (fungal ball, osteoma). C: Bilateral involvement suggests inflammatory polyps. D: Calcified sphenoid mass suggests fungal sinusitis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 'silent sinus syndrome' on CT of the sinuses shows:
options: Opacification of all sinuses bilaterally with no symptoms
Progressive opacification of the maxillary sinus with inward bowing of all walls, enophthalmos, and hypoglobus — without pain
Bilateral ethmoid opacification with intact sinus walls
Frontal sinus expansion with osteoma formation
questions.answer: Progressive opacification of the maxillary sinus with inward bowing of all walls, enophthalmos, and hypoglobus — without pain
questions.explanation: Silent sinus syndrome (maxillary sinus atelectasis) is chronic maxillary sinus obstruction causing progressive negative pressure, leading to inward bowing (retraction) of all sinus walls (especially the orbital floor), resulting in enophthalmos and hypoglobus without pain or obvious sinonasal symptoms. It presents with slowly progressive facial asymmetry and diplopia. A: Asymptomatic bilateral opacification is chronic rhinosinusitis, not this syndrome. C: Ethmoid opacification is part of sinusitis. D: Frontal osteoma expansion is Pott's puffy tumor or mucocele.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Frontal sinus mucocele on CT appears as:
options: A hyperechoic cystic mass within the frontal sinus
An expansile, well-defined, homogeneous soft tissue mass expanding the frontal sinus with thinning of the sinus walls and possible intracranial or orbital extension
A hyperdense mass filling the frontal sinus
Air-fluid level in the frontal sinus
questions.answer: An expansile, well-defined, homogeneous soft tissue mass expanding the frontal sinus with thinning of the sinus walls and possible intracranial or orbital extension
questions.explanation: A mucocele is a mucous-filled cystic expansion of a sinus resulting from chronic ostial obstruction. On CT, it appears as an expansile, homogeneous soft tissue density mass with thinning and remodeling of sinus walls. It can erode into the orbit or anterior cranial fossa. A: Ultrasound terms (hyperechoic) don't apply to sinuses. C: A hyperdense mass suggests fungal sinusitis. D: Air-fluid level suggests acute sinusitis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A sinonasal mass in a young adult with unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and CT showing a soft tissue mass in the nasopharynx with marked contrast enhancement and bone erosion is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma occurs exclusively in adolescent males. Classic presentation: unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis. CT/MRI: intensely enhancing vascular mass at the posterior nasal cavity/nasopharynx (near the sphenopalatine foramen), with bowing or erosion of the posterior maxillary sinus wall (Holman-Miller sign) and extension into the pterygopalatine fossa. A: Antrochoanal polyp is not vascular and arises from the maxillary sinus. C: Carcinoma is more common in older patients, less vascular. D: Fungal sinusitis has different density features.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following CT features is MOST concerning for a sinonasal malignancy rather than chronic inflammatory disease?
options: Bilateral mucosal thickening with air-fluid levels
Bone erosion/destruction with a soft tissue mass crossing anatomical boundaries and perineural spread
Antrochoanal polyp extending to the nasopharynx
questions.answer: Bone erosion/destruction with a soft tissue mass crossing anatomical boundaries and perineural spread
questions.explanation: Bone erosion/destruction, a mass crossing anatomical compartmental boundaries, and perineural spread (enlargement of neural foramina) are the key imaging features of sinonasal malignancy. A: Bilateral mucosal thickening with levels is typical of acute sinusitis. C: Concha bullosa with mucosal thickening suggests inflammatory obstruction. D: Antrochoanal polyp is benign.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On CT of the paranasal sinuses, which finding is MOST diagnostic of acute sinusitis?
options: Complete opacification of a sinus only
Air-fluid level within a sinus in the clinical context of acute infection
Mucosal thickening of less than 2 mm
questions.answer: Air-fluid level within a sinus in the clinical context of acute infection
questions.explanation: An air-fluid level within a sinus (representing accumulated secretions/pus under the air column) in the setting of acute symptoms is the most specific CT sign of acute sinusitis. Complete opacification can be seen in chronic disease or mucocele. A: Opacification alone is non-specific (can be chronic or mucocele). C: <2 mm mucosal thickening is within normal limits. D: Concha bullosa is an anatomical variant.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient with poorly controlled diabetes presents with proptosis, periorbital swelling, and black necrotic tissue in the nasal cavity. CT shows sinus opacification with bone destruction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mucormycosis (invasive fungal sinusitis) is a life-threatening infection caused by Mucorales fungi, occurring in immunocompromised patients (diabetics, transplant recipients, hematological malignancies). Key features: rapid bone destruction, perineural/vascular invasion, proptosis, and black eschar. CT shows opacification with frank bone destruction. A: Acute bacterial sinusitis does not cause this level of destruction. B: Allergic fungal sinusitis causes expansion, not destruction, and occurs in atopic patients. D: Carcinoma progresses more slowly without the systemic context.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Allergic fungal sinusitis (AFS) on CT of the sinuses characteristically shows:
options: Air-fluid levels with thin mucosal thickening
Hyperdense (hyperattenuating) material filling expanded sinuses (due to inspissated fungal concretions and mucin), with thinned but intact sinus walls
Frank bone destruction and soft tissue extension
Normal sinus mucosa with a solitary polyp
questions.answer: Hyperdense (hyperattenuating) material filling expanded sinuses (due to inspissated fungal concretions and mucin), with thinned but intact sinus walls
questions.explanation: AFS occurs in atopic/immunocompetent patients with an allergic response to fungal colonization. CT shows hyperdense material (Ca2+, Mg2+, and fungal concretions in thick allergic mucin) filling expanded sinuses with thinned but intact or bowed sinus walls. MRI shows T2 signal void. C: Frank bone destruction indicates invasive fungal sinusitis, not allergic. A: Air-fluid levels are for acute bacterial sinusitis. D: Normal mucosa with one polyp is not AFS.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A complication of frontal sinusitis called 'Pott's puffy tumor' refers to:
options: A mucocele of the frontal sinus
Osteomyelitis of the frontal bone with subperiosteal abscess causing forehead swelling
questions.answer: Osteomyelitis of the frontal bone with subperiosteal abscess causing forehead swelling
questions.explanation: Pott's puffy tumor is osteomyelitis of the frontal bone complicating frontal sinusitis, with spread through the anterior table to form a subperiosteal abscess, causing forehead edema/swelling. It can also spread intracranially (epidural empyema, meningitis). It is not a tumor despite the name. A: Mucocele is a separate complication. C: It is benign/infectious. D: Epidural abscess can coexist but is not the complete definition.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which sinus is MOST commonly involved in acute sinusitis?
questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus is the most commonly affected in acute sinusitis because: its ostium opens high on the medial wall (poor gravitational drainage), it is large, and the upper teeth roots are close to its floor. A: Frontal sinusitis is less common and more serious. B: Sphenoid sinusitis is least common (isolated) and can cause serious complications (cavernous sinus thrombosis). D: Ethmoid sinusitis often coexists with maxillary sinusitis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 10-year-old child with right-sided proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and orbital pain following untreated acute ethmoid sinusitis. CT shows a rim-enhancing collection medial to the medial rectus muscle. What complication has occurred?
questions.explanation: A rim-enhancing collection medial to the medial rectus (between the periorbita and orbital wall) represents a subperiosteal abscess — a surgical emergency. Ethmoid sinusitis is the most common source (directly adjacent). The Chandler classification stages orbital complications of sinusitis: I (preseptal cellulitis), II (orbital cellulitis), III (subperiosteal abscess), IV (orbital abscess), V (cavernous sinus thrombosis). A: Preseptal cellulitis is pre-septal without orbital collection. B: Orbital cellulitis has no discrete collection. D: Cavernous sinus thrombosis is Chandler V with bilateral findings and severe systemic sepsis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 'fungal ball' (mycetoma) of the maxillary sinus on CT appears as:
options: Diffuse hyperattenuating material filling multiple sinuses bilaterally
A hyperdense, partially calcified concretion within one sinus (usually maxillary) with surrounding mucosal thickening and no bone destruction
Bone destruction with soft tissue extension into the orbit
Air-fluid level with thin mucosal thickening
questions.answer: A hyperdense, partially calcified concretion within one sinus (usually maxillary) with surrounding mucosal thickening and no bone destruction
questions.explanation: A fungal ball (mycetoma, usually Aspergillus) is a non-invasive collection of fungal hyphae in a single sinus (typically maxillary), appearing as hyperdense (with calcification) material within the sinus. Mucosal thickening surrounds it but there is NO bone destruction (non-invasive). A: Multiple sinuses bilaterally is AFS. C: Bone destruction is invasive fungal sinusitis. D: Air-fluid level is acute bacterial sinusitis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Chronic rhinosinusitis on CT is defined as mucosal thickening persisting for more than:
questions.explanation: Chronic rhinosinusitis is defined clinically as symptoms and CT findings persisting for ≥12 weeks (3 months) despite appropriate medical management. A: 2 weeks is too short — this would be acute sinusitis. B: 4 weeks is sub-acute sinusitis. D: 6 months is unnecessarily long; 12 weeks is the standard threshold.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On CT, cavernous sinus thrombosis complicating sphenoid sinusitis is BEST demonstrated by:
options: Widened cavernous sinus with a hyperdense thrombus on non-contrast CT
Lateral convex bulging of the cavernous sinus with filling defects on contrast-enhanced CT and CTV
Absence of the cavernous sinus on CT
Air within the cavernous sinus only
questions.answer: Lateral convex bulging of the cavernous sinus with filling defects on contrast-enhanced CT and CTV
questions.explanation: Cavernous sinus thrombosis on contrast-enhanced CT/CTV shows: lateral convex bowing of the cavernous sinus wall (normally concave), filling defects within the sinus representing thrombus, and engorged superior ophthalmic vein. A: Non-contrast CT alone has low sensitivity. C: The cavernous sinus is never 'absent' — thrombosed but enlarged. D: Air (pneumocephalus) in the cavernous sinus would be very unusual.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A CT report describes 'Lund-Mackay score' of 18/24. What does this indicate?
options: A normal scan — maximum score is 24
Severe bilateral sinonasal disease — the score rates opacification of each sinus group (0=normal, 1=partial, 2=complete) for a maximum of 24
A single sinus with complete opacification
questions.answer: Severe bilateral sinonasal disease — the score rates opacification of each sinus group (0=normal, 1=partial, 2=complete) for a maximum of 24
questions.explanation: The Lund-Mackay scoring system grades CT sinusitis severity: each sinus group (maxillary, anterior ethmoid, posterior ethmoid, sphenoid, frontal) is scored 0 (clear), 1 (partial opacification), 2 (complete opacification) bilaterally, plus the OMC (0 or 2). Maximum total = 24. Score of 18/24 indicates severe bilateral sinusitis. A: A perfect score of 0/24 is normal, not 18/24. C: One completely opacified sinus contributes 2 points. D: Lund-Mackay is for inflammatory disease, not malignancy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the temporal bone is the first-line imaging for which of the following?
options: Conductive hearing loss, cholesteatoma, and ossicular chain pathology
questions.answer: Conductive hearing loss, cholesteatoma, and ossicular chain pathology
questions.explanation: HRCT of the temporal bone is first-line for evaluating the ossicular chain, middle ear, mastoid air cells, and bony structures — essential for diagnosing cholesteatoma, conductive hearing loss, and pre-surgical planning. A: Menière's disease (endolymphatic hydrops) is best evaluated with MRI (delayed post-gadolinium MRI showing endolymphatic space). C: IAC schwannomas are best evaluated with MRI (contrast-enhanced). D: Cochlear nerve aplasia is assessed with MRI.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On HRCT, cholesteatoma appears as:
options: An enhancing soft tissue mass in the middle ear
A non-enhancing, expansile soft tissue mass in Prussak's space (epitympanum) with bone erosion, particularly of the scutum
A fluid-filled cyst in the mastoid
questions.answer: A non-enhancing, expansile soft tissue mass in Prussak's space (epitympanum) with bone erosion, particularly of the scutum
questions.explanation: Acquired cholesteatoma (most common form) originates in Prussak's space (the pars flaccida recess), appears as a non-enhancing soft tissue mass on HRCT (does not enhance — distinguishing it from granulation tissue), and causes progressive bone erosion, particularly the scutum (blunting of the lateral epitympanic wall) and ossicular chain. A: Enhancement distinguishes granulation tissue/infection from cholesteatoma. C: A fluid-filled mastoid cyst would be a mastoid mucocele. D: Calcification is seen in tympanosclerosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: MRI is preferred over CT for evaluation of the internal auditory canal (IAC) because:
options: Greater spatial resolution for fine temporal-bone cortex
Better soft-tissue contrast for small intracanalicular schwannomas
No need for the patient to remain still during acquisition
A consistently shorter examination time than temporal-bone CT
questions.answer: Better soft-tissue contrast for small intracanalicular schwannomas
questions.explanation: MRI with gadolinium contrast is the gold standard for IAC evaluation, detecting acoustic schwannomas (vestibular schwannomas) as small as 1–2 mm with enhancement, and differentiating schwannoma from meningioma, vascular loops, and labyrinthitis. A: CT is superior for bone detail. C: Both require minimal cooperation. D: CT is faster; MRI takes longer.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Otosclerosis on HRCT of the temporal bone is characterized by:
options: A soft tissue mass eroding the ossicular chain
Focal lucent (hypodense) halo around the cochlea (pericochlear lucency / 'double ring sign')
Sclerosis of all mastoid air cells
Widening of the internal auditory canal
questions.answer: Focal lucent (hypodense) halo around the cochlea (pericochlear lucency / 'double ring sign')
questions.explanation: Otosclerosis (otospongiosis) is a pathological bone remodeling of the otic capsule causing conductive hearing loss. HRCT shows focal areas of decreased density (lucency) at the fissula ante fenestram (anterior to the oval window) — the 'halo sign' or 'double ring sign' around the cochlea. A: Soft tissue mass eroding the chain suggests cholesteatoma. C: Sclerosed mastoid = chronic otitis media. D: Widened IAC suggests schwannoma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient presents with pulsatile tinnitus and conductive hearing loss. Otoscopy reveals a pulsatile red-blue mass behind an intact tympanic membrane. CT shows a soft tissue mass in the middle ear at the cochlear promontory with intense enhancement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glomus tympanicum is a paraganglioma (chemodectoma) arising from paraganglia on the cochlear promontory. Classic presentation: pulsatile tinnitus, conductive hearing loss, and a pulsatile red-blue ('rising sun') mass behind the TM on otoscopy. CT shows an intensely enhancing soft tissue mass at the promontory. A: Cholesteatoma is non-enhancing and non-pulsatile. C: AOM has mucosal thickening/fluid but not an enhancing mass. D: Otosclerosis causes fixation of the stapes, not a visible mass.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old woman presents with a midline neck mass that moves upward with tongue protrusion and swallowing. Ultrasound shows a well-defined, anechoic or slightly heterogeneous midline cystic mass at the level of the hyoid bone. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Thyroglossal duct cyst (TGDC) is the most common congenital midline neck mass. Key features: midline or paramidline location (75% at/below hyoid), moves upward with tongue protrusion (tract connects to foramen cecum), cystic on ultrasound. A: Dermoid cysts are midline but don't move with tongue protrusion and have internal echoes. B: Lymph nodes are not cystic midline masses at the hyoid. D: Ranula is a sublingual gland cyst, below the mouth floor.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A branchial cleft cyst on ultrasound and CT is characteristically:
options: A midline solid mass at the thyroid level
A lateral neck cystic mass at the anteromedial border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at the level of the mandibular angle
A midline cystic lesion at the hyoid
questions.answer: A lateral neck cystic mass at the anteromedial border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at the level of the mandibular angle
questions.explanation: Second branchial cleft cysts (most common — 95%) appear as lateral neck cystic masses characteristically located at the anteromedial border of the SCM, anterior to the carotid space, at the angle of the mandible. They are smooth, thin-walled, and uni-locular. A: Midline solid mass at thyroid level suggests thyroid nodule or lipoma. D: Midline cyst at hyoid is thyroglossal duct cyst. C: Posterior triangle nodes are a different location.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: In an adult >40 years presenting with a persistent lateral neck mass, what must be the primary concern until proven otherwise?
options: Reactive lymphadenopathy from a recent URI
Metastatic lymphadenopathy from a head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC)
questions.answer: Metastatic lymphadenopathy from a head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC)
questions.explanation: In adults >40 years, a persistent (>3–4 weeks) lateral neck mass is metastatic lymphadenopathy from HNSCC until proven otherwise. The oropharynx (HPV-related), oral cavity, larynx, and hypopharynx are common primary sites. Full head and neck examination and imaging (CT/MRI) with endoscopy are mandatory. A: Reactive lymphadenopathy is possible but not the primary concern in this age group with a persistent mass. C: Lymphoma is a differential but less common. D: Branchial cleft cysts don't typically present de novo in patients >40 years.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On CT, a lymph node is considered suspicious for metastatic involvement based on all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Short axis diameter >1 cm (in most neck levels)
Extranodal extension (ill-defined margins, surrounding fat stranding)
Uniform oval shape with a fatty hilum
questions.answer: Uniform oval shape with a fatty hilum
questions.explanation: A uniform oval lymph node with a preserved fatty hilum is a sign of a BENIGN reactive node, not malignant. Features suspicious for malignancy include: short axis >1 cm, central necrosis (liquefactive center), extranodal extension (ill-defined/irregular margins), ring enhancement, and round shape (loss of oval morphology). A, B, C: All are criteria for suspicious nodes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A lymphoma presenting as a neck mass on CT typically shows:
options: Necrotic lymph nodes with extranodal extension
Multiple enlarged, homogeneous, non-necrotic lymph nodes ('rubbery' appearance) that may coalesce, often with bilateral involvement
A cystic neck mass with thin walls
