questions.answer: Multiple enlarged, homogeneous, non-necrotic lymph nodes ('rubbery' appearance) that may coalesce, often with bilateral involvement
questions.explanation: Lymphoma (Hodgkin's and NHL) typically presents as multiple enlarged, homogeneous (non-necrotic) lymph nodes, often with a 'rubber' density on CT, bilateral/bilateral involvement, and potential mediastinal involvement. Necrosis can occur in aggressive lymphomas (Burkitt's, T-cell) but is less common than in metastatic HNSCC. A: Necrosis and ECS favor SCC metastasis. C: Calcification in a lymph node (after treatment) can occur but is not typical de novo. D: A cystic neck mass is a branchial cleft cyst.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A cystic neck mass with a 'claw sign' (normal thyroid tissue wrapping around its margins) on CT or ultrasound is most consistent with:
options: Thyroid cyst or intrathyroid colloid cyst
questions.answer: Thyroid cyst or intrathyroid colloid cyst
questions.explanation: The 'claw sign' in the neck describes normal thyroid parenchyma wrapping around a lesion, indicating that it originates within the thyroid gland — most commonly a thyroid cyst or colloid cyst. A: Branchial cleft cysts are parapharyngeal/lateral, not within the thyroid. C: Parathyroid adenomas are typically posterior to the thyroid. D: Cervical thymic cysts are midline/anterior but not within the thyroid.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which neck space is the most common site for deep neck space infections (DNSI) to originate from dental sources?
questions.explanation: The submandibular space is the most common site for DNSI of dental origin, particularly from mandibular molar infections (Ludwig's angina involves bilateral submandibular + submental + sublingual spaces). A: Parapharyngeal space is more commonly involved from tonsillar/pharyngeal sources. C: Retropharyngeal space infections are more common in children from lymph node suppuration. D: Masticator space infection can arise from dental sources but is less common than submandibular.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On ultrasound, a reactive lymph node is distinguished from a malignant node primarily by:
options: Preserved echogenic (fatty) hilum, oval shape, and hilar vascularity on Doppler
questions.answer: Preserved echogenic (fatty) hilum, oval shape, and hilar vascularity on Doppler
questions.explanation: Benign/reactive lymph nodes have: preserved echogenic (fatty) hilum, oval shape (long:short axis ratio >2), and hilar (central) blood flow pattern on Doppler. Malignant nodes lose the fatty hilum, become round, and show peripheral or absent/chaotic vascularity. A: Size alone is not reliable. C: Peripheral vascularity suggests malignancy. D: Posterior enhancement is a cystic feature.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old male with a neck mass is found to have a cystic node with ring enhancement on CT. HPV testing of fine needle aspirate is positive. The primary tumor is MOST likely located in the:
questions.explanation: HPV-associated head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) most commonly originates in the oropharynx (tonsil, base of tongue). Oropharyngeal HPV+ SCC frequently presents with cystic nodal metastases (simulating branchial cleft cysts). Patients are often young, non-smokers. A: Laryngeal SCC is more strongly tobacco-associated, less commonly HPV-driven. C: Hypopharyngeal SCC is tobacco/alcohol-related. D: Oral cavity SCC is tobacco/alcohol-related.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A neonate presents with a soft, compressible, transilluminating posterior neck mass. Ultrasound shows a multiloculated cystic mass with thin walls. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Cystic hygroma (macrocystic lymphatic malformation) typically presents in neonates/infants as a soft, transilluminating, multiloculated cystic mass in the posterior triangle of the neck. Ultrasound shows multiple thin-walled cysts. It is the most common congenital cystic neck mass in this age group and location. A: Hemangioma is solid and vascular on Doppler. C: Cervical teratoma is midline, often calcified, and solid/complex. D: TGDC is midline and at the hyoid level.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which ultrasound feature of a thyroid nodule has the HIGHEST specificity for malignancy?
options: Marked hypoechogenicity relative to the adjacent strap muscle
Isoechoic nodule with a halo sign
Purely cystic appearance with comet-tail artifacts
questions.answer: Marked hypoechogenicity relative to the adjacent strap muscle
questions.explanation: Marked hypoechogenicity (darker than the strap muscle) is the single most specific ultrasound feature for thyroid malignancy (particularly papillary carcinoma). A: Spongiform appearance is the most benign-appearing pattern (high negative predictive value for malignancy). C: Isoechoic nodule with halo is suggestive of a follicular adenoma (benign). D: Purely cystic nodule with comet-tail artifacts (colloid) is benign.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: The ACR TI-RADS (Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System) categorizes thyroid nodules based on a point system. A nodule with marked hypoechogenicity, irregular margins, taller-than-wide shape, and microcalcifications would receive what TI-RADS category?
questions.explanation: Each suspicious feature adds points in TI-RADS: marked hypoechogenicity (3 pts), irregular/lobulated margins (2 pts), taller-than-wide (3 pts), microcalcifications (3 pts) → total 11 points = TR5 (≥7 points). TR5 is highly suspicious, warranting FNA at ≥1 cm. A: TR1 is for benign nodules (0 points). B: TR3 is mildly suspicious (3–4 points). D: TR2 is not suspicious (2 points).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 38-year-old woman with a history of childhood neck irradiation presents with a 1.5 cm isoechoic thyroid nodule with microcalcifications. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Follow-up ultrasound in 12 months — isoechoic nodules are low risk
Fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy given the high-risk history and microcalcifications
CT of the neck with contrast
Radionuclide thyroid scan to assess hot vs. cold nodule
questions.answer: Fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy given the high-risk history and microcalcifications
questions.explanation: Childhood neck irradiation is a major risk factor for thyroid malignancy (papillary carcinoma). Even an isoechoic nodule becomes more suspicious in this context. Microcalcifications are a suspicious feature (associated with papillary carcinoma). FNA is warranted. A: The high-risk history + microcalcifications change management. C: CT is not the primary diagnostic step for a thyroid nodule. D: Radionuclide scan may show a cold nodule (malignancy) but FNA provides cytological diagnosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On ultrasound, 'microcalcifications' within a thyroid nodule are defined as:
options: Coarse calcifications >2 mm with posterior acoustic shadowing
Punctate (<1 mm) echogenic foci without posterior acoustic shadowing (or with comet-tail artifacts if colloid)
Hyperechoic foci of any size within a cystic nodule
questions.answer: Punctate (<1 mm) echogenic foci without posterior acoustic shadowing (or with comet-tail artifacts if colloid)
questions.explanation: Microcalcifications are punctate (<1 mm) echogenic foci without posterior acoustic shadowing, representing psammoma bodies in papillary thyroid carcinoma. They must be distinguished from: coarse calcifications (benign dystrophic changes, A), peripheral eggshell calcification (C, can be benign or malignant), and colloid crystals (comet-tail/ring-down artifact = benign). D: Any hyperechoic foci in a cystic nodule could be colloid.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 'hot nodule' on radionuclide thyroid scan (technetium-99m or I-123) refers to a nodule that:
options: Has increased uptake relative to normal thyroid — almost never malignant
Has decreased uptake relative to normal thyroid — increased malignancy risk
Is a cold nodule with a cystic center
questions.answer: Has increased uptake relative to normal thyroid — almost never malignant
questions.explanation: A hot (hyperfunctioning) nodule has increased radionuclide uptake compared to normal thyroid tissue, indicating autonomous function. Hot nodules are almost never malignant (<1% risk). They are a common cause of hyperthyroidism (toxic adenoma). B: Cold (hypo/non-functioning) nodules have decreased uptake and carry ~15% malignancy risk (higher with suspicious ultrasound features). C & D: These are not nuclear medicine terminology.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which thyroid malignancy is associated with elevated serum calcitonin and is derived from parafollicular C-cells?
questions.explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from calcitonin-secreting parafollicular C-cells, producing elevated serum calcitonin (a sensitive tumor marker). MTC accounts for 5–10% of thyroid cancers and can be sporadic or familial (MEN2). A: Papillary — thyroglobulin is the marker. B: Follicular — thyroglobulin marker, hematogenous spread. D: Anaplastic — most aggressive, no specific marker.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On ultrasound, a thyroid nodule with a 'taller-than-wide' shape (anteroposterior > transverse diameter) is associated with:
options: Increased risk of malignancy — growth across tissue planes rather than along them
questions.answer: Increased risk of malignancy — growth across tissue planes rather than along them
questions.explanation: A 'taller-than-wide' (A/P > transverse) shape indicates that the nodule is growing perpendicular to the fascial planes rather than along them, suggesting invasive growth. This is a suspicious feature for malignancy (particularly papillary carcinoma) and is assigned the highest points in ACR TI-RADS. A: Colloid cysts are oval/round and wider-than-tall. C: Goiter causes diffuse enlargement. D: Taller-than-wide is not a normal variant.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Ultrasound-guided FNA of a thyroid nodule is indicated for ACR TI-RADS TR5 nodules at a size threshold of:
questions.explanation: Per ACR TI-RADS guidelines: TR5 (highly suspicious) nodules: FNA recommended at ≥1 cm. TR4: FNA at ≥1.5 cm. TR3: FNA at ≥2.5 cm. TR1 and TR2: no FNA. A: 0.5 cm would be below the practical threshold even for TR5. C & D: These thresholds apply to lower-risk categories.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On CT with contrast, a thyroid nodule that appears as a hypodense mass with irregular margins, cervical lymphadenopathy, and invasion of the trachea is MOST consistent with:
questions.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is the most aggressive thyroid malignancy, presenting with rapid growth, tracheal/esophageal invasion, and extensive cervical lymphadenopathy on CT. It appears as a heterogeneous hypodense mass with irregular margins and local invasion. A: Multinodular goiter shows multiple nodules without aggressive invasion. C: Adenoma is well-defined and non-invasive. D: Hashimoto's shows diffuse heterogeneous gland without a discrete invasive mass.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is a BENIGN ultrasound feature of a thyroid nodule?
questions.explanation: Spongiform appearance — >50% of the nodule composed of small, uniform cystic spaces — is the most benign ultrasound appearance of a thyroid nodule, with a very high negative predictive value for malignancy (>99%). It represents multiple tiny colloid-filled follicles. A: Irregular margins are suspicious (TI-RADS points). B: Microcalcifications are suspicious (psammoma bodies). C: Marked hypoechogenicity is suspicious.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 50-year-old man presents with sudden onset of painful parotid gland swelling during eating. Ultrasound shows a dilated Stensen's duct with a hyperechoic shadowing focus within the duct. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Sialolithiasis presents with mealtime pain/swelling (stimulated salivation cannot drain past the obstructing calculus). Ultrasound shows a hyperechoic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing within the duct (representing the calculus) with proximal duct dilatation. A: Abscess would be a hypoechoic collection with surrounding inflammation. C: Pleomorphic adenoma is a solid, well-defined parotid mass — not related to eating. D: Sjögren's is chronic inflammation with multiple tiny cysts bilaterally.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: The most common benign salivary gland neoplasm is:
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common salivary gland tumor (70% of all salivary tumors), most often occurring in the parotid gland. It is benign but has malignant transformation potential (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma). A: Warthin's tumor is the second most common benign parotid tumor (bilateral in 10%), associated with smoking. C: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common malignant salivary tumor. D: Oncocytoma is rare.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On MRI, a pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland characteristically appears as:
options: T1 hyperintense, T2 hypointense well-defined mass
T1 hypointense, T2 markedly hyperintense (bright) well-circumscribed mass with lobulated borders
T1 isointense, T2 isointense mass with irregular margins
T1 hyperintense cystic mass with fluid-fluid levels
questions.answer: T1 hypointense, T2 markedly hyperintense (bright) well-circumscribed mass with lobulated borders
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenomas have high water/mucopolysaccharide content, appearing T2 markedly bright (higher than fat), T1 hypointense, with well-defined lobulated borders and a capsule. T2 high signal is characteristic and helps differentiate from Warthin's tumor (T2 intermediate/slightly lower signal). A: T1 hyper/T2 hypo would suggest fat, hemorrhage, or melanoma. C: Irregular margins suggest malignancy. D: Fluid-fluid levels suggest hemorrhagic cyst.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which salivary gland has the HIGHEST proportion of malignant tumors when a mass is discovered?
questions.explanation: The proportion of malignancy increases as salivary gland size decreases — 'smaller gland, higher malignancy rate': Parotid ~20–25% malignant, Submandibular ~40–45%, Sublingual ~50%, Minor salivary glands ~50–80%. D is correct. Note: the parotid has the most absolute number of tumors, but the lowest proportion of malignancies. A: Parotid has lowest proportion (but most overall tumors). B & C: Higher than parotid but lower than minor glands.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Sjögren's syndrome on ultrasound of the parotid glands classically shows:
options: Bilateral heterogeneous parotid parenchyma with multiple small hypoechoic foci/cysts (lymphoepithelial lesions) throughout
Unilateral duct dilatation with a calculus
Bilateral parotid enlargement with homogeneous normal echogenicity
questions.answer: Bilateral heterogeneous parotid parenchyma with multiple small hypoechoic foci/cysts (lymphoepithelial lesions) throughout
questions.explanation: Sjögren's syndrome (autoimmune exocrinopathy) causes bilateral parotid (and submandibular) gland changes: heterogeneous parenchyma with multiple small hypoechoic foci representing lymphoepithelial cysts and lymphocytic infiltration. This is bilateral and diffuse. A: Solitary mass suggests adenoma/carcinoma. C: Calculus/duct dilation is sialolithiasis. D: Uniform bilateral enlargement without heterogeneity is seen in mumps or early sarcoid.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 4-year-old child presents with high fever, neck stiffness, and difficulty swallowing. Lateral neck X-ray shows widening of the retropharyngeal soft tissues. Contrast-enhanced CT neck confirms a rim-enhancing fluid collection in the retropharyngeal space. What is the diagnosis and MOST critical complication?
options: Peritonsillar abscess — risk of airway obstruction
Retropharyngeal abscess — risk of descending mediastinitis
Ludwig's angina — risk of carotid artery erosion
Parapharyngeal abscess — risk of otic barotrauma
questions.answer: Retropharyngeal abscess — risk of descending mediastinitis
questions.explanation: Retropharyngeal abscess (RPA) is most common in children <5 years (retropha ryngeal nodes involute after puberty). CT shows a rim-enhancing fluid collection in the retropharyngeal space. The most critical complication is descending necrotizing mediastinitis via the 'danger space' (potential space between alar and prevertebral fascia), which carries >40% mortality. A: Peritonsillar abscess is lateral, not retropharyngeal. C: Ludwig's is in the submandibular space. D: Parapharyngeal infection can spread to the carotid space.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On contrast-enhanced CT, the finding that MOST reliably distinguishes a deep neck abscess from cellulitis/phlegmon is:
options: Rim-enhancing fluid collection with central low density
Uniform diffuse enhancement of the soft tissues
questions.answer: Rim-enhancing fluid collection with central low density
questions.explanation: A rim-enhancing fluid collection with a central low-density (pus) core on contrast CT is the key finding distinguishing an organized abscess from phlegmon/cellulitis (which shows diffuse, non-rim enhancement without a discrete fluid collection). This distinction is critical for surgical drainage vs. antibiotics-only management. B: Diffuse uniform enhancement is cellulitis. C: Fat stranding is non-specific inflammation. D: Enlarged nodes can be reactive or suppurative.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Ludwig's angina is a severe deep neck infection defined as bilateral involvement of which spaces?
options: Bilateral submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces
questions.answer: Bilateral submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces
questions.explanation: Ludwig's angina is a rapidly spreading bilateral cellulitis/phlegmon of the submandibular (mylohyoid), sublingual, and submental spaces — causing tongue elevation and posterior displacement, with risk of fatal airway obstruction. It most commonly originates from mandibular molar dental infection. A: Parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal is a different infection pattern. C & D: These are not the defining spaces of Ludwig's angina.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A complication of parapharyngeal space abscess involving the carotid sheath can cause all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Parapharyngeal space infection involving the carotid sheath can cause: IJV thrombosis (Lemierre's syndrome — septic thrombophlebitis with septic emboli), carotid artery erosion/pseudoaneurysm, cranial nerve involvement (CN IX–XII), and sympathetic chain involvement (Horner's syndrome). Hypersalivation alone without neurological signs is not a recognized complication of carotid sheath involvement.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Lemierre's syndrome on CT of the neck shows:
options: Retropharyngeal soft tissue widening with air pockets
Internal jugular vein thrombosis with perivenous inflammation, often arising from a peritonsillar or pharyngeal infection
questions.answer: Internal jugular vein thrombosis with perivenous inflammation, often arising from a peritonsillar or pharyngeal infection
questions.explanation: Lemierre's syndrome is septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein, classically following a peritonsillar or oropharyngeal infection (typically Fusobacterium necrophorum). CT shows: intraluminal thrombus within the IJV with perivenous inflammation ('dirty fat') and potential septic pulmonary emboli. A: Submandibular collections suggest Ludwig's. B: Retropharyngeal air-widening suggests RPA. D: Prevertebral abscess suggests vertebral osteomyelitis or discitis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following neck spaces is the 'danger space' that allows rapid inferior spread of deep neck infection into the mediastinum?
options: Danger space (space 4) — between the alar fascia and prevertebral fascia
questions.answer: Danger space (space 4) — between the alar fascia and prevertebral fascia
questions.explanation: The 'danger space' (space 4) is a potential space between the alar fascia (anteriorly) and the prevertebral fascia (posteriorly), extending from the skull base to the diaphragm (mediastinum). It provides an uninterrupted pathway for infection to descend into the posterior mediastinum — hence the name. A: The retropharyngeal space is anterior to the alar fascia and does not extend below T1/T2. C: Parapharyngeal space is lateral. D: Submandibular space is in the floor of the mouth.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: CT of the neck in a patient with a deep neck infection shows air within a soft tissue collection. What does this finding indicate?
options: Gas-forming organism (e.g., Clostridium) or communication with the aerodigestive tract — associated with severe necrotizing infection
A benign finding — small amounts of air are common in any abscess
questions.answer: Gas-forming organism (e.g., Clostridium) or communication with the aerodigestive tract — associated with severe necrotizing infection
questions.explanation: Air within a deep neck collection indicates either gas-forming anaerobic organisms (necrotizing fasciitis, Clostridium) or a fistula/communication with the pharynx/esophagus/trachea. This is a marker of necrotizing infection, which is life-threatening and requires urgent surgical debridement. A: Post-surgical air is possible if there is a recent procedure. C: Air in a deep tissue collection is not an artifact. D: Air in an abscess is never a benign finding in this context.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A peritonsillar abscess on CT appears as:
options: A rim-enhancing fluid collection in the peritonsillar space lateral to the tonsil, displacing the uvula contralaterally
questions.answer: A rim-enhancing fluid collection in the peritonsillar space lateral to the tonsil, displacing the uvula contralaterally
questions.explanation: Peritonsillar abscess (PTA) — the most common deep neck infection in adults — appears on CT as a rim-enhancing collection in the peritonsillar space (between the palatine tonsil capsule and the superior pharyngeal constrictor), with contralateral uvula deviation (due to mass effect) and ipsilateral swelling. A: Midline retropharyngeal collection = retropharyngeal abscess. C: Parotid collections = parotid abscess. D: Prevertebral mass = discitis/osteomyelitis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is the MOST common source of deep neck infections in children under 5 years?
options: Tonsillitis and pharyngitis with reactive/suppurative lymph node involvement
questions.answer: Tonsillitis and pharyngitis with reactive/suppurative lymph node involvement
questions.explanation: In children <5 years, the most common source of deep neck infection (particularly retropharyngeal abscess) is suppuration of retropharyngeal lymph nodes secondary to tonsillitis, pharyngitis, or upper respiratory infection. These nodes involute after age 5, explaining why RPA is predominantly a pediatric disease. A: Dental infection is the most common source in adults (particularly Ludwig's angina). C: Salivary gland infection (sialadenitis) can cause submandibular space infection. D: Traumatic perforation is uncommon.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Descending necrotizing mediastinitis (DNM) complicating a deep neck infection requires which imaging modality for optimal assessment of extent?
options: Contrast-enhanced CT from skull base to diaphragm
questions.answer: Contrast-enhanced CT from skull base to diaphragm
questions.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest (skull base to diaphragm) is the imaging of choice for DNM to: (1) confirm mediastinal extension, (2) delineate the fascial spaces involved, (3) identify loculations, (4) plan surgical drainage (cervical vs. thoracic approach). Plain CXR is often non-diagnostic early. A: CXR misses early or subtle mediastinal changes. C: MRI is too slow for this surgical emergency. D: Barium swallow could identify an esophageal source but not delineate the mediastinal extent.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old male smoker presents with hoarseness of 3 months duration. CT of the larynx shows a hypodense soft tissue mass arising from the true vocal cord with subglottic extension and cartilage erosion. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx
questions.answer: Squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx
questions.explanation: Laryngeal SCC (glottic type, most common) presents with hoarseness, occurs in older male smokers, and on CT shows a soft tissue mass of the vocal cord with subglottic extension and cartilage destruction — the latter indicating advanced T3–T4 disease. A: Vocal cord polyp is a benign soft tissue lesion without cartilage erosion. C: Papillomatosis causes multiple papillary excrescences (HPV), typically in younger patients. D: Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy causes cord paralysis but no mass.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, perineural tumor spread (PNS) of head and neck carcinoma is identified by:
options: Lymph node enlargement along the jugular chain
Enlargement and enhancement of named cranial nerve foramina/canals with obliteration of normal fat pads
Direct invasion of the carotid artery
Soft tissue mass in the parapharyngeal space
questions.answer: Enlargement and enhancement of named cranial nerve foramina/canals with obliteration of normal fat pads
questions.explanation: PNS occurs when tumor cells spread along the perineurium of cranial nerves. CT signs: enlargement and enhancement of named nerve canals (e.g., mental foramen, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, pterygopalatine fossa), loss of normal fat pads in neural foramina, and denervation changes in muscles. MRI is more sensitive than CT for PNS (enhancement of nerve segments). A: Nodal enlargement is lymphatic spread, not PNS. C: Carotid invasion is direct extension. D: Parapharyngeal mass is local extension.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old patient with a history of heavy alcohol and tobacco use presents with a mass at the base of tongue with bilateral level II lymph node metastases. What is the most likely primary diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The base of tongue is an oropharyngeal site. Oropharyngeal SCC in the context of heavy tobacco and alcohol use is the most likely diagnosis. Bilateral cervical nodal metastases are common due to bilateral lymphatic drainage of the tongue base. A: Thyroid carcinoma arises from the thyroid gland. C: Lymphoma can arise at this site but is more often bilateral, painless, and non-smoking-related. D: Salivary gland carcinomas arise from salivary gland tissue.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which imaging modality is MOST sensitive for detecting leptomeningeal carcinomatosis as a complication of head and neck cancer?
options: MRI brain and spine with gadolinium
questions.answer: MRI brain and spine with gadolinium
questions.explanation: MRI with gadolinium is the most sensitive for leptomeningeal carcinomatosis (linear/nodular enhancement along the leptomeninges, cranial nerves, and spinal canal). It is also the best for detecting base of skull invasion and perineural spread. A: Non-contrast CT is insensitive for leptomeningeal disease. C: PET-CT is used for staging/restaging nodal disease and distant metastases. D: Ultrasound cannot image intracranial structures.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old woman with no smoking history presents with a painless swelling at the angle of the jaw. MRI shows a well-defined, T2 hyperintense, homogeneous mass in the superficial lobe of the parotid gland with delayed gradual enhancement on dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma: marked T2 hyperintensity (characteristic), well-defined margins, and gradual/delayed enhancement on dynamic MRI (due to myxoid/chondroid matrix with slow contrast filling). It is the most common parotid tumor and typical in young-middle aged women. A: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is less T2 bright, irregular margins, more aggressive. C: Warthin's tumor is T2 intermediate, often bilateral, associated with smoking, predominantly in elderly males. D: Lymphoma is in intraparotid/periparotid nodes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On FDG-PET/CT, which of the following clinical scenarios is the MOST appropriate indication?
options: First-line evaluation of a new thyroid nodule
Unknown primary head and neck cancer presenting with cervical nodal metastases
questions.answer: Unknown primary head and neck cancer presenting with cervical nodal metastases
questions.explanation: FDG-PET/CT is highly valuable in identifying the occult primary tumor in patients presenting with neck nodal metastases from an unknown primary (HNSCC). PET detects metabolically active foci in the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and hypopharynx that may be too small for CT/MRI. A: PET is not used for thyroid nodule evaluation (incidental thyroid PET uptake is a different finding). C: Benign adenoma requires no PET follow-up. D: Sinusitis has non-specific FDG uptake and PET is not indicated.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 70-year-old with a history of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) treated 15 years ago now presents with temporal lobe memory deficits and hypoglossal nerve palsy. MRI shows T2 signal changes in the temporal lobes and bone marrow replacement at the skull base. What is the most likely cause?
options: Radiation-induced temporal lobe necrosis and base of skull local recurrence of NPC
questions.answer: Radiation-induced temporal lobe necrosis and base of skull local recurrence of NPC
questions.explanation: Late complications of head and neck radiotherapy include temporal lobe radiation necrosis (T2 signal changes in temporal lobes with enhancement) and skull base osteoradionecrosis. NPC has a strong tendency for base-of-skull recurrence. Hypoglossal nerve palsy from skull base disease (XII exits via hypoglossal canal) is a recognized recurrence presentation. A: Primary brain tumor would not explain skull base changes. C: Alzheimer's doesn't cause CN palsy. D: Viral encephalitis is acute/subacute without skull base involvement.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: The 'rule of tens' for paragangliomas of the head and neck states approximately:
options: 10% bilateral, 10% benign, 10% arise from adrenal gland
All paragangliomas are benign in 10% of cases
questions.explanation: The 'rule of tens' for paragangliomas: ~10% bilateral, ~10% multiple, ~10% malignant, ~10% familial (hereditary — SDHx mutations). This is a teaching mnemonic applicable to head and neck paragangliomas (carotid body tumor, glomus jugulare, vagale). B: All paragangliomas can be malignant; they are not defined as benign. C & D: These do not reflect the rule.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A carotid body tumor (chemodectoma) on CT angiography characteristically shows:
options: A hypodense mass compressing the common carotid artery
An intensely enhancing mass in the carotid bifurcation that SPLAYS the internal and external carotid arteries ('lyre sign')
A non-enhancing mass in the carotid space
questions.answer: An intensely enhancing mass in the carotid bifurcation that SPLAYS the internal and external carotid arteries ('lyre sign')
questions.explanation: Carotid body tumors (paragangliomas) arise from chemoreceptor tissue at the carotid bifurcation. Classic finding on CTA: intensely enhancing vascular mass at the carotid bifurcation that splays (widens the angle between) the ICA and ECA — the 'lyre sign' (resembling a lyre instrument). A: Hypodense non-enhancing mass would suggest lymphoma or necrotic node. C: Carotid thrombosis is a separate entity. D: Paragangliomas are characteristically intensely enhancing due to their vascular nature.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is MOST strongly associated with which virus?
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) has the strongest association with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) — particularly non-keratinizing and undifferentiated types. EBV serology (VCA IgA, EA IgA) is used as a biomarker. NPC is endemic in Southeast Asia (Cantonese population) and North Africa. A: HPV is associated with oropharyngeal SCC (tonsil, base of tongue). C: HBV is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma. D: CMV is not associated with head and neck tumors.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient presents with sudden-onset severe headache ('thunderclap headache'). Non-contrast CT of the brain is performed and is negative. What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Discharge — CT is the gold standard for SAH
Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia or MRI brain with FLAIR to detect subarachnoid hemorrhage missed by CT
questions.answer: Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia or MRI brain with FLAIR to detect subarachnoid hemorrhage missed by CT
questions.explanation: Non-contrast CT has >98% sensitivity for SAH within 6 hours but decreases significantly after 12–24 hours. A negative CT in a patient with thunderclap headache requires either lumbar puncture (for xanthochromia — still the gold standard) or MRI with FLAIR/DWI sequences (which can detect SAH missed by CT, especially at >6 hours). A: CT alone is insufficient given the clinical picture. C: Contrast CT doesn't add value for acute SAH. D: EEG is not relevant for SAH diagnosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: MRI is preferred over CT for evaluation of posterior fossa pathology because:
options: Shorter acquisition time than emergency CT scanning
Better tissue contrast without petrous-bone beam hardening
Absence of ionizing radiation during image acquisition
Complete inability of CT to depict cerebellar anatomy
questions.answer: Better tissue contrast without petrous-bone beam hardening
questions.explanation: CT has significant beam-hardening artifact from the dense petrous temporal bones in the posterior fossa, which can obscure small lesions in the cerebellum, pons, and medulla. MRI provides superior contrast resolution of posterior fossa structures without this artifact limitation. C: While MRI uses no ionizing radiation (a true advantage), the specific reason for superiority in the posterior fossa is beam-hardening artifact. A: MRI is slower than CT. D: CT can evaluate the cerebellum but with less clarity due to artifact.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: CT with contrast is the PREFERRED modality for initial evaluation of which of the following?
options: Suspected acute deep neck space infection with abscess
questions.answer: Suspected acute deep neck space infection with abscess
questions.explanation: Contrast-enhanced CT is first-line for suspected deep neck space infection — it rapidly identifies abscesses (rim-enhancing fluid collections), defines their extent within neck spaces, assesses airway compromise, and guides surgical drainage. A: Multiple sclerosis is best evaluated with MRI (white matter plaques). B: Acute ischemic stroke — CT first (exclude hemorrhage), then MRI DWI (more sensitive for early infarct). D: Vestibular schwannoma requires MRI with gadolinium (IAC protocol).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: In a patient with a known head and neck carcinoma, PET-CT is MOST useful for:
options: Detailed local staging (T stage) of the primary tumor
Detecting distant metastases, synchronous primary tumors, and assessing treatment response
questions.answer: Detecting distant metastases, synchronous primary tumors, and assessing treatment response
questions.explanation: FDG-PET/CT in HNSCC is most valuable for: detecting distant metastases (lung, liver, bone), identifying synchronous primary tumors, detecting occult nodal/distant disease, and assessing treatment response (residual/recurrent disease). Local staging (T stage) is better done with dedicated CT/MRI. A: CT/MRI provides superior anatomical detail for local staging. C: Inner ear pathology is assessed with HRCT/MRI. D: Thyroid function is assessed biochemically or with nuclear medicine thyroid scan.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old patient with a pacemaker requires imaging for a suspected neck mass. Which imaging modality is most appropriate?
options: MRI — pacemakers are no longer a contraindication
Ultrasound as first-line; CT with contrast if further characterization needed
questions.answer: Ultrasound as first-line; CT with contrast if further characterization needed
questions.explanation: Traditional (non-MRI-conditional) pacemakers are an absolute contraindication to MRI due to ferromagnetic interaction and induced currents. Ultrasound is an excellent first-line modality for neck mass evaluation (widely available, no radiation, real-time). CT with contrast provides further characterization when needed. A: MRI-conditional pacemakers DO allow MRI in some centers under specific conditions, but this requires knowing the device type and cannot be assumed. C: PET-CT is not first-line for a new neck mass. D: Plain X-ray has no role in neck soft tissue mass evaluation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following describes the correct chronological sequence of steps in the classic Seldinger technique for percutaneous vascular access?
options: Vessel puncture with access needle → insertion of guidewire through needle → removal of needle over wire → advancement of catheter or sheath over wire
Vessel puncture with access needle → advancement of sheath over needle → insertion of guidewire through sheath → withdrawal of needle
Vessel cutdown → direct insertion of guidewire → advancement of needle over wire → placement of sheath
Puncture with access needle → advancement of catheter through needle lumen → insertion of guidewire through catheter → removal of needle
questions.answer: Vessel puncture with access needle → insertion of guidewire through needle → removal of needle over wire → advancement of catheter or sheath over wire
questions.explanation: Correct: The classic Seldinger technique, described by Sven-Ivar Seldinger in 1953, consists of puncturing the target vessel with a hollow access needle, passing a flexible guidewire through the needle lumen into the vessel, withdrawing the needle while maintaining wire access, and then advancing a catheter, dilator, or vascular sheath over the wire into the vessel.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: In fluoroscopy-guided interventional procedures, which operator action is most effective at reducing the radiation dose to both the patient and the interventional team according to the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) principle?
options: Maximizing electronic magnification (zoom) to improve spatial resolution
Utilizing pulsed fluoroscopy at the lowest acceptable frame rate and tight collimation
Positioning the X-ray tube as close to the patient as possible while moving the image detector away
Continuous foot pedal depression during catheter manipulation to ensure uninterrupted visualization
questions.answer: Utilizing pulsed fluoroscopy at the lowest acceptable frame rate and tight collimation
questions.explanation: Correct: Utilizing pulsed fluoroscopy at lower frame rates (e.g., 7.5 or 4 pulses per second rather than 15 or 30 fps) substantially lowers radiation output. Tight collimation restricts the X-ray beam to the region of interest, which diminishes total patient dose and reduces scatter radiation to the operator. This directly adheres to the ALARA principle.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 64-year-old male with cirrhosis and a suspicious 3 cm hepatic mass is scheduled for an elective ultrasound-guided core needle liver biopsy. Pre-procedural coagulation testing reveals an International Normalized Ratio (INR) of 2.1 and a platelet count of 38,000/µL. According to standard interventional radiology safety consensus guidelines for procedures with significant bleeding risk, what is the most appropriate pre-procedure management?
options: Proceed with biopsy immediately; liver biopsies are low-bleeding-risk procedures requiring no correction
Administer fresh frozen plasma (or prothrombin complex concentrate) to achieve an INR < 1.5, and transfuse platelets to achieve a count ≥ 50,000/µL prior to biopsy
Transfuse platelets only, because coagulopathy in cirrhosis is completely reflected by platelet count rather than INR
Cancel the procedure permanently because core needle liver biopsies are absolutely contraindicated in cirrhotic patients
questions.answer: Administer fresh frozen plasma (or prothrombin complex concentrate) to achieve an INR < 1.5, and transfuse platelets to achieve a count ≥ 50,000/µL prior to biopsy
questions.explanation: Correct: Percutaneous solid-organ core biopsy (such as of the liver or kidney) is classified as a high-bleeding-risk procedure. Standard IR consensus guidelines recommend an INR < 1.5 (or correction with FFP/PCC/vitamin K) and a platelet count threshold ≥ 50,000/µL (via platelet transfusion) prior to performing the biopsy to prevent catastrophic intraperitoneal hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which imaging modality provides real-time multiplanar cross-sectional visualization of soft-tissue structures and needle tip progression without the use of ionizing radiation, making it the preferred guidance modality for thyroid and superficial soft-tissue biopsies?
questions.explanation: Correct: Ultrasonography offers continuous real-time cross-sectional visualization of needles and target lesions without ionizing radiation, is portable, and allows Doppler assessment of intervening vascular structures, making it the modality of choice for superficial organs (thyroid, breast, lymph nodes, testicles) and accessible abdominal viscera.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: During moderate (conscious) sedation for a protracted pelvic embolization, a 70 kg patient receives intravenous midazolam and fentanyl. Five minutes later, the patient becomes unarousable, exhibits shallow breathing at 6 breaths per minute, and pulse oximetry drops to 84%. What is the most appropriate immediate sequence of interventions?
options: Administer rapid IV push of 100 mg propofol to facilitate emergency endotracheal intubation
Stimulate the patient, establish airway positioning (chin lift/jaw thrust), apply high-flow supplemental oxygen/bag-valve-mask ventilation, and administer IV naloxone
Administer IV flumazenil immediately as a single large bolus without addressing the airway, as respiratory depression is exclusively caused by benzodiazepines
Continue the procedure while turning the patient into the prone position to relieve tongue obstruction
questions.answer: Stimulate the patient, establish airway positioning (chin lift/jaw thrust), apply high-flow supplemental oxygen/bag-valve-mask ventilation, and administer IV naloxone
questions.explanation: Correct: Severe respiratory depression during conscious sedation is an emergency. The priority is basic life support: stimulate the patient, open the airway (head tilt/jaw thrust), provide high-flow oxygen or bag-valve-mask ventilatory support, and administer the opioid reversal agent naloxone (0.04 to 0.4 mg IV titrated). If benzodiazepine-induced hypoventilation persists, flumazenil can also be carefully titrated.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient is undergoing CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of a 1.5 cm subdiaphragmatic liver lesion. To minimize target motion and ensure identical spatial lesion registration between serial CT validation scans and needle advancement, what respiratory instruction should the patient be coached to maintain?
options: Deep forced inspiration held as long as possible
Continuous deep breathing through an incentive spirometer
questions.explanation: Correct: Consistent suspended respiration at quiet, passive end-expiration (functional residual capacity) is the most reproducible physiological respiratory state. Deep inspiration varies substantially in volume with each breath, leading to significant slice misregistration and geographic miss during CT-guided punctures of upper abdominal organs.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary physical mechanism of scatter radiation generation that poses the principal source of occupational radiation exposure to the operator during fluoroscopic procedures?
options: Photoelectric absorption within the image intensifier
Compton scattering occurring within the patient's body tissues
Bremsstrahlung radiation emitted by the lead shielding apron
Pair production within the primary X-ray tube housing
questions.answer: Compton scattering occurring within the patient's body tissues
questions.explanation: Correct: Compton scattering within the patient's body tissues is the primary source of scatter radiation in diagnostic and interventional fluoroscopy. Incident X-ray photons interact with outer-shell electrons of patient tissue atoms, deflecting photons in all directions toward the interventional team standing near the table.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 58-year-old woman taking apixaban (Eliquis) for atrial fibrillation requires an elective image-guided percutaneous nephrostomy for ureteral obstruction. Assuming normal renal function, what is the recommended minimum withholding period for apixaban prior to this high-bleeding-risk interventional procedure?
options: No withholding required; apixaban can be continued up to the morning of the procedure
questions.explanation: Correct: For Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) like apixaban (half-life ~12 hours) in patients with normal renal function undergoing procedures with high risk of bleeding (e.g., percutaneous nephrostomy, solid organ biopsy), standard Society of Interventional Radiology guidelines recommend discontinuing the drug for at least 48 hours (4-5 elimination half-lives) to ensure near-complete clearance and normal hemostasis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which type of guidewire features a polymer jacket that becomes extremely lubricious when activated by normal saline, making it ideal for navigating tight stenoses and tortuous vessels, but carries an increased risk of vessel dissection if pushed against resistance?
options: Heavy-duty stainless steel wire (e.g., Amplatz Super Stiff)
Straight floppy-tip stainless steel wire (e.g., Bentson)
questions.explanation: Correct: Hydrophilic-coated guidewires (such as the Terumo Glidewire) have a specialized polymer coating that attracts water molecules to create an ultra-low-friction surface. They easily cross tight stenoses and tortuous anatomy, but their lubricity reduces tactile feedback, increasing the hazard of subintimal tracking and arterial dissection if advanced forcefully against resistance.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Immediately following local anesthetic infiltration and introduction of a 6-French vascular sheath into the right common femoral artery, a 28-year-old male becomes diaphoresis, pale, and complains of severe lightheadedness. His blood pressure drops from 125/80 mmHg to 75/40 mmHg, and his heart rate drops from 78 bpm to 42 bpm. What is the diagnosis and initial drug treatment of choice?
options: Anaphylactoid reaction to local anesthetic; administer intramuscular epinephrine
Vasovagal reaction; elevate the patient's legs, administer rapid IV fluid bolus, and administer IV atropine
Retroperitoneal hemorrhage; immediately administer IV protamine sulfate
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST); administer 20% lipid emulsion infusion as first and only step
questions.answer: Vasovagal reaction; elevate the patient's legs, administer rapid IV fluid bolus, and administer IV atropine
questions.explanation: Correct: The combination of acute hypotension and bradycardia (pulse 42 bpm) triggered by pain, anxiety, or arterial puncture is the classic presentation of a vasovagal reaction (neurocardiogenic syncope). Management consists of Trendelenburg positioning, IV fluid bolus, and intravenous atropine (0.5 to 1.0 mg IV) to block excessive vagal tone.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the optimal anatomical target site for common femoral artery (CFA) puncture during conventional retrograde femoral catheterization?
options: Over the medial half of the femoral head, below the inguinal ligament and above the bifurcation into the superficial and deep femoral arteries
Above the anterior superior iliac spine within the pelvic brim
5 cm distal to the inguinal crease over the proximal superficial femoral artery
Directly over the bifurcation of the superficial and profunda femoris branches
questions.answer: Over the medial half of the femoral head, below the inguinal ligament and above the bifurcation into the superficial and deep femoral arteries
questions.explanation: Correct: The common femoral artery should be punctured over the medial half of the femoral head, inferior to the inferior epigastric artery/inguinal ligament and superior to the bifurcation of the CFA into the superficial femoral and profunda femoris arteries. This provides a bony backing against which manual compression can achieve reliable post-procedural hemostasis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Two hours after an uneventful diagnostic pelvic angiography via right femoral artery access, a 68-year-old woman develops ipsilateral flank pain, progressive tachycardia (HR 118 bpm), and hypotension (BP 82/46 mmHg). The right groin puncture site is soft, non-tender, and without visible hematoma or bruit. Fluoroscopic review confirms the arterial puncture occurred superior to the femoral head above the inguinal ligament. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: A 'high puncture' above the inguinal ligament penetrates the external iliac artery. Because this site is located inside the pelvic cavity/retroperitoneum without posterior bony support, bleeding tracks silently into the retroperitoneal space. Large volumes of blood accumulate without external groin swelling, presenting classically with flank pain, unexplained hypotension, and tachycardia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which catheter configuration is designed with multiple side holes and a circular curled tip to enable high-volume, rapid contrast injections into large vessels (such as the abdominal aorta) while preventing jet-induced vessel wall injury?
questions.explanation: Correct: Pigtail catheters feature a curled, atraumatic circular tip and multiple side holes. This configuration disperses rapid, high-pressure power injections of contrast medium uniformly across the vascular lumen, preventing a single high-velocity end-hole jet from dissecting or perforating the aortic wall.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary technical cause of misregistration artifacts during digital subtraction angiography (DSA)?
options: Patient voluntary or involuntary motion between the acquisition of the mask image and contrast-enhanced images
Inadequate concentration of iodinated contrast material
questions.answer: Patient voluntary or involuntary motion between the acquisition of the mask image and contrast-enhanced images
questions.explanation: Correct: Digital subtraction angiography subtracts a pre-contrast 'mask' frame from subsequent contrast-filled frames to eliminate radiopaque background bones and soft tissues. If the patient moves (swallowing, coughing, breathing, or bowel peristalsis) between the mask and contrast frames, the anatomical structures do not align, producing misregistration artifacts.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Carbon dioxide (CO2) angiography is a well-established alternative to iodinated contrast in patients with severe contrast allergy or renal failure. In which of the following vascular territories is CO2 angiography ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED?
options: Thoracic aorta, coronary, and cerebral arterial circulation
Inferior vena cava during filter placement
questions.answer: Thoracic aorta, coronary, and cerebral arterial circulation
questions.explanation: Correct: Carbon dioxide gas injection is strictly contraindicated in the arterial circulation above the diaphragm (thoracic aorta, coronary arteries, and cerebral/carotid arteries). Because CO2 is a gas, delivery into the cerebral circulation can lead to gas vapor locking of intracranial microvessels, resulting in cerebral ischemia, seizures, and fatal stroke.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 72-year-old diabetic male with baseline chronic kidney disease (eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73 m²) must undergo urgent lower extremity diagnostic angiography. Which preventive measure has the strongest clinical evidence for minimizing the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN)?
options: Intravenous volume expansion with isotonic crystalloid (0.9% normal saline) before and after contrast administration
High-dose intravenous loop diuretics (furosemide) administered immediately prior to contrast injection
Routine prophylactic hemodialysis within 1 hour following the angiogram
Oral administration of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) to enhance renal cortical blood flow
questions.answer: Intravenous volume expansion with isotonic crystalloid (0.9% normal saline) before and after contrast administration
questions.explanation: Correct: Intravenous volume expansion with isotonic crystalloids (0.9% normal saline or buffered isotonic bicarbonate) before, during, and after contrast administration is the cornerstone of CIN prevention. Hydration dilutes contrast within the renal tubules, enhances renal blood flow, and mitigates medullary ischemia and toxic tubular epithelial injury.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Following extensive catheter and guidewire manipulation through a severely calcified, atheromatous abdominal aorta for lower-extremity revascularization, a patient develops livedo reticularis, painful purple discolored toes with preserved palpable pedal pulses, and acute renal failure with eosinophiluria. What is the underlying pathophysiology?
options: Atheroembolic renal disease (cholesterol crystal embolization / 'trash foot')
Acute common femoral artery occlusive dissection
questions.answer: Atheroembolic renal disease (cholesterol crystal embolization / 'trash foot')
questions.explanation: Correct: Atheroembolism (cholesterol crystal embolization, or 'trash foot') occurs when mechanical trauma from wires, sheaths, or catheters dislodges friable atheromatous plaque from the aorta. Microscopic cholesterol clefts embolize to small peripheral arterioles (100-200 µm), causing ischemic microvascular signs (livedo reticularis, blue/purple toes) while sparing large named conduit arteries (pedal pulses remain palpable). Renal microvascular occlusion triggers an inflammatory response characterized by eosinophilia and eosinophiluria.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient with suspected acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding undergoes mesenteric angiography. What specific angiographic finding confirms active, ongoing arterial hemorrhage?
options: Tortuous, calcified branches of the gastroduodenal artery
Focal pooling or extravasation of contrast medium that persists beyond the arterial phase into the venous phase and does not wash out
Rapid transit of contrast through the portal vein during late arterial phase
Slight narrowing and pruning of peripheral intestinal arterial arcades
questions.answer: Focal pooling or extravasation of contrast medium that persists beyond the arterial phase into the venous phase and does not wash out
questions.explanation: Correct: Active arterial extravasation is definitively identified on conventional angiography as a focal blush or pool of radiopaque contrast material that accumulates outside the vascular lumen, persists into the parenchymal and venous phases, and does not wash out with normal intravascular blood flow.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Before undertaking transradial arterial access for diagnostic angiography, which assessment is traditionally performed to confirm dual arterial blood supply to the hand via an intact palmar arch?
options: Allen test (or modified Allen test with pulse oximetry)
questions.answer: Allen test (or modified Allen test with pulse oximetry)
questions.explanation: Correct: The modified Allen test (often augmented with plethysmography/pulse oximetry, the Barbeau test) evaluates the patency of the ulnar artery and the completeness of the palmar arch. Both radial and ulnar arteries are compressed until the hand blanches; release of ulnar compression should restore palmar perfusion within 5-10 seconds, ensuring the hand will not become ischemic if the radial artery occludes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is an advantage of digital subtraction angiography (DSA) over standard un-subtracted cut-film angiography?
options: Complete elimination of radiation exposure to the patient
Superior visualization of small, low-contrast vascular branches by removing overlying bone and soft-tissue shadows
Immunity to motion artifacts caused by patient breathing
Lack of requirement for intravascular contrast medium
questions.answer: Superior visualization of small, low-contrast vascular branches by removing overlying bone and soft-tissue shadows
questions.explanation: Correct: The primary advantage of DSA is its high contrast resolution. By subtracting pre-contrast background anatomical structures (bones, bowel, dense soft tissues), even faint intravascular contrast opacification in tiny branch vessels can be clearly visualized and evaluated.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary mechanical mechanism by which percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) successfully restores luminal caliber in an atherosclerotic arterial stenosis?
options: Complete vaporization and thermal ablation of the atheroma
Controlled fracture of the atherosclerotic plaque and stretching/delamination of the media and adventitia
Immediate enzymatic dissolution of cholesterol clefts
Centrifugal compaction of thrombus without affecting the arterial wall
questions.answer: Controlled fracture of the atherosclerotic plaque and stretching/delamination of the media and adventitia
questions.explanation: Correct: The mechanism of balloon angioplasty (as originally demonstrated by Grüntzig and Dotter) involves controlled cracking, fracturing, and dehiscence of the rigid, calcified intimal plaque, along with overstretching and permanent plastic deformation of the muscular media and fibrous adventitia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: When sizing a standard non-compliant angioplasty balloon for treating a focal stenosis in the superficial femoral artery (SFA), how should the nominal diameter of the balloon be selected?
options: Sized 1:1 to the diameter of the adjacent normal, non-diseased reference artery
Sized at least 50% larger than the normal reference vessel to ensure complete plaque effacement
Sized precisely to the minimum luminal diameter of the stenotic segment
Always fixed at 12 mm regardless of vessel caliber
questions.answer: Sized 1:1 to the diameter of the adjacent normal, non-diseased reference artery
questions.explanation: Correct: In peripheral arterial interventions, angioplasty balloons are sized 1:1 relative to the caliber of the healthy, non-diseased vessel segment immediately adjacent to the stenosis. Oversizing balloons increases the risk of vessel dissection, transmural rupture, and acute thrombosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Why are self-expanding nitinol stents preferred over balloon-expandable stents in the superficial femoral artery (SFA) and popliteal artery across the adductor canal and knee joint?
options: Self-expanding stents have significantly higher radio-opacity and rigid hoop strength than balloon-expandable stainless steel stents
Self-expanding nitinol stents exhibit superelasticity and thermal memory, allowing them to resist permanent crush deformation from extrinsic muscular compression and flexion
Self-expanding stents do not require guidewire passage for deployment
Self-expanding stents completely eliminate the risk of in-stent neointimal hyperplasia
questions.answer: Self-expanding nitinol stents exhibit superelasticity and thermal memory, allowing them to resist permanent crush deformation from extrinsic muscular compression and flexion
questions.explanation: Correct: The SFA and popliteal artery are subjected to powerful biomechanical forces including torsion, elongation, bending, and external compression from surrounding thigh muscles. Nitinol (nickel-titanium alloy) self-expanding stents possess superelastic thermal memory; if crushed or deformed by external muscular pressure or knee flexion, they spring back to their circular configuration. In contrast, rigid balloon-expandable stents undergo permanent irreversible plastic collapse when compressed externally.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Immediately following balloon angioplasty of an iliac artery stenosis, completion angiography reveals a persistent, non-occlusive linear intimal flap with contrast hang-up and a significant reduction in downstream distal flow (trans-lesional pressure gradient of 25 mmHg). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Immediately transfer the patient for emergency open surgical bypass
Deploy an intravascular stent across the flow-limiting dissection
Administer high-dose IV protamine sulfate to seal the flap
Withdraw the sheath and apply vigorous external manual compression
questions.answer: Deploy an intravascular stent across the flow-limiting dissection
questions.explanation: Correct: A flow-limiting dissection (manifesting as contrast hang-up and a significant trans-lesional hemodynamic gradient) is a well-known complication of angioplasty. The standard endovascular treatment is placement of a metallic intravascular stent across the dissected segment to tack the mobile intimal flap securely against the vessel wall and restore brisk laminar flow.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which type of endovascular device combines a metallic stent skeleton with an impermeable synthetic fabric lining (such as PTFE or Dacron), making it specifically indicated for exclusionary treatment of traumatic arterial ruptures, pseudoaneurysms, and arteriovenous fistulas?
questions.explanation: Correct: Covered stents (also called stent-grafts or endoprostheses) consist of a metallic stent covered with an impermeable membrane (expanded PTFE or polyester/Dacron). They create a physical seal across the vessel wall defect, excluding pseudoaneurysms, covering perforations/ruptures, and sealing high-flow AV fistulas while preserving primary vessel lumen patency.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 62-year-old patient undergoes successful placement of a bare-metal stent in the right common iliac artery. What pharmacotherapy is routinely prescribed post-procedure to prevent acute and subacute in-stent thrombosis while the metallic struts endothelialise?
options: Dual antiplatelet therapy (e.g., aspirin plus clopidogrel)
questions.answer: Dual antiplatelet therapy (e.g., aspirin plus clopidogrel)
questions.explanation: Correct: Following bare-metal stent placement, the metallic struts are thrombogenic until covered by a layer of host endothelial cells (re-endothelialization, typically taking 4 to 12 weeks). Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), commonly combining aspirin and an ADP receptor antagonist like clopidogrel, is standard practice to prevent platelet activation and acute stent thrombosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary biological and cellular process responsible for late (months to years) in-stent restenosis following bare-metal stent implantation?
options: Neointimal hyperplasia driven by vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation and extracellular matrix deposition
Atheromatous calcification of the metal struts
questions.answer: Neointimal hyperplasia driven by vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation and extracellular matrix deposition
questions.explanation: Correct: In-stent restenosis (ISR) is predominantly caused by neointimal hyperplasia. Mechanical stretch and injury to the media by the stent struts trigger an inflammatory cascade, inducing vascular smooth muscle cells to migrate from the media into the intima, proliferate, and synthesize an abundant extracellular collagenous matrix that encroaches on the lumen.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Drug-eluting balloons (DEB) and drug-eluting stents (DES) used in peripheral vascular interventions are most commonly coated with which anti-proliferative lipophilic chemotherapeutic agent to inhibit neointimal hyperplasia?
questions.explanation: Correct: Paclitaxel (a microtubule-stabilizing mitotic inhibitor) and sirolimus/everolimus (mTOR inhibitors) are the antiproliferative agents used on drug-coated balloons and drug-eluting stents. Their lipophilic properties allow rapid transfer and prolonged retention within the arterial wall during brief balloon inflation, successfully inhibiting smooth muscle cell proliferation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 54-year-old male undergoes angioplasty for a short, severe ostial renal artery stenosis caused by atherosclerosis. Immediately following deflation of the angioplasty balloon, angiography shows that the vessel lumen has snapped back to nearly its original pre-procedure degree of narrowing without any visible dissection flap. What phenomenon has occurred, and what is the definitive endovascular management?
options: Acute stent thrombosis; administer systemic thrombolytic therapy
Elastic recoil; deploy a balloon-expandable stent
Severe catheter-induced vasospasm; administer intra-arterial nitroglycerin
Intimal rupture; perform emergency open nephrectomy
questions.answer: Elastic recoil; deploy a balloon-expandable stent
questions.explanation: Correct: Ostial atherosclerotic lesions (especially at the renal artery origin) contain rigid, elastic aortic plaque that commonly exhibits acute elastic recoil immediately upon balloon deflation. Elastic recoil is the rapid snapping back of the arterial wall without mechanical dissection. The definitive treatment is placement of a rigid balloon-expandable stent with high radial force to hold the ostium open.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: During high-pressure balloon dilation of a calcified common iliac artery stenosis, the balloon suddenly bursts. The patient immediately reports severe lower abdominal pain, and fluoroscopy reveals extravasation of contrast into the retroperitoneal cavity with an immediate drop in systemic blood pressure. What is the immediate, life-saving initial endovascular step?
options: Rapidly withdraw all wires and sheaths and apply firm manual pressure to the groin
Advance a new angioplasty balloon over the wire across the rupture site and inflate it to low pressure to achieve internal balloon tamponade while preparing a covered stent
Inject liquid cyanoacrylate glue directly through the vascular sheath into the iliac artery
Infuse 5,000 units of IV heparin bolus to prevent iliac thrombosis
questions.answer: Advance a new angioplasty balloon over the wire across the rupture site and inflate it to low pressure to achieve internal balloon tamponade while preparing a covered stent
questions.explanation: Correct: Acute arterial rupture is a catastrophic emergency. Maintaining wire access across the lesion is vital. An occlusion or angioplasty balloon should be advanced immediately over the wire to the site of rupture and inflated at nominal/low pressure. This provides immediate internal occlusion/tamponade of the laceration, halting exsanguination and stabilizing hemodynamics while a covered stent (stent-graft) is brought into the room, prepped, and deployed.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following embolic agents is classified as a TEMPORARY mechanical occlusive agent that is typically resorbed by the body within 2 to 6 weeks?
questions.explanation: Correct: Gelatin sponge (Gelfoam) is a temporary embolic agent derived from purified pork skin gelatin. When prepared as a slurry, pledgets, or powder, it induces acute thrombosis and mechanical occlusion. Enzymatic digestion and foreign body reaction resorb the material over a period of several weeks (typically 2 to 6 weeks), allowing potential recanalization of the vessel.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old male sustains severe pelvic fractures in a high-speed motor vehicle collision. Contrast-enhanced CT reveals massive pelvic retroperitoneal hematoma with multifocal active arterial contrast extravasation arising from small distal branches of both internal iliac arteries. The patient remains hemodynamically unstable despite massive transfusion. What is the most appropriate transcatheter embolization strategy?
options: Surgical ligation of the external iliac arteries
Bilateral non-selective temporary gelatin sponge (Gelfoam) slurry or pledget embolization of the internal iliac anterior divisions
Placement of bare-metal stents into the common femoral arteries
Direct injection of absolute ethanol into the inferior vena cava
questions.answer: Bilateral non-selective temporary gelatin sponge (Gelfoam) slurry or pledget embolization of the internal iliac anterior divisions
questions.explanation: Correct: In severe pelvic trauma with multifocal arterial extravasation, 'shotgun' or regional embolization of the internal iliac anterior divisions using Gelfoam slurry or pledgets is life-saving. Gelfoam rapidly reduces arterial perfusion pressure to stop hemorrhage while preserving collateral circulation and eventually resorbing, preventing long-term pelvic organ necrosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary mechanism of action by which metallic embolization coils achieve complete, permanent vascular occlusion?
options: Direct thermal coagulative necrosis of the muscular media
Mechanical cross-sectional space-filling combined with thrombogenicity promoted by synthetic fibers (Dacron/nylon) attached to the metal struts
Osmotic dehydration and denaturation of endothelial proteins
questions.answer: Mechanical cross-sectional space-filling combined with thrombogenicity promoted by synthetic fibers (Dacron/nylon) attached to the metal struts
questions.explanation: Correct: Metallic coils (platinum or stainless steel) provide a mechanical scaffold that fills the vessel lumen. Synthetic fibers (Dacron, nylon, or polyester) attached to the coils accelerate thrombus formation by promoting platelet adhesion and activating the intrinsic coagulation cascade, resulting in dense, organized fibrovascular occlusion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 42-year-old woman with severe menorrhagia and symptomatic uterine leiomyomas elects to undergo uterine fibroid embolization (UFE). Which embolic agent is the gold standard particulate agent specifically calibrated to achieve bilateral terminal arteriolar occlusion of the perifibroid plexus while sparing the normal myometrium?
options: Calibrated spherical microspheres (e.g., Tris-acryl gelatin microspheres)
questions.answer: Calibrated spherical microspheres (e.g., Tris-acryl gelatin microspheres)
questions.explanation: Correct: Calibrated spherical microspheres (such as 500-700 µm or 700-900 µm Tris-acryl gelatin microspheres) are precisely sized to lodge in the feeding arterioles of the perifibroid vascular plexus. This induces targeted ischemic necrosis of the fibroids while normal myometrium survives via rich collateral uterine blood supply.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following liquid embolic agents polymerizes instantly upon contact with ionic solutions (such as blood or saline), requiring the delivery microcatheter to be flushed with non-ionic 5% dextrose solution (D5W) before injection to prevent premature catheter occlusion?
questions.explanation: Correct: N-butyl cyanoacrylate (NBCA) is an adhesive monomer that undergoes rapid, exothermic, permanent polymerization when exposed to anions (hydroxyl ions and blood/saline). To prevent the glue from immediately hardening within and gluing the microcatheter inside the vessel, the delivery catheter must be thoroughly primed and flushed with a non-ionic solution (typically 5% dextrose in water - D5W).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Thirty-six hours following transcatheter arterial chemoembolization (TACE) of a large liver tumor, a patient develops a low-grade fever (38.2°C), mild right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and moderate leukocytosis. A non-contrast CT shows expected gas bubbles and lipiodol retention in the tumor without fluid collections or bowel perforation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Fulminant acute bacterial cholangitis requiring emergent surgical exploration
questions.explanation: Correct: Post-embolization syndrome (PES) is a common, self-limiting constellation of symptoms including fever, localized pain, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, and leukocytosis. It is caused by tissue ischemia, cell necrosis, and the release of inflammatory cytokines following successful embolization of solid organ tumors or vascular beds. Treatment is supportive with analgesics, antiemetics, and antipyretics.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 76-year-old male with massive lower gastrointestinal bleeding from a diverticular hemorrhage refractory to colonoscopy undergoes superselective mesenteric angiography. To achieve durable hemostasis while minimizing the risk of bowel ischemia and perforation, at what level should the microcatheter be positioned for embolization?
options: Main trunk of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA)
Origin of the ileocolic or right colic artery at its takeoff from the aorta
Superselectively within the terminal vasa recta supplying the bleeding diverticulum
questions.answer: Superselectively within the terminal vasa recta supplying the bleeding diverticulum
questions.explanation: Correct: Modern transcatheter embolization for lower GI bleeding utilizes microcatheters to achieve superselective catheterization of the bleeding terminal vasa recta directly adjacent to the bleeding focus. Embolizing only the bleeding vasa recta with microcoils or small Gelfoam pledgets stops the hemorrhage while preserving collateral circulation from adjacent arcades, keeping the risk of bowel infarction below 2-5%.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which liquid sclerosing agent causes immediate denaturation of endothelial proteins, microvascular precipitation, and full-thickness transmural vessel wall necrosis, making it highly effective for low-flow vascular malformations but dangerous if spilled into non-target tissues?
questions.explanation: Correct: Absolute ethanol (100% alcohol) is a potent chemical sclerosant. It causes immediate denaturation of cellular proteins, lysis of red blood cells, and stripping of the endothelial lining down to the media and adventitia, triggering transmural thrombosis. It is used to permanently eradicate vascular malformations (e.g., venous malformations), but requires extreme caution to avoid non-target tissue necrosis, nerve injury, or cardiopulmonary collapse.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What unique anatomical feature of liver blood supply provides the biological basis for transcatheter arterial chemoembolization (TACE) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)?
options: HCC tumors derive ~80-90% of their blood supply from the hepatic artery, whereas normal liver parenchyma receives ~70-75% of its blood flow from the portal vein
HCC tumors are supplied exclusively by the superior mesenteric vein
Normal liver parenchyma has no arterial blood supply, depending solely on the splenic artery
HCC tumors receive blood exclusively from the systemic retroperitoneal lumbar arteries
questions.answer: HCC tumors derive ~80-90% of their blood supply from the hepatic artery, whereas normal liver parenchyma receives ~70-75% of its blood flow from the portal vein
questions.explanation: Correct: The liver has a dual blood supply: normal hepatic parenchyma receives ~70-75% of its blood and ~50% of its oxygen from the portal vein. In contrast, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) develops robust neoangiogenesis supplied almost entirely (~80-90%) by the hepatic artery. Intravenous chemoembolization selectively devascularizes the tumor while the normal background parenchyma is protected by ongoing portal venous flow.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: During embolization of a bleeding left gastric artery, which technical precaution is most vital to prevent accidental 'non-target' reflux of embolic material into the celiac trunk and splenic/hepatic circulation?
options: Injecting the embolic agent rapidly under high manual pressure without fluoroscopy
Using a microcatheter seated deeply within the target vessel and performing slow, controlled contrast-monitored injection under continuous real-time fluoroscopic visualization
Selecting an embolic particle size smaller than 20 µm
Positioning the catheter tip loosely in the mid-abdominal aorta
questions.answer: Using a microcatheter seated deeply within the target vessel and performing slow, controlled contrast-monitored injection under continuous real-time fluoroscopic visualization
questions.explanation: Correct: Preventing non-target embolization requires stable, deep, coaxial microcatheter placement into the selected target artery. Embolics must be administered slowly and under continuous fluoroscopic monitoring (using contrast as a suspension carrier) to detect the onset of vascular stasis. Injections must cease immediately when flow slows to prevent embolic particles from refluxing retrograde into parent vessels.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary diagnostic difference between fine-needle aspiration (FNA) and core needle biopsy (CNB)?
options: FNA obtains intact histological tissue cores preserving architecture, whereas CNB obtains single cells for cytological smear
FNA obtains cellular aspirates for cytopathological evaluation, whereas CNB yields intact tissue cores for histological examination, architectural assessment, and immunohistochemistry
FNA requires a 14-gauge needle, whereas CNB uses a 25-gauge needle
FNA is strictly contraindicated under ultrasound guidance
questions.answer: FNA obtains cellular aspirates for cytopathological evaluation, whereas CNB yields intact tissue cores for histological examination, architectural assessment, and immunohistochemistry
questions.explanation: Correct: Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) uses small-gauge needles (20-25G) to harvest disaggregated cells and fluid for cytological smear examination.
