Core needle biopsy (CNB) utilizes larger cutting needles (14-18G) to excise solid cylinders of tissue, preserving tissue architecture and enabling definitive histological grading, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary advantage of utilizing a 'coaxial' needle system when performing image-guided parenchymal or retroperitoneal biopsies?
options: It completely eliminates the risk of pneumothorax during lung biopsy
A single guide cannula traverses the organ capsule once, allowing multiple core biopsy passes to be obtained through the cannula while permitting track embolization upon withdrawal
It removes the requirement for pre-procedure local anesthesia
It eliminates the need for imaging guidance during the biopsy
questions.answer: A single guide cannula traverses the organ capsule once, allowing multiple core biopsy passes to be obtained through the cannula while permitting track embolization upon withdrawal
questions.explanation: Correct: In a coaxial biopsy system, an outer introducer/guide needle is placed up to or just into the margin of the target lesion under imaging guidance. The stylet is removed, and multiple biopsy passes can be acquired through the stationary outer cannula using an inner biopsy needle. This avoids puncturing the organ capsule or pleura repeatedly, shortens procedure time, reduces pain, and allows injection of gelatin sponge or blood clot to seal the biopsy track upon removal.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 65-year-old smoker has a 2.5 cm solitary pulmonary nodule located deep within the right lower lobe, surrounded entirely by aerated lung parenchyma. Which imaging modality is most appropriate for guiding percutaneous needle biopsy?
questions.explanation: Correct: Computed tomography (CT) is the modality of choice for non-pleural-based lung parenchymal lesions. Normal aerated lung contains air that completely scatters and reflects ultrasound waves, preventing acoustic penetration and visualization. CT provides excellent spatial resolution, clear cross-sectional visualization of the aerated parenchyma, nodule, vessels, and needle path.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 59-year-old woman undergoes an uncomplicated CT-guided core biopsy of a right lung nodule. The immediate post-procedure scan demonstrates a small 10% right apical pneumothorax. The patient is completely asymptomatic, speaking in full sentences, with a respiratory rate of 14 breaths/min and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate emergency insertion of a 28-French surgical chest tube connected to wall suction
Conservative observation with supplemental oxygen, follow-up chest radiograph in 2 to 4 hours, and reassurance
Immediate transfer to the operating room for emergency open thoracotomy
Endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure
questions.answer: Conservative observation with supplemental oxygen, follow-up chest radiograph in 2 to 4 hours, and reassurance
questions.explanation: Correct: Small, asymptomatic post-biopsy pneumothoraces (<15-20% lung volume) in hemodynamically stable patients are managed conservatively. The patient is placed on supplemental oxygen (which hastens pleural nitrogen resorption), observed, and evaluated with an interval upright chest radiograph at 2-4 hours to confirm stability before discharge.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old male with end-stage alcoholic cirrhosis, refractory gross ascites, and marked coagulopathy (INR 2.8, platelets 24,000/µL) requires a liver biopsy to assess for alcoholic hepatitis vs acute decompensation. Percutaneous liver biopsy is contraindicated. Which specialized interventional approach allows safe liver parenchymal biopsy in this setting?
questions.explanation: Correct: Transjugular liver biopsy (TJLB) is specifically designed for patients with severe coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, or massive ascites. A catheter is introduced via the right internal jugular vein, navigated down the inferior vena cava into a right or middle hepatic vein, and a biopsy needle is fired through the venous wall into adjacent liver parenchyma. Because the hepatic capsule is never punctured, any bleeding discharges directly back into the venous circulation, eliminating the risk of hemoperitoneum.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: When planning an image-guided percutaneous biopsy of a suspected musculoskeletal sarcoma in an extremity, which principle is mandatory to prevent compromising future curative limb-salvage surgery?
options: The biopsy tract must be planned in consultation with the orthopedic oncology surgeon so that the needle path traverses only a single compartment and can be entirely excised en bloc during definitive surgery
The needle should traverse as many muscular compartments as possible to evaluate for microscopic margins
Extremity bone lesions should never be biopsied prior to surgical amputation
A transverse incision crossing neurovascular bundles should always be used for needle entry
questions.answer: The biopsy tract must be planned in consultation with the orthopedic oncology surgeon so that the needle path traverses only a single compartment and can be entirely excised en bloc during definitive surgery
questions.explanation: Correct: The biopsy tract is considered contaminated with tumor cells. Therefore, the biopsy route must be planned in close coordination with the orthopedic surgical oncologist. The tract must avoid neurovascular bundles, traverse only a single muscular compartment, and lie directly along the planned surgical incision so that the entire tract can be excised en bloc during definitive tumor resection.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which malignancy carries a well-documented propensity for tumor tract seeding during percutaneous needle biopsy, leading most clinical guidelines to recommend surgical resection or pleural fluid cytology rather than percutaneous biopsy?
questions.explanation: Correct: Malignant pleural mesothelioma has an unusually high rate of chest wall tumor tract seeding (reported in up to 10-20% of instrumentation sites without prophylactic radiation). Testicular germ cell tumors and transitional cell urothelial carcinomas also have high risks of tract seeding, and percutaneous biopsy is generally avoided.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Immediately following an ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy of the right hepatic lobe, the patient should be placed in which recovery position to provide natural mechanical tamponade to the liver puncture site?
questions.explanation: Correct: Placing the patient in the right lateral decubitus position for the initial 1 to 2 hours of post-procedure recovery positions the punctured right hepatic lobe dependent against the lateral abdominal and chest wall. The body weight of the liver and patient creates natural external compression/tamponade on the puncture site, significantly reducing the incidence of post-biopsy subcapsular and peritoneal bleeding.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions represents an ABSOLUTE contraindication to elective percutaneous image-guided core biopsy?
options: No safe needle path avoiding critical structures
Age over 70 years with stable organ function
A solitary kidney with preserved renal function
questions.answer: No safe needle path avoiding critical structures
questions.explanation: Correct: The lack of a safe needle pathway that avoids critical neurovascular structures, non-target visceral organs, or bowel is an absolute contraindication to percutaneous biopsy. Other absolute contraindications include uncorrectable severe coagulopathy and a patient unable to cooperate or remain still.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: When performing an image-guided percutaneous biopsy of a renal cortical mass, which anatomical structure must be strictly avoided by the needle path to prevent urine leakage and urinoma formation?
questions.explanation: Correct: Puncturing the renal pyelocaliceal collecting system (calyces or renal pelvis) can result in persistent urinary extravasation, retroperitoneal urinoma, and urosepsis. The needle path must be confined to the renal cortex and target lesion, staying peripheral to the renal sinus and calyces.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which technique for percutaneous abscess catheter placement involves mounting the drainage catheter directly over an internal stiffening cannula and sharp trocar needle, allowing direct single-step puncture into the collection without serial wire dilation?
questions.explanation: Correct: The trocar technique is a single-step entry method in which the drainage catheter, stiffening metal cannula, and inner sharp trocar stylet are assembled as a single unit and advanced directly into the fluid collection. It is particularly well-suited for large, superficial, tense fluid collections where there is no intervening bowel or critical vascular structures.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary function of the internal locking suture/string mechanism found in modern percutaneous pigtail drainage catheters?
options: To conduct electrical current for abscess cavity cauterization
To secure and maintain the curled pigtail loop within the cavity, preventing accidental catheter displacement or retraction out of the abscess
To deliver continuous micro-infusions of antibiotic solutions
To measure continuous real-time intracavity hydrostatic pressure
questions.answer: To secure and maintain the curled pigtail loop within the cavity, preventing accidental catheter displacement or retraction out of the abscess
questions.explanation: Correct: Percutaneous drainage catheters incorporate an internal monofilament suture running to the distal tip. Once the catheter is positioned in the collection, pulling and fastening the locking suture tightens the tip into a secure, circular 'pigtail' configuration. This prevents the catheter from inadvertently slipping out of the cavity during patient movement or coughing.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 48-year-old male develops a deep pelvic abscess in the rectovesical pouch 8 days following an open Hartmann's procedure for perforated diverticulitis. Contrast CT reveals the collection is shielded anteriorly by loops of small bowel, laterally by the iliac vessels, and superiorly by the bladder. Which minimally invasive image-guided approach provides a safe anatomical drainage route?
options: Direct anterior trans-mesenteric approach traversing multiple loops of small bowel
Transgluteal approach via the greater sciatic foramen under CT guidance, entering close to the sacrum inferior to the piriformis muscle
Direct lateral approach through the common iliac vein
questions.answer: Transgluteal approach via the greater sciatic foramen under CT guidance, entering close to the sacrum inferior to the piriformis muscle
questions.explanation: Correct: The transgluteal approach is the standard, well-established route for deep pelvic abscesses inaccessible from the anterior abdominal wall. Under CT guidance with the patient prone, the catheter is introduced through the greater sciatic foramen, as close as possible to the sacral margin and inferior to the piriformis muscle (in the infrapiriform space). Staying close to the sacrum avoids injury to the sciatic nerve and superior/inferior gluteal neurovascular bundles.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: To maintain catheter patency and prevent occlusion from thick, viscous purulent debris, what routine nursing and post-procedure catheter care protocol should be ordered?
options: Gentle manual flushing with 5 to 10 mL of sterile 0.9% normal saline every 8 to 12 hours
Instillation of 500 mL of hydrogen peroxide twice daily into the cavity
Clamping the catheter permanently after the first 24 hours
questions.answer: Gentle manual flushing with 5 to 10 mL of sterile 0.9% normal saline every 8 to 12 hours
questions.explanation: Correct: Routine catheter maintenance involves gentle manual flushing with small volumes (5-10 mL) of sterile normal saline every 8 to 12 hours. This prevents the side holes and lumen from clogging with fibrinous debris, blood clots, or thick pus without overdistending the cavity or precipitating transient bacteremia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old female has had a percutaneous drainage catheter in an intra-abdominal abscess for 10 days. Which combination of clinical and imaging findings indicates that the catheter can be SAFELY REMOVED?
options: Output remains > 200 mL/day of thick green pus, but the patient is afebrile

Complete clinical resolution of sepsis (afebrile, normalized WBC), minimal clear/serous drainage (<10 to 15 mL/day), and follow-up imaging/sinogram demonstrating complete cavity obliteration without an enteric fistula
Immediate cessation of drainage on post-procedure day 2 with persistent high spiking fevers
When the collection begins draining frank enteric content, indicating successful internal drainage
questions.answer: Complete clinical resolution of sepsis (afebrile, normalized WBC), minimal clear/serous drainage (<10 to 15 mL/day), and follow-up imaging/sinogram demonstrating complete cavity obliteration without an enteric fistula
questions.explanation: Correct: Criteria for safe abscess drain removal include: (1) clinical resolution of infection (patient is afebrile, asymptomatic, with normalized white blood cell count); (2) catheter output decreasing to minimal amounts (<10-15 mL per 24 hours) of clear/serous fluid; and (3) follow-up CT or fluoroscopic abscessogram showing collapse and obliteration of the cavity without evidence of an ongoing fistula.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: When cannulating the internal jugular vein (IJV) under real-time ultrasound guidance, which sonographic characteristic definitively differentiates the vein from the adjacent internal carotid artery?
options: The internal jugular vein has thick, echogenic walls and resists external transducer compression
The internal jugular vein is readily compressible under light probe pressure, lacks visible arterial pulsations, and typically exhibits caliber expansion with the Valsalva maneuver
The internal jugular vein has prominent, pulsatile Doppler flow with high resistance
The internal jugular vein is always located directly medial to the internal carotid artery
questions.answer: The internal jugular vein is readily compressible under light probe pressure, lacks visible arterial pulsations, and typically exhibits caliber expansion with the Valsalva maneuver
questions.explanation: Correct: On ultrasound, veins have thin walls and collapse easily under light external transducer pressure, whereas arteries have thicker, more echogenic walls that resist compression. The IJV displays low-resistance venous phasic flow on Doppler and expands in diameter during a Valsalva maneuver or Trendelenburg positioning.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the recommended anatomical position for the tip of a central venous catheter (CVC) placed via the right internal jugular vein?
options: At the cavoatrial junction or in the lower third of the superior vena cava (SVC)
Deep in the apex of the right ventricle across the tricuspid valve
questions.answer: At the cavoatrial junction or in the lower third of the superior vena cava (SVC)
questions.explanation: Correct: The ideal location for a central venous catheter tip is the lower third of the superior vena cava (SVC) at or just above the cavoatrial junction. This site provides high-volume, rapid blood flow that quickly dilutes hypertonic or irritating infusions (chemotherapy, TPN), while minimizing the risks of vessel wall erosion, thrombosis, and cardiac arrhythmias.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 50-year-old female diagnosed with breast cancer requires central venous access for a planned 12-month course of intermittent outpatient chemotherapy regimens. She desires a device that requires minimal home maintenance and allows her to swim and shower without restriction between treatment cycles. Which device is most appropriate?
options: Peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) with external lumens
questions.explanation: Correct: A totally implantable subcutaneous venous access port (Port-a-Cath) consists of a reservoir placed in a subcutaneous pocket (typically in the anterior chest wall) connected to a central catheter in the SVC. When not in use, the skin is completely closed and intact, allowing normal bathing, showering, and swimming with a very low risk of infection. It is the gold standard for long-term, intermittent oncology infusions.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: During an attempted landmark-guided right internal jugular vein cannulation in an intensive care unit, a 7-French dilator and large-bore sheath are inadvertently advanced into the right common carotid artery. Bright red, pulsatile blood is observed emerging from the sheath. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediately remove the sheath and apply vigorous manual pressure over the carotid artery for 15 minutes
Leave the sheath in place, secure it, and obtain an immediate vascular surgery or interventional radiology consultation for surgical repair or endovascular closure
Inject 5,000 units of heparin through the sheath to prevent stroke
Attach a pressurized flush bag and use the sheath for arterial pressure monitoring
questions.answer: Leave the sheath in place, secure it, and obtain an immediate vascular surgery or interventional radiology consultation for surgical repair or endovascular closure
questions.explanation: Correct: When a large-bore catheter or sheath (≥7-French) is inadvertently placed into the carotid artery, it should be LEFT IN PLACE. Immediately pulling a large sheath from a high-pressure artery carries catastrophic risks of massive expanding cervical hematoma, airway compression, pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula, and stroke. Leaving the sheath in place tamponades the hole while emergency vascular surgery or interventional radiology repair (surgical exploration or covered stent/closure device) is arranged.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient with an indwelling tunneled central venous catheter (Hickman) presents with catheter dysfunction: solutions can be infused easily under gentle gravity pressure, but blood cannot be aspirated from the lumen ('ball-valve' effect). What is the most common underlying cause?
options: Fibrin sheath formation around the catheter tip
Total thrombotic occlusion of the superior vena cava
Catheter fracture at the clavicular junction
Air lock within the infusion hub
questions.answer: Fibrin sheath formation around the catheter tip
questions.explanation: Correct: A fibrin sheath (or fibroepithelial sleeve) is a sleeve of proteinaceous and cellular tissue that develops around indwelling central catheters. It creates a classic 'ball-valve' or 'one-way valve' mechanism: positive pressure during infusion forces the sleeve open, allowing fluids to flow into the vein easily, but negative suction during aspiration pulls the sleeve tightly over the catheter side holes and tip, completely blocking blood aspiration.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: During a percutaneous nephrostomy (PCN) for obstructive pyelonephritis, which anatomical entry route into the renal collecting system is preferred to minimize the risk of major renal vascular laceration?
options: Direct anterior puncture through the renal hilum traversing the main renal artery
Posterolateral puncture directed through an avascular plane (Brödel's line) entering into a posterior calyx
Direct medial puncture through the upper pole renal pelvis
Transperitoneal anterior approach traversing the descending colon
questions.answer: Posterolateral puncture directed through an avascular plane (Brödel's line) entering into a posterior calyx
questions.explanation: Correct: Brödel's line is an avascular boundary plane located on the posterolateral border of the kidney between the anterior and posterior renal arterial divisions. Puncturing along this line into a posterior calyx under combined ultrasound and fluoroscopic guidance traverses the minimum amount of vascular renal parenchyma, avoiding segmental and interlobar arteries and minimizing the risk of severe retroperitoneal hemorrhage or pseudoaneurysm.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of deploying 'T-fasteners' (gastropexy anchors) during a percutaneous radiologic gastrostomy (PRG) tube placement?
options: To mechanically appose and anchor the anterior gastric wall securely against the anterior abdominal wall, preventing gastric displacement and leakage into the peritoneal cavity
To ligate the gastroepiploic arteries to prevent bleeding
To destroy the gastric mucosal acid-secreting parietal cells
To prevent gastroesophageal reflux into the pharynx
questions.answer: To mechanically appose and anchor the anterior gastric wall securely against the anterior abdominal wall, preventing gastric displacement and leakage into the peritoneal cavity
questions.explanation: Correct: T-fasteners (gastropexy anchors) are small metal rods attached to sutures deployed through a needle into the gastric lumen. When retracted, they pull the anterior gastric wall snugly against the parietal peritoneum of the anterior abdominal wall. This apposition prevents the stomach from pulling away during tract dilation and catheter insertion, avoiding catastrophic intraperitoneal leak of gastric contents and peritonitis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 62-year-old male with inoperable Klatskin tumor (hilar cholangiocarcinoma) presenting with severe pruritus, painless jaundice, and acute cholangitis has failed endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). A percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD) is performed. What is the fundamental goal when advancing the catheter in an 'internal-external' drainage configuration?
options: Cross the obstructing biliary stricture to place the catheter tip and side holes into the duodenum, allowing bile to drain both externally into a bag and physiologically into the bowel lumen
Terminate the catheter in the main portal vein to mix bile with systemic circulation
Occlude the ampulla of Vater permanently with a balloon
Drain the gallbladder exclusively while leaving the common bile duct completely obstructed
questions.answer: Cross the obstructing biliary stricture to place the catheter tip and side holes into the duodenum, allowing bile to drain both externally into a bag and physiologically into the bowel lumen
questions.explanation: Correct: In an internal-external biliary drainage configuration, the drainage catheter crosses the obstructing malignant biliary stricture with its distal tip and distal side holes situated within the duodenum, while proximal side holes reside in the dilated biliary ducts above the obstruction. This allows external decompression during acute sepsis/cholangitis and subsequent capping of the catheter so bile flows internally into the gastrointestinal tract, preserving enterohepatic circulation and electrolyte balance.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient with an established percutaneous nephrostomy catheter placed 3 months ago presents for routine tube exchange. The tube is functioning well, and the cutaneous track is completely mature. What is the primary safety principle during a routine catheter exchange?
options: Rip the old catheter out swiftly without a wire and attempt blind puncture with a new catheter
Maintain continuous wire access across the mature tract into the renal pelvis throughout the entire exchange procedure before advancing the new catheter
Inject 100 mL of concentrated contrast into the retroperitoneum prior to wire insertion
Perform an open surgical cutdown to identify the renal capsule
questions.answer: Maintain continuous wire access across the mature tract into the renal pelvis throughout the entire exchange procedure before advancing the new catheter
questions.explanation: Correct: The cardinal safety rule of catheter exchanges (nephrostomy, biliary, gastrostomy) is to maintain continuous guidewire access within the lumen and tract at all times. A guidewire is advanced through the existing catheter into the collecting system/cavity before the old catheter is removed, ensuring the established tract is not lost.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What two vascular structures are connected by an artificial parenchymal tract during the creation of a Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (TIPS)?
options: Hepatic artery and common bile duct
A hepatic vein (usually the right hepatic vein) and an intrahepatic branch of the portal vein (usually the right portal vein)
Splenic vein and left renal vein
Superior mesenteric vein and inferior vena cava
questions.answer: A hepatic vein (usually the right hepatic vein) and an intrahepatic branch of the portal vein (usually the right portal vein)
questions.explanation: Correct: A TIPS procedure creates a low-resistance conduit between an outflow systemic vein (typically the right hepatic vein) and an inflow portal vein branch (typically the right portal vein branch) through the liver parenchyma. An expandable covered stent is deployed across this tract to decompress portal hypertension, treating refractory variceal bleeding and cirrhotic ascites.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following scenarios represents an ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION to performing an elective interventional radiology procedure?
options: A competent patient refusing to give informed consent for the procedure
Mild elevation of serum creatinine (1.4 mg/dL)
Presence of a prosthetic titanium hip replacement
questions.answer: A competent patient refusing to give informed consent for the procedure
questions.explanation: Correct: Informed consent from a competent patient is legally and ethically mandatory. A competent patient's refusal of an elective procedure is an absolute contraindication to proceeding. Other absolute contraindications include an uncorrectable bleeding diathesis or lack of a safe anatomical access path.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old male with a history of a prior severe anaphylactoid reaction (bronchospasm and facial angioedema) to iodinated contrast is scheduled for an elective diagnostic abdominal angiography. Which premedication regimen is most widely recommended prior to elective contrast administration?
options: Oral prednisone (50 mg) administered at 13 hours, 7 hours, and 1 hour prior to the procedure, plus oral diphenhydramine (50 mg) 1 hour prior
Intravenous epinephrine bolus (1 mg) given 5 minutes prior to contrast injection
Oral aspirin (325 mg) and clopidogrel (300 mg) the morning of the procedure
Intravenous furosemide (80 mg) given immediately after contrast administration
questions.answer: Oral prednisone (50 mg) administered at 13 hours, 7 hours, and 1 hour prior to the procedure, plus oral diphenhydramine (50 mg) 1 hour prior
questions.explanation: Correct: The standard Greenberger (ACR) premedication protocol for patients with prior moderate-to-severe allergic reactions undergoing elective procedures consists of oral prednisone (50 mg) taken at 13, 7, and 1 hour before contrast injection, plus oral or IM diphenhydramine (50 mg) administered 1 hour prior to the procedure. Corticosteroids require at least 4-6 hours to exert anti-inflammatory genomic effects.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Two minutes into an angiographic procedure following the initial injection of non-ionic iodinated contrast, a 45-year-old female develops acute diffuse urticaria, marked inspiratory stridor, audible wheezing, and profound hypotension (BP 70/38 mmHg, HR 128 bpm). What is the first-line medication of choice, including dose and route?
options: Intramuscular epinephrine, 0.3 mg (0.3 mL of 1:1,000 [1 mg/mL] solution) into the anterolateral thigh
Intravenous diphenhydramine, 50 mg push as sole therapy
questions.answer: Intramuscular epinephrine, 0.3 mg (0.3 mL of 1:1,000 [1 mg/mL] solution) into the anterolateral thigh
questions.explanation: Correct: This patient is suffering from severe anaphylactoid shock with life-threatening airway compromise (stridor) and hypotension. The primary, first-line life-saving drug is epinephrine administered intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh at a dose of 0.3 mg (0.3 mL of 1:1,000 dilution). IM administration achieves rapid, reliable peak blood concentrations. Antihistamines and steroids are secondary adjuncts and must never delay epinephrine.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 70-year-old woman presents 4 days after a right femoral artery catheterization with a painful, enlarging, pulsatile mass in the right groin. Duplex ultrasonography demonstrates a 3.5 cm cystic cavity adjacent to the common femoral artery with swirling internal red and blue flow ('yin-yang sign') and a communication channel with high-velocity to-and-fro flow. What is the diagnosis and preferred first-line minimally invasive therapy?
options: Femoral artery pseudoaneurysm; percutaneous ultrasound-guided bovine thrombin injection
Arteriovenous fistula; systemic anticoagulation with warfarin
Infected groin abscess; incision and drainage at the bedside
Simple subcutaneous hematoma; apply a heating pad
questions.answer: Femoral artery pseudoaneurysm; percutaneous ultrasound-guided bovine thrombin injection
questions.explanation: Correct: The clinical presentation of a pulsatile groin mass with a duplex ultrasound showing a 'yin-yang sign' (swirling flow) and a connecting neck with characteristic 'to-and-fro' spectral waveform confirms a femoral artery pseudoaneurysm. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous thrombin injection (typically 100-500 IU) directly into the pseudoaneurysm sac is the gold-standard treatment, achieving instant, durable thrombosis in >95% of cases without surgery.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient who underwent a prolonged, complex 6-hour fluoroscopically guided abdominal intervention involving multiple oblique projections accumulates an estimated peak skin entrance dose of 12 Gray (Gy). What potential radiation-induced deterministic injury should the interventional team monitor for, and over what timeframe does it typically manifest?
options: Transient erythema developing within 24 hours, followed potentially by deep skin necrosis, ulceration, or chronic radiation dermatitis appearing weeks to months later
Immediate acute thermal third-degree burns within 5 minutes of procedure completion
Systemic bone marrow failure within 1 hour
No risk; skin doses below 20 Gy cause zero biological changes
questions.answer: Transient erythema developing within 24 hours, followed potentially by deep skin necrosis, ulceration, or chronic radiation dermatitis appearing weeks to months later
questions.explanation: Correct: Radiation-induced skin injury is a deterministic effect with specific dose thresholds: early transient erythema occurs at ~2 Gy; epilation at ~3 Gy; dry/moist desquamation at ~10-15 Gy; and deep ulceration or dermal necrosis can occur at doses exceeding 12-15 Gy. While mild erythema may appear within hours, severe necrosis and breakdown typically manifest weeks to months after the radiation event.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: During the removal of an 8-French central venous catheter from the right internal jugular vein of an upright, sitting patient, the patient suddenly gasps, becomes acutely dyspneic, cyanotic, and hypotensive. Auscultation of the precordium reveals a loud, churning 'mill-wheel' murmur. What complication has occurred, and what is the immediate physical maneuver?
options: Venous air embolism; place the patient immediately in the Trendelenburg and left lateral decubitus position (Durant maneuver), and administer 100% high-flow oxygen
Acute tension pneumothorax; immediately place the patient in high Fowler's position
Acute pulmonary thromboembolism; place the patient in the prone position
Cardiac tamponade; perform immediate blind subxiphoid needle decompression
questions.answer: Venous air embolism; place the patient immediately in the Trendelenburg and left lateral decubitus position (Durant maneuver), and administer 100% high-flow oxygen
questions.explanation: Correct: The entry of atmospheric air into the central venous system causes acute venous air embolism, especially when catheters are manipulated with the patient upright. The classic churning 'mill-wheel' murmur, sudden dyspnea, and collapse are pathognomonic. The patient must be immediately placed in the Trendelenburg and left lateral decubitus position (Durant maneuver). This traps the air bubble at the apex of the right ventricle, preventing it from obstructing the right ventricular outflow tract (pulmonary vapor lock) while 100% oxygen is administered to accelerate nitrogen resorption.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 66-year-old male receives 5,000 units of unfractionated heparin during a complex peripheral angioplasty. At the conclusion of the case, the interventionalist decides to reverse the anticoagulant effect of heparin before pulling the 6-French femoral sheath. Which medication is the specific reversal agent for unfractionated heparin?
questions.explanation: Correct: Protamine sulfate is a strongly basic, positively charged polycationic peptide that binds stoichiometrically to strongly acidic, negatively charged heparin molecules, forming an inactive stable salt that completely neutralizes heparin's anticoagulant activity (approximately 1 mg of protamine neutralizes 100 units of heparin).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following clinical findings is the classic physical examination hallmark of an iatrogenic femoral arteriovenous (AV) fistula following percutaneous catheterization?
options: A continuous palpable thrill and 'machinery-like' continuous vascular bruit heard over the puncture site throughout both systole and diastole
An acutely cold, pale, and pulseless lower extremity with complete sensory loss
A silent, rapidly expanding non-pulsatile soft-tissue swelling in the flank
Isolated petechial rash over the distal digits with normal pulses
questions.answer: A continuous palpable thrill and 'machinery-like' continuous vascular bruit heard over the puncture site throughout both systole and diastole
questions.explanation: Correct: An iatrogenic arteriovenous (AV) fistula forms when a puncture needle traverses both the artery and an adjacent vein, establishing an abnormal persistent low-resistance communication. Because arterial pressure exceeds venous pressure during both systole and diastole, blood flows continuously into the vein, producing a palpable thrill and a continuous, machinery-like vascular bruit on auscultation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient with non-dialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 2.1 mg/dL) requires an urgent CT-guided drainage of an infected intra-abdominal collection. Why is diagnostic or therapeutic percutaneous non-vascular CT intervention associated with a MINIMAL risk of contrast-induced nephropathy compared to vascular procedures?
options: Percutaneous abscess drainage and needle guidance generally require NO intravascular contrast, utilizing non-contrast CT planning or small amounts of dilute non-absorbed intraluminal/intracavity contrast
Abscess drainage patients are physiologically immune to contrast nephrotoxicity
All CT scanners automatically filter iodinated contrast from the patient's blood stream during scanning
Intra-abdominal infections accelerate renal glomerular filtration
questions.answer: Percutaneous abscess drainage and needle guidance generally require NO intravascular contrast, utilizing non-contrast CT planning or small amounts of dilute non-absorbed intraluminal/intracavity contrast
questions.explanation: Correct: Image-guided percutaneous non-vascular procedures (such as abscess drainages and biopsies) under CT or ultrasound guidance are routinely performed without systemic intravascular contrast administration. Guidance relies on non-contrast imaging, direct needle visualization, and cavity assessment with tiny amounts of dilute contrast injected directly into the non-vascular abscess cavity, avoiding any systemic renal toxic exposure.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 74-year-old male on chronic aspirin and clopidogrel therapy for a coronary stent placed 3 years ago presents with acute painless hematochezia and requires diagnostic mesenteric angiography and potential transcatheter embolization. What is the standard management regarding his antiplatelet therapy for this acute emergent procedure?
options: Do not delay emergent angiography; proceed with access using small-gauge needle/micropuncture technique and ultrasound guidance while planning for meticulous manual compression or vascular closure
Cancel angiography and wait 7 days for clopidogrel clearance
Administer 10 units of fresh frozen plasma to reverse clopidogrel immediately
Perform emergency surgical femoral artery cutdown under general anesthesia
questions.answer: Do not delay emergent angiography; proceed with access using small-gauge needle/micropuncture technique and ultrasound guidance while planning for meticulous manual compression or vascular closure
questions.explanation: Correct: In emergent, life-threatening clinical scenarios (such as acute severe gastrointestinal bleeding), urgent diagnostic angiography and transcatheter embolization should not be delayed for antiplatelet clearance. Risk is minimized by utilizing ultrasound guidance, micropuncture access (21G needle) to ensure a single, clean common femoral or radial artery puncture, and meticulous post-procedure manual compression or deployment of an approved vascular closure device.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which anatomical zone of a growing long bone is situated between the epiphysis and the diaphysis and represents the primary site of longitudinal growth?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because the physis (growth plate or epiphyseal plate) consists of specialized hyaline cartilage responsible for endochondral ossification and longitudinal bone growth in skeletally immature individuals. Distractors: A is incorrect because the metaphysis is the flared region of mature/trabecular bone adjacent to the growth plate on the diaphyseal side. C is incorrect because an apophysis is a secondary ossification center that serves as a site of tendon or ligament attachment (traction epiphysis), not longitudinal growth. D is incorrect because the endosteum is the thin vascular membrane lining the inner medullary cavity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On conventional plain radiography of a normal synovial joint, what primarily constitutes the apparent 'joint space' observed between articulating bones?
options: Radiolucent articular hyaline cartilage and joint fluid
Fibrous joint capsule and collateral ligaments
questions.answer: Radiolucent articular hyaline cartilage and joint fluid
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because articular (hyaline) cartilage has water-equivalent soft tissue radiodensity that is not distinguishable from synovial fluid on plain radiographs; thus, the radiolucent gap between opposing subchondral bone plates represents both cartilaginous layers plus intra-articular fluid. Distractors: A is incorrect because synovial fluid is minimal in a normal joint (~1-4 mL) and cartilage occupies the vast majority of this physical space. C is incorrect because the capsule and collateral ligaments surround the joint peripherally rather than lying between articular surfaces. D is incorrect because intra-articular gas is abnormal or a transient traction phenomenon, not standard anatomy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 12-year-old male runner presents with localized pain over the tibial tuberosity. Plain radiographs demonstrate irregular ossification and fragmentation of the tuberosity without joint effusion. Knowledge of normal skeletal anatomy identifies the tibial tuberosity as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because the tibial tuberosity is an apophysis (traction epiphysis) where the patellar tendon inserts and exerts tensile traction force, predisposing adolescents to Osgood-Schlatter disease. Distractors: A is incorrect because pressure epiphyses occur at articular ends of long bones and transmit compressive loads (e.g., distal femoral epiphysis). C is incorrect because nutrient canals are oblique radiolucent cortical channels transmitting blood vessels in the diaphysis. D is incorrect because subchondral bone directly supports articular surfaces inside joints.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Why is the normal periosteum invisible on plain radiographs of healthy adult long bones?
options: It is completely resorbed after skeletal maturity
It is non-mineralized soft tissue closely applied to the cortex and lacks contrast with surrounding soft tissues
It possesses an identical radio-opacity to dense cortical bone
It is located deep to the endosteum within the medullary canal
questions.answer: It is non-mineralized soft tissue closely applied to the cortex and lacks contrast with surrounding soft tissues
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because the normal uninjured periosteum is a thin, fibrous, non-calcified soft-tissue envelope; lacking mineral content, its radiographic attenuation is identical to adjacent muscle and connective tissue, making it invisible until stimulated into producing mineralized reactive bone. Distractors: A is incorrect because the periosteum persists throughout life and remains crucial for fracture healing and appositional bone remodeling. C is incorrect because cortical bone is heavily mineralized (radiopaque/white), whereas periosteum is non-mineralized soft tissue. D is incorrect because the periosteum covers the external outer cortex, not the inner medullary canal.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: An emergency physician orders plain radiographs of a suspected ankle injury. Which fundamental imaging rule must always be observed when evaluating skeletal trauma?
options: Obtain only a single view to minimize radiation dose
Always obtain at least two orthogonal projections and include the joint above and joint below when long bones are involved
Always administer intravenous contrast before radiography
Obtain non-weight-bearing stress radiographs first in all acute trauma
questions.answer: Always obtain at least two orthogonal projections and include the joint above and joint below when long bones are involved
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because the 'rule of two' dictates obtaining at least two perpendicular (orthogonal) views (e.g., AP and Lateral) because a fracture or displacement readily missed on one projection is clearly visible on another. When long bones are traumatized, imaging the adjacent joints ensures non-contiguous injury or associated dislocation (e.g., Maisonneuve fracture) is not overlooked. Distractors: A is incorrect because single-view radiography frequently misses displaced fractures and joint incongruities. C is incorrect because IV contrast is unnecessary for cortical trauma and increases risk. D is incorrect because acute stress views are contraindicated in uncharacterized trauma due to pain and displacement risk.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: In systematic fracture description, 'displacement' strictly describes what spatial relationship?
options: The angular deviation of the fracture fragments relative to the longitudinal anatomical axis
The degree of translatory shift of the distal fragment relative to the proximal fragment, expressed as millimeters or percentage
The shortening of the bone caused by muscle spasm and fragment overlap
Rotational twisting along the long axis of the shaft
questions.answer: The degree of translatory shift of the distal fragment relative to the proximal fragment, expressed as millimeters or percentage
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because displacement (or apposition/translation) describes the linear offset or horizontal translatory shift of the distal fragment in relation to the proximal fragment (e.g., 50% lateral displacement). Distractors: A is incorrect because angular deviation is termed 'angulation'. C is incorrect because shortening or fragment overlap is termed 'shortening', 'telescoping', or 'bayonet apposition'. D is incorrect because twisting along the long axis is termed 'rotation'.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old man sustains a forearm injury. Radiographs reveal a complete transverse fracture of the radial midshaft. The distal radial fragment is tilted 20 degrees towards the dorsal aspect of the wrist. By radiological convention, how should this angulation be accurately reported?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because by universally accepted radiological convention, fracture angulation is named according to the direction in which the distal fragment points or tilts (dorsal angulation). Alternatively, some systems describe the direction of the apex of the angle (which would be volar/apex volar), but describing the distal fragment tilt directly as dorsal angulation is the primary orthopedic standard. Distractors: A is incorrect because volar angulation would mean the distal fragment is tilted anteriorly/volarly. C is incorrect because varus refers to medial deviation in the coronal plane, not sagittal dorsal tilting. D is incorrect because rotation refers to axial twist, not angular tilt.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old motorcyclist sustains a distal femoral fracture. Plain radiograph demonstrates that the distal fracture fragment overlaps the proximal fracture fragment by 3 cm alongside it. What radiological descriptive term designates this specific finding?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because bayonet apposition (or overlap/shortening) occurs when the fracture surfaces do not touch end-to-end but instead slide past each other longitudinally, resulting in skeletal shortening. Distractors: A is incorrect because distraction refers to longitudinal separation of fracture fragments with an increased gap between them. C is incorrect because impaction occurs when bone fragments are driven firmly into one another (shortening with trabecular compression, not side-by-side sliding). D is incorrect because diastasis refers to abnormal separation of bones normally bound tightly together (e.g., distal tibiofibular syndesmosis or pubic symphysis).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A lateral knee radiograph obtained with a horizontal beam (cross-table lateral) following blunt trauma demonstrates a straight, horizontal fluid-fluid interface within the suprapatellar bursa. What does this 'lipohemarthrosis' indicate?
options: Isolated rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament without bony injury
An intra-articular fracture that allowed marrow fat to escape into the joint cavity
Pre-existing degenerative joint disease with synovial cyst formation
questions.answer: An intra-articular fracture that allowed marrow fat to escape into the joint cavity
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because lipohemarthrosis (the FBI sign: fat-blood interface) occurs when an intra-articular fracture breaches both the cortical bone and the medullary cavity, allowing low-density marrow fat to float atop higher-density blood within the joint capsule. Distractors: A is incorrect because isolated soft tissue ACL tears produce hemarthrosis (blood only) without floating marrow fat layer unless accompanied by an osteochondral or plateau fracture. C is incorrect because osteoarthritis does not cause acute fat-blood separation levels. D is incorrect because gas-forming infection displays air-fluid levels (radiolucent air above fluid), not fat floating on blood.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the radiologic significance of identifying an elevated 'posterior fat pad' on a true lateral elbow radiograph in an adult after acute trauma?
options: It is a normal anatomic variant seen in 50% of healthy adults
It is pathognomonic of joint effusion, which in trauma signifies an occult intra-articular fracture (typically radial head)
It represents traumatic rupture of the triceps tendon insertion
It confirms complete posterior dislocation of the ulna
questions.answer: It is pathognomonic of joint effusion, which in trauma signifies an occult intra-articular fracture (typically radial head)
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because the posterior fat pad normally resides hidden deep within the olecranon fossa; visualization of the posterior fat pad on a 90-degree lateral elbow radiograph is always abnormal and indicates a joint effusion distending the capsule. In acute trauma, this strongly indicates an occult intra-articular fracture (most commonly the radial head in adults and supracondylar humerus in children). Distractors: A is incorrect because a visible posterior fat pad is never normal. C is incorrect because triceps tendon rupture is a specific extra-articular soft tissue injury. D is incorrect because dislocation shows overt loss of articular congruity, not merely an effusion sign.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: When describing a fracture involving the articular surface of a joint, which characteristic is MOST critical to report because of its direct correlation with post-traumatic secondary osteoarthritis?
options: The degree of articular surface step-off and diastasis
The color of the overlying cutaneous bruising
The thickness of the adjacent diaphyseal cortex
The presence of nutrient foramina in the shaft
questions.answer: The degree of articular surface step-off and diastasis
questions.explanation: Correct: A is correct because articular incongruity—such as step-off (vertical displacement) and diastasis (articular gap)—disrupts normal joint biomechanics, alters contact pressures, and accelerates cartilage wear, leading directly to post-traumatic osteoarthritis. Distractors: B is incorrect because cutaneous discoloration is a clinical observation, not a radiographic descriptor. C is incorrect because diaphyseal cortical thickness has minimal bearing on articular reconstruction. D is incorrect because nutrient foramina are benign normal anatomic landmarks.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 22-year-old recruit experiences insidious, worsening mid-foot pain during basic training. Initial radiographs taken 3 days after symptom onset are completely normal. Two weeks later, repeat radiographs reveal faint transverse radiolucency with fluffy periosteal cuffing at the second metatarsal neck. This scenario exemplifies which type of fracture?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because a fatigue (stress) fracture results from abnormal, repetitive cyclic stress applied to bone with normal elastic resistance (classic 'march fracture' of the second or third metatarsal). Initial radiographs are frequently negative, with periosteal reaction and subtle fracture lines becoming visible only after 10-14 days of bone remodeling. Distractors: A is incorrect because an insufficiency fracture represents normal stress applied to diseased, mineral-deficient bone (e.g., osteoporotic sacral fractures). C is incorrect because there is no underlying pre-existing destructive bone lesion or lytic tumor. D is incorrect because greenstick fractures occur in flexible pediatric bones following acute acute major trauma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 70-year-old woman with known multiple myeloma trips on a rug and sustains an immediate fracture of her proximal femur. Radiographs show a transverse fracture line centered directly through a well-defined 3-cm lytic marrow lesion with endosteal scalloping. What is the correct designation for this fracture?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because a pathologic fracture is one occurring in bone that has been structurally weakened by a pre-existing localized systemic or focal disease process (such as a primary tumor, metastasis, myeloma, or infection), often with minimal or low-energy trauma. Distractors: A is incorrect because fatigue fractures occur in normal bone subjected to repetitive submaximal stress. C is incorrect because an avulsion fracture is caused by forceful pulling of a tendon or ligament on its bony insertion. D is incorrect because stress remodeling does not describe complete cortical failure through a neoplastic lesion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following descriptions best defines an 'impacted' fracture on plain film radiography?
options: Fracture fragments are pulled apart by muscle spasm leaving a distinct gap
Fracture fragments are driven into each other, characterized radiographically by a dense, opaque line of overlapping, telescoped trabeculae
The bone is shattered into three or more completely separated fragments
One cortex is fractured while the opposite cortex is plasticly deformed
questions.answer: Fracture fragments are driven into each other, characterized radiographically by a dense, opaque line of overlapping, telescoped trabeculae
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because impaction occurs when axial compressive forces drive one fragment into another; instead of a radiolucent fracture line, it frequently produces a zone of increased radiopacity (sclerotic band) representing compacted, collapsed trabeculae. Distractors: A is incorrect because this defines distraction. C is incorrect because this defines a comminuted fracture. D is incorrect because this defines an incomplete greenstick fracture.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient is evaluated 8 months following an open tibial shaft fracture. Radiographs show persistent radiolucency across the fracture site, rounding and sclerosis of the cortical bone ends, and total absence of bridging callus across the gap. What complication is present?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because non-union is characterized by cessation of bone healing processes, marked by cortical rounding, closure of the medullary canal by dense sclerotic bone (eburnation), and a persistent fracture cleft without bridging callus over several months. Distractors: A is incorrect because delayed union implies that healing is progressing slower than expected, but active reparative callus is still present and cortical ends are not sealed off. C is incorrect because malunion describes a fracture that has healed completely, but in an unacceptable mechanical or anatomical alignment. D is incorrect because refracture is a new break occurring through a previously healed site.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A fracture that results in more than two distinct bony fragments is formally classified as:
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because a comminuted fracture is defined as a fracture with three or more pieces (i.e. more than two distinct fragments). Distractors: A is incorrect because a segmental fracture is a specific subtype where two distinct, complete fracture lines isolate a central free segment of shaft. C is incorrect because spiral describes the rotational morphology of the fracture line. D is incorrect because incomplete means only one cortex is broken.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 21-year-old skier experiences severe external rotation of his planted lower leg. Radiographs reveal a fracture line that encircles and winds along the tibial shaft like a corkscrew. Which fracture classification best matches this mechanism and appearance?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because a spiral fracture is produced by a torsional (twisting) force along the long axis of the bone, producing a curving, multiplanar fracture line with sharp pointed tips. Distractors: A is incorrect because transverse fractures are perpendicular to the shaft axis and typically result from direct blow or tension. C is incorrect because axial loading produces impaction, comminution, or vertical split fractures. D is incorrect because pure bending typically results in a transverse fracture or an oblique fracture with a butterfly fragment.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 72-year-old woman falls on her outstretched hand. Radiographs reveal a transverse fracture of the distal radial metaphysis with dorsal displacement, dorsal angulation, and radial deviation of the distal fragment, associated with an ulnar styloid fracture. This classic injury is named:
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because a Colles fracture is the classic extra-articular distal radial metaphyseal fracture with dorsal angulation/displacement ('dinner fork deformity') sustained from a fall on an outstretched hand (dorsiflexed wrist). Distractors: A is incorrect because a Smith fracture ('reverse Colles') features volar (palmar) displacement/angulation resulting from a fall onto a flexed wrist. C is incorrect because a Barton fracture is an intra-articular fracture-subluxation of the radiocarpal joint with a displaced rim fragment. D is incorrect because a Galeazzi fracture comprises a radial shaft fracture with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the defining anatomical configuration of a 'Monteggia' fracture-dislocation?
options: Fracture of the distal third of the radius with dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint
Fracture of the proximal ulnar shaft with dislocation of the radial head
Bilateral fracture of both the radius and ulna without joint dislocation
Fracture of the radial head with distal radioulnar joint disruption and interosseous membrane tear
questions.answer: Fracture of the proximal ulnar shaft with dislocation of the radial head
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because a Monteggia fracture-dislocation consists of a fracture of the proximal or mid ulnar shaft associated with anterior (or posterior/lateral) dislocation of the radial head at the radiocapitellar joint (mnemonic: MUGR - Monteggia = Ulna fracture, Galeazzi = Radius fracture). Distractors: A is incorrect because a distal radial shaft fracture with DRUJ dislocation is a Galeazzi fracture. C is incorrect because this describes a simple 'both-bone' forearm fracture. D is incorrect because this describes an Essex-Lopresti fracture-dislocation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 30-year-old boxer punches a solid wall with a closed fist. Radiographs demonstrate a fracture through the neck of the fifth metacarpal with volar angulation of the metacarpal head. This injury is universally known as:
questions.explanation: Correct: C is correct because a Boxer's fracture is a fracture of the neck of the 5th (and sometimes 4th) metacarpal, typically with volar displacement/angulation of the metacarpal head resulting from direct axial impaction. Distractors: A is incorrect because a Bennett fracture is an intra-articular two-piece fracture-subluxation of the base of the first metacarpal. B is incorrect because a Rolando fracture is a comminuted (three-part or T/Y-shaped) intra-articular fracture of the first metacarpal base. D is incorrect because Gamekeeper's (or Skier's) thumb is an avulsion fracture/sprain of the ulnar collateral ligament of the first MCP joint.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: How does a 'segmental' long bone fracture differ from a routine 'comminuted' fracture?
options: A segmental fracture has two distinct fracture lines that isolate a completely free intercalary shaft segment between them
A segmental fracture only breaks the outer periosteum
A segmental fracture always involves the articular cartilage of both adjacent joints
A segmental fracture is strictly incomplete and occurs exclusively in neonates
questions.answer: A segmental fracture has two distinct fracture lines that isolate a completely free intercalary shaft segment between them
questions.explanation: Correct: A is correct because a segmental fracture is characterized by two distinct, complete fracture levels that divide the shaft into three major portions, creating an isolated, intercalary bony segment between the proximal and distal portions. Distractors: B is incorrect because segmental fractures involve complete cortical disruption at multiple levels. C is incorrect because the segmental block is diaphyseal or metaphyseal and does not require intra-articular extension. D is incorrect because segmental fractures occur in adults with high-energy trauma, not neonates.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old cyclist falls directly onto his thumb. Plain radiograph shows an intra-articular fracture through the base of the first metacarpal with a triangular fragment remaining in articulation with the trapezium, while the main metacarpal shaft is subluxated proximally and radially by the abductor pollicis longus tendon. What is this classification?
questions.explanation: Correct: A is correct because a Bennett fracture is an oblique, intra-articular fracture-subluxation of the base of the first metacarpal: the small anterior/volar lip fragment remains anchored to the trapezium by the anterior oblique ligament, while the major shaft fragment is pulled proximally, laterally, and dorsally by the abductor pollicis longus muscle. Distractors: B is incorrect because a Rolando fracture is a comminuted (T- or Y-shaped) intra-articular base fracture. C is incorrect because a Stener lesion involves the adductor aponeurosis interposing between the ruptured UCL and first MCP joint. D is incorrect because Mallet finger/thumb is an extensor tendon rupture or avulsion at the distal phalanx.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 16-year-old sprinter feels a sudden sharp snap in his anterior hip during a burst of acceleration. Radiographs show a small displaced bone fragment avulsed from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS). Which muscle is responsible for this avulsion?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because the sartorius muscle (and tensor fasciae latae) originates from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS); forceful contraction during sprint starts can cause an apophyseal avulsion fracture at this site. Distractors: A is incorrect because the straight head of the rectus femoris originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS). C is incorrect because the iliopsoas inserts onto the lesser trochanter. D is incorrect because the hamstring muscles originate from the ischial tuberosity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Under the Gustilo-Anderson classification of open fractures, what differentiates a Type III open fracture from Type I and II?
options: Presence of a clean wound less than 1 cm in length
Extensive soft-tissue damage, high-energy mechanism, significant contamination, or severe comminution/periosteal stripping regardless of wound size
Exclusively closed skin with only microscopic epidermal blistering
Involvement of the articular joint space without skin penetration
questions.answer: Extensive soft-tissue damage, high-energy mechanism, significant contamination, or severe comminution/periosteal stripping regardless of wound size
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because Gustilo-Anderson Type III fractures are high-energy open injuries characterized by extensive soft tissue laceration, severe crushing, degloving, periosteal stripping, gross contamination, and severe bone comminution (subdivided into IIIA, IIIB with periosteal stripping requiring flap coverage, and IIIC with arterial injury requiring repair). Distractors: A is incorrect because a clean puncture wound < 1 cm is Type I. C is incorrect because all Gustilo-Anderson categories are open fractures with breach of skin. D is incorrect because an intra-articular fracture without skin perforation is closed.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old construction worker falls from a height. Radiographs of the ankle show a fracture of the distal third of the fibula, tearing of the deltoid ligament with medial clear space widening (>4 mm), and disruption of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis. Under the Weber (Danis-Weber) classification, this injury is classified as:
questions.explanation: Correct: C is correct because Weber Type C fractures occur above the level of the ankle joint (above the syndesmosis) and are almost invariably accompanied by rupture of the syndesmotic ligaments and interosseous membrane, producing joint instability. Distractors: A is incorrect because Weber A is a fracture below the level of the tibial plafond/syndesmosis (avulsion of distal fibula, syndesmosis intact). B is incorrect because Weber B is a spiral/oblique fracture at the level of the syndesmosis, which may be partially torn. D is incorrect because there is no 'Weber D' category in the Danis-Weber system.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is the precise radiological distinction between a 'subluxation' and a 'dislocation'?
options: A subluxation involves bone fracture, whereas a dislocation does not
A subluxation represents partial loss of contact between articulating joint surfaces, whereas a dislocation represents complete loss of contact
A subluxation is spontaneous, whereas a dislocation requires severe trauma
A subluxation affects only pediatric patients, whereas a dislocation affects only adults
questions.answer: A subluxation represents partial loss of contact between articulating joint surfaces, whereas a dislocation represents complete loss of contact
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because subluxation is defined as partial or incomplete disruption of the congruity of a joint, with some remaining contact between opposing articular surfaces; dislocation (luxation) is complete disruption with zero contact between the articulating surfaces. Distractors: A is incorrect because both subluxations and dislocations can occur with or without associated fractures. C is incorrect because both can result from traumatic or atraumatic etiologies. D is incorrect because both conditions occur across all age groups.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 23-year-old rugby player falls on his abducted, externally rotated arm. Radiographs of the shoulder show the humeral head displaced anteriorly and medially, lying inferior to the coracoid process. What is the most common direction of glenohumeral dislocation exemplified here?
questions.explanation: Correct: A is correct because anterior dislocation accounts for approximately 95% of all shoulder dislocations, with the humeral head typically coming to rest in the subcoracoid position. Distractors: B is incorrect because posterior dislocations account for only 2-4% and typically follow seizures or electrocution. C is incorrect because inferior dislocation (luxatio erecta) is rare (<1%) and presents with the arm locked hyperabducted above the head. D is incorrect because superior dislocation is exceedingly rare and requires violent upward force with acromial fracture.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old man presents with severe shoulder pain following an epileptic seizure. Frontal AP radiographs appear deceptively normal at first glance, but close inspection reveals the humeral head is fixed in internal rotation resembling a 'light bulb', with widening of the glenohumeral joint space (>6 mm, 'rim sign'). An axillary or scapular Y view is essential to confirm which elusive diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because posterior shoulder dislocations are notorious for being missed on standard AP radiographs (often following seizures or high-voltage electric shocks due to forceful contraction of the internal rotators); characteristic AP signs include the 'light bulb sign' (profile of the internally rotated humeral head) and the 'rim sign' (joint space >6 mm). A scapular Y, axillary, or Velpeau view readily confirms the humeral head displaced posterior to the glenoid fossa. Distractors: A is incorrect because anterior dislocations are easily recognized on AP views by medial displacement under the coracoid. C is incorrect because calcific tendinopathy shows dense periarticular amorphous calcification without altered glenohumeral alignment. D is incorrect because biceps subluxation does not alter gross humeral head position.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Following successful closed reduction of an anterior shoulder dislocation, follow-up radiographs demonstrate a wedge-shaped compression fracture along the posterosuperior and lateral aspect of the humeral head. What is the eponymous name for this bony impaction injury?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because a Hill-Sachs lesion is a chondral or osteochondral compression fracture of the posterolateral aspect of the humeral head caused by impaction against the hard anterior glenoid rim during anterior dislocation. Distractors: A is incorrect because a Bankart lesion involves injury to the anteroinferior glenoid labrum/rim. C is incorrect because a reverse Hill-Sachs (McLaughlin) lesion occurs on the anteromedial humeral head during a posterior dislocation. D is incorrect because a Bennett lesion is a posterior capsule/glenoid calcification seen in throwing athletes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What is a 'Bony Bankart' lesion?
options: Fracture of the posterolateral humeral head
Detachment of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum with an avulsion fracture of the anteroinferior glenoid rim
Fracture of the acromion process following direct trauma
Subluxation of the sternoclavicular joint with clavicle fracture
questions.answer: Detachment of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum with an avulsion fracture of the anteroinferior glenoid rim
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because a Bankart lesion is a tear of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum; when accompanied by an avulsion fracture of the adjacent anteroinferior cortical bone of the glenoid rim, it is termed a 'bony Bankart' lesion. Distractors: A is incorrect because an impaction fracture of the posterolateral humeral head is a Hill-Sachs lesion. C is incorrect because acromial fracture is an independent scapular trauma. D is incorrect because this describes a sternoclavicular injury.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: An unrestrained driver involved in a head-on motor vehicle collision suffers a 'dashboard injury' where the flexed knee strikes the dashboard. The patient presents with the affected lower limb shortened, adducted, and internally rotated. Frontal pelvis radiograph confirms the femoral head lies superior and lateral to the acetabulum. What injury is present?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because posterior hip dislocation accounts for ~90% of hip dislocations, typically caused by axial force applied through the flexed knee/femur against the dashboard; the limb is classically held in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation, with the displaced femoral head appearing smaller (due to magnification differences) and situated superolateral to the acetabulum on AP view. Distractors: A is incorrect because anterior hip dislocation (10%) presents with abduction and external rotation, with the head projecting over the obturator foramen or pubis. C is incorrect because central dislocation drives the head medially through a shattered acetabular floor into the pelvis. D is incorrect because intertrochanteric fractures present with limb shortening and marked external rotation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Why is an acute traumatic posterior hip dislocation considered a true orthopedic emergency that mandates emergent radiological confirmation and immediate reduction?
options: Risk of rapid development of gas gangrene in the joint
Tension and compression on the ascending retinacular arteries markedly increases the risk of avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head if not reduced within 6 hours
Immediate complete ankylosis occurs within 12 hours
Spontaneous fat embolus syndrome occurs in 100% of cases within 2 hours
questions.answer: Tension and compression on the ascending retinacular arteries markedly increases the risk of avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head if not reduced within 6 hours
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because the femoral head receives its critical blood supply from the medial femoral circumflex artery via ascending retinacular branches; displacement stretches and kinks these vessels, and delay in reduction beyond 6 hours exponentially increases the incidence of irreversible avascular necrosis (AVN) and sciatic nerve palsy. Distractors: A is incorrect because closed dislocations are sterile and do not cause gas gangrene. C is incorrect because ankylosis takes months or years to develop. D is incorrect because fat embolism is a systemic complication of long-bone fractures, not isolated hip dislocation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 10-year-old child falls onto an extended elbow. Radiographs confirm complete posterior displacement of both the radius and ulna relative to the distal humerus. Which anatomical variety of elbow dislocation is this?
questions.explanation: Correct: A is correct because posterior (and posterolateral) dislocations comprise greater than 90% of all elbow dislocations, typically resulting from hyperextension injuries on an outstretched hand where the olecranon drives backward relative to the distal humerus. Distractors: B is incorrect because anterior elbow dislocations are very uncommon and usually involve an olecranon fracture from direct posterior blow. C is incorrect because divergent dislocation (radius and ulna separated in opposite directions) is exceedingly rare. D is incorrect because both forearm bones were displaced together.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old motorcyclist falls onto a hyper-extended wrist. On the lateral wrist radiograph, the capitate and all carpal bones remain aligned along the long axis of the distal radius, but the crescent-shaped lunate is displaced volarly and tilted anteriorly, resembling a 'spilled teacup'. What is the correct diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because in a true lunate dislocation, the lunate loses its normal articulation with both the distal radius and the capitate, squeezing out into the volar carpal tunnel and tilting anteriorly ('spilled teacup' sign on lateral view), while the capitate remains roughly aligned with the radial axis. Distractors: A is incorrect because in a perilunate dislocation, the lunate maintains its normal articulation with the distal radius, but the capitate and remaining carpal bones are dislocated dorsally. C is incorrect because the gross carpal disruption shown is a carpal dislocation, not an isolated scaphoid fracture. D is incorrect because SLAC wrist is a chronic arthritic pattern resulting from untreated chronic scapholunate ligament dissociation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A cyclist falls directly onto the tip of his shoulder. Radiographs demonstrate superior displacement of the distal clavicle relative to the acromion, with widening of both the acromioclavicular (AC) joint and the coracoclavicular (CC) space by greater than 50% compared to the normal contralateral side. What grade of AC joint injury is this according to the Rockwood classification?
options: Grade I (sprain of AC ligament alone)
Grade II (torn AC ligament, intact CC ligament)
Grade III (complete rupture of both AC and CC ligaments with 25-100% superior displacement)
Grade VI (inferior displacement of clavicle under coracoid)
questions.answer: Grade III (complete rupture of both AC and CC ligaments with 25-100% superior displacement)
questions.explanation: Correct: C is correct because Rockwood Grade III acromioclavicular injury is defined by complete rupture of both the AC and coracoclavicular (trapezoid and conoid) ligaments, resulting in superior displacement of the distal clavicle and widening of the coracoclavicular distance by 25% to 100%. Distractors: A is incorrect because Grade I features normal alignment with only microscopic ligament sprain. B is incorrect because Grade II has disruption of the AC ligament with intact/strained CC ligaments (<25% clavicle elevation). D is incorrect because Grade VI features severe inferior displacement of the clavicle beneath the coracoid process.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: What are the four classical, cardinal radiographic hallmarks of osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease) seen on plain radiography?
options: Uniform joint space narrowing, marginal erosions, periarticular osteopenia, and soft tissue swelling
Asymmetric joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, marginal osteophytes, and subchondral cysts (geodes)
Pencil-in-cup deformities, fluffy periostitis, ankylosis, and acro-osteolysis
Chondrocalcinosis, subchondral collapse, loose bodies, and osteoporosis
questions.answer: Asymmetric joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, marginal osteophytes, and subchondral cysts (geodes)
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because the definitive radiographic tetrad of osteoarthritis (OA) consists of: 1) asymmetric joint space loss (reflecting localized mechanical cartilage wear), 2) subchondral sclerosis (eburnation / cortical thickening under load), 3) marginal osteophyte formation (bony outgrowths at joint margins), and 4) subchondral pseudocysts or geodes. Distractors: A is incorrect because these are the hallmarks of inflammatory arthropathies such as rheumatoid arthritis. C is incorrect because these represent psoriatic arthritis. D is incorrect because chondrocalcinosis indicates CPPD (pseudogout) and osteoporosis is not a defining feature of OA.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 64-year-old obese female presents with progressive knee pain aggravated by walking and relieved by rest. An AP radiograph taken with the patient supine appears nearly normal with minimal changes. What is the most appropriate next radiographic step to accurately evaluate joint cartilage loss?
options: CT scan of the knee with IV contrast
Weight-bearing (standing) AP and flexed (Rosenberg) knee radiographs
Knee aspiration prior to repeat supine radiograph
questions.answer: Weight-bearing (standing) AP and flexed (Rosenberg) knee radiographs
questions.explanation: Correct: B is correct because non-weight-bearing (supine) radiographs significantly underestimate the true severity of cartilage loss; standing (weight-bearing) radiographs, particularly in 30-45° of flexion (the Rosenberg view), load the functional contact zones of the femoral condyles and reveal asymmetric joint space narrowing that remains occult when lying flat. Distractors: A is incorrect because CT is not the first-line screening or assessment modality for routine osteoarthritis and exposes the patient to unnecessary radiation.
