questions.explanation: The centre-edge (CE) angle of Wiberg should be greater than 25 degrees in adults to indicate adequate femoral head coverage by the acetabulum. A CE angle less than 20° suggests acetabular dysplasia. Values of 20–25° are borderline. Options C and D represent dysplastic hips and would predispose to early osteoarthritis and dislocation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which of the following is a normal variant on a hand X-ray that can be mistaken for a pathological fracture?
questions.explanation: Nutrient foramina are small linear lucencies that run obliquely through the cortex of bones and can mimic fracture lines. They are distinguished from fractures by their oblique orientation, sharp sclerotic margins, and predictable location. Madelung deformity (Option A) is an actual developmental abnormality. Subchondral sclerosis (Option C) and periosteal reaction (Option D) are pathological findings.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal wrist X-ray, which carpal bone is most commonly fractured but may not be visible acutely?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone (70% of carpal fractures) following a fall on an outstretched hand. Scaphoid fractures may be invisible on initial plain X-ray in up to 20% of cases, requiring MRI or CT for definitive diagnosis. Lunate fractures (Option A) are rare. Triquetrum fractures (Option B) are visible as dorsal chip fractures. Trapezium fractures (Option D) are uncommon.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal AP shoulder X-ray, the subacromial space should measure approximately:
questions.explanation: The normal subacromial space on an AP shoulder X-ray is approximately 7–14 mm. A space less than 7 mm suggests rotator cuff tear, superior migration of the humeral head, or subacromial impingement syndrome. A space less than 1 mm (Option D) is severely abnormal. Options A and C are also abnormal — Option A too narrow, Option C unrealistically large.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a CT abdomen at the level of the pancreatic tail, which structure is typically seen posterior and to the left of the aorta?
questions.explanation: The left adrenal gland is typically located posterior and slightly medial to the upper pole of the left kidney, near the pancreatic tail level, and to the left of the aorta. It has an inverted Y or V shape on CT. The IVC (Option B) is to the right of the aorta. The SMA and SMV (Option A) are anterior to the aorta. The descending colon (Option D) is more lateral and inferior.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a CT chest with contrast, the normal pulmonary artery trunk should measure no more than:
questions.explanation: The main pulmonary artery should measure less than 29 mm in diameter on CT. A measurement ≥29 mm suggests pulmonary arterial hypertension. Option A (15 mm) is too small — the normal PA is larger than this. Options C (45 mm) and D (55 mm) would represent severe dilation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a CT brain without contrast, which window setting is most appropriate for evaluating the brain parenchyma?
questions.explanation: The brain window (width 80, level 40) is used to assess brain parenchyma, optimising contrast between grey matter, white matter, and CSF. Bone windows (Option A) are for evaluating skull fractures. Lung windows (Option B) are for pulmonary parenchyma. Soft tissue windows (Option D) are used for the mediastinum and abdominal organs.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal CT of the chest, at which level does the ascending aorta become the aortic arch?
options: At the level of the pulmonary valve
At the level of the sternal angle (T4)
At the level of the clavicles
questions.answer: At the level of the sternal angle (T4)
questions.explanation: The ascending aorta transitions to the aortic arch at the level of the sternal angle (angle of Louis), corresponding to T4-T5. This is the same level as the carina and the manubriosternal junction. Option A (pulmonary valve) is too inferior. Option C (T8) is the level of the diaphragmatic hiatus. Option D (clavicles) is too superior.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal abdominal CT, what is the typical Hounsfield unit (HU) range for the liver parenchyma on an unenhanced scan?
questions.explanation: Normal liver parenchyma measures approximately 50–70 HU on unenhanced CT. Values lower than 50 HU suggest hepatic steatosis (fatty infiltration). Fat measures approximately −100 to −50 HU (Option D). CSF and water measure ~0 HU (Option A). Bone measures >400 HU. Option C (100–150 HU) would suggest hyperdense lesions such as haematoma.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a T1-weighted MRI, which of the following appears hyperintense (bright)?
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous fat appears hyperintense (bright) on T1-weighted MRI due to its short T1 relaxation time. Cortical bone (Option A) is hypointense on all MRI sequences. Intervertebral discs (Option B) appear hypointense on T1. Acute haemorrhage in the oxyhemoglobin stage (Option D) is actually isointense to hypointense on T1; subacute haemorrhage with methaemoglobin is T1 bright.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which MRI sequence suppresses fat signal and is particularly useful for detecting bone marrow oedema?
questions.explanation: STIR (Short TI Inversion Recovery) suppresses fat signal and is highly sensitive for detecting bone marrow oedema, soft tissue oedema, and stress fractures — conditions that would otherwise be masked by bright marrow fat on standard sequences. T1 (Option A) is best for anatomy and fat. T2* GRE (Option C) is sensitive to blood products. Proton density (Option D) is used for cartilage evaluation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal brain MRI, the corpus callosum is best seen on which plane?
questions.explanation: The corpus callosum, as a midline commissural structure connecting the two cerebral hemispheres, is best visualised in its entirety on a sagittal MRI. On axial images, only cross-sections are seen. Coronal (Option B) shows portions but not the complete structure. Oblique (Option D) is not a standard plane for brain imaging.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A patient undergoes MRI of the liver with gadolinium contrast. On the hepatobiliary phase image, normal liver parenchyma appears:
questions.explanation: On the hepatobiliary phase of gadolinium-enhanced MRI (using hepatocyte-specific agents such as gadoxetate/Primovist), normal liver parenchyma appears hyperintense relative to the spleen because the contrast agent is taken up by functioning hepatocytes. Lesions without hepatocytes (e.g., metastases) appear as hypointense defects. Options A and C do not reflect the normal hepatobiliary phase appearance.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal MRI of the knee, the medial meniscus has what signal characteristics on T2-weighted imaging?
options: Central high signal with peripheral low signal
questions.explanation: Normal fibrocartilage menisci appear uniformly dark (hypointense) on T2-weighted MRI due to their low water content and dense collagen structure. High signal within a meniscus on T2 (Options A, C, D) suggests a tear or degeneration. Grade 1 and 2 MRI changes show intrasubstance increased signal not reaching the articular surface; Grade 3 represents a true tear.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal abdominal ultrasound, the liver parenchyma echotexture is compared to the right kidney cortex. Which statement is correct?
options: The liver is isoechoic to the renal cortex
The liver is slightly more echogenic than the renal cortex
The liver is less echogenic than the renal cortex
They cannot be compared on ultrasound
questions.answer: The liver is slightly more echogenic than the renal cortex
questions.explanation: Normally, the liver parenchyma is slightly more echogenic than the renal cortex. If the liver appears markedly more echogenic, fatty infiltration (hepatic steatosis) should be considered. If the kidney cortex is more echogenic than the liver, renal parenchymal disease may be present. They share a predictable echogenicity relationship that is important for detecting pathology.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal renal ultrasound, the renal pyramids appear:
questions.explanation: Normal renal medullary pyramids appear hypoechoic (darker) compared to the echogenic renal cortex. This distinction is important — medullary nephrocalcinosis or other conditions can alter this pattern. Anechoic with posterior enhancement (Option D) describes simple cysts, not pyramids. Hyperechoic pyramids would suggest nephrocalcinosis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On Doppler ultrasound of a normal abdominal aorta, which flow pattern is expected?
questions.explanation: The abdominal aorta normally demonstrates a triphasic waveform: a large forward systolic peak, brief flow reversal in early diastole, and small forward flow in late diastole. This reflects the high-resistance vascular bed of the lower limbs. Monophasic waveforms (Option A) suggest proximal obstruction. Continuous non-pulsatile flow (Option C) is seen in venous structures. Option D would suggest absence of flow.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal obstetric ultrasound at 18–20 weeks gestation, fetal heart rate is expected to be approximately:
questions.explanation: The normal fetal heart rate at 18–20 weeks is 140–160 bpm. In early first trimester, it is slightly higher. Rates below 100 bpm (bradycardia) and above 200 bpm (tachycardia) are concerning for fetal compromise or arrhythmia. Options A and B represent bradycardia, Option D represents tachycardia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal gallbladder ultrasound, the gallbladder wall should measure no more than:
questions.explanation: The normal gallbladder wall measures up to 3 mm when the gallbladder is adequately distended (ideally after 4–6 hours of fasting). Wall thickening >3–4 mm suggests cholecystitis, but can also occur in non-fasting states, heart failure, liver disease, or hypoalbuminaemia. Option A (1 mm) is thinner than normal. Options C and D indicate significant pathological thickening.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal mammogram, which tissue appears radiolucent (dark)?
questions.explanation: Adipose (fatty) tissue appears radiolucent (dark/black) on mammography because fat attenuates X-rays poorly. Dense fibroglandular tissue (Option A) appears white/radio-opaque. Calcifications (Option B) are very bright/white. Spiculated masses (Option D) are radio-opaque and associated with malignancy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: According to the ACR BI-RADS classification, which category indicates a finding with less than 2% probability of malignancy and recommends routine annual screening?
questions.explanation: BI-RADS 2 indicates a benign finding (0% malignancy probability) with routine annual screening recommended. BI-RADS 1 (Option B) is a normal study. BI-RADS 0 (Option A) means incomplete assessment requiring additional imaging. BI-RADS 3 (Option D) indicates a probably benign finding (< 2% malignancy) requiring 6-month follow-up.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old woman has a routine mammogram. The radiologist notes scattered areas of fibroglandular density. This corresponds to which ACR breast density category?
questions.explanation: Scattered fibroglandular densities correspond to ACR Breast Density Category B. Category A (almost entirely fatty) has minimal glandular tissue. Category C (heterogeneously dense) may obscure small masses. Category D (extremely dense) significantly limits mammographic sensitivity and increases cancer risk.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On breast ultrasound, a normal lymph node within the axilla appears as:
options: A round hypoechoic solid nodule without hilum
A reniform structure with a hyperechoic fatty hilum
An anechoic structure with posterior enhancement
A hyperechoic solid mass with irregular margins
questions.answer: A reniform structure with a hyperechoic fatty hilum
questions.explanation: Normal lymph nodes appear as reniform (kidney-shaped) structures with a hyperechoic fatty hilum and a hypoechoic cortex on ultrasound. Loss of the fatty hilum or cortical thickening >3 mm suggests metastatic involvement. An anechoic structure with enhancement (Option C) describes a cyst. A round hypoechoic node without hilum (Option A) raises suspicion for malignancy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a standard mammogram, which two views are routinely obtained?
questions.explanation: Standard mammography comprises the craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO) views for each breast. The MLO provides the most breast tissue and is the single most important view. The CC view allows for medial-lateral localisation. Straight lateral (ML) is used as an additional view, not a standard view. AP (Option A) is not a mammographic projection.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal chest X-ray of a neonate, the thymus may be visible as a sail-like projection from the superior mediastinum. This is known as:
questions.explanation: The thymic sail sign describes the triangular projection of the thymus into the right hemithorax in neonates and young infants, resembling a sail. It is a normal finding up to 2 years of age. The hilum overlay sign (Option A) is used to determine the origin of a mediastinal mass. The Luftsichel sign (Option C) is associated with left upper lobe collapse. The silhouette sign (Option D) indicates loss of a normal border due to adjacent airspace disease.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On X-ray of a normal 10-year-old child's knee, an epiphyseal growth plate (physis) appears as:
options: A dense sclerotic line across the metaphysis
A radiolucent band perpendicular to the long axis of the bone
A periosteal reaction along the diaphysis
questions.answer: A radiolucent band perpendicular to the long axis of the bone
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal growth plate appears as a radiolucent (dark) horizontal band perpendicular to the long axis of the bone, between the epiphysis and metaphysis. It is normal and must not be confused with a fracture. A dense sclerotic line (Option A) would suggest a growth arrest line. Cortical disruption (Option C) and periosteal reaction (Option D) indicate pathological conditions.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: Which imaging modality is preferred for evaluating a 3-month-old infant with suspected developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is the modality of choice for evaluating DDH in infants under 4–6 months because the femoral head is predominantly cartilaginous at this age and not visible on X-ray. The Graf method uses ultrasound to measure the alpha angle (acetabular angle) and beta angle. X-ray (Option A) is only useful after ossification of the femoral head at ~4–6 months. CT (Option B) involves radiation and offers no advantage. MRI (Option D) is reserved for complex cases.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a normal neonatal cranial ultrasound, what is a normal finding that should not be mistaken for haemorrhage?
options: Hyperechoic choroid plexus in the temporal horns
Subependymal haemorrhage at the caudothalamic groove
questions.answer: Hyperechoic choroid plexus in the temporal horns
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus is a normal hyperechoic (bright) structure seen in the temporal horns of the lateral ventricles on neonatal cranial ultrasound and should not be confused with haemorrhage. Periventricular leukomalacia (Option B) is a pathological finding representing white matter injury. Subependymal haemorrhage (Option C) at the caudothalamic groove is pathological and graded as Grade I IVH. Grade III IVH (Option D) is significantly pathological.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 5-year-old child presents with a limp. X-ray shows a crescent-shaped subchondral lucency in the femoral head. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A crescent sign (subchondral lucency) in the femoral head of a child with a limp is pathognomonic of Perthes disease, representing avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis. It is most common in boys aged 4–8. Normal variants (Option A) do not cause crescent signs. DDH (Option C) presents with acetabular dysplasia. Transient synovitis (Option D) shows joint space widening on X-ray but no bony changes.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On an unlabelled axial CT image, you identify a crescent-shaped hyperdense collection along the inner table of the skull. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A crescent-shaped (concave-convex) hyperdense collection conforming to the inner table of the skull is characteristic of an acute subdural haematoma. It crosses suture lines and follows the brain contour. An epidural haematoma (Option A) is biconvex (lens-shaped) and does not cross sutures. SAH (Option C) fills the sulci and cisterns. Cerebral contusion (Option D) appears as irregular parenchymal haemorrhage.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On an unlabelled PA chest X-ray, you identify fluffy bilateral perihilar infiltrates in a 'bat-wing' distribution. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bilateral perihilar fluffy infiltrates in a 'bat-wing' or 'butterfly' distribution are characteristic of pulmonary oedema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic). Associated features include upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, and pleural effusions. Pneumonia (Option A) tends to be unilateral and lobar/segmental. Pleural effusion (Option C) causes basal opacity with a meniscus. Pneumothorax (Option D) shows absent lung markings.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On an unlabelled abdominal X-ray, you identify a 'double-bubble' sign with no distal bowel gas. What diagnosis does this suggest?
questions.explanation: The double-bubble sign — two distinct air-filled bubbles representing the stomach and proximal duodenum with no distal bowel gas — is the classic radiological sign of duodenal atresia. This is due to complete obstruction at the level of the second part of the duodenum. Jejunal atresia (Option A) produces multiple dilated loops. Hirschsprung's (Option B) shows distal large bowel obstruction. Malrotation with volvulus (Option D) can cause a double-bubble but typically has some distal gas.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On an unlabelled T2-weighted MRI of the knee, you identify a linear hyperintense signal extending to the articular surface of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. This represents:
options: Grade 2 meniscal signal (linear intrasubstance change not reaching surface)
Grade 3 meniscal tear (signal reaching articular surface)
questions.answer: Grade 3 meniscal tear (signal reaching articular surface)
questions.explanation: A Grade 3 meniscal signal on MRI is defined as increased T2 signal that reaches at least one articular surface, indicating a true meniscal tear. Grade 1 (Option A) is globular intrasubstance signal. Grade 2 (Option B) is linear intrasubstance signal not reaching the surface. Both Grades 1 and 2 are considered incidental findings not representing true tears.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On an unlabelled ultrasound image, you see an anechoic structure with well-defined walls, posterior acoustic enhancement, and no internal echoes. This is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: A simple cyst on ultrasound is characterised by: anechoic interior, thin well-defined walls, posterior acoustic enhancement (increased through-transmission), and no internal echoes. Solid tumours (Option A) are echogenic. Abscesses (Option C) typically contain internal echoes and debris. Haematomas (Option D) usually show internal echoes and heterogeneous texture.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 65-year-old smoker presents with progressive dyspnoea. Chest X-ray shows a dense right upper lobe opacity with a concave inferior border and an associated hilum that appears elevated. The inferior border of the mass forms an S-shaped curve. What is this sign called?
questions.explanation: The Golden S sign (reverse S sign of Golden) is seen in right upper lobe collapse combined with a central obstructing hilar mass (typically bronchogenic carcinoma). The superior convex curve is formed by the tumour mass and the inferior concave curve by the collapsed upper lobe, creating a reverse S or Golden S shape. Silhouette sign (Option A) involves loss of normal borders. Air bronchogram (Option C) shows air-filled bronchi within a dense lung. Meniscus sign (Option D) describes fluid-filled cavities.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On a chest X-ray, the right heart border is obliterated by an adjacent opacity. The left heart border is clearly visible. Which lobe/segment is most likely affected?
options: Right middle lobe or right lower lobe medial segment
questions.answer: Right middle lobe or right lower lobe medial segment
questions.explanation: The silhouette sign: the right heart border is formed by the right atrium and is adjacent to the medial segment of the right middle lobe and the medial basal segment of the right lower lobe. Consolidation/collapse in these segments obliterates the right heart border. The right lower lobe posteriorly (Option A) obliterates the right hemidiaphragm. Left upper lobe (Option C) obliterates the aortic knuckle/left heart border. Left lower lobe (Option D) obliterates the left hemidiaphragm.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A chest X-ray shows air-filled branching tubular structures within an area of dense consolidation in the right lower lobe. This finding is called the:
questions.explanation: The air bronchogram sign occurs when air within bronchi is made visible against a background of airspace consolidation or atelectasis — the surrounding alveoli are filled with fluid/pus while the bronchi remain air-filled. This indicates the pathology is parenchymal, not pleural or mediastinal. Silhouette sign (Option A) involves border obliteration. Meniscus sign (Option C) describes fluid in a cavity. Rigler sign (Option D) refers to visualisation of both sides of the bowel wall.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: On an erect abdominal X-ray, the wall of the small bowel is outlined on both sides. The patient has a rigid abdomen. What sign is this and what does it indicate?
questions.explanation: Rigler's sign (double wall sign) is seen when free intraperitoneal air outlines both the inner and outer walls of the bowel, making the bowel wall visible on both sides. This is a sign of pneumoperitoneum and indicates bowel perforation. Normally, only the inner wall (mucosa) is visible because the outer wall is surrounded by soft tissue of equal density. The meniscus sign (Option A) relates to fluid within a cavity. Options C and D describe different signs.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A neonatal abdominal X-ray demonstrates two large gas-filled structures in the upper abdomen with no gas distally. Which sign is this and what is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The double-bubble sign represents gas in the stomach (first bubble) and the distended proximal duodenum (second bubble), with absence of distal gas. This is the hallmark of duodenal atresia or duodenal stenosis with complete obstruction. Approximately 30% of cases are associated with Down syndrome (trisomy 21). Rigler sign (Option A) relates to pneumoperitoneum. Air bronchogram (Option C) is a chest finding. Triple bubble (Option D) suggests proximal jejunal atresia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A chest X-ray shows a well-defined opacity with a concave upper border in the right costophrenic angle that moves with patient positioning. What sign is this and what does it represent?
options: Golden S sign — lung collapse with mass
questions.explanation: The meniscus sign describes the concave upper surface of a pleural effusion on an erect chest X-ray, caused by fluid tracking up the pleural cavity along the lateral chest wall. The concavity results from surface tension at the fluid-air interface. It shifts with positional changes (supine versus erect). Golden S sign (Option C) involves lung collapse. Hampton's hump (Option D) is a wedge-shaped pleural-based opacity from pulmonary infarction.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: An air bronchogram sign within a pulmonary mass is significant because it suggests:
options: The mass is extrinsic to the lung
The pathology is within the alveolar/airspace compartment
There is a pulmonary abscess with cavitation
questions.answer: The pathology is within the alveolar/airspace compartment
questions.explanation: An air bronchogram within a mass indicates the pathology is intra-alveolar (airspace disease), confirming the lesion is in the lung parenchyma. It is classically seen in pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, and bronchoalveolar carcinoma (now lepidic adenocarcinoma). Extrinsic masses (Option A) compress but do not surround bronchi. Cavitation (Option C) is different from air bronchograms. Benignity (Option D) cannot be assumed.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: The silhouette sign is positive when an opacity OBLITERATES the border of an adjacent structure. Which pathological process is the underlying mechanism?
options: The adjacent structure has become calcified
Two structures of similar radiodensity become contiguous, eliminating the visible interface
A pleural effusion separates two structures
questions.answer: Two structures of similar radiodensity become contiguous, eliminating the visible interface
questions.explanation: The silhouette sign occurs when two adjacent structures of similar attenuation (density) lose their visible border on X-ray. Normally, the heart border is visible because it is adjacent to air-filled lung. When the adjacent lung becomes consolidated or collapsed (similar density to soft tissue), the interface disappears. Calcification (Option A) would increase density and create a visible border. Pleural effusion (Option C) can cause this but is not the mechanism of the sign. Hyperinflation (Option D) increases contrast, not reduces it.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: The Rigler sign requires how much free intraperitoneal air to be radiologically visible on an erect abdominal X-ray?
options: A specific amount cannot be defined
questions.explanation: Rigler's sign is highly sensitive and can be seen with as little as 1 mL of free intraperitoneal air. However, in clinical practice, pneumoperitoneum on erect X-ray typically requires at least 50–100 mL of free air to be reliably detected under the diaphragm. CT is far more sensitive and can detect very small amounts. Options A and B are incorrectly large volumes for the Rigler sign specifically.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old man presents with haemoptysis. Chest X-ray shows a lung mass with an air crescent within a cavity, surrounded by a halo of lucency. This describes which sign and condition?
questions.explanation: The air crescent (meniscus) sign within a lung cavity with a soft tissue mass (fungal ball) describes an aspergilloma. The crescent of air surrounds the mobile fungal ball (mycetoma). This is particularly seen in patients with pre-existing cavities (old TB, sarcoid). The halo sign (Option C) is a different sign — ground-glass halo around a nodule, seen in angioinvasive aspergillosis. Air bronchogram (Option B) and Golden S (Option D) describe different findings.

questions.prompt: A 25-year-old motorcyclist is brought to A&E after a high-speed collision. A chest X-ray shows widening of the superior mediastinum (>8 cm), loss of the aortic knuckle, and deviation of the trachea to the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Traumatic aortic injury (aortic transection) is suggested by: superior mediastinal widening >8 cm, obliteration of the aortic knuckle, tracheal deviation to the right, depression of the left mainstem bronchus, and left apical cap. This typically occurs at the aortic isthmus (ligamentum arteriosum). CT angiography is the definitive investigation. Tension pneumothorax (Option A) would show tracheal deviation away from the affected side with absent lung markings. Haemothorax (Option C) causes a unilateral pleural opacity.

questions.prompt: A 70-year-old woman presents with sudden severe headache ('thunderclap'). CT brain without contrast is performed within 2 hours of onset. What is the expected finding?
options: Normal CT — CT has no role in this scenario
Hyperdense blood filling the subarachnoid cisterns
A hypodense area in the MCA territory
questions.answer: Hyperdense blood filling the subarachnoid cisterns
questions.explanation: Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) from a ruptured berry aneurysm classically presents with a thunderclap headache. CT brain within 6 hours of onset has ~98% sensitivity, showing hyperdense (bright) blood in the basal cisterns, sylvian fissures, and sulci. A hypodense MCA territory lesion (Option C) suggests ischaemic stroke. Periventricular changes (Option D) indicate small vessel disease. CT is always the first-line investigation (Option A is wrong).

questions.prompt: On erect chest X-ray, a hyperlucent hemithorax with absent lung markings and a visible lung edge is noted. The trachea and mediastinum are deviated toward the contralateral side. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax is characterised by: hyperlucent hemithorax, absent lung markings, visible lung edge, mediastinal shift AWAY from the affected side (due to positive pressure), and flattening/inversion of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm. Simple pneumothorax (Option A) has no mediastinal shift. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical emergency — treatment should not be delayed for imaging confirmation. Pleural effusion (Option C) causes opacification, not hyperlucency.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Emergency radiology — trauma imaging, acute abdomen, stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, pneumothorax
questions.topicTitle: Emergency radiology — trauma imaging, acute abdomen, stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, pneumothorax
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old hypertensive man presents with sudden onset of left hemiplegia. CT brain at 1 hour shows no abnormality. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: An acute ischaemic stroke may have a normal CT within the first 6 hours. MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is far more sensitive, detecting ischaemia within minutes of onset as restricted diffusion (bright on DWI, dark on ADC map). This guides thrombolysis decisions. Discharging home (Option A) without investigation is dangerous. Repeat CT at 24 hours (Option B) delays treatment. CT chest angiography (Option D) has no role here.

questions.topicTitle: Emergency radiology — trauma imaging, acute abdomen, stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, pneumothorax
questions.prompt: A CT brain shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense collection over the right temporal convexity in a 20-year-old following head trauma. The patient had a lucid interval after injury. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An acute epidural haematoma (EDH) appears as a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense collection, does NOT cross suture lines, and is classically associated with a lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration due to arterial bleeding (typically from the middle meningeal artery after temporal bone fracture). Acute SDH (Option A) is crescent-shaped and crosses sutures. Diffuse axonal injury (Option C) shows subtle punctate haemorrhages at grey-white junctions. Cerebral contusion (Option D) is irregular parenchymal haemorrhage.

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old presents with acute severe central abdominal pain radiating to the back with hypotension. CT abdomen shows a focal outpouching of the infrarenal aorta measuring 7 cm with periaortic haematoma. What is the diagnosis and appropriate management?
options: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) — emergency surgical repair
questions.answer: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) — emergency surgical repair
questions.explanation: A ruptured AAA (>3 cm with outpouching and periaortic haematoma on CT) is a surgical emergency with high mortality. The classic triad is: sudden severe back/abdominal pain, pulsatile abdominal mass, and haemodynamic instability. Emergency open or endovascular repair (EVAR) is required. Aortic dissection (Option A) has a different appearance (intimal flap). Acute pancreatitis (Option C) and mesenteric ischaemia (Option D) do not cause an aortic aneurysm.

questions.topicTitle: Emergency radiology — trauma imaging, acute abdomen, stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, pneumothorax
questions.prompt: On CT of the abdomen in a patient with acute right iliac fossa pain, which specific CT finding is most diagnostic of acute appendicitis?
options: Dilated appendix >6 mm with periappendiceal fat stranding
questions.answer: Dilated appendix >6 mm with periappendiceal fat stranding
questions.explanation: The most specific CT finding for acute appendicitis is a dilated appendix measuring >6 mm in diameter with periappendiceal fat stranding, wall thickening (>2 mm), and sometimes an appendicolith. Free pelvic fluid (Option A) is non-specific. Terminal ileal thickening (Option C) suggests Crohn's disease or ileitis. Right hydronephrosis (Option D) suggests ureteric calculus.

questions.prompt: A 35-year-old male is involved in a road traffic accident. FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) ultrasound is performed. Which area does NOT form part of the standard FAST examination?
questions.explanation: The standard FAST examination assesses four areas for free fluid: (1) Hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch), (2) Splenorenal recess, (3) Pericardium (subxiphoid view), and (4) Pelvis (pouch of Douglas). The retroperitoneum (Option D) is NOT part of the standard FAST because retroperitoneal haemorrhage does not freely collect in the peritoneal cavity and cannot be reliably detected by FAST — CT is required.

questions.prompt: On CT brain, a hypertensive 60-year-old shows an acute hyperdense parenchymal haemorrhage in the basal ganglia. Which vessel territory does this implicate?
options: Lenticulostriate arteries (perforators of middle cerebral artery)
questions.answer: Lenticulostriate arteries (perforators of middle cerebral artery)
questions.explanation: Hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage most commonly occurs in the basal ganglia (putamen, 35%) due to rupture of the lenticulostriate arteries — small perforating branches of the MCA. These vessels are particularly vulnerable to hypertensive lipohyalinosis. ACA (Option A) territory haemorrhage would affect the medial frontal lobe. PCA (Option B) affects the occipital lobes. Basilar artery (Option D) affects the brainstem.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Emergency radiology — trauma imaging, acute abdomen, stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, pneumothorax
questions.topicTitle: Emergency radiology — trauma imaging, acute abdomen, stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, pneumothorax
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old woman presents with periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa, nausea, and fever. Ultrasound is inconclusive. CT scan shows a periappendiceal abscess. What is the Alvarado score range that typically warrants surgical intervention?
options: The Alvarado score is not used in this context
questions.explanation: The Alvarado score combines clinical and laboratory parameters (migration of pain, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, RIF tenderness, rebound tenderness, elevated temperature, leukocytosis, shift to left). A score of 7–10 carries high probability of appendicitis and typically warrants surgical intervention. Score 4–6 (Option B) is equivocal and often prompts CT imaging. Score 1–3 (Option A) is low probability. However, CT confirming a periappendiceal abscess typically mandates intervention regardless of score.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.topicTitle: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.prompt: An imaging study shows a cross-sectional image of the abdomen with the liver appearing dark grey, the aorta appearing bright white, and the vertebra appearing extremely bright. Which modality is this?
questions.explanation: CT with IV contrast shows: bone (vertebra) as extremely bright (>400 HU), contrast-enhanced vessels (aorta) as bright white, and soft tissues (liver) as grey on a black background. MRI T1 (Option A) shows fat as bright but cortical bone as dark. Plain X-ray (Option C) is a 2D projection, not cross-sectional. Ultrasound (Option D) is 2D, real-time, using greyscale but with a characteristic fan-shaped image.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.topicTitle: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.prompt: An image shows a 2D fan-shaped greyscale image of the right upper quadrant. A round anechoic structure with a bright posterior wall and posterior acoustic enhancement is seen adjacent to the liver. What is the most likely finding?
questions.explanation: On ultrasound, a simple hepatic cyst appears as an anechoic (echo-free) round structure with imperceptible walls and posterior acoustic enhancement (increased through-transmission of sound). This is pathognomonic of a simple cyst. Liver metastases (Option A) are solid and echogenic. Hepatic abscess (Option B) contains internal echoes and debris. HCC (Option D) is a solid heterogeneous mass.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.topicTitle: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.prompt: An MRI shows a sagittal image of the brain. A large midline structure connecting the two cerebral hemispheres is absent. The gyri of the medial hemisphere appear to radiate towards the third ventricle. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Agenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC) is characterised by absence of the corpus callosum on MRI, with the medial hemispheric gyri (cingulate gyrus) running vertically towards the third ventricle (rather than over the corpus callosum), widely spaced lateral ventricles ('bull's horns' appearance), and a high-riding third ventricle. Holoprosencephaly (Option B) involves fusion of the cerebral hemispheres. Lissencephaly (Option C) shows smooth cerebral cortex without gyri. This is not a normal variant (Option D).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.topicTitle: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.prompt: A nuclear medicine image shows a patient injected with a radiotracer. Areas of increased uptake (hot spots) are seen in multiple vertebral bodies, ribs, and the skull. The modality is identified as a bone scan. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Multiple hot spots on a Tc-99m bone scan in multiple vertebral bodies, ribs, and skull suggest metastatic bone disease (osteoblastic metastases), most commonly from prostate, breast, or lung cancer. Osteoporosis (Option A) does not cause focal hot spots. Paget's disease (Option B) causes a more confluent pattern of uptake in affected bones. Multiple myeloma (Option D) causes 'cold spots' (photopenic) on bone scan as it is predominantly lytic.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.topicTitle: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.prompt: A CT angiogram of the coronary arteries shows significant narrowing of the proximal left anterior descending (LAD) artery with calcified plaques. This imaging modality is best described as:
questions.explanation: CT coronary angiography (CTCA) is a non-invasive technique that uses multidetector CT with IV contrast to visualise coronary arteries, detecting stenosis and calcified/non-calcified plaques. Conventional coronary angiography (Option A) is an invasive catheter-based technique. Cardiac MRI (Option C) is used for function/viability assessment, not detailed coronary imaging. Nuclear stress test (Option D) assesses myocardial perfusion, not coronary anatomy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.topicTitle: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.prompt: An X-ray image shows a 'snowstorm' appearance of multiple small rounded opacities throughout both lung fields in a patient with known malignancy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Diffuse bilateral small rounded opacities ('snowstorm' or 'cannonball' metastases) in a patient with known malignancy are characteristic of haematogenous pulmonary metastases, typically from thyroid, renal cell, choriocarcinoma, or colon cancer. Miliary TB (Option A) produces smaller, more uniform 1–2 mm nodules. Sarcoidosis (Option C) typically shows upper/mid-zone bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and nodules. Pulmonary oedema (Option D) produces perihilar alveolar opacification.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.topicTitle: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.prompt: On a plain X-ray of the hand, periarticular soft tissue swelling and erosions with overhanging edges ('rat-bite erosions') are seen at the first MTP joint with a large eccentric soft tissue mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tophaceous gout is characterised on X-ray by well-defined 'punched-out' erosions with overhanging edges (Martel hook sign), eccentric soft tissue tophi, and relative preservation of joint space until late stages. The first MTP joint is classically affected. Rheumatoid arthritis (Option A) shows juxta-articular erosions without overhanging edges. Osteoarthritis (Option B) shows subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes. Psoriatic arthritis (Option D) causes 'pencil-in-cup' deformity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.topicTitle: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.prompt: An abdominal CT in portal venous phase shows a low-attenuation lesion in the liver with peripheral nodular enhancement that fills in centripetally on delayed images. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hepatic haemangiomas demonstrate characteristic peripheral nodular enhancement that fills in centripetally (from periphery to centre) on delayed phases, becoming isodense or hyperdense to the liver. This is due to their vascular lakes filling slowly. HCC (Option A) shows arterial enhancement with washout. FNH (Option C) shows homogeneous arterial enhancement with a central scar. Simple cysts (Option D) do not enhance at all.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.topicTitle: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.prompt: On a chest X-ray, an opacity is seen in the left lower zone that does not cause volume loss and obscures the left hemidiaphragm but not the left heart border. Which segment is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Obliteration of the left hemidiaphragm with a preserved left heart border indicates the pathology is in the left lower lobe (not lingula). The left hemidiaphragm is silhouetted by the left lower lobe. The left heart border is formed by the lingula — if preserved, the lingula is clear. If the lingula were affected (Option A), the left heart border would be obliterated. Options C and D would show different patterns.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.topicTitle: Image-based diagnosis — identify modality, abnormality, anatomical location, most likely diagnosis
questions.prompt: An MRI shows a well-defined T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense lesion in the posterior fossa of a 6-year-old with headaches and ataxia. On contrast, it enhances avidly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma (cerebellar astrocytoma) is the most common posterior fossa tumour in children, appearing as a T2-hyperintense cystic mass with an enhancing mural nodule, often with a large cystic component. Medulloblastoma (Option B) is solid, midline (vermis), and restricted diffusion on DWI. Ependymoma (Option C) arises from the 4th ventricle floor and extends through foramina (plastic tumour). Brainstem glioma (Option D) causes diffuse pontine expansion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.topicTitle: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old pregnant woman (16 weeks gestation) presents with right iliac fossa pain. Ultrasound is inconclusive for appendicitis. What is the preferred next investigation?
options: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast
questions.answer: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast
questions.explanation: MRI without gadolinium contrast is the preferred second-line investigation for suspected appendicitis in pregnancy when ultrasound is inconclusive, due to its excellent soft tissue resolution and absence of ionising radiation. CT (Option A) is accurate but involves radiation to the fetus. Plain X-ray (Option C) has poor soft tissue contrast. Immediate laparoscopy (Option D) would be premature before imaging confirmation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.topicTitle: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.prompt: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to MRI?
questions.explanation: A non-MRI-conditional cardiac pacemaker is an absolute contraindication to MRI due to risk of device malfunction, lead heating, device movement, and potentially lethal arrhythmias. MRI-conditional pacemakers exist and can be used under specific protocol conditions. Titanium alloys (Option A) are MRI-safe. Dental amalgam fillings (Option C) are generally safe. Surgical skin staples (Option D) are usually safe but may cause artefact.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.topicTitle: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old man presents with haematuria and is found to have a 4 cm solid renal mass on ultrasound. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis with IV contrast (for staging)
questions.answer: CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis with IV contrast (for staging)
questions.explanation: A solid renal mass >3 cm is highly suspicious for renal cell carcinoma. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast is the investigation of choice for staging, characterising the mass (enhancement pattern, fat content), and evaluating for lymphadenopathy and metastases. MRI (Option A) is used if CT is contraindicated. Watchful waiting (Option B) is inappropriate for a 4 cm solid mass. IVU (Option D) is outdated for renal mass evaluation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.topicTitle: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old woman presents with a hot, swollen, tender right knee. Joint aspiration shows turbid fluid. Which imaging modality is FIRST-LINE to identify the underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Plain X-ray is the first-line investigation for a hot swollen joint. It can identify joint space narrowing, effusion, erosions, chondrocalcinosis (crystal arthropathy), or periostitis. MRI (Option A) is more sensitive and used second-line for soft tissue, cartilage, and bone marrow assessment. CT (Option C) is for complex fractures. Bone scintigraphy (Option D) is for occult fractures or metastases, not acute arthritis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.topicTitle: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.prompt: A 50-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of productive cough and fever. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. She fails to improve with antibiotics. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: A persistent non-resolving pneumonia despite antibiotic therapy requires CT chest to exclude an underlying endobronchial obstruction (e.g., bronchogenic carcinoma) or other pathology (empyema, lung abscess). Repeat X-ray alone (Option A) delays diagnosis of malignancy. Sputum culture (Option C) alone is insufficient. Bronchoscopy (Option D) may be needed but CT should precede it to plan the procedure.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.topicTitle: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.prompt: Gadolinium-based contrast agents are contraindicated in which patient group due to risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF)?
options: Patients with mild renal impairment (eGFR 60–89 mL/min)
Patients with severe renal failure (eGFR <30 mL/min) not on dialysis
questions.answer: Patients with severe renal failure (eGFR <30 mL/min) not on dialysis
questions.explanation: Nephrogenic Systemic Fibrosis (NSF) is a serious fibrosing condition associated with gadolinium contrast agents in patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min) or acute kidney injury. The risk is highest with linear gadolinium agents. Macrocyclic agents have a much lower risk profile. Mild renal impairment (Option A) is generally safe with appropriate agents. Age (Option C) and iodine allergy (Option D) are not direct contraindications to gadolinium.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.topicTitle: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old male presents with acute scrotal pain. The investigation of choice to differentiate testicular torsion from epididymo-orchitis is:
questions.explanation: Doppler ultrasound (colour and power Doppler) is the investigation of choice for acute scrotal pain. In testicular torsion, there is absent or markedly reduced testicular blood flow. In epididymo-orchitis, there is increased flow (hyperaemia). This distinction is critical as torsion requires emergency surgical exploration within 6 hours. Plain X-ray (Option A) has no role. CT (Option B) and MRI (Option D) are not first-line for this condition.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.topicTitle: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.prompt: A 65-year-old man presents with acute onset dysphagia and regurgitation. A contrast swallow study is requested. Why is water-soluble contrast preferred over barium initially?
options: Water-soluble contrast provides better mucosal detail
Water-soluble contrast is safer if aspiration occurs, and avoids peritoneal contamination from perforation
Barium is contraindicated in all elderly patients
questions.answer: Water-soluble contrast is safer if aspiration occurs, and avoids peritoneal contamination from perforation
questions.explanation: Water-soluble contrast (e.g., Gastrografin) is preferred initially in suspected oesophageal perforation or obstruction because, if aspirated into the lungs, it is absorbed without causing pneumonitis (unlike barium, which causes severe chemical pneumonia). If a perforation is present, water-soluble contrast will not cause barium peritonitis. However, if aspiration risk is high, water-soluble contrast can still cause pulmonary oedema — in that case, dilute barium may be preferred. Barium provides better mucosal detail (Option A) — this is a reason to prefer barium, not water-soluble.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.topicTitle: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.prompt: Which is the first-line investigation for suspected pulmonary embolism (PE) in a haemodynamically stable patient with a normal chest X-ray?
questions.explanation: CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the current first-line investigation for suspected PE in most patients. It is fast, widely available, highly sensitive and specific, and can diagnose alternative conditions. V/Q scanning (Option A) is preferred in pregnancy, renal impairment, or contrast allergy. Conventional pulmonary angiography (Option C) is the gold standard but invasive and now rarely used. Chest X-ray alone (Option D) is usually normal or non-specific in PE.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.topicTitle: Investigation of choice — first-line imaging, best confirmatory investigation, contraindications
questions.prompt: A neonate presents with bilious vomiting on day 1 of life. Plain X-ray shows the double-bubble sign. What is the next most appropriate investigation?
options: Upper GI contrast study to exclude malrotation/volvulus
questions.answer: Upper GI contrast study to exclude malrotation/volvulus
questions.explanation: Although the double-bubble sign is highly suggestive of duodenal atresia, bilious vomiting in a neonate must first exclude midgut malrotation with volvulus — a surgical emergency. An upper GI contrast study demonstrates the position of the duodeno-jejunal flexure (DJ flexure): normally to the left of the spine at the level of the pylorus. If the DJ flexure is malpositioned, urgent surgery is required. CT (Option A) involves radiation and is not first-line in neonates. MRI (Option C) is not practical in an emergency. Repeat X-ray (Option D) delays treatment.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.topicTitle: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.prompt: A patient undergoes CT-guided lung biopsy of a right upper lobe nodule. Which is the most common complication?
questions.explanation: Pneumothorax is the most common complication of CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy, occurring in approximately 20–35% of cases, with about one-third requiring chest drain insertion. Risk factors include emphysema, deeper lesions, and smaller lesion size. Haemothorax (Option A) and air embolism (Option B) are rare but serious complications. Significant pulmonary haemorrhage requiring transfusion (Option D) is uncommon.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.topicTitle: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.prompt: A 72-year-old man with intermittent claudication is referred for digital subtraction angiography (DSA). Which statement correctly describes DSA?
options: A pre-contrast mask image is subtracted from post-contrast images to remove background bone and soft tissue
DSA is a non-invasive technique equivalent to CT angiography
DSA uses MRI technology to image blood vessels
questions.answer: A pre-contrast mask image is subtracted from post-contrast images to remove background bone and soft tissue
questions.explanation: Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) works by electronically subtracting a pre-contrast 'mask' image from subsequent post-contrast images, removing background structures (bone, soft tissue) to leave only the contrast-filled vessels visible. This requires intra-arterial contrast injection via a catheter. It is invasive (Option C is incorrect). It uses X-rays and iodinated contrast, not MRI (Option D). Contrast is essential (Option A is wrong).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.topicTitle: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old woman undergoes image-guided percutaneous drainage of a hepatic abscess. During the procedure, she develops hypotension, tachycardia, and rigors. What is the most likely complication?
questions.explanation: Bacteraemia and septicaemia (septic shock) is a well-recognised complication of abscess drainage, occurring when bacteria enter the bloodstream during the procedure. Prophylactic antibiotics are administered before the procedure to reduce this risk. Pneumothorax (Option A) can occur with high-riding abscesses. Contrast reactions (Option B) would present with urticaria/bronchospasm. Haemobilia (Option D) is bleeding into the biliary tree, a later complication.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.topicTitle: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.prompt: ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography) is performed for a patient with obstructive jaundice. Which finding on ERCP confirms common bile duct (CBD) stone disease?
options: A smooth tapering of the CBD
A filling defect within a dilated CBD
Complete obstruction at the porta hepatis
questions.answer: A filling defect within a dilated CBD
questions.explanation: CBD calculi (choledocholithiasis) appear as filling defects within a dilated common bile duct on ERCP, often with a 'meniscus sign' at the superior margin of the stone. Smooth tapering (Option A) suggests a benign stricture or extrinsic compression. Complete porta hepatis obstruction (Option C) may suggest metastatic disease or cholangiocarcinoma. Irregular mid-CBD stricture (Option D) raises concern for malignancy (cholangiocarcinoma).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.topicTitle: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old man undergoes percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Following the procedure, he develops flank pain, a drop in haemoglobin, and a haematoma at the femoral access site. What complication has occurred?
options: Femoral artery pseudo-aneurysm or retroperitoneal haematoma
questions.answer: Femoral artery pseudo-aneurysm or retroperitoneal haematoma
questions.explanation: Femoral access site complications following PCI include pseudo-aneurysm (incomplete arterial wall closure), haematoma, arteriovenous fistula, and retroperitoneal haematoma. Flank pain with haemoglobin drop and groin haematoma following femoral artery access indicates retroperitoneal haematoma — a serious but recognisable complication. Coronary dissection (Option A) would cause chest pain. Contrast nephropathy (Option B) causes rising creatinine. PE (Option D) causes respiratory symptoms.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.topicTitle: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.prompt: A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) is indicated for which condition?
options: Hepatocellular carcinoma with portal vein thrombosis
Refractory variceal bleeding in portal hypertension
questions.answer: Refractory variceal bleeding in portal hypertension
questions.explanation: TIPS is indicated for refractory variceal bleeding, refractory ascites, hepatic hydrothorax, and Budd-Chiari syndrome — all complications of portal hypertension. It creates a shunt between the hepatic vein and portal vein via a transjugular approach, reducing portal pressure. Portal vein thrombosis (Option A) is actually a relative contraindication. Acute cholecystitis (Option C) and hepatic artery aneurysm (Option D) have no role for TIPS.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.topicTitle: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.prompt: During a barium enema examination, barium enters the peritoneal cavity through a colonic perforation. What is the most serious consequence?
options: Barium peritonitis — a life-threatening condition with high mortality
questions.answer: Barium peritonitis — a life-threatening condition with high mortality
questions.explanation: Barium peritonitis following perforation during barium enema is a life-threatening emergency with mortality rates approaching 50–80% if untreated. Barium sulphate causes intense chemical peritonitis, leading to sepsis and multi-organ failure. This is why water-soluble contrast is used when perforation is suspected. Options A and C grossly understate the severity. Temporary obstruction (Option D) is not the primary concern.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.topicTitle: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.prompt: A patient has a PET-CT scan showing an FDG-avid right hilar mass. What does increased FDG uptake in the mass indicate?
options: The mass is a benign lipoma
The mass has high metabolic activity, consistent with malignancy
The mass is a pulmonary hamartoma
The mass is a simple cyst
questions.answer: The mass has high metabolic activity, consistent with malignancy
questions.explanation: PET-CT uses F-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), a glucose analogue, that accumulates in metabolically active (high glucose uptake) cells. Malignant tumours have high FDG avidity due to the Warburg effect (preferential aerobic glycolysis). FDG-avid lesions are suspicious for malignancy or active infection/inflammation. Benign lipomas (Option A), hamartomas (Option C), and simple cysts (Option D) do not accumulate FDG significantly.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.topicTitle: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.prompt: After a percutaneous nephrostomy is placed for obstructed pyonephrosis, the nephrostogram shows contrast outlining dilated calyces with a smooth tapering at the pelviureteric junction (PUJ). What does this indicate?
options: PUJ obstruction as the cause of hydronephrosis
Transitional cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis
questions.answer: PUJ obstruction as the cause of hydronephrosis
questions.explanation: A nephrostogram showing dilated calyces and renal pelvis with smooth tapering at the PUJ — and no contrast passing into the ureter — is diagnostic of pelviureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction. This can be intrinsic (smooth muscle dysfunction) or extrinsic (crossing vessel). A mid-ureteric stone (Option A) would show obstruction lower down. Normal anatomy (Option C) would show free flow of contrast. TCC (Option D) would show an irregular filling defect.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.topic: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.topicTitle: Radiological procedures — indications, complications, interpretation of findings
questions.prompt: A radiologist performs ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of a thyroid nodule. The pathology report returns 'Thy3f' (follicular neoplasm). What does this classification indicate?
options: Definitely benign — no further action required
Follicular neoplasm — surgical hemithyroidectomy recommended for definitive histological diagnosis
questions.answer: Follicular neoplasm — surgical hemithyroidectomy recommended for definitive histological diagnosis
questions.explanation: The Thy3f (Bethesda category IV) classification indicates a follicular neoplasm, which cannot be definitively classified as benign or malignant on cytology alone because follicular carcinoma is distinguished from adenoma by vascular and capsular invasion — features only assessable on surgical histology. Hemithyroidectomy (diagnostic lobectomy) is the standard management. Thy1 = inadequate (Option D). Thy2 = benign (Option A). Thy5 = malignant (Option B).

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old male is scheduled for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During direct laryngoscopy using a Macintosh 3 blade, only the epiglottis is visualized; the vocal cords cannot be seen despite external laryngeal manipulation. According to the modified Cormack-Lehane classification, which grade best describes this view?
questions.explanation: Option C is correct: Grade 3 in the Cormack-Lehane system represents visualization of the epiglottis only, with no glottic aperture or arytenoid structures visible. Option A is incorrect: Grade 2a represents partial visualization of the vocal cords. Option B is incorrect: Grade 2b represents visualization of only the arytenoids or posterior part of the vocal cords, not just the epiglottis. Option D is incorrect: Grade 4 represents visualization of the soft palate only, where even the epiglottis is not visible.

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: An anesthesiologist is evaluating a 9-month-old infant prior to cleft palate repair. Which anatomical feature of the pediatric airway distinguishes it from the adult airway?
options: The larynx is positioned at the level of C1-C2
The epiglottis is shorter, flatter, and stiffer than in adults
The narrowest non-distensible anatomical portion of the pediatric airway is at the cricoid ring
The infant tongue is proportionally smaller relative to the oral cavity
questions.answer: The narrowest non-distensible anatomical portion of the pediatric airway is at the cricoid ring
questions.explanation: Option C is correct: Anatomically and clinically, the non-distensible cricoid ring forms the narrowest circular portion of the infant larynx, making it prone to subglottic edema and post-extubation croup. Option A is incorrect: The infant larynx is positioned more cephalad, typically at the level of C3-C4 (versus C4-C5 or C5-C6 in adults), not C1-C2. Option B is incorrect: The infant epiglottis is long, narrow, floppy, and omega-shaped (U-shaped), angled obliquely over the glottis. Option D is incorrect: The infant tongue is proportionally larger relative to the smaller oral cavity, predisposing to upper airway obstruction.

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: Regarding tracheobronchial anatomy, which of the following statements correctly differentiates the right mainstem bronchus from the left mainstem bronchus?
options: The right main bronchus takes off at a wider angle (45 degrees) from the midline compared to the left
The right main bronchus is shorter, wider, and diverges at approximately 25 degrees from the vertical axis
The right main bronchus gives off its upper lobe bronchus 5 cm distal to the carina
Endobronchial intubation occurs more frequently in the left mainstem bronchus due to cardiac positioning
questions.answer: The right main bronchus is shorter, wider, and diverges at approximately 25 degrees from the vertical axis
questions.explanation: Option B is correct: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter (~2.5 cm long vs 5 cm on the left), and branches more vertically (approx. 25° from the vertical line vs 45° for the left), making accidental right mainstem intubation and foreign body aspiration far more common. Option A is incorrect: The right bronchus diverges at ~25°, whereas the left bronchus diverges at ~45°. Option C is incorrect: The right upper lobe bronchus branches very early, typically only 1.5–2 cm from the carina (sometimes as close as 1 cm). Option D is incorrect: Inadvertent endobronchial intubation overwhelmingly occurs on the right side due to its vertical alignment.

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: During a midline lumbar puncture for spinal anesthesia at the L3-L4 interspace, which is the correct sequence of anatomical structures traversed by the needle from superficial to deep before entering the subarachnoid space?
options: Skin, subcutaneous fat, interspinous ligament, supraspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, dura mater, arachnoid mater
Skin, subcutaneous fat, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura mater, arachnoid mater
Skin, subcutaneous fat, ligamentum flavum, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, dura mater, subarachnoid space
Skin, subcutaneous fat, supraspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, interspinous ligament, subdural space, arachnoid mater
questions.answer: Skin, subcutaneous fat, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura mater, arachnoid mater
questions.explanation: Option B is correct: The standard midline approach traverses: skin -> subcutaneous tissue -> supraspinous ligament -> interspinous ligament -> ligamentum flavum -> epidural space -> dura mater -> arachnoid mater -> subarachnoid space. Option A is incorrect: The supraspinous ligament is superficial to the interspinous ligament. Option C is incorrect: The ligamentum flavum is deep to both the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments. Option D is incorrect: The interspinous ligament lies superficial to the ligamentum flavum.

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: Cerebral blood flow (CBF) autoregulation maintains constant perfusion across a range of mean arterial pressures (MAP). Within what range of MAP does intact cerebral autoregulation typically function in a normotensive healthy adult?
questions.explanation: Option B is correct: In healthy normotensive individuals, CBF remains constant at ~50 mL/100g/min across a mean arterial pressure of 50 to 150 mmHg via arteriolar myogenic response. Below 50 mmHg, ischemia and hypoperfusion occur; above 150 mmHg, hyperperfusion and blood-brain barrier disruption occur. Option A is incorrect: 20 to 80 mmHg is severely shifted to the left and causes cerebral ischemia below 50 mmHg. Options C and D are incorrect: These ranges are shifted too high, representing limits seen only in chronic uncontrolled severe hypertension.

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: A healthy 32-year-old female undergoes induction of general anesthesia with neuromuscular blockade. Induction and muscle paralysis produce an immediate change in respiratory mechanics. What happens to the Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) in the supine position upon induction of general anesthesia?
options: FRC increases by approximately 500 mL due to positive pressure ventilation
FRC decreases by approximately 15% to 20% primarily due to cephalad displacement of the diaphragm
FRC remains unchanged because the chest wall recoil balances lung compliance
FRC drops strictly below residual volume, causing universal lobar collapse
questions.answer: FRC decreases by approximately 15% to 20% primarily due to cephalad displacement of the diaphragm
questions.explanation: Option B is correct: Changing from standing to supine reduces FRC by ~0.5–1 L, and induction of general anesthesia causes muscle relaxation and loss of chest wall tone, allowing abdominal contents to displace the diaphragm cephalad, reducing FRC by an additional 15–20% (~400–500 mL). Option A is incorrect: General anesthesia reduces FRC rather than increasing it. Option C is incorrect: Significant cephalad shift of the diaphragm and loss of tone prevent FRC from remaining constant. Option D is incorrect: FRC consists of Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) plus Residual Volume (RV); FRC cannot fall below RV as RV is the gas remaining after maximal expiration.

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: According to the Hagen-Poiseuille equation for laminar flow through a cylindrical conduit, if the internal radius of an intravenous cannula is doubled while maintaining constant length and pressure gradient, the flow rate increases by a factor of:
questions.explanation: Option D is correct: The Hagen-Poiseuille equation states Q = (pi * DeltaP * r^4) / (8 * eta * l). Flow (Q) is directly proportional to the fourth power of the radius (r^4). Doubling the radius (2^4) increases flow by 16-fold. Options A, B, and C are incorrect: They reflect linear (r^1 = 2), square (r^2 = 4), or cubic (r^3 = 8) relationships, which underestimate the 16-fold increase.

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: During fluid and gas flow across anesthetic breathing systems and endotracheal tubes, flow transition from laminar to turbulent occurs when the Reynolds number exceeds which critical threshold?
questions.explanation: Option C is correct: Reynolds number (Re = (rho * v * d) / eta) predicts flow character. Re < 2000 is predominantly laminar (governed by viscosity), Re between 2000 and 4000 is transitional, and Re > 4000 (with onset often starting above 2000) is turbulent (governed primarily by fluid density). Option A is incorrect: 200 is well within the laminar flow realm. Option B is incorrect: 1000 maintains predictable laminar flow. Option D is incorrect: 10000 is fully developed turbulence, well past the transition point.

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: An anesthesia technician connects a medical gas cylinder to the anesthesia machine yoke. Which pin combination on the Pin Index Safety System (PISS) corresponds specifically to an Oxygen cylinder?
questions.explanation: Option B is correct: Oxygen uses pin index positions 2 and 5. Option A is incorrect: Positions 1 and 5 are designated for Medical Air. Option C is incorrect: Positions 3 and 5 are designated for Nitrous Oxide (N2O). Option D is incorrect: Positions 2 and 6 are designated for Entonox (50% O2 / 50% N2O).

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: At room temperature (20 degrees Celsius), an E-cylinder of Nitrous Oxide contains both liquid and gas, maintaining a constant pressure of 745 psig until the liquid is exhausted. Why can Nitrous Oxide remain liquefied in a cylinder at room temperature while Oxygen cannot?
options: Nitrous Oxide has a critical temperature of 36.5 degrees Celsius, whereas Oxygen has a critical temperature of -118 degrees Celsius
Nitrous Oxide has a lower critical pressure than Oxygen, allowing rapid condensation
Oxygen molecules undergo dimerization at room temperature, preventing liquefaction
Nitrous Oxide reacts with the brass cylinder casing, forming a liquid amalgam
questions.answer: Nitrous Oxide has a critical temperature of 36.5 degrees Celsius, whereas Oxygen has a critical temperature of -118 degrees Celsius
questions.explanation: Option A is correct: Critical temperature is the temperature above which a substance cannot be liquefied regardless of the applied pressure. Nitrous oxide's critical temperature is 36.5°C (above room temperature of 20°C), so it exists as liquid and gas in equilibrium. Oxygen's critical temperature is -118°C (far below room temperature), so it can only exist as a gas at 20°C. Option B is incorrect: Critical pressure is not the limiting physical property preventing liquefaction above critical temperature. Option C is incorrect: Oxygen does not dimerize to prevent liquefaction. Option D is incorrect: Nitrous oxide does not form amalgams with brass.

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: On October 16, 1846, the first successful public demonstration of surgical ether anesthesia was conducted at Massachusetts General Hospital. Who was the dentist/anesthetist who administered the diethyl ether?
questions.explanation: Option C is correct: William T. G. Morton publicly demonstrated diethyl ether ("Letheon") for the excision of a neck tumor by surgeon John Collins Warren on October 16, 1846 ("Ether Day"). Option A is incorrect: Crawford Long used ether earlier in 1842 in Georgia but did not publish or publicly demonstrate his results until 1849. Option B is incorrect: Horace Wells demonstrated nitrous oxide in 1845, which was deemed a failure when the patient groaned. Option D is incorrect: Charles T. Jackson was a chemist who suggested ether to Morton, but did not administer it.

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: Who was the Scottish obstetrician who first introduced chloroform into clinical anesthesia practice in 1847 to relieve labor pain?
questions.explanation: Option A is correct: Sir James Young Simpson discovered the anesthetic properties of chloroform on himself and colleagues and introduced it into clinical obstetric practice in November 1847. Option B is incorrect: John Snow was the first full-time physician anesthetist who famously administered chloroform to Queen Victoria in 1853, but did not discover its clinical utility. Option C is incorrect: Joseph Priestley discovered nitrous oxide and oxygen in the 1770s. Option D is incorrect: Humphry Davy synthesized nitrous oxide and suggested in 1799 that it might alleviate surgical pain.

questions.subject: Anesthesia
questions.prompt: Which Viennese ophthalmologist first introduced local anesthesia into clinical practice in 1884 by demonstrating the topical anesthetic effect of cocaine on the eye?
