Core Concept: DSM-5 requires that continuous signs of the disturbance persist for at least 6 months (which must include at least 1 month of active-phase symptoms that meet Criterion A, alongside prodromal or residual periods) for a diagnosis of Schizophrenia.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: One week is insufficient for any chronic psychotic illness (Brief Psychotic Disorder spans 1 day to 1 month).
• Option B: One month of active symptoms meets criteria for Schizophreniform Disorder in DSM-5 (duration 1 to 6 months), or satisfies the duration criterion in ICD-10.
• Option C: Six months of total illness duration (including prodrome/residual) is the explicit DSM-5 timeline required for Schizophrenia.
• Option D: Two years is the duration required for dysthymia or cyclothymia, not the baseline requirement for schizophrenia.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: Which neurochemical pathway in the brain is primarily hypothesized to be HYPERACTIVE, leading to positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions) in schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: The dopamine hypothesis posits that hyperactivity in the mesolimbic dopamine tract (ventral tegmental area projecting to the nucleus accumbens) mediates positive psychotic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations). Conversely, mesocortical hypodopaminergia contributes to negative and cognitive symptoms.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Hyperactivity of mesolimbic D2 receptors produces positive symptoms; D2 antagonism here treats psychosis.
• Option B: Mesocortical hypofunction (to prefrontal cortex) is linked to negative symptoms and cognitive deficits.
• Option C: Nigrostriatal tract regulates extrapyramidal motor control; D2 blockade here causes drug-induced parkinsonism.
• Option D: Tuberoinfundibular tract inhibits prolactin; D2 blockade here produces hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhea, and amenorrhea.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 26-year-old male with chronic schizophrenia exhibits stupor, mutism, and maintains an awkward, uncomfortable posture against gravity for hours after being passively positioned by the examiner. When the examiner gently tries to move his arm, the patient provides an equal and opposite resistance proportional to the applied force. What two catatonic signs are demonstrated?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: In catatonia, maintaining an uncomfortable posture or offering plastic resistance resembling bending a wax candle is known as waxy flexibility (flexibilitas cerea) or catalepsy. Gegenhalten (oppositional paratonia) is active resistance to passive movements that increases in proportion to the force exerted by the examiner.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Plastic postural maintenance (catalepsy/waxy flexibility) and proportional oppositional resistance (Gegenhalten) are hallmark signs of catatonia.
• Option B: Echolalia is vocal echoing; echopraxia is motor mimicry of examiner actions.
• Option C: Ambitendency is vacillation between conflicting motor impulses; mannerisms are exaggerated caricatures of normal goal-directed movements.
• Option D: Stereotypies are repetitive, purposeless non-goal-directed movements; tics are sudden, rapid, recurrent motor or vocal twitches.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 21-year-old male treated with Haloperidol for 4 days suddenly develops acute, painful, sustained upward deviation of both eyes (oculogyric crisis) and involuntary neck twisting (torticollis). He is extremely distressed. What is the emergency pharmacological treatment of choice?
options: Anticholinergic agent (e.g., Intramuscular/IV Promethazine or Diphenhydramine or Trihexyphenidyl)
questions.answer: Anticholinergic agent (e.g., Intramuscular/IV Promethazine or Diphenhydramine or Trihexyphenidyl)
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Acute dystonia is an extrapyramidal side effect (EPS) occurring within hours to days of starting high-potency D2 antagonists, caused by an acute dopamine-acetylcholine imbalance in the basal ganglia. Central anticholinergic medications (e.g., parenteral diphenhydramine, promethazine, benztropine) promptly restore cholinergic-dopaminergic balance.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Parenteral anticholinergic agents immediately reverse acute dystonic contractions.
• Option B: Increasing haloperidol exacerbates dopamine blockade and intensifies the life-threatening dystonic spasm.
• Option C: Propranolol is the first-line medication for akathisia, not acute muscular dystonia.
• Option D: ECT is reserved for refractory psychosis or malignant catatonia, not acute medication-induced dystonia.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old female with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is started on Clozapine. After 6 weeks of dose titration, she develops a high-grade fever, sore throat, and mouth ulcers. A complete blood count reveals an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 420/μL. What is the diagnosis and mandatory clinical action?
options: Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis; immediately discontinue clozapine, isolate the patient, and administer prophylactic antibiotics/G-CSF
Normal clozapine-induced benign fever; continue clozapine and add paracetamol
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; administer bromocriptine while continuing clozapine
Streptococcal pharyngitis; continue clozapine and give oral penicillin
questions.answer: Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis; immediately discontinue clozapine, isolate the patient, and administer prophylactic antibiotics/G-CSF
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Clozapine carries a 0.5–1% risk of life-threatening agranulocytosis (defined as ANC < 500/μL). When agranulocytosis occurs, Clozapine must be stopped immediately and permanently, the patient isolated, and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) with infectious disease care initiated.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: ANC < 500/μL with fever/sore throat is acute agranulocytosis; immediate permanent discontinuation is mandatory to prevent fatal sepsis.
• Option B: Overlooking severe neutropenia as 'benign fever' leads to fatal septicemia.
• Option C: NMS is characterized by severe 'lead-pipe' muscular rigidity, autonomic instability, and elevated CPK, not isolated severe neutropenia.
• Option D: While pharyngitis is present, it is a secondary manifestation of Clozapine-induced bone marrow suppression.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: Which of the following clinical features is classified as a 'negative symptom' of Schizophrenia?
options: Avolition (Loss of motivation and goal-directed activity)
questions.answer: Avolition (Loss of motivation and goal-directed activity)
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: The negative symptoms of schizophrenia (the '5 A's') represent a loss or deficit of normal mental functioning: Avolition, Alogia (poverty of speech), Anhedonia, Asociality, and Affective flattening.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Delusions are positive symptoms (excess or distortion of normal function).
• Option B: Hallucinations are classic positive symptoms.
• Option C: Avolition is a core negative symptom representing diminished motivation and initiative.
• Option D: Catatonic behavior is classified under disorganized motor/psychomotor behavior.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: Which of the following factors is statistically associated with a GOOD/FAVORABLE prognosis in schizophrenia?
options: Prominent negative symptoms and structural brain changes on neuroimaging
Late and acute onset, presence of precipitating stressor, and prominent affective symptoms
Family history of chronic schizophrenia and poor premorbid social adjustment
questions.answer: Late and acute onset, presence of precipitating stressor, and prominent affective symptoms
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Good prognostic indicators in schizophrenia include: acute onset, late age of onset, female sex, identifiable precipitating life events, married status, good premorbid social/academic functioning, prominent affective (depressive/manic) symptoms, positive symptoms, and absence of structural brain anomalies.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Insidious onset and early age of onset strongly correlate with poor long-term outcomes.
• Option B: Negative symptoms and enlarged ventricles are strong indicators of poor prognosis and treatment resistance.
• Option C: Acute onset with clear stressors and mood symptoms predicts a significantly better prognosis and treatment response.
• Option D: Genetic burden of schizophrenia and poor premorbid functioning correlate with refractory illness.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old male with schizophrenia has been on long-term Haloperidol for 7 years. Over the past 6 months, his family noticed repetitive, involuntary, choreoathetoid movements of his tongue, lip smacking, and grimacing. The movements temporarily disappear during sleep and worsen when he is stressed. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Tardive dyskinesia is a late-onset, potentially irreversible adverse effect of chronic dopamine antagonist therapy, caused by postsynaptic D2 receptor supersensitivity and upregulation in the striatum. It manifests as involuntary oro-facial-lingual movements (lip smacking, tongue protrusion/fly-catcher tongue) and choreoathetoid movements.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Acute dystonia occurs early (days), not after 7 years of maintenance treatment.
• Option B: Involuntary oro-bucco-lingual movements after long-term neuroleptic exposure define tardive dyskinesia.
• Option C: Drug-induced parkinsonism presents with bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor, not choreic orofacial hyperkinesia.
• Option D: Akathisia is a subjective inner motor restlessness compelling the patient to pace or fidget continuously.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: According to DSM-5 criteria, what is the minimum duration of persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood required to diagnose a Manic Episode (unless hospitalization is required)?
options: At least 1 full week (7 consecutive days)
questions.answer: At least 1 full week (7 consecutive days)
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: A Manic Episode requires a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood lasting at least 1 week (or any duration if hospitalization becomes necessary).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Exactly 1 week (7 days) is the DSM-5 threshold for a Manic Episode.
• Option B: Two weeks is the minimum duration required for a Major Depressive Episode.
• Option C: One month is the criteria for disorders like PTSD or schizophreniform active phase.
• Option D: Six months is the threshold for generalized anxiety disorder or schizophrenia.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: What is the key diagnostic boundary separating Bipolar I Disorder from Bipolar II Disorder?
options: Bipolar I requires at least one lifetime Manic episode, whereas Bipolar II requires at least one Hypomanic episode and at least one Major Depressive episode without any history of mania
Bipolar I never has depressive episodes, while Bipolar II only has depressive episodes
Bipolar II involves severe psychosis with mania, while Bipolar I is mild
Bipolar I is diagnosed exclusively in children, while Bipolar II is diagnosed in the elderly
questions.answer: Bipolar I requires at least one lifetime Manic episode, whereas Bipolar II requires at least one Hypomanic episode and at least one Major Depressive episode without any history of mania
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: The presence of even a single lifetime manic episode establishes the diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder (regardless of whether major depressive episodes have occurred). Bipolar II Disorder requires at least one hypomanic episode AND at least one major depressive episode, with NO history of full manic episodes.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Bipolar I is defined by full mania; Bipolar II is defined by hypomania plus major depression with no lifetime mania.
• Option B: Most patients with Bipolar I experience severe depressive episodes throughout their lifetimes.
• Option C: Psychosis by definition upgrades any elevated episode to full Mania (Bipolar I); Bipolar II hypomania cannot feature psychosis.
• Option D: Both disorders can present across adolescence and adulthood.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 29-year-old female presents with low mood, profound fatigue, and sadness. Further inquiry reveals that she experiences mood reactivity (mood brightens in response to positive events), hyperphagia with substantial weight gain, hypersomnia (sleeping 12 hours/day), and 'leaden paralysis' (heavy, leaden feeling in arms and legs). What specific subtype of depression is this?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Atypical depression is characterized by mood reactivity (ability to cheer up temporarily with positive stimuli) combined with reversed vegetative symptoms: hypersomnia, hyperphagia/weight gain, leaden paralysis, and long-standing interpersonal rejection sensitivity.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Melancholic depression features non-reactive mood, terminal/early morning insomnia, anorexia/weight loss, and excessive guilt.
• Option B: Mood reactivity, hyperphagia, hypersomnia, and leaden paralysis are the hallmark criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with atypical features.
• Option C: Catatonic depression presents with posturing, mutism, stupor, or negativism.
• Option D: Psychotic depression requires presence of delusions (e.g., poverty, guilt) or hallucinations.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: Which of the following represents the classic Cognitive Triad of Depression formulated by Aaron Beck?
options: Negative views about the Self, the World (Environment), and the Future
Delusions of persecution, grandiosity, and reference
Fear of spiders, heights, and enclosed spaces
questions.answer: Negative views about the Self, the World (Environment), and the Future
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Aaron Beck's cognitive theory of depression posits that negative automatic thoughts stem from a dysfunctional cognitive triad: negative, distorted evaluation of (1) oneself, (2) the world/current experiences, and (3) the future.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Negative views of the self ('I am worthless'), world ('Everything is terrible'), and future ('Nothing will ever improve') form Beck's cognitive triad.
• Option B: These are psychotic delusions, not Beck's depressive schema.
• Option C: These are specific phobic anxieties.
• Option D: These describe Kluver-Bucy syndrome or atypical/manic features.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 38-year-old male with Bipolar I Disorder on maintenance Lithium therapy presents with progressive coarse tremors, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, and persistent vomiting. His serum lithium level is measured at 2.4 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Reassure the patient and increase the lithium dose
Immediately withhold lithium, give IV normal saline infusion, monitor vitals, and prepare for hemodialysis if clinical status deteriorates
Add oral thiazide diuretics to enhance lithium clearance
questions.answer: Immediately withhold lithium, give IV normal saline infusion, monitor vitals, and prepare for hemodialysis if clinical status deteriorates
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Therapeutic serum lithium levels range from 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L (maintenance: 0.6–0.8 mEq/L). Levels >2.0 mEq/L indicate life-threatening toxicity with neurotoxicity (coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, seizures). Lithium must be stopped, hydration with saline initiated (sodium promotes lithium excretion), and hemodialysis considered for levels >2.5 mEq/L (or >4.0 mEq/L regardless of symptoms).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Increasing the dose would be lethal; 2.4 mEq/L is in the toxic range.
• Option B: Discontinuing lithium, aggressive hydration with isotonic saline, and hemodynamic support/dialysis preparation is standard life-saving therapy.
• Option C: Potassium has no role; lithium excretion is linked to sodium and renal proximal tubule handling.
• Option D: Thiazide diuretics reduce renal lithium clearance and severely worsen lithium toxicity.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 26-year-old female in her first trimester of pregnancy has severe bipolar disorder. The clinician avoids prescribing Sodium Valproate primarily because of its established association with which congenital malformation?
options: Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the cervix
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Sodium Valproate is a potent teratogen associated with a 1–2% risk of neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly), craniofacial defects, and neurodevelopmental impairment when used in early pregnancy.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Ebstein's anomaly (tricuspid valve downward displacement) is classically linked to first-trimester Lithium exposure.
• Option B: Neural tube defects are strongly linked to Valproate teratogenicity due to folate metabolism disruption.
• Option C: Phocomelia (limb malformations) was caused by thalidomide.
• Option D: Clear cell vaginal/cervical adenocarcinoma is associated with in utero diethylstilbestrol (DES) exposure.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: What is the minimum duration of chronic, fluctuating low mood and mild depressive symptoms (without meeting full criteria for a major depressive episode) required to diagnose Dysthymia (Persistent Depressive Disorder) in adults?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Dysthymia / Persistent Depressive Disorder in adults requires a chronic depressed mood for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 years (in children and adolescents, the duration threshold is 1 year).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Six months is the minimum duration for GAD, not dysthymia in adults.
• Option B: One year is the diagnostic duration required for children/adolescents with dysthymia.
• Option C: Exactly 2 years of persistent depressive symptoms is the adult diagnostic standard in DSM-5 and ICD-10.
• Option D: Five years is unnecessarily prolonged; early clinical diagnosis prevents chronic morbidity.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 74-year-old widow presents with severe melancholic depression, refusing food and water for 4 days. She is convinced that her intestines have completely rotted away, her heart has stopped beating, and that she is technically already dead and residing in hell. What specific psychopathological syndrome is this?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Cotard's syndrome (nihilistic delusions / délire de négation) is a severe neuropsychiatric syndrome seen in psychotic depression or organic brain lesions where the patient denies their own existence, believing they are dead, putrefied, or have lost their internal organs, blood, or soul.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Believing that internal organs are rotted and that one is dead represents classic nihilistic delusions of Cotard's syndrome.
• Option B: Capgras syndrome involves the delusion of doubles/impostors replacing loved ones.
• Option C: Othello syndrome is morbid, delusional jealousy regarding partner infidelity.
• Option D: Clérambault syndrome (erotomania) is the delusion of being loved by someone of elevated status.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old male is started on an antidepressant. Three weeks later, he presents to the clinic with severe anorgasmia and delayed ejaculation, which is causing marital distress. Which class of antidepressants is most commonly associated with treatment-emergent sexual dysfunction?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine) cause sexual dysfunction (loss of libido, delayed ejaculation, anorgasmia) in up to 30–70% of patients due to stimulation of postsynaptic 5-HT2A and 5-HT2C receptors in the spinal cord and limbic system.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: SSRIs have the highest rates of sexual dysfunction among commonly prescribed antidepressants.
• Option B: Bupropion acts via norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibition (NDRI) and has virtually no sexual side effects (often used as an antidote).
• Option C: Mirtazapine is a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA) with 5-HT2 blockade, sparing sexual function.
• Option D: Agomelatine acts on melatonergic and 5-HT2C receptors, with negligible sexual side effects.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 31-year-old female with major depression on Phenelzine (a Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitor) attends an Italian banquet where she consumes aged cheese, salami, and red wine. Within an hour, she develops severe occipital headache, palpitations, neck stiffness, and BP spikes to 220/130 mmHg. What substance in the food triggered this hypertensive crisis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Ingestion of aged cheeses, cured meats, and yeast extracts rich in tyramine while on non-selective MAO inhibitors blocks gastrointestinal and hepatic MAO-A. Unmetabolized tyramine enters systemic circulation, gets taken up into sympathetic terminals, and displaces massive amounts of stored norepinephrine into the synaptic cleft, triggering a life-threatening hyperadrenergic crisis ('cheese reaction').

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Tyramine displacement of stored norepinephrine causes the catastrophic hypertensive crisis.
• Option B: Tryptophan is a serotonin precursor linked to serotonin syndrome when combined with serotonergics, not the tyramine cheese crisis.
• Option C: Phenylalanine is an essential amino acid elevated in phenylketonuria, not the trigger for the cheese reaction.
• Option D: Histamine causes scombroid fish poisoning and allergic flush, not sympathetic-mediated severe hypertensive crisis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: What is the defining clinical feature of Delusional Disorder (Paranoia) according to standard diagnostic criteria?
options: Non-bizarre or circumscribed delusions lasting at least 1 month, with well-preserved personality, logical coherence, and absence of prominent hallucinations
Severe formal thought disorder with prominent visual hallucinations and rapid dementia
Continuous catatonic posturing and mutism for at least 6 months
Absence of any delusions or false beliefs
questions.answer: Non-bizarre or circumscribed delusions lasting at least 1 month, with well-preserved personality, logical coherence, and absence of prominent hallucinations
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Delusional Disorder is defined by the presence of one or more non-bizarre or circumscribed delusions lasting at least 1 month, where cognitive functions, intellectual faculties, emotional responsiveness outside the delusional system, and daily functioning remain remarkably well-preserved.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Well-systematized circumscribed delusions with preserved personality and absence of bizarre schizophrenic symptoms define Delusional Disorder.
• Option B: Prominent formal thought disorder and prominent auditory/visual hallucinations fulfill criteria for Schizophrenia.
• Option C: Catatonic posturing belongs to Catatonia or Catatonic Schizophrenia.
• Option D: Delusions are the absolute core sine qua non requirement of Delusional Disorder.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 48-year-old businessman is utterly convinced without any factual basis that his loyal wife of 22 years is secretly sleeping with multiple neighborhood men. He obsessively inspects her undergarments for stains, interrogates her incessantly, secretly installs tracking devices in her car, and searches her mobile phone records daily. What specific subtype of delusional disorder is this?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: The jealous subtype of delusional disorder (morbid/pathological jealousy or Othello syndrome) is defined by the fixed, unshakeable delusion that one's spouse or sexual partner is unfaithful, accompanied by dangerous investigative behaviors, interrogations, and high risk of domestic violence.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Erotomanic type involves the delusion that another individual is secretly enamored of the patient.
• Option B: Grandiose type involves delusions of extraordinary talent, unrecognized status, or divine association.
• Option C: Unshakeable unfounded conviction of marital infidelity accompanied by compulsive searching and stalking defines the jealous subtype (Othello syndrome).
• Option D: Somatic type involves delusions related to bodily functions or sensations (e.g., infestation, foul odor, misshapen body parts).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 33-year-old woman is brought to the clinic by her sister. The patient insists that a famous Bollywood movie actor is deeply and passionately in love with her. She claims he sends her secret coded romantic messages during television interviews by blinking his eyes twice. Despite multiple formal legal restraining orders and complete lack of contact, she insists they are spiritually married. What syndrome is this?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: de Clérambault's syndrome (erotomania) is a delusional disorder subtype in which the patient holds a firm, delusional conviction that another person—invariably of higher social, economic, or celebrity status—is secretly in love with them and initiates secret communications.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Delusion of being loved by an elevated or famous person who communicates secretly is classic de Clérambault's syndrome.
• Option B: Capgras syndrome involves the delusion that a familiar close relative has been replaced by a double or impostor.
• Option C: Fregoli syndrome involves the belief that a persecutor takes on the physical appearance of different strangers.
• Option D: Ganser syndrome involves approximate answers ('parareactions'), clouding of consciousness, and somatic conversion signs.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 60-year-old woman who lives alone in an isolated rural farmhouse with her 32-year-old dependent, socially isolated daughter develops persecutory delusions that neighbors are pumping poisonous gas into their water well. Within 6 months, the daughter adopts the identical delusional system word-for-word. When the daughter is admitted to the hospital and separated from the mother, her delusions disappear completely within 3 weeks without antipsychotic therapy. What is the diagnosis for the daughter's condition?
options: Induced Delusional Disorder (Folie à deux / Shared Psychotic Disorder)
questions.answer: Induced Delusional Disorder (Folie à deux / Shared Psychotic Disorder)
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Induced Delusional Disorder (Folie à deux / Shared Psychotic Disorder) occurs when a delusional belief is transmitted from a primary case (inducer/dominant partner with a psychotic disorder) to a secondary recipient (usually a dependent, socially isolated individual). Upon physical separation from the dominant partner, the recipient's delusions typically resolve spontaneously.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Primary schizophrenia does not resolve spontaneously within 3 weeks upon simple physical separation from a relative.
• Option B: Folie à deux (shared psychosis) classically occurs in isolated pairs where the dependent person adopts the inducer's delusion, which remits on separation.
• Option C: Schizotypal disorder is an enduring trait disorder with odd behavior and eccentric thinking, not an acute adopted shared delusional system.
• Option D: Malingering involves conscious fabrication for external financial or legal gain, absent here.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old woman with a history of right temporoparietal ischemic stroke looks at her husband of 30 years and screams in terror, insisting that the man standing before her is an identical physical impostor and double who has murdered her real husband and taken his place. She recognizes that he looks and sounds identical, yet refuses to believe he is the same person. What delusional misidentification syndrome is this?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Capgras syndrome is a delusional misidentification syndrome characterized by the belief that a familiar person (usually spouse or close relative) has been replaced by an identical impostor or double. It is understood neurobiologically as a disconnection between facial visual recognition (ventral temporal stream) and emotional familiarity/affective arousal (limbic/amygdala network).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: The belief that a familiar relative is replaced by an exact physical double/impostor is Capgras syndrome.
• Option B: Fregoli syndrome is the belief that different strangers encountered are actually one familiar person in various disguises.
• Option C: Intermetamorphosis is the belief that people in the environment physically and psychologically morph into each other.
• Option D: Syndrome of subjective doubles is the belief that a physically identical doppelgänger of oneself exists and leads an independent life.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: What is the defining clinical difference between Schizoaffective Disorder and Mood Disorder with Psychotic Features?
options: Schizoaffective disorder requires at least 2 weeks of hallucinations or delusions in the ABSENCE of prominent mood symptoms during the lifetime duration of the illness
Mood disorder with psychotic features only occurs in elderly demented patients
Schizoaffective disorder never involves any depressive or manic episodes
Mood disorder with psychotic features is caused exclusively by bacterial infections
questions.answer: Schizoaffective disorder requires at least 2 weeks of hallucinations or delusions in the ABSENCE of prominent mood symptoms during the lifetime duration of the illness
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: In Schizoaffective Disorder, active psychotic symptoms must co-occur with a mood episode, BUT there must also be a period of at least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations occurring in the complete absence of significant mood symptoms. In Mood Disorder with Psychotic Features, psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during active mood episodes.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Presence of delusions or hallucinations for ≥2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode is the critical diagnostic differentiator for schizoaffective disorder.
• Option B: Mood disorders with psychosis occur across all age groups from late adolescence onwards.
• Option C: Schizoaffective disorder by definition requires concurrent major manic or depressive episodes during substantial parts of the illness.
• Option D: Mood disorders with psychosis are primary affective psychiatric illnesses, not acute bacterial infections.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: What is the maximum duration of illness allowed to diagnose 'Brief Psychotic Disorder' in DSM-5, before which full return to premorbid level of functioning must occur?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Brief Psychotic Disorder is defined by the sudden onset of at least one positive psychotic symptom (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or grossly disorganized behavior) lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month, followed by eventual full return to the premorbid level of functioning.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: 1 day to less than 1 month with full recovery is the defining DSM-5 duration for Brief Psychotic Disorder.
• Option B: A duration of 1 to 6 months constitutes Schizophreniform Disorder.
• Option C: Beyond 6 months meets the duration threshold for Schizophrenia.
• Option D: An indefinite persistent duration indicates a chronic psychotic disorder (e.g., schizophrenia or delusional disorder).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old male presents with persistent delusions that a male coworker whom he barely knows is disguising himself as various strangers across the city—including his bus driver, a bank teller, and a grocery store clerk—in order to follow and monitor his movements. What delusional misidentification syndrome is this?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Fregoli syndrome (named after the Italian quick-change actor Leopoldo Fregoli) is a delusional misidentification syndrome where the patient believes that one persecutor or familiar person assumes various physical disguises and is masquerading as different strangers.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Delusion of a single familiar individual taking on the identity of different strangers through disguise is Fregoli syndrome.
• Option B: Capgras syndrome is the delusion of an impostor taking the place of a familiar person.
• Option C: Ekbom syndrome is delusional parasitosis (insects crawling in/on the skin).
• Option D: Cotard's syndrome is the nihilistic delusion of being dead or lacking organs.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old woman is evaluated in the emergency room 10 days after the uncomplicated delivery of her first child. Her family reports that she has become agitated, severely insomniac, expresses confusion, and states that she heard a voice telling her that her baby is possessed by the devil and must be drowned to save the world. What is the diagnosis and immediate management?
options: Postpartum blues; reassure and send home
Postpartum psychosis; treat as a psychiatric emergency requiring immediate inpatient hospitalization, suicide/infanticide precautions, and pharmacotherapy
Postpartum fatigue; recommend sleeping pills and leave baby under maternal care alone
Adjustment disorder with anxious mood; outpatient counseling after 2 months
questions.answer: Postpartum psychosis; treat as a psychiatric emergency requiring immediate inpatient hospitalization, suicide/infanticide precautions, and pharmacotherapy
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Postpartum (puerperal) psychosis is a medical emergency with an incidence of 1–2 per 1000 births, typically beginning within the first 1 to 2 weeks postpartum. It features delirium-like confusion, affective symptoms, delusions (often involving the infant), and carries a high risk of infanticide (up to 4%) and suicide. Immediate inpatient admission and separation until safe is mandatory.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Postpartum blues is mild, transient mood lability peaking on day 3-5 without psychosis or infanticidal thoughts.
• Option B: Postpartum psychosis is a life-threatening psychiatric emergency requiring immediate hospitalization and protective separation.
• Option C: Leaving a psychotic, command-hallucinating mother alone with the neonate puts the infant at immediate mortal risk.
• Option D: Psychosis with infanticidal command hallucinations cannot be managed as an outpatient adjustment disorder.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 26-year-old prisoner awaiting trial for armed robbery is examined. When asked: 'How many legs does a cow have?', he replies: 'Five.' When asked: 'What is 2 + 2?', he answers: 'Five.' When asked: 'What color is snow?', he answers: 'Black.' He also exhibits clouding of consciousness and hysterical sensory loss. What is this psychopathological presentation?
options: Ganser syndrome (Symptom of approximate answers / Vorbeireden)
questions.answer: Ganser syndrome (Symptom of approximate answers / Vorbeireden)
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Ganser syndrome (historically termed prison psychosis) is characterized by the production of approximate answers (Vorbeireden)—where the patient gives an incorrect answer that demonstrates they clearly understood the nature of the question (e.g., 2+2=5, a horse has 5 legs). It is associated with clouding of consciousness, conversion symptoms, and pseudohallucinations, classified as a dissociative disorder or condition associated with extreme stress.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Vorbeireden (giving answers just off the mark, showing comprehension of the concept) combined with stress or incarceration is Ganser syndrome.
• Option B: Wernicke's aphasia involves fluent paraphasic jargon speech with impaired comprehension, not deliberately close approximate answers.
• Option C: While secondary gain may be present, classic Ganser syndrome is recognized in psychopathology as an involuntary dissociative phenomenon beyond simple malingering.
• Option D: Simple schizophrenia presents with insidious development of negative symptoms and decline in functioning without prominent Vorbeireden or florid hysterical signs.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old software engineer presents to the emergency department experiencing sudden palpitations, sweating, tremors, chest tightness, and an intense fear of impending doom. Physical examination, ECG, cardiac enzymes, and thyroid profile are within normal limits. She reports having three similar unprovoked episodes over the past month and is persistently anxious about experiencing another attack. What is the most appropriate long-term pharmacological treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: The clinical presentation is classic for Panic Disorder, characterized by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks followed by at least 1 month of persistent concern about additional attacks or maladaptive behavioral changes. SSRIs (e.g., sertraline, paroxetine, escitalopram) are the first-line long-term pharmacological agents due to their efficacy and lack of dependence potential.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. SSRIs are the first-line pharmacological treatment of choice for long-term maintenance in panic disorder, often paired with Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).
• Option B: Incorrect. Short-acting benzodiazepines like alprazolam may be used for rapid symptomatic relief during acute attacks or initial bridging, but monotherapy is contraindicated for long-term management due to risks of tolerance, dependence, and rebound anxiety.
• Option C: Incorrect. Beta-blockers like propranolol control peripheral autonomic symptoms (e.g., performance anxiety) but fail to address the core cognitive and central neurochemical pathology of panic disorder.
• Option D: Incorrect. Typical antipsychotics like haloperidol have no role in uncomplicated panic disorder and carry substantial risks of extrapyramidal symptoms and metabolic adverse effects.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: According to ICD-10 diagnostic guidelines, what is the minimum duration of persistent, generalized, and unfocused anxiety required to establish a diagnosis of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is characterized by excessive, uncontrollable worry ('free-floating anxiety') and apprehension concerning multiple everyday events and activities, accompanied by autonomic hyperactivity and motor tension, lasting for at least 6 months.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Incorrect. A duration of 1 month is typical for diagnosing Acute Stress Disorder or evaluating early adjustment disorders, not GAD.
• Option B: Incorrect. A 3-month duration is insufficient for standard ICD-10/DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for GAD.
• Option C: Correct. Both ICD-10 and DSM-5 require persistent symptoms occurring more days than not for a minimum duration of at least 6 months.
• Option D: Incorrect. 12 months exceeds the minimum diagnostic threshold required for diagnosing GAD.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old accountant spends 4 to 5 hours every evening checking door locks, gas knobs, and electrical outlets repeatedly. He acknowledges that his fears of burglary or fire are irrational and excessive, yet he feels intolerable distress until the checking ritual is completed. What psychological therapy is considered the specific first-line evidence-based intervention for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: The patient presents with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) featuring checking compulsions driven by intrusive obsessions. The insight is preserved (ego-dystonic). Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), a specialized form of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), is the established gold-standard psychotherapy for OCD.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) systematically exposes the patient to obsession-triggering cues while refraining from performing the neutralizing compulsion, leading to habituation and extinction of anxiety.
• Option B: Incorrect. Systematic desensitization is primarily utilized for specific phobias using relaxation pairing rather than the prolonged unneutralized exposure required in OCD.
• Option C: Incorrect. Psychoanalysis is ineffective for resolving primary obsessional neurocircuitry and compulsive rituals.
• Option D: Incorrect. DBT is specifically indicated for Borderline Personality Disorder and emotional dysregulation, not primary OCD.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A survivor of a severe motor vehicle collision presents with intrusive flashbacks, hyperarousal, night terrors, and avoidance of driving starting 10 days after the trauma. What is the most appropriate diagnosis if the symptoms have been present for less than 1 month?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Acute Stress Disorder and PTSD share core symptom clusters (intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, arousal) occurring after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence. The critical differentiating parameter is the duration of symptoms.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Incorrect. PTSD requires symptoms to persist for more than 1 month (4 weeks) following the traumatic event.
• Option B: Correct. Acute Stress Disorder is diagnosed when trauma-related symptoms arise within days and last between 3 days and 1 month following exposure.
• Option C: Incorrect. Adjustment disorder involves an emotional or behavioral reaction to identifiable non-life-threatening stressors (e.g., divorce, job loss) within 1 month, without meeting full trauma-related intrusion criteria.
• Option D: Incorrect. GAD involves pervasive, chronic free-floating anxiety unrelated to a singular life-threatening traumatic catastrophe.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 22-year-old woman suddenly develops bilateral lower limb paralysis following a bitter argument with her fiancé. Neurological examination reveals normal deep tendon reflexes, no muscle wasting, and a positive Hoover's sign. Throughout the examination, she appears remarkably calm and unconcerned about her inability to walk. What is the classic clinical term for this unconcerned attitude?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: This presentation exemplifies Conversion Disorder (Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder / Dissociative neurological symptom disorder in ICD-11). Hoover's sign demonstrates functional weakness (involuntary extension of the paretic leg when flexing the contralateral hip against resistance). 'La belle indifférence' describes the patient's paradoxical lack of distress or inappropriate complacency regarding a severe neurological deficit.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. 'La belle indifférence' is the classic descriptive psychopathological feature seen in a substantial proportion of patients with conversion disorder.
• Option B: Incorrect. Ganser syndrome is characterized by approximate answers ('paralogia'), clouding of consciousness, and somatic conversion features, often seen in forensic settings.
• Option C: Incorrect. Folie à deux (shared psychotic disorder) involves the transmission of delusional beliefs from a primary psychotic individual to a closely associated second individual.
• Option D: Incorrect. Capgras phenomenon is a delusional misidentification syndrome where a familiar person is believed to have been replaced by an identical impostor.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 45-year-old man presents with persistent preoccupation that he has stomach cancer despite exhaustive normal gastrointestinal investigations, negative endoscopies, and repeated oncological reassurance over the past 8 months. He experiences minimal physical symptoms other than mild epigastric awareness, yet his conviction that he harbors a lethal disease severely impairs his daily life. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Illness Anxiety Disorder (historically classified under Hypochondriacal Disorder in ICD-10) is defined by a persistent preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious, undiagnosed medical illness despite medical reassurance, with minimal or absent somatic symptoms.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The patient has a dominant fear/preoccupation of harboring a serious malignancy with negligible somatic symptoms and refusal of medical reassurance, typical of Illness Anxiety Disorder.
• Option B: Incorrect. Somatization disorder (Briquet's syndrome) is characterized by multiple, recurrent, and medically unexplained somatic symptoms across various organ systems (gastrointestinal, pain, neurological, sexual), rather than anxiety about a single specific disease.
• Option C: Incorrect. In delusional disorder somatic type, the belief is held with fixed, unshakeable psychotic conviction completely out of touch with reality, whereas in illness anxiety disorder, the preoccupation is overvalued but not truly psychotic.
• Option D: Incorrect. Factitious disorder involves intentional, deceptive fabrication or induction of signs and symptoms to assume the sick role without external secondary gain.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 19-year-old college student refuses to attend classes because he believes his nose is 'grotesquely deformed and asymmetrical.' Multiple dermatologists and plastic surgeons have examined him and confirmed that his facial features are completely normal. He spends over 4 hours a day examining his face in mirrors and camouflaging it with scarves. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacological intervention?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) is an obsessive-compulsive spectrum disorder characterized by preoccupation with nonexistent or slight defects in physical appearance, leading to repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, excessive grooming). Pharmacologically, BDD responds selectively to SSRIs, often requiring higher doses and longer durations than standard major depression.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. SSRIs at high doses (frequently exceeding standard antidepressant dosages) are the first-line pharmacotherapy for BDD, combined with CBT.
• Option B: Incorrect. Antipsychotic monotherapy is ineffective as a primary treatment for BDD, though atypical antipsychotics may sometimes augment SSRIs in refractory cases with poor insight.
• Option C: Incorrect. Lithium is a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder and has no efficacy in treating BDD obsessions.
• Option D: Incorrect. Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant mood stabilizer with no therapeutic role in BDD.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 26-year-old violinist experiences overwhelming autonomic symptoms including tachycardia, hand tremor, and diaphoresis strictly when performing solo in front of an audience. Her symptoms do not occur during private rehearsals or non-performance social interactions. Which medication taken 30 to 60 minutes prior to a performance is most effective for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Performance-only Social Anxiety Disorder (performance anxiety / stage fright) involves acute autonomic hyperarousal in evaluative public speaking or artistic performances. Non-selective beta-adrenergic antagonists block peripheral beta receptors, mitigating tremors, palpitations, and sweating.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Propranolol (10-40 mg) taken 30-60 minutes before the performance selectively attenuates peripheral sympathetic symptoms without causing sedation or cognitive slowing.
• Option B: Incorrect. Sertraline is an SSRI indicated for generalized social anxiety disorder requiring daily administration over weeks, not as a PRN dose before a single performance.
• Option C: Incorrect. Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist indicated for GAD that requires 2-4 weeks of continuous dosing and is ineffective as a single-dose PRN agent.
• Option D: Incorrect. While benzodiazepines reduce anxiety, they cause sedation, ataxia, and psychomotor impairment that can critically compromise musical or cognitive performance.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old bank manager unexpectedly disappears from his home city following severe financial ruin. Three weeks later, he is discovered 800 kilometers away working as a waiter under a completely new identity. He has no recollection of his past life, family, or profession. A complete organic workup is normal. What is the most specific diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Dissociative Fugue is characterized by purposeful, sudden unexpected travel away from home or customary workplace, accompanied by inability to recall one's past (amnesia) and the assumption of a new partial or complete identity.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The hallmark constellation of unexpected travel, retrograde amnesia for autobiographical memory, and assumption of a new identity/lifestyle confirms Dissociative Fugue.
• Option B: Incorrect. Dissociative amnesia without fugue involves inability to recall important personal information (usually traumatic), but without purposeful travel and identity assumption.
• Option C: Incorrect. Dissociative Identity Disorder (multiple personality disorder) involves the presence of two or more distinct personality states alternating executive control, rather than sudden travel and complete identity abandonment.
• Option D: Incorrect. Depersonalization-derealization disorder involves feelings of detachment from one's body or mental processes (as an outside observer) or feeling unreality of surroundings, with intact memory and identity.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: In the diagnosis of Adjustment Disorder according to ICD-10 criteria, symptoms must arise within what time frame following the occurrence of the identifiable psychosocial stressor, and typically resolve within what duration once the stressor or its consequences have ceased?
options: Within 1 month of stressor onset; resolve within 6 months
Within 3 months of stressor onset; resolve within 12 months
Within 6 months of stressor onset; resolve within 2 years
Within 2 weeks of stressor onset; resolve within 1 month
questions.answer: Within 1 month of stressor onset; resolve within 6 months
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Adjustment Disorder represents a state of subjective distress and emotional disturbance interfering with social functioning, arising during the period of adaptation to a significant life change or stressful life event. Diagnostic time boundaries are strictly defined.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. According to ICD-10, the onset of symptoms must occur within 1 month of the stressor, and symptoms normally resolve within 6 months unless the stressor is prolonged (chronic adjustment disorder in DSM allows longer if stressor persists).
• Option B: Incorrect. While DSM-5 allows symptom onset within 3 months, it still requires resolution within 6 months once the stressor terminates; 12 months is incorrect for standard resolution.
• Option C: Incorrect. A 6-month delay in onset invalidates the temporal causal link required for an adjustment disorder.
• Option D: Incorrect. A 2-week window is too narrow and 1-month resolution is characteristic of acute stress reactions rather than adjustment disorders.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.chapterTitle: Disorders of Adult Personality and Behaviour
questions.topic: Disorders of Adult Personality and Behaviour
questions.topicTitle: Disorders of Adult Personality and Behaviour
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old unmarried man lives in complete social isolation. He dresses in eccentric, mismatched clothing, speaks in an odd, metaphorical manner, and believes that strangers on the street are communicating with him through subtle hand gestures. He expresses strong interest in clairvoyance and telepathy but does not have persistent auditory hallucinations or fixed persecutory delusions. Which personality disorder is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Schizotypal Personality Disorder is a Cluster A disorder characterized by odd beliefs/magical thinking, ideas of reference, eccentric behavior or appearance, unusual perceptual experiences, and social anxiety that does not abate with familiarity.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Odd appearance, magical thinking (telepathy, clairvoyance), ideas of reference, and metaphorical speech are hallmark features of Schizotypal Personality Disorder.
• Option B: Incorrect. Schizoid personality disorder features emotional coldness, detachment, and complete lack of interest in social relationships, but lacks the cognitive-perceptual distortions, eccentric appearance, and magical thinking.
• Option C: Incorrect. Paranoid personality disorder is dominated by pervasive distrust and suspiciousness of others' motives without prominent magical thinking or bizarre eccentricities.
• Option D: Incorrect. Avoidant personality disorder individuals desire social interaction but avoid it due to intense fear of rejection, ridicule, and inadequacy; they do not exhibit odd beliefs or eccentricities.

questions.prompt: A 23-year-old female presents with recurrent non-suicidal self-injury (cutting forearms), chronic feelings of emptiness, intense fear of abandonment, and turbulent interpersonal relationships wherein friends are alternately idealized as perfect and then devalued as cruel. When under extreme stress, she experiences brief paranoid ideation. Which psychological therapy represents the evidence-based treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: The clinical vignette illustrates Borderline (Emotionally Unstable) Personality Disorder, Cluster B. Key traits include affective instability, splitting (dichotomous idealization/devaluation), fear of abandonment, impulsivity, self-harm, and stress-related micropsychotic ideation. Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), developed by Marsha Linehan, is the specialized gold standard.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) specifically targets emotional dysregulation, distress tolerance, mindfulness, and interpersonal effectiveness in borderline personality disorder.
• Option B: Incorrect. Systematic desensitization is used for phobic disorders to desensitize specific conditioned fear responses.
• Option C: Incorrect. IPSRT is specifically designed for stabilizing circadian rhythms and routines in Bipolar Affective Disorder.
• Option D: Incorrect. Applied relaxation is an adjunct behavioral method used in generalized anxiety disorder.

questions.prompt: To establish a definitive diagnosis of Antisocial Personality Disorder (Dissocial Personality Disorder), diagnostic manuals (DSM-5 / ICD-10) require evidence of which disorder having onset before the age of 15 years?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Antisocial Personality Disorder involves a pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others, deceitfulness, impulsivity, irritability, and lack of remorse. A prerequisite criterion is that the individual demonstrated persistent patterns of Conduct Disorder before age 15.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Evidence of Conduct Disorder before age 15 (e.g., aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, theft, serious rule violations) is a mandatory DSM diagnostic criterion.
• Option B: Incorrect. While ODD may precede conduct disorder, it does not satisfy the specific criterion requiring documented Conduct Disorder.
• Option C: Incorrect. ADHD frequently co-occurs with conduct problems but is not the required diagnostic precursor for antisocial personality disorder.
• Option D: Incorrect. Separation anxiety disorder has no etiologic or diagnostic prerequisite link to antisocial personality disorder.

questions.prompt: A 27-year-old actress presents for counseling. Her friends describe her as dramatic, seductive, and constantly demanding to be the center of attention. When she is not the focus of a group, she feels uncomfortable and depressed. Her speech is impressionistic and lacking in detail, and she displays rapidly shifting, shallow expressions of emotion. Which personality disorder does this reflect?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Histrionic Personality Disorder (Cluster B) is characterized by pervasive attention-seeking behavior, inappropriate sexually seductive or provocative behavior, shallow and rapidly shifting emotions, theatricality, and impressionistic speech.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The patient displays classic features: theatricality, discomfort when not the center of attention, inappropriate seductiveness, and impressionistic speech.
• Option B: Incorrect. Narcissistic personality disorder features grandiosity, entitlement, and need for admiration, but focuses on superiority and prestige rather than emotional theatricality and seductiveness.
• Option C: Incorrect. Borderline personality disorder involves intense emotional dysregulation, chronic emptiness, self-harm, and unstable identity, which are absent here.
• Option D: Incorrect. Dependent personality disorder is defined by submissiveness, clinging behavior, and inability to make everyday decisions without advice.

questions.prompt: A 42-year-old corporate executive reacts with intense rage, humiliation, and contempt whenever his subordinates offer constructive feedback. He routinely exaggerates his achievements, expects unconditional compliance, believes he is extraordinarily unique, and exploits his colleagues to achieve personal goals while lacking empathy for their distress. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Narcissistic Personality Disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of grandiosity (in fantasy or behavior), need for excessive admiration, lack of empathy, entitlement, interpersonal exploitation, and severe vulnerability to perceived criticism (narcissistic injury/rage).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Grandiosity, entitlement, lack of empathy, exploitation, and hypersensitivity/rage in response to constructive feedback define Narcissistic Personality Disorder.
• Option B: Incorrect. Antisocial personality disorder features overt criminality, repeated violation of societal laws, physical aggression, and reckless disregard for safety, rather than preoccupation with status and grandiosity.
• Option C: Incorrect. Paranoid personality disorder is dominated by pervasive mistrust and suspicion of malicious intent, not grandiosity and entitlement.
• Option D: Incorrect. Schizotypal disorder involves eccentricities, social oddities, and magical thinking.

questions.prompt: A 30-year-old programmer declines multiple lucrative promotions because they would require leading team presentations. He yearns for intimate friendships and romantic relationships but completely isolates himself because he feels socially inept, unappealing, and fears being criticized or rejected. How does his condition primarily differ from Schizoid Personality Disorder?
options: He actively desires close interpersonal relationships, whereas schizoid patients are indifferent to them
He displays prominent magical thinking and oddities of speech
He has lack of empathy and exploitative tendencies
He exhibits affective flattening and blunted volition
questions.answer: He actively desires close interpersonal relationships, whereas schizoid patients are indifferent to them
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Avoidant Personality Disorder (Anxious/Avoidant in ICD-10) and Schizoid Personality Disorder both involve social isolation. The cardinal differentiating feature is social motivation: avoidant individuals desire social intimacy but avoid it due to intense fear of rejection, humiliation, and feelings of inadequacy; schizoid individuals have no desire for relationships and genuinely prefer solitary activities.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The core distinction is that avoidant patients yearn for social connections but fear rejection, whereas schizoid patients are emotionally detached, aloof, and indifferent to social relationships.
• Option B: Incorrect. Magical thinking and odd speech are characteristic of Schizotypal, not Avoidant personality disorder.
• Option C: Incorrect. Lack of empathy and interpersonal exploitation characterize Narcissistic and Antisocial personality disorders.
• Option D: Incorrect. Flattened affect and blunted volition are negative psychotic symptoms or schizoid features, not seen in avoidant individuals who experience intense internal distress and emotional arousal.

questions.prompt: A 48-year-old supervisor insists that every office file must follow an intricate, multi-step alphabetical and color-coded filing system. Because of his excessive devotion to productivity and perfectionism, deadlines are routinely missed. He is stubborn, miserly with money, refuses to delegate tasks unless colleagues submit exactly to his way of doing things, and views his behavior as rational and essential. Which feature distinguishes his condition from Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)?
options: His traits are ego-syntonic, whereas OCD symptoms are typically ego-dystonic
His condition responds robustly to low-dose clomipramine within days
He experiences prominent intrusive ego-alien obsessional images
He demonstrates lack of insight into the reality of bacterial contamination
questions.answer: His traits are ego-syntonic, whereas OCD symptoms are typically ego-dystonic
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (Anankastic Personality Disorder in ICD-10) is characterized by perfectionism, rigidity, stubbornness, preoccupation with orderliness/details, and workaholism. The key distinction from Axis I OCD is that OCPD traits are ego-syntonic (perceived as acceptable, rational, and desirable by the patient), whereas OCD rituals and obsessions are ego-dystonic (intrusive, unwanted, irrational distress).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. OCPD traits are ego-syntonic (the patient believes his exacting standards are superior and correct). In contrast, OCD patients generally recognize their obsessions/compulsions as irrational and distressing (ego-dystonic).
• Option B: Incorrect. Personality disorders do not respond rapidly to clomipramine or pharmacotherapy; pharmacotherapy has minimal impact on characterological rigidity.
• Option C: Incorrect. Intrusive ego-alien obsessional thoughts/images define OCD, not OCPD.
• Option D: Incorrect. Fear of contamination is a classic OCD presentation, whereas OCPD focuses on generalized control, rules, and perfectionism.

questions.prompt: A 34-year-old woman allows her husband to dictate what clothes she wears, which friends she speaks to, and how she spends her time. When her husband was hospitalized, she felt completely helpless and unable to manage daily chores or make decisions without constant reassurance. She tolerates severe verbal mistreatment out of fear that he will leave her. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Dependent Personality Disorder (Cluster C) is characterized by a pervasive and excessive need to be taken care of, leading to submissive, clinging behavior, difficulty making everyday decisions without advice/reassurance, difficulty expressing disagreement, and urgent seeking of another relationship when one ends.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The patient exemplifies Dependent Personality Disorder through extreme submissiveness, outsourcing personal autonomy, fear of being left alone, and tolerance of abuse to avoid abandonment.
• Option B: Incorrect. Borderline personality disorder features impulsive lashing out, splitting, rage, and self-harm rather than passive submissiveness.
• Option C: Incorrect. Avoidant personality disorder involves social inhibition and fear of humiliation, not dependent submissiveness within an existing relationship.
• Option D: Incorrect. Histrionic personality disorder is characterized by dramatic attention-seeking, flirtatiousness, and emotional expressiveness.

questions.prompt: A 29-year-old wealthy woman is caught pocketing inexpensive cosmetic pencils from a department store. She admits to recurrent, irresistible urges to steal items that she neither needs for personal use nor for their monetary value. She describes mounting tension immediately before the act, followed by intense gratification and relief while stealing, followed by intense guilt afterwards. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Kleptomania is an impulse control disorder characterized by recurrent failure to resist impulses to steal objects that are not needed for personal use or monetary value. The cycle involves increasing tension before the theft, pleasure/relief at the time of committing the theft, and post-theft remorse.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Stealing unneeded items, pre-act tension, immediate gratification, post-act guilt, and absence of financial motivation are definitive for Kleptomania.
• Option B: Incorrect. In antisocial personality disorder, theft is premeditated, motivated by personal gain or spite, and completely devoid of guilt or remorse.
• Option C: Incorrect. Malingering involves intentional fraudulent theft or false illness claims for tangible external secondary gain (money, avoiding legal prosecution).
• Option D: Incorrect. Pyromania involves pathological fire-setting, not shoplifting.
