questions.prompt: Which of the following disorders of impulse control involves recurrent pulling out of one's own hair resulting in noticeable hair loss, preceded by tension and followed by relief, without an underlying dermatological cause?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Trichotillomania (Hair-pulling disorder) is classified under Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders (or Habit and Impulse Disorders in ICD-10). It involves repetitive pulling out of one's hair leading to hair loss, accompanied by repeated attempts to decrease or stop the behavior.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Trichotillomania is the specific psychiatric impulse/repetitive disorder defined by pathological hair pulling.
• Option B: Incorrect. Excoriation disorder (skin-picking disorder) involves recurrent picking of one's own skin resulting in cutaneous lesions.
• Option C: Incorrect. Body dysmorphic disorder involves preoccupation with an imagined or slight physical defect, not repetitive hair pulling for tension release.
• Option D: Incorrect. Alopecia areata is an autoimmune dermatological condition characterized by smooth, non-scarring, circumscribed patches of hair loss with exclamation point hairs, without conscious pulling.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: According to the classic Masters and Johnson human sexual response model, which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of physiological phases?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: William Masters and Virginia Johnson established the linear four-phase physiological model of human sexual response: Excitement, Plateau, Orgasm, and Resolution. (Helen Singer Kaplan later modified this to include Desire as the initiating phase).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The original Masters and Johnson four-phase physiological sequence is Excitement, Plateau, Orgasm, and Resolution.
• Option B: Incorrect. This represents Helen Singer Kaplan's three-phase triphasic model (Desire, Excitement, Orgasm) integrated with resolution.
• Option C: Incorrect. Plateau occurs after excitement (vasocongestion), not prior to it.
• Option D: Incorrect. Plateau precedes orgasm; orgasm does not occur prior to the plateau phase.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 38-year-old male presents with inability to achieve an erection during sexual intercourse with his wife over the past 4 months. He reports sudden onset of symptoms following severe marital discord. Crucially, he notes having firm, spontaneous early morning erections upon waking. What does the presence of intact nocturnal and early morning erections indicate?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: The presence of normal Nocturnal Penile Tumescence (NPT) and spontaneous morning erections demonstrates that the neurovascular, cavernous, and endocrine pathways responsible for penile erection are structurally intact. Preserved NPT in the setting of situational or partner-specific dysfunction confirms a psychogenic (functional) etiology.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Sudden onset, temporal relationship to marital stress, and preserved nocturnal/morning erections are hallmark indicators of psychogenic erectile dysfunction.
• Option B: Incorrect. Arteriogenic erectile dysfunction results in persistent failure of vascular inflow, abolishing nocturnal and morning erections.
• Option C: Incorrect. Autonomic neuropathy (e.g., from diabetes) causes progressive, persistent organic erectile failure and loss of NPT.
• Option D: Incorrect. Hypogonadism causes generalized loss of libido and impaired nocturnal erections.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 25-year-old newly married man complains of persistent ejaculation occurring within 30 seconds of vaginal penetration, causing significant distress to him and his partner. He has no erectile difficulty. Along with behavioral techniques (such as the Semans stop-start and Masters & Johnson squeeze techniques), which pharmacological agent is specifically approved for on-demand oral treatment of premature ejaculation?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Premature (early) ejaculation is defined by persistent ejaculation within approximately 1 minute of penetration, inability to delay ejaculation, and associated personal distress. Dapoxetine is a short-acting, rapidly absorbed SSRI specifically designed and licensed for PRN (on-demand) treatment of premature ejaculation taken 1-3 hours prior to anticipated sexual activity.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Dapoxetine is a fast-acting SSRI with rapid elimination, specifically indicated for on-demand management of premature ejaculation.
• Option B: Incorrect. Sildenafil is a PDE-5 inhibitor used for erectile dysfunction, not primary premature ejaculation (unless co-occurring with ED).
• Option C: Incorrect. Trazodone is a sedating antidepressant associated with priapism, not premature ejaculation.
• Option D: Incorrect. Bupropion is an NDRI that increases dopamine and noradrenaline; it typically improves libido and does not delay ejaculation (and is often used to counter SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 24-year-old woman presents with unconsummated marriage of 1 year. Whenever intercourse is attempted, she experiences involuntary, painful spasm of the outer third of the vaginal musculature, completely preventing penile entry, despite desiring intimacy and experiencing normal arousal. Pelvic examination confirms marked reflex contraction of the pubococcygeus muscle on touch. What is the diagnosis and first-line behavioral therapy?
options: Vaginismus; treated with progressive vaginal dilators and relaxation training
Dyspareunia; treated with systemic estrogen replacement
Hypoactive sexual desire disorder; treated with flibanserin
Female orgasmic disorder; treated with sensate focus therapy
questions.answer: Vaginismus; treated with progressive vaginal dilators and relaxation training
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Vaginismus is characterized by recurrent or persistent involuntary spasm of the musculature of the outer third of the vagina (primarily the levator ani and pubococcygeus muscles) that interferes with sexual intercourse, gynecological examination, or tampon insertion. The first-line treatment is systematic desensitization using progressive graduated vaginal dilators coupled with pelvic floor relaxation exercises (Kegel relaxation).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The clinical presentation is diagnostic of Vaginismus, and progressive graduated dilators combined with relaxation represent the gold-standard first-line therapy.
• Option B: Incorrect. Dyspareunia refers to genital pain associated with intercourse without involuntary muscular spasm preventing entry.
• Option C: Incorrect. Hypoactive sexual desire disorder involves lack or absence of sexual fantasies and desire, whereas this patient has intact desire.
• Option D: Incorrect. Female orgasmic disorder is the delay or absence of orgasm after normal arousal; it does not present as muscular obstruction of vaginal entry.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions is characterized by persistent or recurrent deficiency or absence of sexual fantasies and desire for sexual activity, causing marked distress or interpersonal difficulty?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Disorders of the desire phase of sexual response involve disturbances in sexual appetence. Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder (HSDD) involves a chronic lack of sexual interest, thoughts, and fantasies.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. HSDD specifically denotes persistent deficiency of sexual thoughts, fantasies, and desire leading to distress.
• Option B: Incorrect. Sexual aversion disorder involves active disgust, repulsion, and active avoidance of genital sexual contact.
• Option C: Incorrect. Erectile dysfunction is an arousal/vasocongestive disorder in males, often with completely preserved sexual desire.
• Option D: Incorrect. Female sexual arousal disorder involves lack of physiological lubrication or genital swelling despite potential presence of desire.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 31-year-old man is apprehended by police after secretly installing hidden cameras in his neighbors' bedrooms to view them undressing and engaging in sexual activities without their consent. He achieves intense sexual arousal exclusively by observing unsuspecting individuals. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Voyeuristic Disorder is a paraphilic disorder characterized by recurrent, intense sexual arousal from observing an unsuspecting person who is naked, disrobing, or engaging in sexual activity, acted upon with a nonconsenting person or causing significant distress/impairment.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Secretly watching unsuspecting individuals undressing or engaged in sexual activity for sexual gratification defines Voyeurism.
• Option B: Incorrect. Exhibitionistic disorder involves exposing one's genitals to an unsuspecting stranger.
• Option C: Incorrect. Frotteuristic disorder involves touching or rubbing against a nonconsenting person (typically in crowded public places).
• Option D: Incorrect. Fetishistic disorder involves intense sexual arousal from inanimate objects (e.g., shoes) or highly specific non-genital body parts.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old man achieves sexual gratification and orgasm exclusively by touching and rubbing his genitalia against unsuspecting, fully clothed women in crowded commuter trains. What paraphilia does this behavior describe?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Frotteuristic Disorder is a paraphilia involving recurrent, intense sexual arousal from touching or rubbing against a nonconsenting person, typically executed in crowded transit or public spaces where escape or anonymity is facile.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Rubbing against nonconsenting strangers in crowded environments defines Frotteurism.
• Option B: Incorrect. Exhibitionism is exposing one's genitalia to unsuspecting people.
• Option C: Incorrect. Voyeurism is observing unsuspecting people undressing or engaging in sexual acts.
• Option D: Incorrect. Transvestic disorder involves sexual arousal derived from cross-dressing in clothing of the opposite sex.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: According to DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for Pedophilic Disorder, what is the minimum age the individual must be, and what is the minimum age difference required between the individual and the prepubescent child?
options: Individual must be at least 16 years of age, and at least 5 years older than the child
Individual must be at least 18 years of age, and at least 5 years older than the child
Individual must be at least 18 years of age, and at least 10 years older than the child
Individual must be at least 21 years of age, and at least 7 years older than the child
questions.answer: Individual must be at least 16 years of age, and at least 5 years older than the child
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Pedophilic Disorder involves recurrent, intense sexually arousing fantasies, urges, or behaviors involving sexual activity with a prepubescent child (generally age 13 years or younger). DSM-5 specifies precise chronological thresholds to distinguish this disorder from peer sexual exploration.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The criteria stipulate that the individual must be at least 16 years of age and at least 5 years older than the prepubescent child (aged 13 or younger).
• Option B: Incorrect. The age requirement is 16, not 18.
• Option C: Incorrect. The age cutoff is 16 and the age difference is 5 years, not 10 years.
• Option D: Incorrect. Neither 21 nor 7 years represents the DSM threshold.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: In modern psychiatric classifications (such as ICD-11 and DSM-5), how is marked and persistent incongruence between an individual's experienced gender and assigned sex officially conceptualized?
options: As Gender Incongruence / Gender Dysphoria, removed from the category of mental illness/paraphilias
As Transvestic Fetishism within neurotic disorders
As an ego-dystonic sexual orientation disorder
As a primary psychotic delusional misidentification
questions.answer: As Gender Incongruence / Gender Dysphoria, removed from the category of mental illness/paraphilias
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Contemporary psychiatric taxonomies (ICD-11, DSM-5) have depathologized gender diversity. ICD-11 renamed gender identity disorder to 'Gender Incongruence' and moved it out of the Mental and Behavioural Disorders chapter into a new chapter on Conditions Related to Sexual Health, recognizing that diverse gender identities are not per se psychiatric disorders.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Gender Incongruence (ICD-11) / Gender Dysphoria (DSM-5) focuses on the distress caused by mismatch between experienced gender and assigned sex, de-stigmatizing it and separating it from paraphilias.
• Option B: Incorrect. Transvestic fetishism is a paraphilia involving sexual arousal from cross-dressing, which is fundamentally distinct from gender incongruence.
• Option C: Incorrect. Gender identity relates to one's internal sense of being male, female, or another gender, whereas sexual orientation relates to interpersonal attraction; neither is classified as a psychiatric illness.
• Option D: Incorrect. Gender incongruence has no connection to psychotic delusions or reality distortion.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 44-year-old man treated with an atypical antidepressant presents to the emergency room with a painful, rigid penile erection that has persisted for 6 hours without sexual stimulation. Which psychotropic medication is most classically associated with this medical emergency (priapism)?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Priapism is a persistent, painful erection lasting longer than 4 hours unrelated to sexual stimulation. It is a urological emergency that can lead to corporal fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction. Among psychotropic medications, Trazodone (a serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor with potent alpha-1 adrenergic blocking properties) is famously associated with priapism ('Trazodone causes bone').

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Trazodone is classically implicated in priapism due to alpha-1 adrenergic antagonism preventing penile detumescence.
• Option B: Incorrect. Sertraline causes sexual dysfunction such as delayed ejaculation or anorgasmia, but rarely priapism.
• Option C: Incorrect. Escitalopram carries risks of decreased libido and delayed orgasm, but not classic drug-induced priapism.
• Option D: Incorrect. Venlafaxine is an SNRI that causes sexual arousal dysfunction and anorgasmia, not priapism.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: On a standard normal polysomnogram (PSG), which stage of sleep is characteristically identified by the presence of sleep spindles and K-complexes?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Normal non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep is divided into stages N1, N2, and N3. Stage N2 comprises roughly 45-55% of total sleep time and is neurophysiologically defined by the appearance of sleep spindles (12-14 Hz bursts) and K-complexes (high-amplitude biphasic waves).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Sleep spindles and K-complexes are the pathognomonic electroencephalographic hallmarks of Stage N2 sleep.
• Option B: Incorrect. Stage N1 is characterized by transition from alpha rhythm (8-13 Hz) to low-amplitude, mixed-frequency theta activity (4-7 Hz) and vertex sharp waves.
• Option C: Incorrect. Stage N3 (slow-wave sleep or delta sleep) is characterized by high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves (<4 Hz) comprising >20% of the epoch.
• Option D: Incorrect. Stage R (REM) is characterized by low-amplitude mixed-frequency EEG (sawtooth waves), rapid eye movements, and skeletal muscle atonia.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 52-year-old executive complains of difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep for 4 nights every week over the past 6 months. She experiences daytime fatigue, irritability, and poor concentration. Medical examination and drug screens are unremarkable. According to international clinical guidelines, what is the established first-line intervention for chronic insomnia disorder?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Chronic Insomnia Disorder is defined by sleep initiation or maintenance difficulties occurring at least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months, with daytime functional impairment. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine and international guidelines designate Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) as the first-line therapy, superior to pharmacotherapy in long-term efficacy without risks of tolerance or dependence.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. CBT-I (including sleep hygiene, stimulus control, sleep restriction, and cognitive restructuring) is the definitive first-line treatment for chronic insomnia.
• Option B: Incorrect. Zolpidem is approved only for short-term management (2-4 weeks) due to risks of dependence, complex sleep behaviors, and tolerance.
• Option C: Incorrect. Long-term benzodiazepines like clonazepam are contraindicated due to dependence, tolerance, cognitive blunting, and alteration of sleep architecture.
• Option D: Incorrect. Amitriptyline has high anticholinergic and cardiac toxicity risks and is not a first-line treatment for primary insomnia.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 21-year-old student experiences irresistible bouts of daytime sleepiness occurring multiple times daily. While laughing at a comedy show, he suddenly experienced bilateral knee buckling and dropped to the ground while remaining fully conscious. He also describes terrifying hallucinations upon falling asleep and inability to move for a minute upon waking. What neurochemical deficiency in the cerebrospinal fluid is the hallmark of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: The clinical tetrad of Narcolepsy Type 1 includes: (1) Excessive daytime sleepiness, (2) Cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion with preserved consciousness), (3) Hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, and (4) Sleep paralysis. The underlying pathophysiology is autoimmune destruction of orexin/hypocretin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, resulting in low or undetectable CSF hypocretin-1 (orexin-A) levels.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Loss of hypothalamic hypocretin/orexin neuropeptides is the definitive neurochemical hallmark of Narcolepsy with cataplexy (Type 1).
• Option B: Incorrect. Dopamine deficiency in the substantia nigra underlies Parkinson's disease, not the orexinergic sleep-switch failure in narcolepsy.
• Option C: Incorrect. Serotonin deficiency is implicated in depressive and anxiety disorders, not the primary cause of narcoleptic cataplexy.
• Option D: Incorrect. GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter but its deficiency is not the primary diagnostic marker for narcolepsy.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 55-year-old obese man (BMI 34 kg/m²) is brought by his wife because of loud, irregular snoring, gasping episodes during sleep, and unrefreshing rest. He falls asleep repeatedly while driving and during work meetings. What is the gold-standard diagnostic investigation and the definitive non-invasive treatment of choice?
options: Overnight Polysomnography (PSG); Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP)
questions.answer: Overnight Polysomnography (PSG); Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP)
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is caused by repetitive collapse of the upper airway during sleep, leading to hypoxemia, sleep fragmentation, and excessive daytime somnolence. The gold-standard diagnostic tool is overnight Polysomnography (demonstrating an Apnea-Hypopnea Index [AHI] ≥ 5/hr with symptoms or ≥ 15/hr), and Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) is the definitive first-line therapeutic intervention.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Overnight polysomnography confirms the diagnosis and CPAP provides pneumatic splinting of the upper airway to abolish apneas.
• Option B: Incorrect. MSLT is the diagnostic test for narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia, not the primary test for OSA.
• Option C: Incorrect. Routine EEG evaluates seizures; clonazepam worsens OSA by relaxing pharyngeal muscles and suppressing respiratory drive.
• Option D: Incorrect. Brain MRI is not diagnostic for OSA, and surgery (uvulopalatopharyngoplasty) is reserved for selected anatomical obstructions after CPAP failure.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 7-year-old boy is brought by his parents. Roughly 90 minutes after falling asleep, he abruptly sits up in bed screaming in terror, with marked diaphoresis, tachycardia, and dilated pupils. He appears inconsolable, does not recognize his parents, and resists physical comfort. After 10 minutes, he falls back asleep and has complete amnesia for the event the next morning. Which stage of sleep is this parasomnia arising from?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Sleep Terrors (pavor nocturnus) are NREM parasomnias occurring characteristically during deep slow-wave sleep (Stage N3) in the first third of the night. Features include abrupt terror arousal, intense autonomic activation, unresponsiveness to comforting, and total amnesia the following morning. In contrast, Nightmare Disorder occurs during REM sleep in the latter half of the night, with vivid dream recall and no amnesia.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Sleep terrors arise from slow-wave sleep (Stage N3 / delta sleep), accounting for the lack of dream recall, confusion upon arousal, and timing in the early night.
• Option B: Incorrect. REM sleep parasomnias include nightmares and REM sleep behavior disorder; nightmares feature full awakenings with vivid memory of the frightening dream.
• Option C: Incorrect. Stage N1 is light transitional sleep and does not generate sleep terrors.
• Option D: Incorrect. Stage N2 contains sleep spindles and K-complexes and is not the origin of classic sleep terror parasomnias.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 10-year-old girl is found by her parents walking silently through the kitchen 2 hours after going to bed. Her eyes are open with a blank, staring expression. She does not respond to verbal questions and is easily guided back to bed. The next morning, she has no memory of the episode. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Somnambulism (Sleepwalking) is an NREM arousal parasomnia originating from slow-wave sleep (Stage N3). Individuals exhibit complex motor behaviors (walking, opening doors) while maintaining a low level of awareness and responsiveness, with complete morning amnesia.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Complex ambulatory motor behavior arising from early-night sleep with blank stare, unresponsiveness, and subsequent amnesia confirms Somnambulism.
• Option B: Incorrect. REM Sleep Behavior Disorder occurs in older adults during REM sleep, involving acting out violent dreams due to loss of muscle atonia.
• Option C: Incorrect. Absence seizures occur during wakefulness, last 5-15 seconds, and do not present as sustained wandering during nocturnal sleep.
• Option D: Incorrect. A fugue state is a dissociative amnesic condition involving purposeful travel during wakefulness.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 68-year-old man violently kicks, thrashes, and punches in his sleep, repeatedly striking his bed partner. When awakened, he immediately recalls a vivid, terrifying dream in which he was fighting off aggressive animals. Polysomnography demonstrates abnormal preservation of skeletal muscle tone during REM sleep. What neurodegenerative condition is strongly associated with the future development of this disorder?
options: Alpha-synucleinopathies (e.g., Parkinson's disease, Dementia with Lewy bodies)
questions.answer: Alpha-synucleinopathies (e.g., Parkinson's disease, Dementia with Lewy bodies)
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD) is characterized by loss of normal REM sleep muscle atonia (REM without atonia), allowing patients to enact their dreams with violent motor activity. Over 80% of individuals diagnosed with idiopathic RBD convert within 10-15 years to an alpha-synucleinopathy neurodegenerative disorder (Parkinson's disease, Dementia with Lewy Bodies, or Multiple System Atrophy).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. RBD is the strongest known prodromal clinical marker for alpha-synucleinopathies, notably Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia.
• Option B: Incorrect. Alzheimer's disease is a tauopathy/amyloidopathy that does not show a primary prodromal link with dream-enactment RBD.
• Option C: Incorrect. ALS affects upper and lower motor neurons without characteristic REM sleep atonia loss or dream enactment.
• Option D: Incorrect. Huntington's disease is a CAG trinucleotide repeat disorder affecting striatal GABAergic neurons; it is not specifically linked to RBD.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 40-year-old female complains of an irresistible urge to move her legs in the evenings when sitting or lying down, accompanied by an unpleasant creeping, crawling sensation deep in her calves. The symptoms are temporarily relieved by walking or stretching. Which laboratory investigation is essential in the initial evaluation of this disorder?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS / Willis-Ekbom disease) is characterized by an urge to move the legs usually accompanied by uncomfortable sensations, beginning/worsening during periods of rest, partially or totally relieved by movement, and worse in the evening/night (URGE criteria). Central nervous system iron deficiency in the substantia nigra impairs dopamine synthesis; hence, checking serum ferritin is the mandatory initial step (replacement is indicated if ferritin < 50-75 ng/mL).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Serum ferritin must be measured because iron deficiency is a treatable underlying cause and exacerbating factor for RLS.
• Option B: Incorrect. Creatine kinase evaluates myositis/rhabdomyolysis, which presents with weakness and muscle pain rather than evening motor restlessness relieved by movement.
• Option C: Incorrect. Uric acid is checked for gout, which causes acute inflammatory monoarthritis (podagra).
• Option D: Incorrect. Lumbar puncture is not indicated in the routine evaluation of RLS.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: An 18-year-old college freshman cannot fall asleep before 3:00 AM on any night, regardless of fatigue. However, once asleep, she sleeps soundly and wakes naturally at 11:30 AM feeling refreshed. When forced to wake at 7:00 AM for morning lectures, she suffers severe daytime sleepiness and academic decline. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Delayed Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder (DSWPD) is a circadian rhythm disorder common in adolescents and young adults, characterized by a persistent delay in the timing of the major sleep period (typically by 2 or more hours) relative to societal requirements. Sleep architecture and quality are entirely normal when allowed to sleep on their preferred schedule.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Consistent late sleep onset (3 AM) and late awakening (11:30 AM) with normal sleep quality when unconstrained defines Delayed Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder.
• Option B: Incorrect. Advanced Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder involves early evening sleepiness (e.g., 7 PM) and early morning awakening (e.g., 3 AM), typically seen in the elderly.
• Option C: Incorrect. Irregular sleep-wake rhythm features fragmented sleep throughout the 24-hour cycle without a single consolidated nocturnal sleep bout.
• Option D: Incorrect. Non-24-hour disorder involves a free-running circadian clock that shifts later every single day, commonly observed in totally blind individuals.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: Non-benzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic agents, commonly known as 'Z-drugs' (e.g., Zolpidem, Zaleplon), exert their hypnotic effects primarily by acting selectively as agonists at which specific receptor subunit?
options: Alpha-1 subunit of the GABA-A receptor complex
Alpha-2 subunit of the GABA-A receptor complex
questions.answer: Alpha-1 subunit of the GABA-A receptor complex
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Z-drugs (zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone) are positive allosteric modulators that bind selectively to the alpha-1 subunit (formerly known as BZ1 receptor) of the pentameric GABA-A receptor complex. The alpha-1 subunit mediates sedation, hypnotic effects, and anterograde amnesia, while alpha-2 and alpha-3 mediate anxiolytic and muscle-relaxant properties.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Z-drugs have preferential selectivity for the alpha-1 subunit of the GABA-A receptor, producing hypnotic effects with less muscle relaxation and anticonvulsant activity.
• Option B: Incorrect. Alpha-2 and alpha-3 subunits are targeted non-selectively by classic benzodiazepines to produce anxiolysis and myorelaxation.
• Option C: Incorrect. GABA-B receptors are G-protein coupled receptors targeted by baclofen, not Z-drugs.
• Option D: Incorrect. 5-HT1A is targeted by buspirone, not sedative-hypnotic Z-drugs.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.chapterTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topic: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topicTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.prompt: A 16-year-old girl is brought by her parents with a 15-kg weight loss over 6 months. Her BMI is 14.2 kg/m². Despite severe emaciation, she insists she is 'dangerously fat' and exercises rigorously for 3 hours daily while restricting her intake to 300 kcal/day. Examination reveals bradycardia (44 bpm), hypotension (85/55 mmHg), dry scaly skin, fine downy body hair (lanugo), and secondary amenorrhea. What is the definitive diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Anorexia Nervosa is characterized by restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight (BMI < 18.5 kg/m², severe < 15 kg/m²), intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, and distorted body image. Physical signs include hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, amenorrhea, and lanugo hair.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Severe underweight (BMI 14.2 kg/m²), relentless pursuit of thinness, distorted body image, and classic endocrine/physical signs (lanugo, bradycardia) establish Anorexia Nervosa.
• Option B: Incorrect. Bulimia Nervosa patients typically maintain a normal or slightly above-normal body weight (BMI ≥ 18.5 kg/m²) and engage in objective bingeing followed by purging.
• Option C: Incorrect. Binge Eating Disorder features recurrent binge eating episodes without compensatory purging or weight loss, usually resulting in obesity.
• Option D: Incorrect. ARFID involves food avoidance/restriction leading to weight loss without body image distortion or fear of fatness (e.g., sensory aversion or fear of choking).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.chapterTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors

questions.prompt: A 20-year-old college student with a normal BMI of 22 kg/m² engages in episodes of consuming enormous quantities of food within a 2-hour period while feeling completely out of control. Following each episode, she feels profound guilt and forces herself to vomit by inserting her fingers down her throat. Examination reveals bilateral painless parotid gland enlargement and calluses over the dorsal aspects of her knuckles. What is the eponym for these knuckle calluses?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Bulimia Nervosa involves recurrent binge eating episodes followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors (self-induced vomiting, laxative abuse). Russell's sign refers to calluses, abrasions, or hyperkeratosis on the dorsum of the hand and knuckles caused by repeated trauma against the incisor teeth during self-induced vomiting.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Russell's sign is the classic cutaneous stigma of chronic manual self-induced vomiting in bulimia nervosa.
• Option B: Incorrect. Trousseau's sign is carpopedal spasm induced by inflating a blood pressure cuff, indicating hypocalcemia.
• Option C: Incorrect. Chvostek's sign is facial twitching elicited by tapping the facial nerve, also indicating hypocalcemia.
• Option D: Incorrect. Gottron's papules are erythematous papules over the knuckles pathognomonic for dermatomyositis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.chapterTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topic: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topicTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.prompt: Which of the following eating disorders is characterized by recurrent episodes of eating large amounts of food with a subjective sense of lack of control, accompanied by marked distress, but WITHOUT the regular use of inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as purging or fasting?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Binge Eating Disorder (BED) involves recurrent episodes of eating significantly more food in a short period than most people would consume, accompanied by feelings of lack of control, marked distress, guilt, and eating alone due to embarrassment, in the absence of recurrent compensatory purging, fasting, or excessive exercise.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The absence of compensatory purging/starvation behaviors directly differentiates Binge Eating Disorder from Bulimia Nervosa.
• Option B: Incorrect. Bulimia Nervosa requires regular inappropriate compensatory behaviors (vomiting, laxatives, extreme exercise) to counteract the binge.
• Option C: Incorrect. Anorexia binge-eating/purging type requires significantly subnormal body weight (BMI < 18.5 kg/m²).
• Option D: Incorrect. Pica is the persistent eating of non-nutritive, non-food substances (dirt, chalk, paint flakes).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.chapterTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topic: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topicTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.prompt: A 26-year-old primiparous woman on postpartum day 4 is tearful, irritable, emotionally labile, and anxious about her ability to nurse her newborn. She remains completely in touch with reality, has no suicidal or infanticidal thoughts, and interacts affectionately with the infant. By day 10, her mood stabilizes entirely without medical treatment. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Postpartum Blues (Baby Blues) affects up to 50-80% of postpartum women. It typically peaks around postpartum days 3 to 5 and resolves spontaneously within 10 to 14 days without active pharmacological intervention. Features include mild tearfulness, emotional lability, anxiety, and fatigue without psychotic symptoms or gross impairment in infant care.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The transient onset on day 4, mild lability, preservation of bonding, and spontaneous resolution by day 10 are pathognomonic of postpartum blues.
• Option B: Incorrect. Postpartum depression develops over weeks to months (typically weeks 2-12 postpartum), lasts months, and meets full criteria for major depressive disorder.
• Option C: Incorrect. Postpartum psychosis is a severe psychiatric emergency featuring delusions, hallucinations, confusion, and risk of infanticide.
• Option D: Incorrect. Late luteal phase dysphoric disorder (premenstrual dysphoric disorder) relates to the menstrual cycle in non-pregnant females.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.chapterTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topic: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topicTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.prompt: On postpartum day 6, a 28-year-old woman becomes severely agitated, disoriented, and states that her baby is possessed by demons and must be sacrificed to save the world. She has severe insomnia, auditory hallucinations, and rapid mood swings from mania to depression. What is the immediate clinical priority?
options: Emergency psychiatric admission, separation of the infant from unsupervised contact, and antipsychotic/mood stabilizer therapy
Outpatient supportive counseling and reassurance of the husband
Prescription of on-demand Zolpidem and follow-up in 2 weeks
Encouraging uninterrupted exclusive breastfeeding to enhance maternal bonding
questions.answer: Emergency psychiatric admission, separation of the infant from unsupervised contact, and antipsychotic/mood stabilizer therapy
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Postpartum (puerperal) psychosis is a medical and psychiatric emergency with high rates of suicide (5%) and infanticide (4%) driven by command hallucinations or altruistic delusions. Immediate inpatient psychiatric hospitalization, safety measures (strictly preventing unsupervised maternal-infant contact), and prompt treatment (antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, or ECT) are mandatory.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Immediate psychiatric admission, safety protection for the infant against infanticide, and biological treatments are non-negotiable priorities.
• Option B: Incorrect. Outpatient therapy is life-threateningly inadequate for acute postpartum psychosis.
• Option C: Incorrect. Hypnotic monotherapy does not treat underlying psychotic mania and delays emergency intervention.
• Option D: Incorrect. Leaving the infant alone with an actively delusional mother poses an extreme risk of infanticidal harm.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.chapterTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors

questions.topicTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.prompt: In the category of 'Abuse of non-dependence-producing substances' (ICD-10 code F55), which class of agents is most frequently abused, often covertly by patients with eating disorders or factitious diarrhea?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: ICD-10 category F55 designates 'Abuse of non-dependence-producing substances' (substances that do not produce classic pharmacological addiction/tolerance like opioids or alcohol, but are chronically misused despite harm). Common examples include laxatives, purgatives, diuretics, antacids, vitamins, and steroids. Laxative abuse is classically seen in purging-type eating disorders.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Laxatives (along with diuretics) are the prototype agents in F55, widely abused for weight purging without having true biological addictive properties.
• Option B: Incorrect. Benzodiazepines produce classic pharmacological dependence, tolerance, and withdrawal (classified under F13).
• Option C: Incorrect. Opioids are classic dependence-producing substances (classified under F11).
• Option D: Incorrect. Barbiturates cause profound physical dependence and withdrawal (classified under F13).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.chapterTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topic: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topicTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.prompt: A severely malnourished 17-year-old female with Anorexia Nervosa (BMI 12.8 kg/m²) is admitted to the ICU. Aggressive high-calorie nasogastric feeding is initiated rapidly. On day 3, she develops generalized muscle weakness, cardiac arrhythmias, confusion, and peripheral edema. Which serum electrolyte abnormality is the hallmark mediator of this life-threatening refeeding syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Refeeding syndrome occurs when carbohydrate-rich nutrition is abruptly reintroduced to a chronically starved patient. Glucose intake stimulates massive insulin secretion, driving phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells to facilitate glycolysis and ATP synthesis. The resulting profound hypophosphatemia leads to ATP depletion, cardiac failure, arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, respiratory failure, and death.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Severe hypophosphatemia is the hallmark pathophysiological hallmark of refeeding syndrome due to insulin-driven intracellular shifting.
• Option B: Incorrect. Refeeding causes hypokalemia (intracellular shift of potassium), not hyperkalemia.
• Option C: Incorrect. Refeeding depletes serum phosphate into cells, causing severe hypophosphatemia, not hyperphosphatemia.
• Option D: Incorrect. Magnesium also shifts intracellularly, resulting in hypomagnesemia, not hypermagnesemia.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.chapterTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topic: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topicTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.prompt: A 23-year-old woman with chronic Bulimia Nervosa who purges by vomiting 4 to 5 times daily undergoes arterial blood gas and serum electrolyte analysis. Which classic metabolic and electrolyte derangement is expected?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Repeated self-induced vomiting results in massive loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl), hydrogen ions, chloride, and potassium. In response to volume contraction, aldosterone increases in the renal tubules, accelerating renal secretion of potassium and hydrogen ions in exchange for sodium reabsorption, creating classic hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Gastric HCl loss leads to chloride depletion, alkalosis, and secondary renal potassium wasting, yielding hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.
• Option B: Incorrect. Acidosis does not occur in vomiting; metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap can occur with severe chronic laxative abuse (bicarbonate loss in diarrhea).
• Option C: Incorrect. This pattern is seen in renal tubular acidosis or severe diarrhea, not vomiting.
• Option D: Incorrect. Serum potassium is depleted, not elevated.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.chapterTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topic: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topicTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.prompt: Regarding the pharmacological management of Anorexia Nervosa, what does scientific evidence demonstrate regarding the efficacy of SSRIs (such as Fluoxetine) in acutely emaciated, starved patients?
options: SSRIs are ineffective in acute starvation because starvation depletes brain tryptophan and downregulates serotonin receptors; efficacy is only seen after weight restoration
SSRIs are the primary first-line intervention that directly drives weight restoration in acute starvation
SSRIs are strictly contraindicated due to guaranteed immediate induction of lethal ventricular arrhythmias
SSRIs produce rapid weight gain superior to nutritional rehabilitation
questions.answer: SSRIs are ineffective in acute starvation because starvation depletes brain tryptophan and downregulates serotonin receptors; efficacy is only seen after weight restoration
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Tryptophan is the dietary essential amino acid precursor for serotonin (5-HT) synthesis. In acute starvation and profound malnutrition, severe depletion of tryptophan results in impaired serotonin synthesis, rendering SSRIs essentially ineffective for promoting weight gain or reducing obsessions. SSRIs are only effective for preventing relapse and managing comorbid depression/OCD after substantial nutritional restoration.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Starvation depletes tryptophan and impairs 5-HT neurochemistry, making SSRIs ineffective for acute weight restoration; they are useful only post-restoration to maintain weight and treat comorbid symptoms.
• Option B: Incorrect. SSRIs do not induce weight gain in acute anorexia; nutritional rehabilitation and behavioural management are the cornerstones.
• Option C: Incorrect. While cardiac status must be monitored (QTc prolongation), SSRIs are not categorically contraindicated for arrhythmia reasons, but rather lack acute efficacy.
• Option D: Incorrect. Pharmacotherapy is completely inferior to structured nutritional rehabilitation.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.chapterTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topic: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.topicTitle: Behavioural Syndromes Associated with Psychological Disturbances and Physiological Factors
questions.prompt: Which atypical antipsychotic medication has demonstrated the strongest evidence in clinical trials for promoting weight gain and reducing intense obsessional anxiety regarding food in severely underweight patients with Anorexia Nervosa?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: While psychotherapy and nutritional rehabilitation are the primary modalities, Olanzapine (an atypical antipsychotic with 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, and H1 receptor antagonism) has demonstrated efficacy in randomized controlled trials for facilitating weight gain and attenuating ruminative, obsessional anxiety surrounding meals in Anorexia Nervosa.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Olanzapine has the best empirical trial evidence for facilitating weight restoration and reducing obsessional distress in anorexia nervosa.
• Option B: Incorrect. Aripiprazole is weight-neutral or can cause weight loss and has less robust evidence for anorexia weight gain.
• Option C: Incorrect. Ziprasidone is known for being strictly weight-neutral and carries risk of QTc prolongation.
• Option D: Incorrect. Typical neuroleptics like haloperidol do not promote weight gain effectively and increase extrapyramidal risks in malnourished individuals.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: According to traditional psychiatric classification (ICD-10) based on standardized intelligence quotient (IQ) testing, what is the defined IQ range for Moderate Mental Retardation (Intellectual Disability)?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Intellectual Disability (Mental Retardation) is categorized by IQ score bands: Mild (IQ 50-69, 'Educable'), Moderate (IQ 35-49, 'Trainable'), Severe (IQ 20-34), and Profound (IQ < 20).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The IQ range for Moderate Intellectual Disability is 35 to 49 (mental age equivalent roughly 6 to under 9 years).
• Option B: Incorrect. IQ 50 to 69 corresponds to Mild Intellectual Disability.
• Option C: Incorrect. IQ 20 to 34 corresponds to Severe Intellectual Disability.
• Option D: Incorrect. An IQ below 20 defines Profound Intellectual Disability.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: What is the single most common GENETIC cause of intellectual disability, and what is the most common INHERITED genetic cause of intellectual disability, respectively?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is the most common overall genetic cause of intellectual disability (due mostly to maternal meiotic non-disjunction, which is non-inherited/sporadic). Fragile X syndrome (caused by CGG trinucleotide expansion in the FMR1 gene) is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Down syndrome is the commonest genetic (chromosomal) cause, whereas Fragile X is the commonest inherited (familial) cause.
• Option B: Incorrect. This reverses the classic genetic vs. inherited epidemiological distinction.
• Option C: Incorrect. Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes are genomic imprinting disorders of chromosome 15 and are less prevalent.
• Option D: Incorrect. Phenylketonuria is a rare inborn error of metabolism, far less common than Fragile X syndrome.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 14-year-old boy with moderate intellectual disability is evaluated. Physical examination reveals an elongated face, a prominent jaw (prognathism), large everted ears, high-arched palate, joint hypermobility, and bilateral macroorchidism. He exhibits hand-flapping stereotypies and poor eye contact. What is the underlying genetic mechanism responsible for this syndrome?
options: CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome
questions.answer: CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: The clinical constellation of post-pubertal macroorchidism, long face, large prominent ears, high-arched palate, and autistic behavioral features is diagnostic of Fragile X syndrome. It is caused by an expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat (>200 repeats in full mutation) in the 5' untranslated region of the FMR1 gene, causing hypermethylation and transcriptional silencing of fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Fragile X syndrome is caused by unstable CGG triplet repeat expansion on the FMR1 gene at Xq27.3.
• Option B: Incorrect. Microdeletion of 7q11.23 causes Williams syndrome (elfin facies, cocktail party speech, supravalvular aortic stenosis).
• Option C: Incorrect. Maternal deletion of 15q11-q13 causes Angelman syndrome ('happy puppet' syndrome with inappropriate laughter and ataxia).
• Option D: Incorrect. Paternal deletion of 15q11-q13 causes Prader-Willi syndrome (hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: An 8-year-old boy presents with severe insatiable appetite (hyperphagia), absence of satiety, and extreme tantrums if food is denied. He has morbid obesity, almond-shaped eyes, small hands and feet, short stature, and hypogonadism. Chromosomal microarray reveals loss of paternal expression of genes in the 15q11-q13 region. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Prader-Willi Syndrome is a genomic imprinting disorder caused by the loss of paternally expressed genes on chromosome 15q11-q13 (via paternal deletion in 70% or maternal uniparental disomy in 25%). It presents with infantile hypotonia and poor feeding, followed in early childhood by uncontrollable hyperphagia leading to severe obesity, intellectual disability, hypogonadism, and short stature.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Loss of paternal 15q11-q13 expression, hyperphagia, morbid obesity, and hypogonadism establish Prader-Willi Syndrome.
• Option B: Incorrect. Angelman syndrome is caused by loss of maternal expression of UBE3A at 15q11-q13 and presents with microcephaly, paroxysmal laughter, and ataxia without hyperphagia.
• Option C: Incorrect. Fragile X syndrome is characterized by macroorchidism and large ears, not obesity and microphallus.
• Option D: Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) features tall eunuchoid habitus, gynecomastia, and testicular atrophy.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 2-year-old child presents with global developmental delay and fair complexion with blonde hair and blue eyes, despite both parents having dark Indian skin and hair. The mother notes a distinct 'musty' or 'mousy' odor in the child's urine. Laboratory investigation confirms deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase. What dietary modification is mandatory to prevent progressive, irreversible intellectual disability?
options: Diet strictly low in Phenylalanine with Tyrosine supplementation
questions.answer: Diet strictly low in Phenylalanine with Tyrosine supplementation
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism caused by mutations in the phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) gene, preventing conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. Accumulation of phenylalanine and phenylketones leads to progressive brain injury, microcephaly, severe intellectual disability, musty/mousy odor, and hypopigmentation (due to impaired melanin synthesis from tyrosine). Early dietary restriction of phenylalanine with tyrosine supplementation prevents neurological damage.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. A low-phenylalanine diet initiated in infancy combined with tyrosine supplementation prevents brain accumulation of toxic metabolites and normalizes cognitive development.
• Option B: Incorrect. High phenylalanine is neurotoxic and causes profound mental retardation.
• Option C: Incorrect. Gluten-free diet is indicated for celiac disease, not PKU.
• Option D: Incorrect. Low-copper diet and penicillamine are used for Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 9-year-old boy presents with intellectual disability and intractable seizures. Physical examination reveals hypopigmented ash-leaf macules on his trunk under Wood's lamp, adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas) across the butterfly distribution of his nose and cheeks, and a shagreen patch in the lumbosacral region. Cranial MRI demonstrates subependymal calcified nodules. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (Bourneville's disease) is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder (TSC1/TSC2 genes) classically defined by Vogt's triad: intellectual disability, intractable epilepsy, and adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas). Hallmark dermatological signs include hypomelanotic macules (ash-leaf spots), shagreen patches, and ungual fibromas (Koenen's tumors).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Ash-leaf spots, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patches, seizures, and subependymal nodules are diagnostic of Tuberous Sclerosis.
• Option B: Incorrect. Neurofibromatosis Type 1 presents with café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, axillary freckling (Crowe sign), and Lisch nodules.
• Option C: Incorrect. Sturge-Weber syndrome presents with a facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) in the V1 trigeminal distribution, leptomeningeal angiomas, and tram-track calcifications.
• Option D: Incorrect. Ataxia Telangiectasia features progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasias, and immunodeficiency.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: In standard clinical practice, adaptive functioning in individuals suspected of having intellectual disability is commonly assessed in India using the Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS). What is the formula used to calculate the Social Quotient (SQ)?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Adaptive behavior measures an individual's ability to cope with everyday life demands. The Vineland Social Maturity Scale (VSMS) assesses social and adaptive competence across domains such as self-help, locomotion, communication, and socialization, yielding a Social Age (SA). The Social Quotient (SQ) expresses this ratio relative to Chronological Age (CA).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The standard formula is SQ = (Social Age / Chronological Age) × 100, analogous to the historical Binet IQ formula (MA/CA × 100).
• Option B: Incorrect. This inverts the numerator and denominator.
• Option C: Incorrect. Chronological age is the benchmark denominator, not mental age.
• Option D: Incorrect. Mental age is not used as the denominator for calculating social quotient.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: Individuals with Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) who survive beyond the age of 40 years demonstrate an exceptionally high risk (nearly 100% neuropathologically) of developing which neurodegenerative condition?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: The gene encoding the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) is localized on chromosome 21 (21q21.3). In Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), the resulting gene dosage effect causes lifelong overexpression of APP, accelerated cleavage into amyloid-beta 42 peptides, and universal formation of neurofibrillary tangles and senile plaques by age 40, leading to early-onset Alzheimer's disease dementia.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Gene dosage of APP on chromosome 21 causes early neuropathological and clinical Alzheimer's disease in Down syndrome patients.
• Option B: Incorrect. Parkinson's disease is an alpha-synucleinopathy and is not driven by chromosome 21 gene dosage.
• Option C: Incorrect. ALS affects motor neurons; while familial ALS type 1 is linked to SOD1 on chromosome 21, Trisomy 21 specifically predisposes to Alzheimer's pathology.
• Option D: Incorrect. Huntington's disease is caused by CAG repeats on chromosome 4.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 3-year-old girl is evaluated for developmental regression. Her parents report that she developed normally until age 14 months, at which point she progressively lost previously acquired purposeful hand skills and expressive language. She developed deceleration of head growth (acquired microcephaly), ataxia, hyperventilation episodes, and constant, stereotypic hand-wringing movements. What genetic mutation on the X chromosome is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Rett Syndrome is an X-linked dominant neurodevelopmental disorder affecting almost exclusively females (lethal in hemizygous males). Characterized by 6-18 months of normal development followed by developmental regression, loss of spoken language, deceleration of head growth, gait ataxia, and stereotypic hand movements (hand-wringing, hand-washing). Over 90% of cases are caused by mutations in the methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene at Xq28.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Loss-of-function mutations in the MECP2 gene on the X chromosome cause Rett syndrome.
• Option B: Incorrect. FMR1 expansion causes Fragile X syndrome, which does not present with hand-wringing regression and acquired microcephaly in young girls.
• Option C: Incorrect. TSC1 mutations cause Tuberous Sclerosis.
• Option D: Incorrect. DMD gene deletion causes Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A newborn is evaluated for dysmorphic features. Physical examination demonstrates microcephaly, a smooth and elongated philtrum, a thin vermilion border of the upper lip, short palpebral fissures, and low birth weight. Maternal history reveals heavy binge drinking of spirits throughout pregnancy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Maternal ethanol consumption during pregnancy exerts teratogenic effects on neural crest migration and CNS development. Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (FAS) is the most common preventable non-genetic cause of intellectual disability, defined by the triad of: (1) Facial dysmorphism (smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures), (2) Prenatal and postnatal growth deficiency, and (3) Central nervous system neurodevelopmental abnormalities (microcephaly, cognitive deficits).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The classic facial features (smooth philtrum, thin upper lip vermilion, short palpebral fissures) with microcephaly and maternal alcohol history confirm Fetal Alcohol Syndrome.
• Option B: Incorrect. Congenital Rubella features sensorineural deafness, cataracts, microphthalmia, and congenital heart disease (patent ductus arteriosus).
• Option C: Incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism presents with prolonged neonatal jaundice, coarse facial features, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, and hypotonia.
• Option D: Incorrect. Cornelia de Lange syndrome features synophrys (confluent eyebrows), long curly eyelashes, micromelia, and hirsutism.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: An 8-year-old boy cannot sit still in his classroom, frequently leaves his seat, blurts out answers before questions are completed, and intrudes on peers' games. At home, he loses his schoolbooks and pencils, cannot organize homework, and is easily distracted by extraneous stimuli. These behaviors have been persistent for 10 months and cause impairment in both school and home settings. What is the first-line pharmacological treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: The clinical vignette illustrates Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) combined presentation, fulfilling criteria of persistent inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity across two or more settings for at least 6 months. Psychostimulants (Methylphenidate, Amphetamines) are the first-line medications of choice, working as dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors in the prefrontal cortex.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Methylphenidate is the gold-standard, first-line psychostimulant for ADHD, significantly improving attention span and impulse control.
• Option B: Incorrect. Antipsychotics like haloperidol are not indicated for uncomplicated ADHD and carry risks of tardive dyskinesia and cognitive blunting.
• Option C: Incorrect. Fluoxetine is an SSRI used for depressive and anxiety disorders, without primary efficacy for ADHD core symptoms.
• Option D: Incorrect. Valproate is an anticonvulsant mood stabilizer used for pediatric bipolar disorder or epilepsy, not ADHD.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 4-year-old boy is brought by his parents due to lack of speech. He avoids eye contact, does not respond when his name is called, and does not use gestures such as pointing to show interest. He spends hours spinning the wheels of toy cars and lining them up in rigid rows, becoming intensely distressed if any toy is moved out of order. Hearing evaluation is completely normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is characterized by persistent deficits in two core domains: (1) Social communication and social interaction (impaired eye contact, lack of joint attention, absence of reciprocal conversation/gestures), and (2) Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities (stereotyped motor movements, lining up toys, insistence on sameness, rigid adherence to routines).

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Severe deficits in social-emotional reciprocity and joint attention combined with stereotyped, repetitive motor behaviors and rigid routines define Autism Spectrum Disorder.
• Option B: Incorrect. Childhood schizophrenia is exceptionally rare before age 5 and requires psychotic phenomena (delusions, auditory hallucinations).
• Option C: Incorrect. Developmental language disorder involves speech delay but social reciprocity, non-verbal pointing, eye contact, and imaginative play remain intact.
• Option D: Incorrect. Reactive attachment disorder arises from severe early social neglect, presenting with inhibited, emotionally withdrawn behavior toward adult caregivers without restricted, repetitive stereotypies.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 10-year-old boy exhibits multiple involuntary motor twitches, including eye blinking, shoulder shrugging, and facial grimacing, as well as vocal tics consisting of involuntary throat clearing, grunting, and occasional barking sounds. These tics have waxed and waned but have been continuously present for the past 18 months, causing social embarrassment. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Tourette Disorder is diagnosed when an individual exhibits both multiple motor tics AND at least one vocal tic (not necessarily concurrently), present for more than 1 year (with onset before age 18 years), not attributable to substance use or another medical condition.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The presence of both multiple motor tics and vocal tics for a duration exceeding 1 year fulfills diagnostic criteria for Tourette Disorder.
• Option B: Incorrect. Chronic motor tic disorder features motor tics ONLY (or vocal tics only), never both motor and vocal tics.
• Option C: Incorrect. Transient (provisional) tic disorder lasts less than 1 year.
• Option D: Incorrect. Sydenham chorea presents with rapid, non-stereotyped, purposeless, flowing movements associated with rheumatic fever, rather than brief stereotyped tics.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 15-year-old adolescent is brought to a clinic after being suspended from school. He has a history of physically assaulting younger peers, torturing stray dogs, setting small fires behind a warehouse, and breaking into cars to steal electronics. He shows complete absence of remorse or guilt. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Conduct Disorder is a repetitive and persistent pattern of behavior violating the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms/rules. Key categories include: aggression to people/animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness/theft, and serious rule violations. It serves as the developmental precursor to Antisocial Personality Disorder.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Cruelty to animals, physical aggression, fire-setting, theft, and lack of remorse in an individual under 18 define Conduct Disorder.
• Option B: Incorrect. Oppositional Defiant Disorder involves anger, argumentative behavior, and vindictiveness directed at authority figures, but lacks severe physical cruelty, destruction of property, or theft.
• Option C: Incorrect. DMDD is characterized by chronic, severe persistent irritability with frequent temper tantrums out of proportion to provocation, without predatory aggression or theft.
• Option D: Incorrect. Antisocial Personality Disorder cannot be diagnosed prior to 18 years of age.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 9-year-old girl is frequently argumentative with her parents and teachers. She loses her temper easily, deliberately annoys her elder brother, defies classroom rules, and blames others for her mistakes. However, she has never engaged in physical violence, has never destroyed property, does not steal, and has never been cruel to animals. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) is defined by a pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness lasting at least 6 months. Crucially, it does not involve the severe violation of societal norms, physical cruelty to animals/humans, destruction of property, or deceitful theft seen in conduct disorder.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Defiance, blaming others, argumentativeness, and irritability without physical cruelty, property destruction, or theft define Oppositional Defiant Disorder.
• Option B: Incorrect. Conduct disorder requires aggressive violations of human/animal rights, destruction of property, or criminality.
• Option C: Incorrect. Pediatric bipolar disorder features distinct episodic cycles of mania (grandiosity, decreased sleep, flight of ideas), which are absent here.
• Option D: Incorrect. Intermittent explosive disorder involves recurrent discrete behavioral outbursts of physical or verbal aggression that are disproportionate and impulsive.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 7-year-old boy wets his bed nearly every night. Thorough physical examination, urinalysis, urine culture, and renal ultrasound are completely normal. The child has never achieved nighttime urinary continence. What is the diagnosis, and what is the most effective long-term behavioral treatment?
options: Primary Nocturnal Enuresis; Bell-and-pad (enuresis alarm) conditioning
Secondary Diurnal Enuresis; Fluid overload therapy
questions.answer: Primary Nocturnal Enuresis; Bell-and-pad (enuresis alarm) conditioning
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Enuresis is the repeated involuntary voiding of urine into bed or clothes in children aged 5 years or older (or equivalent developmental level). Primary enuresis means urinary continence has never been established for 6 continuous months. The enuresis alarm (bell-and-pad / conditioning device) is the most effective long-term intervention, achieving high cure rates with low relapse via classical Pavlovian conditioning.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Involuntary nocturnal bedwetting in a 7-year-old with normal physical investigations is Primary Nocturnal Enuresis; the enuresis alarm conditioning represents the gold-standard first-line behavioral intervention.
• Option B: Incorrect. Diurnal enuresis refers to daytime wetting; fluid overload would exacerbate enuresis.
• Option C: Incorrect. Neurogenic bladder has structural or neurological pathology (e.g., spina bifida), which is ruled out here.
• Option D: Incorrect. Encopresis refers to passage of fecal matter into inappropriate places, not urination.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 6-year-old boy is brought by his mother because he repeatedly soils his underwear with semi-formed stool 2 to 3 times per week. Physical examination reveals a large, hard fecal mass palpable in the suprapubic area and rectal vault dilation. The mother reports that he has a history of painful, infrequent bowel movements dating back to age 3. What is the underlying pathophysiology and the most appropriate initial medical management?
options: Encopresis with constipation and overflow incontinence; Bowel cleanout with osmotic laxatives followed by scheduled toileting
questions.answer: Encopresis with constipation and overflow incontinence; Bowel cleanout with osmotic laxatives followed by scheduled toileting
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Encopresis (fecal soiling) in children aged 4 years or older is most commonly (>80-90%) associated with chronic constipation and overflow incontinence (retentive encopresis). Painful defecation leads to stool withholding, rectal distension, blunting of the defecation reflex, and eventual liquid stool leaking around a hard fecal impaction. Initial management requires fecal disimpaction using osmotic laxatives (e.g., polyethylene glycol) followed by maintenance laxatives and behavioral toileting.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. The presence of a palpable fecal mass and history of stool withholding confirms retentive encopresis with overflow incontinence; osmotic disimpaction and behavioral retraining is the treatment of choice.
• Option B: Incorrect. Non-retentive encopresis occurs without constipation or impaction; imipramine is not an initial treatment for retentive encopresis and has constipating anticholinergic effects.
• Option C: Incorrect. Hirschsprung disease typically presents in the neonatal period with failure to pass meconium and enterocolitis; an empty rectal ampulla on DRE is typical, unlike fecal impaction here.
• Option D: Incorrect. Encopresis is rarely willful, and punitive approaches worsen anxiety, withholding, and stool retention.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: An 8-year-old girl screams, cries, and vomits every morning before school. She worries incessantly that her mother will be killed in an accident or kidnapped while she is away. She refuses to sleep alone or attend sleepovers, repeatedly insisting on sleeping in her parents' bed. When her mother is present, the girl is completely calm and happy. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Separation Anxiety Disorder involves developmentally inappropriate and excessive fear or anxiety concerning separation from major attachment figures. Typical features include distress when anticipating separation, persistent worry about harm befalling attachment figures, reluctance/refusal to go to school or leave home, and refusal to sleep away from attachment figures.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Fear of harm to the mother, morning somatic symptoms before leaving mother (school refusal), and refusal to sleep alone are hallmark features of Separation Anxiety Disorder.
• Option B: Incorrect. Social anxiety disorder involves fear of embarrassment, scrutiny, or negative evaluation by peers/adults, not anxiety over physical separation from parents.
• Option C: Incorrect. Agoraphobia is fear of being in situations/places from which escape might be difficult in the event of panic-like symptoms.
• Option D: Incorrect. 'School phobia' is usually a manifestation of separation anxiety (fear of leaving parent) rather than a specific phobia of the school building.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 6-year-old girl speaks fluently, loudly, and animatedly at home with her parents and siblings. However, since enrolling in kindergarten 8 months ago, she has not spoken a single word to her teacher or classmates, communicating only through nodding or gestures when at school. A complete speech, language, and hearing assessment confirms normal linguistic competence. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Selective Mutism is defined as a consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where there is an expectation to speak (e.g., at school), despite speaking in other situations (e.g., at home). The disturbance interferes with educational or social achievement, lasts at least 1 month (not limited to the first month of school), and is not due to lack of knowledge or communication disorder.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Normal speech at home coupled with complete inability to speak at school lasting >1 month confirms Selective Mutism.
• Option B: Incorrect. ASD involves pervasive deficits in social communication across all environments, with restricted repetitive interests, rather than context-specific mutism.
• Option C: Incorrect. Language disorders cause expressive or receptive deficits across all environments, not situation-specific inhibition.
• Option D: Incorrect. Selective mutism is an anxiety-driven disorder, not an oppositional refusal driven by hostility or spite.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 4-year-old child who spent his infancy in an overcrowded, neglectful orphanage is adopted. His adoptive parents observe that he rarely seeks comfort when distressed, shows minimal social or emotional responsiveness, exhibits unexplained episodes of irritability and fearfulness during non-threatening interactions with caregivers, and displays a complete lack of positive affect. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD) is characterized by a consistent pattern of inhibited, emotionally withdrawn behavior toward adult caregivers (rarely seeks or responds to comfort when distressed), minimal social responsiveness, and episodes of unexplained fearfulness/irritability, stemming directly from extreme pathogenic care and neglect in early infancy.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Correct. Inhibited emotional withdrawal, failure to seek comfort when hurt, and lack of positive affect following severe early institutional neglect are pathognomonic of Reactive Attachment Disorder.
• Option B: Incorrect. Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder (DSED) is the opposite attachment phenotype (also stemming from neglect), characterized by overly familiar, indiscriminate approach toward unfamiliar adult strangers without reticence.
• Option C: Incorrect. While social responsiveness is reduced, the child's presentation is secondary to documented severe early neglect and lacks the restricted, repetitive stereotypies and sensory abnormalities of ASD.
• Option D: Incorrect. Pediatric MDD can cause irritability, but the persistent failure of attachment behaviors directly linked to institutional neglect defines RAD.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder maintained stably on lithium carbonate (900 mg/day; serum level 0.8 mEq/L) presents with coarse hand tremors, ataxia, dysarthria, and vomiting. Her family reports she recently started an over-the-counter medication for severe knee pain following a sports injury. Which of the following drugs is the most likely culprit behind her clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic window (acute mania: 0.8–1.2 mEq/L; maintenance: 0.6–0.8 mEq/L). NSAIDs (like ibuprofen, naproxen, indomethacin, and celecoxib) inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis, reducing renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate, which decreases renal lithium excretion and precipitates toxic accumulation.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Incorrect. Acetaminophen does not inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis significantly and does not substantially affect renal lithium clearance; it is considered the safest analgesic in patients taking lithium.
• Option B: Correct. Ibuprofen is an NSAID that reduces renal blood flow by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, leading to decreased lithium clearance, marked serum level elevation, and overt clinical lithium toxicity (coarse tremors, ataxia, vomiting, dysarthria).
• Option C: Incorrect. Aspirin is a notable exception among classical NSAIDs; at standard anti-inflammatory doses, it does not significantly elevate serum lithium levels compared to other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents.
• Option D: Incorrect. Tramadol is an opioid analgesic that may carry a risk of serotonin syndrome or seizures when combined with certain psychotropics, but it does not cause decreased renal excretion or classical toxicity of lithium.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.prompt: A 28-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is initiated on clozapine. Four weeks after starting therapy, routine laboratory monitoring reveals an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 850/mm³ and total leukocyte count of 2,200/mm³. He is currently afebrile and asymptomatic. According to standard clozapine safety guidelines, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Continue clozapine at the same dose and repeat CBC in 48 hours
Reduce clozapine dose by 50% and repeat CBC twice weekly
Immediately discontinue clozapine, monitor ANC daily, and consult hematology
Add lithium carbonate to stimulate granulocyte colony production while maintaining clozapine
questions.answer: Immediately discontinue clozapine, monitor ANC daily, and consult hematology
questions.explanation:
Core Concept: Clozapine carries a serious risk of severe neutropenia and life-threatening agranulocytosis (ANC < 500/mm³). Under standard hematological monitoring protocols, an ANC < 1,000/mm³ constitutes severe neutropenia, mandating immediate cessation of clozapine, urgent hematology consultation, daily blood counts until recovery, and strict avoidance of rechallenge unless benefits overwhelmingly outweigh risks under specialized protocols.

Option Analysis:
• Option A: Incorrect. Continuing clozapine when ANC drops below 1,000/mm³ risks progression to fatal agranulocytosis and fulminant septic shock.
